I Proclamation for dissolving Parliament.

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION,

For dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the Calling of another.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS We have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to Tuesday the Sixth Day of April next: We do, for that End, publish this Our Royal Proclamation; and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are discharged from their Meeting and Attendance on

Tuesday the said Sixth Day of April next. And We being desirous and resolved, as soon as may be, to meet Our People, and to have their Advice in Parliament, do hereby make known to all Our loving Subjects, Our Royal Will and Pleasure to call a new Parliament: And do hereby further declare, That, with the Advice of Our Privy Council, We have this Day given Order to Our Chancellor of Great Britain, to issue out Writs, in due Form, for calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Teste on Friday the Twenty-sixth of this instant March, and to be returnable on Tuesday the Eighteenth Day of May following.

Given at Our Court at The Queen's House, the Twenty-fifth Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four, in the Twenty-fourth Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the K i n g.

Parliamentum inceptum et tentum apud civitatem Westmouasteri-ensem die Martis, 18° die Mail, anno regni Domini nostri Georgii Tertii, Dei gratia, Magnae Britanniae, Francias, et Hiberniae, Regis, Fidei Defensoris, &c. 24° annoque Domini 1784.

THE King’s most Excellent Majesty having, by His Royal Proclamation (hereunto annexed) dated the 25th Day of March last, dissolved the last Parliament, and by His Writ of Summons, issued under the*Great Seal of Great Britain, bearing . Teste at Westminster, on Friday the 26th Day of March, called a new Parliament, and appointed the same to meet and sit this Day; the most Noble James Duke of Chandos, Lord Steward of His Majesty’s Houshold, came, about Twelve of the Clock, into One of the Rooms belonging to the Clerk of the House of Commons, where the Oaths appointed to be taken by the Members returned to serve in Parliament are usually administered; and John Hatscll, Esquire, Clerk of the House of Commons, and Mr. Ley, Clerk Assistant, and the other Clerks, attending according to their Duty; and the honourable John Yorke, Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, having delivered to the said Mr. Hatsell a Book, containing a List of the Names of such Members &s had been returned to serve in this Parliament, the Lord Steward did himself, in Person, administer the Oaths appointed to several of the Members who appeared, and afterwards made a Commission or Deputation under his Hand and seal (hereunto also annexed) impowering several of the Members who had before been sworn to administer the said Oaths to the rest of the Members returned; some of which Commissioners administered the same accordingly to such other Members as appeared: Which being done, the Members repaired to their Seats in the House of Commons.

After which, a Message was delivered by Sir Francis Molyncux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod.

Gentlemen,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly the House went up to attend His Majesty in the House of Peers; where the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, by His Majesty’s Directions, said,

My Lords and Gentlemen,

HIS Majesty has been pleased to command me to acquaint you, That He will defer declaring the Cause of calling this Parliament, till there shall be a Speaker of the House of Commons: And therefore it is His Majesty’s Pleasure, that you, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, do immediately repair to the Place where the Commons usually sit, and there choose a fit Person to be your Speaker; and that you present Vox. 40.

such Person, who shall be so chosen, to His Majesty here, for His Royal Approbation, Tomorrow at Two of the Clock.

And the House being returned;

The most honourable James Marquis of Graham, Son and Heir apparent of the most noble the Duke of Montrose, and One of the Burgesses for the Borough of Great Bedwyn, in the County of Wilts, addressing himself to the Clerk (who, standing up, pointed to him, and then sat down) proposed to the House for their Speaker the Right honourable Charles JVolfran Cornwall; in which Motion he was seconded by Sir George Howard, Knight of the most honourable Order of the Bath, and One of the Burgesses for the Borough of Stamford, in the County of Lincoln.

The House then calling Mr. ConwaU to the Chair, he stood up in his Place, and expressed the Sense he had of the Honour proposed to be conferred on him; and having recommended the Choice of a properer Person, he submitted himself to the House.

The House then again unanimously calling Mr. Cornwall to the Chair* he was taken out of his Place by the said Marquis of Graham and Sir George Howard, and conducted to the Chair; where, standing on the upper Step, he returned his humblest Acknowledgments to the House for, the great Honour they had been pleased to confer on him; but hoped that the House would permit him to state the Circumstances he'had before mentioned in another Place.

But the Members cried, No, No.

And thereupon he sat down in the Chair; and then the Mace (which before lay under the Table) was laid upon the Table.

Then the Right honourable the Lord Viscount Gallway, in the Kingdom of Ireland, Comptroller of His Majesty’s Houshold, and One of the Citizens for the City of York, having congratulated Mr. Speaker elect, moved to adjourn till To-Morrow, Twelve of the Clock.

And the House accordingly adjourned till Tomorrow, Twelve of the Clock.

TI ! F, House being met, and Mr. Speaker elect having taken the Chair;

A Message was brought from His Majesty, by Sir Francis Molymux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod.

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker elect, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty in the House of Peers: Where Mr. Speaker elect was presented to His Majesty, for His Royal Approbation: And

Then the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain after receiving Directions from His Majesty, signified His Majesty’s Approbation of Mr. Speaker elect.

The House being returned:

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had been in the House of Peers: Where His Majesty had been pleased to approve of the Choice the House had made of him to be their Speaker; and that he ha.!, in their Name, and on their Behalf, by humble Petition to His Majesty, laid Claim to all their ancient Rights and Privileges, particularly that their Persons, their Estates, and Servants might be free from Arrests, and all Molestations; that they may enjoy Liberty of Speech in all their Debates, may have Access to His Majesty’s Royal Person whenever Occasion shall require; and that all their Proceedings may receive from His Majesty the most favourable Construction; which, he said, His Majesty had confirmed to them in as toll and ample Manner as they have been hen totore granted or allowed by llis Majesty, or any of His Royal Predecessors.

And then Mr. Speaker repeated his most respectful Acknowledgments to the House for the Honour they had done him.

Mr. Speaker then put the House in Mind, that the first Thing to be done, was to take the Oaths, and make and subscribe the Declaration, and to take and subscribe the Oaths of Abjuration and Qualification, by Law required.

And thereupon Mr. Speaker, first alone, standing upon the upper Step of the Chair, took the said first mentioned Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the said Oath of Abjuration; and also delivered in to the Clerk of the House, an Account of his Qualification, and took and subscribed the Oath of Qualification.

And, after him, several other Members took the said first mentioned Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration; and such of the said Members as are by Law required to deliver in to the Clerk of this House an Account of their Qualification, and to take and subscribe the Oath of Qualification delivered in such Account, and took and subscribed the said Oath accordingly.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Usual Ordered, That all Persons who will question any

Orders. Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, do question the same within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in; and that all Members, w ho are returned for Two or more Places, do make their Election t by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place; and, if any Thing shall come in Question touching the Return or Election of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate; and that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That, in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lists, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters

excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver, the like Lists, on their Part, to the Petitioners or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stanger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is sitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speakers Chamber every Day before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House or Gallery thereof, while the House is sitting.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where this House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Con>-mittee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High v>rime and Misdemeanor; and this House

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers? of Middlesex and Westminster, do take Care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take Care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminslei' Hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance, by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do see the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting, or losing, of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Post Master General, do for the future, evefy Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the least immediately after the Rising of the House, and also from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take Care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members sending for the dame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Postmaster General.

The Sheriff of the County of Middlesex certifies and returns, that by virtue of the Writ to him directed, he, on the 26th March, in the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, duly made and delivered his Precept to the Bailiff of the Liberty of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Church of Saint Peter, at Westminster, whereby he commanded him, without Delay, to cause Two Citizens to be elected for the said City; and that on the 17th May, in the Year aforesaid, he did receive from the said Bailiff a Return, or Answ er, to the said Precept, and which he hath annexed to the Writ to him the said Sheriff directed, and which Return, or Answer, is in the Words and Figures following:

The King's Mr. Speaker reported to the House* That when the Speech. House did attend His Majesty, upon Wednesday last, in the House of Peers, His Majesty was pleased to make a Most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is os followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have the greatest Satisfaction in meeting you in Parliament at this Time, after recurring, in so important a Moment, to the Sense of My People. I have a just and confident Reliance, that you are animated with the same Sentiments of Loyalty, and the same Attachment to our excellent Constitution, which I have had the Happiness to see so fully manifested in every Part of the Kingdom. The happy Effects of such a Disposition will, I doubt not, appear in the Temper and Wisdom of your Deliberations, and in the Dispatch of the important Objects of public Business which demand your Attention. It will afford Me peculiar Pleasure to find that the Exercise of the Power, entrusted to Me by the Constitution, has been productive of Consequences so beneficial to My Subjects, whose Interest and Welfare are always nearest My Heart.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Estimates for the current Year to be laid before you; and I trust to your Zeal and Affection to make such Provisions for their farther Supply, and for the Application of the Sums granted in the last Parliament, as may appear to be necessary.

I sincerely lament every Addition to the Burthens of My People; but they will, I am persuaded, feel the Necessity, after a long and expensive WTar, of effectually providing for the Maintenance of the National Faith and Our Public Credit, so essential to the Power and Prosperity of the State.

Vol. 40.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The alarming Progress of Frauds in the Revenue, accompanied in so many Instances with Violence, will not fail on every Account to excite your Attention.

I must at the same Time, recommend to your most serious Consideration, to frame such Commercial Regulations as may appear immediately necessary in the present Moment. The Affairs of the East India Company form an Object of Deliberation deeply connected with the general Interests of the Country. While you feel a just Anxiety to provide for the good Government of Our Possessions in that Part of the World, you will, I trust, never lose Sight of the Effect which any Measure to be adopted for that Purpose may have on Our own Constitution, and Our dearest Interests at Home. You will find Me always desirous to concur with you in such Measures as may be of lasting Benefit to My People: I have no Wish but to consult their Prosperity, by a constant Attention to every Object of National Concern, by a uniform Adherence to the true Principles of Our free Constitution, and by supporting and maintaining, in their just Balance, the Rights and Privileges of every Branch of the Legislature.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That whenever several Petitions, complaining of undue Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, shall, at the same Time, be offered to be presented to the House, Mr. Speaker shall direct such Petitions to be all of them delivered in at the Table, where they shall be classed and read in the following Order; viz. Such Petitions as complain of Double Returns, in the First Class; such as complain of the Election or Return of Members returned to serve for Two or more Places, in the Second Class; and the Residue of the said Petitions, in the Third Class: And the Names of the Places to which such Petitions (contained in the First Class, if more than One) shall relate, shall, in the first Place, be written on several Pieces of Paper of an equal Size, and the same Pieces of Paper shall be then rolled up, and put by the Clerk into a Box or Glass, and then publicly drawn by the Clerk; and the said Petitions shall be read in the Order in which the said Names shall be drawn: And then the like Method shall be observed with respect to the several Petitions contained in the Second and Third Classes respectively;

A Petition of Roger Wilbraham, Esquire, was read; Midshall Setting forth, That at the last Election for Members El«ction. to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Midshall', otherwise Mitchell, in the County of Cornwall, the Petitioner, David Howell, Christopher Hawkins, and William Boscawen, Esquires, were Candidates to represent the said Borough in Parliament; and that the said Christopher Hawkins, by himself and his Agents, was guilty of Bribery and other corrupt Practices, and of using undue Influence in procuring, and endeavouring to procure, Persons to vote for him at the said Election, and also in preventing Persons who would have given their Voices in Support of the Petitioner, from attending and appearing at the Poll for that Purpose; and that a considerable Majority of Persons, legally entitled to vote at the said Election, gave their Voices in Favour of the said Devoid Howell, who was duly elected and returned to serve as one of the Burgesses for the said Borough; and that a Majority also of Persons legally entitled to vote at the said Election polled and tendered their Voices for the Petitioner, but that the Portreeve of the said Borough, before whom the Poll was taken, rejected the Votes of several Persons having a Right to vote, which were tendered on Behalf of the Petitioner, and admitted many Persons to give their Voices in Favour of the said Christopher Hawkins, who were not legally qualified as Electors, by which Means there appeared upon the Poll an equal Number of Voices in Favour of the Petitioner and of the said Christopher Hawkins; and that although the said Portreeve, in Consideration of such Equality of Numbers, claimed, as Returning Officer, to have a casting Voice, and actually gave such casting Voice in Favour of the Petitioner, nevertheless the said Portreeve hath returned, That Twenty-one Persons, having a Right of voting at the said Election, elected the Petitioner, and that the like Number of Twenty-one Persons, having a Right of voting, elected the said Christopher Hawkins, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Mitchell: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into their Consideration, and give such Relief as the Circumstances of the Case require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 15th Day of June next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of the Right honourable Charles James Fox was read; Setting forth, That, at the late Election of Two Citizens to serve in this present Parliament for the City of Westminster, the Right honourable Sir Samuel Hood, Baronet, Baron Hood of the Kingdom of Ireland, Sir Cecil Wray, Baronet, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that, a Poll being demanded, the same was opened by Thomas Corbett, Bailiff of the Liberty of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Church of Saint Peter at Westminster, on the 1st Day of April 1784, and continued from Day to Day, Sundays excepted, until the 17th Day of May, being the Day before the Day on which this present Parliament was summoned to meet, and when the Writs for the Election of Members to serve therein were commanded to be returned; on which said 17th Day of May, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon, the said Thomas Corbett finally closed the said Poll; and that the Numbers upon the said Poll, at the final Close of the same were as follows, viz. For Lord Hood 6694 — For the Petitioner 6233 — For Sir Cecil Wray *5998; and that, in consequence of an Agreement proposed by Lord Viscount Mahon, pa the Part Vol. 40.

of Lord Hood and Sir Cecil Wray, and entered into between the said Candidates at the Commencement of the said Poll, Eleven Inspectors on each Side, and Five Friends on each Side, constantly attended the said Poll, and no Vote, to which any Objection was made, was received for the Petitioner on the said Poll, without an Appeal to the presiding Officer, and his Decision that such Vote was good; and that, in the early Part of the said Poll, Sir Cecil Wray obtained a Majority of Votes thereon, to the Number of 318, and that, from the Time such Majority began to be diminished, to the final Close of the said Poll, almost every Vote which was tendered for the Petitioner was vehemently contested, and every Objection w'hich could be suggested, either by Inspectors, Friends, or Counsel, was made thereto; and that the said Poll was finally closed by the said Thomas Corbett, neither by the Consent of the Candidates, nor after a certain Interval without the Tender of any Vote, but by his the Bailiff’s own Authority, because the King’s Writ to the Sheriff commanded the same to be returned by the 18th Day of May 1784; and that the said Precept from the Sheriff to the Bailiff of Westminster, after informing the said Bailiff that he the said Sheriff had received a certain Writ of the King to him directed, which is in such Precept set out in the very Words thereof, commands the said Bailiff to cause Two Citizens to be elected for the said City, according to the Exigency of the said Writ, and in what Manner he shall have executed that Precept, immediately after the said Election, to make known to the said Sheriff so that he may certify the same to the King in His Chancery, as by the said Writ he is commanded; and that not only the plain and precise Terms of the said Writ and Precept, but the constant and invariable Usage of Parliament, require a Return of Members to serve in Parliament on or before the 18th Day of May, being, in this Instance, the Day on which the Parliament was summoned to meet; and that the Act of the Tenth and Eleventh of King William the Third, Chap. 7, doth positively and unequivocally require the Sheriff, or other Officer, having the Execution and Return of any Writ for the Election of Members to serve in any new Parliament summoned and called, to make Return of the same on or before the Day that such Parliament shall be called to meet; and that, after the final Close of the said Poll, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon, on the 17th Day of May, a Scrutiny of the said Poll was demanded on Behalf of Sir Cecil Wray, which was immediately objected to by the Petitioner, who strongly urged that such Scrutiny could not be proceeded upon by the said Bailiff after the Time on which, by Law, he was required to return the said Writ, and that, when he had finally closed the said Poll, because by Law he had no Power to continue the same any longer, it would be inconsistent and absurd to grant a Scrutiny into such Poll, to commence and be proceeded upon by him after his Power to continue such Poll was terminated; yet the said Bailiff did take upon him, contrary to the Exigency of the Writ, the positive Injunctions of the said Statute, and the invariable Law and L^sage of Parliament, in the most arbitrary and illegal. Manner, to declare that he would grant such Scrutiny, to commence and be proceeded upon after the Day appointed for the Return of the Writs for summoning this Parliament; and that, immediately after the final Close of the Poll, and casting up the Numbers, which appeared to be in favour of Lord Hood and the Petitioner, the Electors of the said City and Liberty caused an Indenture of Return of Lord Hood and the Petitioner, executed by the said Electors, to be tendered to the said High Bailiff, but he positively refused to accept or to execute the same; and that, notwithstanding such Pretence of granting a Scrutiny, the said Bailiff, being well aw^re that be was bound E by

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 8th Day of June next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon;

The House was moved, That an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to regulate the Trials of controverted " Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition does not come within the Description of a Petition complaining of an undue Election or Return of a Member or Members to serve in Parliament, the Proceedings upon which are regulated by Two Acts, made in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, for regulating the Trials of controverted Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament;

Mr. Fox withdrew.

Resolved, That the said Petition does not come within the Description of a Petition complaining of an undue Election or Return of a Member or Members to serve in Parliament, the Proceedings upon which are regulated by Two Acts, made in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, for regulating the Trials of controverted Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Petition be withdrawn.

and that a Commission of Bankrupt was issued against the said Christopher Potter on the 17th of April 1783, and he was thereupon found and declared a Bankrupt, and on the Second Day of the Month of May following an Assignment of all his Estate and Effects whatsoever was made for the Benefit of his Creditors, and that at such Time the said Christopher Potter had no Freehold Estate whatsoever, and from the Estate and Effects of the said Christopher Potter, the Petitioner is informed, no more than Two Shillings and Six Pence in the Pound has been paid to his Creditors; Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 6th Day of July next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being resident Freemen, and resident Freeholders, of and in the Borough of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, having a Right to vote in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was also read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election of Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, the Honourable Henry Fane, the Honourable Thomas Fane, Robert Wood\ Esquire, and John Cator, Esquire, were Candidates; and that, at the Poll taken upon the said Election, William Peterson, the Returning Officer, permitted many Persons to vote, who, not being resident within the said Borough, had no Right so to do, and refused to admit several others, being resident Freeholders, who had a Right as such to have given their Votes at the said Election, whereby the said Henry Fane and Thomas Fane were unduly returned, although the said Robert Wood and John Cator were duly elected by a very great Majority, and ought to have been returned; which Proceedings of the said Returning Officer the Petitioners apprehend to be a Violation of the Rights of themselves, and others, the legal Electors of the said Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief thereupon as shall be just.

A Petition of Sir Ralph Payne, Knight of the most honourable Order of the Bath, was read; Setting forth, That, at a Court held in the Borough of Ashburton, On Monday the 5th Day of April 1784, by William Winsor and Joseph Sunter, Portreeves and Returning n

Officers of the said Borough, for the Purpose of electing Two Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, and Robert Mackreth, Esquire, having been put in Nomination as Candidates, John Tonkin, an Elector of the said Borough, stated some Objections to such Nomination, and himself nominated the Petitioner to the said Returning Officers, and recommended him to the Electors then there assembled as a fit and proper Person to be one of the Representatives of the said Borough of Ashburton in Parliament, and accordingly demanded a Poll to be opened for the said Sir Ralph Payne, which Nomination, Recommendation, and Demand, were seconded by John Winsor, another Elector of the said Borbugh; and that the Petitioner being thus proposed, the other Tw'o Candidates then in Nomination, Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, and Robert Mackreth, Esquire, who were both personally present, produced on Oath their respective Qualifications, under the Act of the Ninth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, to sit in Parliament, and the like Qualification of the Petitioner was by some of the Electors required to be then and there immediately produced, previous to the Admission of the Petitioner as a Candidate, or to the opening of any Poll for him; and that the Petitioner not being in Person present, the said Requisition could not be then complied with, and it was insisted on Behalf of the Petitioner, that the Law did not require the Production of his Qualification at the Place of Election previous to his being received as a Candidate, or to the opening of a Poll for him, yet the said Returning Officers, partially contriving to procure the Return of the said Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, and Robert Mackreth, Esquire, did in Breach of their Duty, refuse to admit the Petitioner as a Candidate to represent the said Borough of Ashburton in Parliament, and to open a Poll for him, to the great Injury of the Petitioner, and in manifest Violation of the Freedom of Election; and that, in pursuance of the said partial and illegal Design of the said Returning Officers to procure the Return of the said Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, and Robert Mackreth, Esquire, the said Returning Officers did then and there proceed to open a Poll for the said Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, and Robert Mackreth, Esquire, together with the Right honourable Fredtrick Lord North, to the Exclusion of the Petitioner, and have returned the said Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, and Robert Mackreth, Esquire, duly elected Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Ashburton; and that the Petitioner did, on the j 7th Day of May Instant, before William Addington and Edmund Kelly, Esquires, Two of his Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the City and Liberty of Westminster, duly take the Oath of Qualification, prescribed by the Act of the Ninth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for securing the Freedom of Parliaments by the further qualifying the Members to sit in the House of Commons; and that the Petitioner conceives, and is advised, that sue hr partial and illegal Conduct of ’the said Portreeves, Returning Officers of the said Borough of Ashburton, touching the said Election and Return of Members to serve, in Parliament for the said Borough of Ashburton, has rendered such Election and Return null and void: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to grant him such Relief, and take such other Measures thereupon, as the Nature of his Case shall, in the Judgment of the House, require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 8th Day of July next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of Joshua Smith and George Jackson, Esquires, was read; Setting forth, That at the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Petnyn, in the County of Cornwall, Sir Francis Bassett, Baronet, Sir John Saint Aubyn, Baronet, and the Petitioners, were Candidates; and that Eduard Hodge, the Portreeve of the said Borough, who presided as the Returning Officer at the said Election, shewed a great and manifest Partiality in Favour of the said Sir Francis Bassett and Sir John Saint Aubyn, and in the Course of the Poll rejected the Votes of many Persons who had a right to vote, and who tendered their Votes for the Petitioners, and did admit many Persons to vote for the said Sir Francis Bassett 'and Sir John Saint Aubyn who had no Right whatsoever to vote in the Election of Members to represent the said Borough; and that the said Sir Francis Bassett and Sir John Saint Aubyn, by themselves and their Agents on their Behalf, and others by their Privity and Direction, previous to and during the said Election, were guilty of Bribery, and other corrupt and illegal Practices, in order to procure themselves to be elected, and for the same Purpose did, by Promises and other undue Influence, of themselves, their Friends, and Agents, prevent, and attempt to prevent, divers Persons from voting for the Petitioners; and that by the Means aforesaid a colourable Majority of Votes appeared upon the Poll for the said Sir Francis Bassett and Sir John Saint Aubyn, and the said Portreeve returned them as Burgesses duly elected to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, whereas the Petitioners were duly elected, and ought to have been returned duly elected to represent the said Borough in Parliament; and that such Proceedings are in Prejudice of the Rights of a Majority of the legal Electors of the said Borough, in Violation of the Laws of Elections, and to the manifest Injury of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 13th day of July next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Pontefract thereunto subscribed, being Burgesses Electors for Election. Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Pontefract in the County of York, on Behalf of themselves and divers other Burgesses Electors of the said Borough, was also read; Setting forth, That Pontefract is an ancient Borough of Burgage Tenure, and an ancient Corporation; that the Corporation consists of Persons having Freeholds of Burgage Tenure, paying a Burgage Rent, and of no others, and down to 1768 there appears by the Journals to have been several contested Elections for Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that at neither of such contested, nor at any other Elections there down to that Time, did any other Persons vote than such as were Freeholders of Burgage Tenure of the said Borough; and that, upon a Contest in 1768, the Return having been made by Freeholders of Burgage Tenure only, agreeably to the Constitution and uninterrupted Usage of the Borough, an Attempt was made for the first Time by the then Petitioners, and by Persons calling themselves Electors, to overthrow the Right of Election in the Freeholders of Burgage Tenure, and to establish a Right in the Inhabitants Householders, Resiants within the said Borough; and that the said Petition w^as heard at the Bar of the House, on the 6th of February 1770, and at the said Hearing Tw o obscure Entries in Two Journals of the 28th of May 1624, different in Expression, w'ere read,

Counsel on both Sides were heard thereupon, and the House solemnly considered the same in a Debate of many Hours, when it was determined, upon a Division of 161 to 32, that the said Two Entries, appearing in Two several Journals of the same Date, should not be admitted to be read to the Counsel at the Bar as the last Determination of the House touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for that Borough, and thereupon the House permitted Evidence to be offered to establish the Right of Election in the Borough, and the Counsel proceeded accordingly to give Evidence, that the Right of Election for the Borough of Pontefract is in Persons having a Freehold of Burgage Tenure within the said Borough, paying a Burgage Rent; and that Witnesses were examined, Returns produced, and other Evidence given, to prove the said Right, and several Entries in the Journals of the House, and Reports from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, touching Elections for the Borough of Pontefract, were read, and the House, upon the whole, resolved, " That the " Right of Election for Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Pontefract, in the County of " York, is in Persons having within the said Borough " a Freehold of Burgage Tenure, paying a Burgage " Rent;" and that, at the Third Election which happened after the said Resolution, viz. at the General Election in 1774, the Inhabitants Householders, Resiants within the said Borough, in open Defiance of that clear and recent Determination of the House, repeated their Attempt to overturn the ancient Constitution of the said Borough, and destroy the Right of Election therein, by claiming a Right to poll, but their Votes were rejected by the Returning Officer; a Petition was, in consequence, presented against the Sitting Members, and referred to a Select Committee of the House, when the first Question before the said Committee was, whether the aforesaid Entries in the Two Journals of the 28th of May 1624, or either of them, or the Resolution of the House of the 6th of February 1770, should be read, as the last Determination of the House of Commons touching the Legality

Cricklade A Petition of John Walker Heneage and Robert

Election. Nicholas, Esquires, was read; Setting forth, That at the

late General Election for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, Robert Adamson, Charles Westley Core, Esquires, and the Petitioners, were Candidates; and that many indirect and unwarrantable Practices were made use of By the said Robert Adamson and Charles Westley Core, and also by other Persons in their Interests, to procure a colourable Majority for them, the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core; and that Richard Townsend was the Bailiff and Returning Officer of the said Borough, and before the Poll did attempt, by undue and improper Influence, to prevail upon Persons, who had no Right of voting, to appear and tender their Votes in favour of Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, promising, and giving them Reasons to believe, that he would admit them upon the Poll at all Events; and that during the Poll

the said Richard Townsend did behave himself with marked and continued Partiality and Preference towards Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, and did illegally and arbitrarily admit a great Number of Voters who had no Right to vote, nor were qualified in any Manner to give their Votes at such Election for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, and did wilfully and knowingly reject many Voters who were duly qualified to vote, and who tendered their Votes in favour of the Petitioners, and did, by a Variety of other undue and illegal Devices, attempt to procure a fraudulent and colourable Majority for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, and did, against the earnest and continued Remonstrances of the Petitioners and their Counsel, admit without proper and sufficient Enquiry all Persons to vote for Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, and did discourage all Enquiry into the Rights or Titles of those who tendered their Votes for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core; and that the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, by themselves and their Agents, before and at the said Election, were guilty of gross Bribery, in order to corrupt the Voters of the said Borough; and as well by giving! as by promising to give, Money and other Rewards "to the Voters of the said Borough, and by other illegal, corrupt, and indirect Means, did prevail on many of the Voters of the said Borough to give their Votes at the said Election for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core; and that in consequence thereof, and by the partial, arbitrary, and illegal Conduct of the Returning Officer, a colourable Majority of Votes was obtained for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, under which the said Returning Officer has endeavoured to protect himself for the illegal Return which he has made of the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, in Prejudice of the Petitioners, who had a clear Majority of legal and uncorrupted Votes, and ought to have been returned for the said Borough, and in Subversion of the true and sacred Rights of Election, ami of the Law and Constitution of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 27th Day of July next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s

Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former

Cases, were sent to the several Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Times on which the said several Petitions were ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Address on Mr. John James Hamilton reported from the Corn-

King’s mittee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address

Speech. to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty our humble Thanks for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

We beg Your Majesty will be assured, that we are animated with the warmest Sentiments of Loyalty, and an inviolable Attachment to our excellent Constitution, which are, we trust, inseparably united in the Hearts of Your Faithful Subjects.

We acknowledge, with the warmest Gratitude and Satisfaction, Your Majesty’s Wisdom and Goodness in recurring, at so important a Moment, to the Sense of Your People; and we trust that so seasonable an Exercise of the Power entrusted to Your Majesty by the Constitution will not fail to be attended by the most happy and beneficial Effects.

Your Majesty may be assured, that Your Faithful Commons will be ready to take proper Measures for the Application of the Sums voted in the last Parliament, and to grant such further Supplies as may

appear to be necessary; having the fullest Confidence that all Your Majesty’s Subjects will, from Loyalty to Your Majesty, and Zeal for the Interests of the Country, be ready to support those heavy Burthens which, in Consequence of a long and expensive W ar, are now unavoidable; and that they will be sensible of the Necessity of effectually providing for the Maintenance of the National Faith and the Public Credit, so essential to the Power and Prosperity of the State.

We also beg Leave to assure Your Majesty, that we shall apply our utmost Attention to the Means of preventing the increasing Frauds in the Revenue: That we shall take into our most serious Consideration such Commercial Regulations as the present Situation may immediately require.

That, in our Deliberations on the Affairs of The East India Company, so deeply connected with the general Interests of the Country, we shall be truly anxious to provide for the good Government of our Possessions in that Part of the World.

That we shall be careful never to lose Sight of the Effects which any Measure, to be adopted for the Purpose, may have on our excellent Constitution, and our dearest Interests at Home; and that we are deeply penetrated with the Gracious and Parental Expressions of Your Majesty’s Affection and Goodness to Your People, and have the most dutiful Reliance on Your Majesty’s Royal Attention to every Object of National Concern, and to the true Principles of our free Constitution, which can only be secured by maintaining, in their just Balance, the Rights and Privileges of every Branch of the Legislature.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to II is Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

A Petition and Representation bf Sir Ashton Lever, Knight, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, in the early Part of his Life, having a Turn for Natural History, began to collect Specimens and Articles of every Kind, and, being flattered by his great Success, resolved to remove his Museum to the Metropolis, not doubting but he could make it, by its Pre-eminence over all other Collections, of Public Benefit, and a National Honour; and that, notwithstanding the Difficulty and Expence of this Undertaking, he entered upon it with determined Spirit, and pursued it in such a Manner as to have secured every capital Article that has offered itself, and, by selecting out of some Hundred thousand Specimens, has actually formed a Collection superior to any Thing of the Kind in Europe, or perhaps to them all united, as it comprehends Subjects so rare and valuable as are not to be found in any other Cabinet; and that the Petitioner has persevered in this Pursuit at a very great Expence, encouraged by a firm Belief that it might be rendered worthy the Attention of the Public, in which he has been confirmed by the Opinion of Persons of the first Consequence, but it is nowr grown too great a Concern for an Individual; and that, notwithstanding this Collection has been made in Hopes that it would have been purchased for the Use and Benefit of the Public, yet Vol. 40.

from the critical Situation of the Times it has been thought improper to apply for the Indulgence of Parliament in the Mode he intended otherwise to have done,* and it cannot easily be disposed of in the common Way of Sale: And therefore praying, r£hat Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to authorize and impower the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, to sell and dispose of the said Museum and Collection, and the several Pieces composing the same, in such Manner as the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, shall think proper, without being liable or subject to any Penalty or Forfeiture, imposed by any Act or Acts of Parliament against any Sale or Sales by Way of Lottery, or Lots, Tickets, Numbers,' or Figures; and that such Sale or Sales, so to be made of the said Museum, and of the several Pieces composing the same, by the Petitioner, hb Executors, Adminbtrators, or Assigns, before a Day in the Act to be specified, may be good and valid, any Law or Statute to the contrary thereof notwithstanding, or otherwise as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition and Representation be referred to the Consideration of a Committee;

And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House: ,

And it is referred to Mr. Gascoyne, Junior, Sir William Middleton, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber.

A Petition of Sir James Maxwell, of Pollock, Baronet, Robert Bogle, Robert Craufurd, John Maxwell, and John Craig, Proprietors of the Soap Manufactory of Glasgow, and Copartners under the Firm of Robert Craufurd and Company, Merchants in Glasgow, and of James Corbet, James Dunlop, George Brown, Andrew Blackburn Colville, John Cross, Hugh IVyUie, Thomas Dunmore, Robert Dunmore, Junior, James

Robert Craufurd, George Kippen, Thomas Connell, James Genrmil, John Craufurd, James Scott, and William Semple, Proprietors of the Rope Manufactory of Glasgow, and Copartners under the Firm of James Corbet and Company, Merchants in Glasgow, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That by several Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, and, among others, by an Act passed in

the Year 1661, in the First Parliament of King Charles the Second, intituled, " Act for erecting of Manufactories;" by another Act, passed in the Year 1669, in the Second Parliament of the said King Charles the

Mail. 1784, '

Second, intituled, 11 Act concerning the Excise and " Customs;" and by another Act, passed in the Year' 1681, in the Third Parliament of his said Majesty King Charles the Second, intituled, u Act for encouraging Trade and Manufactories," certain Privileges and Immunities were granted, and Rules made,- for encouraging and promoting Manufactories in Scotland, and particularly, Materials useful for Manufactures were allowed to be imported, for the Use of such Manufactures, free of Customs and Excise, and alt other Public Burthens; and, in order to prevent all Questions and Debates in relation to the said Privileges and Immunities, the Lords of the Exchequer and Privy Council in Scotland were, by certain of the said Acts, authorized to enquire and declare what Manufactories already were, or thereafter should be, duly qualified to enjoy the Benefit of the Privileges and Immunities by the said Acts bestowed; and that, under the Encouragements held forth by the said Acts of Parliament, Two Manufactories were erected in Glasgow, the one in the Year 1674, for making of Soap, and the other in the Year 1696, for making of Ropes and Cordage, the Proprietors of each of which Manufactories did obtain from the Exchequer and Privy Council of Scotland an Order, or Act, declaring their respective Works to be duly qualified in Terms of the Statutes in that Behalf, and which Manufactories, so established and approven, have been continually carried on since the respective Times of their Erection, and do now, by Course of regular Successions and Conveyances, belong to the following Persons, viz. the first mentioned Manufactory for making of Soap, to the Petitioners Sir James Maxwell, Baronet, Robert Bogle, Robert Craufurd, John Maxwell, and John Craig, by Way of Copartner, known by the Appellation of the Soap Work Company of Glasgow, and transacting Business under the firm of Robert Craufurd and Company, and the other Manufactory for making of Ropes and Cordage, to the Petitioners James Corbet, James Dunlop, George Brown, Andrew Blackburn Colville, John Cross, Hugh Wyllie, Thomas Dunmore, Robert Dunmore, James Somma'vitle, Robert Craufurd, George Kippen, Thomas Connell, James Getnmil, John Craufurd, James Scott, and William Semple, also by Way of Copartner, known by the Appellation of the Rope Work Company of Glasgoa\ and transacting Business under the Firm of James Corbet and Company; and that, by the 6th Article of the Treaty of Union, settled and agreed upon in the Fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, between the Two Kingdoms of England and Scotland, Provision is made,

" That all Parts of the United Kingdom, for ever,

" from and after the Union, shall have the same " Allowances, Encouragements, and Drawbacks, and " be under the same Prohibitions, Restrictions, and " Regulations of Trade, and liable to the same Customs and Duties on Import and Export; and that " the Allowances, Encouragements, and Drawbacks,

" Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Regulations of Trade,

" and the Customs and Duties on Import and " Export, settled in England when the Union cominences, shall, from and after the Union, take Place " throughout the whole United Kingdom, excepting " and reserving the Duties upon Export and Import " of such particular Commodities from which any " Persons, the Subjects of either Kingdom, are specially " liberated and exempted by their private Rights,

" which, after the Union, are to remain safe and " entire to them, in all respects, as before the same and that, upon the Commencement of the said Union, Doubts and Disputes did arise between the Officers of her Majesty’s Customs and the Proprietors of the said Soap and Rope Works, who claimed the Privilege of importing Materials for their respective Manufactories free of Duties, as a private Right, constituted by the Acts of Parliament and Acts of 7 Privy

24 Geo. III. Mail.

Privy Council before mentioned, and, as sufch, saved by the Exception in Favour of private Rights contained in the aforesaid 6th Article of the said Treaty of Union; to which Claim the Officers of the Revenue objected, that the Exemption from Duties, given by the Acts of Parliament and Privy Council of Scotland, was not in the Nature of a private Right, but of a public Encouragement to Trade, and as such was determined and at an End by the Treaty of Union; in respect of which Disputes it was agreed upon, as an interim Expedient, that the Proprietors of the aforesaid Manufactories should grant Bonds for the Duties of the Materials to be imported by them, with Condition to pay the same in case the Parliament of Great Britain, or Court of Exchequer in Scotland, should adjudge the said Materials liable to the Payment of Duties, which Agreement of taking such Conditional Bonds, as aforesaid, was for some Time carried into Execution, until the Commissioners of the Customs at Edinburgh gave Orders for levying the Duties upon all such Materials, imported for the Use of the said Manufactories, as were by Law chargeable with Duties upon being imported for other Purposes; whereupon the Proprietors of the said Manufactories paid the Duties accordingly, but under Protest that the Right of Exemption claimed by them should not thereby be hurt, nor themselves precluded from reclaiming such Duties as already had been, or afterward should be, paid by them; and, for bringing the Right of Exemption so claimed by them to Trial, the Proprietors of the said Rope Work did some Time since institute an Action in the Court of Exchequer at Edinburgh, at the Suit of the said James Corbet, One of the said Proprietors, and Assignee of the rest of those Proprietors, against Edward Burrow, Collector of the Customs at the Port of Port Glasgow, and John Clerk, then the Deputy of the said Edward Burrow, at the Member Port of Greenock, for that they had, against Right, refused to re-pay Duties levied by them on certain Materials imported for the Use of the said Rope Work; in the Course of the Proceedings on which Action a special Verdict was agreed upon and settled by the Parties, and returned by a Jury, upon which Verdict Counsel were heard by the Lord Chief Baron and other Three Barons of the said Court, and the Judges having been equally divided in their Opinion, the Question remains hitherto undetermined; since the Time of which Hearing, certain Propositions have been offered by the Petitioners, the Proprietors of the said Works, for accommodating the Matter in Dispute; and that it has been alledged by the Officers of the Revenue, that the Claim of Exemption made by the Petitioners, the Proprietors of the said Manufactories, would, on the one Hand, if established, be very prejudicial to the Public Interest, being capable to be exercised in an unlimited Extent with respect to the Commodities which are the Subject thereof, to the great Diminution of the Revenue, and the Breach of that Equality in Trade which ought to have Place in all Parts of the United Kingdom; while, on the other Hand, the Petitioners, by Means of the aforesaid Treaty of Union, and the Doubts and Disputes thereupon arising in relation to the Right of Exemption claimed as aforesaid, as well as by Reason of the Proceedings consequent upon such Doubts and Disputes, and in firm Reliance upon the public Faith of the Kingdom, laid out a considerable Sum of Money towards carrying on the said Works, have suffered considerable Loss and Inconveniency, the Exemption from the Payment of Duties enjoyed by them, under the Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, having, by the aforesaid Means, been abridged or interrupted, and much Expence incurred by Law Suits, and otherwise; and that, in a Case so circumstanced, it is submitted to be reasonable and just that some Compensation should be made to the Petitioners for the private Loss Vol. 40.

they have suffered in Consequence of the said Treaty of Union, a Transaction calculated for National Advantages, and, it is at the same Time expedient to remoVe all such Doubts and Disputes, as aforesaid, in future: And therefore praying, That Leave msly be given to bring in a Bill to explain the Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, herein above recited, and for granting Relief to the Petitioners, and for extinguishing or abolishing all Claims or Pretensions of the Proprietors of the said Two Manufactories, called the Soap and Rope Manufactories of Glasgow, and their Successors, to'any Exemption from the Payment of Customs or Duties.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to the Lord Advocate of Scotland,

Mr. Dempster, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

and that the said John Dagge hath taken upon himself falsely, partially, and illegally, to make a Return of the said Edward Bouverie and William Scott, and not of the said Henry Seymour Conway and Robert Shafto, who were duly elected Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, to the Prejudice of the said Henry Seymour Conway and Robert Shafto, and in direct Violation of the Rights and Franchises of the Petitioners, and the other legal Electors of the said Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as shall appear to be just.

PRAYERS.

A PETITION of the Right honourable Charles Howard, commonly called Earl of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Town of Sheffield, in the West Riding of the County of York, is a large and populous trading Town, wherein a public Market is holden Twice in every Week, and a public Fair Twice in every Year; and that the present Market Place within the said Town is too small for the Use of the Inhabitants and others frequenting the said Market, and the Passage along the public Streets adjoining to the Market Place is greatly obstructed, and rendered very inconvenient to Travellers, by the Stalls and Standings necessarily placed therein on Market Days, and the present Slaughter Houses stand in a very improper Situation, and are frequently very offensive to the Inhabitants of the said Town; and that the Petitioner is Owner of the said Market Place and the Shops and other Buildings erected thereon, and entitled to the Right of holding the said Market, and is also Owner of a very considerable Estate within the other Parts of the said Town, and the Neighbourhood thereof; and that the said Market Place might be much enlarged, and made more convenient, and the Passages through the adjacent Streets rendered safe and commodious, if certain ancient Houses and other Buildings, belonging to the Petitioner and others, situate on the East Side thereof, were taken down, and the Scites thereof, and some vacant Ground adjoining thereto, were added to the present Market Place, and, that a proper Place for slaughtering of Cattle might be built in some more convenient Situation; and that Application hath been made to the Petitioner by many of the principal Inhabitants of the said Town and Neighbourhood, requesting him to enlarge the said Market Place, and to erect proper Shops and other Buildings thereon, and to remove the said Slaughter Houses; which Improvements the Petitioner believes would be of very great Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and all Persons resorting thereto, and would also be advantageous to the Petitioner and the future Owners of his said Estate; wherefore the Petitioner is willing and desirous to cause the said Improvements to be done, in case he shall be enabled to raise, by Sale and Mortgage of some Parts of the said Estates, a sufficient Sum of Money to defray the Expence thereof: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable him to make the several Improvements before mentioned, and to raise a competent Sum of Money to defray the Expences thereof, by such Ways and Means, and under such Restrictions, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Wilberforce and Mr. Duncombe do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Phillips* A Petition of Henry Phillips, of Knightsbridge, being Preservation offered to be presented to the House; of Provisions. Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That in March 1781 the Petitioner presented a Petition to the House of Commons, stating, that having been informed of the Ravages and Devastations made during Sea Voyages on the dry Provisions in His Majesty’s Navy by Weevils and other Insects, he had, after many Years incessant Study and Assiduity, discovered a cheap Composition, easy in its Application, and the Expence not exceeding Five Guineas, in eradicating Weevils, Spiders, Maggots, and Cockroaches, out of a First-rate Man of War; and that the House is in Possession of numerous and incontrovertible Testimonies of the great Utility of the Petitioner’s Discovery; and that the Petitioner having been the Author of an Invention of the utmost Consequence to the Health and Lives of Seamen in His Majesty’s Service, as the Commissioners for victualling the Navy, and several Vol. 40.

respectable Naval Officers, testified in a Committee of the House in 1781, a Bill was, in consequence thereof, submitted to Parliament, for providing a Reward of £. 3,600 to the Petitioner, on his making a proper Discovery, for the Use of the Public, of the Composition of his Powder for the Destruction of Insects, but which Reward the House of Lords postponed until further Proofs of the Success of the Petitioner’s Invention, and ordered a particular Account of the Result of such Experiments as were then making, or should be made, on board any of His Majesty’s Ships of War, of the Efficacy of the Petitioners Powder, to be laid before them; in Obedience to which, the Commissioners of the Admiralty have laid before Parliament a Number of Certificates, incontestibly proving the great Importance of the Petitioner’s Invention; and that the Petitioner, conscious, from the Addition of the numerous and incontrovertible Testimonies in Support of his Invention, that the Utility of his Discovery gives him a Claim to Public Protection, and to Public Reward, is induced, notwithstanding the Invention has been acquired by Eighteen Years unremitted Application, at the Expence of £. 4,000, and at the Hazard of his Life (he being now almost blind) to make known to the House, that he is ready and willing to lay open the Nature and Manner of preparing his Composition, that all His Majesty’s Subjects may reap the Benefit of it, upon receiving such Compensation for his Trouble and Expence as the House shall think fit to grant.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do ^examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr John Luttrell, Mr. Medley, 8cc.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Mom- .

ing, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cases, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty Yesterday with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most Gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return you My most cordial Thanks for this very loyal and dutiful Address.

The affectionate Expressions of Attachment from My Faithful Commons, and their zealous Regard to the Principles of Our invaluable Constitution, must ever afford Me the most sincere Satisfaction.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, residing at Sleaford and Boston, and the Country adjacent thereto, in the Parts of Kestcven and Holland, in the County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, anjl read; Setting forth, That a certain Stream or River, and the Branches thereof, from Sleaford Castle Causeway, through the several Parishes of New Sleaford, Old Sleaford, and Evedon Haverholm Priory, and the several Parishes of Amcick, Ewerby, North and South Kyme, Billinghay, and Swineshead, in the Parts of Kesteven and Holland, in the County of Lincoln, to the Junction of the said Stream or River with the River Wit ham, near Chapel Hill, in the same County, extends to the Distance of Twelve Miles, or thereabouts; and that, if the said River.was made navigable for Boats,

Barges*, and other Vessels, a Communication would thereby be opened with the Port of Boston, the City of Lincoln, and the River Trent, whereby great Benefit would arise to the Land Owners, Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants of the several Parishes adjacent to the said River or Stream from Sleaford to the Wit ham, by facilitating the Carriage of Coals,

Wool, Corn, and other Goods and Commodities, at less Expence than is now paid for the same by Land Carriage, greatly tend to the Increase of Trade and Commerce, and be of public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making the said Stream or River, and the Branches thereof, navigable from Sleaford Castle Causeway to the Junction of the said Stream with the River Wit ham, making such Cuts, and maintaining the said Navigation, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Anderson Pelham, Sir Robert Laze ley. See.: And 'they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records,

A Petition of the respective Companies of Proprie- Birmingham tors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation, and the Navigation. Birmingham and Fazelcy Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act was passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut or Canal from Birmingham to Bilston, and from thence to Autherley, there to communicate with the Canal then making between the Rivers Secern and Trent, \md for making Collateral Xuts up to several Coal Mines; and that another Act was passed in the Ninth Year of His said Majesty, to rectify a Mistake in the said first-mentioned Act, and to explain and amend the same; and that another Act was passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from a Place near Riders Green, in the County of Stafford, to Broadwater Fire Engine, and Six Collateral Cuts from the same to several Coal Mines, and also a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Binningham, to join the Coventry Canal, at or near Fazcley, in the Parish of Tamworth, in the said County of Stafford, with a Collateral Cut to the lower Part of the said Town of Birmingham; and that the Canal and Collateral Cuts, authorized to be made by virtue of the said last mentioned Act, will communicate with the Canal and Collateral Cuts made and completed by virtue of the Powers granted by the said first-recited Act, and nearly the Whole of the Proprietors of the said Birmingham Canal Navigation, and the Proprietors of the said Bh'mingham and Fazcley Canal Navigation, are the same Persons; and that, as the said respective Navigations will communicate with each other, and great Expences and Inconveniences would be avoided by incorporating the same, and making them one common Concern, it hath been agreed that the same should be consolidated, and the respective Companies of Proprietors of the said Two Undertakings have entered into Agreements for that Purpose; and that, by a Clause in the said last-meu-tioned Act, it is recited, That, at a Meeting held at Coleshill, in the County of Warwick, upon the 20th Day of June 1782, by certain Delegates from the respective Companies of Proprietors of the Oxford,

Coventry, and Grand Trunk Canal Navigations, and from certain Subscribers to a new-proposed Navigation from the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury to Birmingham, and from thence to join the Coventry

Canal

Canal in the Neighbourhood of Fazdeyr, it was proposed and agreed, by such Delegates, on the Part of their respective Companies or Constituents, That, in order to effect a General Communication between the Oxford, Coventry, and Grand Trunk Canals, the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury, and Town of Birmingham, it would be necessary that the Coventry Canal should be completed between Atherstone and Fradley Heath, that the Oxford Canal should be completed from Oxford to Banbury, and that the new' Subscribers should execute a Canal from such Coal Mines to Birmingham and to Fazeley; and, the more easily to effect the Communication between Fazeley - and Fradley Heath, it was further agreed, that the Proprietors of the Coventry Canal should, by Authority of Parliament or otherwise, relinquish to the Proprietors of the Grand Trunk Canal, and to the Subscribers to such proposed Canal, that Branch of the said Coventry Canal lying between Fazdey and Fradley Heath, and that the same should be executed by them, at their joint Expence, in Manner and on the Terms therein mentioned, and that, when the same should be completed, it should be equally divided between, and each Part considered as the several and distinct Property of, the said Parties, and be supported accordingly; and it was therein expressed to be further understood and agreed, that the Tonnage to be taken for all Coals navigated from Birmingham, throughout the intended Canal, to Fazeley, and upon all or any Part or Parts of the Coventry and Oxford Canals, should not exceed One Penny per Ton per Mile; but it was thereby also understood, that the Subscribers to the said intended Canal were not to be restrained from taking any additional Tonnage for all Coals passing from the Collieries, and discharged at Birmingham, or any Distance upon the intended Canal, short of Fazeley; and it is further recited, that the Canals and Collateral Cuts authorized to be made by the Company of Proprietors incorporated by that Act, and under the Authority of the same, had been substituted in the Place and Stead of the said proposed Canal from the Collieries at Wednesbury to Biimingham} and from thence to Fazeley aforesaid, and that the said Company had, in Consideration of the same, agreed to ratify and confirm the aforesaid Agreement, so entered into by the said former Subscribers, with respect to the Execution of that Part of the Said Coventry Canal from Fazeley to Fradley Heath aforesaid, it is thereby enacted, that the said Agreement so entered into by the said former Subscribers, and the several Matters and-Things therein specified and contained to be done by, and on their Parts, shall be binding and conclusive on the Company of Proprietors incorporated by the said Act, as fully and effectually as if they had been Parties thereto; and that, although by the said last mentioned Act it is enacted, that the Agreement so entered into by the said former Subscribers at Coles-hill, and the several Matters and Things therein specified and contained to be done by and on their Parts, should be binding and conclusive upon the Company of Proprietors incorporated by the said last mentioned Act, yet it is conceived that the Authority of Parliament is necessary to enable such Proprietors to carry the said Agreement into Execution; and that, for the more speedily and effectually completing the said Birmingham and Fazeley Canal, it Will be necessary to borrow a large Sum of Money, by Way of Loan, upon the Credit of the Tolls of the said respective Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazdey Canal Navigations, and it will be likewise necessary that some of the Clauses in the said last mentioned Act should be explained, altered, and amended, and some further Powers given for the better carrying on, completing, and improving the said Navigations: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to consolidate Vol. 40.

the said Two respective Undertakings of the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, and for incorporating the said Tv.o respective Companies of Proprietors, and the several Powers, Privileges, and Authorities, by the said respective Acts of Parliament granted; and that such farther Powers may be granted to the Petitioners as m&y be necessary to enable them to borrow Money for completing the said last mentioned Undertaking, to carry into Execution the Agreement so entered into at Coleshill, for explaining and amending several Clauses in the said last mentioned Act, and for such other Purposes as the House shall see fit and expedient for the Support and Improvement of the said respective Navigations.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names pawn-are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and brokers, others, Pawnbrokers within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the more effectual Punishment of Persons who shall attain, or attempt to attain, Possession of Goods or Money by false or untrue Pretences, for preventing the unlawful Pawning of Goods, for the easy Redemption of (Goods paw ned, and for other Purposes, certain Regulations were established for conducting the Business of a Pawnbroker; and that the said Act does not limit or ascertain the Amount of Charges for Warehouse Room to be paid to the Pawnbroker, and therefore the Petitioners have almost ever since the making of the said Act taken such Sums of Money for the Warehouse Room of the Goods pledged as have, in their Appre-» bensions, been reasonable, and were necessary for the decent Maintenance of themselves and Families; and that the Petitioners, and others, in the conducting of the said Business, have oftentimes refused to take Money tendered to them for the Redemption of Goods pledged, because such Money was inadequate to their Expences, and, in consequence of some of such Refusals, Actions at Law have been brought against several Pawnbrokers, in which such Tenders have been considered to be sufficient, and Yerdicts have been given K thereon
