theneon against such Pawnbrokers; and the Petitioners and others, in endeavouring to obtain a reasonable Profit in their said Business, are liable, notwithstanding tke said Act, to be sued at Law for supposed Offences against the Laws relating to Usury; and that, in case the Petitioners were to receive such inadequate Tenders, and the Trade is to be conducted on such low Terms, the Petitioners will not be able to carry on the same, but it must be totally annihilated, whereby the Petitioners, and their Families, and all other carrying on that Business, must be driven to seek their Livelihoods by other Employments; and, the said Act is, in other Respects, defective, and insufficient to answer the good Purposes for which it was intended; and that the Petitioners, being conscious of having always carried on their Business with the utmost Integrity, and being desirous of gaining by their Trade no more than a reasonable Profit upon their Capital for the decent Support of themselves and Families, hope they shall be found a useful Body of Tradesmen, and deserving of the Countenance and Protection of the Legislature: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and render more effectual, the said Act of the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, so far as the same relates to the preventing the unlawful Pawning of Goods, and the easy Redemption of Goods pawned, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Alderman Newnham and Mr. Watson do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to ascertain the Manner and Form of taking an Oath, by certain Persons, Protestants of the ancient Church of Scotland: And that Mr. Dempster and the Lord Advocate of Scotland do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Salford A Petition of the Trustees appointed for putting

Road. in Execution an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for repairing and widening " the Road from a certain Place in the Town of " Salford, to the Towns of Warrington and Bolton and " through Wardley Lane to the Town of Wigan, and " to the Stocks in the Township of Duxbury, and to a " Place called The Broad Oak in Worsley, in the " County Palatine of Lancasterand also, of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the said County of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in pursuance of the said Act, the Trustees therein named have caused great Part of the said Roads to be repaired, widened, and amended, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, which is now owing; and that the said Act is near expiring, and unless the same is renewed, and the Term and Powers enlarged, the Money advanced upon the Credit of the said Tolls cannot be repaid, nor the said Roads be effectually amended; and alleging, that there is a Public Bridle Way djr Horse Road leading from a Place called The South Sea, upon the Road between the Towns of Salford and Bolton, in the said Act mentioned, through the several Townships of Pendlebury and Prestwick, in the said County, into the Public Turnpike Road be-ween Manchester and Bury, in the same County, which if repaired, widened, and improved, and made into a Public Highway, would be of great public Utility, by forming a nearer Communication between the said Towns of Warrington and Bury, and Rochdale, in the said County, and also between Part of the Two Counties of Lancastet' and York, but the same is at present very narrow and inconvenient, and in many Places deep and founderous, and cannot be made and kept in Repair by the Laws now in being: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, not only to continue and enlarge the Term and Powers of the said recited Act, hut also to make, repair, and amend, the said Road from South Sea aforesaid, to the said Road leading between Manchester and Bury aforesaid, under such Powers and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Matthew White Ridley, Mr. Stanley, &c.: And they are to1 meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

that Colonel John Thomson, of Charktom, was legally elected Delegate for the Borough of Anstruther-Easter, by a Majority of the real and qualified Counsellors, but by admitting Persons to vote who were not in Truth Counsellors, nor qualified to be of the Council, an apparent Majority was created in favour of the said Sir John Anstruther, and besides a general Objection lay against the Election of that Borough; that the Magistrates who were an essential and integral Part of the Corporation, and without which it could not subsist, never had qualified themselves to exercise their Offices; that the Commission to a Delegate for Anstruther-Wester was void, as being granted by Persons who were not legal Administrators of the Boroughs, contrary to the united Voice of the Inhabitants, and who had not qualified themselves to exercise their Office; Trent and A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, was pre- sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Petitioners were impowered to make a Navigable Cut or Canal from the River Trent, at or near Wilden Ferry, in the County of T>erhy, to the River Mersey, in the County of Chester, which they have several Years since completed; and that, by an Act made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Persons therein named were united into one Body Politic and Corporate, by the Name of The Company of Proprietors of the Coventry Canal Navigation, and were impowered to make a Navigable Cut or Canal from the City of Coventry, to join the Canal of the Petitioners on Fradley Heath; and that, by another Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Persons therein also named were united into one other Body Politic and Corporate, by the Name of The Company of Proprietors of the Oxford Canal Navigation, and were impowered to make a Navigable Cut or Canal from the said Coventry Canal Navigation to the City of Oxford; and that the said Canal, so authorized to be made from Coventry to the Canal of the Petitioners at Fradley Heath, hath been completed from Coventry to At her-stone, in the County of Warwick; and the said Canal, authorized to be made from Coventry to Oxford, hath been completed from Coventry to Banbury, but the other Parts of the said several Undertakings remain yet to be executed; and that, at a Meeting held at Coleshill, in the County of Warwick, upon the 20th Day of June 1782, by certain Delegates from the Petitioners, and the respective Companies of Proprietors of the Coventry and Oxford Canal Navigations, and from certain Subscribers to a new-proposed Navigation from the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury to Birmingham, and from thence to join the Coventry Canal, in the Neighbourhood of Fazcley, it was proposed and agreed by such Delegates, on the Part of their respective Companies or Constituents, that, in order to effect a general Communication between the Canal of the Petitioners and the said Coventry and Oxford Canals, the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury, and the Town of Birmingham, it would be necessary that the Coventry Canal should be completed between Atherstone and Fradley Hsath, that the Oxford Canal should be completed from Banbury to Oxford, and that the Subscribers to the said new-proposed Navigation should execute a Canal from the said Collieries to Birmingham and to Fazely; and, the more easily to effect the Communication between Fazely and Fradley Heath, it was agreed that the Proprietors of the Coventry Canal should, by Authority of Parliament, or otherwise, relinquish to the Petitioners, and to the Subscribers to such proposed Canal, that Branch of the said Coventry Canal lying between Fazely and Fradley Heath, and that the same should be executed by them at their joint Expence, and that, when the said Canal between Fazely and Fradley. Heath should be completed, it should be equally divided between, and each Part cojqsidered jis Vol. 40.

the separate and distinct Property of, the Petitioners and the said Subscribers, and be supported accordingly; and that, by an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for making and " maintaining a Navigable Canal from a Place called " Rider's Green, in the County of Stafford, to Bivad " Water Fire Engine, and Six Collateral Cuts from " the same, to several Coal Mines; and also a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Birmingham,

and that, at the said Election, a great Majority of Votes, over those which were given for the said Henry Cruger and Samuel Peachy were given by the Petitioners, and others duly qualified to vote, in Favour of the said George Daubeny, who was duly chosen at the said Election, and ought to have been returned as one of the Members to serve in Parliament for the said City and County; but the Sheriffs and Returning Officers of the said City and County admitted a great Number of Persons to vote for the said Henry Cruger at the said Election, who had no Right, and ought not to have been admitted, to vote at the said Election, and rejected the Votes of divers Persons who tendered their Votes for the said George Daubeny, and had a Right to vote at the said Election, and by such Means, and other Acts of Partiality, created a colourable Majority on the Poll in Favour of the said Henry Cruger over the said George Daubeny, and have unduly returned the said Henry Cruger as one of the Members to serve in Parliament for the said City and County, to the great Injury of the Petitioners, and of the said George Daubeny: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Thomas Stanley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees appointed for putting in Execution an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His late Majesty King Geot'ge the Second, intituled, "An Act for repairing and " widening the Road from a certain Place in the " Town of Salford, to the Towns of Warrington and " Bolton, and through Wardley Lane to the Town of " Wigan, and to the Stocks in the Township of " Duxbury, and to a Place called The Broad Oak, in #< Worsley, in the County Palatine of Lancasterand also, of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders of the said County of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And

Thomas Butta'worth Bayley, Esquire, being examined, informed your Committee, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution thereof, and have borrowed several Sums of Money, to the Amount of upwards of £. 2,000, upon the Credit of the Tolls; which Money now remains due, and cannot be repaid, nor the said Roads effectually amended, unless the Term of the said Act be further continued, and the Powers thereof enlarged.

That the public Bridle Way or Horse Road leading from a Place called The South Sea, upon the Road between the Towns of Salford and Bolton, in the said Act mentioned# through the several Townships of Pendlebury and Prestxviok, into the public Turnpike Road betw'een Manchester and Bury, is at present very narrow and inconvenient, and in many Places deep and founderous; and that it would be of public Utility, if the same was made a Turnpike Road, whereby the Communication between several Parts of the Country would be shortened Four or Five Miles. — Then,

Mr, James Cooke was examined, who confirmed the above Evidence, with respect to the said Bridle Way; and added, that the Estimate for repairing it amounts to £.277. 3*. and that £.600 has been subscribed for that Purpose.

Mr. Bayley being again examined, said, That many Alterations and Additions are nepessary to be made to the said Act; and it is proposed to repeal the Clause which exempts the Inhabitants of Worsley from Statute Work upon any Part of the Road between The Guide Post in Swinton, through Wariley Lane, to The Stocks in Worsley — That the Inhabitants of Worsley have now the Enjoyment of a large Road of Communication instead of a Bridle Way; and that it is proposed to say out £. 800 in repairing that Part of the Road, which is to be applied prior to any other Expenditure of Money upon the Roads.

A Petition of the Trustees of the British Museum being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the said Trustees represented to Parliament, that the Sum allowed them for the Establishment and Support of the said Museum was reduced to a Capital of £. 30,000 Reduced Bank Annuities, the Dividend of which, amounting to £.900, was, notwithstanding their utmost Attention to the forming their Establishment with Frugality, greatly insufficient for that Purpose, upon which Representation they have, at sundry Times, obtained from this House various Sums to supply the Deficiency of their Income, which Sums, together with the Salary allotted to the King’s Librarian Yearly, amounting to about £. 250, have proved insufficient to defray the necessary Expences of the said Museum, and what now remains in the Hands of the Trustees is not sufficient to defray the Expences of the current Year: And

therefore praying the House to grant the Petitioners such farther Support, towards enabling them to carry on the Execution of the Trust reposed in them by

Parliament, for the general Benefit of Learning and useful Knowledge, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of the Money granted by Parliament for the Use of the British Museum, and of the Expenditure thereof.

A Petition of the Reverend Thomas Weelccs Dolby, of Chippenham, in the County of Witts, Clerk, Executor of the last Will and Testament of Edward Dowries, deceased, who was Executor of the last Will and Testament of Charles Weekes, late of London. Merchant, deceased, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the said Charles IFcekes, being Owner of the Ship Hope, Burthen 133 Tons, or thereabouts, and she being, at the latter End of the Year 1743, Outward-bound from London, to bring Home a Loading of Sugars from Nevis, was, about the 1st of December 1743, let by Charter-Party to the Commissioners for victualling His Majesty's Navy, to carry Stores to Gibraltar or Port Mahon, the Sailing Part whereof she performed, from the The Doxcns to Gibraltar, in Nineteen Days, and from The Downs to Port Mahon in Forty Days; but the said Ship was, nevertheless, contrary to the Spirit and true Meaning of the Charter Party, detained by Government more than Twelve Months, and during the Time used as if she had been hired as a Monthly Transport, in the Course of which Time she received considerable Damage, and her said Voyage to Nevis (where a Cargo was ready for her) and from thence to London, was totally defeated; and that the Government, in the War which began in 1739, had Two Methods of hiring Ships, viz. one for Transports, to be used at their Will and Pleasure, so long as the Service required, at about 15s. or 16$. a Ton per Month, taken into immediate Pay, and so continued till discharged, and, if discharged Abroad, such Pay was continued for a reasonable Time, for the Ship either to return Home, or to proceed elsew here, as the Owner had directed; the other Method of hiring Ships by Government was in the Manner The Hope had been hired as above mentioned, under certain Restrictions for particular Voyages, upon much cheaper Terms than the other, because the Owners of Ships Outward-bound, in order to bring Home Cargoes to Europe, having the Homeward-bound Freight for the chief Object, contracted with Government to carry Stores to Places lying near the Outward-bound Course, for very insignificant Freights, and Demurrages in Proportion to the true Value of the Use and Hire of the Ships for any Length of Time; and that, according to the Mode of hiring after the Manner of a Monthly Transport, the Money due to the said Weekes, in respect to the said Ship, amounted to £.1,700, and upwards, together with Interest, to commence at a certain Time, the Whole of which, both Principal and Interest, would now amount to upwards of £.5,000; and, according to the other Mode of hiring, the Money so due under the Charter-Party, and for the special Damages sustained by the said Weekes, from Government having deviated from the true Spirit and Meaning of the Contract, has already, in a Suit formerly instituted by the said Weekes against the said Commissioners, been proved to amount to £.2,000 and upwards, besides Interest; and that, although the said Weekes and Downes, in their Life Time, sought Satisfaction, both at Law and in Equity, and by other Means, for the said

A Petition of the several Persons whose Hands and Names are thereunto subscribed, Voters for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts, in Behalf of themselves and other Voters in the said Borough, was delivered in at the Table and read; Setting forth, That at the last Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts, which came on the 2d Day of April last past, Eduard Cotsford, Esquire, was a Candidate, and a Poll was demanded to be taken in his Favour, he being present at the said Election; and, at the said Election, William Egerton, Esquire, and Edward Bear croft, Esquire, were also Candidates, and a Poll was also demanded to be taken in their Favour, they being also present at the said Election; and that, at the said Election, the Petitioners voted for the said Edward Cotsford, and others, Voters of the said Borough, voted for the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft; and that the said William Egcj'ton and Edward Bearcroft, by themselves or Agents, previous to and during the said Election, were guilty of gross Bribery in Vol. 40,

corrupting the Voters; that a general System of Bribery and Corruption prevailed in the said Borough, and the Voters were influenced to vote for the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft, by large Sums of Money given to them previous to the said Election, and by beneficial Promises made to them by the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft, or their Agents; and that several illegal Threats were made use of, previous to the said Election, by the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft, or their Agents, to influence Persons to vote for them, the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft, some of which Threats have been performed and carried into Execution, and several Bargains were made with many of the Voteris, previous to the said Election, by the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft, or their Agents, to vote as they directed; and that the Returning Officer was guilty of the most illegal Partiality, previous to and during the said Election, by going round and canvassing the Borough with the said William Egertbn and Edward Bearcroft, or their Agents, previous to the said Election, and by admitting Persons to vote for the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft, who had no legal Right to vote, and rejecting other Persons who had respectively a legal Right to vote, and who tendered themselves at the Poll to vote for the said Edward Cotsford; and that, by these and various other corrupt and illegal Means, a Majority of Votes was obtained, on the Face of the Poll, in Favour of the said William Egerton and Edward Bearcroft, and theywere declared duly elected, in direct and manifest Violation of the Freedom of Election, and to the Prejudice and manifest Injury of the Petitioners and others, Voters in the said Borough, their 'Franchises being materially affected and lessened thereby:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein as to the House shall meet.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

and that not only the plain and precise Terms of the said Writ and Precept, but the constant and invariable Usage of Parliament, require a Return of Members to serve in Parliament on or before the 18th Day of May, being, in this Instance, the Day on which the Parliament was summoned to meet; and that the Act of the Tenth and Eleventh of King William the Third, Chapter 7, doth positively and unequivocally require the Sheriff, or other Officer having the Execution and Return of any Writ for the Election of Members to serve in any new Parliament summoned and called, to make Return of the same on or before the Day that such Parliament shall be called to meet; and that, after the final Close of the said Poll, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon on the 17th Day of May, a Scrutiny of the said Poll was demanded on Behalf of Sir Cecil Wray, which was immediately objected to by the Petitioners, who strongly urged, that such Scrutiny could not be proceeded upon by the said Bailiff, after the Time in which by Law he was required to return the said Writ, and that when he had finally closed the said Poll, because by Law he had no Power to continue the same any longer, it would be inconsistent and absurd to grant a Scrutiny into such Poll, to commence and be proceeded upon by him after his Power to continue such Poll was terminated, yet the said Bailiff' did take upon him, contrary to the Exigency of the Writ, the positive Injunction of the said Statute, and the invariable Law and Usage of Parliament, in the most arbitrary and illegal Manner, to declare that he would grant such Scrutiny, to commence and be proceeded upon after the Day appointed for the Return of the Writs for summoning this Parliament; and that, immediately after the final Close of the Poll and casting up the Numbers, which appeared to be in Favour of Lord Hood and the Right honourable Charles James Fox, the Petitioners caused an Indenture of Return of Lord Hood and the Right honourable Charles James Fox, executed by the Petitioners, to be tendered to the said High Bailiff, but he positively refused to accept or to execute the same; and that, notwithstanding such Pretence of granting a Scrutiny, the said Bailiff* being well aware that he was bound by Law to make a Return on or before the 18th Day of May, and that it was not lawful for him on any Pretence to refuse or neglect to make a Return, did, on the said 17th Day of May, make to the Sheriff of Middlesex the Return herein after set forth; Haddington, A Petition of George Johnstone was delivered in at Ac. Election. read; Setting forth, That, at the late

Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the District of Boroughs of Haddington, Dunbar, North Berwick, Lauder, and Jedburgh, in that Part of Great Britain called ScotlandFrancis Charteris, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that, by Means of divers notorious, illegal, and corrupt Practices, committed by the said Francis Charteris, or his Agents, the said Francis Charteris was chosen a Delegate, or Commissioner, from Jedburgh, and was afterwards returned by a Majority of the Commissioners, who met at Haddington on the 26th of April last, the Member to serve in Parliament, in manifest Injury to the Petitioner, who had the Votes of Two of the Commissioners legally chosen from the said District of Boroughs, and ought to have been returned, as the said Francis Charteris had, by the said notorious, illegal and corrupt Practices, which were duly notified to the other Commissioners, rendered himself ineligible: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises under their Consideration, and grant the Petitioner such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 28th Day of September next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cases, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders lor their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken, into Consideration.

OrderedThat Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Sheppard’s Mr. Penruddocke reported from the Committee, to Shord Road, whom the Petition of several of the Trustees for executing certain Acts, passed in the Fifth Year of Queen Anne, the Eleventh of King George the First, and the Eighteenth and Twenty-ninth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing the Highways between Sheppard's Shord and The Devizes, and from Stert Stone, in the Parish of Urshfont, to Rorwd Ford, in the County of Wilts, and for changing and altering Part of the said Highways, and for repairing the Road from the Top of Red Hone to Stert Stone aforesaid, and of several Persons living near to or travelling the said Roads, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts, passed in the Fifth Year of Queen Anne, the Eleventh of King George the First, and the Eighteenth and Twenty-ninth of King George the Second, were read: And,

Mr. John Flower being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded to put the said Acts in Exe-# cution, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of

Money upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, which, together with the Tolls, have been applied according to the Directions of the said Acts — That the Roads cannot be kept in Repair, nor the Money now ow ing be repaid, unless the Terms granted by the said Acts be further continued, and the Powers thereof amended and enlarged.

That the altering and diverting the present Road between The Devizes and Sheppard's Shord, and the making a new Road to join the Turnpike Road from Sheppard's Shord to Beckhampton, will be a great Convenience to Travellers, by avoiding the several steep Hills over which the present Road passes, and of public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for completing and keeping in Repair the Highways between Sheppard's Shord and The Devizes, and from Stert Stone, in the Parish of Urshfont, to Road Ford, in the County of Wilts; and for changing and altering Part of the said Highways; and for repairing the Road from the Top of Red Hone to Stert Stone, in the said County of Wilts: And that Mr. Pem'uddockc and Mr. Goddard do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Supply Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Twenty-six thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four, including Four thousand Four hundred and Ninety-five Marine}.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committed,

That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Twenty-six thousand Men, for Thirteen Months, including Ordnance for Sea Service.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, Ways and resolve itself into a Committee of the w hole House, to Weans, consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of several of the Trustees for executing an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present, Majesty, intituled, "An Act for repairing and widening the Road from Alford to Boston, and from " thence to Cowbridge, in the County of Lincoln" and of several of the Creditors on the Tolls granted the said Act, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That considerable Progress has been made in repairing and widening the Road described in the said Act; and that the Sum of £. 8,12-5 has been borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls, which is still owing, and the Term granted by the said Act is near expiring; and that, in the Execution of the said Act, several Alterations and Amendments thereof, and further Provisions, have been found necessary, and unless the Term and Powers of the said Act are enlarged, the Money borrowed cannot be repaid, nor the Road continued to be kept in proper Repair: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes above mentioned, in such Manner, and under such Provisions, as to the House shall seehA meet

The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir James Maxwell, of Pollock, Baronet, Robert Bogle, Robert Crau* Jurd, John Maxwell, and John Craig, Proprietors of the Soap Manufactory of Glasgou\ and Copartners under the Firm of Robert Craujurd and Company, Mer* chants in Glasgow, and of James Corbet, James Dunlop, George Brown, Andrew Blackburn Colville, John Cross, Hugh Wyllie, Thomas Dunmare, Robert Dunmore, Junior, James SommemUe, Robert Craujurd, George Kip-pen, Thomas Connell, James Gemmil, John Craujurd, James Scott, and William Semple, Proprietors of the Rope Manufactory of Glasgow, and Copartners under the Firm of James Corbet and Company, Merchants in Glasgow, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; mid afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of the Parliament of Scotland, passed in the Year 1661, in the First Parliament of King Charles the Second, intituled, "An Act for erecting of Manufactories :" And also,

An Act of the said Parliament, passed in the Year 1669, *n die Second Parliament of the said King Charles the Second, intituled, "An Act concerning the Excise and Customs:" And also,

An Act of the said Parliament, passed in the Year 1681, in the Third Parliament of his said Majesty King Charles the Second, intituled, "An Act for encouraging Trade and Manufactories/’ were read; whereby it appeared, that certain Privileges and Immunities were granted, and Rules established, for encouraging and promoting Manufactories in Scotland, and, in particular, Materials useful for Manufactures were allowed to be imported for the Use of such Manufactures, free of Customs and Excise, and all other Vol. 40.

public Burthens; and that* in order to prevent all Questions and Debates concerning the said Privileges and Immunities, the Lords of the Exchequer and Privy Council in Scotland were, by certain of the said Acts, authorized to enquire and declare what Manufactories already were, or thereafter should be, duly qualified to enjoy the Benefit of the Privileges and Immunities by the said Acts granted.

Mr. James Chalmers then produced to Your Committee a Certificate from the Deputy King’s Remembrancer in the Court of Exchequer in Scotland, and an Extract of an Act of the Privy Council of Scotland, of the 7th May 1696; by which it appeared, that under the Encouragements held forth by the said Acts of Parliament, Two Manufactories were erected in Glasgow, the one in the Year 1674 for making of Soap* and the other in the Year 1696 for the making of Ropes and Cordage, the Proprietors of each of which Manufactories obtained from the Exchequer and Privy Council of Scotland an Order, or Act, declaring their respective Works to be duly qualified in Terms of the Statutes in that Behalf: And the said Witness being examined, said, That the said Manufactories so established and approved have been continually carried on since the respective Times of their Erection, and do now by Course of regular Successions and Conveyances belong respectively to the several Persons who have signed the said Petition.

The Sixth Article of the Treaty of Union, settled and agreed upon in the Fifth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, between the Two Kingdoms of England and Scotland, was then read; whereby it appeared, that Provision is made that all Parts of the United Kingdom, for ever from and after the Union, shall have the same Allowances, Encouragements, and Drawbacks, and be under the same Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Duties on Import and Export; and that the Allowances, Encouragements, and Drawbacks, Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Regulations of Trade, and the Customs, Duties on Import and Export, settled in England when the Union should commence/ should, from and after the Union, take place throughout the whole Kingdom, excepting and reserving the Duties upon Export and Import of such particular Commodities from which any Persons, the Subjects of either Kingdom, were specially liberated and exempted by their private Rights, which, after the Union, were to remain safe and entire to them in all respects as before the same.

A Member present then informed Your Committee, That, upon the Commencement of the said Union, Doubts and Disputes arose between the Officers of the Customs and the Proprietors of the said Soap and Rope Works, who claimed the Privilege of importing Materials for their respective Manufactories free of Duties, as a private Right constituted by the Acts of Parliament and Acts of Privy Council before mentioned, and as such saved by the Exception in Favour of private Rights, contained in the aforesaid Sixth Article of the said Treaty of Union; to which Claim the Officers of the Revenue objected, that the Exemption from Duties, given by the Acts of Parliament and Privy Council of Scotland, was not in the Nature of a private Right, but of a public Encouragement to Trade, and as such was determined and at an End by thq Treaty of Union — That, in consequence of these Disputes, it was agreed, as a temporary Expedient, that the Proprietors of the aforesaid Manufactories should give Bonds for the Duties of the Materials to be imported by them, with Condition to pay the same, in case the Parliament of Great Britain, or Court of Exchequer in Scotland, should adjudge the said Materials liable to the Payment of Duties; which Agreement for taking such conditional Bonds, as aforesaid, was for some Thne carried into Execution, until the Commissioners of the Customs at Edinburgh gave Orders

R for

62 2°.?

for levying the Duties upon all such Materials imported for the Use of the said Manufactories, as were by Law chargeable with Duties upon being imported for other Purposes; whereupon the Proprietors of the said Manufactories paid the Duties accordingly, but under Protest that the Right of Exemption claimed by them should not thereby be hurt, nor themselves precluded from reclaiming such Duties as already had been or afterwards should be paid by them; and for bringing the Right of Exemption so claimed by them, the Proprietors of the said Rope Work, did some Time since cause an Action to be instituted in the Court of Exchequer at Edinburgh, at the Suit of the said James Corbet, One of the said Proprietors, and Assignee of the rest of those Proprietors, against Edward Burrow, Collector of the Customs at the Port of Port Glasgow, and John Clerk, then the Deputy of the said Edward Burrow, at the Member Port of Greenock, for that they had against Right refused to repay Duties levied by them on certain Materials imported for the Use of the said Rope Work — That in the Course of the Proceedings in the said Action, a special Verdict was agreed upon and settled by the Parties, and returned by a Jury, upon which Verdict Counsel were heard by the Lord Chief Baron and other Three Barons of the said Court; and the Judges having been equally divided in their Opinion, the Question remains hitherto undetermined; since the Time of which Hearing, certain Propositions have been offered by the Petitioners, the Proprietors of the said Works, for accommodating the Matter in Dispute.

That it has been alledged by the Officers of the Revenue, that the Claim of Exemption made by the Petitioners, the Proprietors of the said Manufactories, would, on the one Hand, if established, be very prer judicial to the public Interest, being capable to be exercised in an unlimited Extent with respect to the Commodities, which are the Subject thereof, to the great Diminution of the Revenue, and the Breach of Siat Equality in Trade which ought to take place in all Parts of the United Kingdom; while, on the other Hand, the Petitioners, by means of the aforesaid Treaty of Union, and the Doubts and Disputes thereupon arising in relation to the Right of Exemption claimed as aforesaid, as well as by reason of the Proceedings consequent upon such Doubts and Disputes, and in firm Reliance upon the public Faith of the Kingdom, laid out and employed a considerable Sum of Money towards carrying on the said Works, have suffered considerable Loss and Inconveniency, the Exemption from the Payment of Duties enjoyed by them, under the Acts of Parliament of Scotland, having by the aforesaid Means been abridged or interrupted, and much Expence incurred by Law Suits and otherwise.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report

Shafton A Petition of Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, and

Election. William Richard Rumbold, Esquire, was read; Setting forth, That at the late Election for Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Shafton, otherwise Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset, the Petitioners, Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, and, William Richard Rumbold, Esquire, and Hans Wintrop Mortimer and Adam Drummond, Esquires, were Candidates; and that the said Hans Wintrop Mortimer and Adam Drummond, by themselves and their Agents, previous to and during the Course of the said Election, were guilty of many gross and notorious Acts of Bribery and Corruption, whereby many of the Electors were influenced to give their Votes in Favour of the said Hans Wintrop Mortimer and Adam Drummond, and, by such unlawful Means, and divers other corrupt and unwarrantable Practices of the said Hans Wintrop Mortimer and Adam Drummond, their Agents and Abettors, they have procured themselves to be returned to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioners, and in Violation of the Rights of the said Borough; and that Persons were admitted to vote at the said Election for the said Hans Wintrop Mortimer and Adam Drummond, who were not duly qualified to vote at the said Election, and several good Votes, who tendered themselves as such, and offered to vote for the Petitioners, were rejected by the Returning Officer; and the Petitioners conceive, a great Majority of the legal and uncorrupted Voters at the said Election polled for the Petitioners, and that they ought to have been returned: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 30th Day of September next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of the several Persons, resident in the Exporting Cities of London and Westminster, in the Borough of Pare Skins, Southwark, and Parts adjacent, employed in the making and vending Beaver Hats, and Hats mixed with Beaver, Hare Wool, Coney Wool, Goats Wool, and other Materials, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others concerned in the said Manufacture in Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Hat Manufactory of this Kingdom is a very considerable Branch of Trade, in which several Thousand British Subjects are employed; and that Hare Wool and Coney Wool, the Growth of this Kingdom. are better in Quality than any other, and, as those are the staple Articles of the said Manufactory,

English Hats have acquired such Reputation, that great Quantities of them are exported to Foreign Parts; and that, in Addition to the Produce of this Country, great Quantities of Hare Wool and Coney Wool have been usually imported from Ireland, Flanders, Russia, and Germany, but, for some Time past, very little of the said Articles have been imported from any of those Parts, owing, as the Petitioners apprehend, to their being detained for the Supply of Foreign Manufactures; and that Goats Hair, or Turkey Goats Wool, is an Article much used in the said Manufactory, and pays a Duty of about Six Pence per Pound on Importation, though Foreigners, who buy at the same Market as the English, receive it, as the Petitioners believe, free of Duty, and as there is a Drawback, on its being exported, of Four Pence per Pound, our Rivals can have it cheaper, even from this Kingdom, than the British Manufacturer; and that, owing to their superior Excellence, considerable Quantities of British Hare Wool and Coney Wool and Skins have lately been exported to France, Flanders, and other Foreign Parts, for the Support of Foreign Manufactures, and to the great Injury of our own; and that there is at present a great Scarcity of those necessary Materials, and, if the Practice of exporting them to Foreign Countries is not by some Means prevented, the British Hat Manufactory will be rendered of little Consequence, and many Families thereby left unprovided for; and that the Public Revenue is materially injured by the Frauds constantly practised by Foreigners, and others, in dressing British Hare Skins and British Coney Skins, so as to evade the Duties intended to be imposed thereon by the different Acts of Parliament now in Force for that Purpose, and the Petitioners conceive that the only Method of remedying those Mischiefs, and preserving the said Manufactory, would be, by laying an additional Duty on the Exportation of all undressed Hare Skins and Hare Wool, and Coney Skins and Coney Hair or Wool, from this Kingdom, or by prohibiting the Exportation thereof, and by allowing the Importation of Goats Hair or Goats Wool Duty-free; and that some further and other Regulations be established for the collecting of the Duty imposed upon such of the said Skins as are tawed or dressed: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House, shall seem meet.

Turkey A Petition of the Governor and Company of Mer-

Company. chants of England, trading into The Levant Seas, being

offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protect His Majesty’s Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been tbund necessary that an Ambassador should be sent from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in the other Parts of Turkey where British Subjects reside, and w here the English Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence w hereof has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with many other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on this Trade, has of late Years amounted to about £9,000 per Annum; and that the Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishing, is now, from many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance, granted to the Petitioners by Parliament, enabled them to support their Expences during the past Year, but the Petitioners are sensible they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not, in the present Situation of the Trade, declare their Inability to support their necessary Expences, unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary ana proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

plate Glass A Petition of the Governor and Company of British Manufacture. Cast piate Glass Manufacturers being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, from their first Institution, by an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty’s lleign, intituled, "An Act to incorporate i€ certain Persons therein named, and their Successors, with proper Powers for the Purpose of estaWishing One or more Glass Manufactories within " the Kingdom of Great Britain, and for the effectually supporting and conducting the same upon " an improved Plan, in a peculiar Manner calculated " for the Casting of large Plate Glass," they have, with unremitting Attention, endeavoured to forward a Work, which Parliament, by its Sanction, meant to countenance, as an Object of public and national Concern; the Result has been a real Performance of what was held up as a Plea to warrant the Privileges Vol. 40.

granted by Parliament to the said Company, who have brought the Manufactory to such a Degree of Perfection as already td stand forth a Rival, and to become an Object of Envy to the French Nation in that Branch of Manufacture, which in France has been upheld for more than a Century by peculiar Indulgences of Monopoly in the Trade, and Total Exemption from Duties; and representing to the House, that the Petitioners have expended in the Progress of their Works upwards of £ 100,000, without receiving the smallest Dividend, owing to a Variety of Circumstances to which an Infant Manufactory, upon an entire new Plan, must naturally be liable; and, amongst other Hardships, they have found the Duties payable to Government very oppressive, from the Mode in which they are collected, and the peculiar Manner in which Glass is made by Casting, differing much from all other British Manufactories wherein the Glass is made by Blowing, and on which the Duties fall much lighter, although the Quantum of the Duty charged by Law on the Materials is the same, and this appears to be owing to a Waste of Metal through the whole Process of the Casting Work, exceeding in Quantity more than double the Waste of the Blowing Work, whereas the Allowance for Waste (being One Fourth Part of the whole Quantity of clean Metal in the Pot) is equal to both, and therefore it compensates for the Loss by Waste, in a Manner much more advantageous to the Blowing than it does to the Casting Glass Manufactory, and the Petitioners can prove that they have paid Duties upon an extra Waste of Metal not known in the Blowing Glass Manufactories, to the Amount of £6,000, and upwards; and that, from some Error in the Mode of Gauging the Pots, the Petitioners have actually paid Duty for more Glass Metal than was ever melted by them, to the Amount of £2,000, and upwards, making in the Whole a Sum of £ 8,000, and upwards, which, they apprehend, has been a Charge upon their Manufactory beyond the equitable Intention of the Law, and is a singular Excess beyond the Duties collected upon all other Plate Glass Manufactories in this Kingdom; and that, from such heavy Burthens upon the Produce of the Manu-r factory, they find themselves unable to continue their . Endeavours to support it without some Relief shall be given by Parliament, as there appears 1o be a considerable Annual Loss, upon an Average Balance stated for some Years past, which must soon destroy the Company, unless by such Relief their Income can be increased: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and further enforce, the said Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, to enlarge the Company’s Capital Stock, and to give such further Relief, in regard to the Payment of Duties, as may repair the Losses already sustained by the Company, and prevent the like in future, by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Herbert Maclavorlh, Sir William Dolben, &c.: And they are to meet To-morrowr Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records; and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day for the House Prevention of to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, Smuggling, to consider of the Laws made to prevent the clandestine Importation and Running of prohibited Goods, and Goods liable to the Payment of Duties, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Flection. of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Church of Saint Peters, Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is informed that a Petition has been presented to the House, from certain Electors of the City of Westminster, complaining of the Conduct of the Petitioner, and that the said Electors are to be heard by Counsel at the Bar of this House: And therefore praying, That he may be permitted to be heard by Counsel against the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petitioner be permitted to be heard by his Counsel* at the Bar of this House, against the Allegations contained in the said Petition of the Electors of the City of Westminster.;

Ditto. A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are

thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, Electors of the City and Liberty of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in pursuance of Proclamation, made on the 26th Day of March last, for the Election of Two Citizens to serve in the then ensuing Parliament for the said City and Liberty, Thomas Corbett, Esquire, Bailiff* of the said City and Liberty, did, on the 1st Day of April last,. proceed in such Election, when Sir Samuel Hood, Baronet, Lord Hood of the Kingdom of Ireland, the Right honourable Charles James Fox, and Sir Cecil Wray, Baronet, were proposed as Candidates; and that the Poll continued until the 17th Day of May last, when the same w as closed, and the Numbers, as they then stood on the Poll, appeared to be, for Lord Hood, 6,694; for Mr. Fox, 6,234; and for Sir Cecil Wray, 5,998; and that the said Sir Cecil Wray, one of the said Candidates, and several of the Electors, signed a Requisition to the said Thomas Corbett, demanding a Scrutiny of the Votes that had been polled at that Election, which the said Bailiff*

(after hearing what was alledged by the said Charles James Fox and his Counsel, and also by Sir Cecil Wray and his Counsel, and also Counsel for the said Electors who had signed such Requisition) granted accordingly, and appointed the 28th Day of May for proceeding the rein; and that the Petitioners are well assured, that no true and decisive Judgment can be formed as to the Majority of legal Votes in Favour of any Two of the said Candidates, without such an Investigation as could not be entered into during the Course of the Poll; and that the Petitioners are informed, that Proceedings are carrying on in this House for the Purpose of requiring the said Bailiff to make a Return of Members as the Numbers stood at the Close of the Poll, which, they conceive, would be highly injurious to their Rights and Franchises:

And therefore praying, That, the Premises being taken into Consideration, the House will permit the said Bailiff to proceed in the said Scrutiny, and that the House will grant such further or other Relief as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration at the same Time that the Petition of the Right honourable Charles James Fox, relating to the late Election for the City of Westminster, and to the Return or Answer of the Bailiff of the said City to the Precept of the Sheriff of Middlesex, is taken into further Consideration.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House Ways and to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, Means, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The Counsel were directed to withdraw.

A PETITION of George Bishop, Proprietor of Bishop's the Maidstone Geneva Manufactory, was pre- Geneva, sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, by a considerable Residence in Holland, and great Attention to the Method of making Spirits there, which are known by the Name of Geneva, made himself Master of the Art and Mystery of preparing the same; and that the Spirit so manufactured in the United Provinces was always allowed to be far superior in Quality to the same Kind of Spirit made in any other Country, until the Petitioner, after repeated Experiments, and a very great Expence in providing and constructing the necessary Buildings and Implements, established his said Manufactory at Maidstone, where he has, till lately, made Spirits fully equal in Flavour, Strength and Purity, to the best made in Foreign Countries, insomuch that it is very difficult, if not impossible, to distinguish the same from the best Holland's Geneva; and that, in order to make the Spirit he manufactures, the Nature of his Process requires a much larger Proportion of Wash to a given Quantity of Geneva than by a lately made Law is permitted, for which Reason the Petitioner applied to the House in the last Parliament, to be exempted from the Provision of an Act, intituled, "An Act for repealing the Duties payable on Chocolate made " in Great Britain, and for granting certain Inland cc Duties upon Cocoa Nuts in lieu thereof; for the " better and more effectual securing the Revenue " of Excise, and of the Inland Duties under the Ma*

" nagement of the Commissioners of Excise, and for " preventing Frauds therein; for the more punctual " and ready Payment of the Allowances to be made " to Brewers out of the additional Duties imposed on " Malt; and for rectifying a Mistake in an Act made " in this present Session of Parliament, with respect to " the exempting of Candles from the additional Duty " of £. 5 per Centum upon the Duties of Excise imposed by the said Act;" and that the Petitioner, not succeeding in his Application, and being most grievously injured in his Property, and embarrassed in his Trade? by the Provisions of the said Act, hath ever since used his utmost Skiff and Diligence to discover some Mode of Working, by which he might make Spirits as good as those he used to do, conformably to the Provisions and Restrictions of the said Act, but ‘ without Success; and therefore the Petitioner hopes, if some Relief was to be granted him respecting the Method of charging and collecting the Excise Duty on the Spirit he manufactures, he may be enabled to carry on his Trade as well as he did before the passing of the said Act, by w'hich the Revenue would be very materially benefited, and the smuggling of Holland's Geneva into this Country in some Degree prevented:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant him such Relief as the singular Hardship of his Case may be found to merit, and as to the House shall seem meet and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

N. B. The Sum of £. 3,000, voted in 1783 for building a Chapel at the new Barracks at Woolwich, was not applied to that Service, but entered in the foregoing List as a Saving, upon a Supposition that the Purchase of the House, late Sir Gregory Page's, at Blackheath, would have taken Place; in which Case the present Academy would have been converted into a Chapel. This Purchase not taking Effect, it becomes necessary to carry into Execution the building of a Chapel according to the former Vote of Parliament.

A Petition of Robert Barlow, Esquire, John Tun-nard, Thomas Turmard, and Richas'd Yerburgh, Gentlemen, Owners and Proprietors of Lands and Grounds in the Parish of Frampton, in the County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are within the said Parish several Open Fields, Parcels of Common, Fen, and Waste Grounds, whereon the Petitioners are entitled to Right of Common, and also certain Plots of Land called the Reaches, Marsh, and Holmes s, in and near to the said Parish, which contain in the Whole, by Estimation, about 1,500 Acres; and that the Lands lie dispersed and intermixed with each other in small Parcels, and are in general so inconveniently situated as to render the Cultivation thereof difficult and expensive, and, in their present Situation, are incapable of much Improvement; and that it would be for the mutual Advantage and Convenience of the Owners and Proprietors of Lands within the said Parish, and tend greatly to the Improvement of their respective Estates, if a general Division and Inclosure could be had of the said Open Fields, Parcels of Common, Fen, and other the Commonable Lands and Waste Grounds, and the said Plots of Land, within and near to the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Open Fields, Parcels of Common, Fen, and other Commonable Lands and Waste Grounds within the said Parish of Frampton, and also the said Plots of Land called the Reaches, Marsh, and Holmes s, in and near to the said Parish, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir John Thorold and Mr. Anderson Pelham do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Combing Wool, Worsted Yam, and Goods made from Worsted, in the County of Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Yams spun in the said County have greatly declined in their Value, occasioned principally by the fraudulent Reeling thereof; and that, in consequence of the Preference given to the Yarns of other Counties, where a Regulation, under £he Sanction of an Act of Parliament, has taken Place (unless the Petitioners are authorized to make such Regulations) it is to be feared their Trade will greatly decline, and with it the Employment and Sup^ pprt of the Poor in the said County; and that, by an Act, made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for the more effectual preventing of Frauds and Abuses committed by Persons employed in the Manufacture of Hats, and in the Woollen, Linen, Fustian, Cotton, Iron, Leather, Fur, llemp, Flax, Mohair, and Silk Manufactures, and for preventing unlawful Combinations of Journeymen Dyers and Journeymen Hotpressers, and of all Persons employed in the said several Manufactures, and for the better Payment of their Wages; and, by Two other Acts, made in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Penalties

'unit. . 1784.

and Punishments are inflicted upon all Persons who shall reel false or short Yarn, and on Persons embezzling Materials used in the said Manufactures; and that the gpod Purposes of the said Laws have been greatly frustrated, from the Petitioners being unwilling to expose themselves singly to the Loss attending the Resentment of the Spinners and Work People, by prosecuting them for Offences against the said Acts; and that this important Branch of the Woollen Manufactory of the said County will be greatly prejudiced thereby, unless the Petitioners are enabled jointly to carry those Laws into effectual Execution, which cannot be done without the Aid of Parliament; and that, by an Act made in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the more effectual preventing Frauds and Abuses committed by Persons employed in the Manufactures of Combing Wool,

Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the Counties of York, Lancaster, and Chester, certain Powers were given for the Appointment of a Committee of the Manufacturers of the said Counties, with Power to nominate proper Persons to be Inspectors for the Purposes therein mentioned, and also, to have the Direction of all Prosecutions of Offenders against that and the aforementioned Acts, and also the Management of the Fund therein created, and to do such other Matters and Things for carrying the said Act into Execution, as they should think best for the Interest and Advantage of all the said Manufacturers, by which the Yarns of the said Counties have been greatly improved: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, with similar Powers to the aforesaid Act, and for such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House may seem meet, and the Necessity of the Case requires.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir John Rous and Mr. Grigby do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Right honourable Ralph Earl of Verney, in the Kingdom of Ireland, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Wendover, in the County of Buckingham, Robert Burton, Esquire, John Ord, Esquire, William Jolliffe, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that the said Robert Burton and John Ord, after the Dissolution of the last Parliament, and the issuing of the Writ for the Election, and previous to, and during the Poll, by themselves and their Agents; and by other Ways and Means, on the Behalf and at the Charge of the said Robert Burton and John Ord, did give, present, and allow to the Electors of the said Borough, and to several Persons who had, or claimed to have, a Right to vote in the Election for the said Borough, Meat, Drink, Reward, Entertain* ment, and Provision, in order to procure themselves to be elected for the said Borough, and the said Robert Burton and John Ord were guilty of Bribery and Corruption, and attempting to bribe and corrupt those who had a Right to vote in the said Election, in order to procure themselves to be returned as duly elected; and that, by the said and other indirect Means, the said Robert Burton and John Ord obtained a Majority on the Poll, and were returned accordingly, in Prejudice of the Petitioner and the Electors of the said Borough, and in open Defiance of the Law and Freedom of Elections: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief therein, as shall, upon Examination, appear to be just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 14th Day of October next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 31th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cases, were sent to the several Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Times on which the said several Petitions were ordered to be taken into Consideration.

A Petition of Captain William Brereton, late Lieutenant Governor of the City of Cavite, and Commander of His Majesty’s Ships stationed at The Philippine Islands, being offered to be presented to the House; ,

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the , House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That an Expedition having been concerted against the Spanish Settlements in The Phillip-pine Islands, the same was undertaken by Troops composed of His Majesty’s 79th Regiment of Foot; and Europeans and Sepoys in the Service of the East India Company, who were transported to the Island of Luconia in His Majesty's Squadron commanded by Vice Admiral Cornish, assisted by some Ships belonging to the Lidia Company, and, on the 6th of October 1762, the City of Manila was taken by Storm, and the City of Cavite surrendered without an Attack; and that the City of Manila, on the 2d of November following, was delivered up to certain Agents authorized by the East India Company to receive the same, in Conformity to the Directions given by His Majesty to General Draper, who commanded the Land Forces employed upon the Expedition; and that His Majesty, anxious to preserve the said Conquest, gave Directions to His Admirals and Generals to be assisting to the Officers of the East India Company in holding Possession thereof, until His Royal Will and Pleasure should be further signified with regard to the future

o

Dispdsition of the said Conquest, which was to depend entirely and absolutely upon His Majesty; and, the India Company not having sent more Officers and Servants upon the Expedition than were necessary to take Charge of the City of Manila, and it being judged of great Importance that a Sea Officer should command at Cavite (where the Naval Arsenals and Storehouses were situate) Captain Kcmpenjdt was appointed Governor of the City and District of Cavite; and that Admiral Cornish, thinking it proper to scud Captain Kempenfclt to England with his Dispatches, appointed the Petitioner to succeed him in the Government of Cavite, and the Petitioners Commission, under the Admirals Hand and Seal, bears Date the 14th of November and he actually entered upon

the Charge of Lieutenant Governor accordingly by virtue of the said Commission; and that Admiral Cornish having nearly repaired his Squadron by the Beginning of February 1763, and being about to depart from Manila, the India Company’s Deputy Governor, on the 3d of that Month, represented to Admiral Cornish that he had not the faintest Hope of preserving the Conquest with so small a Garrison, unless he would leave a Naval Force for their Protection; and, in Consequence of the said Representation, Admiral Cornish left the Petitioner Commander in Chief of the King’s and Company’s Naval Forces, and he continued in the Government of Cavite; and that, during the Siege of Manila, the Spanish Governor dispatched a Lieutenant General into the Field to levy Forces, and to defend the Provinces in case Manila should fall into the Hands of the English, which Event taking Place the 6th of October, the War was still carried on; and that the Resources of the Spaniards in The PhiUippine Islands were infinite, and the Treasure brought from Nczv Spain in the Philippino Galleon falling into the Spanish General’s Hands, he soon levied a powerful Army, with which he surrounded Manila, and cut off all Supplies of Provisions from the Garrison, and made it dangerous for any Person to go without the Walls; and that the Representation made by the Deputy Governor of Manila to Admiral Cornish was manifested soon after his Departure with the Squadron, as the Spaniards appeared in Arms in great Multitudes in all Parts, and the Petitioner foresaw there was no Prospect of maintaining the Conquest, unless Means were found to detach the principal Inhabitants and Natives of the District of Cavitt from the Views and Interest of the Spaniards in Arms; the Petitioner therefore deemed it absolutely , necessary to keep a Public Table at Cavite, and entertain them liberally, in order to conciliate their Minds, which put him to a heavy Expence, but it had the desired Effect, as through their Influence the Petitioner was enabled to procure Provisions for the Crews of His Majesty’s Ships and the Garrisons of Manila and Caviti, which otherwise must have been abandoned; and that, in the Month of March 1764, the Petitioner received a Warrant under the King’s Sign Manual, for restoring the Conquest to the Spaniards, and in negotiating that Business the Petitioner was put to a very considerable Expence in entertaining the Spanish Governor and his Commissioners, and doing the National Honours upon that Occasion; and that when the Petitioner received the Orders for evacuating the Conquest, he had no more than Four Ships with

him

Supply.

34 Geo. III.

f Junii.

him to carry away the Troops that had been brought to Manila in Fifteen, which obliged him to fit up Two old Spanish Ships to serve as Transports, which enabled him to embark all the Troops, and to push thefm on to the Company’s Setdements in Lidia, where the Company were involved in fresh Troubles with the Country Powers; and that the Ships under the Petitioner's Command being mostly old and rotten, and badly supplied with Provisions, and the Troops and Seamen being very sickly, he was driven into the Port of Bataviain great Distress; ar)d that the Petitioner resided on Shore Six Months at Batavia, at a great Expence, in Hopes of being able to repair His Majesty’s Ship Falmouth, of which Ship the Petitioner was Commander, but, upon repeated Surveys held upon her, it was found utterly impracticable to repair her, and she was obliged to be left there, and die Petitioner, having procured other Ships to carry the Troops to Madras, and disposed of the Falmouth's Crew, he was under the Necessity of taking a Passage to Europe for himself, some of his Petty Officers, and Servants, in a Dutch East Indiaman, which was attended with great Expence and Inconvenience; and that the Petitioner also incurred very heavy Expences by the Loss of Exchange on Money taken up at Batavia for the Use of His Majesty’s Sick Seamen and Troops employed upon the Expedition, and for Costs and Damages of a Suit at Law brought against him for Matters that were indispensably necessary in carrying on His Majesty's Service, and several other Expences were incurred by the Petitioner during the Course of his Command in The Philippine Islands; and that the Petitioner has not yet received any Compensation for his said Disbursements, but, on the contrary, has been at very considerable Expence in prosecuting several Memorials, particularly to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, who are of Opinion he cannot be relieved but by the Justice and Wisdom of the Legislature: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and indemnify him for his said Expences and Disbursements, the detaining of which, for so great a Length of Time, has been attended with great Injury to his private Fortune, acquired by a long and faithful Service to his King and Country.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Adam, the Master of the Rolls, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the w hole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of One Million be granted to His Majesty, for paying off and discharging the Exchequer Bills made out by virtue of an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for raising a certain Sum of Money, by Loans " or Exchequer Bills, for the Service of the Year One " thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-three," and charged upon the first Aids to be granted in the then next Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of One Million Five hundred thousand # Pounds be granted to His Majesty, for paying off and discharging the Exchequer Bills made out by virtue of an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for raising a further Sum of Money, by Loans or " Exchequer Bills, for the Service of the Year One thou-u sand Seven hundred and Eighty-three," and charged upon the first Aids to be granted in the then next Session of Parliament.

A Petition of the Persons w'hose Names are there- Honiton unto subscribed, Electors of Members to serve in Par- Electio11* liament for the Borough of Honiton, in the County of Devon, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, at the last General Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Honiton, Sir George Yonge, Baronet, Sir George Collier, and John Bailey, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the said George Yonge and Sir George Collier, by themselves and Agents, were guilty of gross Bribery and Corruption, by giving and promising the Voters of the said Borough, Money, and other Rewards for their Votes, and thereby corrupted and influenced the said Voters, and the said Sir George Collier, previous to the Election, deposited Money in the Hands of his Agents for the Purpose of procuring Votes, and which was applied for that Purpose, by which Means he corrupted and influenced the Voters; and that the said Sir George Yonge and Sir George Collier, and their Agents, after the Teste of the Writ, and before the Close of the Poll, treated the Voters with Meat and Drink, and thereby, influenced their Voices; and, by the undue Influence the said Sir George Yonge and Sir George Collier had over the Returning Officer, many unqualified Persons were brought to vote, whose Votes were actually received, notwithstanding Remonstrances were made to the contrary; and that, by such and other Means of undue Influence, the said Sir George Yonge and Sir George Collier procured themselves to be returned Members for the said Borough, although the said Mr. Bailey had a Majority of legal Votes, in direct Opposition to the Rights of Election, and the Injury of the Petitioners Rights and Franchises: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday, the 19th Day of October next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.
