Mr. Gascoyne, Junior, reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition and Representation of Sir Ashton Lexer, Knight, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition and Representation; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition and Representation, Mr. Thomas Waring being examined, said, That he had been Manager and Superintendant of the Collection of Natural and Artificial Curiosities belonging to Sir Ashton Lever, ever since it was brought to London, in the Year 1775 — That Sir Ashton Lever had been diligently employed for Twelve Years before that Time, in forming his Collection — That it consists of Natural Curiosities and Productions of Art, and that the various Specimens and Articles are in Number upwards of 26,000, which have been selected from more than 150,000, that have been in Sir Ashton Lexer's own Possession, exclusive of a great Number procured from Foreign Cabinets — That his Collection is the most extensive and valuable of any in England, and contains many Articles not to be found in any other — That according to his Judgment Sir Ashton Lever must have expended at least £. 40,000 in making his Collection, and that it may probably have cost him near £. 50,000 — That Sir Ashton has from Time to Time received considerable Presents of curious Things, but that the preparing those Articles for public Inspection has put him to a considerable Expence — That if the Collection shall be kept in a Place proper for its Reception, and due Care and Attention be given to it, the Articles may be preserved for Ages in their present beautiful and perfect State; and that the Expence of keeping it at Leicester House, where it now is, amounts Annually to about £. 1,200, of which £.660 is paid for House Rent and Taxes. — And being asked, How the Public are admitted to the sight of the Collection? he said, On paying a certain Sum for each Persons Admission; and that the Money collected by those Means has amounted, from the Opening of it in February 1775 to February 1784, to about the Gross Sum of £. 13,500. — And the Witnesss added,

'unit. A. 1784.

That, in his Opinion, it would be a great Loss to Sir Ashton Leoer, if he were to dispose of his Collection by the common Way of Sale.

Mr. Waring being desired to explain his Estimate of the Expence Sir Ashton Lever had been at in collecting and supporting his Museum? said. That he formed it from his Knowledge of what Money Sir Ashton has received, and what he owes, and what the Witness has Reason to suppose he has expended in his Family, together with the Witness’s Knowledge of the Expence of some of the Articles, which corroborates his Opinion. Then,

Mr, Thomas Tenant was examined, who said, That he had been upwards of Twenty Years a Collector of Subjects of Natural History, and had seen all the Cabinets of Curiosities, both public and private ones, of any Note, in Holland, France, and Portugal, and those at Brussels, Dresden, Brunswick, and Vienna, and had also seen the Spanish Cabinet while collecting in Holland — That he had never seen any Collection more rare, more curious, or more instructive, than Sir Ashton. Lexer's, nor any that can be compared with it — That it exceeds all others in the Beauty and Preservation of the numerous Articles it contains, which are better selected than any he had seen elsewhere. — And being asked, Whether he had heard of any Commissions to purchase any of the Articles in Sir Ashton Lever's Collection? he said, That an Idea being entertained Abroad, that the Collection is to be sold, he had Commissions to buy a great Number of the Articles for Private Cabinets. — And being further examined, he said, That in his Opinion this Collection is of such Value and Rarity, as to be an Object of National Attention, and worth being purchased by the Public. — And he concluded with saying, that if a Sovereign Prince was to endeavour at forming such a Collection, it could not be done in less than Twenty Years, nor ever be made so extensive and complete, there being many Specimens in this that could not be procured at any Expence; and he thinks it would be attended with great Loss to dispose of this Collection by the common Way of Sale, it being of greater Value, as it now is, than it would be if separated.

Mr. John Church being then called, informed your Committee, That he had amused himself many Years in collecting Natural Curiosities; that he had seen all the Collections of any Note in England, and that the W’hole of them put together would not form one so rare and valuable as that at Leicester House — That the Articles there are in complete Beauty and Preservation — That he had taken great Pains to form an Estimate of their Value, ascertained by the Prices he had known similar Articles sell for at public Sales, or otherwise; and that, according to his Calculation, the Value of the Whole to be sold is upwards of £.53,000, in which Valuation he includes the Cases and other Matters connected with the Articles as now exhibited — That he does not believe such another Collection could be made in a Man’s Life, and many of the Articles are so rare they could not be procured at all; and that if the same proper Care be continued to be taken of the Collection as is now, he thinks the Articles in it would preserve their Beauty for Ages. — And the Witness added, That, in his Opinion, Sir Ashton Lever & Collection is well worthy the Attention of the Public, to save it from being dispersed again, by the present Possessor’s being obliged, or being induced, to part with it to Individuals, which would be a Discredit to this Country; and that it would be a great Loss to Sir Ashton Leva' to separate the Articles, in disposing of them by the common Way of Sale.

Your Committee also examined Sir William Hamilton, Knight of the most honourable Order of the Bath, who said, That he had seen Sir Ashton Levers Collection of Curiosities very often; and having a particular Love for Natura} History, he has had an Opportunity, in

A Petition of the Guardians of the Standard of Sheffield Wrought Plate within the Town of Shffield, assembled at their last Annual Meeting, appointed by an Act of Parliament, passed in the 13th Year of the Reign of His Majesty King George the Third, intituled,

" An Act for appointing Wardens and Assay Masters " for assaying Wrought Plate in the Towns of Shesfeld and Bh'jningham," and of the principal Manufacturers of Wrought Plate, and of Silver Plated Goods, within the Town of Sheffield aforesaid, and its Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and read'; Setting forth, That by the said Act it is enacted, that it shall be lawful for the Assayer, or such other Person as the Wardens for the Time being shall appoint, to ask, demand, take, and receive, of and from all such Person and Persons as shall, from Time to Time, bring to the Assay Office any Piece of Wrought Plate to be assayed, tried, and marked, such Prices, Sums of Money, or Rewards, as they shall > think fit, so as the same do not exceed the Sum of One Shilling for every Pound Troy, and proportionably for every greater or lesser Quantity of Plate so assayed and marked, which Prices, Sums of Money, or Rewards, allowed to be taken for assaying Wrought Plate, are inadequate to defraying the necessary Expences of the said Assay Office; and that it is also by the said Act enacted, that if any Working Silversmith or Dealer in Wrought Plate, or any other Metal plated or covered with Silver, shall strike, or cause to be struck, any Letter or Letters upon any Vessel or other Thing made of Metal plated or covered with Silver, or upon any Metal Vessel or other Thing made to look like Silver, such Persons so offending shall forfeit the Sum of £.100; and that, upon the wording of the said Clause, Doubts have arisen whether the Manufacturers of Goods plated with Silver (without being liable to the said Penalty) can or may strike their Names upon such Goods, and, in Consequence of such Doubts, several of the Petitioners, and other Manufacturers of plated Goods, have been deterred, since the passing of the said Act, from striking their Names upon plated Goods, whereby a proper Distinction betwixt the best and worst plated Goods is prevented, and all Emulation in that Branch of Business is done away, to the certain and manifest Prejudice thereof:

And therefore praying such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

The said Copy is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said Translation is as followeth; viz.

TREATY of Peace between His Majesty the King of Great Britain and their High Mightinesses the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries.

In the Name of the most Holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. So be it

Be it known to all those whom it shall or may in any Manner concern. The most Serene and most Potent Prince and Lord George the Third by the Grace of God, King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick and Lunenburgh, Arch-Treasurer and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, Sgcf, and the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, having laid the Foundation of Peace by the Preliminary Articles, signed at Paris the 2d of September last, and His said Majesty and the said States General being desirous to complete so great and salutary a Work, have named and authorized, to wit, on the Part of His Britannic Majesty, Daniel Hailes, Esquire, His said Majesty’s Minister Plenipotentiary to his Most Christian Majesty; and on the Part of their High Mightinesses the said States General, the most Noble and most Excellent Lords Mathew Lestevenon, Lord of Berkerrroode and Strycn, Deputy to the Assembly of the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries from the Province of Holland\ and their Ambassador in Ordinary to his Majesty the Most Christian King; and Gerard Brantsen, Burgomaster and Senator of the City of Arnhem^ Councillor and Grand Master of the Mint of the Republic, Deputy to the States General of the United Provinces, and their Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to his Most Christian Majesty: Who, after having duly communicated to each other their full Powers, in good Form, have agreed upon the following Articles.

Article 1.

There shall be a Christian, universal, and perpetual Peace, as well by Sea as by Land, and a sincere and constant Friendship shall be re-established between His Britannic Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, Kingdoms, Dominions, and Subjects, and their High Mightinesses the said States General, and their Dominions and Subjects, of what Quality or Condition soever they be, without Exception either of Places or Persons, so that the High contracting Parlies shall give the greatest Attention to the maintaining between themselves and their said Dominions and Subjects, this reciprocal Friendship and Intercourse, without permitting hereafter, on either Part, any Kind of Hostilities to be committed, either by Sea or by Land, for any Cause or under any Pretence whatsoever: And they shall carefully avoid, for the future, every Thing which might prejudice the Union happily re-established, endeavouring, on the contrary, to procure reciprocally for each other whatever may contribute to their mutual Glory, Interests, and Advantage, without giving any Assistance or Protection, directly or indirectly, to those who would do any Injury to either of the High contracting Parties. There shall be a general Oblivion of every Thing which may have been done or committed before or since the Commencement of the War which is just ended.

Article 2.

With respect to the Honors of the Flag, and the Salute at Sea, by the Ships of the Republic towards those of His Britannic Majesty, the same Custom shall be respectively followed as was practised before the Commencement of the War which is just concluded.

Article 3.

All the Prisoners taken on either Side, as well by Land as by Sea, and the Hostages carried aw'ay or given during the War, and who have not yet been restored, conformably to the Preliminary Treaty, shall be restored as soon as possible without Ransom; each Power respectively discharging the Advances which shall have been made for the Subsistence and Maintenance of their Prisoners, by the Sovereign of the Country where they shall have been detained, according to the Receipts, attested Accounts, and other authentic Vouchers, which shall be furnished on each Side; and Sureties shall be reciprocally given for the Payment of the Debts which the Prisoners may have contracted in the Countries where they may have been detained, until their entire Release. And all Ships, as well Men of War as Merchant Ships, which may have been taken since the Expiration of the Terms agreed upon for the Cessation of Hostilities by Sea, shall likewise be restored, bond Jidc, with all their Crews and Cargoes: t And the Execution of this Article shall be proceeded upon immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty.

Article 4.

The States General of the United Provinces cede and guaranty, in full Right, to His Britannic Majesty, the Town of Ncgapatnam, with the Dependencies thereof; but in Consideration of the Importance which the States General of the United Provinces annex to the Possession of the aforesaid Town, the King of Great Britahiy as a Proof of His good Will towards the said States, promises, notwithstanding this Cession, to receive and treat with them for the Restitution of the said Town, in case the States shall hereafter have an Equivalent to offer him.

Article 5.

The King of Great Britain shall restore to the States General of the United Provinces Trinquemale, as also all the other Towns, Forts, Harbours, and Settlements, which, in the Course of the War, have been conquered in any Part of the World whatever by the Arms of His Britannic Majesty, or by those of the English East India Company, and of which He might be in Possession; the Whole in the Condition in which they shall be found.

Article 6.

The States General of the United Provinces promise and engage not to obstruct the Navigation of the British Subjects in the Eastern Seas.

Article 7.

Whereas Differences have arisen between the English African Company and the Dutch West India Company, relative to the Navigation on the Coasts of Africa, as also on the Subject of Cape Appollonia; for preventing all Cause of Complaint between the Subjects of the Two Nations upon those Coasts, it is agreed, that Commissaries shall be named on each Side to make suitable Arrangements on these Points.

Article 8.

All the Countries and Territories which may have been, or which may be conquered, in any Part of the World whatsoever, by the Arms of His Britannic Majesty, as well as by those of the States General, which are not included in the present Articles, neither under the Head of Cessions, nor under the Head of Restitutions, shall be restored without Difficulty, and without requiring any Compensation.

Article 9.

Whereas, by the 9th Article of the Preliminary Treaty, a Period wa3 stipulated and appointed by the 9 High

24 Geo. III. 7 0 Junii01

High contracting Parties for the Restitutions and Evacuations to be made, on each Side, of the Towns, Fortresses, and Territories which should have been conquered by their respective Arras, and of which they should be in Possession, excepting such as had been ceded; and whereas the Term specified in the aforesaid 9th Article is already expired, the High contracting Parties engage reciprocally, and bond, side, to observe the said Stipulations; and in case, by any Accident or otherwise, the Cessions and Restitutions therein comprized should not have taken place, to expedite immediately the necessary Orders, to the End that there may be no further Delay in the Accomplishment of the said Stipulations.

Article 10.

His Britannic Majesty, and their High Mightinesses the aforesaid States General, promise to observe sincerely and bond side all the Articles contained and established in this present Treaty; and they will not suffer the same to be infringed, directly or indirectly, by their respective Subjects: And the said High contracting Parties guaranty to each other, generally and reciprocally, all the Stipulations of the present Treaty.

Article 11.

The solemn Ratifications of the present Treaty, prepared in good and due Form, shall be exchanged in this City of Paris, between the High contracting Parties, in the Space of One Month, or sooner, if it can be done, to be computed from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty.

In Witness whereof, we the underwritten, their Ambassadors and Ministers Plenipotentiary, have signed with our Hands in their Names, and by virtue of our full Powers, the present Definitive Treaty, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at Paris, the Twentieth Day of May, One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four.

(L.S.) Daniel Hailes. (L.S.) Lestevenon Van

Berkcnroode.

(L.S.) Brant sen.

Separate Article.

It has been agreed and determined, that the French Language, made use of in all the Copies of the present Treaty, shall not form an Example which may be alledged or quoted as a Precedent, or in any Manner prejudice either of the contracting Powers, and that they shall conform for the future to what has been observed, and ought to be observed, with Regard to and on the Part of Powers, who are in the Practice and Possession of giving and receiving Copies of like Treaties in a different Language from the French; the present Treaty having nevertheless the same Force and Virtue as if the aforesaid Practice had been therein observed.

In Witness whereof, we, the underwritten Ambassadors and Ministers Plenipotentiaries of His Britannic Majesty and the States General of the United Provinces, have signed the present Separate Article, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at Paris, the Twentieth Day of May, One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four.

(L. S.) Daniel Hailes. (L. S.) Lestevenon Van

Berkcnroode.

(L.S.) Brantsen.

Cricklade A Petition of those whose Names are thereunto sub-

Election. scribed, Voters for Burgesses to serve in Parliament

for the Borough of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, was read; Setting forth, That, at the late General Election for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, Robert Adamson, Charles West ley Coxe, John Walker Heritage, and Robert Nicholas, Esquires, were Candidates; and that many indirect and unwarrantable Practices were made use of by the said Robert Adamson and Charles Westley Coxe, and also by other Persons in their Interests, to procure a colourable Majority for them the said Mr. Adamson, and Mr. Coxe; and that Richard Tmnsend was the Bailiff and Returning Officer of the said Borough, and, before the Poll, did attempt, by undue and improper Influence, to prevail upon Persons, who had no Right of voting, to appear and tender their Votes in favour of Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care, promising, and giving them Reasons to believe, that he would admit them upon the Poll at all Events; and that, during the Poll, the said Richard Townsend did behave himself with marked and continued Partiality and Preference towards Mr. Adamson and Mr. Coxe, and did, illegally and arbitrarily, admit a great Number of Voters, who had no Right to vote, nor were qualified, in any Manner, to give their Votes at such Election, for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Coxe, and did wilfully and knowingly reject many Voters, who were duly qualified to vote, and who tendered their Votps in favour of the said Mr. Hcneage and Mr. Nicholas, and did, by a Variety of other undue and illegal Devices, attempt to procure a fraudulent and colourable Majority for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care, and did, against the earnest and continued Remonstrances of Mr. Heneage and Mr. Nicholas, and their Counsel, admit, without proper and sufficient Enquiry, all Persons to vote for Mr. Adamson and Mr. Coxe, and did discourage all Enquiry into the Rights or Titles of those who tendered their Votes for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Coxe; and that, in consequence of such unwarrantable Practices, and by the partial, arbitrary, and illegal Conduct of the Returning Officer, a colourable Majority of Votes was obtained for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care, under which the said Returning Officer has endeavoured to protect himself for the illegal Return which he has made of the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Coxe, in Violation of the Franchises -of the Petitioners and other Voters for the said Mr. Heneage and Mr. Nicholas, who had a clear Majority of legal and uncorrupted Votes, and ought to have been returned for the said Borough, and in Subversion of the true and sacred Rights of Election, and of the Law and Constitution of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 27th Day of July next, at the same Time that the Petition of John Walker Heneage and Robert Nicholas, Esquires, is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the 'Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Drink, Entertainment, and Provision, and make Presents, Gilts, Rewards, and Entertainment, and make Promises, Agreements, Obligations, and Engagements, to give and allow Meat, Drink, Provisions, Presents,

Rewards, and Entertainments, to divers Persons so having Voice or Vote in the said Election, in order to be elected, and for being elected, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that, by the aforesaid corrupt, illegal, and undue Means, the said Anne Pou-lett and Alexander Hood obtained a Majority of Votes at the said Election over the said Sir Gilbert Elliot, and the Returning Officer of the said Borough hath returned the said Anne Poulett and Alexander Hood as the Persons duly elected to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, whereas the said Anne Poulett and Alexander Hood were, by the corrupt and illegal Practices aforesaid of themselves and their Agents, disabled and incapacitated upon the said Election to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, and the said Election of them the said Anne Poulett and Alexander Hood was void, and they ought to be deemed and taken as no Members of this Parliament, and as if they had never been returned or elected for this Parliament; and the said Election and Return of the said Anne Poulett and Alexander Hood were and are contrary to Law, and the Rights and Privileges of Parliament, and highly injurious to the Petitioners, and the other legal Electors of the said Borough, as well as to the said Sir Gilbert Elliot: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and declare the said Election and Return of the said Anne Poulett and Alexander Hood to be void, and grant to the Petitioners such further Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet. t

Borough of Cai'ntirvon, was read; Setting forth, That, at the last General Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Car-nan'on, which, came on the 9th Day of April last, the Right honourable Sir Thomas Wynn, Baronet, Baron Newborough of the Kingdom of Ireland, and Glynn Wynn, Esquire, were declared Candidates, and a Poll was demanded in Favour of the said Lord Newborough, then and now Abroad out of this Realm; and that, by Means of various illegal and corrupt Practices, committed by the said Glynn Wynn and his Agents, he the said Glynn Wynn procured himself to be returned a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, and particularly the said Glynn Wynn, before and during the said Election, was, by himself and by his Agents, guilty of bribing divers of the Burgesses of the said Boroughs, in order to influence them to give *their Votes at the said Election, and did, by himself and by his Agents, after the Teste of the Writ or Precept for holding the said Election, and before and during the Poll taken at the same Election, directly and indirectly give; present, and furnish, to a very great Number of Persons having Voice in the said Election, divers Sums of Money, Meat, Drink, Entertainment, and Provisions, and also by Promises and Undertakings to give and allow Money, Meat, Drink, Provisions, Rewards, and Entertainments, to a great many Persons so having Voice at the said Election, in order to be elected, and for being elected, a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the pretended Mayor, and the Two pretended Bailiffs, of the said Borough of Carnaj'von, who assumed and arrogated to themselves the Character, and the Power, and Authority, of Returning Officers for the said Borough at the

# O O

said Election, had not, nor had any or either of them, any legal Power or Authority to act as such on that Occasion, inasmuch as they, nor any or either of them, were duly elected or appointed to such Offices respectively, in such Manner as is by Law required, so as to enable them to make a Return of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, or to do any other Corporate or Official Act whatsoever; and that the said pretended Mayor and Bailiffs, so having assumed to themselves such Power and Authority, were afterwards guilty of the most illegal Partiality during the said Election, by admitting Persons to vote for the said Glynn Wynn w*ho had no legal Right to vote, and by rejecting the Votes of other Persons who had severally a good and legal Right to vote, and who offered and tendered themselves at the Poll to vote for the said Lord Newborough; and that the said Mayor, or pretended Mayor, to whom the Custody of the Books and Records of the said Borough of Carnarvon belongs, at the Instance of the said Glynn Wynn, his Attornies, Solicitors, and Agents, kept back and concealed several of the Books and Records belonging to the said Borough of Carnarvon, although he was frequently called upon and requested to produce the same to the Electors and the Agents of the said Lord Nrwborough, as well before as during the said Election, and the said Mayor, or pretended Mayor, caused or suffered other of the said Books and Records to be altered and mutilated, thereby leaving out the Names of very many Persons wfoo were and are legal Burgesses of the said Borough of Carnarvon, and who had severally served and exercised the said Office of Burgess, and other Corporate Offices, within the said Borough, for a great Number of Years preceding the said Election, and who would have voted, and many of whom offered and tendered their Votes, for the said Lord New* borough, and which the said pretended Returning Officers arbitrarily refused to admit on the Poll, although their flight to vote at the said Election was notorious, and well known to the said pretended Returning Officers,

and that the Town Clerk of the Borough of Pwllheli, one of the said Contributary Boroughs, or the Person acting as such, and who had the Custody of the Books ana Records of that Borough, and who was in the Interest of the said Glynn Wynn, and acted as his Agent at the said Election, conducted himself in a most arbitrary, unjust, and illegal Manner, previous to and at the said Election, in refusing the Inspection of the said Books and Records, and giving Copies of the same when duly required, as by Law he ought to have done, and in refusing to enter on Stamp the Names of divers of the Burgesses of that Contributary Borough w*ho were in the Interest of the said I/>rd Newborough, and who, or many of whom, tendered their Voles in his Favour, although due Application had been made for such Purposes; and that a great Number of Persons were admitted to poll at the said Election for the said Glynn Wynn, as Burgesses of the said Contributary Borough of Pwllheli, w ho had no Right to vote, and others who had a legal Right to vote for the same, and who offered to vote for the said Lord Newborough, were rejected by the said pretended Returning Officers at the said Election; and that the said Glynn Wynn, together with the said Mayor, or pretended Mayor, of Carnarvon (who was, at and previous to the said Election, greatly in the Interest of the said Glynn Wynn) a long Time before, that is to say, One Year before the said Election, applied themselves severally to the said Recorder, or Town Clerk, of the Borough of Nefn, another of the said Contributary Boroughs, to give up and deliver to them, or One of them, the Books, Records, and Papers, belonging to the said last mentioned Contributary Borough, and the same were accordingly delivered to them, at different Times, by the said Recorder or Town Clerk, and the said Glynn Wynn, and the said Mayor, or pretended Mayor, kept the same in their Custody or Possession, or in the Custody or Possession of One of them, up to the Time of, and until the said Election had been proceeded in, and have kept the Possession thereof ever since, in order to prevent the Agents of the said Lord Newborough, and the said Electors, from obtaining the Inspection and Copies of the same Records, from the said Officer, as by Law they were entitled to; and that the said last mentioned Recorder, or Town Clerk, alleged, when Application was made to him for the Purposes aforesaid, that he could not comply therewith, for that the said Glynn Wynn, and the said Mayor, or pretended Mayor, had got the said Books and Records out of his Custody, and that they would not restore the same to him again; and the said Mayor, or pretended Mayor, as well as the said Glynn Wynn, refused the Agents of the said Lord Newborough, and the said Electors, the Inspection of the same, or to grant Copies thereof, or any of them, although duly applied to for that Purpose, whereby the Agents of the said Lord Newborough could not, nor could the Petitioners, or the said Electors, obtain that Information and Satisfaction respecting the Premises, or avail themselves thereof in such Manner as they were by Law entitled to; and that by the Means aforesaid, and other illegal and undue Means, a colourable Majority, on the Poll, was obtained in favour of the said Glynn Wynn, who has been unduly returned by the said pretended Mayor and Bailiffs as duly elected to Vol. 40.

serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Carnarvon, and its Contributary Boroughs, whereas the said Lord Newborough ought to have been returned at the said Election, to represent the same, instead of the said Glynn Wynn, who w as and is, by Reason of the Premises, incapable of sitting in Parliament for the said Borough, upon the said Election; and that, by the aforesaid corrupt and illegal Practices, the Rights and Privileges of the Petitioners and the other Electors for the said Borough of Carnarvon, and its Contributary Boroughs, have been grossly and manifestly violated, and the Petitioners, and the said Electors, have been greatly injured: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief, and to adopt such other salutary Measures for vindicating the Rights and Privileges of Electors against such Practices, and the arbitrary, partial, illegal, and unjust Conduct of Returning Officers, and others, whom it may concern, as the Nature of this Case shall in the Judgment of the House require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 16th Day of November next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of Sir John Henderson, Baronet, was Fife Election, read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election for the County of Fife, Lieutenant General Robert Skene and the Petitioner were the only Candidates; and that General Skene was returned as having a Majority of Electors in his Favour, but the Petitioner is advised that the Votes given for General Skene are to be considered as thrown away, inasmuch as the Office of Inspector of Military Roads in Scotland, though no longer in General Skene's own Name, as formerly, yet is still held by his Brother Captain David Skene, in Trust for, or for the Benefit of, General Skene, which Office was adjudged on a former Occasion to be a new Office created since the 25th Day of October 1705, and as such by the Act of the Sixth of Queen Anne, rendering any Person, for whose Benefit it is held, ineligible to serve in Parliament; and that, at the Meeting for Election, the Petitioner, before the Vote was put for the Choice of Member of Parliament, did publicly apprize the Freeholders, that General Skene was ineligible for the Reasons stated above, and did also enter a Protest in the Minutes of Election, that the Votes given for General Skene should be held to be of no Avail, and that the Petitioner should be held to be duly elected, and should be returned accordingly: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 18th Day of November next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed. Electors of the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, was also delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, at the late Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port, the honourable Lewis Thomas Watson, the honourable Henry Neville, Sir Peter Parker, Baronet, and Thomas Alves, Esquire, were Candidates; and that Robert Stone, Esquire, who was Bailiff and Returning Officer at the said Election, on the 30th Day of March last proceeded to the Election of Two Barons to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port, without giving Four Days Notice of the Day appointed for such Election, as by the Statute, made in the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, "An Act for the u further regulating Elections of Members to serve " in Parliament, and for the preventing irregular c< Proceedings of Sheriffs, and other Officers, in the <c electing and returning such Members," he is required; and that, at such Election, the said Hemy Neville and Sir Peter Parker were returned duly elected to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port of Seaford, and the Petitioners are advised, and conceive, that, by reason the said Returning Officer proceeded to such Election without giving Four Days Notice of the Day appointed for such Election, the same, and the Return made thereon, are null and void: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into their Consideration, and grant such Relief therein as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration at the same Time that the last preceding Petition is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matters of the said Petitions.

Memwandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cases, were sent to the several Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Times on which the said several Petitions were ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Mr. Hunter Blair reported from the Committee, to Corn im-whom the Petition of Messieurs Allan, Steuart, and ported into Co. Charles and Robei't Fall, Sir William Forbes, Sco 80 James Hunter, and Co. Samuel Anderson, James

and Co. John Chalmers, and Co. Beadie, Scougal and Ogilvie, Adam Keir, John Thomson, James Thomson,

Martin and Kerr, Robert Hart, George Hall, Whitiet Pullar and Hutton, James and John Stein, and Joseph Lamb, William Batson, and Co. was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: WThere the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition is as follows:

It appeared, by an Act passed in the Twenty-third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, that the Importation of Corn, upon Payment of the Low Duties, was allowed for a certain limited Time.

And, by the Evidence of Mr. George Chambers, it appeared to your Committee, that in the Scarcity occasioned by the Failure of the Crop in the Year 1782, the Petitioners (being Merchants) imported sundry large Cargoes of Corn from The Baltic, for the Relief of Scotland and Newcastle, in procuring Which they risked a considerable Sum of Money — That in order to have entitled the Merchants to the Benefit of entering the said Com, upon Payment of the Low Duties, the same should have arrived before the 25th of September 1783, but the Ships were detained beyond that Time by a most uncommon long Duration of stormy Weather and contrary Winds — That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances of the Case, the Lords of the Treasury, upon Application made to them, authorized the Commissioners of the Customs, in England and Scotland, to admit the Vessels to an Entry upon Payment of the Low Duties, Bonds being given for the Payment of the High Duties, until Application should be made to Parliament for Relief; and that Bonds were given accordingly.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, to authorize the Commissioners of the Customs, in England and Scotland, to cancel Bonds given for the High Duties on certain Parcels of Corn imported into Great Britain, on certain Conditions therein mentioned: And that Mr. Hunter Blair and the Lord Advocate of Scotland do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Shrewsbury Mr. TVillidm Pulteney repotted from the Committee#

Poor. to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose

Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, assessed towards the Relief of the Poor of the Parishes of Saint Chad, Saint Mary, Saint Alkmand, Saint Julian, The Holy Cross, and Saint Giles and Meole Brace, otherwise Biace Meole, in the County of Salop, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter' of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table; Where the same was read; and is as followed; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, jVII-Ham Smithy Esquire, being examined, said, That the Poor of the several Parishes within the said Town and Liberties are very numerous, and are supported at a great Expence — Hi at if proper Powers were given for providing a convenient Place for their Reception, and for their being orderly and well governed therein, it would not only tend to the more effectual Relief of such as by Age or other Infirmities are rendered incapable of supporting themselves, but to the better Employment of the able and industrious.

And the Witness further said, That if Provision was made for allowing Contracts to be entered into for the Maintenance of the Poor, belonging to any of the other Parishes within the County, in such Place of Reception, it would be an Ease and Advantage to such parishes as may be willing to make such Contracts, and be of public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor belonging to several Parishes within the Town of Shrewsbury^ and the Liberties thereof, in the County of Salop: And that Mr. William Pulteney, Sir Charlton Leigh tan, and Sir Richard Hilly do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Scotland — A Petition of John Bitshby, Sherriff Clerk of the

hfsof Shire of Dumfries, on Behalf of himself and the rest emffs, &c. of Sherriffs and Stewarts Clerks in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland) was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act 4‘ for taking away and abolishing the Heretable Jurisdictions in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and for making Satisfaction to the Proprietors "thereof, and for restoring such Jurisdictions to the €i Crown, and for making more effectual Provision " for the Administration of Justice throughout that " Part of the United Kingdom by the Kings Courts " and Judges there, and for obliging all Persons acting as Procurators, Writers, or Agents in the Law " in Scotland to take the Oaths, and for rendering the " Union of the Two Kingdoms more complete," Power was given to the Court of Session to regulate the Fees to be paid to the Clerks or other Officers officiating in the Circuit Courts, or in the Courts of Sherriffs or Stewarts, in Civil Causes, and such Regulations were by the said Act directed to be binding on all Parties concerned, unless or until the same be altered by Act of Parliament; and that, in pursuance of the said Act, the Court of Session did regulate a Table of Fees to be demanded and taken by the Sherriffs and Stewarts Clerks, but, by the Increase of Commerce and Population in that Part of the United Kingdom, Cases frequently occur which are not provided for by the said Table of Fees, and in other Instances the Fees already provided are inadequate to Vol. 40.

the Labour and Trouble of the SHgrriffs and'Stewarts Clerks, and some Articles of Trouble and Duty appear to have escaped the Attention of the Court, which Circumstances have Occasioned different Practices in different Counties, and have been productive of Litigation: And therefore prayings That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to irtipower the Court of Session to fix and ascertain reasonable Fees for such Articles of Duty as were not regulated and provided for by the aforesaid Table, and to make such Variations as shall appear just, where the Fees are inadequate to the Trouble.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that the Lord Advocate of Scotland and Mr. Dempster do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of John Lord Viscount Dudley and Ward\ Lord of the Manor of the Borough and Parish of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, and the humble Petition of Joseph Cartwright, Clerk, Vicar of the said Parish of Dudley, and of the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Burgages, Lands, and Tenements, within the said Manor and Parish, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Owners and Proprietors of Burgages, Lands, and Tenements, within the said Manor and Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are, within the said Manor and Parish, several Commons and Waste Lands, called Dudley Wood, and divers other Parcels of Waste Lands and Commonable Places, containing in the Whole, by Estimation, One thousand Acres, or thereabouts, upon which the Petitioners, and the rest of the said Proprietors, have, or respectively claim, a Right of Common; and that the said Commons, Waste Lands, and Commonable Places, in their present Situation, yield very little Profit to the Petitioners, and the rest of the Proprietors aforesaid, and, in their present State, are incapable of any considerable Improvement; but, if the same were divided, inclosed, and allotted unto and amongst the Petitioners, and all other Persons interested in the same, according to their respective Interests therein, the said Commons might thereby be greatly improved, and become very profitable to the Petitioners, and the rest of the said Proprietors, as well as a public Advantage: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Commons, Waste Lands^ and Commonable Places, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir John Wrottesley, Sir Edward Littleton, &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Nicholas Mills being examined, said, That the Trustees acting under the said Acts have, in pursuance of the Powers thereby given, borrowed the Sum of £.7,102. 115. 7 d. upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted on the said Roads leading from the Lower Market House in Tavistock aforesaid, over Horrabridge, by Manadon Gate aforesaid, to the Old Pound near Plymouth Dock, which hath been laid out and expended according to the Directions of the said Acts — That the said last mentioned Roads are in bad Repair, and in some Parts so ruinous as to be unsafe for Passengers, and some Parts thereof are now under Indictments for Want of Repair. — And the Witness further added,

Poor, incorporated by an Act of Parliament, made in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the better Relief arid Employment of the Poor of the Borough of -heved, otherwise Launceston, tfnd the Parish of Saint Mary Magdalen, in the County of and also

of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and others contributing to the Maintenance of the Poor of the said Borough and Parish, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the said Governor and Guardians have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, but the Money thereby authorized to be raised hath been found insufficient for the Maintenance of the Poor of the said Borough and Parish, and a considerable Debt hath been incurred for the necessary Purposes of carrying the said Act into Execution, which now remains due, and the said Act hath, in several Respects, been found ineffectual for the Purposes intended; and that there is now standing, in the Name of the Mayor and Corporation of the said Borough, the Sum of /. 384. 1 o s. 8 d.Consolidated Bank Annuities, the Interests or Dividends of which is applicable to the Relief of the Poor, but the Petitioners apprehend it would be more beneficial to the said Borough and Parish, if the said Sum was wholly vested in the said Governor and Guardians of the Poor, in order to sell or dispose of the same, and the Money arising therefrom applied towards discharging the said Debt; and that there are, within the said Borough, several Common Lands, called Great Pemygiltam, Little -gillam, Hay, Windmill, and Longland, the Aftermowth of which hath, of ancient Right and Custom, been enjoyed by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Free Burgesses, and the Widows of Free Burgesses, which is of little Benefit to the several Persons entitled thereto; and it would be advantageous to the Petitioners, if the same was to be sold, or let, for the best Price or Rent which could be had for the same, and the Money arising thereby applied towards repairing the Church, repairing and lighting the Streets, or any other Purpose, for the Ornament of the said Town, or the Convenience of the Inhabitants: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a BUI for altering and amending the said Act, and other the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Rose, the Lord Maitland, &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

This Enquiry into the Proceedings of the Auditor of the Imprest, relative to the Accounts of the Treasurer of the Ordnance, gave us no Insight into the Manner in which the Business of the Ordnance is conducted: To obtain this Knowledge we had Recourse to the Chief Clerks, as the efficient Officers in the several Branches of this Department. We’examined N*4- John Boddinglofi, Esquire, Secretary to the Board of n*5- Ordnance; Robert Mackenzie, Esquire, Secretary; and 6* Mr. Nicholas JVittwer, Minuting Clerk to the Lieu-N*7»8- tenant General; John Vidgen, Esquire, First Clerk in N* 9, 10. the Office of the Surveyor General; William Nettleship, Esquire, First Clerk to the Clerk of the Ordnance; N*n. Mr. Thomas Day, late Clerk in the Office of the N° 12. Storekeeper; and Mr. William Weaver, First Clerk to the Clerk of the Deliveries. From these Examinations, and from the Instructions for the Government of the Office of Ordnance, given by King Charles the Second, in the Year 1683, submitted to our Inspection, and which, with very few Alterations, are the Rules that govern the Office at this Day, we have been enabled to obtain some Knowledge of the Manner in which this extensive Branch of the Public Expenditure is transacted.

The Office of Ordnance is governed by a Master General, and a Board under him, all appointed by separate Letters Patent.

The Board consists of Five principal Officers — the Lieutenant General — the Surveyor General — the Clerk of the Ordnance — the Storekeeper — and, Clerk of the Deliveries, — any Three of whom form a Board. The Master General and Lieutenant General are each, by virtue of his Office, in Two Capacities; the one Military, the other Civil: In their military Capacity the Master General is Commander in Chief, and the Lieutenant General Second in Command, over the Artillery and Engineers.

In his civil Capacity the Master General is intrusted with the entire Management of, and Controul over, the whole Ordnance Department: All Warrants from the King, Privy Council, or, in Sea Affairs, from the Board of Admiralty, and all Letters from Secretaries of State, conveying Orders relative to the Ordnance, are directed, not to the Board, but to the Master General; and the Board carry them into Execution under his Authority, and in consequence of his Direction: He can do alone any Act, which can otherwise, if he does not interpose, be done by the Board: He can order the Issue of Money; but that Order must be executed in the established Mode, that is, by Debenture signed by Three Board Officers.

The Board are subordinate to the Master General: They act under him, pursuant to his Significations < or Directions: If he does not interpose, they are competent of themselves to carry on all the official Business: They make Contracts and Agreements for the Purchase of Stores and Performance of Services, and direct the Issue of Money and Stores; but if the Master General chuses to exert the Power intrusted to him, he can controul all their Actions.

During the Absence of the Master General, or the Vacancy of the Office, the whole executive Power devolves upon the Board: All Warrants, Letters, and Orders, are directed to the Lieutenant General and principal Officers: They can order, sign, execute, transact, and perform every Service or Matter incident to the Office of the Ordnance.

Vol. 40.

The Lieutenant General, in his civil Capacity, is Twelfth the first in Rank among the Members that compose the Board: His Signature is essential to a Debenture, Accounts, to warrant the Payment of it by the Treasurer; unless he is absent Abroad, in which Case any other of the principal Officers is impowered by the King’s Instructions to sign it in his stead; or unless, as has been usual, His Majesty appoints an Assistant and Deputy to the Lieutenant General, to act for him in his Absence. The present Lieutenant General has no Deputy: The last Appointment of this Kind was that of the Surveyor General, by Warrant dated the n? 13. nth of April 1750. It is the Duty, likewise, of this Officer, to superintend all the Officers and Ministers in the various Departments of the Ordnance, and to see that they perform the Duties of their several Employments.

The other Four Principal Officers hav&each of them, independent of his being a Member of the Board, a separate and distinct Branch of Business committed to his Management.

The Surveyor General, or Master Surveyor, as he is stiled in his Patent, is the Second Board Officer:

His peculiar Duty is, as his Title imports, to survey all Stores received or returned into the Storehouses of the Ordnance: He is interposed as a Check upon the Quality and Quantity of the Stores received into the Magazine: At the Totver he executes this Duty by his Clerks; at the Out Ports, and Foreign Garrisons, Officers called Clerks of the Survey are appointed to this Service, who regularly make their Returns into his Office. It is his Province to examine the Account of every Expenditure; and therefore the Price Book, which contains the Price allowed by the Board for every Species of Stores and Service, is lodged with him; and all Bills for Pay for Stores delivered and Services performed, with their proper Vouchers, are transmitted to him for his Examination and Allowance: He compares the Prices charged, and sees that they agree with the Terms of the Contract, Agreement, Warrant, or Order, on which they are grounded: He examines and passes the Accounts of those Officers, or others, to whom the Money has been issued on Account; and after he has finished his Examination of any Demand or Expenditure, he forms a Bill, signs it, and transmits it to the Clerk of the Ordnance, as the Ground for a Debenture for Payment.

The Repairs of the Buildings belonging to the Ordnance at the Tower, and the Direction of the Artificers, Workmen, and Labourers there employed, are intrusted to his Care.

The Clerk of the Ordnance presides in that Office in which are recorded and preserved all the original Authorities, Instruments, and Vouchers, that warrant, describe, and authenticate the Proceedings of the Ordnance: He is the Accountant of the Ordnance; and, as such, keeps the Accounts of all the Cash and Stores belonging to the whole Department: *

He draws up the Annual Estimate for Parliament, and the Monthly Estimate for the Treasury. The Treasurer sends him an Account of the Imprests from the Exchequer, as soon as he receives them: The Articles that compose the Voluntary Charge, and the Imprests Vacated, originate from Accounts examined and settled in his Office; and the Instruments by which Money is paid, or issued, are formed by him.

He makes out the Quarter Books for the Payment of the Officers, from the Appointments, whether they are by Commission, Patent, . Warrant, Signification, or Order; all of which, with the Salaries annexed to them, are entered in his Office. All Debentures for the Payment of Money, either for Stores delivered or Services performed, are made out by him, from the Bills transmitted to him from the Surveyor General.

He vacates the Imprests issued to, or the Debts due from, the Persons named in the Debentures or G g Quarter

The Board of Ordnance have it in Contemplation to call upon the Sub-Accountants to clear their Imprests; and for this Purpose, by their Order dated the 22d of January last, they have directed the Clerk of the Ordnance to prepare for them a List of the Imprests remaining in force, and of the Debts due to the Ordnance.

That most useful and necessary Regulation, the Abolition of ail Fees, Gratuities, and Rewards, and the Substitution of certain fixed Salaries in their Stead, being, adopted in the Office of Ordnance, and estate. Wished by His Majesty’s Warrant of the 24th of June 1783, before alluded to (with the Exceptions therein mentioned) we are relieved from any Enquiry into the Quantum and Sources of the Profits of the several Officers employed in this extensive Department. In the Establishment annexed to, and carried into Execution by, that Warrant, a Salary is appointed to each Office; and the annual Amount of them, together, £ 34457* 1. 6. is Thirty-four thousand Four hundred and Fifty-seven Pounds, One Shilling, and Six Pence.

In every Office, those Persons who preside, and are intrusted with the superintending Power and Controul over the Whole, having full Knowledge of the Business allotted to each Division, are the proper Judges what Number of Officers and Ministers are necessary, and what Industry and Talents are requisite, for the Performance of every Branch of the Duty: It must rest upon their Judgment and Fidelity to the Public, that neither the N umber nor Salaries exceed the Demands of the Service. Before this Regulation was in force, Fees aOd Gratuities, under the Sanction of Custom, were paid by the Contractor in various Stages of his Transaction with the Office, from the procuring his Contract to his Payment by Debenture: A Contract for the Hire of a Ship of Seven hundred Tons Twenty Months in the Service, cost the Contractor, in Agency, Fees, and Gratuities, Three hundred and Eighty-two Pounds. One per Cent. the customary a, 180,396. Poundage for Agency only, upon Two Millions One N#2i. hundred and Eighty thousand Three hundred and Ninety-six Pounds, the Amount of the Freight, is £.*1,803. Twenty-one thousand Eight hundred and Three Pounds. Whatever Saving accrues from this Regulation is Gain to the Public; for the Contractor, to insure his Profit, will charge it in its fullest Extent to the Account of the Public.

This Regulation is a Part of that System of Occo-nomy that ought to be extended to every Revenue Department, whether of Receipt or Expenditure. The Exertion of the Authority of the superior Officer, vested in him by virtue of his Office, with His Majesty’s Approbation and Confirmation, has effected it in the Ordnance: Were the same Steps taken in other Offices, the same End would be attained: There is hardly any Office but possesses the like Powers, lodged either with the supreme Officer or a Board; and, should any Defect or Obstruction check the Exercise of the Power, the Legislature can lend their Aid. The Utility of the Regulation has the Sanction, not only of high Authority, in the Instance before us, but of the declared Sense of the Legislature, by their establishing it in the Office of the Paymaster General of His Majesty’s Forces.

It appears from this Enquiry, that the Auditor of the Imprest is employed upon the Ordnance, as upon the Navy and other Accounts that have been before us, in little more than comparing different Entries of the same Sums, and examining the Formality of Vouchers, and the Accuracy of Computations and Castings: Those Circumstances of the Account in which the Interest of the Nation is the most mate-Vol. 40.

rially concerned, the Terms of the Contract, find the Twtlfifi Fidelity of the Execution, are not within his Reach: Report The Board of Ordnance alone are intrusted to decide accouqu upon them; and, upon the Authority of the Signature of the Board Officers, he admits, the Voucher for an Expenditure to be true in every Circumstance, except in those which, being considered as the least important, are usually committed to the Care of inferior Clerks.

This Account first undergoes, in the Office of Ordnance, an Examination similar to that given to it by the Auditor of the Imprest: Every Article is checked by the proper Officer; and the final Examination of the Ledger with the Vouchers is made by the Board previous to their Signature: A Second Examination of the same Kind, in another Office, at the Expence to the Public of Three hundred and Ten Pounds a Year, the customary Fee ta the Auditor for the Business transacted by him, seems to be of no Use; and, therefore, we are of Opinion, that auditing the Accounts of the Treasurer of the Ordnance in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, is an unnecessary Expence to the Public, and ought to be discontinued; that, after those Accounts have been fully examined by the Board of Ordnance, the Articles should be ranged under distinct and separate Heads of Service, and the Accounts reduced into the official Form, by the Treasurer of the Ordnance, and by him passed through the necessary Offices of the Exchequer.

Office, we have wot been able to discover, from those which have hitherto come under our Consideration, any solid Advantage derived to the Public from the Examination given to them by the Auditor of the Imprest; and, for that Reason, we have suggested the Propriety of exempting them from his Jurisdiction, and the urgent Necessity of relieving the Nation from so heavy, and, to all Appearance; so unnecessary an Expence,

The Account of the Fees and Gratuities claimed by him, and his Officers and Clerks, and his Certificate of the Accounts depending in his Office, transmitted every Half Year to the King’s Remembrancer of the Exchequer, exhibit a Number and Variety of other Accounts, subject to his Cognizance, to which our Enquiry has not yet been extended; and therefore, how far the Security of the Public may require the Intervention of the Auditor, to establish the Truth and Accuracy of those Accounts, we can form no Judgment: But we have proceeded far enough to warrant our Opinion upon the Propriety and Necessity of introducing into this Office the Regulation we have so frequently had Occasion to enforce in relation to other Offices.

The Office before us is an Office of Controul: It is insrituted as a Check upon the Public Accounts: The Allowance of the Auditor being necessary to every Article both of the Receipt and Expenditure, the State of the Account, as between the Public and the Accountant, must continue unknown till the Balance is ascertained by the Auditor at the Completion of his Examination; and, consequently, that Balance, however great it may be, if in Favour of the Public, remains with the Accountant, if in Favour of the Accountant, remains with the Public, until that Period. Hence it may be the Interest of the Accountant to purchase, at a high Price, either Delay or Expedition in passing his Accounts; and, should an Officer be corrupt, the Permission to receive Fees and Gratuities is an obvious Method to obtain it; and, therefore, we are of Opinion, that the Payment of Fees and Gratuities by the Person accounting, however confined by Usage as to the Quantum, is a Mode ill adapted to the Constitution of this Office, and to the Nature of the Business there transacted.

We do not say, or mean to insinuate, that we have discovered any Instance of such Abuse in this Office; but the Mode is open to it; and a wise Government does not wait for the Mischief: It guards, as far as human Prudence can guard, against the Possibility of the Evil; it prevents or removes the Temptation.

But there is another, and still more weighty Reason for a Reform in the Mode of defraying the Expence9 of this Office.

The Service of the presiding Officer bears no Proportion to the Magnitude of his Profits. A Deputy Auditor tells us, in his Examination annexed to our Eighth Report, -that the whole Business of the Office is transacted by the Deputy and Clerks; from the Year 1745 until the Year 1781, that is for Thirty-six Years, he did not recollect that the Principal ever executed any Part of it: To him, therefore, it was a perfect Sinecure. The Business of the Office is of the same Kind now it was then; the Quantity is increased; and that Increase requires an Addition to the Number of Clerks; but it does not make the Intervention of the principal Officer more necessary; the Whole of the Business is properly the Labour of Clerks only; and, therefore, though the present Auditors have paid an Attention beyond their Predecessors, by regulating their Offices, accelerating the Public Accounts, and bringing up the Arrears, yet, should Men less active hereafter fill these Stations, they may again sink into Sinecures, and excessive Vol. 40.

Junii. 125

Stipends be paid every Year to Officers unprofitable to the Public. In the Year 1782, One of these Officers received Nett Sixteen thousand Five hundred and Sixty-five Pounds, Eight Shillings and Eight Pence: the other, Ten thousand Three hundred

and Thirty-one Pounds, Five Shillings, and Eleven Pence: In the Year 1783/the one received Nett Sixteen thousand Two hundred and Thirty Pounds, Four Shillings; the other, Sixteen thousand Three hundred and Seventy-three Pounds, Three Shillings, and Four Pence.

The Public cannot afford to maintain Officers of any Description at such an Expence. This Nation is in Debt above Two hundred and Thirty Millions: It raises every Year, to pay the Interest and Charges attending that Debt, above Eight millions Seven hundred thousand Pounds; of which above Nineteen thousand Eight hundred Pounds, the Bank Fee alone, is to be paid every Year to these Officers, for Business from whence the Public derive no Benefit; and should additions be made this Year to the Public Debt, unless the Legislature will interpose their Authority, these Fees of Office will have their Addition likewise: The Profits of the Auditors of the Imprest rise in Proportion to the Increase of the Public Distress. Upon these Reasons we ground our Opinion, that the Public Good requires that all Fees and Gratuities in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest should be forthwith abolished; that the Profit of the Auditors themselves should be reduced to a reasonable Standard; and that every Officer and Clerk in the said Office should be paid, by the Public, a certain fixed Annual Salary, in Proportion to his Rank and Employment, in lieu of all Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities whatsoever: And we continue to adhere to the Opinion we have stated in our last Report, seeing no Reason to depart from it, That no Right is vested in the Auditor, either by the Letters Patent by which he holds his Office, or by Usage, that can be opposed to this Reduction and Regulation.

Office of Accounts, T. Anguish, (l.s.)

Surrey Street, A. Piggott, (l.s.)

June 8th, 1784. Richd Neave, (l.s.)

Samf Beachcroft, (l.s.)

Geo. Drummond, (l.s.)

The Sums imprested from the Exchequer are either for the Land Service, the Sea Service, or Exceedings; but the Treasurer make9 no Distinction of these Receipts in his Ledger — he has only One Cash Account. The Examination of Cuthbert Fishery Esquire; taken upon Oath, 17th February, 24th and 26th March, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That the Account of Imprests paid, entered in the Ledger, contains all the Sums issued by way of Imprest during the Period of the Account; it is signed at the End by all the Board Officers; the Treasurer does not produce the Imprest Bills to the Auditor of the Imprest, he retains them in his own Office until they are vacated by Debentures, after which they are deposited in the White Tower. — When Money is directed for the Payment of Debentures payable in Course, it is immediately advertised, which is Notice to the Holders of those Debentures: No particular Notice is given to the Holders of Ready Money Debentures, but a List of them, as well as of the Debentures in Course, is hung up in the Hall. — Whatever Money is directed by the Board to be paid, the Treasurer takes Credit for that Sum, and omits it in his next Cash Account laid before the Board; but at the End of the Year, should any Part of it be unpaid, he gives Credit to the Public for that Sum, when he makes up the Account of the Year: This Sum has never been considerable, for it is very seldom that Debentures in Course of Payment continue long without being produced to the Treasurer.

When a Treasurer resigns, the Board continue to direct him to make Payments, until his Cash is nearly exhausted; and when he makes up his final Account, the Board direct him to pay over the Balance in his Hands to his Successor. — The Money imprested from the Exchequer is placed to the Account of the Treasurer at the Bank; his First Clerk, by virtue of a
