4.

The Examination of John Boddinglon, Esquire, Secretary to the Board of Ordnance; taken upon Oath, January 12th, 14th, February 4th, 13th April 20th and 23d, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Secretary to the Board of Ordnance; he has been Forty-five Years in the Office of the Clerk of the Ordnance: In the Year 1763 he was appointed Chief Clerk in that Office; as such it was his Business to attend constantly at the Board, to lay before them such Letters and Papers as he received, and to take Minutes of their Proceedings. — In the Year 1777 the Title of Secretary to the Board was given, by Warrant to the First Clerk, without making any material Alteration in the Duty of the Office. — In January 1783 the Office of Secretary to the Board was taken from the Department of the Clerk of the Ordnance, and formed into a distinct Office, with Clerks subject to, and in the Appointment of, the Secretary. — As Chief Clerk in the Office of the Clerk of the Ordnance, it was his Duty to examine the Accounts of the Captains and Gunners of the Navy, relative to the Expenditure of the Ordnance and Stores delivered to them. This Branch is continued to the present Secretary. — All Contracts for Stores are made by the Board, sometimes in consequence of Advertisements and Proposals delivered in (in which Case the Board elect the lowest Terms, unless there is Reason to the contrary) sometimes in consequence of Proposals delivered in without Advertisements: The Contract is reduced into Form, and signed' by Three Board Officers, and the Contractor. — In general, the Persons who are to supply particular Kinds of Stores, or execute particular Branches of Business for the Ordnance, are appointed by the Master General; the Prices they are to receive are stated in Proposals delivered in by them; which Proposals are referred to, and regulated by, the Surveyor General, agreed to by a Minute of the Board, and entered in the Price Book.

The Board relies upon the Surveyor General that the Contract is executed according to the Terms. Before t he Year 1777 the Manner of procuring Ships for Freight was by Advertisement; in that Year a Su-perintendarit for Shipping was appointed, whose Duty it is to look out for such Ships as may Be wanted.

K k — Most

Twelfth Report on Public Account*.

%l6

— Most of the Ships that have been employed by the Ordnance since that Time have been procured by the Superintendant, who is answerable for their being fit for the Service: He produces the Owner of the Ship to the Board, and settles the Freight. — After the Ship is fitted out, the Superintendant, with a Clerk from the Surveyors Office, and with One from the Clerk of the Ordnance Office, take an Inventory, and settle the Value of the Ship, in case she should be lost or taken.

Where Government determines upon erecting a Fortification, an Engineer, in consequence of Directions from the Master General, forms a Project and Estimate; which is examined by the Chief Engineer, and if approved of by the King, is communicated to the Board by the Master General, who directs the Engineer to carry his Plan into Execution. — He receives Proposals for different Parts of the Work, and sends them to the Board for their Approbation; he procures Labourers himself, and settles their Wages, and superintends the Execution. — The Board, in the Beginning of the Year 1782, came to a Determination to advertise for the different Articles wanted in every Branch in the Ordnance Service, pursuant to the original Instructions to the Officers of the Ordnance; and this Resolution has been carried into Execution ever since. — An Engineer in England neither receives nor pays Money; the Storekeeper pays, in consequence of his Order, and passes his Account in the Surveyors Office. — The Engineer serving with the Army Abroad passes no Account in the Office of the Ordnance, for he receives no Money from the Ordnance.

Ever since he has been in the Ordnance, their Debentures have carried no Interest, unless by particular Agreement; it has been frequently recommended by the Board to the Treasury, that they should bear Interest: He believes the Discount upon these Debentures has been, at some Times during the Two last Years,

28 per Cent.

In every Agreement with the Board, either for Stores or Service, the Person Contracting understands that he is to be paid in Course, unless the Agreement specifies to the contrary. — The Plans for the Fortifications at Chatham, Portsmouth, and Plymouth are very extensive, and will occasion a great Expence — they are not yet njearly completed. — Estimates of the whole Expence for completing each of them, and keeping them in Repair, are at this Time in the Contemplation of the Master General.

In the Year 1775 a Contract for Horses, Conductors, and Drivers, for the Ordnance, was entered into by the Board of Ordnance with Thomas Fitzherbert, Esquire, to continue for Seven Years. — The Contractor is bound to find and provide for the Ordnance all such Horses, Conductors, and Drivers, as he should from Time to Time be required to find. — The Commander in, Chief regulates from Time to Time the Number wanted, the Board send the Requisition to the Contractor; hence, as Circumstances have varied, the Number of Horses, Conductors, and Drivers, employed by the Ordnance, has been different; the first Number lhat was called for, was in the Year 1778, and many were continued, either upon Full Pay or Half Pay, until the End of the War.

The Contractor is to provide Forage for his Horses; but he is to be furnished from the King’s Magazines at the Rate of Six Pence the Ration; and the Conductors and Drivers are to find themselves with Provisions. — The Orduance agreed to allow 10 for every Horse killed or taken by the Enemy.

The Business of the Ordnance is conducted by the Master General and a Board — The Master General is appointed by Letters Patent. He has in himself the complete executive Power, and pan do any Act without the Intervention of the Board, except what

wii. A. 1784.

regards the Instruments for the Payment of Money; he may direct the Issue, but those Instruments must be signed by Three Officers of the Board, of whom, in some of them, the Lieutenant General and the Clerk of the Ordnance must be Two; in others, any Three of the Board are sufficient.

The Master General is, by virtue of his Office, Commander in Chief both of the Artillery and Engineers, which is his Military Character.

The Board consists of Five Officers — the Lieutenant General, the Surveyor General, the Clerk of the Ordnance, the Storekeeper, and Clerk of the Deliveries; these are called the principal Officers. — These Officers are each of them appointed by Letters Patent; each, except the Lieutenant General, has a distinct Civil Duty allotted to him: Any Three of them form a Board, and can make Contracts and Agreements, direct the Issue of Stores, and order Payments, without the Intervention of the Master General; but, if he chuses to interpose, he has a controlling Power over all they do. — The Lieutenant General has no particular Civil Duty, but as one of the Board Officers; in his Military Capacity he is Second in Command both in the Artillery and Engineers; in his Absence the Surveyor General has been appointed by the King's Warrant to act for him. — The present Lieutenant General has no Deputy The rest of the Board Officers have no Military Character.

The Duty of the Surveyor General, or (as he is called in his Patent) Master Surveyor, is to survey all Stores received or returned; he has Clerks under him for that Purpose at the Tower; and at the Out Ports and foreign Garrisons Clerks of the Survey are appointed to do that Duty, and make their Returns to him. He is to examine and allow all Bills for Stores delivered, and Services performed — to see that the Prices are conformable to the Contract, Agreement, Warrant, or Order — to examine the Account of every Expenditure, and allow such Articles as are warranted by the Instructions to the Officers intrusted with that Expenditure; — the Repairs of the Storehouses, Barracks, and all other Buildings belonging to the Ordnance at the Tower; and the Artificers, Workmen, and Labourers, there employed, are under his Direction.

The Duty of the Clerk of the Ordnance is to examine and keep all the Accounts of Stores and Cash, as a Check upon the Storekeeper and Treasurer; ta make out the Quarter Books and Debentures for all the Payments, pursuant to the Bills transmitted to him from the Surveyor General; and to make out Imprests pursuant to the Orders of the Master Gene* ral or Board; which Imprests may be signed by any Three of the Board Officers. — This Officer keeps an Account of the Sums imprested; and it is a Part of his Duty to call upon those Persons to whom Money has been advanced on Account, to clear their Accounts.

The Storekeeper has the Custody, and keeps the Account, of the Ordnance and Stores at the Tower — The Storekeepers at the Out Ports and Garrisons have the Custody, and keep the Accounts, of the Ordnance and Stores committed to their Charge, and transmit their Accounts of the Receipts and Issues to the Board, which are examined by the Storekeeper and Clerk of the Ordnance jointly.

The Clerk of the Deliveries superintends and keeps the Account of the Issues of the Ordnance and Stores: He prepares, pursuant to the Directions of the Board, an Instrument, called " A Proportion," directed to any Storekeeper, authorizing him to deliver certain Stores to Persons therein named; this Instrument must be signed by any Three Board Officers. He takes a Receipt for the Stores, which is generally an Engagement to account for them. — Upon every

9 Receipt

24 Geo. III. n° jfumi.

Receipt or Return of Stores, the Account of them is taken by the Storekeeper, Surveyor, and Clerk of the Ordnance. — The Storekeeper keeps a Journal of the Receipts, Returns, and Issues, from which he forms his Ledger; the Clerk of the Ordnance keeps a Check Ledger, which he forms from his ow n Journal of the Receipts and Returns, and from the Journal of the Clerk of the Deliveries of the Issues. — It is not usual for the Storekeeper to pass any Account; but upon the Resignation or Death of a Storekeeper, a general Survey and Remain is taken of the Ordnance and Stores at the Tower, and is made a Charge upon the Successor. — The Storekeeper at the Out Ports send to the Board every Year an Account of their Receipts, Issues, and Remains. — All the original Authorities for Payments, Contracts, and Securities, and all the Vouchers for the Bills, are preserved in the Record Room in the White Tower, under the Clerk of the Ordnance; the Receipts for the Deliveries are kept by the Clerk of the Deliveries.

The Orders under which the Board of Ordnance act are, Warrants from the King or Privy Council; and, in Sea Affairs, from the Admiralty; Letters from Secretaries of State, and Significations from the Master General. — The Warrants and Letters must be directed to the Master General, and he directs the Board to carry them into Execution; from this Direction of the Master General the Board derive ‘ their Authority to^act; when there is no Master General, these Instruments are directed to the Lieutenant General, and the rest of the principal Officers. — The Regulations and Instructions by which the Office of Ordnance is at present governed, are those of the Year 1683, which, with very few Alterations, have been confirmed at the Beginning of every Reign since that Time.

Since the Resolution, no Offices in the Department of the Ordnance have been allowed to be executed by Deputy.

The Terms of the Contracts for making Gunpowder are these: — The Board supply the Contractor with Eighty Pounds of double-refined Saltpetre; h6 agrees to make that Quantity into & Barrel of Gunpowder of One hundred Pounds Weight, to pass such Proof as the Board shall think proper; for which fie is to be paid One Pound Seven Shillings and Six Pence.

The Terms of the Contract for Iron Ordnance are these: — The Contractor is bound to cast them agreeably to Moulds delivered to him by the Board, at Eighteen Pounds a Ton, subject to such Survey and Proof as the Board shall direct.

N° 9.

The Examination of William Nettleshipp, Esquire, First Clerk to the Clerk of the Ordnance; taken upon Oath, December 15th, 16th, 23d, and 24th, 1783.

This Examinant saith, That he is First Clerk to the Clerk of the Ordnance; he has been in that Department since the Year 1762, and was appointed First Clerk in June 1782. Formerly the Office of Clerk of the Ordnance included the Business of the Secretary (which was called the Minuting Department) as well as the Business of the Accountant. From the 1st of January last the Business of the Secretary has been separated from the Clerk of the Ordnance, and now forms a distinct Branch. — Keeping the Accounts of various Branches of the Ordnance is the present Business of the Clerk of the Ordnance. The Annual Estimate is drawn up in this Office; it contains the Sum that will probably be wanted for the Service during the Year, and the Sum wanted to defray Services performed and not provided for. After it is voted, an Estimate of the Sums that will probably be wanted for each Mopth, distinguishing the current Services from Payments in Course, is drawn up in this Office, and transmitted to the Treasury pursuant to their Requisition. The Monthly Memorial contains the Sum stated in that general Estimate for the Month. — The Treasurer, as soon as he has received the Sum, notifies it to this Office and to the Secretary. — These Sums, im-prested from the Exchequer, are kept under Tw?o Heads — the Land, and the Sea Service. The Annual Estimate contains the Money for the Land Service only; that for the Sea Service is £. 5 per Cent. of the Money voted for the Seamen, and is included in the Monthly Estimates. — After every Board, where there has been an Alteration in the Cash, the Treasurer gives the CJerk of the Ordnance an Account of the State of his Cash, with his Receipts and Payments since his last Account; and a similar Account every Month. — The Directions to the Treasurer, to receive the Sums contained in his Voluntary Charge, originate in this Office. — These Sums are, the estimated Value of such Stores as are deficient or wanting at the Time when the Accounts of the Person to whom they have been intrusted are examined — Sums arising from the Sale of old Stores — Sums remaining unpaid, in a Debenture containing Payments to various Persons: The Treasurer takes Credit for the whole Sum therein contained, and charges himself with the Sum not paid — some Rents of Lands and Houses belonging to the Ordnance — and every Payment not included under the Heads of Imprests from the Exchequer, or Imprests Vacated. Where Stores are intrusted, the

Vo l. 40.

Account of them is, as he believes, usually taken by an Officer of the Ordnance at the Out Port, and transmitted to this Office, where the Deficiency is estimated. — Upon every Sale of Old Stores the Board in general attend. — The Imprests Vacated, are either Deductions from Debentures, or Sums which the Treasurer is directed to receive by Letters from the Board. — Where Sums have been imprested, and Part only expended, the Clerk of the Ordnance settles the Account, and the Board direct the Balance to be paid to the Treasurer. Where a Sum is advanced to any Person who is paid upon a Quarter Book, this Imprest is vacated in like Manner upon the Quarter Book. — All Debentures are made out in this Office from Bills transmitted from the Office of the Surveyor General, and signed by him. All the Expenditures are examined in the Office of the Surveyor General. — A complete Bill, containing the Stores received, or Services performed, with their Price and Computation, is sent to this Office, where the Bill is reduced into the Form of a Debenture; and if the Person entitled has received Money by way of Imprest, such Imprests are inserted in the Margin. If he is indebted for Stores, the Sum he owes is likewise inserted in the Margin, and is entered by the Treasurer in his Voluntary Charge. — All Debentures are paid pursuant either to Letters or Lists — those paid in consequence of Letters are called ready Money Debentures, or those which the Board have agreed to pay as soon as they are enabled to do it — those paid by Lists are called Debentures in Course. The Persons entitled to these Debentures know, when they contract, that no Time is limited for the Payment; and that they are to be paid as their Debentures come in Course of Time for Payment — At every Board the Clerk of the Ordnance lays before them the State of the Cash, and an Account of such Ready Money Debentures as require Payment, and such Sums as ought to be advanced on Account- — he prepares the Official Letters to the Treasurer for the Payment of such Sums as they direct. — These Ready Money Debentures are principally for Transport Service, Home Freight, and Salaries. When the State of the Cash is sufficient, the Clerk of the Ordnance lays before the Board an Account of the Amount of the Debentures made out in Course, for as many of those Months, next the Month last paid, as the Cash, from the then State of it, will probably be sufficient to discharge.

The Board determine how many Months they will pay, always taking them in Course. — A List of the Debentures of those Months is made out by the Clerk of the Ordnance, and transmitted, signed by him, to the Treasurer — the original List, signed by the Board, is kept in this Office. — In general, the Debts due from the Ordnance carry no Interest; — at this Time there are Two Kinds that carry Interest — some Ready Money Debentures, and certain Sums becoming due on Contracts, which (the Board being unable to discharge them) were, by the Consent of the Creditors, converted into a Security, called an Imprest, signed by the Board; by which they engage to pay Interest at £.5 perCent. for the Sum therein mentioned, from a certain Day therein named — these Imprests are in Course of Payment. — The other Debt carrying Interest, is One Third Part of the Sums due for Iron Ordnance, at £. 5 per Cent, to a limited Time, pursuant to an Agreement between the Board and the Gun-founders, by the Directions of the Treasury. — The Month next in Course of Payment is September 1781. — No Debentures are made out but pursuant to Bills transmitted from the Office of the Surveyor General, and allowed by him; after they are made out, they remain in the Office of the Clerk of the Ordnance until they are either applied for, or ordered for Payment; they are then laid before the Board to be signed, and delivered to the Proprietors. — A List of all L1 the

tftfe Debentures, both Ready Money and in Course, ordered for Payment, is hung up in the Office. The List of Ready Money Debentures laid before the Board for Payment usually contains all the Debentures made out each Month, except such as require more immediate Payment by the Terms of the Contract, as for Transport Service and Salaries; these are laid before the Bbard as soon as made out The Date of the Debenture is not the Time it is made out, but the Time the Service is performed. — The Date of the Authority which directs the Debenture to be made out, is usually inserted in it — That Authority must be either the Order of the Master General, or the Board, or the Privy Council, or the King’s Sign Manual. A Debenture is often not made out until long after the Service is performed, as where the Surveyor General has a Difficulty in making out the Account, or Objections are niade to it: As soon as can be, after the Bill is sent to the Office of the Clerk of the Ordnance, the Debenture for it is made out. The Heads under which the Accounts of the Payments are kept in the Ledgers are, as near as possible, the Heads of the Estimate delivered to the House of Commons. The Two Quarter Books, in the Civil and Military Branches, are made out of course in this Office every Quarter; they contain the Titles of the Offices, the Names of the Officers, and their respective Salaries. The Military Quarter Book contains the complete Establishment of the Corps of Engineers; they are all appointed by Commission, and have Pay according to their Rank; their Commissions are entered in this Office: — The Civil Quarter Book contains the Master General, the Board Officers, and Officers under them, and some others whose Duty is mixt, consisting both of Land and Sea Service. — Where the Duty of the Officer is either by Land or Sea only, or he is upon a Foreign Establishment, he is paid by Debenture. — The Officers in the Civil Branch are appointed either by Patent, Warrant, or Signification by the Master General or Order; all of which are entered with the Clerk of the Ordnance; and each Office has its Salary annexed to it Where it is necessary that Money should be advanced for any Service, the Board direct the Clerk of the Ordnance to make out an Instrument called an Imprest, which contains the Sum to be advanced, the Name of the Person, and the Service; this Imprest is signed by the Board, and delivered to the Person entitled. The Expenditure of all Money issued upon Account is examined in the Office of the Surveyor General. Before the Treasurer’s Ledger is sent to the Office of the Auditor, all the Articles in the Charge are examined by the correspondent Entries in this Office, and the Articles of his Payments are examined with the Debentures and Quarter Books by the Board. — The Treasurer’s List of Letters is examined by the Letters themselves — after this Examination each Quarterly Account in the Ledger is signed by the Board, together with the Amount of the Imprest, Voluntary Charge, and Imprest Vacated.

N* 10.

The Examination of William Nettleshipp, Esquire; taken upon Oath, March 17th, 26th, 31st, April 20th, 21st, 23d, and 26th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That the Annual Estimate consists of Two Branches — the Ordinary, and the Extraordinary. The Ordinary comprehends the perma-

nent Establishments, and the computed probable Sums that will be wanted for certain usual Services; the Computations for these Services are made upon what has been found to be the usual Expenditure for such Services: The Extraordinaries consist of Sums not permanent, Sums that will probably be wanted in various Garrisons, both in Great Britain and elsewhere, and for other Services; the Calculations of these Expences are grounded either upon Estimates of the Engineer relative to the Works, or the usual Annual Expence of particular Services. — Every Annual Estimate since the Year 1720 has been attended with an Account of Services performed and not provided for: These Services have been in general either not foreseen, or such as have exceeded the Sums provided for them. Several of them have been foreseen, and yet, by the Custom of Office, have been omitted to be provided for: But the Estimates for the Years 1783 and 1784 were formed on- the Principle of avoiding, as much as possible, the Necessity of coming to Parliament with an Account of unprovided Services; every probable Expence, as far as was foreseen, having been brought forward in those Estimates.

The £. 5 per Cent, of the Money voted for the Seamen, has not, during the late war, discharged the Expence of the Ordnance for Sea Service; in One of the Years it appeared to have been deficient above Two hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds: It is very difficult to keep an accurate and distinct Account of it, because the Services are frequently blended together; but as distinct an Account as can conveniently be, is kept in the Office. — The State of the Debt of the Ordnance, annexed to the Estimate, comprehends the Debt incurred by the Ordnance, not provided for in the Year preceeding the Estimate, and also the Debt incurred in former Years, and not provided for; the Debts included in this Account have some of them not been inserted in the Accounts of Services performed and not provided for, annexed to the Estimates of the preceding Years; those that have been inserted remain unpaid. — The Monthly Estimate to the Treasury contains a Monthly Division of Three Sums: — The £.5 per Cent, for the Sea Service — the Sum voted upon the Estimate for the Land Service — and the Sum voted for the unprovided Services of the preceding Year. — The Imprest Ledger is kept by the Clerk of the Ordnance; no Account of any Article in that Ledger is given officially to the Board, unless they call for it, or unless any particular Circumstance renders it necessary to produce it to them. — The Clerk of the Ordnance has never, in his Knowledge, of himself called upon any Sub-Accountant to clear his Imprest.

The Clerk of the Ordnance keeps an Account of the Receipts and Issues of all Stores — He takes his Account of the Receipts at the Tower, by his Receiving Clerk; and of the Issues, from the Clerk of the Deliveries — He takes his Account of the Receipts and Issues of Stores at the Out Ports and Garrisons from the Ledger transmitted from those Store-keepers to the Clerk of the Ordnance, with the Vouchers.

Where a Debenture contains a Payment for Services, some of which are Land and some Sea Services, it is expressed in the Debenture to be for that Service for which the greatest Part of the Expence is incurred. — During the last War, the Commissaries and Paymasters of the Artillery Abroad have drawn upon the Board of Ordnance for the Subsistence of the Artillery, and sometimes the Board have remitted Money to them for that Service; these Sums have all been charged to the Agent for the Artillery in England, who receives the Agency, and settles the Accounts with the Commissary, and passes his own Accounts in the Office of the Surveyor General. — The Two Lists of Insupers, transmitted from this Board to the Office of Ordnance, have been examined, as far as they could 2 be,

About September 1782 the Master General called for an Account of the Establishment of the Ordnance, and of the Salaries paid on the Ordinary, and all Allowances made by the Board to each Officer; having received such an Account, he new modelled the Establishment, and regulated the Salaries of every Officer, and then procured His Majesty’s Warrant for the Abolition of al! Gratuities, Fees, and Rewards, except in the Instances therein mentioned, and the Substitution of certain Salaries in their Stead.

Order of the Board: This Proportion is signed by any Three Board Officers, entered in the Proportion Book in this Office, and then delivered to the Storekeeper, as his Warrant for the Issue. — The Issuing Clerk, who is the Second Clerk in this Office, having entered in the Issuing Book the Articles contained in the Proportion, carries that Book to the Storekeeper, and receives those Articles from him, sees them packed, sends them away, and takes a Receipt from the Person intrusted to convey them; which Receipt is kept by the Clerk of- the Deliveries, as his Voucher. The Storekeeper at an Out Port issues Ordnance and Stores.pursuant to the Orders, either of the Board, or of the Commanding Admiral, or of the Commanding Officer in that District. The Board send their Orders, either in consequence of Letters from the Board of Admiralty, in which Case they send them to the Storekeeper at the Out Port, without the Intervention of the Clerk of the Deliveries; or upon an Application of the Commanding Officer of any Regiment, in which Case the Board order a Proportion for the usual Supply to be drawn by the Clerk of the Deliveries, who sends it to the Storekeeper at the Out Port. — Every Quarter every Storekeeper at the Out Ports sends to the Clerk of the Deliveries Accounts of all the Issues made by him during that Quarter, in consequence of the Orders either of the Board or of the Commanding Admiral or Commanding Officer, with the Vouchers ' for such Issues, signed generally by the Storekeeper, Clerk of the Survey, and Clerk of the Checque: — The Clerk of the Deliveries draws a Proportion for each Voucher, which, when signed by the Board, and entered in the Proportion Book, is sent down to the Storekeeper, as his Justification, and is transmitted by him to the Out Port Ledger-keeper, with the Ledger and Vouchers.

N* 13.

GEORGE R.

Whereas We have thought fit, by Our Letters Patent, under Our Great Seal of Great Britain, bearing Date the Tenth Day of this Instant April, to constitute and appoint Our Trusty and Well-beloved Charles Frederick, Esquire, to be Master Surveyor of Our Ordnance, Ammunition, and Habiliments of War, within Our Tower of London, Our Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, and all other Our Dominions, during Our Pleasure; We do by these Presents nominate, constitute, and appoint the said Charles Frederick, Esquire, to be Assistant and Deputy to Our Lieutenant General of Our Ordnance for the Time being, in such Manner as Sir Henry Shercy Knight, John Charlton, William Bridges, Michael Richards, Esquires, Colonel John Armstrong, and Colonel Thomas Lascellesy were heretofore nominated, constituted, and appointed; and, in the Absence of the said Lieutenant General of the Ordnance for the Time being, to do, execute, and perform all Matters to the said Office or Place of Our Lieutenant General of Our Ordnance belonging, in as ample Manner, to all Intents and Purposes, as the Lieutenant General of Our Ordnance for the Time being could or might have done, if he were actually present, and as fully and freely as Sir Hemy Shere9 Knight, John Charltony William Bridges, and Michad Richards, Esquires, Colonel John Armstrongy and Colonel Thomas Lascelles, or any former Deputy or Deputies, had enjoyed, or exercised, the said Office or Deputation: We have also thought fit to authorize and require you to cause an Allowance to be made unto him the said Charles Frederick, out of the Treasury of Our Ordnance, of the Sum of Three hundred Pounds per Annum, to be paid to him the said Charles Frederick, or his Assigns, Quarterly, by equal Proportions, Bill, and Debenture, according to the Usage of Our said Office, and in such Manner as the same was allowed and paid to the said Sir Henry Shere9 John Charlton, William Bridges, Michael Richards, John Armstrong, and Thomas Lascelles; the said Allowance to commence and be accounted from the Day of the Date hereof, and to continue during Our Pleasure: And for so doing this shall be, as well to you as to the Auditors of Our Imprests, and all others whom it may concern, a full and sufficient Warrant Given at Our Court at St. James s, the Eleventh Day of April 1750, in the Twenty-third Year of Our Reign.

By His Majesty’s Command,

Bedford.

This Examinant saith, That he has frequently, since the Year 1775, supplied the Ordnance with Transports, sometimes in consequence of Advertisements, sometimes by the Intervention of a Broker, and sometimes by Means of the Superintendant of Shipping.

In the Year 1776 he let to the Ordnance the I/yrd

Torwnshend Transport, Captain Spence, of about Seven hundred Tons — she continued in the Service about Thirty Months; her freight amounted to about Eighteen thousand Four hundred and Sixty Pounds. All the Fees, Expences, and Gratuities, paid by him to Persons employed by the Ordnance Office in consequence of this Contract, amounted to about One hundred and Ninety Pounds. — In the Year 17S0 he let to them the Raynham Hall, Captain Butcher, of about the same Burthen; her freight, for about Twenty Months, was about Twelve thousand Two hundred Pounds; the like Expences in consequence of this Contract amounted to Three hundred and Eighty-two Pounds; the Increase of this Expence arose from Two Articles — he paid to a Person in the Ordnance Office a Gratuity of One hundred Pounds for procuring the Contract, and he also paid One hundred and Twenty-two Pounds, being at the Rate of One per Cent. upon the Freight, to an Agent, who was a Person employed in the Ordnance; — in his Contract for the Lord Torwnshend he did not employ an Agent. — In the year 1782 he let to them the Juliana, Captain iVUliam, nearly of the same Burthen; her Freight for Twelve Months was about Six thousand Two hundred Pounds; the Expences of this Contract amounted to Ninety-six Pounds,- of which Sixty Pounds was for Agency; before the rest of the Fees were paid, a Regulation in the Office relative to the Payment of Fees took place. — He never considered himself as bound by the Valuations of his Ships taken by the Ordnance Officers, unless he signed them: — Some of the Valuations he has sighed, others he has refused to sign, and some he has not seen. He has lost only One Ship, for which ^the Ordnance have paid him, and for that he was paid according to the Valuation.

N* 15.

The Examination of Mr. John Thornpson; taken upon Oath, January 26th and February 2d 1784,

This Examinant saith, That in the Year 1776 he first supplied the Board of Ordnance with Ships, and has frequently since that Time furnished them with such as they wanted. — Whenever he found that they were in want of Ships, and he had them ready, he wrote Letters to the Board offering to supply them, and mentioning his Terms. — He has now some Ships in their Service, but all of them, as he believes, hired before the Year 1783. After a Ship is taken up, and completely fitted out, she is valued, usually at Graves-endy by Officers of the Ordnance: He was never himself present at the Valuation of any of his Ships. — When he first furnished the Ordnance with Ships, the Valuation was generally produced to him before the Ship sailed; and if he approved of it he signed it, and was then bound to abide by that Valuation: For these Two or Three last Years, the Valuations of his Ships have not been produced to him as usual, and consequently he has not considered himself as bound by those Valuations Three or Four of his Ships have been taken, and he has been paid for them according to their Valuations, though he had not signed them, having no Objection, upon the Whole, to the Valuations, taken together, One of the Ships being valued as much Vql, 40.

above, as another was under the real Value. — Before Twelfth the late Regulations in the Ordnance Office, all Report the Expences attending the letting to them a Ship °n ?ubIlc of Four hundred Tons, amounted to about One ccoun s’ hundred and Forty or One hundred and Fifty Pounds. — No Fees of any Kind were demanded; but he understood upon Enquiry, that it was Customary to give Gratuities in the different Departments; these Gratuities amounted to about Thirty-five Pounds; the rest was Agency, to a Person employed in the Ordnance, of One per Cent. upon the Freight, and a Gratuity to the Superintendent appointed by the Board, who sails with the Ship, and cotitrouls the-Captain. Since the Regulation no Gratuities have been paid at the Ordnance Office, nor any other Payment made, except the Agency, and to the Superintendent, above-mentioned. — The Consideration for the Agency is, the expediting the Business of each Contract through the several Departments of the Ordnance, a Communication when the Board are in want of Ships, and When Money is teady to be paid.

N* 16.

The Examination of Thomas Dickinson, Esquire, Superintendant of Shipping to the Office of the Ordnance; taken upon Oath, 21st January, 2d and 4th February, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Superintendant of Shipping to the Board of Ordnance; he was appointed to that Office in June 1781. For about the first Six Months of hb being in this Office, in consequence of Directions from the Board, he procured for them such Ships as they required; ever since that Time, the Board have advertised for Ships, at hb Recommendation, and the Proposals laid before the Board have been sent to him, that he might examine the Ship, and report to the Board whether she was fit for the Service. — Where no Ships have been tendered in pursuance of the Advertisements, the Board have directed him to look out for Ships. — The Proposals generally contain the Time of Service, and the Rate per Ton; he gives to the Board his Opinion upon these Terms, and they decide upon them. — The Agreement for the Payment of Freight for the Hire of Ships has been, during this War, to pay Two Months in Advance, and Two , Months Pay at the End of every Four Months after the Expiration of the first Two Months.

The principal Persons he has contracted with for Shipping have been Sir William James, Mr. Angerstein, Mr. Thompson, Mr. Thackary, and Mr. Hubbard. — If the Ships were employed in the Service longer than the Time mentioned in the Charter Party, they continued upon the same Terms as are mentioned in that Instrument. — After a Ship is completely fitted out, the Ship, her Rigging, and her Stores, are valued, almost always at Gravesend; an Inventory of all her Rigging and Stores is taken on the Part of the Ordnance by the Superintendant, the Purveyor, a Clerk from the Surveyor’s Office, a Clerk from the Office of the Clerk of the Ordnance^ and a Person appointed by the Board to assist in valuing the Rigging and Stores. — The Owner or Master may attend at taking thb Inventory if he thinks proper, but it has not been customary to give him Notice of the Time of the Valuation — The same Persons assist in forming a M m Valuation

twelfth Report on Public Accounts.

iH.

Valuation of the Rigging and other Articles. — The Ship is valued by the Superintendant, the Purveyor, and the Person assisting in taking the Inventory. — The Valuation is . sighed by all the Persons taking the Inventory, and lodged in the Office of the Clerk of the Ordnance. — If the Ship is taken or destroyed by the Enemy, the Sum stated to be her Value in that Valuation, is paid to , the Owner, deducting Eight Shillings Ton per Annum for the Wear and Tear. — The usual covenant in the Charter Party is, That the Ship is not to be discharged until her Arrival at Deptford, and after a few Days Notice. — Upon her Arrival at any Port in England, unless she is wanted for the Service, she is ordered immediately to Deptford. — The Rate at which a Ship is valued is according to her Age, Condition, Place where built, and the Price of Shipping at the Time. — Since he has been appointed Superintendant, Five Ordnance Storeships and Six Cutters have been taken by the Enemy, and Three Ships sunk at Gibraltar; all of which were valued by him, and, except one, not yet settled, the Owners have been paid for them according to those Valuations.

Since the late Regulation he has been paid by a Salary of One hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year, in lieu of all Fees, Perquisites, and Gratuities whatever.

The? Dickinson.

The Examination of William Adam, Esquire; taken upon Oath, February 6th, 10th, and 11 tb, 17 84*

This Examinant saith, That in the Year 1781, he entered into a Contract with the Board of Ordnance, in consequence of an Advertisement, for the Delivery of Eight millions of Bricks, cither at the Gun Wharf at Chatham, or within a certain limited Distance of the Works, at One Guinea a Thousand for the Bricks, and Three Shillings per Thousand for the Carriage: The whole Quantity, and more, have been made and delivered, and he has received Imprests to the Amount of them. — The Check on the Part of the Ordnance, upon the Execution of this Contract, was, the Principal Engineer, and the Officers under him. He received the Money due to him, from Time to Time, from the Treasurer of the Ordnance.

He was appointed in December 1781, by the Signification of the Master General, to succeed the late Mr. Morris as Master Carpenter: Under this Appointment he supplied the Ordnance with a Part of the Timber and Deals, for Exportation and for Home Consumption, to a very considerable Amount, and did all the Carpenters Work in particular Districts, under the Direction of the Board of Ordnance. The whole Demand for these Materials and Work, partly tinder the Signification of the Year 1781, and partly under new Contracts entered into last Year, in consequence of public Advertisements, have amounted to, ate he believes* above Fifty thousand Pounds — for these he was to be paid by Debentures in Course; but be has received, upon Application to the Board, < Imprests, from Time to Time, in Part of Payment, to the Amount of Seven thousand Pounds. He has beep informed, and believes, that the Ordnance Debentures have been lately offered to Sale at Thirty-three per Cent. Discount. There is in every District

The Examination of Colonel Matthew Divert] taken upon Oath, March 24th and 26th 1784.

This Examinant saith, He has been employed aa Commanding Engineer at Plymouth ever since the Year 1777. It was his Business, by virtue of that Appointment, to superintend the Construction and Ue^ pairs of all the Fortifications in that Division. The Commanding Engineer receives his Directions either from the Master General or the Board of Ordnance, relative to any Project approved of by them; he forma an Estimate* of the Expence, according to the Prices established by the Board for different Species of Work, and transmits that Estimate to them. — The Prices from which Estimates have generally been hi- therto formed, were established several Years ago, and taken from Proposals then delivered in to the Board pursuant to Advertisements. — Since October last the Prices of some of the material Species of Works have been reduced, more reasonable Terms having been delivered in to the Board, in consequence of Advertisements. — By the Order of the Master General and Board, lie formed an Estimate for the Works ift the Plymouth Division for the Year 1784; he sent thd Original to the Master General, and a Duplicate to the Board — that Estimate was formed upon the old Prices, the Alterations in the Prices not having beer* then communicated to him; he is now, pursuant to Orders from the Master General* forming a nc\* Estimate for the same Works at the reduced Prices. — No Part of a Work is executed, or Materials for any Work provided, without the express Direction iw^ Writing of the Master General or the Board.

The several Species of Work, except the Day La^ hour, are executed by Contract. — The Execution \i superintended by the Commanding Engineer, and the subaltern Engineers and Overseers under him. — Theso Engineers and Overseers are appointed, and their Pay settled, by the Master General. They every Day make Reports to the , Commanding Engineer, in Writing, signed by One or more of them, as to the Day Labour and Repairs, of the Progress ;of the Work at their several Stations, specifying the Materials expended and the Persons employed. — The Engineer or Overseer who superintends a Work to be paid for by Measure, ftvery Week reports to the Commanding 6 Engineer

The Examination of Major William Congreve, of the Royal Artillery; taken upon Oath, March 5th, lbth, and 22d, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Deputy Comptroller of the King’s Laboratory at Weolvich, during the Absence of the Comptroller, and was appointed to this Office in April 1783. It is a Part of his Duty to attend the„ Proof of all Gunpowder made use of by Government. — This Proof is made At Purfieet only, before it is received into the Magazines as serviceable, hr paid for. — The Gunpowder is either newly made, bt returned back from Ships of War, or foreign Gar* fisons, to be re-proved.

When a Proof becomes necessary, the Board of Ordnance direct the Deputy Comptroller to attend at Purfieet at a certain Time; the Officers who attend with him are, the Chief Fire Master, the Assistant fire Master, and the Three Ordnance Officers at

Purfieet, the Storekeeper, the Clerk oiF the Survey, Twelfth and the Clerk of the Checque. — Formerly the Mode of Proof was the raising a given Weight, in d Frame AccouQt^ called a Vertical Eprouvette; by a given- Quantity of *

Powder; but this Mode has, by a Course of Experiments lately made by Order of Lord Townshend' been found not to be a certain Proof of the Goodness of the Powder; for a Powder that with Two Drachms raised the Vertical Eprouvette Four Inches and Five Tenths, with. Three Pounds, in a Thirteen Inch JMor-tar, tanged the Shell One thousand One hundred and Three. Yards; and a Powder that with the same Quantity raised the Eprouvette only One Inch and Nine Tenths, with Three Pounds, in a Thirteen Inch Mortar, ranged the Shell One thousand One hundred and7.Twelve Yards. — A Report of these Experiments* drawn up and signed by him and the Two Fire Mas* ters, he delivered' to Lw&Tatcnshend; a Copy of it, signed by himself, is now before the Board of Ord^ nance,-for them to settle the 'Mode of Proof for the future. — Hence it appears, that great Quantities of Powder proved by the former Method (the only esta-Wkhefl' Mode to prove the Strength of Government Powder, as appears by the Copies of the official Papers subjoined^ which were probably fit for Service* may have been condemnedy and either sold as unser* viceable, or Used in Triumph, or the Saltpetre extracted, to be worked up again at Feversham and near Eleven thousand Bamis of foreign* Powder, nbw ini the Magazines* are condemned, great Part of which* when proved by Mortars, may probably be found fit for the heavy Artillery for Land Service* which will* save Government a considerable Sum of Money. — After a Proof at Purfieet, a Report is made to the Master General and Board of the Quantity of Powder proved, and the State of it; this* Report is signed by the De* puty Comptroller, the Two Fire Masters, and the Storekeeper. The Powder is not received into the Magazines as serviceable, until the Board direct it, in consequence of that Report.

The only Manufactory for Gunpowder, belonging to Government, is at Feversham; the rest of the Gunpowder is made by Powder Merchants or Contrac* tors.

The great Deposit for the Government Gunpowder, in this Part of the Kingdom, is at Purfieet; — it con*, -sists of Five. Magazines, at the Distance of Fifty-eight Feet from each other; Four of them are calciK Iated to contain Thirty-eight thousand Four hundred Darrels; the other is intended only for laying Powder dovVn for Proof. Shook! any one of these Magazines* be blown up, it is scarcely possible* but they must all be btoWrt up.- — By the last Return of the respective Officers of the Ordnance at Puijleet, dated the i3tte Instant, the Quantity of Powder then in Store was . 17th March 1784.

The MODE of preparing Gunpowder for Proof at Purfieet; together with ail Account of the Marks made Use of at that Office, to distinguish it afterwards.

When Powder is received at the King’s. Magazines at Purfieet, whether Merchants, Returned, 4r,

it is stacked in Bays separately; the Weighing of the Returned from the Shipping being first attended to by the Clerk of the Survey, allowing One hundred and Two Pounds for every Whole Barrel, and Fifty-one Pounds for every Half Barrel; it having been found that One hundred Pounds, being but Six Weeks at Sea, has gained Two Pounds in One hundred Pounds, by the Damps, 85c. of the Ship.

When a Proof is ordered, it is separately laid down, for that Purpose. The Merchants and Parcel by Parcel, is sent into the Proof House in a Box, with Six Thimbles, from Six Barrels, to burn on the Plates, and the same in another Box to try in the Eprouvette; then a State is sent from the Proof House to the Magazines, specifying which of these Six are passed as Extra, Sea or Land, Triumph, and Crossed; which are marked on the Barrels accordingly. The Returned is first hand-proved; and such as is not condemned by that Method, is sent into the Proof House in the Manner described, and from thence into the Magazines, to be marked as before — it is then stacked up distinctly, every Parcel of Powder as proved, distinguishing the Passed, Triumph, and Crossed, in order to lay down more for Proof.

The next Process is to get up the -Powder; which is done after this Manner: — The Merchants Powder that is Crossed, is headed up in order to be returned them when sent for: The Passed Powder of the Merchant* is then shifted into King’s Barrels, Whole or Half, Copper or Hazle: — The Feoersham and Returned, Passed, and Triumph, the same. — The Barrels that the Crossed Powder is in are tared, and the Powder shifted back

Sinto them — then the Clerk of the Survey attends the Weighing, $c. of the Whole, both Passed, nph, and Crossed, allowing to a Whole Barrel One hundred Pounds, and to Half a Barrel Fifty Pounds. The Passed for Sea and Land is sent to Tilbury with the utmost Dispatch, by a general Order of the Board, and elsewhere if a particular Order; the Extra to Woolwich, or the Tower, as demanded; the Triumph and Crossed as demanded.

N* 20.

The Examination of Major Thomas Blomefield; taken upon Oath, March 10th and 16th

1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Inspector of Artillery, and was appointed to that Office in March 1780. By that Appointment it is his'Duty to examine all Guns designed for His Majesty's Service, and to make his Report upon them to the Master General and Lieutenant General of the Ordnance; and to inspect all Foreign Arms, Powder, or Military Stores, that may be contracted for by the Board of Ordnance.

By the King’s Warrant, of the Year 1783, he is also directed to superintend the Proof of Guns; which Duty was, before that Time, executed by the Surveyor General and Proof Masters. — All Brass Ordnance are now cast at the Royal Foundry at Wool-wich; all Iron Ordnance are cast by Contract, at Foundries in different Parts of the Kingdom, and are to be delivered at Woolwich to the Charge of the Storekeeper, who gives the Inspector of Artillery an Account of the Number and Nature of those he has received. — The Examination is performed by certain Instruments; One of which, invented by the late General Desaguiliers, is calculated to discover any Error in the Form of the Bore, or in its Position; and by other Instruments, to discover whether it is constructed in every Respect conformable to the Draft sent to the Gun Founder as his Pattern. — The Gun is then laid down for Proof; it is fired on Two different Days, and searched after each Firing, in order to discover any Flaws or Holes. — It is then proved by forcing Water into the Bore; after which, the inward Surface

is inspected, by throwing into it a sufficient Quantity of Light, which frequently discovers concealed Defects that escape every other Examination.

The Founder is subject, by his Contract, to have all his Guns laid down for Proof rejected, upon the Discovery of a concealed Defect in any One of them.

If the Gun stands these Proofs to a sufficient Degree of Precision, in the Judgment of the Inspector, he reports it* as proper to be received into His Majesty’s Stores; if it does not stand the Examination and Proof, a Cross is cut upon it, and it is returned to the Founder. — There are generally from One hundred and Twenty to One hundred and Thirty Guns laid'down for Proof at One Time. — Previous to the Appointment of General Desaguiliers to the Office of Inspector of the Artillery, a very superficial Examination, if any, was given to the Guns, previous to their Proof; for many that were received have since been condemned as defective; and the usual Proof was by Fire and the Searcher. — The First Day’s Proof was made by the Surveyor General and Civil Officers only; on the Second the Board used to attend. — This Duty is now taken from the Civil Department, and intrusted to Military Officers. — The Inspector, Assistant Inspector, and Proof Master, who assist in the whole Process, are Officers of the Artillery.

It is his Duty to examine all Brass and Iron Ordnance used in His Majesty’s Service, and report whether they are proper to be retained in the Service, or condemned as unserviceable. All Brass Ordnance undergo the like Examination and Proof, except that in some Instances the Water Proof has been dispensed with.

Tho. Blomefield.

T. Anguish,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Wiltr Roe.

This Sum is all that* is now wanted; but being for Repairs, it is impossible to ascertain what may be wanted in future. To judge from the past, it may amount Annually to nearly the same Suin'.

Colonel Archer, the Engineer, reports, that the completing the Works at Cumberland Fort will amount to £. 20,830. 11. 2.

Colonel Archer's Estimate to complete these Works is £. 101,000; but if other Plans for securing Portsea Island are carried into Execution, it is probable a great Part of this Expence may be saved.

The Engineer, Lieut. Colonel Monadef, being Abroad, the exact Estimate cannot so well be ascertained; but it is supposed may amount to about £. 20,000 more.

To this Expence of the Wall must be added that of a Parapet, which will amount to £.609. 1.

Colonel Moncrief's Estimate to complete this Work, amounts to £.40,676. 5. 11.

O U T H:

This Sum is all that is now wanted; but being for Repairs, it is impossible to ascertain what may be wanted in future; to judge from the past, it may amount Annually to nearly the same Sum.

The Plans and Estimates for the Works at Merri-field are not yet sufficiently settled, so as to fix the precise Sum that will be required to finish them.

H A M:

This Sum is all that is now wanted; but it is impos* sible to ascertain what Repairs may be wanted in future; to judge from the past, it may Annually amount to nearly the same Sum.

The further Expence of completing these Lines will depend upon the System of Fortifications that may be adopted in respect to this Post; but, from the Report of the Engineers, the present Demand seems necessary at all Events.

" It is at present proposed to confine future Works to the principal Dock Yards. — It is computed, that to " render Portsmouth and Plymouth complete will require or £.500,000, which, at £.50,000 per Annum, will " be done in Eight or Ten Years."

The System for Chatham is now under Consideration; until it is determined, no Guess can be made as to the whole Expence that may attend it.

Will. Nettlcshipp.

Twelfth’

Report

on Public; j^o 26

Accounts.

GEORGE R.

Whereas you have represented unto Us, that the present Establishments, in the several Branches of the Ordnance, are in many Repects defective, and ill calculated for carrying on the Business of that Office with Regularity and (Economy, and particularly in respect to the Proofs of Powder and Ordnance, which have lierc-tofore been under the Inspection of the principal Officers and their Clerks, and other inferior Officers, whose frequent Attendance at Woolwich and Purjlect for this Purpose occasioned considerable Expence, and was attended with much Loss of Time, whereby other material Business was neglected:

And you having also represented unto Us, that the Salaries of the Clerks, and others, are in no Degree proportioned to their several Duties, being, in some Instances, multiplied under various Titles, which are mere Sinecures, whilst in other Cases they are very inadequate to the Labour performed; from whence Temptations have arisen to some of the said Persons to take illegal Fees, and to receive unwarrantable Perquisites, under the Pretence of expediting Business, in consequence of which the Charges on' the Public have been necessarily enhanced; and many of the said Clerks have also been induced to act as Agents for Artificers, Contractors, and Persons supplying Stores for the Office of Ordnance, and for others employed therein; by which Means the Business thereof has been subject to great Partiality and Irregularity:

I11 order, therefore, to remedy these Evils, We have thought fit to approve of the Plan of Establishment which you have proposed to Us, hereunto annexed, for the several Branches of the Office of Ordnance, amounting to £.34,457* 1. 6. per Annum; which, notwithstanding the reasonable Increase of Salaries it contains, yet, from Savings in the Expence of Proofs, and other Articles, appears still to be within the Sums heretofore expended for the same Services.

Our Will and Pleasure therefore is, That you cause the said Establishment to be carried into Execution, and that the same shall take place from the 31st of December last.

And whereas the several Salaries contained in the said Establishment are to be considered as a full and ample Compensation for the respective Services to be periotmed; Our Will and Pleasure is, That from henceforth no Gratuity, Fee, or Reward, shall be demanded, received, or taken, under any Pretence whatsoever; nor shall any Agency for any Artificer, Contractor, or Persons supplying Stores for the Office of Ordnance, or for any Person employed therein; nor any Contract, or Share of Contract, for the Supply of Stores, Materials, Work, or Goods of any Kind for the said Office, be permitted or allowed to be held or enjoyed by any Person or Persons possessing any of the Offices in the said Establishment contained: Ex cepting only from this Prohibition, the Agencies to any Officer of the Royal Regiment of Artillery, or Corps of Engineers, the Contract for keeping Bedding in Repair at the several Barracks, and the following Fees, allowed by our Royal Predecessors, or received by ancient Custom; viz.

Junu. 1784.

nifications for Admission, of any Under Minister, Clerk, Artificer, or Tradesman, Four Pounds.

For making out and entering the Commission of any Gunner, or Warrant for any Labourer, or Workmen, either in Our Office of Ordnance, or Armoury, to be borne upon the Quarter Books, Three Pounds.

From each Regiment in Great Britain, for the Annual Delivery of Ammunition, One Pound One Shilling.

From each Regiment, on Delivery of new Anns, One Pound One Shilling.

From each Gunner of Ships of War, for Certificate on settling his Accounts, Ten Shillings and Six Pence.

From each of the Captains of Ships of War, for Certificate on settling the Gunners Accounts, Five Shillings.

And the several accustomed Gratuities received from Persons permitted to see the several Armouries and Places under the Direction of our Board of Ordnance.

With respect to the Proofs of Powder and Ordnance, it is our further Will and Pleasure, That the Superinteiulance of Salt Pctre, and making of Powder, shall, under the Directions of the Master General, or Board of Ordnance, be committed to the Care and Inspection of the Comptroller of our Laboratory at Woohckh: And that all Proofs of Powder shall he made in Presence of Our said Comptroller, the Fire Master, and Assistant Fire Master, or any Two of them, with One of the respective Officers of Our Magazine at Purjlect.

That the Superintendance of casting Brass and Iron Ordnance, and of making Gun Carriages or Mortar Beds, and the preparing Drafts for the same, shall (under the Direction of the Master General, or Board of Ordnance) be committed to the Care of the In spector of our Artillery; and that all Proofs of Ordnance shall be made in the Presence of Our said Inspector, with his Assistant, and the Proof Master, or any Two of them.

And We do hereby confirm the Power heretofore given to you, or the Board of Ordnance, in like Cases, to make such further Alterations as from Time to Time shall be found more agreeable to the Service, provided that the whole of the Establishment and Allowances approved and confirmed by this Our Warrant be not exceeded.

And for so doing this shall be, during Our Will and Pleasure, a sufficient Warrant and Authority, as well to you, as to all other Our Officers and Ministers herein concerned.

Given at our Court at St. Jamess, this 24th Day of January, 1783.

By His Majesty’s Command,

Thomas Tuunshend.

To Our Right Trusty, and Right Entirely beloved Cousin and Counsellor Charles Duke of Richmond, Lenox, and Aubigny,

Master General of Our Ordnance.

Ordered, That if any Person* possessing any of the Offices in the aforesaid Establishment contained, shall hereafter directly or indirectly demand, receive, or take any Gratuity, Fee, or Reward, under any Pretence whatsoever (excepting only such as are included in \he said enumerated List of Fees) he shall be instantly dismissed from the Office he holds, and shall never again be admissible into the same, or any other Office under the Ordnance.

Ordered, That if any Person, possessing any of the Offices in the aforesaid Establishment contained, shall hereafter directly or indirectly hold any Agency for any Artificer, Contractor, or Person supplying Stores for this Office, or for any Person employed therein (excepting only the Agencies to any Officer of the Royal Regiment of Artillery, or Corps of Engineers) he shall be instantly dismissed from the Office he holds, and shall never again be admissible into the same, or any other Office under the Ordnance.

Ordered, That if any Person, possessing any of the Offices in the aforesaid Establishment contained, shall hereafter directly or indirectly hold or ertjoy, or be in any Way concerned in the holding or enjoying, any Contract, or Share of Contract, for the Supply of Stores, Materials, Works, or Goods of any Kind for this Office, he shall be instantly dismissed from the Office he holds, and shall never again be admissible into the same, or any other Office under the Ordnance.

By Order of the Board,

John Boddington, Secrjr.

*The Examination of Mr. John Daniel Lauzun;

„ taken upon Oath, March 17th and 22d 1784.

This Examinant saith. That he is Messenger to the Board of Ordnance, and has been in that Office about4 Thirteen Years. — It is his Business to make certain Payments on Account of the Ordnance; the Persons he is employed to pay are, the Furbishers, the Artificers, and the Labourers at the Tower; he pays likewise the Stoppages of Artificers belonging to the Train of Artillery Abroad, and such other Sums as he is directed to pay by the Board. To enable him to make these Payments, Sums are from Time to Time imprested to him by the Board. When he is in Want of Money, he makes up a State of his Cash, and sends it to the Board, with a Letter desiring a Sbpply.

Three Bills are sent to him every Month for Payment; the Furbishers Bill is sent to him by the Master Furbisher, signed by him and a Clerk in the Office of the Storekeeper; he sends this Bill to the Board, who direct the exact Sum to be imprested to him, to discharge that Bill: — He himself pays the Persons therein named the Sums set opposite their Names, and they either w rite their Names, of set their Marks.

The Artificers Bill is sent to him, signed by the Modeller; he pays the Persons named in this Bill, of Course, upon the Authority of the Signature of the Vol. 40.

O (V

11 Junii.

Modeller. — He receives the Labourers Bill from the Twelfth-Clerk of the Check at the Tower, signed by him; he sends it to the Board; it is returned to him with ^Junis^ an Entry of the Order of the Board directing him to pay it. The Stoppages are paid pursuant to an Order of the Board; and an Imprest Bill is sent to him from the Clerk of thfe (Jrdnance. — All other Payments, except some very small ones of Course, as Postage of Letters, are paid by him in consequence of Orders from the Board.

His Accounts are passed every Six Months, by the Surveyor General, examined by the Clerk of the "Ordnance, and a Debenture made out to vacate his Imprest.

He pays the Land Tax and Window' Tax for the Tower, in consequence of Imprest Bills sent to him by the Board for that Purpose.

The Examination of Richard Bethel Cox, Es-

quire; taken upon Oath, April 2d and 7th

1784.

This Examinant saith, That Messrs. Richard Cox and Arthur Mair were Paymasters of the Artillery, from the Year 1772 to the 30th April 1782, when they were superseded: He w as employed in the Office under his Father Richard Cox, from the Year 1773 the Year 1782; the Cash Account of Messrs.- Cox and Mair with the Board of Ordnance, delivered by him to this Board, and dated the 31st March 1784, contains, to the best of his Knowledge and Belief, a true State of that Account, down to the 30th April 1782.

The Board of Ordnance are at this Time indebted to them in the Sum of Fifteen thousand and Fifty-six Pounds Teh Shillings and Eleven Pence Three Farthings, including their Agency and Salaries. — The Sums issued by the Board of Ordnance to the Paymaster, for the Monthly Subsistence of the Artillery, are computed upon the Establishments in Great Britain and in the Mediterranean; but the Sums issued by him include the Subsistence not only of those Establishments, . but also of Supernumeraries, who are mustered in the Companies of Artillery at Home, in order to recruit the Companies Abroad, and of Soldiers doing Duty at Home, but belonging to Companies Abroad; and for these the Board never issue the Subsistence to the Paymaster, yet the Commanding Officers of the different Detachments and Companies draw upon him for Sums on Account, to pay this Subsistence, for which they return to the Paymaster Monthly Pay Lists, as their Vouchers: The Subsistence of thfcse Supernumeraries and jSbldiera at Home, is considered as a Part of the Subsistence of the Companies iri Aiiierica and in the West Indies; those Companies are paid by Paymasters there appointed by the Board. The Paymaster in Canada receives his Money by Drafts upon the Paymaster in London; the Paymasters in the other Parts of America, and in the West Indies, either draw for their Money upon the Board of Ordnance, or receive it by Remittances from Contractors; all these Sums issued to the Paymasters Abroad; are charged to the Account of the Paymaster at Home, who himself passes their Accounts, and passes his own Account of the Issues and Expenditures of the whole Regiment, in the Office of the Surveyor General. The last Account passed by the Paymaster in England, is an Account of the Year Pp *7/6:

COPY of Part of a Report of the Surveyor General to the Board of Ordnance.

The Plan of a Military Work being approved of, I presume that the next and immediate Considerations are, the Time, and Money requisite to complete it; consequently, that it becomes the Duty of the Board of Ordnance to adopt that Mode of executing the Plan, which is attended with the greatest Dispatch and least Expence. There are Two Ways of carrying on Works in the Ordnance; one by Measure and Contract, the other by Day Work; both under the Controul of the Engineer: In the First, the Work is measured on the Spot, and the Bills are1 sent to the Surveyor General’s Office, to be monied agreeable to Contract or Office Prices: In the Second, some of the Materials are purchased by Contracts made at the Board, and others are purchased by the Engineers on the Spot; and the Work is done by Artificers and Labourers, at a daily fixed Pay. Which of these Two Modes is likely to be the most expeditious, I believe there can be little Doubt of; and the Sloth of the Men working for daily Wages, compared to the Activity of the Man whose Labour (being paid for by Measure) has a Profit proportionate to his Industry, increases the Expence, by lengthening the Time; as will appear by the following Account of the Money already expended at Portsmouth, compared with the Value of the Works, supposing them to be executed by Contract and Measurement.

Account of Bills allowed for Materials, and for Pay of Artificers and Labourers by Day Work, Vide

Accounts. The Examination of Charles Hams, Esquire

taken upon Oath) 2d and 4th June 1784.

This Examinant saith, That the Profits of the Auditors of the Imprest arise from Salaries and Fees: The Salaries are ancient Payments from the Exchequer and other Offices, and amount together to about One hundred Pounds a Year to each Auditor: The Fees upon the Ordinary Accounts consist either of certain fixed Annual Allowances for auditing certain Accounts, or of Sums bearing a certain Proportion to the Amount of the Account; and, in the Army, a certain Annual Sum for the Account, and a certain Sum for every Troop and Company contained in the Account.

The other Fees are, small Payments for the Inrolment of public Instruments in the Office, according to a Table of Fees long established, and amounting to about Two hundred Pounds a Year. 'Hie Fees for the Extraordinary Accounts are in Proportion to the Length and Period of the Account, and the Trouble it gives to the Office. — -All these Fees (except for some of the Inrolments) are paid by the Public. — -The Authority by which the Auditor claims his Fees is, either the Warrant of the Lord High Treasurer Godolphin, dated the 4th of July 1704, or a Warrant under the Sign Manual, or a Warrant from the Treasury.

The Profits of the Deputy Auditors arise from Salaries paid to them by the Auditor, and from Fees and Gratuities; — the Fees are certain fixed Sums on

Junii. A. 1784.

particular Accounts, and paid by the Public; the Gratuities are such Presents as the Deputy understands to have been usually paid by the Accountants.

The Profits of the Clerks arise from Salaries paid to them by the Auditors — from certain Sums, or a certain Proportion, out of the Auditor’s Fees — Allowances for ingrossing, and extra Business — and Gratuities from Individuals.

The Deputy receives, both for the Auditor and Clerks, all the Profits of the Office, and accounts to them for such Profits.

All the Expences of the Office are defrayed by the Auditor; he is rated to the Land Tax and Twelve Penny Duty. — In the Year 1781 the Establishment of the Office was increased by the Addition of One Deputy and Four Clerks; and in that and the following Year Six or Seven extra Clerks were added; and all the Clerks were paid for Extra Work, which occasioned the great Increase of the Expences in those Years.

The Fees and Gratuities paid by the Accountants to the Deputies and Clerks, are some of them charged and allowed in the incident Bills of the Accountants, and therefore paid by the Public; others do not appear to be charged to the Account of the Public; and therefore what Part of those Fees are paid by the Public, and what Part by the Individuals, cannot be ascertained.

Cha* Harris.

T. A aguish,

Rich* Neave,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for repairing and amending the several Roads leading from Woodstock, through Kiddington and Enstone, to Rollright Lane, and from Enslow Bridge to Kiddington aforesaid, in the County of Oxon; and, an Act made in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by the said last mentioned Act, and for making the said Act more effectual; and also, an Act made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by the said last mentioned Act, and for making the said Act more effectual, were read: And

Acts, and have borrowed the Sum of £. 300 upon the Credit thereof, which Money now remains due. — And the Witness further said, That the said Money cannot be repaid, nor the Roads kept in Repair, unless the Terms granted by the said Acts be further continued, and the Powers thereof altered and amended; and that it is proposed to reduce the said Acts into One Act of Parliament.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Supply* Committee of the whole House, to wdiora it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Eighty-one thousand One hundred and Forty-one Pounds Six Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Expence of Services performed by the Office of Ordnance for Land Service, and not provided for by Parliament, in the Year 1783.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Four hundred Twenty-nine thousand and Eight Pounds Two Shillings and Seven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance for Land Service, for the Year 1784.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Four thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to be advanced to the Governor and Company of Merchants of England trading into the Levant Seas, to be applied in assisting the said Company in carrying on their Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, towards enabling the Trustees of the British Museum to carry on the Execution of the Trusts reposed in them by Parliament.
