A Motion was made, and the Question being put, Reprewn-That a Representation be presented to His Majesty, J?tl0"oa, most humbly to offer to His Royal Consideration, that w^"8* the Address of this House upon His Majesty’s Speech from the Throne, was dictated solely by our Conviction of His Majesty’s own most gracious Intentions towards His People, which, as we feel with Gratitude, so we are ever ready to acknowledge with Cheerfulness and Satisfaction.

Impressed with these Sentiments, we were willing to separate from our general Expressions of Duty,

Respect, and Veneration to His Majesty’s Royal Person, and to His princely Virtues, all Discussion whatever with Relation to several of the Matters suggested, and several of the Expressions employed, in that Speech.

That it was not fit or becoming that any decided Opinion should be formed by His faithful Commons, on that Speech, without a Degree of Deliberation adequate to the Importance of the Object: Having afforded ourselves due Time for that Deliberation, we do now most humbly beg leave to represent to His Majesty, That, in the Speech from the Throne, His Ministers have thought proper to use a Language of a very alarming Import, unauthorized by the Practice of good Times, and irreconcileable to the Principles of this Government.

Humbly to express to His Majesty, that it is the Privilege and Duty of this House to guard the Constitution from all Infringement on the Part of Ministers, and, whenever the Occasion requires it, to warn them against any Abuse of the Authorities committed to them: But it is very lately, that, in a Manner not more unseemly than irregular and preposterous, Ministers have thought proper, by Admonition from the Throne, implying Distrust and Reproach, to convey the Expectations of the People to us, their sole Representatives; and have presumed to caution, us, the natural Guardians of the Constitution, against any Infringement of it on our Parts. This dangerous Innovation we, His faithful Commons, think it our Duty to mark; and as these Admonitions from the Throne, by their frequent Repetition, seem intended to lead gradually to the Establishment of an Usage, we hold ourselves bound thus solemnly to protest against them.

This House will be, as it ever ought to be, anxiously attentive to the Inclinations and Interests of its Constituents: Nor do we desire to straiten any of the Avenues to the Throne, or to either House of Parliament. But the ancient Order, in w'hich the Rights of the People have been exercised, is not a Restriction of these Rights; it is a Method providently framed in Favour of those Privileges, which it preserves and enforces by keeping in that Course which has been found the most effectual for answering their Ends. His Majesty may receive the Opinions and Wishes of Individuals under their Signatures, and of Bodies Corporate under their Seals, as expressing their own particular Sense; and He may grant such Redress as the legal Powers of the Crown enables the Crown to afford. This, and the other House of Parliament, may also receive the Wishes of such Corporations and Individuals by Petition; the collective Sense of His People His Majesty is to receive from His Commons in Parliament assembled. It would destroy the whole Spirit of the Constitution, if His Commons were to receive that Sense from the Ministers of the Crown,

9 or

34 Geo. III. i 40 Juniu 109

or to admit them to be a proper or a regular Channel for conveying it.

That the Ministers in the said Speech declare, " That His Majesty has a just and conhdent Reliance, " that we (His faithful Commons) are animated with u the same Sentiments of Loyalty, and the same Attachment to our excellent Constitution, which He " had the Happiness to see so fully manifested in " every Part of the Kingdom."

To represent, That His iaithful Commons have never failed in Loyalty to His Majesty. It is new to them to be reminded of it. It is unnecessary and invidious to press it upon them by any Example. This Recommendation of Loyalty, after His Majesty has sat for so many Years, with the full Support of all Descriptions of His Subjects, on the Throne of this Kingdom, at a Time of profound Peace, and without any Pretence of the Existence or Apprehension of War or Conspiracy, becomes in itself a Source of no small Jealousy to His faithful Commons, as many Circumstances lead us to apprehend that therein the Ministers have Reference to some other Measures and Principles of Loyalty, and to some other Ideas of the Constitution, than the Laws require, or the Practice of Parliament will admit.

No regular Communication of the Proofs of Loyalty and Attachment to the Constitution, alluded to in the Speech from the Throne, have been laid before this House, in order to enable us to judge of the Nature, Tendency, or Occasion of them, or in what particular Acts they were displayed: But if we are to suppose the Manifestations of Loyalty (which are held out to us as an Example for Imitation) consist in certain Addresses delivered to His Majesty, promising Support to His Majesty in the Exercise of His Prerogative, and thanking His Majesty for removing certain of His Ministers, on Account of the Votes they have given upon Bills depending in Parliament: If this be the Example of Loyalty alluded to in the Speech from the Throne, then we must beg Leave to express our serious Concern for the Impression which has been made on any of our Fellow-Subjects by Misrepresentations, which have seduced them into a seeming Approbation of Proceedings subversive of their own Freedom: We conceive, that the Opinions delivered in these Papers were not well considered; nor were the Parties duly informed of the Nature of the Matters on which they were called to determine, nor of those Proceedings of Parliament which they were led to censure.

We shall act more advisedly. — The Loyalty we shall manifest will not be the same with theirs; but, we trust, equally sincere, and more enlightened. It is no slight Authority which shall persuade us (by receiving "as Proofs of Loyalty the mistaken Principles lightly taken up in these Addresses) obliquely to criminate, with the heavy and ungrounded Charge of Disloyalty and Disaffection, an uncorrupt, independent, and reforming Parliament. Above all, we shall take Care that none of the Rights and Privileges, always claimed, and since the Accession of His Majesty’s illustrious Family constantly exercised, by this House (and which we hold and exercise in Trust for the Commons of Great Britain, and for their Benefit) shall be constructively surrendered, or even weakened and impaired, under ambiguous Phrases, and Implications of Censure on the late Parliamentary Proceedings: If these Claims are not well founded, they ought to be honestly abandoned; if they are just, they ought to be steadily and resolutely maintained.

Of His Majesty’s Own gracious Disposition towards the true Principles of our free Constitution, His faithful Commons never did, or could, entertain a Doubt: But we humbly beg Leave to express to

His Majesty our Uneasiness concerning other new and unusual Expressions of His Ministers declaratory of a Vol. 40.

Resolution " tq support, in their just Balance, the " Rights and Privileges of every Branch of the " Legislature."

It were desjrable that all hazardous Theories concerning a, Balance, of Rights and Privileges (a Mode of Expression wholly foreign, to Parliamentary Usage) might have been forborne: Your Commons are well instructed in their own Rights and Privileges, which they are determined to maintain on the Footing upon which they were handed down from their Ancestors; They are not unacquainted with, the Rights and Privileges of the House of Pqers, and they know and respect the lawful Prerogatives of the Crown: But

they do not think it safe to admit any Thing concerning the Existence of a Balance of those Rights, Privileges, and Prerogatives, nor, are they able to discern to what Objects Ministers would apply their Fiction of a Balance, nor what they . would consider as a just one: These unauthorized Doctrines have aTendency to stir improper Discussions, and to lead to mischievous Innovations in the Constitution.

That His faithful Commons most humbly recomr mend, instead of the inconsiderate Speculations of unexperienced Men, that, on all Occasions, Resort should be. bad to the happy Practice of Parliament, and to those solid Maxims of Government which have prevailed since the Accession of His Majesty’s illustrious Family, as furnishing the only safe Principles qn which the Crown and Parliament can proceed.

We think it the more necessary to be cautious on this Head, as, in the last Parliament, the present Ministers had thought proper to countenance, if not to suggest, an Attack upon the most clear and undoubted Rights and Privileges of tins House.

Fearing, from these extraordinary Admonitions, and from the new Doctrines, which seem to have dictated- several unusual Expressions, that His Majesty has been abused by false Representations of the late Proceedings in Parliament, we think it our Duty respectfully to inform His Majesty, that, no Attempt whatever has been made against His lawful Prerogatives, or against the Rights and Privileges of the Peers, by the late House of Commons, in any of their Addresses, Votes, or Resolutions: Neither do we

know of any Proceeding by Bill, in which it was proposed to abridge the Extent of His Royal Prerogative: But, if such Provision had existed in any Bill, we protest, and we declare, against all Speeches, Acts, or Addresses, from any Persons whatsoever, which have a Tendency to consider such Bills, or the Persons concerned in them, as just Objects of apy Kind of Censure and Punishment from the Throne: Necessary Reformations may hereafter require, as they have frequently done in former Times, Limitations and Abridgements, and in some Cases an entire Extinction of some Branch of Prerogative: If Bills should be improper in the Form in which they appear in the House where they originate, they are liable, by the Wisdom of this Constitution, to be corrected, and even to be totally set aside, elsewhere; . this is the known, the legal, and the safe Remedy: But whatever, by the Manifestation of the Royal Displeasure, tends to intimidate Individual Members from proposing, or this House from receiving, debating, and passing Rills, tends to prevent even the Beginning of every Reformation in the State, and utterly destroys the deliberative Capacity of Parliament: We therefore claim, demand, and insist upon it as our undoubted Right, that no Persons shall be deemed proper Objects of Animadversion by the Crown, in any Mode whatever, for the Votes which they give, or the Propositions which they make, in Parliament.

We humbly conceive, that besides its Share of the Legislative Power, and its Right of Impeachment, that, by the Law and Usage of Parliament, this House has other Powers and Capacities, which it is bound

That His Majesty’s Ministers, misled by their Ambition,. have endeavoured, if possible, to form a Faction in the Country against the popular Part of the Constitution, and have therefore thought proper -to add to their slanderous Accusation against a House of Parliament, relative to His Majesty’s Prerogative, ;another of a different Nature, calculated for the Purpose of raising Fears and Jealousies among the Corporate Bodies of the Kingdom; and of persuading uninformed Persons belonging to those Corporations to look to, and make Addresses to them as Protectors of their Rights, under their several Charters, from the Designs winch they, without any Ground, charged the then House of Commons to have formed against Charters in general: For this Purpose they have not scrupled to assert, that the Exertion of His Majesty’s Prerogative in the late precipitate Change in His Administration, and the Dissolution of the late Parliament, were Measures adopted in order to rescue the People and their Rights out of the Hands of the House of Commons, their Representatives.

We trust that His Majesty’s Subjects are not yet so far deluded as to believe that the Charters in any other local or general Privilege can have a solid Security in any Place but where that Security has always been looked for, and always found, in the -House of Commons: Miserable and precarious indeed, would be the State of their Franchises, if they were to find no Defence but from- that Quarter from whence they have always been attacked; but the late House of Commons, in passing that Bill, made no Attack upon any Powers or Privileges, except such as an House of Commons has frequently attacked, and will attack, (and they trust, in the End, with their wonted Success) that is, upon those which sue corruptly and oppressively administered; and that we will correct, and, if necessary for the Purpose, as far as in us lies, will.wholly destroy every Species of Power and Authority exercised to the Oppression, Wrong, and Detriment of the People, and to the Impoverishment qnd Desolation of the Countries subject to it.

Abettors and Supporters of the Persons who have been guilty of the Misdemeanors which Parliament has reprobated, and who for their own ill Purposes have given Countenance to a false and delusive State of the Company*s Affairs, fabricated to mislead Parliament, and to impose upon the Nation.

Your Commons feel, with a just Resentment, the inadequate Estimate which your Ministers have formed of the Importance of this great Concern: They call to act upon the Principles of those who have not enquired into the Subject, and to condemn those who, with the most laudable Diligence, have examined and scrutinized every Part of it: The Delilierations of Parliament have been broken; the Season of the Year is unfavourable; many of us are new Members, who must be wholly unacquainted with the Subject, which lies remote from the ordinary Course of general Information.

We are cautioned against an Infringement of the Constitution; and it is impossible to know, what the secret Advisers of the Crown, who have driven out the late Ministers for their Conduct in Parliament, and have dissolved the late Parliament for a pretended Attack upon Prerogative, will consider as such an Infringement: We are not furnished with a Rule, the Observance of which can make us safe from the Resentment of the Crown, even by an implicit Obedience to the Dictates of the Ministers who have advised that Speech; We know not how soon those Ministers may be disavowed, and how soon the Members of this House, for our very Agreement with them, may be considered as Objects of His Majesty’s Displeasure: Until by His Majesty’s Goodness and Wisdom the late Example is compleatly done away, we are not free.

We are well aware, in providing for the Affairs of the East, with what an adult Strength of Abuse, and of Wealth and Influence growing out of that Abuse, His Majesty’s Commons had, in the last Parliament, and still have, to struggle: We are sensible that the Influence of that Wealth, in a much larger Degree and Measure than at any former Period, may have penetrated into the very Quarter from whence alone any real Reformation can be expected.

If, therefore, in the arduous Affairs recommended to us, our Proceedings should be ill adapted, feeble, and ineffectual; if no Delinquency should be prevented, and no Delinquent should be called to Account; if every Person should be caressed, promoted, and raised in Power, in Proportion to the Enormity of his Offences; if no Relief should be given to any of the Natives unjustly dispossessed of their Rights, Jurisdictions, and Properties; if no cruel and unjust Exactions should be, forborne; if the Source of no Peculation, or oppressive Gain, should be cut off; if, by the Omission of the Opportunities that were in our Hands, our Indian Empire should fall into Ruin irretrievable, and in its Fall crush the Credit, and Overwhelm the Revenues of this Country, we stand acquitted to our Honour, and to our Conscience, who have reluctantly seen the weightiest Interests of our Country, at Times the most critical to its Dignity and Safety, rendered the Sport of the inconsiderate and unmeasured Ambition of Individuals, and by that Means the Wisdom of His Majesty’s Government degraded in the public Estimation, and the Policy and Character of this renowned Nation rendered contemptible in the Eyes of all Europe.

It passed in the Negative.

Prayers.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration Midshall the Petition of Roger Wilbraham, Esquire; and Election, also, the Petition of Christopher Hawkins, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and double Return for the Borough of Midshall, otherwise Mitchell, in the County of Cornwall, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Sixty Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.-

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Forty-nine Members then present were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Thirteen Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Seven, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; Three, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees; and Three on Account of their having already, in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside* being complete, the Counsel for Mr. Wilbraham named George Dempster, Esquire, and the Counsel for Mr.

Hawkins named Philip Rashleigh, Esquire, to serve on the said Select Committee.

And Lists of the said Forty-nine Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

Phillips’ Pre- Mr. John Luttrell reported from the Committee, to servation of whom the Petition of Henry Phillips of Provisions, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth: viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

----- Wright,from the Admiralty Office, produces,

according to Order, Copies of several Certificates and Letters, shewing the Efficacy of certain Powders, invented by the Petitioner for destroying Weevils, Maggots, Spiders, and Cockroaches, and which Powder has been used on board Ships of War, by Order of the Admiralty Board, at the Recommendation of the Victualling Board.

Mr. John Watts, from the Victualling Office, presents the like Certificate and Letters from that Office.

And both Witnesses said, That no Letter or Account had been received at their Offices, stating that the Powder had ever failed doing what it was used for.

From the Perusal of the Letters and Certificates so produced to your Committee, it appeared to them, that the Powder invented and prepared by the said Mr. Phillips, the Petitioner, had been used for the Preservation of Grain, Biscuit, and dry Stores, on Board His Majesty’s Ships Union, Fox, Daedalus, Diligent, Brune, Ambuscade, Princess Caroline, Leocadia,

Britannia, Iphigenia, Ocean, Eurydice, Agamemnon, Alarm, Jason, Maiiboi'ough, and Diligente; and that it had fully answered the Ends proposed, of destroying the above-mentioned Insects, and preventing their Return,

whereby the Ships Provisions had been preserved from being wasted or spoiled during Voyages of considerable Length.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Watson reported from the Committee, to whom , the Petition of the several Persons, resident in the Cities of London and Westminster, in the Borough of Southwark, and Parts adjacent, employed in the mak-irtg and vending Beaver Hats, and Hats mixed with Beaver, Hare Wool,' Coney Wool, Goats Wool, and

Junii. A. 1784.

other Materials, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others concerned in the said Manufacture in Great Britain, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Collinson being examined, said, That the Hat Manufactory of this Kingdom is a very considerable Branch of Trade, in which several Thousand British Subjects are employed-i — That Hare Wool and Coney Wool, the Growth of this Country, are better in Quality than any other, whereby the English Hats have acquired such Reputation, that great Quantities of them are exported to Foreign Parts — That he has worked Hare Wool and Coney Wool imported from different Foreign Countries, and has found by Experience that the same is greatly inferior to that of Great Britain, and cannot be worked up so well, without a Mixture of the English — That of late Years very little of the said Articles have been imported, owing to their being detained for the Supply of Foreign Manufactures.

The Witness further said, That Turkey Goats Hair (or Wool) is a very material Ingredient in the Hat Manufactory — Then

Mr. John Renkin confirmed the above Evidence; and added, That the said Turkey Goats Hair pays a Duty of about Six Pence per Pound on Importation, rather more than Four Pence of which is drawn back by Foreigners when exported; and further said, That Hare Wool is exceedingly scarce.

This Evidence, respecting the above Duty, was corrobdrated by Mr. Philip Coxe, who said, He is of Opinion, that the taking off the Duty on Importation of this Article would be a great Encouragement to the Hat Manufactory, the said Duty being rather more than Ten per Cent. upon its Average Value at this Market.

Mr. William Waldeck being then examined, said, That, owing to the superior Excellence of British Hare and Coney Wool, considerable Quantities have lately been exported to France, Flanders, and America — -That the Orders for Exportation have been so great, that they could not be executed — That an Agent for a House in Flanders had given him Orders for Ten, Twenty, or more Thousands of Skins, and that he had sold him Two hundred Pounds Weight of Hare Wool, which was exported — That he had sold several Parcels to other Agents, which he had Reason to believe were for the Purpose of Exportation to Foreign Markets — That if he had had the Skins, he could have sold them for Nine Shillings per Dozen, which was an exorbitant1 Price, the medium Price being from Six to Seveiv Shillings per Dozen. — He further added, That the Demand for Exportation still continues to increase, he having lately sold considerable Quantities of unmanufactured Hare and Coney Wool for that Purpose, and has sent several Samples to Foreign Parts for Approbation, all of which passed through the Hands of Robertson, the Broker.

Mr. Collinson being further examined, said, That if the present Exportation of Hare and Coney Wool is not prevented, he thinks there will not be a sufficient Quantity left in the Kingdom to supply the Demand of the Manufactory; and he is of Opinion, that if the Exportation is prohibited, the Manufactory of this Country will consume the whole Quantity grown.

And being asked as to the Prices of Hare and Coney Wool, he said, That Coney WTool, which was last Year at Twelve Shillings per Pound, now sells for Fifteen Shillings; and that Hare Wool has advanced in the same Proportion, which he imputed to Two

Causes,


a a Geo. III. i 6213

Caused, the Exportation of the said Articles, and the increased Demand for Hats to America.

Mr. Thomas fV&ntner, a Feltmaker, being examined, said, That he had some Time since discharged Eight Men out of Twenty-four, for Want of Materials to employ them; and that he had now at work Twenty Men in the Hat Manufactory; and could he procure a Sufficiency of Hare and Coney Wool, he could employ Twenty more.

Mr. Miller Christy, Hat Manufacturer, corroborated the last mentioned Evidence, respecting the great Scarcity of Materials; and added, That he had Demands for more Hats than he could supply. — And

Mr. Josiah Baughan, Hat Manufacturer, added, That he has sold for Exportation, to Boston in New England, great Quantities of Hare and Coney Wool, and has now an Order to execute for the same Place, the Americans not being able to manufacture Hats without these Materials.

Mr. Richard Warrcner, a Leather Dresser, being also examined, said, That Foreigners employed in dressing Hare and Coney Skins, evade the Duties imposed by Law, by working in unentered Places, and consequently are not visited by the Exciseman — That if the Witness was to dress the said Skins, he would be obliged to pay a Duty of Thirty per Cent. ad Valorem. — Which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Thomas Bands, an Excise Officer.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Twenty Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were by the Clerk taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

Roads, reditaments, distinguished by the Out Grounds, in the Parish of Saint Andrews, within the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, and of the principal Inhabitants of and within the Manor and Parish of Stonehouse, in the same County, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also, the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the Town of Plymouth Dock, in the Parish of Stoke Damarel, in the County of Devon, on Behalf of themselves and other Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish; and also, the Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty and several of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with, in respect to the first-mentioned Petition; but that the said Orders, so far as relates to the Notices required to be given at the Michaelmas Quarter Sessions, and in the Newspapers in the Months of August or September, had not been complied with in respect to the second-mentioned Petition, as the Parties did not know of the Application for repairing the Road in the first-mentioned Petition, until it was too late to give the Notices required by the said Standing Orders; and that the Committee had examined the Matters of the first and, second-mentioned Petitions, no Party having appeared in Support of the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. Christopher Harris being examined, said,

That from the great Increase of Buildings in the Towns of Plymouth, Stonehouse, and Plymouth Dockf and on Account of a commodious Stone Bridge having been erected over the Creek of Stonehouse, by Means of which a safe, convenient, and short Communication was effected between the Borough of Plymouth and Plymouth Dock, the High Road leading from the Shambles through Frankfort Gate, within the said Borough, to the said Bridge, having been so much more used than formerly, is become so much out of Repair, as to render the Expence of keeping the same in proper Repair a great Burthen to the Petitioners, and others, who are in certain Proportions con tributary by Law for the necessary Repair thereof —

That the Sum of £. 333. 4$. 6 d. was last Year expended 3 K in

in repairing the same — That the Parish Rates collected for that Purpose; viz. yd. in the Pound, and 6d. Composition, amounted only to £.124. 6 s. and therefore a Debt of £.208. )8s. 6d. now remains due from the Parish, besides the Expence of Indictments, amounting to Thirty Guineas — That the above Rates are as high as the Law allows, and that the Road is much better now than it was before this Money was expended; but the Witness supposes Part of it must be taken up again for the Purpose of making tnore Drains.

And the Witness further said, That the Laws in being are inadequate for the Purpose of altering, making, and maintaining the said Road, and of lighting, watching, watering, and cleansing the same; and also for regulating the Stands and Fares of Carriages using the said Road; all which are necessary for the Accommodation of the Public.

Then, to prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Harris informed your Committee, That the Road leading from the Western End of the said Bridge to the Inner Barrier Gate next the Playhouse in the Parish of Stoke J>amarel, befog in Length about Five hundred Yards, is ruinous, and is not properly lighted, watched, or watered; and that if Power was granted for those Purposes, it would be of great public Utility.

Sir Herbert ftfackporth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Churchwardens of the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Middlesex, and of several of Jthe Oyerspers of the Poor, and Trustees, and Vestrymen, for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King Georgp thp Second, more effectually to enable the Parishioners of the said Parish to purchase, hire, or erect a Workhouse for the employing and maintaining the Poor of the said Parish, and for the more effectual Support and Employment of the Poor therein; and also, for puttting in Execution one other Act of Parliament, made in the Eighteenth Year of His present Majesty, to amend the said first-mentioned Act; and also, the Petition of several of the Vestrymen of the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Middlesex, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the same, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, the said Acts were read; and it appeared by the said first-mentioned Act, that Power was given to the Trustees therein nominated, to purchase or build a House, and to provide the same with Furniture for the Use of the Poor of the said Parish. And

Mr. Francis Child being examined, said, That at the Time of passing the said Act, there was no House or Building fit for the Purpose within the said Parish, and therefore the Trustees and Vestrymen hired a Workhouse at Mile End New T(rm> in the Parish of Stepney, which they have been obliged, from the great Increase of the Number of Poor, to make considerable additional Buildings thereto, and in so doing,

have incurred a very heavy Expence upon the said Parish.

Mr. John Scott confirmed the above Evidence, and added, That notwithstanding the several additional Buildings above mentioned, the said Workhouse is too small, and the Lodging Rooms very inconvenient, the People being obliged to sleep Four or Five in a Bed — That the Rent, Taxes, and common Repairs of the said Workhouse, amount to full £.120 per Annum. Then

Mr. John Stevens, the Master of the said Workhouse, being examined, confirmed the last mentioned Evidence, and said, That the Poor are dajly increasing, insomuch, that since lie has been Master, there has been an Increase of above One hundred in a Year; and that more than One hundred and Fifty have been Relieved out, there not having been sufficient Room in the House.

Mr. Richard Wooding, Surveyor, being next examined, produced a Plan and Estimate for building a new Workhouse, which is calculated to accommodate Five hundred Persons upon the most frugal Plan, the Amount of the Estimate being between £3,500 and £-4,000.

Mr. Scott being further examined, said, That by the said Act of the Eighteenth Year of the present Reign, the usual Mode of making the Rates for the Relief\)f the Poor of the said Parish, was altered to a Pound Rate in different Classes, according to the Yearly Renjt or Value of the Houses, which has been found very inconvenient, and productive of much Collusion between Landlords and Tenants, whereby the Rates have repeatedly proved deficient to defray the necessary Charges of maintaining the said Poor, and a considerable Debt hath been unavoidably contracted thereby, which cannot be discharged, unless Power be given to alter the present Method of assessing the Monies, and for raising a further Sum of Money to discharge the said Debt.

Mr. John Phillips added, That the Poor’s Rate, at the Commencement of the last mentioned Act, produced about £.3*000 a Year, from which Time it has been gradually decreasing; and that although in the Year 1782 an additional {Sixth was laid on, which was estimated to raise £. 600 a Year, the Rates have nevertheless so much decreased as to produce now not more than the original Sum of £.3,000.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Phillips further said, That the present Method of chusing Overseers is very inconvenient, and it would be more useful and advantageous to the Parish, if Power was given to elect Two in each Half Year.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for providing a Workhouse within the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Middlesex, and for raising Money for that Purpose, and to discharge Debts already contracted on Account of the Poor, and for further regulating the Manner of rating to the Poor, appointing Overseers, and preserving all Accounts relating to the Offices of Churchwarden and Overseer of the Poor and Treasurer of the same Parish: And that Sir Herbert Mackworth and Mr. Mainwaring do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Adam reported from the Committee, to whom Brereton'g the Petition of Captain William Brereton, late Lieute- Expenses nant Governor of the City of Cavite, and Commander at Cavilv* of His Majesty’s Ships stationed at The Philippine Istands, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Commisyon, under the Hand and Seal of Rear Admiral Cornish, Commander in Chief of His Majesty’s Ships and Vessels in the East Indies, dated the 14th of November 1762, directed to Captain William Brereton, Commander of His Majesty’s Ship Falmouth, appointing him Lieutenant Governor of the Castle, Town, and District of Cavite; and also, an Order, dated 1st March 1763, together with Instructions from Rear Admiral Cornish to Captain Brereton, whom he left Commander in Chief in the Naval Department, as senior Officer, were read; and it appeared to your Committee, That, by virtue of the said Commission, and in pursuance of the said Order and Instructions, he took upon himself the Government of the said Castle, Town, and District, on the 14th November 1762; and that he continued to exercise the Office of Lieutenant Governor, until the 1st of April 1764, the Day on which the Conquest of The Philippine Islands was delivered over by him to the Agents of the King of Spain2 in Obedience to an Order, under His Majesty’s Royal Sign Manual, directed to the Commander in Chief of Isis Ships at the said Islands; and that during that Period he was at very considerable Expence, amounting to upwards of £. 1,400.

And Captain Philip Bromfield, an Elder Brother of the Trinity House, and late a Commander of a Ship in the East India Company’s Service, informed your Committee, That he was at Manilla at the Time when Captain Brereton commanded there; and that, on Account of the Hostilities w'hich continued to rage in the Country after the Capture, he was put to considerable Difficulty and Expence in procuring Provisions for the Supply of the Garrisons and Fleet — That he kept a regular public Table, for all Persons of Rank in the Country, as well as the King’s and Company’s Officers, which, among other Measures taken by Captain,

Brereton, was necessary to conciliate the Minds of the Inhabitants; and that the Expence of a Table in that Country amounted to more than double the Sum it would cost in England. — And the Witness further said.

That Captain Brereton, from his Situation, and in Order to support his public Character, was put to the additional Expence of £.600, in keeping a Carriage and riecessary Attendants.

also, the Order from Rear Admiral Cornish, dated 21st of August 1763, to concert Measures with the Commanding Officer of the King’s Troops, and the India Company’s Governor\and Council at Manilla, for the Removal of the Kings and Company’s Troops from thence as early as possible, and the Consultations of the 10th March 1764, held in consequence thereof* were also read.

And by the said Consultations it appeared, that there were only Two of His Majesty’s Ships, Two of the Company’s Ships, and a Spanish Ship called The Siam, which Ships could only carry 1,160 Men, to transport about 1,500 Men (exclusive of the Company’s Civil Servants and Domestics) from thence to India.

And Captain Bromjicld further informed your Committee, That the Ships left at the Philippine Islands were not sufficient to carry away all the Troops upon the Surrender of the Conquest to the Spaniards — That a Aiutiny was threatened among the Troops, unless they were assured they should ail be embarked; in consequence of which^ Captain Bratton was obliged to fit up the Siam, and another old Spanish Ship, which he did without any Expence to the Public, in order to remove all the Troops and Stores, and in performing that Service he had great Merit; and that the Time employed therein detained him so long as to make it impossible to save the Passage to Madras, and obliged him to undertake the dangerous and tedious Passage to Batavia, through the Philippine and Molucca Islands — That the W itness sailed, with Captain Brereton, and continued in Company for more than Two Months, when he was obliged to bear away for Zoloo, and whilst he continued in Company, was often on board the Falmouth, and observed that the Commanding Officer, and Ten other Officers of the Mili-' tary, sailed in that Ship, and lived at Captain Brere-toils Table, at his Expence, which the Witness conceives could not have been less than Twelve Dollars a Day beyond his ordinary Charges as Commander of the Squadron.

The Claim made by Captain Brereton on this Account, amounts only to the Sum of £. 200.

It also appeared to your Committee, that the Falmouth was in a very leaky Condition on her Departure ipom the Bay of Manilla; and upon her Arrival at Batavia, repeated Surveys were held upon her by the Carpenters belonging to her, as likewise by those of the Princess Augusta, the Duke of Richmond, and the Duke of Gloucester, East India Company's Ships then riding in that Port.; the Result of which was, that it was totally impracticable to repair her, so, as to go to Sea again; and that, by many unavoidable Delays, he was detained on Shore at Batavia for more than Six Months, and put to the additional Expence of more than £. 400.

And it appeared to your Committee, that during his Detention at Batavia, a very general Sickness prevailed among the Seamen and Soldiers, and that it became necessary to establish an Hospital on Shore; and that he was obliged to take up Money for defraying Hospital Expences. — And by the Contracts produced to your Committee, it appeared, that he contracted for the Maintenance and Cure of the Men, at the Rate of Two Shillings per Man per Diem, the usual and accustomed Rate in that Country — That the Money he so took up, was charged to him at the Rate of Five Shillings per Rix Dollar; but those Dollars, when offered in Payment, could be received after the Rate of only Four Shillings each, the then Rate of Exchange at that Place; upon which there was incurred a Loss of One Shilling upon each Dollar. — And by a Certificate under the Hand of his Agent, it appeared, that upon passing his Accounts at the Navy and Victualling Boards, for Expences incurred at the same Time, the said Loss of Exchange was allowed; but upon the Hospital Accounts being presented to the Vol. 40.

Commissioners of Sick and Hurt* for their Inspection Brereton's and Examination, they objected to the Allowance of Expences the One Shilling Loss of Exchange, alledging, that at Cavite* the Contracts made by him being for Two Shillings per Man per Diem, and not for Half a Rix Dollar, therefore they were of Opinion, that the Loss of One Shilling per Rix Dollar ought to fall upon himself —

But it appeared to your Committee, that this Loss arose from an Error of Captain Brereton, in expressing^ in the Contract, Two Shillings per Man per Diem, instead of Half a Rix Dollar per Man per Diem; and that the Loss accruing to him on this Head amounted to the Sum of £5,13.

And it further appeared to your Committee, that His Majesty’s Ship the Falmouth, being in the Condition before stated, so as to render it impossible for her to pnt to Sea, Captain Brereton acquainted the Secretary of the Admiralty thereof by a Letter, dated Batavia, the 8th of November 1764; and that he, after providing Passage for, and otherwise disposing of her Complement of Men, was under the Necessity of taking a Passage to Europe for himself, and some of his Petty Officers and Servants, in a Dutch'East Indiaman, which he procured with great Difficulty.

And, by a Certificate under the Hand of Captain Brereton s Agent, it appeared to your Committee, that he had not been reimbursed the Expence of his Passage from Batavia to Europe in that Ship, which he stated to your Committee to have amounted to at least £.350; anci which Sum of £. 350, if allowed him, will not be any additional Expence to the Public, so far as respects the Victualling, as the Victualling at the King’s Expence ceased Irorn the Time the Falmouth vvas rendered unfit lor Service.

And by the Evidence of Captain Bromfield, the above Charge ot £-35° appeared to be extremely reasonable, as the Passage in an English East Indiaman would have been charged £. 1,000 at least.

Upon the Evidence of Mr. William Birch, Captain Breretons Attorney, it appeared, that an Action was brought against Captain Brereton, by Charles Peter Saulnier, Commander of an armed Vessel under his Command, for an Assault and false Imprisonment, in taking him out of his Ship, and detaining him on board the Falmouth; and that it appeared in Evidence, upon the Trial of this Action, that Saulnier was going off with the* Ship without Leave, and, disobeying the Signal^ for bringing his Vessel to, was taken and brought before Captain Brereton, as the Commander in Chief, and there detained to answer for his Conduct, and another Person put in command of the Vessel; and that Admiral Cornish, in giving his Evidence at the Trial, declared, that had Captain Brereton done otherwise than he did, that he would not have done his Duty, and that, as his Admiral, he should have called him to a Court Martial; but the Jury thought proper to give a Verdict against him, for £. 400 Damages, with Costs, and that the taxed Costs amounted to £. 84, and which, with his own Costs, and the Expences paid to Witnesses, some of whom were brought from France, and other distant Parts, could not amount in his Opinion to less than £. 600.

And Captain-Brereton assured your Committee, that he has never received any Allowance or Compensation whatsoever for the said Expenditures and Disbursements, or any Part thereof, making altogether the full Sum of £. 3,463, besides the total Loss of Interest upon so large a Sum.

And your Committee cannot close their Report, without doing Captain Brereton, the Petitioner, the Justice to declare, that they find, from the Papers which have been produced to them, and the Testimony of Captain Bromfield, that the Security of the Conquest wholly was attributed to the judicious Management of the Petitioner, and by his Influence over the Spaniards and Natives in the District where he 3 L governed;

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown had, this Morning, a Tender made to him of an Indenture of Return of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the District of Burghs of Inverness, Nairn, Forres, and Fortrose, which had not been annexed to the Return of the Sheriff of the Shire of Elgin, at the Time when the same was delivered into the Office of the Clerk of the Crown, upon the 30th Day of April last; and that the Deputy Clerk of the Crown desired the Directions of this House, whether he should accept the same, and annex it to the Return of the Sheriff of the Shire of Elgin.

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown do attend this House upon Monday Morning next.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of the Debt of the Ordnance, as far as the same can be made up, with the Amount of the Debentures now standing out; distinguishing the Amount of the Debentures issued in each Month.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now read,

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the Ordinary Estimate of His Majesty’s Navy for the Year 1784, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of what may be necessary for the Buildings, Rebuildings, and Repairs of Ships of War in His Majesty’s and the Merchants Yards, and other Extra Works, over and above what are proposed to be done upon the Heads of Wear and Tear and Ordinary for the Year 1784, be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Monday Morning next.

Sir Herb&'t Mackworth repotted from foe Committee, Plate Glass to whom foe Petition of the Governor and Company Manufactory, of British Cast Plate Glass Manufacturers was referred f That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and bad directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where foe same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition* an Act passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act to incorporate certain Persons therein-named, and their Successors*

" with proper Powers for the Purpose of establishing " One or more Glass Manufactories within the Kingdom of Great Brit cun, and for the effectually supporting and conducting the same upon an improved " Plan, in a peculiar Manner, for the casting of large " Plate Glass," was read: And

Mr. Alexander Blacky Secretary to the said Company, being examined, said, That under the Sanction and Authority of the said Act of Parliament, the Company have, with unremitting Attention, endeavoured to forward the abovementioned Work, not merely with a View to their own Emolument and Advantage, but as an Object of Public and National Concern — That the Result has been a complete Performance of every Thing that was held up as a Plea, to warrant the Privileges granted by Parliament to the said Company, who have brought the Manufactory to such a Degree of Perfection, as to become an Object of Envy and Jealousy to the French Nation in that Branch of Manufacture, which in France has been upheld for more than a Century by peculiar Indul-gencies of Monopoly, and total Exemptions from Duty.

And he produced to your Committee, a Copy of an Order of the French King’s Council of State, dated the 13th of October 1781, as published by Authority; from which it appeared, that the Proprietors of the Royal Glass Manufactory in France, having represented to the King the Injury they should sustain if the new Duty on Glass, imposed by an Edict of the Month of August preceding, were to be rigorously levied on their Manufacture, the King in Council made the said Order, whereby the said Company of Proprietors were allowed to compound for the said Duties, at the Rate of 150,000 Livres per Annum, payable Quarterly; and that, as a further Encouragement, the whole Amount of the new Duty (as imposed by the said Edict) on such Glass as they should furnish for the Use of the Royal Palaces, or send Abroad, should be deducted from the said Composition; and it further appeared from the said Order, that with a View to enabling the said Proprietors to recover the Amount of the Duty, which under the said Composition they should actually pay, the Tariffe of their Prices of Glass was increased 10 per Cent.

Mr. Black being further examined, said, That the Company of British Cast Plate Glass Manufacturers have expended, in the Progress of their Works, upwards of One hundred Thousand Pounds, without receiving any Dividend whatever, owing to a Variety of Circumstances to which an Infant Manufactory, upon an entire new Plan, must naturally be liable; in Confirmation of which, he produced to your Committee certain Accounts hereunto annexed, Appendix,

APPENDIX, N‘6.

CAST PLATE GLASS MANUFACTURERS.

Plate Glas* Maimfi^tore;

STATE OF FACTS, submitted to the Commissioners of Excise, with regard to their Losses from the Contraction of Pots, and the Waste; the 28th Ffebhiary 1783.

Sheweth,

1st. That by the Fire contracting the Pots (a Matter till lately unnoticed) they haVfe paid a Duty upon a Quantity of Glass Metal supposed to have been contained in thie Pots, as appealed by the Officers Gauge, amounting to One Sixth of the whole Contents, which in Fact the Pots did not nor could contain, owing to the Contraction subsequent to the Time of first gauging them, to ascertain what they would contain; One Sixth, therefore, of the Duty paid, ought to be refunded as an unjust Overcharge, pirdceeding from Error.

2dly. That by an extraordinary and unavoidable Waste of Metal lil the Mode of carrying on their Business, they have paid at least 70 to 100 per Cent, or in that Proportion at least, varying from Accidents, a Duty for such Waste, calculated from the Time of gauging the Metal in the Pot to the squaring of the Glass, and which is not protected by the Allowance of One Fourth of the gauged Mfctal in the Pot: This can be proved by a great Variety of Experiments; and Mr. Jackson admits it to be 50 perCent. upon 28 Experiments made by himself. The Difference in such Calculations can easily be reconciled, by considering that any particular Nuitiber of Journies may vary considerably by, maity Accidents; therefore, a long taken on

a great Number of Journiies, is the most likely to bring oilt a fniiCiijCaldultition. 1 / .

3dly. That the Waste of Metal in the Blowing Plate Glass Manufactory (calculated in the same Manner from the gauging to the squaring) has varied from 6 to 12 per Cent upon Experiments hitherto pt?4e; which shews how much the;Oa&tabg Work, amounting from 70 tq too per Cent, has Need of a further Allowance,

4thly. That in the Casting Work, the Waste charged with Duty exceeds the Quantity discharged by the Allowance more than double; when the same Species of Waste in the Blowing Work does not exceed it One Fifth: This brings it to the Proportion of 120 to 20, or rather more, with respect to the Relief given, under the present Allowance, to the Two Manufactories. — In one Case, it compensates very fairly for the Loss by Waste; in the other, it falls extremely short of the intended Benefit.

5thly. That the Waste by Evaporation is too insignificant to deserve Notice.

EXPERIMENTS in December 1782, and January 1783.

To ascertain the Diminution of the Pots by Contraction, through the Heat of the Fire.

By the above Experiments it appears, that the Pots shrink from One Fourth to One Sixth nearly; on which the Average or Medium would be One Fifth, supposing the y shrank in that Proportion in equal Numbers; but as that cannot be ascertained without great Difficulty, in a prodigious Number of Experiments, the Company take the Contraction at the lowest or smallest Diminution, most in Favour of the Duty, and against themselves, which is One Sixth, as was before represented in their Memorial; from whence this Conclusion follows, that upon every Pot of Metal they have paid for One Sixth Part more in Quantity than what the Law required; as, from the Manner of taking the Gauge, One Sixth Part more than the real Contents was actually taken by the Measurement, through an Error in not noticing the above Contraction of the Pots, and which indeed Mr. Jackson did not believe to be the Case, but is now fully proved.

After much Consideration, the Commissioners gave to understand to the Committee, that they would not give them any Relief; but admitted, that there was a greater Waste in the Casting than in the Blowing, by the Evidence of their Supervisor Mr. Jackson.

Navy and A Petition of Merchants and Owners of Ships em-Victualling pl0yed in His Majesty’s Service as Transports and 1 8* Victuallers, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommepds it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, during the late War, supplied the Commissioners of the Navy and Victualling Boards with Ships for Transports and Victuallers, for the Freight of which they received Navy and Victualling Bills, subject to a Discount at the Time of contracting, on an Average about Ten per Cent. \ and that the Petitioners have, from Time to Time, advanced very large Sums, on account of their Ships, for Outfits, arid Bills drawn from America at an immense Premium, which, with their Ships arriving daily from America, and being discharged from His Majesty’s Service, obliges them to advance much larger Sums for defraying the Debts contracted during the Voyage, and for discharging Seamen’s Wages, which must be done with Ready Money; and that the Petitioners have been greatly distressed by not having it in their Power to sell their Navy Bills at the above Discoynt; and, as they are the original Holders of these Bills, they are much alarmed at the present high Discount of Twenty per Cent, which they are obliged to pay, and that only for Bills of small Sums, as they>cannot sell large Bills at any Rate; and that the very, great Loss winch has befallen the Petitioners in their Shipping, from the Severity of their Services* and: by being confined to Government Service by His Majesty’s Commissioners, contrary to the Interest of the Petitioners, who, in many Instances, made Application for their Discharge, without Effect, has reduced their Value near Fifty per Cent, since the Peace, added to the above Circumstances, renders the Situation of their Property truly alarming and distressing: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Petitioners Distress into Consideration, and order the Navy and Victualling Bills to be paid off, or grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordend, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Vol. 40.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Sir George Paul, Baronet, being examined, said, That the Common Gaol, and also the several Bridewells, for the County of Gloucester, arc too small for the Occasions of the County, very inconvenient, and much out of Repair; and that it is absolutely necessary, for the safe Custody of Persons who may be committed thereto respectively, that a New Gaol and some additional Bridewells should be built, and that proper Rules should be established for the Government and Regulation thereof.

Mr. William Blackburn being then examined, said,

He made a compleat Survey of the said Gaol and present Bridewells, and confirmed the Whole of the foregoing Evidence of Sir George Paul.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for erecting a New Gaol, and several New Bridewells, in the County of Gloucester, and for the due Regulation and Management of such Gaol, and of the Bridewells in the said County: And that Mr. Berkeley and Mr. Masters do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Duty on A Petition of Richard Bush, of London, Merchant, Barley was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

imported. That, in November, 1782, One hundred and Eight

Quarters and Three Bushels of Barley were imported into the Port of London from Ostaid, in a Vessel called The Good Fortune, and, in December 1782, Three hundred and Fifty Quarters of Barley were imported into the Port of London from Ostend, in a Vessel called The Two Good Brothers; and that the said several Parcels of Barley could not, at the Times of Importation,

be admitted to Entry on Payment of the Low Duties, and certain Bonds, with the Approbation of the Commissioners of the Treasury, were entered into by the Petitioner, to whom the said Barley was consigned,

for Pay merit of the High Duties for the said Parcels of Barley, until Application should be made to Parliament for Liberty to admit the same to be entered upon Payment of the Low Duties: And, that as the said Importation was greatly for the Benefit of the Public at a Time when there was a great Scarcity of Barley in this Kingdom, therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the Bill now depending in the House, to authorize the Commissioners of the Customs in England and Scotland to cancel Bonds given for the High Duties on certain Parcels of Corn imported into Great Britain, on certain Conditions therein mentioned, to direct the Commissioners of the Customs to order the Low Duties to be taken for the said Parcels of Barley, and to order the Bonds given for Payment of the High Duties to be cancelled.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Whitbread, Mr. Ord, 8cc.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

That, in the last Session of Parliament, d Petition was presented to the House, signed by several Magistrates of the said County, stating, That the County Gaol at Stafford is greatly gone to Decay, and insufficient for the Security and Accommodation of Prisoners, and that the House of Correction at Stafford is insecure and incommodious; that the building of a new Gaol, and converting of the present Gaol into a House of Correction, would be a great Convenience to the County; that certain Sums of Money, which have; from Time to Time, been raised within the said County'for public Purposes, remained unapplied; and, praying for a Bill fof biiilding a nefw Griol for the said County, purchasing Lands whereon to erect the same; converting the present Gaol into' a House of Correction, and applying the said Money to those Purposes; and that, on Account of the sudden Dissolution of

Parliament, no Proceedings were had upon the said Petition, and the said Application was not renewed in this Session within the Time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for Private Bills, because it was not at that Time ascertained that His Majesty’s Consent would be obtained to appropriate the Money, so raised as aforesaid and unapplied, to the Purposes mentioned in the said Petition, which Consent is required by a Standing Order of the House, previous to the receiving of any such Petition; and that the Petitioners have now obtained His Majesty’s Consent to apply the said unappropriated Money to the above-mentioned pressing Occasions of the said County: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to exhibit a Petition for the Purposes mentioned in the said Petition, presented to the House in the last Session of Parliament.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the present County Gaol at Stafford is ill constructed, too small, greatly gone to Decay, and insufficient for the Security and Accommodation of Prisoners; and that the House of Correction at Stafford aforesaid, belonging to the said County, to which there is no Court or Outlet, is an insecure and incommodious Building, over a Gateway belonging to the Corporation of Stafford; and that the building of a new County Gaol, in a proper Situation, ana converting the present Gaol into a House of Correction, would be of great Convenience and Advantage to the said County; and that, in the Year 1771, the Sum of £.2,200 was raised on the Inhabitants of a Part of the said County, as a Forfeiture for not raising the Militia, and is now in the Hands of the Receiver General of the said County, and, in the Year 1775, the Sum of £.1,125. ni. tild. was raised in the same Manner, on the like Account, and is now in the Hands of the Treasurer of the said County: _And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for building a new County Gaol for the said County of Stafford, purchasing Lands whereon to erect the same, converting the present Gaol into a House of Correction, and applying the Sums of Money above mentioned towards those Purposes, or that such other Relief may be given in the Premises as the House shall judge necessary.

Nevis Trade A Memorial and Petition of the Council and As-

America semMy of the Island of Nevis,- in Behalf of themselves a* and the rest of the Planters and Inhabitants of the said Island, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Event of Peace, amidst the general Joy which it hath diffused, hath excited in the Breasts of the Petitioners Sensations no less of Gratitude than of Happiness for the invaluable Blessing it confers upon them in the Restoration of their Island to the British Realms, and consequently in putting an End to the Distresses and-Losses they have borne by their Capture and Detention in the Enemy’s Hands for nearly Two Years; and that the Petitioners in contemplating the happy Consequences of Peace, have not restrained their Expectations from extending themselves to the Benefits of an open Trade with America, for, being conscious that their very Existence as a Sugar Colony depends on such an Indulgence, they flattered themselves that Government would become sensible of their Situation, it being not peculiar to them alone, but common to all the Leeward Sugar Islands; they therefore hoped that no Obstacle would arise to their Intercourse with a Country, which, from its local and other natural Advantages, hath afforded the only possible Means of carrying on the Cultivation of those Islands, and without the continued Assistance of which those Islands must become ruinous to the Proprietors of their Lands, and useless Burthens to the Nation; and that they have never alarmed themselves with the least Apprehension of Governments prohibiting their free Communication with the United States of America, from an Idea of Nova Scotia and Canadas being competent to supply them, it being an indisputable Fact, that the uncultivated State of the former Province subjects it to almost an entire Dependence for its Support on the more Southern and fruitful Provinces, whilst Canada, from its Distance, and from its difficult and indeed impracticable Navigation during Six Months of the Year, cannot be regarded as a regular Source of Supplies; and that, being thus buoyed up with the Hopes of renewing so necessary a Trade, and foreseeing in their own Conceptions no probable Impediment thereto, they have been the more surprised to hear that, in the Period of their Captivity, which

! withheld them from seeking and experiencing the

Clemency of Government, a Misfortune which rather enhances than diminishes their Title to Favours, that, in the very Instant of such their Distress, the Island of Antigua hath availed herself of her more fortunate Lot, and petitioned Government to be made a free Port; and that, if such an Indulgence be granted to Antigua, and if the other Islands of the Leeward Government be thereby excluded from a direct Trade with America, it must ultimately end in their Ruin; it would through Necessity oblige the other Islands to send to Antigua for Provisions and Lumber at an enhanced Expence, a Measure severely burthensome to them, and beneficial to Antigua alone, as it would in no wise concur with the Policy of Great Britain, should such be her Object, to diminish American Imports, Vol. 40.

such an exclusive Indulgence to Antigua would also establish it as the only Mart through which the other Islands could procure a regular Vent for their Rum, and the Profits of it, after deducting the heavy Charge of Freight, would be reduced to a Value very inadequate to the Labour' and Expence of distilling it; and, these Disadvantages, great in themselves, would be yet aggravated by unavoidable Interruptions to the Importation of Supplies from Antigua, and that more especially in the Hurricane Months, when, from the Dread of violent Winds and the usually Tempestuous Weather, the Trading Vessels arc mostly laid up, and scarcely any Communication preserved betwixt the Islands; no Vessels, during that Period of the Year, can be hired, unless at the most exorbitant Prices, and, after all, the Success of their Voyage would be a very precarious Dependence; but, even at more favourable Seasons, Disappointments would too frequently occur, from the Windward Situation of Antigua, and from the Calms and Currents so prevalent in those Seas; nay, the very Coast of Antigua would increase the Evil, as, from its natural Disadvantages, all Access to it is singularly difficult; weak, thereiore, as are her natural Pretensions to a free Port, her eventual ones seem no less so, for, if exclusive Privileges are to be granted to any one Island for its particular Benefit, at the Expence and manifest Injury of the rest, a Regard to the Sufferings and Losses of those which have been captured in the Course of the War would no Doubt, in Justice and Humanity, mark one of them as the fittest Object of Partiality; and that the Petitioners, however, presume not to harbour a Thought so injurious to the Justice and Impartiality of Government, as to apprehend the Possibility of Success to a Petition from any one Island, to the Detriment of the rest, but, having thus stated the Dependence of these Colonies on the Continent of America, as well for the Sale of their Rum, as for the necessary Supplies of Lumber and Grain, with which neither Great Britain nor any of her Territories can furnish them but upon the most ruinous Terms, must also submit to the House, as a farther reasonable Plea for thus approaching them, their present embarrassed Situation, in consequence of heavy local Taxes, additional Duties on Sugars in England, the reduced Price of that Article, and their late unfortunate Crops: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into their most serious Consideration, and grant them such Relief as may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read. And,

Mr. Thomas Jago being examined, said. That the Money authorized to be raised hath been found insufficient for the Maintenance of the Poor of the said Borough and Parish, and a considerable Debt hath been incurred for the necessary Purposes of carrying the said Act into Execution, which now remains due; and that the said Act hath in several Respects been found ineffectual for the Purposes thereby intended.

And the Witness further said, That there is now standing, in the Name of the Mayor and Corporation of the said Borough, the Sum of £384. io*. 8 d. Consolidated Bank Annuities, the Interest of which is applicable to the Relief of the Poor; but it is apprehended, that it would be more beneficial to the said Borough and Parish, if the said Sum was wholly vested in the said Governor and Guardians of the Poor, in order to sell or dispose of the same, and the Money arising therefrom applied towards discharging the said Debt.

And the Witness added, That there are, within the said Borough, several Common Lands, called Great Pennygillam, Little Pennygillam, Hay, Windmill, and Longland, the Aftermowth of which hath of ancient Right and Custom been enjoyed by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Free Burgesses, and the Widows of Free Burgesses, which is of little Benefit to the several Persons entitled thereto; and that it would be advanta-% geous to the Petitioners, if the same was to be sold or let for the best Price or Rent which could be had for the same, and the Money arising thereby applied towards repairing the Church, repairing and lighting the Streets, or any other Purpose, for the Ornament of the said Town, or the Convenience of the Inhabitants.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Considera- Ivelchester tion the Petition of John Harcourt, Esquire, and Election. Sir Samuel Harmay, Baronet; and also the Petition of John Pitt, John Shorland, and others, Electors in the Borough of Ivelchester, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Peregrine Cust and Benjamin Bond Hopkins, Esquires, for the said Borough, being come;

Tfie House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions. '

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent; and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

And several Members present having taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, and delivered in an Account of their Qualifications, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Qualification, according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Fourteen Members being found to be present;

llie Counsel and Agents for the Petitioners, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Peregrine Cust,

Esquire, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Benjamin Bond Hopkins, Esquire, were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Counsel for the said Sitting Members respectively informed the House, That they were different Parties, and desired to separate in their Defence:

And the Counsel for the Petitioners being called on by Mr. Speaker, informed the House, that if the Counsel for the Sitting Members would assure the House, upon their Honour, that their Cases were distinct, and had no Connection with each other, he could make no Objection to their separating in their Defence; and the Counsel for the Sitting Members having thereupon assured the House, that there was no Connection between their respective Clients; and, having also stated to the House, that there was no Communication between their respective Clients, and that the Petition was grounded upon a Charge of Bribery, which is distinct in its Nature, the House proceeded to the Appointment of the said Select Committee, as in the Case of there being more than Two Parties, on distinct Interests, before the House.

Then the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Forty-nine Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

to close the Poll at Three o’Clock on the Third Day of the said Election, it was most particularly necessary that there should be no Sort of Interruption of the Proceeding at the said Election, and from the numerous Persons who had a Right to vote therein, that there should not be, in the smallest Degree, any Interruption or Delay in taking the Poll; but the said Paul Le Mesurier, not regarding the Premises and the Freedom of Election, by himself, his Friends and Agents, caused and procured a turbulent Band of Sailors, and others, to be led up to and about the Hustings, from Time to Time, during the said Election, who, by Threats, Insult, and Violence, greatly interrupted the said Election, and thereby intimidated and prevented many of the Voters of the said Borough from polling for the Petitioner at the said Election, and delayed others, who were not to be so intimidated, so long, that the Poll was finally closed before they could, without great Damage and Risque to themselves, be permitted to poll at the said Election; and that many of the Voters of the said Borough, voting for the said Paul Le Mesurier, did ask, receive, and take Money, and other Rewards, of the said Paul Le Mesurier, his Friends and Agents, by way of Gift, Loan, and other Devices, and agreed and contracted with the said Paul Le Mcsurier, his Friends and Agents, for Money, Gifts, Offices, Employments, and Rewards, to give their Votes at the said Election, and, divers others of such Voters, for such illegal and corrupt Considerations as aforesaid, were persuaded by the said Paul Le Mesurier, his Friends and Agents, to forbear to give their Votes at the said Election; and that the said Paul Le Mesurier, before and during the said Election, by himself, his Friends and Agents, was guilty of Bribery, Corruption, and undue Influence, by giving and promising to give Money and other Rewards to the Voters of the said Borough, w hereby, and by other illegal and corrupt Means, nnny of the Voters of the said Borough were induced and prevailed upon to give their Votes at the said Election for the said Paul Le Mesurier, and others of the said Voters were induced and prevailed upon to forbear to give their Votes at the said Election; and that the said Paul Le Mcsurier, in the Time of this present Parliament, and after the Vacancy occasioned by the Death of the said Sir Barnard Turner for the said Borough, by himself, and by other Ways and Means, in the said Paul Le Mesurier s Behalf, and at his Charge, and before his Election for the said Borough (herein after mentioned) gave, presented, and allowed to several Persons, having Voices and Votes in such Election, Money, Meat, Drink, Entertainment, and Provision, and made Promises and Engagements to allow Money, Meat, Drink, Provision, Reward, and Entertainment, to and for several such Persons in particular, as well as to the said Borough in general, in order to be elected, and for being elected, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, contrary to the Statute; and that, by the aforesaid, and other undue and illegal Means, the said Paul Le Mesurier obtained a colourable Majority of Eleven Votes upon the Poll at the said Election, and was accordingly returned as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in Violation of the sacred Purity of Election, in Derogation of the Rights of the legal and uncorrupt Electors of the said Borough, and in Prejudice of the Petitioner, who, having a Majority of legal and uncorrupted Votes on the said Poll (and no Disability whatever) was duly elected at the said Election, and ought, in Justice to himself, and to the Voters of the said Borough, to have been returned a Burgess to serve in the present Parliament for the said Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to grant to the Petitioner such Relief therein as to the House shall seem just Vol. 40.
