A Petition of Elisha Tebb, Joseph Bromley, Thomas Southwark King, Thomas Birt, James Sayle, Thomas Edwards, Election. John Kent, James Whitaker, Samuel Moult en, Benjamin Shaw, Thomas Thomas, Thomas Citibank, John Windsor, John Easton, Thomas Baxter, Thomas Homersham,

Michael Craiston, Andrew Mann, Thomas Pooley, Joseph Marshall, and others, Electors of the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, was also delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in the room of the late Sir Barnard Turner, deceased, Sir Richard Hotham, Knight (lately One of the Representatives for the said Borough in Parliament) and Paul Le Mesurier, Esquire, were the Candidates; and that, at the said Election, many Persons who had no Capacity to vote at any Election for Members to serve in Parliament, and many others who were not qualified to vote at such Election for the said Borough, according to the last Determination of the House of Commons (settling the Right of Election in and for the said Borough, and the Law’ of the Land) were admitted to vote for the said Paul Le Mesurier; and that, the said Candidates having agreed finally to close the Poll at Three o'Clock on the Third Day of the said Election, it was most particularly necessary that there should be no Sort of Interruption of the Proceedings at the said Election, and that the numerous Persons w ho had a Right to vote therein should not be, in the smallest Degree, interrupted or delayed in giving their Suffrages; but the said Paul Le Mesurier, not regarding the Premises and the Freedom of Election, by himself, his Friends and Agents, caused and procured a turbulent Band of Sailors, and others, to be led up to the Hustings, from Time to Time, during the said f lection, who, by Threats, Insults, and Violence, greatly interrupted the said Election, and thereby intimidated and prevented many of the Voters of the said Borough from polling for the said Sir Richard Hotham, and also delayed others, who were nut to be intimidated, so long, that the Poll was finally closed before they could, without great Danger and Risque to themselves, be permitted to poll at the said Election; and that many of the Voters of the said Borough, voting for the said Paul Le Mesurier, did ask, receive, and take Money and other Rewards of the said Paul Le Mesurier, his Friends and Agents, by Way of Gift, Loan, and other Devices, and agreed and contracted with the said Paul Le Mesurier, his Friends and Agents, for Money, Gifts, Offices, Employments, and other Rewards, to give their Votes at the; said Election, and, divers others of them, for such illegal and corrupt Considerations as aforesaid, were persuaded, by the said Paul Le Mesurier, his Friends and Agents, to forbear to give their Votes at the said Election; and that the said Paul Le Mesurier, before and during the said Election, by himself, his Friends and Agents, was guilty of Bribery and Corruption, by giving and promising Money, Securities for Money, and other Rewards, to the Voters of the said Borough, whereby, and by other illegal Means, many of the Voters of the said Borough were induced and prevailed upon to give their Votes, at the said Election, for the said Paul Le Mesurier, and others of the said Voters were induced and prevailed upon to forbear to give their Votes at the said Election; and that the said Paul Le Mesurier, in the Time of this present Parliament, alter the Vacancy for the said Borough, occasioned by the Death of the said Sir Barnard Turner, and before the Election of the said Paul Le Mesurier (herein after mentioned) by himself, and by other Ways and Means in his Behalf, and at his Charge, gave, presented, and allowed to several Persons, having

Voices and Votes in such Election, Money, Meat, Drink, Entertainment, and Provision, and made Promises and Engagements to give and allow Money, Meat, Drink, Provision, Reward, and Entertainment, to and for several such Persons in particular, as well* as to the said Borough in general, in order to be elected, and for being elected to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, contrary to the Statute, §c.; and that, by the aforesaid, and other undue and illegal Means, equally destructive of the Freedom and Purity of Elections, the said Paul Le Mesurier procured himself to be unduly elected and returned a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioners, and others, Electors in the said Borough, who voted at the said Election for the said Sir Richard Hotham, the Petitioners and such Electors being a Majority of legal Votes, who gave their Voices at the said Election, and thereby duly elected the said Sir Richard Hotham to be the Representative for the said Borough in this present Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and to grant the Petitioners, and the other Electors of the said Borough, such Relief therein as to the House shall seem just.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the loth and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cases, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel,. or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petitions were ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matters of the said Petitions.

The Counsel and Agents, before-mentioned, being again returned to the Bar, the Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee delivered in to the House one of the said Lists, which had been struck by the said Counsel in his Presence, together with a new List of the Names of the Thirteen Members then remaining unstruck; which last mentioned List was read; and is as follows:

Sir William Mansel, Baronet, John Langston, Esquire, John Baring, Esquire, Philip Metcalfe, Esquire, George Osbaldeston, Esquire, Charles Lefevre, Esquire, John Moore, Esquire, the Honourable Richard Howard, Henry James Pye, Esquire, Bame Borne, Esquire, Alexander Hood, Esquire, Sir Charles Kent, Baronet, Thomas Boothby Parkins, Esquire.

A Bill to discontinue the Petty Custom on Aliens Goods imported into Great Britain, and the Duty of One per Centum on Goods exported to, or imported from, The Mediterranean Seas in unqualified Ships; and for repealing so much of an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as enacts, that no Part of the Old Subsidy shall be drawn back upon Goods exported to the British Colonic* or Plantations in America, was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House w ill, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

The Thirteen Members, before-mentioned, being returned to the House, the said Counsel and Agents were again called in to the Bar.

And the Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee informed the House, that the said Thirteen Members had by themselves chosen Thomas Powys, Esquire, and the Earl of Morning ton, to serve on the said Select Committee.

And the Names of the said Thomas Powys, Esquire, and the Earl of Mornington, were added to the said List of Thirteen Members.

And the said Fifteen Members, being the Select Committee for trying the Merits of the said Petition of John Harcourt, Esquire, and Sir Samuel Hannay, Baronet; and also, the Petition of John Pitt, John Shorland, and others, Electors in the Borough of Ivelchester, now taken into Consideration, were sworn by the Clerk at the Table, in the usual Manner.

And thereupon the Counsel and Agents withdrew.

Ordered, That the said Select Committee do meet forthwith in the Third Committee Chamber appointed for hearing the Trials of controverted Elections.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Church, thereunto subscribed, Landlords, Owners, and Inha* Middlesex, bitants of Houses and Land, within the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for providing a Workhouse, within the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Middlesex, and for raising Money for that Purpose,* and to discharge Debts already contracted on Account of the Poor, and for further regulating the Manner of rating to the Poor, appointing Overseers, and preserving all Accounts relating to the Offices of Churchwarden and Overseer of the Poor, and Treasurer of the same Parish; and Setting forth, That, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, as it is now formed, it will he extremely prejudicial to the Petitioners and other Landlords, Owners, and Inhabitants of Houses and Land in the said Parish, and will interfere with and lessen the Security of the several Persons who have advanced their Monies, by way of Annuities, on the Security of the Poor Rates of the said Parish, and will alter, and in Effect repeal or render ineffectual, Part of the Statute of the Forty-third of Queen Elizabeth, touching the Appointment of Overseers of the Poor: And therefore praying. That they may have Leave to be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill; and that they may receive such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit

Mr. Rolle reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill to amend and render more effectual Two Acts, made in the Second and Twelfth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing, widening, and altering several Roads leading from Tavistock to Plymouth, and other Plades, in the County of Devon, and for repairing and widening the Road from the Guildhall, in Tavistock aforesaid, through Matthew Street and Lower Brook Street, to Chtrrybrook, and to Dunna Bridge Pound, and from the Callmgton Turnpike Road to Moru'clham and New Quay, in the said County, was committed That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That so much of His Majesty’s Most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 19th Day of May las^ as relates to providing effectually for the Maintenance of the National Faith, and the Public Credit, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do consider of a proper Provision to be made for discharging the Unfunded Debt of the Public.

Ordered, That the Account shewing the Amount of the Course of the Navy, Victualling, &c. from the Time to which the same was last paid to 31st Deem-ber 1783, with the Interest computed to 5th July 1784, upon such of the Bills as carry an Interest, and distinguishing the Amount of the Interest and Non-Interest Bills in each Month, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of the Debt of the Office of Ordnance, as far as the same can be made up, with the Amount of the Debentures now standing out, distinguishing the Amount of the Debentures issued in each Month, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of extraordinary Expences of the Anny, incurred and paid by the Right honourable the Paymaster General of His Majesty’s Forces, from the 1st of February to the 24th of December 1783, both inclusive, and not provided for by Parliament, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of Savings on the Pay voted for His Majesty’s Forces during the Years 1781 and 1783, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of Guards, Garrisons, and other His Majesty’s Land Forces in Great Britain, Guernsey, and Jersey, from 25th December 1783 to 24th December 1784, both inclusive, being 366 Days, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of His Majesty’s Forces in the Plantations, including those in Garrison at Gibraltar, from 25th December 1783 to 24th December 1784* both inclusive, being 366 Days, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, for the Year 17^4> be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of the Inn Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, and of the Expences of the said Hospital for the Year 17S4* be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of Additionals to Three Regiments of Foot, for the respective Times within mentioned, in the Year 1783, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of the Pensions to be paid to the Widows of Commissioned Officers, for the Year 1784, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That Surplusses, stated the 5th Day of April 1783, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That Surplusses, stated the 10th Day of October 1783, be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee;

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert took the Chair of the Committee. j

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair. j

Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Mr. Gilbert also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Ordered, That the Bill for the more effectual Pre- Prevention of vention of Smuggling in this Kingdom, be read a Second lu& Time upon Monday Morning next.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Considera- ColcWtr lion the Petition of Sir Robert Smyth, Baronet, KUctivo. complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Colchester, in the County of Essex, being come; °

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and Ont £ . hundred

24 Geo. III. i° Juliu 275

hundred and Seven Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House , being locked, the Clerk Was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Two Members, then present, were draw n, who were not objected to;

And the Name of John Morllock, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Thirty-four other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Sir Joseph Alawbey, Baronet, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioner, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Thirteen other Members, then present, were drawn, who w ere not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Fifty-two other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Twenty on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; Two, on Account of their being Petitioners to this House, complaining of undue Elections and Returns; Twenty-one, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees; Four, on Account of their having already, in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees; Four, on Account of their Returns to serve in Parliament not having been brought in Fourteen Days; and One, on Account of his having voted at the sakl Election.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and, not excused, or set aside, being complete, Lists of the said Names w ere delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

'Dye Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

An ingrossed Bill for amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Roads leading from the Meeting House in the Parish of Llanegwad, to the Lime Kilns in the Parish of Llanddarog, and from Dan-yr-Allt in the said Parish of Llantgwad', to Pont-y-Berem in the Parish of Llangendeirne, in the County of Carmarthen, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Roads leading from the Meeting House in the Parish of Llanegwad, to the Lime Kilns in the Parish of Llanddarog, and from Dan-yr-Allt in the said Parish of Llanegwad, to Pont-y-Berem in the Parish of Llangendehne, in the County of Carmarthen.

Ordered, That Sir William Marisel do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

That every Contributor towards raising the said Sum of Six millions shall, for every One thousand Pounds contributed, be entitled to Six Tickets in a Lottery to consist of Thirty-six thousand Tickets, amounting to Three hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds, upon Payment of the further Sum of Ten Pounds for each Ticket, the said Three hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds to be distributed into Prizes for the Benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery, which shall be paid in Money, at the Bank of England, to such Proprietors, upon Demand, as soon after the 1st Day of March 1785, as Certificates can be prepared, without any Deduction whatsoever.

That every Contributor shall, on or before the 9th Day of July next, make a Deposit of Fifteen Pounds per Centum on such Sum as he or she shall chuse to subscribe towards raising the said Sum of Six millions, with the Chief Cashier or Cashiers of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, and also a Deposit of Fifteen Pounds per Centum with the said Cashier or Cashiers, in Part of the Monies to be contributed towards raising the said Sum of Three hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds by Lottery, as a^ecurity for making the future Payments respectively on or before the Days or Times herein after mentioned; that is to say,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon all Stuffs wholly made of Cotton spun in Great Britain, to be so printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain (except as aforesaid) the Sum of Three Pence for every Yard in Length, reckoning One Yard wide, and after that Rate for a greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon all Linens and Stuffs (except as before excepted) to be printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain, the Sum of Three Pence for every Yard in Length, and after that Rate for a greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon all Ribbands made in Great Britain, and manufactured wholly of Silk, or whereof the greater Part in Value shall be Silk, not exceeding One Third of an Inch in Breadth, a Duty of One Penny for every Twelve Yards in Length, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon all such Ribbands above One-third, and not exceeding Three-fourths of an Inch in Breadth, a Duty of One Farthing for every Yard in Length, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon all such Ribbands above Three-fourths of an Inch, and not exceeding Two Inches and One-half in Breadth, a Duty of One Halfpenny for every Yard in Length, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon all such Ribbands exceeding Two Inches and One-half in Breadth, a Duty of One Penny for every Yard, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon every Yard of Gauze made in Great Britain, and manufactured wholly of Silk, or in which there shall be any Mixture of Silk, being striped or figured Gauze, and not exceeding One Yard in Breadth, a Duty of Three Pence, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon every Yard of such Gauze, being striped or figured Gauze, exceeding One Yard in Breadth, a Duty of Four Pence, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon every Yard of such Gauze, being plain Gauze, and not exceeding One Yard in Breadth, a Duty of Two Pence, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for and upon every Yard of Gauze, being plain Gauze, and exceeding One Yard in Breadth, a Duty of Three Pence, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Maker of Mead for Sale be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Twenty Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Brandy Dealer, or Person selling Brandy or other Spirituous Liquors, not being a Retailer or Rectifier, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Five Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every other Distiller for Sale or Exportation be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Ten Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Corn Distiller, or Maker of Low Wines or Spirits from Corn or Grain for Sale or for Exportation, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Fifty Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Maker of any Kind of Sweets, other than Mead for Sale, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Five Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person in Great Britain qualified, in respect to their Property, to kill Game, shall, previous to their shooting at, killing, or destroying any Game, register their Qualifications with the Clerk of the Peace, and Annually take out Certificates thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Certificate Annually granted to any Person qualified, in respect of his Property, to kill Game, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, there shall be paid a Stamp Duty of One Pound One Shilling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Deputation, or Appointment of a Gamekeeper, granted to any Person (not qualified in respect of his Property) by any Lord or Lady of a Manor, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, there shall be paid a Stamp Duty of One Pound One Shilling, over and above the Duty now imposed on Deeds.

The Ninth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by inserting, after the Word " Tiles," and before the Word " commonly," the "Words " which shall " be made in Great Britain."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That there be charged, for and upon all Tiles which shall be made in Great Britain, commonly called or known by the Name of Pan or Ridge Tiles, a Duty of Eight Shillings for every Thousand, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

The Tenth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by inserting, after the Word " Tiles," and 'before the Word " commonly," the Words " which shall be " made in Great Britain."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That there be charged, for and upon all Tiles which shall be made in Great Britain, commonly called or known by the Name oi'Peeving Tiles, not exceeding Ten Inches Square, a Duty of One Shilling and Six Pence for every Hundred, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

The Eleventh Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by inserting, after the Word " Tiles," and before the Word " commonly," the Words " which shall be " made in Great Britain."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That there be charged, for and upon all Tiles which shall be made in Great Britain, commonly called or known by the Name of Paving Tiles, exceeding Ten Inches Square, a Duty of Three Shillings for every Hundred, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

The Twelfth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by inserting, after the Word " Tiles," and before the Word " other," the Words " which shall be made " in Great Britain "

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That there be chargedj for and upon all Tiles which shall be made in Great Britain', other than such as are before enumerated) and described, by whatsoever Name or Names such Tiles now are, or hereafter may be called or known, a Duty of Three Shillings for every Thousand, and so in' Proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

The Thirteenth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution;

The House divided.

The Noes went forth.

A Petition of Captain Elliot Salter, of His Majesty’s Salur's ' Royal Navy, was presented to the House, and read; Prizei Setting forth, That the Petitioner, on the 29th of July 1782, being then Commander of His Majesty’s Ship Santa Margaretta, fell in with, and took, a French Frigate, called The Amazone, but, being the next Morning chased by the whole Ft'ench Fleet, was compelled to abandon his Prize, on Account of her disabled State, notwithstanding he might at that time easily have destroyed her, but was prevented from so doing by Motives of Humanity, on Account of the Number of the Wounded on board of her, whom it was impossible to remove; and that the Navy Board have conceived him not to be entitled, under those Circumstances, to the Head Money given by Act of Parliament, and the Petitioner is therefore compelled to apply to the House, on Behalf of himself and of the Officers and Crew of the Santa Margarettay for such Relief as to the House shall seem meet; and that this Petition could not be prepared and offered to the House on or before the 16th Day of June last, being the last Day appointed for receiving Petitions for private Bills, on Account of the Petitioner not having obtained His Majesty’s Royal Approbation, which is required, by a Standing Order of the House, before a Petition of this Nature can be received; but that Approbation having now been obtained, the Petitioner hopes that, under these Circumstances, the House will permit a Petition to be offered.

Ordered, That in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Captain Elliot Salter.

Then a Petition of Captain Elliot Salter, late Commander of His Majesty’s Ship Santa Margarettay of 36 Guns, and 255 Men, in Behalf t)f himself, her Officers and Ship’s Company, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

the said Petition was brought up, and read;

4 D Setting

﻿Distress of Shetland.

86 2* JuliL784.

Setting forth, That the Petitioner, being on a Cruize off Cape Henry, on the Coast of North America, on the 29th of July 1782, fell in with, at Day-break, and gave Chace to, a Sail, which was soon after discovered to be a French Frigate, of equal force to the Santa Margaretta, hut at the same Time perceiving Eight Sail of large Ships bearing down under a Press of Sail (which proved to be Part of a Fleet of Thirteen Sail of the Line, under the Command of Monsieur Vaudrieut) he wore Ship and stood from her, having not only an Enemy but a Lee Shore to encounter; that the Frigate then gave Chace till 3 P. M. when she tacked and stood back to her Fleet, which the Petitioner had then lost Sight of from the Mast-head, excepting only a Second Frigate (supposed to be the Iris) which continued in Sight; and the Petitioner, his Officers, and Ship’s Company, having an eager Desire to bring the first-mentioned Frigate to an Action, it was judged proper to tack and stand after her for that Purpose; in a Quarter of an Hour she also tacked, and at 5 P. M. the Action commenced within Pistol-shot of each other, and continued warmly on both Sides for an, Hour and a Quarter, when she was obliged to surrender, having upwards of 80 Men killed, and 70 wounded, and proved to be LAmazo?ie> mounting 36 Guns, long 12 and 6 Pounders, and having 291 Men on board, commanaed by the Viscomte de Montguiotl, who was killed in the early Part of the Action; and that the Petitioner immediately sent a Lieutenant and One Third of his Ship’s Company on board, to take Possession of her, and shift the Officers and all such Prisoners as it jvas practicable to remove; but the Situation of L'Amazone, soon after she struck, was critical, her Main and Mizen Masts over her Side, her Hull in a most shattered Condition, several Guns dismounted, and Four Feet Water in her Hold; it was therefore judged most prudent to take her in Tow, and at Day-break the next Morning the whole French Fleet was discovered in Chace, and near up with the Petitioner, who was under the Necessity of recalling his Officers and People (after cutting away the small Remains of her Rigging) and to abandon the Prize, which might have been easily destroyed, but not being able to remove the wounded Prisoners, his Feelings could not admit of their Destruction, which in that Case must have been inevitable; and that the Petitioner, having applied to the Navy Board for Head Money for the Capture of the above-mentioned Ship, which was in his Possession Twelve Hours, and having received for Answer, that the Act of Parliament did not allow of that Bounty, as the Ship was not entirely destroyed, the Petitioner, in Behalf of himself, his Officers, and Ship’s Company, finds himself and them entirely precluded from those Advantages, which he' presumes were intended by the Legislature as an Encouragement to His Majesty’s Navy, and to which, under the Spirit of the Act, he conceives his Ship’s Company entitled from their Gallantry and very good Conduct on the above-mentioned Occasion: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief as shall appear just and proper.

Ordercdy That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Mr. William JVyndham Gremilk, Sir Peter Parker, &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had lira Majesty’s Commands to lay before this House, a Petition from the Commissioners of Supply, Clergy, and Heritors, of the Country or

Islands of Shetland, in 'Behalf of the Inhabitants of those Islands, now in extreme Distress for Want of Bread, which had been presented to his Majesty, and which His Majesty recommends to the Consideration of the House.

And Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer delivered the said Petition in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Unto the King’s Most Excellent Majesty,

The Petition of the Commissioners of Supply, Clergy, and Heritors, of the Country or Islands of Shetland? in Behalf of the Inhabitants of those Islands, now in extreme Distress for Want of Bread;

Most humbly sheweth,

That the Soil, and still more the Climate, of those Islands, unpropitious to Agriculture even in the best Seasons, produce but a scanty Support for the Inhabitants, in Number about 20,000, their principal Dependence for Subsistence being upon Fish, and the Produce of their Sheep and Cattle, which in general have hitherto enabled them to buy such a Proportion of Bread as their Support required, which their small Farms seldom or never produced: In the last Seven Years Crops, there have been Four, which together, reserving Seed Corn, did not yield above One Year’s Supply of Bread, so that Three Years Provision for about 20,000 Persons has been imported in the Period mentioned (including 1,200 Bolls humanely sent them by Government) and the greatest Part of it at exorbitant Prices; their Two last Crops especially have failed in a greater Degree than ever known, and, by the Length and Severity of last Winter, most of their Sheep and Cattle have died, and also some of the poorer People themselves, for Want of the real Necessaries of Life; the Fishing too has almost totally failed; the Heritors of the Country have supported the Inhabitants until all their Resources are gone; Sir Thomas Dundas, of Kerse9 one of the greatest Proprietors, has been most benevolent; there is now indeed Bread to be bought, but the Heritors Funds being already expended, and the poorer People’s Sheep and Cattle now dead, their Distress is only aggravated by seeing a Relief which they are incapable of purchasing.

From the detached Situation of those Islands, no other Part of Your Majesty’s Dominions can, at any Time, feel an equal Degree of Distress to that now felt by their wretched Inhabitants, their Distance from the Continent rendering it impossible for them to procure a Supply of Meal in Time, which forced them to eat their Seed Corn: This Distress is, with the utmost Candour and Fidelity, now represented to Your Majesty.

However far removed, by our local Situation, from those Blessings and Advantages which Your Majesty’a Subjects derive from Your exalted Virtues, and mild and equitable Government, we, notwithstanding, feel the happy Effects of that Government, and have hitherto, and always will join our Fellow Subjects in adoring that Providence which placed Your Majesty and Your Royal Ancestors upon the British Throne, by that happy Event communicating to Millions the Blessings of Liberty, Security, and National Felicity: With all Humility and Loyalty we implore Your Royal Benevolence in Behalf of a People, who, however remote, and perhaps otherways insignificant, yet, considered. as a Nursery of Seamen, we will venture to prove, hath contributed more to the Naval Power of Your Majesty’s Empire, than any other equal Number of Your Subjects.

May it therefore please Your Majesty, . to extend Your Beneficence and Clemency to the immediate Relief of this distressed and afflicted People, in such 5 Proportion*

Distress in The Marquis of Graham, according to Order, re-

Shetiand. ported from the Committee of the whole House, to

whom it was referred to consider of the Petition, which had been presented to His Majesty, from the Commissioners of Supply, Clergy, and Heritors, of the Country or Islands of Shetland, in Behalf of the Inhabitants of those Islands, now in extreme Distress for Want of Bread, That he was directed by the Committee to move the House, that an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, most humbly to thank His Majesty, for His Majesty’s gracious Attention to the Wants and Distresses of His People, in the Communication , His Majesty has been pleased to make to this House, of the Petition of the Inhabitants of Shetland to His Majesty; and to assure His Majesty that this House has taken the same into their earliest Consideration, and most humbly beseech His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give such Directions as may tend most effectually to avert the Evils that are to be apprehended from the calamitous State of the Inhabitants of the Shetland Islands; and to assure His Majesty, JLhat this House will make good, out of the first Aids that shall be granted by Parliament, such Expences as shall be incurred by His Majesty, in relieving the Misery to which His Majesty’s unhappy Subjects may be reduced.

And the Marquis of Graham moved the House accordingly.

Sir John Wrottesley reported from the Committee to whom the Petition of certain of His Majesty’s 4

Justices of the Peace, acting in and for the County of Stafford, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, William Inge, Esquire, being examined, said, That the present County Gaol at Stafford is ill constructed, too small, greatly gone to Decay, and very inconvenient and inadequate for the Security and Accommodation of Prisoners — That the House of Correction at Stafford is in a ruinous Condition, and very insecure and incommodious, there being no Yard or Outlet for the Convenience of separating the Prisoners; — that the said Prison belongs to the County of Stafford, and is situate over a Gateway belonging to the Corporation of Stafford.

And the Witness further said, That the building of a New County Gaol in a proper Situation, and converting the present County Gaol into a House of Correction, would be a great Convenience and Advantage to the said County; and that, at a very respectable Meeting of Gentlemen at the Quarter Sessions, it was unanimously agreed, that Directions should be given for an Application to Parliament for effecting the above Purposes.

And the "Witness added, That there is now in the Hands of the Treasurer of the said County, the Sum of £. 2,200, which, in the Year 1771, was raised upon the Inhabitants of a Part of the said County, as a Forfeiture for not raising the Militia; and also, the Sum of £.1,125. 11 id. which, in the Year 1775>

was raised in the same Manner, and on the like Account.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House* to consider of the said Report.

Election. was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That at the last Election of Alembers to serve in Parliament for the County of Bedford, the Right honourable the Earl of Upper Ossoiy in the Kingdom of Ireland, the Right honourable Robert Henley, Lord Ongley, of the said Kingdom of Ireland, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that William Goldsmith, Esquire, the Sheriff of the said County, who presided at the said Election, declared that the Numbers on the Poll were, for the Earl of Upper Ossory 1,050, for the Petitioner 974» and for the said Lord Ongley 973; -and, the said Lord Ongley presented his Petition to the House, stating, among other Things, that of the Votes

given and received by the said Sheriff at the said Election, a greater Number was given in Favour of him the said Robert Henley Lord Ongley, than in Favour of the Petitioner, and that the said Sheriff ought to have returned the said Lord Ongley as one of the Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said County of Bedford, instead of the Petitioner, and praying, that the Return of the said Sheriff might be amended, and the said Lord Ongley9s Name inserted therein in the Stead of the Petitioner; and that the said Petition was, by an Order of the House, referred to a Select Committee, and came on to be heard cm the 2 2d Day of June last, and the said Committee, on the 29th Day of the same Month, resolved, That the said Sheriff ought to have taken the Vote of William Lugsden from the Poll of the Petitioner, and added it to the Poll of the said Lord Ongley, and on the 1st Day of July Instant determined, that the said Lord Ongley ought to have been returned, and the said Resolution having been reported to the House, the said Return h&th accordingly been altered; and that the said Lord Ongley, after the Dissolution of the last Parliament, and after the issuing of the Writ for the said Election, and previous to and during the Poll, by himself and his Agents, and by other Ways and Means, on the Behalf, and at the Charge, of the said Lord Ongley, did give, present, and allow, and did promise, agree, and engage to give, present, and allow, to the Electors of the said County, and to several Persons who had, or claimed to have, a Right to vote in the Election for the said County, Aleat, Drink, Reward, Entertainment, and Provision; and, the said Lord Ongley did give, present, and allow, and did promise, agree, alid engage to give, present, and allow, to the Electors of the said County, and to several Persons who had, or claimed to have, a Right to vote in the Election for the said County, Meat, Drink, Reward, Entertainment, and Provision, as aforesaid, in order to procure himself to be elected for the said County; and that the said Sheriff rejected a great Number of Persons who tendered their Votes for the Petitioner, and who ought to have been admitted, having a Right to vote at the said Election, and admitted upon his Poll for the said Lord Ongley a great Number of Persons w'ho were not Freeholders, or were otherwise disqualified from voting, and ought to have been rejected; and that the said Lord Ongley, by himself and his Agents, after the Dissolution of the last Parliament, and previous to and during the said Election, was guilty of Bribery, and other corrupt and illegal Practices, in order to procure himself to be returned for the said County; and by such illegal and undue Aleans, the said Lord Ongley obtained the Admission of so many Votes in his Favour on the Poll as, upon a Deduction of One Vote from the Petitioner’s Number on the Poll, and an Addition of it to his own, have caused his Name to be inserted in the Return, in Prejudice of the Petitioner, who was duly elected by the Alajority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as the Nature of the Petitioners Case shall require.

A Petition of the Tanners in London, on Behalf of themselves and the Manufacturers of Tanned Leather throughout the Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the* Petitioners observing, by the Votes, that a Bill has been brought in, to revive the High Duties upon the Importation of Oak Bark into this Kingdom, which, if passed into a Law, will prove detrimental to the Manufacture of Tanned Leather, one of the principal Staple Commodities of this Kingdom, and eventually injurious to the Revenue, the Petitioners submit to the Consideration of the House, the Expediency of reviving Duties which, as they amount to a Prohibition, must prove unproductive to the Revenue, and a Check upon an important Manufacture: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief as they shall see meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for reviving the Duties upon Oak Bark imported into Great Britain, and for extending several Acts of Parliament, relative to the Manufacture of Leather, to that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, is committed.

Sir William J)olben reported from the Committee, ,to whom the Petition of the Reverend Thomas JVeekes Dalby, of Chippenham, in the County of Wilts, Clerk, Executor of the last Will and Testament of Edward Downes, deceased, who was Executor of the last Will and Testament of Charles JVeekes, late of London, Merchant, deceased, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and bad directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove foe Allegations ,of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Gray produced to Your Committee the Probates of the Wills of Charles JVeekes, and of Edward Dmmes, whereby it appeared, that Thomas JVeekes Dalby, the Petitioner, is Executor of the last Will and Testament of the said Edwcu'd Downes, who was the Executor of the last Will and Testament of foe said Charles IVeekes.

Mr. Gray also produced an authenticated Copy of an original Record, containing certain Proceedings ,in Equity, in His Majesty’s Court of Exchequer, between Cfmles JVeekes and the Commissioners of the Victualling Office, and others, respecting the £hip Vox. 40.

an

Hope; from whence it appeared, by the Deposition of John Scoles, made in the said Cause, That Charles JVeekes was Owner of the Ship Hope, Burthen 140 Tons, or thereabouts, and was, at the latter End of the Year 1743, Outward bound from London, to bring home a Loading of Sugars from Nevis.

And it appeared by Charter Party, produced to Your Committee, dated 1st December' 1743, That the said Ship was let to the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Navy for One Voyage, to carry Stores from London to Gibraltar or Port Mahon; and that the said Ship should, Wind and Weather permitting, sail under Convoy for Gibraltar or Port Mahon, as should be required: And from the Depositions of Nicholas Feriter and Henry Harley, Mariners, and of John Scoles, it appeared that the sailing Part of the said Voyage was performed from the Downs to Gibraltar in 19 Days, and from the Downs to Port Mahon in 40 Days, and that a Voyage from London to Port Mahon is generally performed in 6 or 7 Weeks.

That the said Ship was nevertheless detained by Government more than 12 Months, in the Course of which Time she received considerable Damage; and her said Voyage to Nevis (where a Cargo of Sugars was ready for her, at the Rate of Eight Shillings per Hundred Weight for Freight, and from thence to London) was totally defeated; and that after she was unloaded *at Port Mahon, she necessarily remained them near Two Months to be repaired and victualled, anq that she sailed from thence without any Cargo, and put into Gibraltar: And it appeared that such Detention of the said Ship was contrary to the Spirit and true Meaning of the said Charter Party; and that the said Ship was, during the said Voyage, used by Government in the Nature of a Monthly Transport.

And it appeared by several Charter Parties, dated in the Years 1741 and 1743, and by the Reports referred by the House to Your Committee, That the Government, in the War which began in 1739, had Two Methods of hiring Ships; foe one for Transports to bp used at their Will and pleasure, so long as the Service required, at 14$. per Ton per Calendar Month, taken into immediate Pay for Six Months certain, and so continued till discharged; and if discharged Abroad, such Pay wps continued for a certain Time, for the Ship either to return Home, or to proceed elsewhere, as fthe Owner had directed.

The other Method of hiring Ships by Government was in the Manner die Hope bad been hired, as abovp mentioned, under certain Restrictions for particular Voyages.

And it appeared to Your Committee, from the Deposition of the said Nicholas Feriter, That the Reason or Inducement of the said Charles JVcekes's letting oqt the said Ship to Freight to the said Commissioners was, as he believed and apprehended, that the said JVeekes doubted not but that she would be able to compleat her Voyage to Gibraltar and Port Mahon in about 7 Weeks, and then have proceeded to Nevis, which would have been little or no Hindrance of her intended Voyage to Nevis; and on that Account4 the Stores and Provisions were carried at a very small Price, the same being done only so help the $pid Ship out, she having bpt little Lading from England.

It fuifoer appeared to your Committee, That ’ ap-cprding to foe Mqdc of hiring, after the Mapner of a Monthly Transport, the Money due to the said JVeekes, in respect to the said Ship, amounted to £.1,524. 11. 2J, besides Interest; and that, according to the other Mode of hiring, the Money due under foe Charter Party, and for the Special Damages sustained by the said JVeekes, from Government having deviated from the true Spirit and Meaning of the Contract, has already, in the said Suit against the said Commissioners of foe Victualling Office, been proved to amount to £. 2,034. 6. . besides Interest; which said Sum of

and that the said School was, as the Petitioners conceive, and as appears to them, originally founded for the Benefit of the Inhabitants of Middleton, otherwise Milton, and the neighbouring Parishes, and Boys in the Neighbourhood of Milton, who can go in the Morning and return at Night, and such Inhabitants of Milton, and the Neighbourhood thereof, have a Right to, and always have enjoyed, the Benefit of the said School, and had their Chrildren educated gratis at the said School, and so the Right honourable Lord Milton, the present Lord of the Manor of Milton, understands the Right and Usage to be, and in a Bill by him exhibited in the High Court of Chancery, in the Year 1758, against the then Feoffees touching the said Schoolr his Lordship insisted that the said School was founded chiefly if not solely for the Benefit of Milton, and its Neighbourhood, the Inhabitants whereof, at the Time of the Foundation, were all Tenants of the Abbot and Convent; and that the Petitioners are not warranted in consenting to the School's being removed out of the Parish of Milton, or its Neighbourhood, as thereby they should destroy the Intention of the Founder of the said School, and deprive the Inhabitants of Milton, and the neighbouring Parishes, of the Right they are entitled to, and have always enjoyed, of sending their Children to be educated gratis in the said School, and for whose peculiar Advantage the said School was at first founded; and that, although Lord Milton well knew the Intention of the Founder of the said Free School to be for the Use of the Inhabitants of Milton and the Neighbourhood, and, that the same was originally built, and has ever since, for now Years, remained in the Place where it now stands, and yet thought proper to rebuild and improve his Mansion House of Milton Abbey, the Petitioners, though the said Lord Milton had made no Requisition to them upon the Subject of the Removal of the said School previous to his Rebuilding and Improvement as aforesaid, and, under such Circumstances, had no reasonable Claim to have his private Convenience accommodated by the Removal of the said School, after such his Rebuilding and Improvement, were nevertheless so far from being averse to any reasonable Indulgence of his Lordship’s Wishes, that they did offer to gratify the same in such Manner as appeared to them in any Degree consistent with the Duties of their Trust, and did, by their Agent, declare their Readiness to remove, or consent to the Removal of the School to any other convenient Spot, in the Parish of Milton, dry, healthy, and otherwise adapted to the Purpose, at whatever Distance he might choose from hb Mansion House, upon hb erecting, instead of the present School House, another comjnodious one for the Master and Scholars, with suitable Conveniences, and conveying such Premises, with the Appurtenances, in Fee, with "hn indisputable Title to the same, to the Petitioners, for the Habitation and Use of the Master and Scholars; and that, as the Petitioners were so ready to accommodate Lord Miltons Convenience, and had, to consult his Ease, offered to put the School House in any other Part of the Parish, and, as the same may easily be removed a considerable Distance from his Mansion House, the Parish extending Vol. 40.

more than Three Miles therefrom, and as it can be no Inconvenience to hb Lordship to have the School at such considerable Distance from him, the Petitioners are much alarmed by a Bill brought into Parliament by Lord Milton, and now depending in the House, for removing the said School to the Town of Dorchester, which the Petitioners cannot by any Means consent to, and they have no such Authority, and it would be a flagrant Violation of their Trust to consent to remove the School from Milton and its Neighbourhood, for whose sole Benefit it was founded, and where the Boys in Milton, and the adjoining Parbhes, can resort to School, and return Home at Night, and be educated gratis, without putting their Parents or Friends to the Inconvenience and Expence of boarding or keeping them from their own Homes, and Dorchester is Ten Miles from Milton, and, if nearer, would be a very improper Situation, because there is already in that Town a Free Grammar School, well endowed, and it must be very improper to have Two Free Schools in the same Place; and that, as the Petitioners are seised of the School House and Premises thereto belonging in Fee, being purchased by their Predecessors for a valuable Consideration, the Petitioners rely on their undoubted Right, and the Justice of the House, that no Parliamentary Aid will be given to take away from the Petitioners their Property without their Consent, or to remove the School out of the reach of those for whose Benefit it was founded, and thereby utterly to defeat the Ends of its Foundation: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law7.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting a Cottage or Tenement used as and for a School House, and other Hereditaments, in or near the Town of Milton, in the County of Dorset, in Joseph Lord Milton, and his Heirs, in Lieu of, and in Compensation for, a Messuage or Tenement and Garden, situate and being in the Town of Dorchester, of greater Value, be read a Second Time: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Soap in the Cities of London and Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, confiding in the Protection of the Laws, have erected Buildings, and purchased Utensils, at a very great Expence, for carrying on the Manufacture of Soap, and, alarmed at the Depredations which Smugglers and fraudulent Manufacturers have committed on their Trade, and consequently on that important Branch of the Revenue which depends upon it, are impelled, by a Sense of public Duty, as well as of private Interest, to submit the following Facts to the /Consideration of Parliament: That, by the Tenth of Anne, a Duty of One Penny per Pound was imposed*on all Soap manufactured in Great Britain, and, by the Twelfth of the same Ileign, a further Duty of One Halfpenny per Pound was laid; which Two Duties, the Petitioners apprehend, will be found to have produced, on an Average of the Years 1780, 1781, and 1782, a Net £211,444. 7s. 6Id; and that, by the Twenty-second of the present Reign, a further Sum of Three Farthings on hard, and One Farthing per Pound on soft, was directed to be raised on Soap, the Produce of which last Duty, though estimated at £ 104,500, has actually produced, for the Year 1783, no more than £12,406! 8s. Sid.; and, it appears, that the Three Duties on Soap, which, according to the Amount of the Two first alone, before the Third was laid, ought to have produced, for the Year 1783, £317,166. n s. 4 <L has actually produced (stating the increased Drawback on the additional Duty) no more than £223,850. 15 s. 9and that the >Petitioners have every Reason to believe, from attentive Observation, and diligent Enquiry, that the Consumption of Soap in the Island, far from being diminished, is exceedingly increased, and that the Deficiency in the Produce of the late Tax is entirely owing to the secret Practices of the fraudulent Manufacturer, and the illicit Importation of Soap by the Smuggler; and that the Petitioners are convinced, from the best Information they are able to obtain, that more than One Vol. 40.

Half of the Soap made in Great Britain escapes the Payment of the Duty, and, they have equal Reason to assert, that the illicit Importation of Soap from Jf'ranee and Guernsey, and especially from Ireland, is such at, in a great Measure, to supply the Consumption of Wales, and that of a considerable Part of the Maritime Counties of England: — Under these Circumstances of a total Failure in the Profits of their Trade, by which they are no longer able to live, and of impending Ruin to what remains of a valuable Branch of tb? Public Revenue, the Petitioners are induced to sub* Blit their Distress to the Consideration of Parliament, and humbly to intreat Relief; and that the Petitioners; desirous of submitting to all such Regulations as are necessary to the Collection of the Revenue, consistently with the Freedom of the Subject, propose, that an Act may be passed to give the Excise Officer the same free Access, by Night as well as by Day, to the entered Premises of the Soap Manufacturer, which he now has to those of the Glass-maker, and that the Officer shah have Liberty to take an Account of the Raw Materials in the Stock of every Manufacturer of Soap, and be empowered to charge the Duty on the Materials, whenever the Quantity of hard Soap produced shall be less than in the Proportion of One Ton from 14 Hundred and £of Oil, or from 13 Hundred of Tallow or Grease; and the Petitioners also beg Leave to suggest the Necessity of prohibiting Pipes, Cocks, and Perforations in the Sides or Bottoms of the Coppers made use of in the Manufacture of Soap; and likewise propose, that no hard Soap shall be sold, except in the Shape of Cakes or Bars, by which Means the many Frauds committed in consequence of the present Allowance of the Use of Scraps or Parings (under which Names all Kinds and Quantities of hard Soap, of an irregular Shape, are sold) will in future be completely prevented; and, the Petitioners are further convinced that, for the more effectual Prevention of Fraud, no Soap Manufacture shall be carried on except in a City, Market Town, or within the Limits of the Foot-walk of an Officer; and that the Petitioners beg Leave also to suggest their Opinion, that the Power which the Commissioners of Excise and the Justices of the Peace possess, to mitigate Penalties at their Discretion, has not only weakened, but almost destroyed the Operation of the Law, for which Reason they submit to the House the strong Conviction they feel, that the Laws which guard the Revenue would be more effectual, if the Commissioners of Excise and Justices of the Peace had no other Discretion than that of either exempting from all Penalty, on Proof that no Fraud was designed, or of levying the whole Penalty on Proof of intentional Offence, as by that Means Impunity could not be granted under the Semblance of Punishment; and that the Petitioners are induced to propose these Regulations from the full Conviction they feel, that no Measures less forcible will be of any Avail, especially as the fraudulent Manufacture of Soap is now an established Trade, and as the Smuggler ha3 the Advantage of purchasing in Ireland Soap which has not only paid no Duty, but which is made from untaxed Materials, while Soap manufactured in England is loaded with its own Taxes, and likevvise charged with another heavy Burthen in the Duty of 5$. 2 il per Hundred Weight on Barilla, and in the Duty of 1 s. 6 d. per Hundred Weight, paid in Ireland on all Tallow imported from that Kingdom, which Tw o Duties, added to the 21 s. per Hundred Excise on Soap, amount to a Charge of 24 s. per Hundred Weight on hard Soap manufactured in England; and that the Petitioners hope, that their venturing to submit to the Consideration of the House any Opinion of theirs will not be attributed to an unbecoming Presumption, but that the House will ascribe it to its true Motive, viz. a Desire to preserve an important Branch of the Revenue from Decay, and themselves and their 4 N Families

A Petition of James Retmel late Major of Engineers, in the Service of the East India Company, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner served His Majesty and the East India Company Seventeen Years in India, and, having suffered by Wounds and severe Service, the Petitioner, in the Year 1777, resigned his Commission in the East India Company’s Service on Condition of receiving a Pension in England, which Pension has been his chief Support since that Time, the Court of Directors of the said Company having granted it on the fullest Conviction of the slender state of his Fortune; and that the said Pension granted by the Favour of one Court of Directors, and revocable at the Will of another, and moreover subject to be affected by the future State of the Company’s Concerns, becomes a kind of Contingency, which makes it necessary for the Petitioner, in case of the Failure of his Pension, to secure a Re-admission into a Service in which he has spent the best Part of his Life, or be compelled to lose the Fruits of his long Services: And therefore praying, That his Case may be taken into Consideration, and an Exception made in his Favour in the Bill now depending in the House, for the better Regulation and Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, in which is a Clause to prevent the Return of certain Semnts of the Company to The East Indies, for the Purpose of holding any Office under the said Company.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better Regulation and Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, ana of the British Possessions in Indiaand for establishing a Court of Judicature, for the more speedy and effectual Trial of Persons accused of Offences committed in The East Indies, is committed.

Royal Assent A Message by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman

to Bilk Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. "Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of . Peers, to bear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission aforementioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also empowering his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, and several othet-Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Sydney, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; which Bills are as followed); viz.

An Act for laying additional Duties upon all Candles (except Wax and Spermaceti Candles) and for moFe effectually securing the Duties upon Candles.

An Act for appointing and enabling Commissioners further to examine, take, and 6tate, the Public Accounts . of the Kingdom.

An Act for dividing and inclosing certain Open and Common Fields, Meadows, and Commons, or Waste Lands, within the Parish of Lower in the County of Warwick.

An Act for confirming and establishing an Exchange agreed upon between the Reverend James Dalton, Rector of the Parish of in the County of

Middlesex, and George Drummond, Esquire, of certain Lands within the said Parish.

An Act to explain and amend a Power vested in John Dalton, Esquire, to grant Leases, so for as it concerns certain Lands and Hereditaments within the Town or Precincts of Lancaster, called The Fryerage, and for the other Purposes therein mentioned.

Exeter Poor. A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others who pay the Rates for Relief and Maintenance of the Poor within the City and County of the City of Exon, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to explain and amend several Acts of Parliament for erecting Hospitals and - Workhouses within the City and County oT the City of Exon, for the better employing and maintaining the Poor, and to raise further Sums of Money for the more effectually carrying the Purposes of the said Acts into Execution; and Setting forth, That the said Bill, if passed into a Law, as it now stands, will be highly prejudicial to, and grievously burthensome on, the Petitioners and others paying the Rates for Relief of the Poor within the said, City and County of the City of Exon: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Witnesses, Agents, and Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass as it now stands, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Ordered, That all, who come to the said Committee, have Voices.

Gibbs* Loss A Petition of Francis Gibbs, late of Portsmouth, by taking Master House Carpenter and Ironmonger, but now of

Lands for the Kings Bench Prison, was presented to the House,

Dockyards. ancj rea(j. Setting forth, That the Petitioner is in great Distress, occasioned by an Act of the Twenty-second Year of His present Majesty, for vesting certain Lands and Tenements near Portsmouth in the Hands of Trustees, for the Purpose of enlarging the Fortifications erecting for the Security of His Majesty’s Dock Yards, by which Act the Fee of such Lands and Tenements are taken from the Proprietors, and the Petitioner has been debarred these Three Years past from executing his Right of selling, or borrowing Money on, his Estate, from which Circumstance he is reduced to the most distressed Situation, although he has a Real Estate in new Houses of £. 120 per Annum, clear of all Incumbrances, but from being deprived of selling or mortgaging his Property during the Pleasure of Parliament, he has been unable to raise Money to pay his Debts, the Whole of which does not amount to £.1^0, and has been obliged to

Vo 1.40.

submit to Confinement in Prison for near Twelve Months past, and thereby been prevented from cm Tying on his Business, which has been attended with Ruin to himself and Family,; apd that the Petitioner had sold Part of his Land, and had entered into an Agreement to build Two more Houses, but the King’s Solicitor and Two Engineers came on the Premisses after the passing of the said Act, and warned him not to proceed, and these Causes have produced his Ruin, and that of his Family: And therefore praying,

That the House will consider his deplorable Situation, and grant him common Justice for the Injuries he b^s suffered, in order that he may get his Liberty, and be in a Situation to provide for his Wife and Family, as he formerly did, by his Industry.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for vesting certain Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments in Trustees, for better securing His Majesty’s Docks, Ships, and Stores at Portsmouth and Plymouth; and also, for re-vesting certain Messuages,
