A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to the House,

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House an Account of the Money granted in the Year 1782, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act* of the Twenty-third of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for extending and improving the Trade to " Africa;" and that they have invested the Money granted in 1783 for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast; and that the said Forts and Settlements were delivered to the Petitioners in a very ruinous Condition by the Royal African Company, and the Sums Annually granted by Parliament for their Support and Maintenance being nearly expended in the Civil and Military Establishments, and in the necessary contingent Charges, there remained little or nothing for the Purpose of Repairs, so that several of them still continue in a very defenceless State; and that sundry Abuses having been alledged to exist in the Conduct of the Officers employed by the Petitioners on the Coast of Africa, and more particularly in the Management of the Public Money committed to their Care, the Petitioners thought proper, in the Year 1779, to suspend their Governor in Chief and the Council at Cape Coast Castle, and to appoint certain Commissioners to examine in Africa into the Conduct and Accounts of the Officers, from the Beginning of the Year 1770, and the said Commissioners having made their Report upon the Accounts of Richard Miles, Esquire, Governor of Cape Coast Castley and the Petitioners having themselves gone through a very long and most careful Examination of the said Accounts, they find, in Confirmation of the Report of the Commissioners, that the Sura of £.5,544. 9$. 5d. Company’s Pay, is due to the said Richard Miles, which they are not at present in any Condition to pay without the Assistance of the House; and that there are several other Sums of Money claimed by the said Officers, which the Petitioners cannot at present deride upon, the Report of the Commissioners upon the Accounts of the said Officers being but lately arrived from Africa, and not yet examined; and that the Petitioners, by Advices from Africa, find, that a very considerable Expence has been incurred by the Hostilities on that Coast between the Subjects of this Country and of the States General of the United Provinces, for which po Provision has been made, but having received no particular Accounts of the said Expenditure, they cannot at present ascertain the exact Amount; and that the Petitioners being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum as may be necessary for the effectual Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements in Africa, for the Payment of the Debt already ascertained to be due to Richard Milesy Esquire, for discharging any other Debts which may

Vol. 40.

appear to be justly due to their Officers and Servants, and likewise such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Accounts do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being a Committee appointed at a General Meeting of Proprietors of Navy and Victualling Bills, on behalf of themselves and of the said Proprietors, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners find, by a Resolution of the House of the 30th of July last, that it is intended to fund all Navy and Victualling Bills made out between the 31st of May 1781, and the 30th of June 1782, upon certain Terms expressed in the said Resolution, and that the Petitioners are Holders of Navy and Victualling Bills made out within that Period, to a very considerable Amount; and representing to the House, that it has not hitherto been usual for Government to suffer Navy and Victualling Bills to remain undischarged so long as even the latest of those now proposed to be funded, and, there is no Precedent for any Deduction or Abatement whatever from the Principal and Interest of such Bills; and that the Petitioners, relying on the Faith of Government, which they apprehend to be pledged to them for the Payment of the entire Sum of their Bills, together with the Interest due thereon, conceive that they shall be essentially injured if they accept the Terms proposed in the said Resolution, or, if they refuse them, be obliged to wait an indefinite Time, without any certain Prospect of Payment; and, the Petitioners submit to the House, whether a Choice of Two Evils, either Composition or indefinite Time (when the Debt is not only specific as to the Sum, but actually due according to acknowledged Precedent and Custom) can be considered as a fair Option, or whether it does not rather partake of the Nature of Compulsion, which the Petitioners are confident would be contrary to the Intentions of the House; and that, when the Petitioners became possessed of this Species of Public Security, they had every Reason, from the Consideration of sound Policy as well as of Justice, to expect the same Punctuality which the Public Creditors of Great Britain of all Denominations have ever experienced; And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as to the House shall appear just and equitable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,

Prevention of Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from

Smuggling, the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Laws made to prevent the clandestine Importation and Running of prohibited Goods, and Goods liable to the Payment of Duties, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report ta the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rates and Duties granted and imposed upon Low* Wines and Spirits for Ilome Consumption, by any Act or Acts now in Force, be discontinued for a Time to be limited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Seven Pence be laid upon every Gallon of Fermented Wort or Wash brewed or made for extracting Spirits, for Home Consumption, from any Malt, Corn, Grain, or Tilts, or any Mixture with the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Five Pence Halfpenny be laid upon every Gallon of Cyder or Perry, or other Wash or Liquet made or brewed from any Sort or Kind of British Materials (except such as are before mentioned) or from any Mixture therewith for extracting Spirits, for Home Consumption.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Ten Pence be laid upon every Gallon of Fermented Wort or Wash made or brewed from Vol. 40.

Melasses or Sugar, or any Mixture therewith for extracting Spirits, for Home Consumption.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Shilling be laid upon every Gallon of Wash composed of Foreign Refused Wine, or Foreign Cyder or Wash prepared from Foreign Materials (except Melasses and Sugar) or any Mixture therewith for extracting Spirits, for Home Consumption.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several additional Rates and Duties imposed by an Act of the Twentieth Year of His Majesty’s Reign, upon Rum and Spirits imported into Great Britain, being of the Growth, Production, and Manufacture of the British Sugar Islands in The West Indies, and also the several and respective additional Imposts and Duties after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centumy imposed by Three several Acts made in the Nineteenth, Twenty-first, and Twenty-second Years of His Majesty’s Reign, upon Rum and Spirits imported into this Kingdom, be suspended for a Time to be limited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exemption from the Duties of Excise payable upon Spirits made from Corn growing within the Lands of Ferrintosh, claimed by Arthur Forbes, of Culloden, in the County of Inverness, Esquire, be wholly taken a.way and extinguished.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second, Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House. .

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the said. Resolutions: And that Mr. Gilbert, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Butler, the Marquis of Graham,

Resolved’ That, from and after the present Session of Parliament, no Member of this House do frank any Letter or Packet, unless the whole Superscription be in his own Hand-writing, and unless, together with the Name of such Member, the Name of the Post Town from which the said Letter or Packet is intended to be sent, and the Day of the Month and Year when the same shall be put into the Post Office, shall be at the same Time superscribed upon such Letter or Packet, which Day of the Month shall be in Words at Length; ai^d that no Member of this House do permit any letter or Packet to be directed to him at any Place, except where he shall actually be at the Time of the Delivery thereof, or at his usual Place of Residence in Londont or at the Lobby of this House.

Ordered, That a Message be sent to the Lords, to acquaint them, that this House hath come to a Resolution, That, from and after the present Session of Parliament, no Member of this House do frank any Letter or Packet, unless the whole Superscription be in his own Hand-writing, and unless, together with the Name of such Member, the Name of the Post Town from which the said Letter or Packet is intended to be sent, and the Day of the Month and Year when the same shall be put into the Post Office, shall be at the same Time superscribed upon such Letter or Packet, which Day of the Month shall be in Words at Length; and that no Member of this House do permit any Letter or Packet to be directed to him at any Place, except where he shall actually be at the Time of the Delivery thereof, or at his usual Place of Residence in London, or at the Lobby of this House.

Ordered, That Mr. Rose do go to the Lords, with the said Message.

A Message from the Lords, by "Mr. Montagu and Mr, Thomson:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have taken the Subject Matter of the Message from this House into Consideration, and have come to the following Resolutions:

Pranking Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, by the Lords Spiri-MUCbe anc* ^emPora^ *n Parliament assembled, That,

em rs' from and after the End of the present Session of Parliament, no Member of this House do frank any Letter or Packet, unless the whole Superscription be' in his own -^land-writing, and unless, together with the Name of such Member, the Name of the Post Town from which the said Letter or Packet is intended to be sent, and the Day of the Month and Year when the same shall be put into the Post Office, shall be at the same Time superscribed upon such Letter or Packet, which Day of the Month shall be in Words at Length.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal in Parliament assembled, That, from and after the End of the present Session of Parliament, no Member of this House do permit any Letter or Packet to be directed to him at any Place, except where he shall actually be at the Time of Delivery thereof, or at his usual Place of Residence in London: And also,

Supply Bill; The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Bricks, &c. Act for granting to His Majesty certain Rates and Duties upon Bricks and Tiles made in Great Britain, and for laying additional Duties on Bricks and Tiles imported into the same; without any Amendment: And also,

Prize Bounty. The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue the Term, and alter and enlarge the Powers, of an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for amending, repairing, and widening several Roads in the Counties of Radnor and Hereford\ and for repairing and widening several other Roads in the said Counties; w ithout any Amendment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Fifteen thousand Six hundred Twenty-six Pounds Four Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Three Regiments of Foot, from the 25th Day of June 1784 to the 24th Day of December following, both Days inclusive, being One hundred and Eighty-three Days.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Nine thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to enable His Majesty to make Compensation to the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and state, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom, for their Diligence, Accuracy, and Ability in the Execution^ of the Tru^t reposed in them by Parliament; and that the said Sum be issued and paid without any Fee or other Deduction whatsoever.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven, thousand Pounds,

Augusti A, 1784.

be granted to His Majesty, to make good to His Majesty the like Sum which has been paid to the Secretaries of the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and state, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom, and to the Commissioners appointed to enquire into the Losses of the American Loyalists, and which has not been made good by Parliament.

Resolved, That It is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-six thousand Eight hundred and Forty-one Pounds One Shilling and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to make good to His Majesty the like Sum which has been issued by His Majesty’s Orders, in pursuance of the Addresses of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Thirteen thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to be employed in repairing* maintaining, and supporting the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That a Sum, not exceeding Twelve thousand Two hundred and Twelve Pounds Eleven Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to replace the like Sum which has been issued, by His Majesty’s Orders* to Duncan Campbell, Esquire, for the Expence of confining, maintaining, and employing Convicts on the River Thames.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Seven thousand Eight hundred and Fifty Pounds be granted to His Majesty, to perfect the Purchase of the Soil of the Bahama Islands, and to support the Civil Establishment of the said Islands, in Addition to the Salaries now paid out of the Duty Fund to the Public Officers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum not exceeding Five hundred Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for the Salary proposed to be allowed to the Chief Justice of the Bermuda or Somers Islands, from the 24th Day of June 1784 to the 24th Day of June 1785.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Maltster, or Maker of Malt for Sale, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Two Pounds, if the Quantity of Malt made by him shall exceed, within the Year ending the Twenty-third Day of June in each Year previous to his taking out the Licence, the Quantity of Three hundred and Fifty Quarters, and be under Four hundred Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Maltster, or Maker of Malt for Sale, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Two Pounds Five Shillings, if the Quantity of Malt made by him shall exceed, within the Year ending the Twenty-third Day of June in each Year previous to his taking out the Liqence, the Quantity of Four hundred Quarters, and be under Four hundred and Fifty Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Maltster, or Maker of Malt for Sale, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Two Pounds Ten Shillings, if the Quantity of Malt made by him shall exceed, within the Year ending the Twenty-third Day qS June in each Year previous to his taking out the Licence, the Quantity of Four hundred and Fifty Quarters, and be under Five hundred Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Maltster, or Maker of Malt for Sale, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Two Pounds Fifteen Shillings, if the Quantity of Malt made by him shall exceed, within the Year ending the Twenty-third Day of June in each Year previous to his taking out the Licence, the Quantity of Five hundred Quarters, and be under Five hundred and Fifty Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Maltster, or Maker of Malt for Sale, be obliged to take out a Licence, which Licence shall be charged with the Yearly Sum of Three Pounds, if the Quantity of Malt made by him shall exceed, within the Year ending the Twenty-third Day of June in each Year previous to his taking out the Licence, the Quantity of Five hundred and Fifty Quarters.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Rolls Record Mr. Attorney General reported from the Committee

Office. who were appointed to consider of a proper Piece of Ground, for erecting an Office for the Clerk of the Records kept in the Rolls Chapel, and to report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee find, by the Evidence of John Kipling, Esquire, Clerk of the Records in the Rolls Chapel, That the House now occupied by him as his Office, is Part of the Rolls Estate, and was purchased in the Year 1772, under the Direction of the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s 'Treasury, in pursuance of an Address of this House to His Majesty, for the Term of Eleven Years, being 'the Remainder of a Lease held by the Earl of Mac-clesfield, as Residuary Legatee in the Will of Sir Thomas Clarke, late Master of the Rolls; That the said Lease expired on the 5th Day of January, 1783, and that in consequence of an Act passed in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Master of the Rolls is restrained from granting Leases other than at Rack Rent of any Part of the said Estate; That if the present House was to be continued to be used as an Office for the Clerk, it will be necessary to provide an Annual Fund to defray the Expence of Rent, Taxes, and Repairs; That the said J House is inconveniently situated, being at a Distance

from the Rolls Chapel, and the Rooms are not sufficiently large for the Purpose of transacting the Public Business of the said Office; and that the present Master of the Rolls has therefore consented that a New Office should be erected upon a Piece of Ground adjoining to the Rolls Chapel, which will be more conveniently situated for transacting the Business of the said Office.

And it appeared to Your Committee, by the Evidence of Sir William Chambers, principal Officer of His Majesty’s Works, That an Office may be conveniently erected upon the said Piece of Ground, and that the Expence of the said Building will amount to the Sum of 1,500; and he added, that there is included in the said Estimate, an Apartment for the necessary Accommodation of the Secretaries to the Master of the Rolls, the Expence of which will amount to Three hundred Pounds.

Upon which Your Committee came to the following Resolution:

V o l. 40*

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a certain Piece of Ground adjoining to the Rolls Chapel, and belonging to the Master of the Rolls in Right of his Office, is a proper Piece of Ground whereon to erect an Office for the Clerk of the Records in the Rolls Chapel, including an Apartment for the Secretaries to the Master of the Rolls.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

The said Copy is as followeth; viz.

/ The Company’s \ TREATY of Peace with the Na-V Sod- t bob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder.

t Tippoo Sultaun’s \ _ _ , _ .

\ Seal.,) Treaty of perpetual Peace and

Friendship, between the Honourable the English East India Company and the Nabob Tippoo Saltaun Bahauder, on his own Behalf, for the Countries of Seringapatam, Hyder Nagur, &c\ and all his other Possessions, settled by Anthony Sadlier, George Leonard Staunton, and John Huddleston, Esquires, on Behalf of the Honourable English East India Company, for all their Possessions,' and for the Carnatic Payen Gaut, by virtue of Powers delegated to the Right honourable the President and Select Committee of Fort Saint George for that Purpose, by the Honourable the Governor General and Council, appointed by the King and Parliament of Great Britain to direct and controul all Political Affairs of the Honourable the East India Company in India, and by the said Nabob, agreeably to the following Articles, which are to be strioly and invariably observed, as long as the Sun and Moon shall last, by both Parties; (that is to say) by the English Company and the Three Governments of Bengal, Madras, and Bombay, and the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder.

Article 1st.

Peace and Friendship shall immediately take place between the said Company and the Nabob Tippoo Sul-taun Bahaudet'j and their Friends and Allies, particularly including therein the Rajahs of Tanjore and Trail encore, who are Friends and Allies to the English and the Carnatic Payen Gaut; also Tippoo Sultaun s Friends and Allies, the Biby of Cannanore, and the Rajahs or Zemindars of the Malabar Coast, are included in this Treaty. The English will not, directly or indirectly, assist the Enemies of the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder, nor make War upon his Friends or Allies; and the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder will not, directly or indirectly, assist the Enemies, nor make War upon the Friends dr Allies of the English.

Article 2d.

Immediately after signing and sealing the Treaty by the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder, and the Three English Commissioners, the said Nabob shall send Orders for the complete Evacuation of the Carnatic, and the Restoration of all the Forts and Places in it now possessed by his Troops, the Forts of Amboorgur and Satgur excepted; and such Evacuation and Restoration shall actually and effectually be made in the Space of Thirty Days, from the Day of signing the Treaty; and the said Nabob shall also, immediately after signing the Treaty, send Orders for the Release of all the ‘Persons who were taken and made Prisoners in the late War, and now alive, whether European or Native, and for their being safely conducted to and delivered at such English Forts or Settlements as shall be nearest to the Places where they now are, so that the said Release and Delivery of the Prisoners shall actually and effectually be made in Thirty Days from the Day of signing the Treaty; the Nabob will cause them to be supplied with Provisions and Conveyances for the Journey, the Expence of which shall be made good to him by the . Company: The Commissioners will send an Officer, or Officers, to accompany the Prisoners to the different Places where they are to be delivered; in particular, Jbuul JVahab Cawn, taken at Chitoor, and; his Family, 40. . -

shall be immediately released, and, if willing to return to Treaty with the Carnatic, shall be allowed to do so. If any Person Tippoo or Persons belonging to the said Nabob, and taken by the Company in the late War, be now alive, and in Person w in Bencoolen, or other Territories of the Company, such Person or Persons shall be immediately released, and, if willing to return, shall be sent without Delay to the nearest Fort or Settlement in the Mysore Country;

Baswapa, late Amuldar of Palicacherry, shall be released, and at Liberty to depart.

Article 3d.

Immediately after signing and sealing the Treaty, the English Commissioners shall give written Orders for the Delivery of Onore, Carwar, and Sadashevagada, and Forts or Places adjoining thereto, and send a Ship or Ships to bring away the Garrisons. The Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder will cause the Troops in those Places to be supplied with Provisions, and any other necessary Assistance for their Voyage to Bombay (they paying for the same): The Commissioners will likewise give at the same Time written Orders for the immediate Delivery of the Forts and Districts of Caroor, Auracourchy, and Daraparam; and immediately after the Release and Delivery of the Prisoners, as before mentioned, the Fort and District bf Dindigul' shall be evacuated and restored to the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder, and none of the Troops of the Company shall afterwards remain in the Country of the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahaiuler.

Article 4th.

As soon as all the Prisoners are released and delivered, the Fort and District of Cannanore shall be evacuated and restored to Ali Rajah Biby, the Queen of that Country, in the Presence of any One Person, without Troops, whom the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder may appoint for that Purpose; and at the same Time that the Orders are given for the Evacuation and Delivery of the Forts at Cannanore and Dindigul, the said Nabob shall give written Orders for the Evacuation and Delivery of Amboorgur and Satgur to the English, and in the mean Time none of the Troops of the said . Nabob shall be left in any Part of the Carnatic, except in the Two Forts above mentioned.

Article 5th.

After the Conclusion of this Treaty, the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder will make no Claim whatever in future on the Carnatic.

Article 6th.

All Persons whatsoever, who have been taken and carried away from the Carnatic Payen Gaut (which includes Tanjore) by the late Nabob Hyder Alt Cawn Bahauder, who is in Heaven, or by the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder, or otherwise, belonging to the Carnatic, and now in the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder s Dominions, and willing to return, shall be immediately allowed to return, with their Families and Children, or as soon as may be convenient to themselves; and all Persons belonging to the Vencatagcherry Rajah, who were taken Prisoners in returning from the Fort of Vellour, to which Place they had been sent with Provisions, shall also be released, and permitted immediately to return. Lists of the principal Persons belonging to the Nabob Mahomed Ali Cawn Bahauder, and to the Rajah of Vencatagcherry, shall be delivered to the Nabob Tippoo Sultauns Ministers; and the Nabob will cause the Contents of this Article to be publicly notified throughout his Country.

Article 7th.

This being the happy Period of general Peace and Reconciliation,4 the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder, as a Testimony and Proof of his Friendship to the English, agrees that the Rajahs or Zemindars on this 5 P Coast,

The Nabob Tippoo Sultaunhereby re-

Article 9th.

The Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bdhauder shall restore the Factory and Privileges possessed by the English at Callicut until the Year 1779 (or 1193 Hegira) and shall restore Mount Dilly and its District, belonging to the Settlement of Tellicherryand possessed by the English, till taken by Sadar Cawn at the Commencement of the late War.

Article t oth.

This Treaty shall be signed and sealed by the English Commissioners, and a Copy of it shall afterwards be signed and sealed by the President and Select Committee of Fort Saint George, and returned to the Nabob Tippoo Sultaun Bahauder, in One Month, or sooner, if possible; and the same shall be acknowledged under the Hands and Seals of the Governor General and Council of Bengal, and the Governor and Select Committee of Bombay, as binding upon all the Governments in India; and Copies of the Treaty, so acknowledged, shall be sent to the said Nabob in Three Months, or sooner, if possible.

A PETITION of the several Persons whose j)ownto Names are thereunto subscribed, Freeholders of Election? the Borough of Downton, -in the County of Wilts, was delivered m at the Table, and read; Setting forth,

That, at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Dazvnton, the Honourable William Seymour Conway, and the Honourable Edward Bouverie, were Candidates; and that the said Election came ou at Downton aforesaid on the 26th Day of July last, and a Poll being demanded, the same was taken before James Serle, Esquire,

Bailiff of the Hundred and Borough of Downton aforesaid, who acted as the Returning Officer for the said Borough; and that John Dagge, Esquire, under an Appointment as Deputy to Joseph Elderton, Esquire, the Steward of the Manor and Borough of Downton aforesaid, did also take upon himself to act as the Returning Officer of the said Borough, and a Poll was also taken by the said John Dagge; and that a very great Majority of the legal Votes of the said Borough were tendered in Favour of the said William Seymour Conway by the Petitioners and divers other Freeholders of the said Borough unto the said James Serle, and also' to the said John Dagge; and that the said James Serle did unlawfully reject divers legal Votes which were tendered unto him in Favour of the said William Seymour Conway, as aforesaid, and received several illegal Votes in Favour of the said Edward Bouverie, yet nevertheless a very great Majority of legal Votes having been tendered and given at the said Election, and admitted by the said James Serle in Favour of the said William Seymour Cqnway, the said James Serle did thereupon declare the said Widiam Seymour Conway to be duly elected, and hath accordingly returned him as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the said John Dagge, at the said Poll so taken by him, did unlawfully and partially reject several legal Votes which were so as aforesaid tendered in Favour of the said William Seymour Conway, and did receive many illegal Votes in Favour of the said Edward Bouverie, and under Colour of a pretended Majority in Favour of the said Edward Bouverie, did declare him to be duly elected, and, notwithstanding the said real Majority in Favour of the said William Seymour Cofizcay, hath taken upon himself falsely and illegally to make a Return of the said Edward Bouvei'ie as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, to the Prejudice of the said William Seymour Conway, and in direct Violation of the Rights and Franchises of the Petitioners, and of the other legal Electors of the said Borough, and, the Sheriff of the said County of Wilts hath annexed to his Writ the Indentures of both the said Returns; and that the said Edward Bouverie, by himself and his 5Q Agents,

Mr. Edwards reported from the Committee, to Bishop* whom the Petition of George Bishop, Proprietor of the Geneve. Maidstone Geneva Manufactory, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Samuel Bicknell being examined, said, That he is a Dealer in Spirits, and lives in Bishopsgate Street —

That he was employed by Mr. Bishop, of Maidstone (the Petitioner), merely as his Agent for the Sale of Geneva, in London — That he opened the Warehouse in Bishopsgate Street in 1779 > Mr. Bishop residing at his Manufactory at Maidstone, making it necessary for him to have some House in Town for the Sale of the Geneva — That Mr. Bishop lived in Holland a considerable Time — That Holland Geneva was universally allowed to be superior to any other, till Mr. Bishop brought his to Perfection; when his was esteemed to be at least equal, if not superior, to that made in Holland, insomuch that it is very difficult, if not impossible, to distinguish the one Spirit from the other —

That many People who have dealt in Spirits, and have bought Mr. Bishop's Geneva, have declared they could not distinguishsit from Foreign — That he is acquainted with the Nature of Mr. Bishops Process in making the Geneva, and knows, that the larger the Quantity of Wash is that is used in making the Geneva, the better the Quality of it is.

That when Mr. Bishop'first brought this Geneva to Market, he had a great Sale for it, and the Demand increased very much — That he had no Complaint with regard to the Quality; and that Orders were received for such great Quantities, that Mr. Bishop could not make it fast enough to supply his Customers; but that since- Mr. Bishop was prevented l^y the Law from working in the Manner he used to do, he has received Two or Three hundred Letters, complaining that the Quality of the Spirit then manufactured by him was so bad, that it was not saleable — That Mr. Bishop's greatest Sale was where the most Smuggling was carried on; and that, the Smugglers could not supply themselves with Foreign Geneva on lower Terms than they could be supplied with it from Mr. Bishop — That there are People called Duffers, who hawk Liquors about Town, who used to buy Spirits from Ships, and run it in; but when Mr. Bishop made iiis Geneva, of the Quality he did (till stopped working by the Act of Parliament) they bought it of him, and sold it for smuggled Holland Geneva* — That Mr. Bishop used

24 Geo. III.

io° Aug

427

to send great Quantities of Geneva to the tVest Indies, whither scarce a Ship went without some; that before they were supplied from his Manufactory, they used Xo take British Brandy and smuggled Geneva, as he has been informed, but it not being so good as Mr. Bishop's Spirit, they had not a proper Sale for it. — And being asked, What he should suppose the Price per Gallon of the Maidstone Geneva as distilled by Mr. Bishop would be, supposing the Prayer of his Petition to be granted? he said 5s. 6d. per Gallon, if the Duties are taken off, and 6$. 6d. if not — That the Proportion of the Proof of the Maidstone Geneva to that smuggled from Abroad is, as near as can be calculated, One Shilling per Gallon in Favour of the former.

That the Price of smuggled Holland Geneva in London, is from 6s. to 6s. 6d. per Gallon; and that generally only the ordinary Sort of Geneva is smuggled. — And being asked, What Price Mr. Bishop's Geneva sold for in London ? he said. The same as at Maidstone; the Carriage being by Water, and so low, as not to be a Farthing a Gallon.

Mr. Edward Layton being then examined, said, That he is a Backmaker in Southwark — That Mr. Bishop's Geneva is entirely different from any other British Spirit that he ever tasted or heard of — That he travels a great deal in Kent and Sussex, and particularly those Parts where Smuggling has been greatly carried on — That during the Time Mr. Bishop's Distillery was in fullest Work, the People of the Towns and Villages on the Coast preferred his Geneva to that smuggled from Abroad; and that in general it was called for in particular by Name.

That during the first Ten Years of Mr. Bishop's Manufactory, his Bill to him as a Backmaker did not exceed £ 500; but in the Space of Two Years and an Half from the Year 1780, he received of Mr. Bishop £. 1,099. 9* for Work done in his Branch of Business only.

Mr. John Rixon being examined, said, That he is a Cooper — That about Ten Years ago he was in the Spirit Trade — That he was employed by Mr. Bishop to sell his Geneva in London, and sold it with great Success before the Time he opened the said Warehouse in Bishopsgate Street — That he found some Difficulty at first, from Persons having imbibed a Prejudice against JSri/isA-made Geneva, from having tasted the Spirit then made by some Dutchmen at Islington, which Manufactory has since been discontinued; but that some Time after he began to sell it, he had so great a Demand, that he sold it as fast as he could draw it — That it was equal to the best Holland Geneva; that it mixes perfectly fine with Water, and better than any other British Geneva, which mixes foul, and with h Blue Cast — That he never met with any Person who could distinguish it from Holland Geneva; and that, could he have been furnished with it at 6d. a Gallon cheaper, he could have sold great Quantities to the People called Duffers — That the Reason why he gave up the Sale of the Geneva, was, that when he made Application for more, Mr. Bishop had stopped working.

Mr. James Dace being then examined, said, That he is a Merchant, and has been a Captain in the French and Dutch Trade for near 30 Years — That he has often, in the Course of Trade, brought home some Quantities of Holland and Dunkirk Geneva — That while Mr. Bishop made his Geneva in its full Perfection, it was preferred to the Holland Geneva — That the Average Price of Geneva Abroad is about 18 d. per Gallon — That the Smugglers now sell it in the Medway from 4*. to 6,?. per Gallon — That he has known One Man bring into the River Medway near 40,000 Gallons in a Month — That he has known the Smugglers buy Mr. Bishops Geneva, in order to sell it again for Holland Geneva.

V^l. 40.

Your Committee thinking it necessary to be in- Bishop’s formed of the Nature of the Process used by Mr. Geneva-Bishop, in the making of his Geneva, called him before them; when he informed Your Committee, That the Materials from which his Geneva is made, are Barley, Rye, and Malt; that he is obliged to use a large Portion of Rye, which is an indispensable Article in the Manufactory, and is of such a glutinous 1 Quality, that it must be diluted very much, or the Wash made from it will burn out the Bottom of the Still, which is frequently the Case in Holland, where they often burn out the Bottom of a Still in Six Weeks — That if he was to make the Wash from the Materials not so diluted, and strong enough to produce One Gallon of Spirits (One in Ten over Hydrometer Proof) out of every Six Gallons of Wash, the Still would be destroyed perhaps in One Day; and that supposing it could be made without destroying the Still, he could not from such Wash make the Sort of Spirit that could be put in Competition with the Holland Geneva.

Mr. Bishop wras then asked, Whether there is any Mode of ascertaining the proportional Density of his best Wash, compared with that of other Distillers, as allowed by Law ? to which he said, That the best Mode is by a small Still, to distil a Part of it; that Method would do it to the greatest Nicety, and the Officer might do it in a small Time — The Officer might try out of every Back 12 Gallons, out of 3,000. —

And being asked, What Length of Time it would take to distil 12 Gallous? he said, From Three to Four Hours —

That Nobody ever made this Sort of Geneva in England, except himself.

Mr. Bishop being then asked, If he could form any Idea of the Quantity of Geneva smuggled into this Country? said, That, according to the best Calculation he can make, it must be about Four Millions of Gallons annually. — Being asked, What he thinks the Average Price of Holland Geneva landed on our Coast, and not lowered, to be? he said, 3s. 6d. a Gallon; and that he believes no Geneva is smuggled but what is lowered; that they lower it on the other Side of the Water; and that they grant a false Proof likewise, but that such Proof will be detected by the Hydrometer.

And being then asked. What the Price of Holland Proof Spirit is at Amsterdam ? he said, 1 s. 6d> a Gallon; but that it is of Two per Cent, lower Proof than that made by him.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

The House w as moved, That the Report which Rolls Record was Yesterday made from the Committee who were Office, appointed to consider of a proper Piece of Ground for erecting an Office for the Clerk of the Records kept in the Rolls Chapel, and to report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House, might be again read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s Most Honourable Privy Council.

A Petition of General James Murrdy, late C&ptain General and Governor in Chief of the Island of Afi-norca, and Vice Admiral of the same, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in consequence of a Verdict obtained against the Petitioner, for the Payment of a Sum of Money, a Minute was made by the late Board of Treasury, on the 15th Day of December last, for paying to the Petitioner the said Sum, which, he is informed, the present Commissioners of the Treasury do not think themselves warranted to pay; and, under these Circumstances, he finds himself compelled to the Necessity of seeking Relief from the House; but, not having been aware of any Difficulty in the Payment of the Money above-mentioned, he did not present a Petition within the Time limited by the House for receiving private Petitions: And therefore praying That the

Then a Petition of General James Murray, late Captain General and Governor in Chief of the Island of Minorca, and Vice Admiral of the same, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read Setting forth, That the Petitioner, being entrusted with those arduous and important Offices in the said Island, did conceive himself, agreeable to his Commissions and Instructions, invested with the Power of removing or suspending till His Majesty’s Pleasure should be known, any Officer whose Conduct appeared either seditious or disobedient to the just and necessary Regulations of his Government; and repre* senting to the House, that James Sutherland, being Commissary or Judge of the Vice Admiralty Court of the Island of Minorca, did commit divers Things, tending to involve the former Governors, as well as the Petitioner, in Disputes with the Natives of the Island, by raising Jealousies and Discontents amongst them, and did likewise hold a secret Correspondence with Doctor Franklin, the American Ambassador to the Court of France, as appears by his intercepted Letters in the Office of His Majesty’s Secretary of State; and when it appeared to the Petitioner, that the Deputy Registrar of the Admiralty Court, a Man of very mean Circumstances, and of a suspicious Character, was interested in most of the Privateers of the Island, which created Jealousy and Suspicion of Partiality, not only in the Minds of the Inhabitants, but of the Neutral Powers, and the Petitioner judged it indispensably necessary that such Deputy Registrar should be suspended, he publicly and peremptorily refused, in open Court, to accept another, appointed, pro Tempore, by the Petitioner, and thereby endeavoured to obstruct all Proceedings at Law in the said Court; and, to such Breaches of Duty, in his Official Situation, did add the most insolent and gross Behaviour towards the Petitioner, thereby endeavouring to destroy all Obedience to Government, and Subordination whatever: Thus circumstanced, the Petitioner found it absolutely necessary, for the Peace of the Island, and to prevent the Anarchy into which it was falling in the latter End of July 1780, to suspend the said James Sutherland from his Office, until His Majesty’s Pleasure should be known, and to send an 5 R Account

and that the Petitioner, immediately thereupon, presented a Memorial to His Majesty, stating the great Hardship he had suffered, from no other Cause than liia Zeal for His Majesty’s Service, and, that his Conduct having been fully and decidedly approved of by His Majesty’s then Ministers, he expressed his Hope, that he should be relieved* and which the Petitioner apprehends he is entitled to, as his Conduct was so approved, and the great Amount of the Damages was calculated upon the Length of Time the said Mr. Sutherland was continued; in Suspension by His Majesty’s Ministers after the Matter was laid before them; and that, in consequence of his Representation, the Petitioner’s Case was referred to the late Board of Trear sury, who, after a due Consideration, had, as appears by a Minute of that Board, agreed to discharge the same; and; that the Petitioner, in Expectation, from Time to Time, of being reimbursed the said. Sum of £. 5>525* 17$. which he intended, to appropriate to the defraying of some private. Debts* which he has since contracted, had at last the Mortification of being informed, that, notwithstanding the Minute before referred to, some Doubts: have appeared to the Board of the Propriety of defraying the same, agreeably to that Minute, but that it would be proper to apply to this House for Relief: And therefore hoping, That the House will be convinced that the Petitioner, in the Measure he pursued in the Removal of Mr. Su+ therland from hia Office* was actuated by no other Motives than his Zeal for the proper Execution of His. Majesty’s Service* and that the House will grant hin> such Relief as to them shall seem meet

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Freeholders of the Borough of Downton, in the County of Wilts, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, the Honourable Edward Bouverie and the Honourable William Conway were Candidates; and that the Election came on the 26th Day of July last, and a Poll being demanded, the said Edward Bouverie had a clear Majority of legal Votes, and was returned by John Dagge, Gentleman, who is the only proper and legal Returning Officer for the said Borough; and that James Scrie, Gentleman, took upon himself to act also as Returning Officer (although he had no Right so to do) and, on the Poll taken by him, to reject several Votes that offered to poll before him for the said Edward Bouverie, and to admit several Votes for the said William Conway that ought not to have been admitted, and has made a Return of the said William Conway as duly elected, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and in manifest Violation of the Freedom of Election, and the Law of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Merits of the said Election into their Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem just

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Osborne, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Rates and Duties upon Bricks and Tile9 made in Great Britain, and for laying additional Duties on Bricks and Tiles imported into the same.

An Act for laying an additional Duty on Hackney Coaches; and for explaining and amending several Acts of Parliament relating to Hackney Coaches.

An Act for granting to His Majesty an additional Duty upon Licences for retailing Beer, Ale, and other Exciseable Liquors.

Downton A Petition of the Honourable William Seymour Con-Election. way, complaining of the last Election and Return for the Borough of Downton, in the County of Wilts, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Certificate of the Deputy Clerk of the Crown, signifying, That the Indenture, whereby the Honourable William Seymour Conway is returned a Burgess for the said Borough, was delivered into the Office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery the 31st Day of July last, was read.

And the Order of the House, made the 24th Day of May last, requiring all Persons that will question any Returns to do it w’ithin Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in, was also read.

But the House not having proceeded upon Business since Friday last;

And the House being informed that the said Petitioner would have petitioned this House within Fourteen Days next after the said Return was brought in, if the House had proceeded upon Business on Saturday last;

Ordered, That the said Petition be now admitted to be received, the same not being presented in due Time, because the House have not proceeded upon Business since Friday last, until this Day.

Then the said Petition was delivered in, and read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Downton, in the County of Wilts, the Petitioner and the Honourable Edward Bouverie were Candidates; and that the said Election came on at*Downton aforesaid on the 26th Day of July. last, and a Poll being demanded, the same was taken before James Serle, Esquire, Bailiff of the Hundred and Borough of Downton aforesaid, who acted as the Returning Officer for the said Borough; and that John Dagge, Esquire, under an Appointment as- Deputy to Joseph Elderlon, Esquire, the Steward of the Manor and Borough of Downton aforesaid, also took upon himself to act as the Returning

Vo l. 40.

Officer for the said Borough; and a Poll was also taken before the said John Dagge; and that the said James Serle did, unlawfully and unjustly, reject divers legal Votes, which were tendered in Favour of the Pe- . titioner, and received sundry illegal Votes in Favour of the said Edward Bouverie, yet nevertheless a very great Majority of legal Votes having been tendered and given at the said Election, and admitted by the said James Serle in Favour of the Petitioner, the said James Serle did thereupon declare the Petitioner to be duly elected, and hath accordingly returned him as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the said John Dagge did, at the said Poll so taken by him, partially, illegally, and wrongfully reject several legal Votes which were tendered m Favour of the Petitioner, and did receive many illegal Votes in Favour of the said Edward Bouverie, and, under Colour of a pretended Majority in Favour of the said Edward Bouverie, did declare him to be duly elected, and, notwithstanding the said real Majority in Favour of the Petitioner, hath taken upon, himself falsely and illegally to make a Return of the said Edward Bouverie as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioner, who was duly elected, and, that the Sheriff of the County of Wilts hath annexed both Indentures of the said Returns to his Writ; and that the said Edward Bouverie, by himself and his Agents, and divers other Persons in his Behalf, were guilty of Bribery, and divers other corrupt and illegal Practices, at and before the said Election, in order to procure him the said Edward Bouverie to be returned for the said Borough, to the Prejudice of the Petitioner, and in open Defiance and Violation of the Law and Right of Election: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioner such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 9th Day of December next, at the same Time that the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Freeholders of the Borough of Downton, in the County of Wilts, is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and nth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections* or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cases, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker de issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

THE House being met, pursuant to the last Parliament Prorogation; and Mr. Speaker being in the further Country; prorogued.

A Message was brought from the Lords, by Mr. Sutherland, Deputy Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

After which His Majesty was pleased to make a Most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I cannot close this Session of Parliament without returning you My warmest Thanks for the eminent Proofs you have given of your zealous and diligent Attention to the Public Service.

The happiest Effects may be expected from the Provisions which you have made for the better Government of India, and from the Institution of a Tribunal so peculiarly adapted to the Trial of Offences committed in that distant Country.

I observe, with great Satisfaction, the Laws which you have passed for the Preservation and Improvement of the Revenue. No Exertions shall be wanting on My Part to give them Vigour and Effect.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Zeal and Liberality with which you have provided for the Exigencies of the Public Service, and the Assistance which you have given Me to prevent a growing Arrear in the Expences of My Civil List, demand My particular Thanks.

I feel in common with you for the unavoidable Burthens of My People.

The Importance of effectually supporting our National Credit, after a long and exhausting War, can alone reconcile Me to so painful a Necessity. I trust, the same Consideration will enable My faithful Subjects to meet it, as they have uniformly done, with Fortitude and Patience.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Definitive Treaty which has been signed with the States General of The United Provinces, and the Peace concluded in India, as well as the Assurances which I receive from Foreign Powers, promise the Continuance of General Tranquillity.

I trust, therefore, that, after so laborious a Session, it will not be found necessary to call you again together at a very early Period.

Voi~40.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly the House, with the Clerk, went up to the House of Peers: Where the Commission was read, for the further proroguing of the Parliament, until Thursday the 2d Day of December next: And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until Thursday the 2d Day of December next

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended His Majesty, in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

After the laborious Attendance of the last Session of Parliament, it has given Me peculiar Pleasure that the Situation of Public Affairs has admitted of so long a Recess.

Among the Objects which now require Consideration, I must particularly recommend to your earnest Attention the Adjustment of such Points in the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland as arc not yet finally arranged: The System which will unite both Kingdoms the most closely on Principles of reciprocal Advantage, will, I am persuaded, best ensure the general Prosperity of My Dominions.

I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that, notwithstanding any Appearance of Differences on the Continent, I continue uniformly to receive from all Foreign Powers the strongest Assurances of their good Disposition towards this Country.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Estimates for the ensuing Year to be laid before you: I confide in your Liberality and Zeal to grant the necessary Supplies, with a just Regard, as well to the Oeconomy requisite in every 5 Z Department,

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty our most humble and hearty Thanks for His Gracious Speech from the Throne:

To assure His Majesty, That we shall resume the Consideration of Public Business, with the same Principles of Duty to His Majesty, and Regard to the Interests of our Constituents, which we have endeavoured to manifest in all our Proceedings:

That we will not fail to give our most earnest Attention to the Adjustment of such Points as are not yet finally arranged in the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, fully agreeing with His Majesty in thinking, That the System, which will unite both Kingdoms the most closely on Principles of reciprocal Advantage, will best ensure the general Prosperity of His Dominions:

That it affords us the truest Pleasure to be informed, That notwithstanding any Appearance of Differences on the Continent, ilis Majesty continues to receive such satisfactory Assurances of the good Disposition of Foreign Powers towards this Country:

To beseech His Majesty to believe, That we shall at all Times be ready to grant such Supplies as are necessary for the Maintenance of the National Credit, and the real Exigencies of the Public Service:

That we are deeply sensible of His Majesty’s paternal Goodness and Care for His People, in recommending to us at the same Time a just Regard to the Oeconomy requisite in every Department; a Duty which His Majesty’s faithful Commons feel always incumbent upon them, and at this Time peculiarly indispensable:

To assure His Majesty, That we see the Importance of every Exertion which can tend to the Suppression of Smuggling, and the Improvement of the Revenue; and that we shall continue to apply ourselves with unwearied Assiduity to those important Objects:

That we shall also proceed, with as much Expedition as possible, to the Consideration of the Reports of the Commissioners of Accounts, as well as of such

further Regulations in the different Offices of the Kingdom as may appear likely to conduce to the Public Advantage:

To entreat His Majesty to be assured, That our utmost Endeavours shall not be wanting to justify His Gracious Reliance on our diligent Attention to every Part of eur Public Di|ty: f

And that we receive, witH the warmest Gratitude and Satisfaction, the Assurances of His Majesty's Concurrence in every Measure which can tend to alleviate the National Burthens, to secure the true Principles of the Constitution, and to promote the general Welfare of the People.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by inserting, after the Word " indispensable," at the End of the Sixth Paragraph, these Words, " and convinced, as we are, by the most decisive and most melancholy Experience, that all Waste u of the Public Treasure in the East Indies, itnmedintety or mediately applicable to the Company's " Use, and all Diversion of that Treasure from Public " Service to the private Emolument of Individuals, iC must not only bring an unsupportable Burthen on " the Natives of those Countries (Multitudes of whom u are our Fellow Citizens, and ought to be the Objects " of our most tender Concern) but has a Tendency to " bring Home the same Burthens on the Inhabitants of " Great Britain, we will, with a Care worthy of the " Magnitude of the Objects which such an Abuse may " effect, employ our most diligent Researches to discover, and our best Endeavours to bring to condign " Punishment, the Authors of such Misdemeanors, if 41 they shall be found to exist."

And the Question being put, That those Words be there inserted;

It passed in the Negative.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Undertakers for raising Thames Water> in York Buildings, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in- the Second and Third Years of King IViMunn and Queen Mary, for incorporating the Proprietors of the Water Works in York Buildings, and for the encouraging, carrying, on, and settling the said Waterworks, the said Governor and Company were incorporated, and euabled to purchase, enjoy, and alien Lands and Hereditaments, Goods and Chattels, and to do and execute all other Things, by their Name of Incorporation, that to them should appertain, and to use a Common Seal, to serve for all their Business; and that said Act appointed a Governor, and Six of the said Company, to be called Assistants, to have the Direction of all the Affairs of the said Company; and that the said Company, in pursuance of the Power vested in them by the said Act, did, in the Year 1719, order a Subscription to be opened for raising a Stock of £.1,200,000, to be laid out in the Purchase of Estates in Great Britain, to be a Fund for granting Annuities for Lives, and for assuring Lives, for the Benefit of all the Subscribers to the said Joint Stock; and that the Sum of £.308,093. 14s. 7d. was, by the said Company, invested in the Purchase of certain Estates in Scotlaiid\ of the Annual Value of £. 12,000, and in Ncn'thumber-land of the Annual Value of £.2,684, which Estates were sold under the Authority and Directions of an Act, passed in the Fourth Year ot King George the First, for Sale of the forfeited Estates in Great Britain and Ireland; and that, in pursuance ot Powers vested in the Company by Two other Acts, passed; in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the said Kings Reign, in VP hr 40.

order to raise! Money? the better to, enable them tOi make good their said Purchases, theyj granted. < Annuities for Lives, to the Amount of<£.12,000 per num, by; Bonds to the Annuitants, and charged the said Company’s Lands in Scotland> with the Payments of the said Annuities; and that, subsequent, to this,' Transaction, the Affairs of the said. Company were*, by a Course of Mismanagement and Misconduct ini the then Directors, , greatly deranged and embarrassed,.-and their Estates, Stock, and Property were, from; Time; to Time, loaded with divers other Incumr brances,. and the Company, byrfhe Fraud or: Misma? nagement of the said, Directors, sustained many heavy. Losses, the Consequence of which was, that the several) Annuitants, by virtue of the Powers, contained ini their Security, entered into Possession of the Company’s Estates in Scotland, and - continued to hold the same; and, subject to their Right and Security, thei Estates have been sold under the Directions andj Authority of certain Acts of Parliament, and Decrees* in Law; and that, by virtue of certain, Clauses contained in an Act of the Seventeenth of His presentt Majesty, for expediting the Sale of the Estates in; Scotland belonging to the York Buildings Company,. for the Relief of their Creditors, it was provided, that, the Judges of the Court of Session in Scotland should} proceed, under certain Regulations therein expressed, to the Sale of the Company's Estates in Scotland, to the classing of their Creditors, and to adjudge and j satisfy their respective Claims, out of the Purchase. Money arising from such Sale, and in the Manner directed by the Act; and that, by the < Powers given by the said Act* all the Estates and Baronies in> Scotland belonging to the said Company, except the Superiorities and Duties of the Town and Village of Stonehaven, have been sold, under the Authority of the Judges of the Court of Session; and that sundry large. Sums of Money have, under the special Provisions in the said last mentioned Act, been paid by the Purchasers of the said Estates of the Company, by virtue of the Warrants of the Court of Session in Scotland\ and, out of the Money so paid, certain Persons, claiming as Creditors of the Company, have receivedi Sums to a considerable Amount, hut there are still very large Sums of Money remaining in the Hands of certain of: the Purchasers, amounting, in the Whole, as is apprehended, to more than sufficient; to pay all; the just and legal Debts of the Company, to the Surplus of which Monies the Petitioners the Company are entitled, in virtue of their Reversionary Right; and that the Liquidation of the fair Debts of the Company is a Matter of great Importance to them, as well as to their just and lawful Creditors, and the Method of Liquidation directed by the Act before-mentioned is. not only highly inconvenient and expensive, but extremely dilatory and difficult, as the Debts of the Company are, for the most Part, contracted by Securities unknown to the Laws of Scotland, and upon which Questions must necessarily arise in the Scotch Courts, which ought to be determined according to the English Law; and that the said Company being an English Company, and their Debts contracted under the Forms and Principles of the English Laws, they are desirous that the said Debts may be fairly liquidated according to those Forms and Principles, and in the most expeditious, equitable, and certain Manner, and that their different Creditors may accordingly receive Satisfaction for their respective Claims in the English Courts, but which cannot at present be done, as the Produce arising from the Sale of their Estates is in Scotland, and out of the Jurisdiction of the said Courts; and that, if it shall appear that any of the Debts of the Company have been contracted in, Scotland, and according to the Forms and Principle of the Scotch Laws, the Company are wilting that a sufficient Sum shall be retained in the

A Petition of Robert Wood, Esquire, and John Cator, Lyme Regig Esquire, was read, Setting forth, That, at the last ElecLion-Election for Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, the Honourable Henry Fane, the Honourable Thomas Fane, and the Petitioners, were Candidates; and that at the Poll taken upon the said Election, before William Peterson, the Returning Officer, a great Majority of Legal Electors appeared in Favour of the Petitioners, some of whom actually voted, and the rest of th<em tendered their Votes, for the Petitioners; and that the said Returning Officer, during the Time of taking the said Poll, acted with great Partiality in Favour of the said Henry Fane and Thomas Fane, and admitted so many illegal Votes in their Favour, and rejected so many legal Votes which were duly tendered in Favour of the Petitioners, as to leave a Majority upon the Face of the Poll in Favour of the said Hairy Fane and Thomas Fane, under Colour whereof the said Henry Fane and Thomas Fane were returned, although the Petitioners were duly elected by a great Majority, and ought to have been returned; and that several of the Votes given at the said Election, in Favour of the said Henry Fane and Thomas Fane, were procured to them, and their Agents, by Means of Bribery and Corruption: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief as shall appear to be just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 15th Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being resident Freemen, and resident Freeholders, of and in the Borough of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, having a Right to vote in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was also read; Setting forth,

That at the last Election of Burgesses to serve" in this present Parliament for the Borough of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, the Honourable Henry Fane, the Honouable Thomas Fane, Robert Wood, Esquire, and John Cator, Esquire, were Candidates; and that, at the Poll taken upon the said Election, William Peterson, the Returning Officer, permitted many Persons to vote who, not being resident within the said Borough, had no Right so to do, and refused to admit several others, being resident Freeholders, who had a Right, as such, to have given their Votes at the said Election, whereby the said Henry Fane and Thomas Fane were unduly returned, although the said Robert Wood and John Cator were duly elected by a very great Majority, and ought to have been returned; which Proceedings of the said Returning Officer the Petitioners apprehend to be a Violation of the Rights of themselves and others the legal Electors for the said Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief thereupon as shall be just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration at the same Time that the last preceding Petition is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Record's, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the.

Hearing of the Matters of the said Petitions.

A Petition of Joshua Smith and George Jackson,. Penry* Esquires, was read; Setting forth, That at the last Electl,'n* Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Penryn, in the County of Cornwall, Sir Francis Bassett, Baronet, Sir John Saint Aubyn, Baronet,

and the Petitioners, were Candidates; and that Edward Hodge, the Portreeve of the said Borough, who presided as the Returning Officer at the said Election, shewed a great and manifest Partiality in Favour of the said Sir Francis Bassett and Sir John Saint Aubyn, and, in the Course of the Poll, rejected the Votes of many Persons who had a Right to vote, and who tendered their Votes for the Petitioners, and did admit many Persons to vote for the said Sir Francis Bassett and Sir John Saint Aubyn, who had no Right whatsoever to vote in the Election of Members to represent the said Borough; and that the said Sir Francis Bassett and Sir John Saint Aubyn, by themselves and their Agents on their Behalf, and others by their -Privity and Direction, previous to and during the said Election, were guilty of Bribery, and other corrupt and illegal Practices, in order to procure themselves to be elected, and, for the same Purpose, did, by Promises and other undue Influence of themselves, their Friends and Agents, prevent, and attempt to prevent, divers Persons from voting for the Petitioners; and that, by the Means aforesaid, a colourable Majority of Votes appeared upon the Poll for the said Sir Francis Bassett and Sir John Saint Aubyn, and the said Portreeve returned them as Burgesses duly elected to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, whereas the Petitioners were duly elected, and ought to have been returned duly elected, to represent the said Borough in Parliament; and that such Proceedings are in Prejudice of the Rights of a Majority of the legal Electors of the said Borough, in Violation of the Laws of Elections, and to the manifest Injury of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the Seventeenth Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Word " Seventeenth," and inserting the Words " Twenty-fgurth" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Word " Seventeenth" stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words u Twenty-fourth" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Aflirmative.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

OrderedThat the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 24th Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant,' or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary, by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Kirkwall,&c. A Petition of John Sinclair, Esquire, of Ulbster, was

Election. read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner was a Candidate at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the District of Boroughs of Kirkwall, I Vick,

Dornoch, Tain, and Dingwall, in Scotland’ which Elec-

tion was held on Monday the 26th Day of April 1784; and that, at the said Election, John Gordon, Esquire, of Carrol, and John Campbell Sutherland, Esquire, of Forse, the Delegates for the Boroughs of IVick and Dornoch, duly chosen and appointed for those Boroughs, voted for the Petitioner; and John Riddoch, Esquire, Major General Charles Ross, and Duncan Munro, of Culcairn, pretending to have the legal Commissions, and to have been duly chosen Delegates from the Boroughs of Kirkwall, Tain, and Dingwall, voted for the Right honourable Charles James For; and that the Commission produced by the said John Riddoch, Esquire, as Commissioner or Delegate for Vol. 40.

the Borough of Kirkwall, was not only in itself void and null, having been brought' about by open Force and Violence, contrary to the Votes given by a Majority of the legal Electors, and not having the Common Seal of the Town appended by the Town Clerk, according to an express Act of Parliament to that Effect, but also, the said Borough of Kirkwall had no Right or Title to send or make Choice of a Delegate to vote at the said Election, on account of the Want and unjust Exclusion of certain constituent ^Members essentially necessary to have been present by the Set and Constitution of the Borough; and that the Commission produced by the said Major General Charles Ross is void and null, in respect that the said Commission bears, That Devoid Ross, Writer in Tain, was appointed Assessor, to act in the Absence of the said Major General Charles Ross, which is manifestly contrary to Law, no Borough being entitled to name above One Commissioner; and that the said Duncan Munro, Esquire, of Culcairn, was not entitled to give a Vote at the said Election, in respect he did not produce the Precept of the Sheriff of Ross to the Magistrates of Dingwall, nor any Evidence that the Orders and Directions of the Legislature, in regard to the Choice of a Commissioner, had been complied with, nor any Authority upon ,w>hich his Commission was founded; and that the said Right honourable Charles James For was ineligible, not being a legal qualified Burgess in any One of the said Boroughs, and having no , Connection with, or Property in, them, nor paying Tax and Stent to His Majesty, according to the Laws and Acts of Parliament directing the same; and also, that his Election is contrary to an Act of the Scots Parliament for settling the Manner of electing Sixteen Peers, and Forty-five Commoners, to represent Scotland in the Parliament of Great Britain, which Act declares that none shall be capable to elect, or be elected, to represent a Shire or Burgh, in the Parliament of Great Britain, for Scotland, except such as were then capable, at the Time of the Union, to elect, or be elected, Commissioners for Shires or Boroughs to the Parliament of Scotland, which no Person was capable of, being born out of Scotland, unconnected with that Country, and who had no Estate or Property therein; and that the Petitioner having had the Voles of the Delegates of the Boroughs of Wick and Dornoch, at the Election aforesaid, and the Delegate, or Commissioner, from Wick, having also declared, that in the Event of an Equality of Votes, by the Incapacity of any One or more of the Four other Commissioners, that he gave his casting or decisive Voice in Favour of the Petitioner, he had thereby a Majority of legal Votes; notwithstanding which, the said Right honourable Charles James For has been returned as the Burgess duly elected to serve in Parliament for the aforesaid District of Boroughs, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioner: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, to permit him to be heard by Counsel, and to grant him such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 5th Day of April next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.
