A Petition of Christopher Cunningham Vickry, Noah Oakhampton Cartwright, John Youlden, Henry Gale, Joseph Harris, Elcclioil* Henry Jole, William Jole, John Lane, John Limebcar,

William Weekes, Edward Paltridge, Thomas Earle, and Thomas Gliddon, Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Oakhampton, in the County of Devon, in Behalf of themselves and many other Electors of the same Borough, w>as also read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election of Members to serve in this Parliament for the said Borough, which began on Monday the 5th Day of April 1784, the Right honourable George Capel Conningsby, Esquire, commonly called Lord Viscount Malden, Humphry Minchin, Esquire, John Luxmoore, Esquire, and Thomas Wiggens,

Esquire, were Candidates; and that the said Lord Viscount Malden and Humphry Minchin were duly elected, and ought in Justice to have been returned, as Members to represent the said Borough in this present Parliament, but that Hairy Luxmoore, then Mayor and Returning Officer of the said Borough, was very partial in Favour of the said John Luxmoore and Thomas Wiggens, admitting many Persons to poll for them who had no Right to vote at the said Election, and rejecting many Persons who were entitled to vote, and offered to poll for the said Lord Malden and Mr. Min- chin; by Means whereof and of other undue and illegal Practices of the said Returning Officer, and of the said John Luxmoore and Thomas Wiggens, the said John Luxmoore and Thomas Wiggens are returned as duly elected, to the great Violation of the Rights of the Petitioners, and of the said Borough: And therefore praying, That the Premises may be taken into Consideration, and that such Relief may be granted to the Petitioners therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration at the same Time that the last preceding Petition is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary, by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matters of the said Petitions.

A Petition of John Walker Heneage and Robert Cricklade Nicholas, Esquires, was read; Setting forth, That, at the Election, late General Election for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, Robci't Adamson, Charles Westley Coxe, Esquires, and the Petitioners, were Candidates; and that many indirect and unwarrantable Practices were made use of by the said Robert Adamson and Charles Westley Coxe, and also by other Persons in their Interests, to procure a colourable Majority for them the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care; and that Richard Townsend was the Bailiff and the Returning Officer of the said Borough, and, before the Poll, did attempt, by undue and improper Influence, to prevail upon Persons who had no Right of voting, to appear and tender their Votes in x Favour

5 Geo. III. 28° Janu 463

Favour of Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care, promising and giving them Reasons to believe that he would admit them upon the Poll at all Events; and that, during the Poll, the said Richard Townsend did behave himself with marked and continued Partiality and Preference towards Mr. Adamson and % Mr. Core, and did illegally and arbitrarily admit a great Number of Voters who had no Right to vote, nor were qualified in any Manner, to give their Votes at such FJection for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care, and did wilfully and knowingly reject many Voters who were duly qualified to vote, and who tendered their Votes in Favour of the Petitioners, and did, by a, Variety of other undue and illegal Devices, attempt to procure a fraudulent and colourable Majority for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care, and did, against the earnest and continued Remonstrances of the Petitioners and their Counsel, admit, without proper and sufficient Equity, all Persons to vote for Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, and did discourage all Enquiry into the Rights or Titles of those who tendered their Votes for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core; and that the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, by themselves and their Agents, before and at the said Election, were guilty of gross Bribery in order to corrupt the Voters of the said Borough, and, as well by giving, as by promising to give, Money and other Rewards to the Voters of the said Borough, and by other illegal, corrupt, and indirect Means, did prevail on many of the Voters of the said Borough to give their Votes at the said Election for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core; and that, in Consequence thereof, and by the partial, arbitrary, and illegal Conduct of the Returning Officer, a colourable Majority of Votes was obtained for the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Core, under which the said Returning Officer has endeavoured to protect himself for the illegal Return which he has made of the said Mr. Adamson and Mr. Care, in Prejudice of the Petitioners, who had a clear Majority of legal and uncorrupted Votes, and who should have been returned for the said Borough, and in Subversion of the true and sacred Rights of Election, and the Law and Constitution of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem just.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the Tenth Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Word " Tenth" and inserting the Word " Seventeenth" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Word " Tenth" stand Part of the Question;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 10th Day of Febniary next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Freeholders of the Borough of Doumton, in the County of Wilts, was read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Doumton, the Honourable William Seymour Conway and the Honourable Edward Bowoerie were Candidates; and that the said Election came on at Downton aforesaid on the ?6th Day of July last, and a Poll being demanded, the same was taken before James Serle, Esquire, Bailiff of the Hundred and Borough of Downton aforesaid, who acted as the Returning Officer for the said Borough; and that John Dagge, Esquire, under an Appointment as Deputy to Joseph Elderton, Esquire, the Steward of the Manor and Borough of Downton aforesaid, did also take upon himself to act as the Returning Officer of the said Borough, and a Poll was also taken by the said John Dagge; and that a very great Majority of the legal Votes of the said Borough were tendered in Favour of the said William Seymour Conway by the Petitioners, and divers other Freeholders of the said Borough, unto the said James Serle, and also to the said John Dagge; and that the said James Serle did unlawfully reject divers legal Votes which were tendered unto him in Favour of the said William Seymour Conway as aforesaid, and received several illegal Votes in Favour of the said Edward Bowoerie; yet nevertheless, a very great Majority of legal Votes having been tendered and given at the said Election, and ad minted fey the said James Serle in Favour of the said William Seymour Comvay, the said James Serle did thereupon declare the said William Seymour Comvay to be duly elected, and hath accordingly returned him as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the said John Dagge, at the said Poll so taken by him, did unlawfully and partially reject several legal Votes which were so as aforesaid tendered in Favour of the said William Seymour Comvay, and did receive many illegal Votes in Favour of the said Edward Bowoerie, and, under Colour of a pretended Majority in Favour of the said Edward Bouverie, did declare him to be duly elected, and, notwithstanding the said real Majority in Favour of the said William Seymour Conway, hath taken upon himself falsely and illegally to make a Return of the said Edward Bowoerie, as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, to the Prejudice of the said William Seymour Conway, and in direct Violation of the Rights and Franchises of the Petitioners, and of the other legal Electors of the said Borough, and, the Sheriff of the said County of Wilts hath annexed to his Writ the Indentures of both the said Returns; and that the said Edward Bouverie, by himself and his Agents, and divers other Persons in his Behalf, were guilty of Bribery, and divers other corrupt and illegal Practices, at and before the said Election, in order to procure him the said Edward Bouverie to be returned for the said Borough, to the Prejudice of the said William Seymour Comvay, and in Violation of the Rights of the Petitioners, and of the Law of Elections: And therefore praying the House, as ivell on the Behalf of the said William Seymour Conway, as of themselves and Others, Electors of the said Borough, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein as shall seem meet.

A Petition of Elisha Tcbb, Benjamin Shaw, John Southwark King, John Kent, Thomas Thomas, Joseph Bromley, Election-and James Sayle, and others, Electors in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, was read; Setting forth, That at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in the Room of the late Sir Barnard Turner, Knight, deceased, Sir Richard Hotham, Knight (lately One of the Representatives for the said Borough in Parliament) and Paul Le Mesu~ rier, Esquire, were the Candidates; and that, at the said Election, many Persons who had no Capacity to vote at any Election for Members to serve in Parliament, and many others who were not qualified to vote at such Elections for the said Borough, according to the last Determination of the House of Commons (settling the Right of Election in and for the said Borough) and the Law of the Land, were admitted to vote for the said Paul Le Mesurier; and that the said Candidates, having agreed finally to close the Poll at Three o’Clock on the Third Day of the said Election, it was most particularly necessary that there should be no Sort of Interruption of the Proceedings at the said Election, and, that the numerous Persons who had a Right to vote therein should not be in the smallest Degree, interrupted or delayed in giving their Suffrages; but the said Paul Le Mesurier, not regarding the Premises, and the Freedom of Election, by himself, his Friends, and Agents, caused and procured a turbulent Band of Sailors, and others, to be led up to the Hustings, from Time to Time, during the said Election, who, by Threats, Insults, and Violence, greatly interrupted the said Election, and thereby intimidated and prevented many of the Voters of the said Borough for polling for the said Sir Richard Hotham, and also delayed others, who were not to be intimidated, so long, that the Poll was finally closed, before they could (without great Danger and 'Risque to themselves) be permitted to poll at the said Election; and that many of the Voters of the said Borough, voting for the said Paul Le Mesurier, did ask, receive, and take Money, and other Rewards, of the said Paul Le Mesurier, his Friends, and Agents, by Way of Gift, Loan, and other Devices, and agreed and contracted with the said Paul Le Mesuiier, his Friends and Agents, for Money, Gifts, Offices, Employments, and other Rewards, to give their Votes at the said Election, and divers others of them, for such illegal and corrupt Considerations as aforesaid, were persuaded by the said Paul Le Mesurier, his Friends, and Agents, to forbear to give their Votes at the said Election; and that the said Paul Le Mesurier, before and during the said Election, by himself, his Friends, and Agents, was guilty of Bribery and Corruption, by giving and promising Money, Securities for Money, and other Rewards, to the Voters of the said Borough, whereby, and by other illegal Means, many of the Voters of the said Borough were induced and prevailed upon to give their Votes at the said Election for the said Paul Le Mesurier, and, others of the said Voters were induced and prevailed upon to forbear to give their Votes at the said Election; and that the said Paul Le Mesurier, in the Time of this present Parliament, after the Vacancy for the said Borough (occasioned by the Death of the said Sir Barnard

Newport, Isle A Petition of the Electors of the Borough of New-

of Wight, town, otherwise Fran/cvi/te, in the Isle of Wight, in the

Eleetion. County of Southampton, whose Names are thereto

subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, Electors of the said Borough, was read; Setting forth, That, at the late Election of a Burgess to represent the said Borough in Parliament, in the room of James Worsley, Esquire, who had vacated his Seat by the Acceptance of a Place, Sir Gilbert Elliot, Baronet, and Mark Gregory, Esquire, were the only Candidates; and that the said Mark Gregory was incapable of being elected, not being duly qualified in Point of Estate, and, being directly or indirectly concerned in a Contract or Contracts, was made ineligible by the Act of the Twenty-second of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act M for restraining any Person, concerned in any Contract, Commission, or Agreement, made for the €t public Service, from being elected, or sitting and " voting as a Member of the House of Commons;" and that William Clarke, Esquire, who took upon himself and acted as Mayor and Returning Officer of the said Borough at the said Election, was not legal Mayor and Returning Officer thereof, not being possessed of a legal Borough Land within the said Borough; and that, by an illegal Agreement in Writing entered into by Sir Richard Worsley, Baronet, Sir Fitz Williams Barrington, Baronet, John Barrington, Esquire, and others, it was agreed, that from the Date thereof the Election of Burgesses to represent the said Borough in Parliament should be jointly in them, to the Exclusion of all others, legal Electors of the said Borough, or to that Effect; and, that most of the Voters who polled for the said Mark Gregory, Esquire, knew of the said illegal Agreement, and voted under the Influence thereof; and that the said William Clarke, Esquire, did likewise admit many other Persons to vote for the said Mark Gregory, Esquire, whom he ought not to have admitted, and, by these Practices, and by Bribery, the said Mark Gregory, Esquire, did procure himself to be returned a Representative in Parliament, in manifest Injury to the Rights of the Electors, and in open Violation of the Law and Constitution of Parliament: And therefore praying, That the said Return of the said Mark Gregory, Esquire, may be set aside, and that the said Sir Gilbert Elliot, Baronet, who was the only Candidate capable of being elected, may be declared duly elected to represent the said Borough in Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 21st Day of April next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary, by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of several of the Trustees for executing Derby, &c; an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His Road, present Majesty, intituled, €i An Act for repairing " and widening the Road from Derby to Mansfield, in the County of Nottingham, and several other Roads " therein mentioned," and also of several of the Creditors who have advanced Money on the Tolls granted by the said Act, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That the Trustees have proceeded to put the said Act into Execution, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, which, together with the Tolls, has been duly applied in repairing and widening the said Roads; and that the Term granted by the said Act is near expiring, and several of the Provisions of the said Act have been found inconvenient, and further Pow’ersare wanting; and that, unless the Term of the said Act is enlarged, the Money borrowed on the Credit thereof cannot be repaid, nor the Roads kept in proper Repair: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said Act, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Lord George Cavendish, Lord George Augustus Henry Cavendish, &c.: And they are to meet upon Tuesday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of Henry Boldero Barnard, Esquire, the South Cave Reverend William Watford, Clerk, and the several Inclosure, other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Messuages, Cottages, and Lands, in the Township of South Cave, in the East Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are, within the said Township, several Open and Common Fields, Ings, and Uninclosed Meadows, wherein the Lands of the respective Proprietors thereof lie intermixed and dispersed in small Parcels, and, in their present Situation, are incapable of any considerable Improvement; but if the same were divided and inclosed, it would be very advantageous to all the Parties interested therein: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes above mentioned, under such Restrictions and Regulations as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Robert Smith, and Mr. Duncombe' do prepare, and bring in, the same.

bitants of the Hundreds of Faversham and Boughton, in the said County, and of the several Parishes of Qspnnge, Scasaltcr, and Whitstable, in the same County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Town of Faversham is large and populous, and there is a Creek or Branch of the Sea which runs up to the same, forming a commodious Haven, by Means whereof a considerable Trade is carried on in the said Town, and also in the said Hundreds of Faversham and Boughton, and the said several Parishes of Ospringe, Seasalter, and Whitstable, on Account of their near Situation to the said Town; and that there are many Persons to whom the Traders of the said Town, Hundreds, and Parishes, are obliged to give Credit for small Sums of Money, who frequently refuse, although able, to pay the same, presuming on the Discouragements which their Creditors lie under, from the great Expence they are unavoidably put to, and the Delays they meet with, in suing for such Debts; and it would tend greatly to promote Industry, and support useful Credit, in the said Town, Hundreds, and Parishes, if a more easy and speedy Method of recovering Small Debts within the same could be obtained: And therefore praying. From the House of Commons, the 1st 1785.

Sir,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to acquaint you. That you are, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, to attend their Service in Parliament, on this Day Fortnight, the 15th Day of this Instant February; and you are to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereon, upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure Of the said House.'

I am, Sir,

Your humble Servant,

C. W. Cornwall, Speaker.

From the House of Commons, the 1st February 1785.

My Lord,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to desire your Lordship, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Members of Parliament for the Cinque Ports to attend their Service in Parliament, on this Day Fortnight, the 15th Day of this Instant February; you Lordship will also be pleased to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereon.

I am, with the utmost Respect,

My Lord,

Your Lordship’s Most humble and obedient Servant,

C.W. Cornwall, Speaker.

To the Right honourable Frederick

Lord North, Lord Warden of the

Cinque Ports.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of die Clock.

Hereditary Right to a Seat is preserved in a family, or assigned at Pleasure (an Evil which the Petitioners presume will be a maiq Object of Attention in the proposed Reform) but involves in it the dearest Interests and mdst important Concerns of many Thousand Citizens, Inhabitants of this- extensive, populous, and flourishing City: That the Scrutiny, which is still carrying on in the City of Westminster, hath lasted for a Period of nearly Eight Months, and, judging by the Progress already made, it appears extremely probable, that, should it proceed with the t same Pace, and the Petitioners do not understand that any Complaint hath been made of undue Delay, the present Parliament may be advanced- to its last Session by the Time the High Bailiff has decided on his Poll: That the Petitioners are well informed, that every Prediction of the Futility, Insignificance, Expence, and Injustice, which must attend the Proceedings of such a Court, hath been abundantly verified by the Event; but the Petitioners forbear any Detail of the Progress or Consequences of a Measure, the Origin and Principle of which they solemnly protest against, as contrary to the Spirit and Practice of the Constitution, to the plainest Provisions both of Common and Statute Law, and to the Rights and Privileges of the Electors of Great Britain; for the same Reason, the Petitioners forbear to meddle with the Motives, Reasons, or Imaginations, alledged by the High Bailiff of Westminster in Defence of his Conduct, or with the Claims and Pretensions of the respective Candidates: But the Petitioners do humbly pray, That the House 1 immediately take such Measures as shall restore the City of Westminster to its undoubted Right of having its Representatives in Parliament, there being no farther or other Relief suited to the Nature of the Injury complained of in the Premises, or which can be satisfactory to the Petitioners.

A PETITION, as well of the Trustees acting Callington under and by virtue of , an Act of Parliament, Road*, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening several Roads leading from Callington, in the County of Cornwall, as of the Creditors on the Tolls of the said Roads, as also of the principal Inhabitants residing near the same, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in pursuance of the Powers given by the said Act, the Sum of £. 1,600 hath been borrowed on the Credit of the said Tolls, which hath been laid out in making, repairing, and improving the said Roads, and the Tolls and Composition Money collected upon the same have also from Time to Time been applied to the Payment of the Interest due upon the Monies borrowed on the Credit thereof, and in the Repair and Improvement of the said Roads; and that the Term of the said Act is near expired, and the said Roads are now in bad Repair, and cannot be kept in good Repair, and the Creditors paid the said Sum of £. 1,600, unless the said Act is continued for a further Term of Years, and the Powers thereof enlarged and amended; and alledging, that the Road leading from Bushford, in the Parish of Stoke Climsland, to Beal's Mill, in the said Parish, and also, the Road leading from Penterscross, in the Parish of Pillaton, to a Place called The Fighting Cocks, in the Parish of Botes Fleming, all in the County of Cornwall, are very ruinous and dangerous, and in many Places so narrow that Carriages cannot pass without the greatest Difficulty, and the same cannot be? sufficiently widened, altered, and repaired, by the ordinary Course of Law: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in One or more Bill or Bills, for the Purpose of continuing the Term, and enlarging and amending the Powers, of the said Act of Parliament, and for extending the said Roads in manner above mentioned, and for giving the Petitioners such further and other Securty apd Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Nottingham A Petition of the several Persona whose Names are Small Debts, thereunto subscribed, Inhabitants of, or residing and trading in* the Town and County of the Town of vNottingham, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the said Town is large and populous, and by reason of the many extensive Trades and Manufactories carried on therein (particularly Framework-Knitting) several Thousands of People are constantly employed, many of whom contract small Debts, and, although well able, refuse to pay the same, presuming on the Discouragements and Difficulties their Creditors lie under, in suing for the Recovery thereof by the usual Course of Law, on Account of the Delays and great Expence they are unavoidably subject to in such Suits; and that the Petitioners conceive, that an easy and speedy Method of recovering Small Debts within the said Town and County of the Town of Nottingham would not only tend to remedy the Inconveniencies above mentioned, but to improve the Trade thereof, as well as promote Industry and Sobriety, arid support useful Credit: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, subject to sjjch Provisions and Regulations as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition, purporting to be the Remonstrance and Memorial of the Operative Weavers of the City of Glasgow, Borough of Ruth erg le?i, and of all those Operators who have entered into a Correspondence with the Glasgow Committee, humbly offered unto the Honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That we who hereunto subscribe our Names are the Operative Weavers of the Places above mentioned, and, having taken into our serious Consideration the very alarming Nature of the late Taxes on printed linens and British manufactured Muslins, beg Leave, with all Deference, to submit our Sentiments thereon to His Majesty’s Ministers, and to Parliament; therefore, as a Body of Operative Tradesmen and Free-born Sons of Britainf acting for the present Interest of the Nation, and for the Advantage of After-Ages, claim the Liberty, as free Subjects, to offer to your Honourable House in the First Place our Opinion of these unpopular, unwise, and ruinous Taxations; and Secondly, as our Ultimatum, to crave a Repeal thereof: It is therefore the Opinion of us all, without Reserve of Sentiment, as we do not mean to be prolix, nor to detain this Honourable House with a Chain of fine-spun Arguments, that these late Duties on the printed Linens and British manufactured Muslins are, in our Views of Matters, and in Reality we presume, the most unwise, imprudent, and, in short, ruinous Laws, that could possibly be devised by any Minister who wished his King and his Country well: And farther, Honourable Gentlemen, we, as a Body of Operative Tradesmen and Free Subjects, in giving our Opinion, do not mean to count our Loss by per Cent.; but we make bold to say, that if these Laws are allowed to continue, they will go far in extirpating these Branches, particularly the British Muslins (and Cotton Machinery, which on these Branches of Manufacture has its Dependance) from this Country: We presume, there is not a Member within the Walls of this Honourable House unacquainted with the infinite Toil and Industry with which these Branches of British Manufacture have been reared and cultivated, and yet are scarce arrived at the Half Stage of Perfection, cultivated we say at very great Expence and Labour, and even imminent Hazard of wasting Fortunes; and much of the Cotton Machinery in Scotland, and even in England, though in a fair Way of doing well, yet have not paid their Cost, nor even produced a Farthing of Profit: The Consequence of these Laws, therefore, if allowed to continue in Force, will be Emigration and Depopulation, and all the Train of Miseries which are the usual Attendants of such National Misfortunes: It is the greatest Curse that can come upon a Land, next to a Judgment from

Heaven, to have Industry curbed---- And farther, we

cannot help observing, that these Laws give an immediate Preference to the Muslins and Callicoes imported by the East India Company, at the immediate Risque and Hazard of the Non-consumption of our ow n British Manufacture: We mean to speak our honest Sentiments, which we presume we have naturally a Right to: The East India Company import their Articles of Callicoes and Muslins from a Country where Tyranny and Oppression reign, and where too the spontaneous Gifts of Almighty God early established the Growth of the Whole of the Materials of their Manufacture within their own Boundaries; on the contrary, we have every Difficulty to struggle with, and to import our Raw Materials for the Printing and Muslin Branches from Foreign Countries, on most of which high Duties are paid, for the Support and Dignity of the Crown, which we think right; why, therefore, in the Name of God, should we be engaged in a* threefold War of Competition and Rivalry with this Company of Foreign Merchants, who, at the Expence of the Blood and Treasure of the Nation, are held up and supported at all Hands ? And moreover, the present flourishing and patronized State of these Manufactures in Ireland, France, and Sxviizerland, and other Places on the Continent, render the present Laws alluded to an Expedient extremely dangerous, and by no Means ultimately beneficial to Government: All these Arguments were fully and clearly set before your Honourable House last Session of Parliament, by the Convention of the Royal Boroughs of Scut land, by the Chamber of Commerce of the City of Glasgow, and by the Manufacturers of this City of Glasgow and Neighbourhood: And we have only farther to set before your Honourable House, that we are deeply interested, each for 1 ourselves individually, with the Rise or Downfall of the Linen and Cotton Manufactures; and we have the Vanity to say, and secure when we say it, that these Branches of Manufacture have already proved a Source of Wealth to the Nation, and give Bread to many Thousands of His Majesty’s industrious and loyal Subjects, and produce all those Advantages which naturally arise from Population and well-directed Industry; and farther, the Memorialists take the Liberty to say, that if these Laws are not repealed, that the Result and Consequences will naturally be a more limited and contracted Sale, and Reduction of the Employment of the laborious Operative Weavers and their Dependents, who are many Thousands; the Consequences then before mentioned may be dreaded, viz. Emigration and Depopulation; or to remain at Home, a Scarcity of Bread, and Misery to stare us in the Face, which cannot fail to render desperate a great Part of this Nation: Honourable Gentlemen, the Desire of the Nation, and us Operative Weavers who. hereunto subscribe, is, that you would take into your serious Consideration the Propriety and Necessity of repealing these Taxes: We presume your Honours will immediately see it necessary; therefore the unanimous Voice of us all is, Repeal! Repeal! We have particularly in our Eye the lute Duties on printed Linens and British manufactured Muslins; but we would beg Leave to call your Attention not only to these, but to the Encouragement of all the Manufactures of this Country in general: Other Objects of Taxation, less dangerous, less obnoxious and destructive, may easily be substituted; why therefore curb Ingenuity and Industry? If you are designed, Honourable Gentlemen, under the Great Ruler of the Universe, to be happy Instruments of raising this drooping Nation to its wonted Splendour, you have an arduous Task allotted for you indeed; you have to undo the Mistakes of many Years, and to pilot this sinking Nation into that Channel of Rest, which

Nature, Experience, and the Circumstances of the Times, point out: And this (taken to be your Lot) lays open a large unbounded Field for the Display of true Roman-like Patriotism, and for the Suppression of all frivolous or selfish Considerations: You are, as Members of the British Senate, Heaven's Trustees for the Nation and all its Dependencies; and the Trust, which Heaven has reposed in you, ought therefore to be a Matter of the most serious Concern and Import: You are the Stewards of the Nation; therefore you are bound, by every Tie, effectually to redress Grievances, and to diffuse universal Justice, common, or at least should be so, to all Hanks and Classes of Mankind: The Confidence of the Nation will be

confirmed to the Legislature, by Manufactures being unshackled, unfettered, and encouraged by Bounties: By these Means also your Names will be transmitted to Posterity, as the Saviours of your Country, and Guardians of the British Liberties: We, the Operative Weavers of the Places aforesaid, will close their Observations by again expressing their serious Apprehensions that the woeful Consequences arising from these Taxes, if allowed to continue in Force, are such as deserve the most serious Attention of the Legislature, to whom they at present look up with that Anxiety and Solicitude incident to a Situation so peculiarly interesting: Hoping for' that Protection which will

enable them to continue useful Subjects of the State, and prevent them from adopting the painful Expedient of seeking Encouragement Abroad, which, by a Continuation of these Laws, they consider as being denied us in our Country: Our ardent Desire is, to be useful Members of the Community; and we presume, or rather flatter ourselves, that our Arguments and Cause, now' submitted to Parliament, will have their full Weight; and we hope that a Repeal of these Laws will be the Decision of the Honourable Parliament of Great Britain: The Memorialists have it not in their Power to appear personally; but we beg Leave to have it understood, that our united Voices surround the Parliament House at the Hour of Decision; and, in humble Expectation that our Wishes on this Business will be crowned with Success, we the Memorialists beg Leave most humbly and most respectfully to subscribe this Remonstrance and Memorial.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Noblemen, ttnd the humble IrelwidWard* Pet*d°n of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and others, of the County of Anglesey, and of other Parts of Great Britain, and also of the Kingdom of Ireland, w as presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Improvement of the Great Road leading through the Counties of Anglesey and Carnarvon towards Ireland is an Object of great Public Importance, as it tends to facilitate the Intercourse between both Kingdoms, and, for several Years past, great Sums of Money have been Annually expended in amending the said Road, and making Bridges, Dams, and other Works, for the Improvement thereof; and that the Passage of Porthaethwy Ferry, over an Arm of the Sea, between the Counties of Anglesey and Carnarvon, called The Streights of Menai, is frequently attended with very great Delay, Inconvenience, and Danger to Persons travelling with Mails and Expresses between England and Ireland, and to all other Persons having Occasion to pass the said Ferry: And representing to the House, that it appears, from the concurrent Opinions of several very eminent Engineers, that a safe and convenient Passage may be made across the said Arm of the Sea, by a Bridge or Embankment, with a Lock or Drawbridge, from the County of Anglesey to the opposite Shore, in the County of Carnarvon, at a Place, near the stud Ferry, called Ynysgeint and, in case the same shall be made, it will be necessary to make a new Road through certain Lands on each Side of the said Bridge, in order to open a Communication with the said Great Road; and that the making such safe and convenient Passage will be of great Benefit, Safety, and Convenience to all Persons having Occasion to travel the said Road, and of Public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making such safe and convenient Passage, and opening proper Communications with the said Great Road as aforesaid, by such Ways and 1 Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Ordered, That the said Petition be refeired to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Francis Reynolds and Abram Rawlinson, did give, present, and allow, and did promise, agree, and engage to give, present, and allow, to the Electors of the said Borough, and to several Persons, who had, or claimed to have, a Right to vote in the Election for the said Borough, Meat, Drink, Reward, Entertainment, and Provision, and the said Francis Reynolds and Abram Rawlinson, did give, present, and allow, and did promise, agree, and engage to give, present, and allow, to the Electors of the said Borough, and to several Persons who had, or claimed to have, a Right to vote in the Election for the said Borough, Meat, Drink, Reward, Entertainment, and Provision, as aforesaid, in order to procure themselves to be elected for the said Borough; and that the said Francis Reynolds and Abram Rawlinson, previous to, and during the Poll, were guilty of Bribery and Corruption, and of attempting to bribe and corrupt those who had a Right to vote in the said Election, in order to procure themselves to be returned as duly elected, and by the said, and other undue, illegal, and unwarrantable Means, the said Francis Reynolds and Abram Rctwlinson obtained a Majority on the Poll, and were returned accordingly, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners and other Electors of the said Borough who voted for the said John Lowther, and in open Defiance of the Law and Freedom of Election; and that the Mayor and Low Bailiff, Two of the Returning Officers of the said Borough, behaved with great Partiality at the said Election, in Favour of the said Francis Reynolds, and Abram Raxvlinson, and admitted many Persons to vote for the said Francis Reynolds and Abram Raxvlinson, who had no Right to vote, and refused to admit to poll others who had a good Right to vote, or were in the same Situation with those whom they allowed to/vote for the said Francis Reynolds and Abram Raxvlinson, and who offered their Votes for the said John Lowther, and the said Mayor and Low Bailiff were otherwise guilty of the most gross Partiality; and that, on a Scrutiny being duly demanded when the Polling was over, on the 26th Day of April last, in Behalf of the said John Lowther, the Petitioners, and other Electors of the said Borough (which Scrutiny, as the Petitioners contend, would have clearly shewn that the said John Lowther had a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned) the said Returning Officers peremptorily refused to grant the same, without giving any substantial Reasons for their so doing, notwithstanding that they had admitted several Votes on the Poll with Queries, in order to re-consider and determine on the Legality of such Votes at some subsequent Time before the Return should be made, notwithstanding the re w as sufficient Time to have gone through and finished the said Scrutiny before the Precept and Writ of Election were returnable; and that the said Francis Reynolds &nd Abram’Razclinsoji, and the said Mayor and Low Bailiff, were guilty of those, and divers other illegal and corrupt Practices, at and before the said Election, to the great Prejudice of the Rights and Franchises of the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 10th Day of May next, at Three of the Clock in the'Afternoon.

Harbour,&c. iras presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Cromarty Bay, in the County of Cromarty, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, has at all Times been a most safe Road-stead to Ships of all Nations, overtaken with Storms in any Part of The German Ocean, and the Erection of a Pier and Harbour has been judged beneficial to Navigation in general, and to the Commerce of that Part of the United Kingdom in particular; and that the Petitioner, Proprietor of the Barony of Cromarty, and of the Port and Harbour, has made a Present to the Public of the Ground and Coast necessary to be occupied by the said Harbour and Pier, and His Majesty has been pleased to grant the Sum of £. 5,000 out of the Produce of the Forfeited Estates in Scotland, towards erecting the said Harbour and Pier; that the Main Pier is erected, and Two other Piers, or Jettees, are begun to be erected, to complete the said Harbour; and that the above Sum of £, 5,000 not being sufficient for erecting and completing the said Piers and Harbour, the Petitioner has undertaken to complete the same, at his own Expence, but the said Harbour and Piers cannot be maintained and preserved without such Tolls are levied as may be adequate to that Purpose: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better preserving and maintaining the Harbour and Piers of Cromarty, in the County of Cromarty, in North Britain.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Samuel Hey wood, being examined, said, That by Reason of the many extensive Trades and Manufactories carried on in the Town of Nottingham (particularly Framework Knitting) several Thousands of People are constantly employed, many of whom contract small Debts, and, although well able, refuse to pay the same, presuming on the Difficulties their Creditors lie under in the Recovery thereof by the usual Course of Law; and that if a more speedy Method of reco* vering such Debts was established, it would be of great Benefit and Advantage to the Inhabitants of the said Town.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more speedy and easy Recovery of Small Debts within the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham: And that Mr. Robert Smith and Mr. Coke of Nottingham do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Memorandum:

By the Act passed in the Year 1781, intituled, "An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, &c"." the East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in Proportion to the Number of Troops sent, or to be sent, to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company.

This Sum the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in the East Indies only; and as it will be necessary to provide for the Subsistence of the Recruiting Companies remaining in Great Britain, there will be wanting at present, for this Purpose, the Sum of Six thousand Nine hundred Sixty-eight Pounds Nine Shillings and Nine Pence; which it will be necessary to vote on Account of the above Estimate.

Callington A yf R. Call reported from the Committee, to whom

Roads. ivl the Petition as well of the Trustees acting under and by virtue of an Act of Parliament, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening several Roads leading from Callington, in the County of Cornwall, as of the Creditors on the Tolls of the said Roads, as also of the principal Inhabitants residing near the same, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with, in respect to the Application for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said Act, but that no Notices were given of the Application for repairing the Road from a Place called Bushford, in the Parish of Stoke Climslandto a Place called Beat's Mill, in the said Parish, and also the Road leading from a Place called Penterscross, in the Parish of Pil-laton, to a Place called The Fighting Cocks, in the Parish of Botes Fleming; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. William Datisey being examined, said, That the . Trustees have borrowed several considerable Sums of Money, which have been laid out in making, repairing, and improving the said Roads — That the Sum of One thousand Six hundred Pounds now remains due, and cannot be repaid, nor the said Roads kept in Repair, unless the Term and Powers of the said Act are enlarged and amended.

And the Witness further said, That the Road leading from Bushford to Beal's Mill, in the Parish of Stoke Climsland, is about Two Miles in Length; and the Road leading from Penterscross, in the Parish of Pil-laton, to a Place called The Fighting Cocks, in the Parish of Botes Fleming, is about Three Quarters of a Mile in Length — That the said Two Pieces of Road are in a very ruinous Condition, and when repaired will be a Continuation of the old Road, in order to meet the Turnpike Road from Launceston to Callington, and from Callington to Saltash.

And he added, That all the principal Inhabitants, and many others, in the Parishes through which the said Pieces of Road lead, have either signed the Petition, or otherwise consented to the Application for repairing the said Roads. Then

Mr. William Gill informed your Committee, That the above-descnbed Pieces of Road are very much out of Repair, and in some Parts impassable for Two

Carriages, and that it would be Of great public Utility to have the same amended and kept in Repair.

Ordered, That the said Report be re-committed.

Ordered, That the said Report be re-committed to the Committee, to whom the said Petition was referred.

That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clrrk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act passed in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from a Place called Nightingale s, in the Township of Heath Charnock, to the Bridge at the West End of the Towm of Bolton in the Moors, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was read: And

Mr. John Cooper being examined, said, That by virtue of the Powers of the said Act, which expired with the last Session of Parliament, a great Progress hath been made in repairing the said Roads, in the doing of which a considerable Sum of Money borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls was expended —

That the Money so borrowed still remains due, but the Persons w’ho lent the same have not now any Security for the Re-payment thereof, the said Act being expired; that the sudden Dissolution of Parliament, and the short Session that succeeded, prevented an Application for the Renewal of the said Act in the usual Course, as the Standing Orders of the House could not then be complied with — That the said Highway now is, and long hath been, the great Carriage Road from the South of Lancashire to Carlisle, and from London and the Southern Counties of the Kingdom to the Western Parts of Scotland — That the Laws in being are not sufficient for the due repairing of the said Road, for which Reason, and for the Indemnification of the Creditors, it is expedient and necessary that the said-Act should be revived, and the Term and Powers thereof continued and enlarged.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for reviving, continuing, and enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act passed in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from a Place called Nightingale s, in the Township of Heath Charnock, to the Bridge at the West End of the Town of Bolton i?i the Mcors, in the County Palatine of Lancaster: And that Mr. Blackburne and Mr. Thomas Stanley do prepare, and bring in, the same.

and that, at the Time of the said Election, the said Henry Cruger was incapable of being elected to serve in Parliament for the said City and County, because the said Henry Cruger, previous to the said Election, and after the Congress of the United States of America had declared the said States to be free and independant, and absolved from all Allegiance to the British Crown, and also, after His Majesty had, in a lawful Manner acknowledged the said States to be free, sovereign, and independant States, did take an Oath or Oaths, or subscribe a Declaration or Declarations, of Allegiance to the said United States, or one of them, and did thereby, and otherwise, actually or virtually renounce his Allegiance to His Majesty, and to this Country, and became an Alien, and not entitled to the Privileges of the natural-born Subjects of this Country; THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of John Walker Heneage and Robert Nicholas, Esquires; and also, the Petition of those whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Voters for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough* being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Thirty-five Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And a Counsel also appeared at the Bar on the Part of the Returning Officer, who, as the said Counsel alledged, was criminated by the said Petitions, or One

Februarii. 785.

of them; but he was directed by the House to withdraw.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Two Members then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Robert Vyner, Esquire, being drawn, be required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being‘Sixty Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Nine other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Select Committee, that there are various Matters of public Business to which he is required to attend, and which, as he apprehends, cannot be delayed without great Inconvenience to the Public; and the Substance of what was so alledged by him being taken down by the Clerk, in Manner before mentioned, and Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon, Mr. Speaker putting the Question to the House, That Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (in respect of what he has now alledged, and verified) be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, which being agreed to by the House, he was excused accordingly.

And the Name of One other Member, then present, was drawn, who was not objected to.

And the Name of Charles Brett, Esquire, being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Twenty-four other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of George Medley, Esquire, being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Thirteen other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note. That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the' Names of Eighteen other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Two, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, which they had before verifiea upon Oath; Twelve, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; One, on Account of his being a Petitioner to this House, complaining of an undue Election and Return; One, on Account of his Return to serve in Parliament not having been brought in Fourteen Day9; and Two, on Account of their having voted at the said Election.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused, or set aside, being complete;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, td take into Consideration so touch of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as recommends to the Consideration of the House, the Matters suggested in the Reports of the Commissioners of Public Accounts, and such further Regulations as may appear to be necessary in the different Offices of the Kingdom.

Ordered, That the several Reports, which have been presented to this House in any former Session of Parliament, from the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and state the Public Accounts of the Kingdom, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of th&Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Morpeth, in the County of Northumberland, in the room of Sir James Erskine, Baronet, who, since his Election for the said Borough, has become Entitled to, and accepted of, a beneficial Interest in the Office of Director of Chancery in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

have proceeded in the Execution- of the said Aety. and have borrowed a Considerable Sum. of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls arising from the said Roads, which still remains due; and that, unless the Term granted by the said Act; which is near expiring, and the Powers thereof, are enlarged, the said Road cannot be completely repaired, and kept in Repair, nor. die Money borrowed upon the Credit of the Tolls arising therefrom (which are a very scanty Security for the same) be repaid: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said Act, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Roads, tion several Acts of Parliament, of the Fourth, the Sixth, and the Tenth Years of King George the First, the Fourth, the Tenth, and the Twenty-fifth Years of King George the Second, and the Sixth Year of His present Majesty, for repairing several Roads leading from the Stone’s End at Blackman Street, in the Parishes of Saint George, Southwark, and Sqint Mary, Newington, to High gate, at the Entrance into Ashdown Fo~ rest, in the Parish of East Grinstead, and to Sutton and Burton Common, and from Vauxhall Bridge, through Stockwell, to join the said Road leading to Highgate, at the Bottom of Bristow Causeway Common, and the Road lying between Nonesuch and Worcester Parks, in the Parish of Cuddington, in the Counties of Surrey and Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have caused the said Roads to be amended according to the Directions of the said Acts, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls authorized to be collected on the said Roads, which still remains due; and that the Term of the said Acts is near expiring, and the Money borrowed cannot be paid off, and the said Roads kept in good Repair, unless the said Term be enlarged, and some further Powers given for those Purposes; and AUedging, that the Road leading from Highgate aforesaid, to IVitchcross, in the County of Sussex, being about Twd Milesj is in a ruinous Condition, and incommodious for Travellers and Carriages, and cannot be effectually amended!, and kept in good Repair, by the oirdiriary Course of Law; that the said Road communicates with the Roads comprised in the said Acts, and might be conveniently amended and repaired, if the same was put under thO Care and Management of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners apprehend; that the several Powers and Provisions necessary for repairing and amending the several Roads before mentioned might be more conveniently executed, if the same were comprised in One Act of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging thti Term and Powers of the said Acts, so for as relate to the said Roads, and for amending, and keeping in Repair, the said Road leading from Highgate tb IVitchcross, in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of the Freeholders of the County of

York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting Represent forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the original Excellence of the Constitution of this Country, most ariiimeD ardently wish to have it maintained upon the genuine Principles on which it was founded; and that it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation; and that, in the present State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, the Commons of this Realm are partially and inadequately represented, and consequently cannot have that Security for their Liberties, which it is the Aim of the Constitution to give them: And therefore supplicating the House, to take into their most serious Consideration the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy to this great Constitutional Evil, as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And being returned;

And a Member present, and a Member returned upon a new Writ, having taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Ninety-six Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

A Petition of the Acting Commissioners, and several Mortgagees, of the Turnpike Roads leading from the Town of Cheltenham, in the County of Gloucester, to Pewsdown Ash and Combend Beeches, and also from the Town of Cheltenham to a certain Place in the Road leading to Tewkesbury, in the same County, called Piff"s Elm, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Petition is presented to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making and repairing a Road, from the Town of Cheltenham, through Birdlip, to join the great Turnpike Road from Gloucester to Bath, at or near the Town of Painswick, through the several Parishes of Cheltenham, Charlton Kings, Leek-hampton, Coberley, Cowley, Brimpsfield, Cranham, and Painswick, and from the said new-intended Road in the Parish of Cranham, down Portway, to join the said Turnpike Road from Gloucester to Bath, at or near a Place in the Parish of Upton Saint Leonard's, in the said County of Gloucester, called The Harrow, and frorh the said Town of Cheltenham, through the several Parishes of Cheltenham, Charlton King's, Wit-tington, Withington, and Dowdeswell, in the said County, to join the Great Turnpike Road from the said City of Gloucester to London at or near a Public House, in the said Parish of Dowdeswell, called Kilkenny, but which they were not apprized of till too late to give the necessary Public Notices required for an Application to Parliament; and that the Petitioners conceive, the new-intended Roads will be very detrimental to the several Mortgagees of the old Turnpike Road, but admit that they will be very advantageous for the Nobility, Gentry, and others, resorting to Cheltenham for the Benefit of drinking the Waters, and also for the Farmers and others carrying Commodities to the Markets of Cheltenham and Gloucester, and therefore they admit, they cannot with Propriety make any Objection to the said new-intended Roads, but troin their rendering the Mon^y advanced upon the Credit of the old Turnpike Roads less secure, and very precarious, the only Prevention whereof, as they conceive, will be by consolidating the old Turnpike Roads with the new-intended Roads under One Trust, and to be a Security not only for the Money already advanced upon the old Turnpike Roads, but also for such Money as may be advanced upon the Credit of, and for making, altering, widening, turning, and keeping in Repair, the said new-intended Roads: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and permit the said old Turnpike Roads, and the new-intended Roads, to be consolidated, and, for that Purpose, that the said old and new-intended Roads may be divided into separate Districts, as to the House shall seem meet; and that the Tolls arising from such Districts may be applied in Discharge of the Principal Money and Interest already advanced, and to be advanced, upon the Credit thereof, and for making, altering, widening, and keeping in Repair, the said old and new-intended

Roads, and the Overplus arising from each respective District,. if any such shall happen to be, may be applied in discharging the Principal and Interest due, and to become due, thereon, and for making, altering, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Roads in the other District or Districts; and that the Term of the old Turnpike Act may be enlarged; and that the Petitioners may have sucl^ further and other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Tradesmen, and others, residing in and near the several Towns and Parishes of Cheltenham, Charlton Kings, Leckhampton, Dozvdeszvell, &c. is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Nottingham Mr* Robert Smith presented to the House, according Small Debts. to Order, a Bill for the more speedy and easy Recovery of Small Debts within the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Ditto. A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses

of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, in Common Council assembled, and of the Gentlemen, Manufacturers, Tradesmen, and other principal Inhabitants of the said Town, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been informed, that several Retail Shopkeepers, Publicans, and others, Inhabitants of the Town of Nottingham, in order to obtain the Establishment of a Court of Requests, under the Sanction and Authority of Parliament, for the Recovery of Small Debts within the said Town, have lately presented their Petition to the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for that Purpose 5 and that the Petitioners conceive, and submit to the Consideration of the House, that a very limited Credit to the common Manufacturer, Mechanic, and Labourer, is ever to be preferred to a more liberal and extensive one; that it calls forth the Exertion of their Diligence and Industry, and, by urging than to labour for the necessary Support and Maintenance of themselves and Families, prevents that Excess and Intemperance, the too frequent Attendance of easy Credit, preserves Sobriety, Respect and Decorum in the lower Orders of Society, and promotes and extends the Welfare and Advantage of the Public in general; and that the Petitioners, from their long Knowledge and Acquaintance with the Trade and Manufactures, and the Condition and Circumstances of the greatest Part of the Inhabiants of the said Town, assure the House,' that they behold with Dread and Concern the numerous Evils which will unavoidably result from the Establishment of such a Judicature; the Publican arid Retailer, sanguine in the Certainty of a short and speedy Remedy for the Recovery of their Demands, and allured by the Prospect of larger Acquirements, will hold forth a delusive and dangerous Credit to the inferior Class of People, which will invite to Irregularity, gradually relax their Industry, and ultimately involve Numbers of them in Calamity and Distress,

Vol. 40.

hot only to the entire Ruin of themselves and Families, but to the great Injury and Prejudice of the Trade and Manufactures of the Town; and that the Petitioners are the more firmly persuaded of the Impropriety and Extravagance of su£h a Tribunal, not only from the above Reasons, but also from there being at present a very easy, ample, and competent.

Provision for the Recovery bf Small Debts within the said Town, by a Court of'Record, held Once in every Fortnight, in which the Mayor and Sheriffs for the Time being preside, and also by a County Court before the Sheriffs, with Trial by Jury: And therefore beseeching, the House, That the Prayer of the said Petition may, not pass into a Law.:

A Petition of the Aldermen, Sheriff, Commoti Council, Livery, Manufacturers, principal Tradesmen, and Inhabitants of the Towtt and County of the Town of Nottingham, was also presented to the Housed arid read; Setting forth, That the said Town is lhrge and populous, and, by rerisori of the many extensivb Trades and Manufactories carried on therein (parti-ciilarly Frame-work Knitting) several Thousands of People are constantly employed, many of whom contract small Debts, and, although well able, refuse to pay the same, presuming on the Discouragements and Difficulties their Creditors lie under in suing for thfe Recovery thereof by the usual Course of Law, on Account of the Delays and great Expence they are uria1 voidably subject to in such ’Suits; and that the Peti-tioriers conceive, that a speedy and easy Method of recovering Small Debts within the said Town and County of the Town of Nottingham would not only tend to remedy the Inconveniences above-mentioned, but tb improve the Trade threof, as ’well as promote Industry and Sobriety, and support useful Credit: And therefore praying, That the Bill, now depending in the House, for the Purposes aforesaid, may, with such Alterations, Provisions, and Regulations, as to the House shall seeni meet, pass into a Law.

And the said Petition's were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the mote speedy and easy Recovery of Small Debts within the Town and County of the Town of Not ting-ham, be read a Second Time.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Land Forces, including Two thousand and Thirty Invalids, amounting to Eighteen thousand and Fifty-three effective Men, Commission and Non-Commissioned Officers included, be employed for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred Fifty-five thousand Nine hundred and Sixty-three Pounds Four Shillings and Three Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Eighteen thousand and Fifty-three effective Men, for Guards, Garrisons, and other His Majesty’s Land Forces in Great Britain, Guernsey, and Jersey, including the Charge of the Pay. of Commission and Non-Commissioned Officers and Private Men, the Charge of Cloathing of the Non-Commissioned Officers and Private Men, the Charge of Agency, and the Charge of Allowances to be made to Captains, Paymasters, Surgeons, and for Riding Masters, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Twenty-two thousand and Twenty-one Pounds Four* Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for maintaining His Majesty’s Forces and Garrisons in the Plantations, and those in Garrison at Gibraltar, in-

cluding the Charge of the Pay of the Commission, Non* Commissioned Officers, and Private Men, the Charge of Cloathing of Non-commissioned Officers and Private Men, the Charge of Agency, and the Charge of Allowances to be made to Captains, Paymasters, and Surgeons, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Three hundred and Fifty-five Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Eight Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Difference between the Charge of the British and Irish Establishment, of Six Battalions of Foot serving at Gibraltar, in North Amenca, and the West Indies, including the Charge of the Pay of Commission and Non-Commission Officers and Private Men, the Charge of Cloathing of the Non-Commission Officers and Private Men, the Charge of Agency, and the Charge of Allowances to be made to Captains, Paymasters, and Surgeons, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Nine hundred and Sixty-eight Pounds Nine Shillings and Nine Pence, be granted to His Majesty, on Account, for the Pay necessary to be advanced to One Regiment of Light Dragoons, and Five Battalions of Foot, for Service in East India, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty-five thousand Seven hundred Eighty-four Pounds Eight Shillings and Nine Pence Halfpenny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Full Pay, for Three hundred and Sixty-five Days, to reduced or supernumerary Officers of His Majesty’s Forces, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Two hundred and Thirty-six Pounds Ten Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Pay of the General and General Staff Officers in Great Britain, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seventy-four thousand Two hundred Twenty-one Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Five Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Allowance to the Paymaster General of His Majesty’s Forces, to the Secretary at War, to the Commissary General of the Musters, to the Judge Advocate General, to the Comptrollers of the Accounts of the Army, their Deputies, and Clerks, including the contingent Expences of their respective Offices, for the Amount of Exchequer Fees to be paid by the Paymaster General, and on Account for Poundage to be returned to the Infantry of* His Majesty’s Forces, for the Year One thousand . Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Resolved, That it is Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight thousand Nine hundred and Four Pounds Six Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Five Battalions of His Majesty’s Hanoverian Infantry in the Pay of Great Britain, from the Twenty-fifth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four, to the respective Times of their Return.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Ninety-one thousand Two hundred Twenty-six Pounds and Six Pence, and Three Eighth Parts of a Penny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the In and Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, and of the Expences of the said Hospital, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five.

Ramsgate A Petition of the Persons whose Names are there-

Paving. unto, subscribed, Inhabitants of, and Land Owners

within, the Vill of Ramsgate, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of Kent, in Behalf of themselves and many other Inhabitants and Land Owners of the same, was

Presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, hat the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is intended to be offered to the Consideration of Parliament, for paving the Streets of the Vill of Ramsgate, which, if passed into a Law, will be a very unnecessary and heavy Burthen on the Petitioners; that proper Mate-' rials for the Repair of Roads, Flint, Gravel, and Chalk, may be had on the Sea Shore adjoining to the Town, at no other Cost than that of Carriage, and, the Petitioners apprehend, that, to bring other Materials from a Distance, at very high Prices, will be an useless and unnecessary Expence; and that the whole Extent of Roads and Streets to be repaired by the said Town does not exceed Two Miles, and was, till within the last Twenty Years, kept in as good Repair as at present, for the Annual Expence of about £. 13, but of late there has been Annually raised near £ 80 for the same Purpose, which would, if properly applied, be amply sufficient, in the Apprehension of the Petitioners, to keep the Roads and Streets in exceeding good Repair; and that the Streets of the said Vill being in many Places only irom Fourteen to Sixteen Feet wide, and in very few above Eighteen, the Petitioners conceive a Foot and Carriage Pavement cannot be made so as that Two Carriages may pass abreast, which will npt only be a great Obstruc- lion to, but may frequently endanger the Lives of, the petitioners and their Families; and that the Mode in wm<ih, as the Petitioners are informed, the Money is proposed to be raised for the Purpose of paving, is unfair, partial, and a heavy Imposition on some particular Trades, and peculiarly burthensome on the Poor,

namely, by continuing the present Highway Assessment of Six Pttice in the Pound on all Rents, and an additional Tax*f One Shilling a Chaldron on Coals, by which Means, few Houses being assessed at above £. 8, no Composition under Two Shillings, and the poorest Family consuming Yearly almost Two Chaldrons, whilst many of the wealthiest burn not more than Four, the most indigent Householders will pay Half as much as their opulent Neighbours; and that the whole Rents of the Town do not, as the Petitioners believe, exceed £ 2,700 a Year, and being already loaded in Poor, Church, and Highway Rates, with Land, House, Window, and Commutation Taxes, to the Amount of near Ten Shillings in the Pound, will, as the Petitioners conceive, be incapable to suppoit an additional Burthen of £ 3,000, which they are informed will be requisite for the Purposes of the said intended Bill; and that Coals are almost the only Fuel in the Town of Ramsgate, which will make any additional Imposition on that necessary Article more severely felt by the poorer Inhabitants; and that, of the Coals landed in the Port of Ramsgate, about One-fourth Part is consumed in the adjacent Country, which, the Petitioners believe, will no longer be the Case, when they can be supplied, at less Expence, from the neighbouring Harbours, and not only be a Detriment to the small Trade of the Town, but occasion a Deficiency in the Tax, which, the Petitioners fear, they shall hereafter be called upon to make good; and that the principal Promoters of the Bill, who style themselves a Committee appointed by the Inhabitants, were chosen at a partial Meeting, to which none were invited, except those who were supposed favourable to the Design, nor have they given any public Notice of their Intention, except by a printed Hand-bill, circulated about the Town previous to the last Session of Parliament, and not since repeated, which the Petitioners apprehend to be contrary to what the Usage in these Cases requires: And therefore praying, That

the intended Bill may not pass into a Law, but, in case the House shall not judge proper to grant the Prayer of this Petition, in that Behalf, the Petitioners intreat that some other Mode may be adopted for raising the Money necessary for carrying the Purposes of the said Bill into Execution, so as that what is said to be intended for the general Good may be supported at the general Expence.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Vill of Ramsgate, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred.

Resolved, That this House will, at the Rising of Adjoum-the House this Day, adjoprn till Monday Morning raent-next.
