to Ip&cich, in the said County, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth, viz.;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Hare being examined, said. That the Road from Becdes to Ipszcich, through Weston, Willingham, Kesgrave, and Rush more, and the other Places mentioned in the Petition, is, from the Nature of the Soil, very deep and ruinous; that it is in many Parts narrow and incommodious, and subject to be much annoyed by Currents of Water; and that it cannot be effectually amended, widened, and kept in Repair, by the Laws now in being, but that it might be made a good Road, if the Sums of Money specified in the Estimates annexed to the Petition were to be expended thereon.

Thomas Trusson, Esquire, being then examined, said, That the properly amending, widening, and keeping in Repair of the said Road, would be a great Benefit and Convenience to the Neighbourhood, and of public Utility; and that it would be the Means of shortening the Communication between Ipswich and Yarmouth, by nearly Nine Miles.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending and keeping in Repair the Road leading from Ipswich to Beccles, in the County of Suffolk: And that Sir John Rous, and Sir Gerard William Vanneck do prepare, and bring in, the same.

N. B. The Ships in this Estimate are the most proper Objects of Expence, under the present View of the Works carrying on at His Majesty’s several Yards; and the Sums that may be laid out upon them calculated accordingly.

But in the Course of the Survey of the Fleet, it may be found that other Ships are in a better Condition than those here proposed, and that it will be more beneficial to the Service to give them a Preference: It will, in such Case, become necessary to apply the Money accordingly.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Namea are thereunto set and subscribed, on behalf of themseiyes and others, ‘Owners of Estates within the Manor and Parish of Pickering, in tins North Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for dividing and inclp§ing the Commons and Waste Lands within the Manor of Pickering, in the North Riding of the County of York;

9

ftnd Setting forth* That the Petitioners are convinced that the Proportion of Land intended to be allotted to them by the said Bill will not fye a reasonable Allow-

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices Who come to the Committee to whom the said Bil[ is committed.

Resolved, That the Counsel be called in; and that the Counsel be restrained from going into any Matters, but such as tend to prove the Evidence, offered at the Bar of this House on Wednesday the 9th Day of this Instant February, defective and incomplete, or such other Matters as may have been discovered since the Order of this House of the same Date.

Then the Counsel were called in.

And the said Petition was read.

And Mr. Speaker acquainted the Counsel with the said Resolution.

And One of the Counsel for the Petitioners informed the House, That, the House having come to that Resolution, the Counsel declined offering any Thing to the House in Support of the said Petition.

A Petition of several Manufacturers and Bleachers Vol. 40,

of, and Dealers in, Linens, within the respective Counties of York and Durham, was presented to the House, and read: Setting forth, That there is a very considerable Manufacture of Linens carried on in the said Counties, but that Deceits and Frauds are often practised therein, as well by the false reeling of the Yarn spun within the same Counties, as by many of the Manufacturer^ making Sale of Pieces of such Linens for a greater Length and Width than the same are really of, and also by selling damaged Pieces of such Linens for such as are sound or undamaged, to the great Discredit of the said Manufacture, and the Prejudice of the fair Trader; and that the putting a Stop to the Deceits and Frauds before mentioned may be a Means of restoring and preserving the Credit, and encouraging the said Manufacture within the said respective Counties: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for preventing the Deceits and Frauds practised as aforesaid within the said Counties of York and Durham, in such Manner, and by such Ways and Means, as the House, shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Duncomhe, Sir John Eden, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Be^mondse w^om the Petition of the several Persons whose Sheets!* Names are thereunto set, Inhabitants of the Waterside Division of the Parish of Saint Mary Magdalen, Bermondsey, in the County of Surrey, in Behalf of themselves and the other Inhabitants of the said Division, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

' Mr. Thomas Carter being examined, said, That he knows the several Streets, Lanes, Ways, Passages, and other Places within the said Division of the said Parish — That the same are very ill paved and cleansed, and badly lighted, and in some Places very narrow and incommodious, and dangerous not only to the Inhabitants, but to all others passing thereon; and that the same are greatly incumbered with Posts and Gutters, and other Obstructions projecting into and over the same.

That, there is no regular Watch within the said Division of the said Parish, for Want whereof the Houses, Persons, and Property of the Inhabitants, and others, are greatly exposed to the Violence of Robbers, and other wicked Disturbers of the public Peace — And the Witness added, That if proper Powers were given to pave, cleanse, light, watch, widen, and regulate the several Streets, Lanes, Ways, Passages, and Places, within the said Division of the said Parish, and to remove all Annoyances and Obstructions, by Spouts, Signs, Gutters, Cellars, Bulks, Penthouses, Steps, Po3ts, Filthy and other Annoyances; and to prevent the same for the future, it would greatly tend to the Health and Convenience, as well as to the Safety, of the Inhabitants of the said Division of the said Parish, and be of great public Utility.

Mr. William Brent being then examined, confirmed the above Evidence.

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, the said Acts of the Fourth, Sixth, and Tenth Years of King George the First, the Fourth, Tenth, and Twenty-fifth of King George the Second, and the Sixth of His present Majesty, were read: And

Mr. Roger Peck, Clerk to the Trustees, being examined, said, That a considerable Progress hath been made in repairing the said Roads, and a large Sum of Money borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls, hath been expended; that £.6,000 of the Money so borrowed still remains due, and cannot be paid off, and the Roads be completely amended and kept in Repair, unless the Terms of the said Acts be enlarged, and some further Powers granted.

And being further examined, he said, That the Road leading from Highgate aforesaid, to IVitchcross, in the County of Sussex, being of the Length of about Two Miles, is in a ruinous Condition, and incommodious for Passengers and Carriages, and cannot be effectually amended and kept in Repair by the ordinary Course of Law — That the said Piece of Road communicates with the Roads comprised in the said Acts, and might be conveniently amended and repaired, if the same were put under the Care and Management of the Trustees for the said several Roads — And he con-'eluded with saying, that the several Powers and Provisions necessary for repairing and amending the several Roads before-mentioned might be more conveniently executed, if the same were comprized in One Act of Parliament.

To prove the Allegations of the Second-mentioned Petition, the said Acts of the Sixth and Tenth Years of King George the First, and the Eleventh and Twenty-fifth Years of King* George the Second, were read, by which it appeared, that the Annual Sums of One hundred Pounds and Sixty Pounds were settled to be paid, by the Trustees for those Acts, to the Trustees for the Care and Management of the Roads in the said Second-mentioned Petition described, for the Repair of the Road from Newington, through Camberwell, to New Cross: And the said Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, was also read, by which it appeared, that the Trustees under that Act are directed to pay Annually to those Trustees the Sum of Ninety Pounds, to be applied towards the Repair of the said Road from Ncicington, through Camberwell, to New Cross: And

Claude Champion Crespigny, Esquire, Treasurer of the said Camberwell Trust, being examined, said, That those Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the Powers wherewith they are invested, and have borrowed the Sum of £.2,000 on the Credit of the several ‘Annual Sums so granted and made payable to them as aforesaid, which Money hath been expended towards amending and repairing the said Roads, but that those Annual Sums are found insufficient for the Amendment and Repair of the said Roads, and the Payment of the Interest of the Money so borrowed as aforesaid — That the said Camberwell Road Trustees, apprehending that the said Roads might be more effectually amended and kept in Repair than at present, if the same were put under the Care and Management of the Trustees for the Roads described in the said First-mentioned Petition, have applied to those Trustees to 9 '

take these Roads' under their Inspection, receiving the said Annual Payments, and subject to the Payment of the Debt contracted as aforesaid, and the Interest payable in respect of the same, to which those Trustees have consented; but the same cannot be done without the Aid of Parliament.

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses; and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Forty-nine Members then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Twenty other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House j Two, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Six, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; and Twelve, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Inhabitants of the Borough of Arundel, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Streets, Lanes, Ways, and Passages, within the said Borough, are not properly paved, cleansed, or lighted, but are subject to various Obstructions and Annoyances, and it would be a great Advantage to the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and all Persons resorting thereto, if the same were properly paved, cleansed, and lighted, and all Encroachments, Obstructions, and Annoyances therein were removed and prevented for the future; and that it would be also for the Benefit and Accommodation of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and of all Persons resorting thereto, that there should be a Market for the Sale of all Kinds of Meat, Fish, Poultry, Butter, and Garden Stuff*: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for paving, cleansing, and lighting the Streets, Lanes, and Places, within the said Borough of Arundel, for removing Nuisances and Annoyances, and preventing the like for the future, and for holding and regulating a Market within the said Borough.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Fitzherbert, the Earl of Surrey, bcc.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the Lord Provost and Magistrates, and Council, of the City of Edinburgh, for themselves, and on Behalf of the Community of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act of the Twenty-sixth of his late Majesty, certain Commissioners were appointed for erecting various public Buildings, and for forming an easy and commodious Communication between the High Vo l. 4(h

Street and the Country Northward, Southward, and Westward, which Act expired in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty; and, by an Act of the Eighth of His present Majesty, the Royalty of the City of Edinburgh was extended over certain Grounds to the North of the said City; and that, in Consequence of the said Acts, public Buildings have been 1 erected, and a Communication formed by a Bridge t> the Northward; but the Avenues to the City from the South being still narrow', steep, and inconvenient, it is highly expedient to open a Communication by a Bridge over The Cozvgate, and by Streets from the said Bridge, to the Squares, Streets, and Rows on the South Side of the City; and, it is also necessary to form a Communication between The Launmercate and the Streets on the West Parts of the new-extended Royalty, and to enlarge the public Markets, and make convenient Roads and Passages to them; and that several of the Buildings in the University of Edinburgh are in a ruinous Condition, and the Apartments, from the Increase of Students, incommodious, so that it is necessary to rebuild the said University, or Part thereof; and that, as the present Mode of levying certain Taxes on the Citizens in Edinburgh, the Liberties and Suburbs thereof, is attended with much Expence and Trouble, it is proposed to establish, instead of them, other Taxes for supporting the Police of the City, on a more equal Principle, and a less expensive Collection; and that, as there exists not at present any Revenue whatsoever for lighting the City, it is highly necessary that a Tax, under the Administration of Commissioners, should he established for that Purpose; and that the Extension of the City, and increased Number of Inhabitants, require an additional Supply of Water, which must be procured from the Springs of the adjacent Country; and that it is also necessary to extend the Royalty over certain Grounds lately purchased by the City, and over Grounds belonging to such Persons as, by their Title Deeds, are bound to pay the ordinary Taxes payable by the Citizens; but that, in order to carry those Measures into Execution, it will be necessary to purchase certain Lands and Houses, to equalize the Land Tax payable by the City and its Liberties, to extend a Proportion of the said Tax over the Districts to the South of the City, and to obtain such Powers and Authorities as to the House shall seem proper, for carrying on and perfecting thbse useful and necessary Designs: And therefore, praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes before-mentioned, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Adam Fergusson, the Lord Advocate of Scotland, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of George Johnstone, Esquire, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That by virtue of His Majesty’s Writ to the Sheriff of Somerset directed, and his Precept founded thereon, for electing a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Ilchester, in the County aforesaid, in the room of Peregrine Cust, Esquire, lately deceased, an Election was had and holden, in the Town Hall of the said Borough, on Thursday the 3d Day of February , in the Year of our Lord 1785, and, at such Election John Harcourt, Esquire, and the Petitioner, wei£ Candidates, and Thomas Palmer, Apothecary (being Bailiff of the said Borough) was the Returning Officer presiding at the said Election, and at the Poll thereat demanded and taken; and that, previous to the said Election, and in Expectation of a Vacancy, great Numbers of Persons were secretly and fraudulently introduced into the said Borough by the said John Harcourt, or his Agents, for the Purpose of

influencing the said Election, not having any legal Right to vote thereat, and, by the Partiality and Corruption and previous Contrivance of the said Thomas Palmer, the said Persons so introduced were received on the Poll for die said John Harcourt, and by Means thereof, and also by Means of great Numbers of other Persons being admitted, by the said Thomas Palmer, to poll at the said Election, for the said John Harcourt, who had no Right to vote thereat, a Majority of pretended Votes was procured upon the said Poll for the said John Harcourt, and he hath been returned to serve in Parliament by the said Thomas Palmer; whereas the Petitioner had a legal Majority of Electors of the said Borough, who offered themselves to the said Thomas Palmer to vote for the Petitioner, and he ought to have been accordingly returned a Burgess for the said Borough at such Election; and that the said Thomas Palmer, the Bailiff, during the said Election, behaved himself with evident Marks of Partiality and Corruption, in the Course of the said Election, in Favour of the said John Harcourt, as well by receiving Voters, which he ought not to have admitted, in Favour of the said Mr. Harcourt, and by rejecting others, which he ought to have accepted, in Favour of the Petitioner, as in several other Instances; and that the said John Harcourt, by Means of illegally treating the said Electors, by himself or his Agents, and by Bribery, and other corrupt and undue Influence, practised by himself or his Agents, caused many Persons to vote for the said John Harcourt, and to abstain from voting for the Petitioner, who otherwise would have voted for the Petitioner, and by Means thereof, and of many other corrupt and illegal Practices, the said John Harcourt procured a Majority of pretended Electors on the said Poll, and was thereby returned to Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the several Matters aforesaid into Consideration, and to afford the Petitioner such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 24th Day of March next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " Thursday the " 24th Day of March" and inserting the Words " Tuesday the 14th Day of June" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Thursday the 24th Day of March " stand Part of the Question;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

A Petition of the Freemen and Inhabitants of the City of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, sensible of the original Excellency of the Constitution of this Country, most ardently wish to have it maintained upon the genuine Principles on which it was founded; and that it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation; and that, in the present State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, the House of Commons do not sufficiently speak the Voice of the People: And therefore praying the House to take into their most serious Consideration the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy to this great and alarming Evil as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Alderman Wilkes reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several of the principal Inhabitants of the Town of Uxbridge, in the County of Middlesex, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Thomas Bishop, Esquire, beina examined, said, That the High Road within the said town is in several Parts narrow

and dangerous for Travellers, that the Foot Ways are ill paved, and the Town very inconvenient, by Means of Nuisances and Annoyances; that in order to render the said High Road safe and commodious for Carriages and Travellers, it will be necessary to remove the present Market House within the said Town, and certain Tenements near or adjoining to the said Market House, and also to lay into the said High Road certain Garden Grounds between Merca's Bridge, and High Bridge, within the said Town, and to widen the said Bridge, called Mercers Bridge; that the widening of the said High Road, and re-building the said Market House in a more convenient Situation, and the paving and cleansing of the said Foot Ways, and also the lighting of the said High Road, and other Places within the said Town, and removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein, will, be of great Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and of public Utility.

Mr. George Clark being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence, and produced a Plan of the Parts of the said Road which it will be necessary to widen.

Ordwed, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for taking down the present Market House, and certain other Buildings, in the Town of Uxbridge, for the Purpose of widening the High Street; and for paving the Foot Ways, and lighting and cleansing the Streets and other Places within the said Town, and removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein; and for changing the Course of the Road between Mercers Bridge and High Bridge; and for re-building the said Market House: And that Mr. Alderman Wilkes and Mr. Mainwaring do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Commercial Intercourse with Ireland.

thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an equal Participation in all the Privileges and Advantages of a Community should, by every Rule of Right, Reason, and Justice, include in it a mutual Obligation to encourage, maintain, and defend those Rights, and to contribute equally to their Support; that the Island of Great Britain, when first united in Legislation, Manufactures, Navigation, and Commerce, became united also in Taxation towards the general Support of the common Good; that Admission of any neighbouring Kingdom to a full Share in all these Rights, without subjecting her to sustain a due Proportion of the general Burthen too, would be a great Deviation from those Principles upon which the Union of this Island was wisely founded; that our American Colonies, first established by ourselves, still supported by our Consumption of their Productions, and protected by our Navy, at a constant and immense Expence, make only 'an equitable Return to the Parent State, by rendering Britain the grand Mart of their Intercourse with Europe; that, from the Vicinity of Ireland, and its great Extent of Coast, no inconsiderable Part of the West India Productions, especially such Articles as arc subject here to the heaviest Duties, might be smuggled in upon us, to the great Detriment of the Revenue of this Part of His Majesty’s Dominions; and that, as the Productions of Fqreign Plantations may be legally imported into Ireland, they may from thence be clandestinely introduced amongst us, and our own Colonies thereby deprived of the Advantages they now derive from the exclusive Supply of this Country: And therefore praying, That the Privilege of supplying her own Markets with the Produce of her ow n Colonies may be preserved inviolate to this Kingdom, and that every further Extension of Trade between Great Britain and Ireland may be established upon such equitable Principles as will redound equally to the mutual Benefit of both Countries.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Westminster thereunder written, Electors of the City and Liberty Election, of Westminster, in Behalf of themselves and several Thousand Electors, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election for the said City^ many Hundred Persons polled who by no Means were entitled so to do; and that, at the Conclusion of the said Election, which had continued Forty Days, a Scrutiny was demanded by Sir Cecil Wray and certain Electors, which Scrutiny was granted by the High Bailiff, who has been since ordered, by this Honourable House, to proceed in the same; and that the Petitioners, anxious to discover and expose any Imposition which may have tended to violate the Right of Election, and apprehending that Endeavours may be made use of to rescind the late Order of the House, respecting the Continuance of the Scrutiny, do most earnestly entreat the further Indulgence of die House, in full Persuasion that, from the farther Prosecution of the Enquiry, they shall be able to procure Justice, the only Motive for demanding the Scrutiny, and the sole Object of the Petitioners Application.

Ordered, That the said Petition do . lie upon the Table.

Sir John Eden reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners of the River Wear, and of the Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, named and appointed by virtue of an Act of Parliament, made in the Thirty-second Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act " for continuing, amending, and rendering more effectual, so much of an Act, made in the Twentieth

" provement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven " of Sunderland, in the County of Durhamas " relates to the Port and Haven of Sunderland, and " the River Wear, between South Biddick, or Biddick " Ford, and the said Port and Haven," whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the several other Commissioners named and appointed by, and in pursuance of, the said Act, was referred;

'That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act, made in the Thirty-second Year of his late Majesty, was read: And

John Thornhill, Esquire, informed your Committee,

That the Commissioners have been at a great Expence in erecting a Pier and Quay at or near the Mouth of the River, in deepening the Channel, and in other necessary Works, for the Improvement and Security ot’ the Navigation of the River, Port, and Haven, and from whence great Benefits and Advantages have arisen — That the Pier is now in so ruinous a State, that it is expected to fall; by which Means the Harbour would be greatly injured: Then

Mr. Robert Shout, Engineer for the Port of Sunderland, being examined, said, That the outer Part of the present Pier is in so ruinous a State, that it is more adviseable to build a new one, than to attempt to repair the old one — That a new Pier is actually begun, and some Progress made in it — That he has not the least Doubt but the new-intended Pier will be of great Utility to the Harbour, by standing more to the Southward, and making the Harbour easier of Access than it is at present; and that a greater Depth of Water will be obtained upon the Bar — That he apprehends the Expence of performing the new Works will amount to £60,000, and upwards; to answer which the present Duties are very inadequate — That there remains £500 due of Money heretofore borrowed, and near £700 to different Tradesmen.

And Mr. Shout produced and explained a Plan of the Harbour, with the intended Alterations pointed out; which Plan, it appeared to your Committee, had been approved of by Mr. Smeaton, the Engineer.

Mr Martin Wilkinson confirmed Mr. Shout's Evidence, with respect to the Money borrowed, and now due on Security.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham: And that Sir John Eden, General Lamb ton, and Mr. Tempest, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition, of the principal Inhabitants and freeholders within the Borough of Launceston, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House* and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the original Excellence of the Constitution of this Country, most ardently wish to have it maintained upon the genuine Principles on which it was founded; and that it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation; and that, in the present State of the People in Parliament, the Commons in this Realm are partially and inadequately represented, and consequently cannot have that Security for their Liberties, which it is the Aim of the Constitution to give them: And therefore supplicating the House, to take into their most serious Consideratioil the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and apply such Remedies to this great Constitutional Evil, as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir John Rous reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, of the County of Suffolk; and also, the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty of the Borough of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, in Common Council assembled; and also, the Petition of several Gentlemen, Merchants, and others, of the Town of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had not been complied with; but that Mr. Peter Jermyn, Junior, informed the Committee, that the Persons who have signed the said Petitions were prevented complying with the said Standing Orders, because the Notices which were regularly given to apply to Par* V o l. 40.

liamerit for the Act, under which these Petitioners pray that the Roads described in their Petitions may be included, were not inserted in the Newspapers till the Three last Weeks in the Month of September, and because the Road was originally intended to be continued from Bulcamp to Beccles; but the Inhabitants of Beccles had since come to a Resolution to oppose the Bill if it extended beyond Bulcamp aforesaid, which is Nine Miles short of Beccles; that for this Reason the Inhabitants of Lowestoft and Yarmouth have, with general Consent* petitioned that the Line of Road should be changed as expressed in the said Petitions: and that the Road from Bulcamp, through Lowestoft to Little Yarmouth, should be amended instead of the Road from Bulcamp to Beccles; and he proved to the Committee, that Notices in the usual Form had been inserted in the Country Newspapers Twice in the Month of January, and Once iii the Month of February last; and that the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the same, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the Said Petitions*

Mr. John Hare, a Surveyor, being examined, said,

That the Road from Bulcamp through Lowestoft to Yarmouth, is considerably shorter than the Road through Beccles, and may be repaired at a less Expence; and that the Road between Beccles and Yarmouth is frequently, in the Winter Time, so overflowed, ps to be impassable; and he concluded with saying, that it would be a great Advantage to Yarmouth, and of public Utility, that the now proposed Line of Road should be amended.

George Bitton, Esquire, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence; and added, That Materials may much more easily be procured on the Line of Road through Lowestoft, than they can on the Road through Beccles.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Inhabitants and Owners of Houses and Lands within the Town, Township, and Barony of Stockport, in the County Palatine of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Town of Stockport is very populous, and a Place of great Trade, and the Inhabitants thereof, and Persons resorting thereto, suffer great Inconvenience for Want of the same being properly lighted, cleansed, and watched, and several of the ancient public Highways, Streets and Passages, in the said Town, are very narrow and inconvenient, and greatly obstruct the Commerce of the said Town; and that the Place assigned for the Market w'eekly held in the said Town is, from the great Increase of Provisions and other Articles brought to Market, become insufficient for that Purpose, and the said Market Place, and the Avenues leading thereto, are much incommoded by several Houses and other Buildings standing therein and adjoining thereto, and the Scite of the said Market Place is very high, uneven, and in great Want of being reduced to a proper and convenient Level; and that there are several Common Lands and Waste Grounds, within the said Township, to the Herbage whereof the Owners of Houses and Lands in the Township are entitled, by Reason of their Freeholds, which Common Lands and Waste Grounds are of little Use to the Owners of Houses and Lands within the said Township; and that Sir George Warren is the present Lord of the Manor and Barony of Stockport, and entitled to a Toll upon all Goods exposed to Sale in the public Markets held therein, and to the Soil of the said Common Lands and Waste Grounds; and that within the said Town, Township, and Barony of Stockport, and also within the Parish of Stockport, there are several considerable Manufactures, as throwing of Silk, Wool-combing, making of Hats, Buttons, and Twist, and Spinning, Twisting, Weaving, and manufacturing of Cotton and Yarn, and printing of Linen and Cotton Goods, which employ great Numbers of People, who contract many small Debts, amounting Yearly to a great Sum of Money, and, although they are well able, refuse to pay such Debts, presuming on the Difficulties their Creditors lie under by the Expence they are unavoidably put to, and the Delays they meet with in suing for the same, and, a more easy and speedy Method of recovering small Debts within the said Town, Township, Barony, and Parish, would tend to improve the Trade thereof, and to support useful Credit therein; and that if Powers were given to light and watch the said Town, and to remove all Obstructions, Projections, Nuisances, and Annoyances therein, and to widen, enlarge, and cleanse the said narrow Streets and Passages, and to enlarge and improve the said Market Place, and a discretionary Power to purchase such Houses, Buildings, and Grounds, as may be necessary for that Purpose, and to establish a Court of Requests, or other Court for recovering of small Debts within the said Town, Township, and Parish, and to build a Prison for the Use of the said Court, and to vest the Appointment of the Officers of the said Court of Requests in the Lord of the said Manor and Barony of Stockport for the Time being, and to sell the said Common Lands and Waste (Sounds within the said* Township of Stockport, and to apply the Money arising from the Sale thereof in defraying the Expences attending the Execution of such Powers, and also to make Rates Vol. 40.

arid Assessments on the Owners arid Occupiers of Houses and Lands within the said Town and Township of Stockport, in Aid of the Money to arise from the Sale of the said Common Lands and Waste Grounds for the said Purposes, it would tend greatly to the Safety, Convenience, and Advantage of the Petitioners, and of all Persons resorting to and Travelling through the said Town: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in One or more Bill or Bills for promoting and carrying into Execution Designs so useful and beneficial to the Inhabitants, and Owners and Occupiers, of Houses and Lands within the said Town, Township, Barony, and Parish of Stockport in particular, and the Public in general.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Cordage Mr. Alderman Watson reported from the Commit-

Mamuacture. to whom the Petition of several Ropemakers within the Port of London, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Ropemakers within the said Port, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same w as read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, "An Act for the avoiding of Deceit " used in making and selling of Twicelaid Cordage, and " for the better preserving of the Navy of this Realm, " was read And

Mr. James Mitchell being examined, said, That the said Act hath been found insufficient for preventing the Frauds and Deceits therein mentioned, the compound Term <c Overworn," therein used, being quite indefinite — That various other Frauds and Abuses have for some Time been practised in the manufacturing of Cordage for Shipping, by using Hemp which is damaged, condemned, or of an inferior Sort or Kind; the Quality of which, after such Cordage is tarred, is not discernible from sound or staple Hemp — That under the Words of the Act ij is difficult to ascertain, whether Goods that have been re-manufactured were Overworn or not — That, by Means of the Frauds and Deceits now practised, the Credit of the Trade is greatly injured; and that the putting a Stop to such Practices will be the only Means of restoring and preserving the Credit of the said Manufactory in Foreign Markets, and of preserving the Lives and Properties of many of His Majesty’s Subjects.

Mr. William Walton, Captain of a Vessel in the Baltic Trade, being then examined, said, That he

had a Ship of his own — That Cordage is manufactured in other Countries besides this — That Foreign Cordage is imported, and used by British Captains, without paying Duty, which is a great Prejudice to the Manufacturers of Cordage within this Kingdom, and to the Public Revenue — That he had frequented the Port , of Saint Petersburgh several Years — That it is usual for Captains of British Ships to purchase Cordage there when £hey were in Want of it — It is about Two or Three Shillings per Hundred Weight cheaper there than in England, but that depends upon the Course of Exchange; and that he never took out with him a less Quantity of Cordage than he should otherwise have done, on Account of his being bound for Saint Petersburgh.

Mr. Ralph Willis being then examined, said, He was Captain of a Ship belonging to Messrs. Thornton and Company — That he had used the Baltic Trade Forty Years constantly — That Ships generally buy at Saint Petersburgh the little Matters of Cordage they may want — That he never had a Cable in that Country in his Life but Once, and that was from Necessity — That he had not known Masters of Ships in the Baltic Trade buy more Cordage at Saint Petersburgh than they wanted — That he believed where the same Person is Owner of several Ships, One of which is in the Baltic Trade, he would, by Means of the Vessel that should go to Saint Petersburgh, supply his other Ships with C ordage — That British Rope Manufacturers have settled at Saint Petersburgh — That the Difference ot Price between a Cable made at Saint Petersburgh, and one in London, may be Ten or Twelve Shillings per Hundred Weight cheaper at the former Place — That he last Year paid Thirty-six Shillings per Hundred in London, and about Twenty-five at Saint Petersburgh.

Mr. William Welbank, a Hemp Broker, being then examined, said, That it is generally complained of, and generally understood, that the Masters of Ships in the Saint Petersburgh Trade buy Cordage at that Place, instead of supplying themselves in London, or elsewhere in Great Britain — That out of the Quantity of Hemp imported, Seven or Eight hundred Tons generally come damaged by Means of the Voyage, so much as not to be fit to make sound merchantable Cordage — That he has always understood it to be very difficult to distinguish this damaged Hemp wrhen tarred from that which is sound and perfect — That this damaged Hemp is generally sold at public Sale, and most of it is purchased by Twine Spinners; and there are many inferior Uses for Rope, to the making of which this damaged Hemp may be applied.

Mr. Mitchell being then examined, said, That the said Act of Queen Elizabeth's Reign does not extend to new Cordage.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for more effectually preventing. Deceits and Frauds in the manufacturing of Cordage for Shipping, and to prevent the illicit Importation of Foreign-made Cordage:

And that Mr. Alderman Watson and Mr. Brett do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That Mr. Daniel Parker Coke have Leave to go the Midland Circuit.

Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and

and Turkey, has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by d Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protect His Majesty's Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary, that an Ambassador should be sent from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in the other Parts of Turkey, where British Subjects reside, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade, the wholb Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with many other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on this Trade, has of late Years amounted to about £.9,000 per Annum; and that the Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishing, is now, from many unavoidable Events, and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance granted to the Petitioners, in the last Session of Parliament, enabled them to support their Expences during the past Year; but the Petitioners are sensible, they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not, in the present Situation of the Trade, declare their Inability to support the necessary Expences, unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper.

ty aforesaid, To the Bailiff of the Liberty of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Church of Saint Peter at Westminster, in the said County; Know, That I have received a certain Writ of our Lord the King, to me directed, which follows; (that is to sajjr) George the Third, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, King, Defender of the Faith, and so forth, To the Sheriff of the County of Middlesex, Greeting. Whereas, by the Advice and Assent of Our Council, for certain arduous and urgent Affairs concerning Us, the State and Defence of Our Kingdom of Great Britahu and the Church, We have ordered a certain Parliament to be holden at Our City of Westminster, on the Eighteenth Day of May next ensuing, and there to treat and have Conference with the Prelates, Great Men, and Peers of Our Realm;- We command and strictly enjoin you, that Proclamation being made of the Day and Place aforesaid, in your next County Court to be holden after the Receipt of this Our Writ, Two Knights of the most fit and discreet of the said County, girt with Swords, and of every City of your County Two Citizens, and of every Borough in the same County Tw’o Burgesses, of the most sufficient and discreet, freely and indifferently, by those who at such Proclamation shall be present, according to the Form of the Statutes in that Case made and provided, you cause to be elected; and the Names of those Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, so to be elected, whether they be present or absent, you cause to be inserted in certain Indentures, to be thereupon made between you and those who shall be present at such Election, and them, at the Day and Place aforesaid, you cause to come in such Manner, that the said Knights, for themselves and the Commonalty of the same County, and the said Citizens and Burgesses, for themselves and the Commonalty of the said Cities and Boroughs respectively, may have from them full and sufficient Power to do and consent to those Things which then and there, by the Common Council of Our said Kingdom (by the Blessing of God) shall happen to be ordained upon the aforesaid Affairs, so that for Want of such Power, or through an improvident Election of the said Knights, Citizens, or Burgesses, the aforesaid Affairs may in no wise remain unfinished: Willing nevertheless, that neither you nor any other Sheriff of this Our said Kingdom be in any wise elected; and the Election in your full County, so made distinctly and openly under your Seal, and the Seals of those who shall be present at such Election, certifie you to Us in Our Chancery, at the Day and Place aforesaid, without Delay, remitting to Us Our Part of the aforesaid Indentures annexed to these Presents, together with this Writ. Witness. Ourself at Westminster, the Twenty-sixth Day of March, in the Twenty-

fourth Year of Our Reign.....Thomas

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Monday Morning next.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

St. George A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and

Hanover Vestrymen, of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover

\Vorkhouse, Square, within the Liberty of the City of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of King George the Second, several Powers were granted to the Petitioners, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the said Parish; and that the Poor within the said Parish are very numerous, and for many Years have been maintained and employed in a Workhouse belonging to the said Parish, which is at present in a very ruinous and decayed State, and is also too small, incommodious, and inconveniently situated, and it would conduce to the Health of the several Persons maintained by the said Parish, if a proper Workhouse was built for their Reception in a more open and airy Situation; and that the Burial Ground belonging to the said Workhouse is not only too small, but is situated in the most populous Part of the Parish, and it is highly necessary that burying in the said Ground should be discontinued in future, without Leave of the Rector and Churchwardens first obtained in Writing, a new Burial Ground having been provided; and that the before-mentioned Act is, in many Respects, defective, and several Powers are wanted by the Petitioners, for the proper Relief and Employment of the Poor in the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, by such Ways and Means, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Jennings, the Lord Hood,

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning,

at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber;

and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records. *

Severn A Petition of the Gentlemen, Land Owners, Trades-

Navigution. men, Manufacturers, and others, residing in the County of Berks, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by virtue of several Acts of Parliament, a Navigable Canal hath been made from the River Severn, at or near Framiload, in the County of Gloucester, to Wallbridge, near the Town of Stroud, from which Place another Navigable Canal is now making, and intended to be continued to the River Thames, at or near Leachlade, in the said County of; Gloucester; and that, notwithstanding divers Acts have at various Times been passed for improving the Navigation of the River Thames, or Isis, little or no Improvement hath been made in that Part thereof situate between the Town of Leachlade, in the County of Gloucester, and Abingdon, in the County of Berks; and, it appears, from the Reports of an able and experienced Engineer, who hath surveyed the said River Thames, within the District above described, and explored the Country between the Towns last mentioned, that there are many natural Impediments which must ever render the said River Thames, between Leachlade and Abingdon, incapable of being made a safe, certain, expeditious, reasonable, and beneficial Navigation, oil which Advantages may be obtained by forming a Canal from some Place at or near Abingdon, to communicate with the Thames and

Severn Canal, at or near Inglhham, in the County of Berks, and Kemps ford, in the County of Gloucester, the Practicability of which hath been ascertained by Levels and correct Surveys taken for that Purpose; and 1 that the making such Canal would not only be advantageous to those Individuals who have strenuously engaged in the Accomplishment of that Undertaking, but would also, in a great Degree, increase the Woollen Manufacture, promote the Circulation of Trade, by reducing the Price, and expediting the Carriage, of Goods, between the Port of London and the principal trading Towns in the Kingdom, and would likewise improve the Landed Interest, be a great Relief to the Poor, tend to the Preservation of the Public Roads, and every Way contribute to the'National Prosperity: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining such Canal as before described, together with Railways and Roads of Communication to and with the same Canal, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House

Page, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Commonalty of the Borough of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Bridge over Yarmouth Haven, which is the only Entrance into the Town of Great Yarmouth from the County of Suffolk, is a Timber Bridge, and so much decayed, that, in the Opinion of experienced Workmen, it is necessary the same should be taken down, and a new Bridge built; and, by an Estimate made of the Expence of taking down the present Bridge, and building a safe and commodious one in the Room thereof, it appears that the same will amount to about £4,000; and that, by virtue of an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Duties, or Sums of Money, or some Part thereof, are applicable towards repairing the said Bridge during the Term of the said Act, but the same are insufficient to defray the Expence of taking down and re-building the Bridge, and the same cannot be done unless the Term of the said Act is Vol. 40.

enlarged, and a further Sum of Money granted to the Petitioners for that Purpose: And therefore braying,

A Petition of several of the Vestrymen and Inhabi- Saints Mutants of the Parishes of Saint Margaret and Saint John Westminster the Evangelist, in the City of Westminster. was present- Parish: ed to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, an Act was made for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said Parishes, and die Vestrymen of the said Parishes are thereby authorized to make a Rate or Assessment upon the Inhabitants, not exceeding Six Pence in the Pound of the Yearly Rent of Value of their respective Houses, Tenements, and other Buildings, for defraying the Expence of maintaining and supporting the said Watch and Beadles; and, in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, another Act was made for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said City and Liberty, which directs, that the Number of Watchmen within the said Parishes of Saint Margaret and Saint John, having Beats or Stands, shall be Forty or more, and the Number to patrol the Streets shall be Six at the least; and that, since the passing of the said Act of the Fourteenth of His present Majesty,'it was judged necessary, for the Safety and Protection of the Persons and Properties of the Inhabitants, that a greater Number of Watchmen than is required by the said Act should be constantly employed within the said Parishes, the Annual Expence whereof has amounted nearly to the whole Money received from the said Rate or Assessment; and that, notwithstanding the great Number of Watchmen employed as aforesaid, several very daring Robberies and Burglaries were, in the Year 1782, committed within the said Parishes, whereupon it was found necessary to employ an additional Number of Men as a Patrol, but the Money arising from the Rate or Assessment authorized to be made as aforesaid not being sufficient to defray the Expence thereof, a Subscription was entered into by many of the said Inhabitants, whereby a sufficient Sum hath been collected for defraying such Expence; and that the Petitioners are convinced, that the establishing the said additional Patrol hath been the Means of preventing many Robberies and Burglaries within the said Parishes, and it is highly expedient the same should be continued; but as there is no other Mode of raising Money to defray the Expence there- of than by voluntary Subscription, which is not only partial and uncertain, but has of late greatly‘decreased, the Petitioners have Reason to apprehend, that the said additional Patrol cannot be continued, unless some certain Provision be established for raising Money to defray the Expence thereof: And therefore praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioners to raise a small additional Rate upon the Inhabitants, for defraying the Expence of supporting a proper and sufficient Patrol within the said Parishes, in such Manner a9 the House shall think proper.

Setting forth, That from their first Institution, by an Act passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign* intituled, "An Act to incorporate " certain Persons therein named, and their Successors*

" with proper Bowers for the Purpose of establishing " One or moire Glass Manufactories within the King*

" dom of Great Britain, and for the effectually sup*

" porting and conducting the same, upon an improved Plan, in a peculiar Manner calculated for " the casting of large Plate Glass," they have, with unremitting Attention, endeavoured to forward Work which Parliament, by its Sanction, meant to countenance as an Object of Public and National Concern; the Result has been, a real Performance of what was held up as a Plea to warrant the Privileges granted by Parliament to the said Company, who have brought the Manufactory to such a Degree of Per* section as already to stand forth a Rival, and to become an Object of Envy, to the French Nati6n in that Branch of Manufacture, which in France has been upheld for more than a Century by peculiar Indulgences of Monopoly in the Trade, and total Exemptions from Duties; and Representing to the House, that the Petitioners have expended, in the Progress of their Works, upwards of £ 100,000 without receiving the smallest Dividend, owing to a Variety of Circumstances to which an Infant Manufactory upon an entire new Plan must naturally be liable; and, amongst other Hardships, they have found the Duties payable to Government very oppressive, from the peculiar Manner in which Glass is made by Casting, ffifferhtg much from all other British Manufactories wherein the Glass is maide by Blowing; and this appears to be owing to an Extra Waste erf Metal through the whole Process of the Casting Work, and the Petitioners can prove, that they have paid Duty upon such Extra Waste of Metal, to the Amount of £. 7,000 and upwards; and that, from such heavy Burthens upon the Produce of the Manufactory, they find themselves unable to continue their Endeavours to support it, Without some Relief from Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring id a Bill to explain, amend, and enlarge the Powers of the said Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, and to authorize them to increase their Capital Stock, and to give such further Relief in regard to the Payment of Duties, as may repair the Losses already sustained by the Company, and prevent the like in future, by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet

Prizes at A Petition of Sir George Collier, Knight, late Com-

Ex^tion zander in Chief of His Majesty’s Fleet in America, xpe 1 on. jQggtijgj. with the Captains whose Names are thereunder signed, in Behalf of themselves and others, and also of the Officers and Men under their Command, on the late Expedition to Penobscot, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That having received authentic Intelligence at New York, in' August 1779, of His Majesty’s Garrison at Penobscot being besieged by Sea and Land by a considerable Number of American Forces, the Petitioners proceeded from thence with His Majesty’s Squadron for its Relief, and in' a few Days were so ‘fortunate as to accomplish the Passage, and to get Sight of the Enemy’s Fleet, who, on the King’s Ships giving Chance, retreated soon after up Penobscot Bay and River, where they were all run ashore, set fire to, and destroyed, to the Amount of Seventeen Sail of Ships of War, and several Transports, besides a great Number of smaller Vessels designed for the Purpose of Annoyance; and that the Enemy’s Ships of War had on board alive at the Time of the Chace Two thousand Seven hundred and Forty-five Men (exclusive Vo l. 40.

of their Army and the Seamen in the Transports and other Vessels) and which Ships of War were intended for proceeding immediately to cruize upon the British Trade, so soon as the Reduction of the King’s Garrison was completed, which they expected would have happened the same Day the British Squadron appeared, as a general Assault was about to take Place by Land and Sea; and that the Petitioners having made Application to the Navy Board for the Head Money for the before-mentioned Two thousand Seven hundred and Forty-five Men (who were on Board the Ships of War when destroyed) have received for Answer, that it cannot be granted for Want of the necessary Affidavits required by Act of Parliament from Three of the principal Officers of each Ship so destroyed or taken; and Representing to the House, that it was not possible to comply with the Forms prescribed, from the Circumstance that all the Enemy’s Officers and Men got on Shore from their Ships, and took their Way through Woods and desart Wilds, where the greater Part perished for Want of Provisions, &c: The Petitioners therefore, in Behalf of themselves, the Officers, and Men concerned, finding themselves precluded from the Advantage which they conceive was intended by the Legislature as an Encouragement for His Majesty’s Navy, by the Impossibility of their being able to comply with the Form prescribed (though from the Spirit of the Act they presume they are entitled to such Advantage, from their good Conduct and Success on the before-mentioned Occasion) pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief as shall appear just and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. James Luttrell, Sir Charles Middleton, &c.: And they are to meet To-mor-

row Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

Total General of the probable Amount of the Expence which will be incurred for completing new Works, for the Purchase of Land, and for altering, re-building, and finishing old Works, for the better Security of His Majesty’s Dock Yards at Portsmouth and Plymouth -

51

As this Computation for new Works exceeds, by about £ 36,000, that of or £ 500,000 given by the Master General, in his Report on the Estimate for 1783, the following Reasons are submitted, as the Cause of this Difference.

That Computation was made from a rough Calculation of the Number of Posts necessary to be occupied, in order to keep an Enemy out of Distance of bombarding the Dock Yards, and of the Sort of Expence that new Works, sufficient for those Posts, might amount to; of which it was thought right that Parliament should have such a general Idea as could then be formed, previous to any Money being asked, with an Intention to begin Works on that System.

Until the Ground was purchased and cleared, and the Levels and Sections taken, the particular Plan for each 'Situation could not be determined, and consequently no correct Estimate could be formed.

The Manner in which these Works might be constructed, would also very much vary the Expence.

Hie

5 Geo. III. of Mar HL i

The same Works, which are now computed to cost £ 536,00b, if executed frith fevetmen, of Sod of Grass, as is frequently done, would cost only £295,000; if with Demi-Revetments and Counter Escarps in Masonry, of the same Section as the Works immediately coveripg the Dock Yarji at Portsmouth, £ 346,000; if with whole Revetments and Counter Escarps in Masonry, £417,006; if, besides whole Revetplelifc and Counter Escarps in Masonry, Casemated Defences, Magazines, Storehouses, arid‘Lodgment for Tthe Troopk (all Bomb-Proof) and Barracks for the Garrison, are included; ds at present intended, the Expence (as dbove computed) will be £536,000, and exceed the First rough Computation by about £3^6,000; if upon a less durable Construction, and with fewer Powers of Resistance, they Would be much within it. 1 ‘ ' ,; 1 O

The Purchase of Lands, Alterations, re-building, and finishing old Works,! Were not included in that Computation. ( , v; J *

It is necessary to explain, that it has been judged expedient to increase she Dimensions first intended for the Fort at Stokes Bay, to strengthen it by Inundations, and to construct every Part in solid Masonry, with such additional Advantages as may be derived from advanced Works, and covered Defences in all the Tlanks, in order to render this important Post as Secure as possible.

The Plan for Frater Lake is of smaller Extent, and has not the Benefit of Inundations; but it is intended to have the same Solidity of Construction; advanced Works, and covered Defences: And it has been thought, that the Two Flanks of the Approach on thd Gosport Side, being sd effectually fortified by these Two strong Forts, the intermediate Work, at first proposed for the Ground near Rowner Church, might be dispensed with. If it should ever be thought adviseable to erect it, the Expence will be ajboiit the same as the Fort at Frater Lake. V

It is also necessary to observe, that the Plan of the Work proposed for Merrlfield (although included in this Computation) has been suspended, from a Desire of avoiding to subject Mr. Carepo to the Incoriveniencies which he apprehends from having a Work within Half a Mile of his House, and in Hopes that some pther Situation may be found, whose combined Advantages may, without Increase of Expence to the Public,\afibrd, equal Protection to the Dock Yard. ’ 1 ,

The re-building South Sea Castle is become indispensable, from the Sea having lately undermined the Foundation, and demolished great Part of the Wall. The great Expence which has from Time to Time been incurred, in various Attempts to secure the Sea Wall, has been found ineffectual against the violent Surf that rages ther^. The old Work is of too bad a Form to deserve the Expence necessary to repair it. A square Redoubt, of a modern Construction, more advantageously and securely placed, a little further from the Sea, is proposed to be built in its Stead.

It is conceived, that the Two new Forts on the Gosport Side, and the Third near Hilsea Lines, together with the Completion of Fort Monckton, the re-building South Sea Castle, and the Improvement of Cumberland Fort, will be sufficient to keep an Enemy out of Distance of bombarding the Dock Yard at Portsmouth; and that the Two Forts on the Heights of Maker, and at Merrifield, with their Dependencies, will afford an equal Degree of Security for the Dock Yard at Plymouth, against a Bombardment from an Enemy landed to the Westward of that Port. The Eastward Side of Plymouth would require at least Five considerable Forts to keep an Enemy out of Reach of Bombardment, by Means of Fortifications: But the Distance at which an Enemy must land on that Side, the vast Detour he must make, and the Difficulties of the Country he must pass through, are so great, that there can be little Doubt but that the Garrison of the Place, assisted by the numerous Inhabitants of the Country, whose Zeal was so generously manifested on the late Alarm, will be sufficient to prevent the Approach of an Enemy on that Side, until effectual Succours can arrive.

A Garrison of 12,000 Men for Plymouth, and 10,000 Men for Portsmouth, with such Help as they may always get from the neighbouring Country, will, it is presumed, be sufficient for the Defence of these Ports, fortified in the Manner proposed, and give sufficient Time for the Strength of the Country to be collected, and to arrive for their Relief.

The Time in which the present Plans will be completed, will depend entirely on the Grants of Parliament. If the Money is supplied in Three or Four Years, the Works may be all finished in that Time. But there is this peculiar Advantage in this System of fortifying by detached inclosed Works, that the Benefits are not postponed till the Whole ms completed; for, as fast as each Work is clone, it adds so much Strength, not only by diminishing the Number of Points of Attack, but by rendering those that remain much more hazardous to an Enemy, who must leave a Fort on his Flank, or in his Rear, that must greatly annoy him. If only the Two Works proposed to be begun upon this Year, at the important Points of Stokes Bay, and the Heights of Maker, were finished, they would add very considerable Strength to the Defences of Portsmouth and Plymouth.

The Object of the proposed Fortifications is to obtain perfect Security for the valuable Stores of the Two principal Naval Arsenals of the Kingdom; blit these Works will besides operate as actual Increase of the Navy, by enabling that Part of it to become active wherever it may be warited, which must otherwise remain stationary at Home, for the Protection of the Dock Yards.

If the Master General and Board of Ordnance have in this Report gone beyond the Order of this Honourable House, to state the probable Amount of Expence, and have shewed the Grounds on which their Computation is founded, and the Object of the W'orks proposed, they trust it will be imputed to their Desire of giving the fullest Information in their Power. Intrusted by His Majesty with this important Branch of the Defence of the Country, they have thought it incumbent on them to offer such Ideas as they conceived would most effectually attain that. End. — Having discharged their Duty, it remains with Parliament to determine upon the System to be pursued, by suffering the Grant of £ 50,000, made last Year to His Majesty, to be employed on the extended Plan for which it was voted, or to restrict it to more confined Works, or to resume it entirely, and risk the Safety of the Dock Yards w ithout any Fortifications.

Then the skid Petition Was ‘brought up, and read; Setting forth, That In or about ‘the Year 1716, the late Charles Hadcli'ffe, Esqriire, the Petitioners "Father, although then brily in the Nineteenth Year of his Age, Was attainted df Hiojh Treason; and that, by an Act passed in the First Year of the Reign of King George the Fir^t, all the Mririots, Lands, and Hereditaments, whereunto any such Attainted Persons were then, or afterwards, 'entitled, were forfeited to, and Were thereby vested in, his then Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, for the Use of the Public, according to the several Estates and Interests Which such attainted Persons had therein respectively, and where they were seized of an Estate in Tail in Possession, the same, it was thereby exacted, Should be vested in his Majesty, his Heirs and SucfceSsbifs, in Fee Simple; and that the Petitioner's Father, after his Attainder, became seised, m Tail Male, tn Possession, of certain Lands and Hereditaments, comprised in a Settlement made in the Year 1691, which therefore became vested in his Majesty in Fee Simple, by virtue of the aforesaid Act; and that the Petitioner’s Father also, after his Attainder, became Tenant, for Life, of certain other Lands and Hereditaments, comprized in a Settlement made in the Year 1712. with Remainder to his First and other Sons in Tail Male; and that the Petitioner was born in France. in the Year 1725, of the said Charted Radcliffe, ana the Right honourable Charlotte Countess of Newburgh, his Wife, and the Petitioner confides, that the Forfeiture in Fee Simple of the most lucrative Part of the Derwentwater Estates, and the Receipt of the Rents and Profits of the remaining Part of the said Estates, by the Public, for upwards of Fifty Years, will have fully atoned for the Crime of his attainted Ancestor; and that, although the Petitioner, by the Forfeiture of his attainted Ancestors, has suffered the loss of an aricient English Earldom, and of the greatest Parts df his Family Estates, yet is he kept out of the remaining Part of them, not on account of their having been forfeited by the Attainder of his Ancestors, but because the Petitioner has hitherto been presumed an Alien, for, after the Attainder of the Petitioner’s Uncle, the late Eatl of t>er-wentveater, his Son, Mr. John Radcliffe, claimed, arid actually enjoyed, for near Seventeen Years, the Estates in Question, as Tenant in Tail Male, under the very same Settlement of 1712, and there is no other Objection, than the Presumption of Alienage, against the Petitioner’s enjoying this very Estate, for, by one and the same Settlement, each Father had a Life Estate, which he forfeited by his Attainder, and each Son, after his Father’s Death, had the same Estate entailed upon him precisely in the same Mariner; and that the Petitioner, in the Year 1749, after the Death Vol. 40.

6f his Father, 'from a Confidence that parliament Wbuld riot have presumed hirp to be an Alien, if he Were not such by Law; out of Respect and Deference to she Legislature, and from a total Ignorance of the Law, as well' as from an absolute Inability to(bear the ‘Expences of litigating the (Question, accepted of the 'Sum of £. 24,000 (as the Act expresses it) as a Re-Tief’fdr his Support; and that the Petitioner, under 1 the implicit Copviction of his being an, Alien, and consequently of his Incapacity to take an Estate Ta*j» under the Settlement of 1712, is recited, in,an Act of Parliament, parsed in the Twenty-second Year of King have consented, th^t all

'the Rights Title, and Interest, which he, or his Issue Male, had, or could have, to the Estates corapijzed in the said Settlement of 1712, should be extinguished; arid -th^t, by the established Law of this Country, ah Estate Tail cannot be barred or defeated, as against lthe Issue in Tail, but by a Common Recovery, or a Fine, or an Act of Parliament, expressly dispensing With these necessary Forms of Law, and it is gleaj* the Legislature did not rhean to defeat the Estate Tail of the Petitioner, since they did not make ai^y Mention of this Estate Tail throughout the Act, but divested the Fee Simple out of his Majesty, which, in the Supposition of the Petitioner’s t being no Alien, was riot yet come into Possession; and that, by the said Act, the petitioner is to remain, in 'respect to his "Claim, to be deemed to bq a natural-born Subject, in the same Condition as he would have been, in case the Act had not been made; and that the Petitioner confides, that he is not precluded from claiming to be a Subject of this Country in Law^ as he is in Heart and Desire, and that, although the Petitioner, as the Son of an attainted Father, born Abroad, seems, by the Fourth of King George the Second; to be precluded from claiming the Benefit of the Act of the Seventh of Queen Anne; by which latter Act the Children of all natural-born Subjects, born out of his Majesty’s Allegiance, are declared to be natural-born Subjects to all Intents and Purposes, yet, by the said Act of the Fourth of king George the Second, the Petitioner is expressly declared, in respect of his being an Alien, to be and remain in the same Condition as he would have been in case the said Seventh of Queen Anne, and the Fourth of King George the Second, had not been made; and that the Petitioner is advised, that, before either of these Acts had passed, he was, by the Common Law and Statute Law of this Realm, a natural-born Subject, yet, in as much as Parliament, in the First Instance, undertook the Consideration of the Petitioner’s Case^ though they expressly avoided deciding upon it, the Petitioner thinks it a proper Submission and Deference to the Legislature rather to submit his Pretensions to the Justice and Equity of Parliament, than to enter into a strict legal Disquisition of his Right, against the seeming Presumption Of the Legislature; and that, by the said Act of the < Twenty-second of King George the Second, his theh Majesty consented that the Parliament should make any Disposition rind Settlement they should think fit of the Interest his Majesty then had, or might have, in the Premises, for the Benefit of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, and by the same Act, such Estate was divested out of his Majesty, and was vested in the Governors of the said Hospital; and that no Estate or Interest whatsoever in the Premises comprised in the said Settlement of 1712 was vested in his then Majesty, if the Petitioner was by Law a natural-born Subject, and therefore the Estate Tail, which, in that Supposition, was vested in the . Petitioner, was neither divested out of him by that Act, or barred as against his Issue Male, and that, if Parliament have so recently restored the forfeited Estates of several loyal Descendants of attainted Ancestors, the Petitioner confidently relies, that the same gracious Bounty and
