Mercy will not be shut against the loyal Descendant of an Ancestor who was attainted in the Nineteenth Year of his Age, and who had not, like the Ancestors of those whose Estates have been lately restored, experienced, for upwards of Thirty Years, the mild and happy Government of His present Majesty’s Royal Family; and that the Petitioner might well hope, that an Application on his Behalf, for a Restoration of all the Estates which were forfeited by his attainted Ancestor, would be attended to upon the same Principles which lately actuated the Liberality of the Legislature towards the like Sufferers for the same Cause, yet, in Consideration of the very useful and charitable Appropriation of the forfeited Estate of his attainted Ancestor, the Petitioner forbears to apply for the Restoration of any Part of those Estates of Vrhich his Father was seised in Tail Male in Possession, and which tvere forfeited to the Crown in Fee Simple, in the same Manner as those Estates which have lately been restored; and that the Petitioner begs Leave to suggest, that the forfeited Estates which have been lately restored were, by the Twenty-fifth of King George the Second, as effectually vested in the Crown, for the Use of the Public, as the Derwentrvater forfeited Estates were, by the Twenty-second of King George the Second, vested in the Governors of Greemoich Hospital, for the Service of the Public; and that the Petitioner is confidently assured, that an Application for his Estate Tail, in the remaining Part of his Family Estates, which the Forfeiture never has reached, will be consonant to the Principles of Justice, Humanity, and Mercy of the House; and the Petitioner forbears to urge any personal Claims upon the Bounty and Mercy of the House, as in the late Restoration of the Scotch forfeited Estates the Principle of Liberality and Mercy w>as so general, that the Person is still unknown and uncertain to whom the Estate of Perth is restored; and that although the Petitioner should be deemed an Alien, yet he confidently hopes, that as Parliament has heretofore granted Estates to a considerable Amount, w'hich had escheated to the Crown, by Reason of Alienage, even to the illegitimate Issue of a foreigri Woman, they will not reject the Application of the legitimate Issue of a British Peeress for a similar Favour, and if the Estates which were vested in the Petitioner’s Father, in Tail, and were forfeited to the Crown, in Fee Simple, should continue appropriated to the Support of Greemvich Hospital\ yet will the Petitioner even then be punished with infinitely more Rigour and Severity than any other Person whomsoever for the Crime committed by his Father, at the inconsiderate Age of Nineteen Years, and under Circumstances of much less Criminality than attended the Treason for which those Estates were forfeited that have been lately restored; and that the Petitioner, in case he shall be admitted as Tenant in Tail of the Premisses in Question, will restore the Bounty which Parliament gave him for his Support at a Time when they presumed him incapable of taking such an Estate, with as much Readiness as he then received it with Gratitude; and that, to complete the grievous Hardship of the Petitioner’s Case, his Claim has never been agitated before a Court of Justice, nor the Grounds of his Pretensions to be a natural-born Subject by Common Law, or by the Statute de natis ultra mare, have ever been submitted to the Consideration of the Legislature, who seem nevertheless to have left the Question open to future Discussion, by their having constantly expressed, in every Act that concerned the Petitioner, that in that Respect he should remain in the same Condition as he would have been, in case such Act had not been made; and that although the Petitioner should not be found to be a natural-born Subject of this Country by the Common Law, or by the Statute de natis ultra marc, yet he begs Leare to submit to Parliament that this Right would evidently

have accrued to - him under the plain Words of the Seventh of Queen Anne, by which the Children of all natural-born Subjects, born out of His Majesty’s Allegiance, are declared to be natural-born Subjects to all Intents and Purposes, if it had not been enacted by the Fourth of King George the Second, that nothing in the said Act of Queen Anne did oc should extend to give the Rights of a natural-born Subject to any fcf

Child born out of his Majesty’s Allegiance, whose ®

Father was attainted of High Treason at the Time of his Birth; and that the Petitioner was born near Six Years before the Fourth of King George the Second was passed, and his Mother, the Countess of Newburgh, in resolving to be delivered of t}er eldest Child in a Foreign Country, relied upon the Faith of the Law, as it then stood; and, the Petitioner has been constantly informed, that his said Mother was confirmed in this Confidence: by the Opinions of His then Majesty’s Attorney General, and other eminent Counsel, who were unanimous in, their Opinions, as the Law then w'as, that, as,to the inheritable Capacity of her Child, it mattered not where the Child was born, provided the Father and Mother were English, and such the Petitioner’s Father and Mother certainly were, otherw ise it would have been very easy for her to have been delivered of the Petitioner in England, in which Case his Right to the Estates comprized in the Settlement of 1712 would have been equally clear with that of the said John Radcliffe, his Cousin German, who actually enjoyed, after the Attainder of his Father, that Estate under the same Settlement, as that upon which the Title of the Petitioner is now founded; and that if the Petitioner should be deemed an Alien, and consequently incapacitated to take an Estate of Inheritance in this Country, under and by virtue of the Fourth of King George the Second, then will he be the First Instance of a Subject of a free Government being deprived by an ex post facto penal !f|

Law, of a Right which attached and was vested in him for the First Six Years of his Life, which Right, without any Day given him to appear in, he will be thus made to forfeit, in the Age. of Innocence, when he was incapable of committing Offence, and in his Absence, when no Friend coukl be applied to to interpose in his Behalf; and that if a Circumstance, expressly warranted by a Statute in Force, may at a future Day be declared to be the immediate Cause of depriving a Subject of his Birthright and Inheritance, this will directly go to establish an unprecedented System of Tyranny and arbitrary Power, against which no human Prudence can protect, no Submission or Obedience to the Laws and Constitution of his Country can defend the Subject: And therefore praying the House, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for granting to the Petitioner' such Redress and Relief as in their Humanity, Mercy, and Justice, the singular and unprecedented Hardships of his Case shall appear to deserve.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A PETITION of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, Merchants, and Traders, of the County of Carnai'von: And also,

A Petition of the* Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, Merchants, and Traders of the County of Cardigan;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appears by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Bridge over an Arm of the Sea, between the Counties of Anglesey and Carnarvon, called The Streights of Menai, at a Place, near Porthaethwy Ferry, called Ynysgcint; and Alledging, That the free Navigation of The Streights of Menai is an Object of public Importance, the said Streights being navigable throughout for Vessels of very large Burthen, and frequently Annually by several Thousand Sail of Vessels, loaded with different and valuable Merchandize, and the making a Bridge, as aforesaid, will very materially injure the Navigation of The Streights of Menaiy and thereby be detrimental to the Trade and Commerce,' Maritime Strength and Revenue, of this Nation, and to the Interests of die Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the Bill for making a Bridge as aforesaid.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council of the City of Chester, in Common Council assembled, wa9 also presented to the House, and read; Tailing Notice of the Application mentioned in the preceding Petitions; and Setting forth, That the free

Navigation of The Streights of Menai is an Object of public Importance, the said Streights being navigable throughout for Vessels of Very large Burthen, frequented by some Thousand Sail in the Year, and in particular by many Vessels which, on certain Winds, have a secure and speedy Passage there, when they could not otherwise proceed to their Destinations; and Alledging, That the making the said Bridge will very materially injure, if not totally ruin, the Navigation of the said Streights, and thereby be detrimental to the Trade and Commerce, Maritime Strength and Revenue, of this Nation, and to the Interests of the Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying, That the Bill for making the said Bridge may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee to whom the Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and others, of the County of Anglesey, and of other Parts of Great Britain, and also of the Kingdom of Ireland, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty Coventry of the City of Coventry, and of the several Persons Poll Booth, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Electors of *c* Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That, by an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty, for better regulating Elections of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the City of Coventry, it is enacted, that the Returning Officer or Officers should, at all future Elections of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City, cause the Booth for holding such Election to be erected in the widest and most convenient Part of the open Market Place, called Cross Cheaping, not contiguous to any other Building; and that the Sheriffs of the said City were, at the last Election, put to great Expence in erecting the Election Booth, a Moiety whereof was repaid them by the successful Candidates, but the other Moiety hath not hitherto been reimbursed, although the Payment thereof has been frequently demanded; therefore, to prevent the like Injustice in future, the Petitioners conceive it to be expedient, that there should be a law declaring at whose Expence the Election Booth should be erected; and, it is apprehended that it would tend much to prevent Riots, and to preserve the Peace, at all future Elections of Members for the said City, if the Returning Officer or Officers were obliged to take the Poll by Taffies, agreeable to the Plan adopted at the last General Election: And therefore praying That Leave may

be given to bring in a Bill for declaring that the Booth for holding future Elections for Members of Parliament for the said City, shall be erected at the joint and equal Expence of all the Candidates, and also for obliging the Returning Officer or Officers at such Elections to take the Poll by Tallies, or for giving such further or other Relief to the Petitioners, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as ft shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Wilmoty Sir Sampson Gideon, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

church, habitants of the Parish of Christchurch, otherwise The

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are British thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and Assurance others, Members of a Society called or known by the Sociel' Description of The British Assurance Society, and now held at the Queens Arms Tavern, Newgate-street, in the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, and several other Persons, about the Year 1773, established a Fund, for the Relief of Members and their Families, in Cases of Sickness and other Misfortunes (particularly stated in the Petition) and as it was necessary for them to be known by some certain Description, to distinguish themselves from other Societies, which might be simile* ia some Respects to that formed by $ the

25 Geo. III. 8° Martiu 611

the Petitioners, they styled themselves, on account of their voluntary Subscriptions, and being British Subjects, The Free British Society, and, under that Description, held Meetings, and chose certain Persons as Trustees, and otherwise, to collect and apply the Subscriptions from Time to Time made for the Pur-

f)$es set forth in the Petition; and that about the ear 1779 the said Society very much increased, from which, and from some Variance happening between the Petitioners and other Members of the said Society, it became necessary to regulate their farmer Rules and Orders; and accordingly, a Deed (by way of Policy) with certain Covenants therein specified, was prepared, and the Petitioners were styled therein The British Assurance Society, an Exemplification of which Dqed was, for the Purpose of every Member having Access thereto, as Evidence, inrolled in the Court of Kings Bench at Westminster, in Trinity Term 1779; and that, since the making of the said Deed, several other Persons have become Members of the said Society, and the same are daily increasing; yet, notwithstanding the Covenants mentioned in the said Deed, the Petitioners, for want of being regularly incorporated, find, that not only several of the salutary Purposes, which, by their original Institution, and the Improvements thereof, are evaded, and rendered ineffectual, by the designing Part of Mankind, but several well-disposed Persons, who would willingly become Members of the said Society, are prevented from so doing, through Doubts of the said Society’s Property being sufficiently secured by the present Mode of Establishment; and that for want of Incorporation, the Title they now have, as a Society, is merely assumed, by which therefore they can neither sue or be sued, but are reduced to the Necessity of proceeding in the Names of certain Members appointed for that Purpose, which not only occasions great Expence, but is constantly attended with Delays and Difficulties, especially as the Courts at Westminster vary in their Opinions respecting the Rights of the Petitioners to maintain or defend Suits; and that, as the said Society’s present Stock is daily increasing, it has been considered, that, if the same was placed out either on Government Security, or Freehold Lands, in the Name of the Society, not only every Member would be the better secured in his just Claims, but such Stock would be thereby much improved; and that, by the Rules and Regulations of the said Society, not only the several Parishes in and round this Metropolis, but also some of the most distant Parishes in Britain, will be greatly disencumbered of their Poor, from the several Members, and their Families, being, by the above Benefits, prevented the miserable Alternatives of absolute Want, or the disagreeable Effects attendant on a Parish Maintenance; and the said Society being open to all British Subjects, of the Protestant Religion, Inmates as well as Householders are equally entitled to its Benefits, whereby many industrious Tradesmen, Labourers, and their Families, are enabled to stem the Torrent of temporary Misfortunes, till, by the Fruits of their own Labour, they can enjoy that Independence ever dear to the British Subject: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, whereby the Petitioners, and such other Person or Persons, who, from Time to Time, may be desirous of becoming a Member or Members of the said Society, may be incorporated and perpetuated as One Body, and may be called upon and enabled to sue and be sued, and to hold Lands and otter Estates, and to do, execute, and perform, every other lawful Act, Deed, Matter, and Thing, by the Name, Style, or Title of The British Assurance Society, as may be necessary for the Purposes aforesaid, with such Presidents, Treasurers, and other Officers, and subject to such Provisoes and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

and that, by an Act made in tte Twenty-second Year of King George the Second, for the more effectual preventing of Frauds and Abuses committed by Persons employed in die Manufacture of Hats, and in the Woollen, Linen, Fustian, Cotton, Iron, Leather, Fur, Hemp, Flax, Mohair, and Silk Manufactures, and for preventing unlawful Combinations of Journeymen Dyers and Journeymen Hot-pressers, and of all Persons employed in the said several Manufactures, and for the better Payment of their Wages: and, by Two other Acts, made in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Penalties and Punishments are inflicted upon all Persons who shall reel False or Short Yarn, and on Persons embezzling the Materials used in the said Manufactures; Mr. Itolle reported from the Committee to whom the Petition of the Governor, Deputy Governor, Assistants, and Guardians of the Poor, of the City and County of 'Exon, under their Common Seal, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Ninth and Tenth Years of King William the Third, for establishing the said Corporation; and also, an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for impowering the said Corporation to raise a Sum of Money to discharge a Debt then incurred; and also, an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for raising a further Sum of Money for discharging other Debts then incurred, were read: And,

Mr Joseph Burrow, Clerk to the said Corporation for Relief of the Poor, being examined, said, That by the great Increase of the Poor of the said City and County of Exon, the high Price of Provisions, and the Expences incurred by the embodying of the Militia, the Corporation have been obliged to contract further Debts, to the Amount of Five thousand Pounds and upwards, which they are incapable to discharge without the Aid of Parliament; and that, from the above Causes, the said Corporation are become wholly unable to fulfil the several Purposes for which they were instituted.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to render more effectual several Acts of Parliament for erecting Hospitals and Workhouses within the City and County of the City of Exon, for the better employing and maintaining of the Poor there; and to raise further Sums of Money for the better carrying the Purposes of the said Acts into Execution: And that Mr. Rollc, Mr. Bastard, Sir Charles Warwick Bampfylde, and Mr. Baring, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Designs for Mr. Alderman Nezrnham reported from the Com-

Vrinting mittee, to whom the Petition of several Persons, whose nens, c. Barnes are thereunto subscribed, Callicoe Printers, Artists, Designers of Drawings, Engravers, and others, Proprietors of original Patterns for printing Linens, Cottons, Callicoes, and Muslins, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth, viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Kilburne being examined, said, That he is a Callicoe Printer, at Wallington, in Surrey — That he draws his own Patterns — That his Patterns have been copied to his great Injury — That out of the Number of Patterns he has drawn, several have not succeeded, and, when any of them have pleased the Public, base and mean Copies have been made immediately, to his very great Loss — That a Thousand Pounds worth of Prints have been obliged to be laid by as useless, on Account of the Imitations. The Witness then produced an original Pattern of his own, executed at his Manufactory, and also a ba.se Copy of the above Pattern, much inferior in Quality, but which prevented the Sale of the Original.

Mr. Thomas Hatcher being examined, said, That he is a Callicoe Printer and Draftsman, at Mitcham, in Surrey: He then confirmed the above Evidence of Mr. Kilburne, and added, That about Twelve Months ago he produced a new Pattern for a Lady’s Dress, which was much admired, and Ladies of the highest Rank had some of them — That he produced but a small Quantity of them at first, thinking that by Reason of the high Price of them they might not sell, but finding a considerable Demand for them, he set about finishing others; and before he could complete them, another Person produced a mean Copy, and offered a considerable Quantity to the Linen Draper that sold the Patterns in London \ which inferior Copy was printed upon a very coarse Linen, and of course was sold at a much inferior Price, by which Means the Sale of his original Design was totally frustrated: Then

Mr. Francis Moore being examined, said, That he is a Wholesale Linen Draper of Cheapside, London — That he purchased a Pattern of Linen of Mr. Kilburne, about a Year and a Half ago, of which he expected a considerable Sale; but that about a Month after the Beginning of the Sale, a base Copy, at a 7

reduced Price, and of inferior Cloth and Materials, was produced for Sale; in consequence of which his Pieces were left upon his Hands, and he thereby sustained a great Loss.

Mr. Thomas Browne being also examined, said, That he is a Wholesale Linen* Draper in Cheapside — That the same Circumstance had happened to him as to the last Witness, by Means whereof he also sustained a great Loss. — And being further examined, he said,

That by the Exportation of mean and inferior Copies to Foreign Markets, the Credit and Sale of our Manufactures are greatly diminished. And he produced, to Your Committee s Letter from Baltimore, in America, to himself, which states, that fine printed Cottons and Chintzes are not in Estimation there equal to the French — That there is now a great Sale of French and Foreign Chintz, which he apprehends would be totally prevented, if Encouragement were given to our Manufactures; and the same might be carried to a greater Extent and much higher Perfection, if the Copy Right, for a limited Time, was secured to the Inventors — That he does not doubt but that, if the Copy Right was obtained, our Manufacturers would be able to excel all the Foreign Manufactures, even the East India Chintz: And the Witness added, That the Foreign and India Chintz are all clandestinely imported, and therefore the Revenue would be greatly benefited by our own being sold in their Stead.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Encouragement of the Arts, of designing and printing Linens, Cottons, Callicoes, and Muslins, by vesting the Properties thereof in the Designers, Printers, and Proprietors, for a limited Time: And that Mr. Alderman Newnham, Mr. Alderman Watson, and Sir Joseph Mawbey, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Bounty on A Petition of James Stuart, of Thames Street, Lo?i-Curing fish, don, Merchant, on Behalf of divers Persons residing in Scotland, who are Carers of Fish, particularly of Red Herrings and Tusk Fish, and who are, or may be, desirous of exporting the same into Foreign Parts, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act made in the Filth Year of King George the First, for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in Foreign Parts, and better securing the Duties on Salt, certain Rates are directed to be paid for all such Fish therein mentioned, as shall be exported from any Place in Great Britain into Parts beyond the Seas; and that, by an Act made in the Twenty-ninth Year of King George the Second, for encouraging the Fisheries in Scotland, it is enacted, that the said Act, made in the Fifth Year of King George the First, and also other Acts therein mentioned, so far as relates to the Curing of Fish for Exportation, with Salt, and likewise to the several Rates, or Sums of Money, allowed upon the Exportation of Fish from England (except as therein is excepted) Should be, and the same were, thereby declared to Vo l* 40.

extend to Scotland, and thatj from and after the 25th of June 1756, it should be lawful to carry, and bring, from any Port of Scotland to any Port of England, for Home Consumption, any Salmon, Cod, Ling, Tusk, and other White Fish, the Persons bringing such Fish into England, Wales, and Berwick upon Tweed, paying such Duties thereon as therein mentioned; and, it is further enacted, that it should be lawful to carry, or bring, from any Port or Place of Scotland to any Port of England, for Re-exportation, any Herrings, Salmon, Cod, Ling, Tusk, and other White Fish, and, that all such Fish, so brought Coastwise from Scotland into England, Wales, and Berxvick upon Tweed, should, upon Exportation thereof to Foreign Parts, be entitled to the same Bounties as, by the said Act passed in the Fifth Year of King George the First, were granted on the Exportation of Fish cured in England; and that, in the said Act of the Twenty-ninth of King George the Second, no mention is made of Red Herrings, by Reason, as the Petitioners apprehend, that Red Herrings were never before that Time cured in Scotland, therefore they are not entitled to any Bounty for the Exportation thereof, within the Letter of the said last mentioned Act; and that, although, by the said last mentioned Act, all such Herrings, Salmon, Cod, Ling,

Tusk, and any other White Fish, brought Coastwise from Scotland, into England\ Wales, and Berwick upon Tweed, should, upon Exportation thereof into Foreign Parts, be entitled to the same Bounties as, by the Act of the Fifth of King George the First, were granted on the Exportation of Fish cured in England, yet, as no Mention is made in the said last mentioned Act of Tusk Fish, the Clause so allowing, or intending to allow, a Bounty on the Exportation of Tusk Fish, is rendered ineffectual, and of no Use to the Persons curing, and desirous of exporting, that Fish, and the Petitioners, as Curers of such Fish in Scotland, are deprived of the Benefit of such Bounties obviously intended them by the said Act of the Twenty-ninth of King George the Second; and that, since the passing of the said Act of the Twenty-ninth of George the Second, great Quantities of Keel Herrings have been cured in Scotland, and exported by the Petitioners into Foreign Parts, but, nevertheless, they are not entitled to any Bounty on the Exportation thereof, by Reason that there is no Provision made for that Purpose in the last mentioned Act; and that the Petitioners have been informed, that it is in the Contemplation of the House soon to take into Consideration the State of the Fisheries in Scotland: And therefore praying, That when the State of the said Fisheries is taken into Consideration, the House will grant the Petitioners Relief, so far as regards allowing a Bounty on Red Herrings and Tusk Fish, brought from Scotland, into England, Wales, or Berwick upon Tweed, Coastwise, and from thence exported into Foreign Parts, as the Petitioners conceive that a Bounty was intended to be allowed on such Fish by the Legislature, when they passed the said Act of the Twenty-ninth of George the Second, although not expressly directed in the said Act, or that the House will afford the Petitioners such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Combing Wool, W°°V Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the combinS-County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Yarns spun in the said County have greatly decreased in their Value, occasioned principally by the fraudulent Heeling thereof; and that, in consequence of the Preference given to the Yarns of other Counties, where Regulations under the Sanction of recent Acts of Parliament, have taken Place, the Petitioners have great Reason to fear, that,

unless

616 8 Martiu ’ 1785*

unless they are authorized to make the like Regulations, their Trade will greatly decline, and with it the Employment and Support of numerous Poor in the said County; and that, by an Act made in the Twenty-second Year of King 'George the Second, for the more effectual preventing of Frauds and Abuses, committed by Persons employed in the Manufacture of Hats, and in the Woollen, Linen, Fustian, Cotton, Iron, Leather, Fur, Hemp, Flax, Mohair, and Silk Manufactures, and for preventing unlawful Combinations of Journeymen Dyers, and Journeymen Hot-pressers, and of all Persons employed in the said several Manufactures, and for the better Payment of their Wages; and by Two other Acts, made in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Penalties and Punishments are inflicted upon all Persons who shall reel False or Short Yarn, and on Persons embezzling the Materials used in the said Manufactures; and that the good Purposes of the said Laws have been greatly frustrated, from the Petitioners being unwilling to expose themselves singly to the Loss attending the Resentment of the Spinners and Work-People, by prosecuting them for Offences against the said Acts; and that this important Branch of the Woollen Manufacture of the said County of Lincoln will be greatly prejudiced thereby, unless the Petitioners are enabled jointly to carry those Laws into effectual Execution, which cannot be done without the Aid of Parliament; and that, by Two Acts made in the Seventeenth and Twenty-fourth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for more effectually preventing Frauds and Abuses, committed by Persons employed in the Manufactures of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the Counties of York, Lancaster, Chester, and Suffolk, certain Powers are given for the Appointment of Committees of the Manufacturers of the said Counties, with Power to appoint proper Persons to be Inspectors of Worsted Yarn, within the same Counties, for the Purposes in such Acts mentioned, which Inspectors are thereby directed to use due Diligence for bringing to Justice all Offenders against the said Two last mentioned Acts, and the said former Acts, and such other Powders and Remedies are, by the said Two last mentioned Acts, given to, and vested in, such Committees, Inspectors, and others, respecting the Funds therein respectively directed to be established, and respecting such other Matters and Things for carrying those Acts into Execution, as have a manifest Tendency to the Advantage of all the Manufacturers of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the said Counties of York, Lancaster, Chester, and Suffolk, whereby the Yarns, and consequently the Trade, of those 'Counties, have been greatly improved: And therefore

praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, with similar Powers to those comprised in the said

Two last mentioned Acts, and for the Purpose of obtaining such other Relief in the Premises as to the House may seem meet* and the Necessity of the Case requires.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Manufacturers of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted* in the several Counties of Northampton, Huntingdon, Cambridge, and The Isle of Ely, Bedford\ Leicester, and Rutland, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the same, as ibshall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of several of the principal Inhabitants of the Village of Clapham, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the said Village is become large and populous, and, from its Vicinity to the Metropolis, the Inhabitants thereof, and also all Persons passing to and from the same in the Night Time, are much exposed to Robberies, and other Outrages; and that it would be a great Security to the Petitioners, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Village, and to all Persons having Occasion to pass to and from the same in the Night Time, if the Road from and including the House in the Occupation of Mrs. Mount, in the said Village, leading towards London, and ending at the Entrance of the Village of Newington, and at the Roads over Clapham Common, and also the said Village and Common, were properly lighted and watched during certain Hours of the Night: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Benjamin Lacam, Proprietor of New Harbour, in foe Bay of Bengal, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner had been many Years engaged in making a Refitting Harbour in The Ganges, capable of receiving and accommodating, with Dry Docks and Supplies, the Ships of His Majesty’s Navy, as well as those of the East India Company, to any Extent of Number and Size; and that the Pe* titioner received, and still holds, his Right and Title to the said Place and Possessions, by a Grant, called a Pottah, executed under the express Direction of the Governor General and Council of Bengal, and sealed with the Official Revenue Seal of the East India Company, in full and accustomed Form, and with as free and absolute a Title and Deed as any Subjects of this Realm hold their Chartered Rights, Grants, and Estates; and that, after the Petitioner had, in foe Couiae^f Six Years, expended about £> 30,000 in

Lacam’s Harbour at Bengal.

Scotland — Bewly, &c. Bridges.

&° Martit. A. 17 85.

Such Works, Vessels’, and Preparations, as best suited to the Nature of his extensive Undertaking, his Grant and Title were revoked arid annulled, by the same Governor General and Supreme Council, to his sudden Disappointment, arid entire Ruin; and that the Petitioner applied and waited for Redress at Ben±

gal, for the Space of Four Years, without Effect, and was then permitted, and generously assisted, by his Creditors, to come to Englan, and appeal to the Sovereign Powers and Justice of his native Country; and that, upon a Representation of his Case to this House, in 1783, at His Majesty’s Recommendation, the House was pleased'to refer it to a Committee, and a Report was made thereon, horn which Report, as the Petitioner conceives, the Truth of the above Allegations will sufficiently appear; and that it likewise appears, from the said Report, that, during the late War, His Majesty’s Ships upon the East India Station were greatly distressed for Want of a Windward Relilting Harbour in the Bay of Bengal, and compelled to quit that Bay at a riiost important Crisis, leaving the Coast of Coromandel, and the whole British Interest and Cause, exposed to the French Fleet, which therefore penetrated almost to the Mouth of The Ganges; and that the Ships of His Majesty’s Squadron, by going round to Bombay, left the Enemy in full Possession of the Bay of Bengal, were absent from their Station Six Months, and thereby prevented from co-operating with the British Forces before Cuddalore till the Month of June, whereas, had there been at that Time a Refitting Harbour at Bengal, His Majesty’s Ships might have returned to the Coast in January, and conveyed in proper Time the necessary Supplies of Troops, Provision, and Money, to the Relief of the then famishing and distressed Garrison of Fort Saint Geot'ge; and that, notwithstanding these Facts do fully appear, and that the French and , by the Re-capture and Partition of can al-

ways command the whole Bay of Bengal (during the Absence of the Fleet at Bombay) the Petitioner has "not been able to obtain any Redress, Decision, or Assistance, from the East India Company, by whose Servants be has been thus entirely ruined, and a great and national Object discouraged, and prevented for the Space of Eight Years, nor can he find any other Mode of Relief than by supplicating the Justice and Protection of the House: And therefore praying,

That the House will take the said Report and the Petitioner’s Case into Consideration, and grant him such Relief and Support, in the Furtherance of the said Work, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Right honourable Lord William Gordon, Sir Thomas Dundas, Baronet, John Sinclair, of Ulbster, Esquire, Arthur Forbes, of Esquire,

George Ross, of Cromarty, Esquire, Alexander Gray, of Overskibo, Esquire, Duncan Davidson, of Esquire, John Mackenzie, of Esquire, John

Mackenzie, of Lentron, Esquire, Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Dundas, John Anstruther, and James Baillie, Esquires, for themselves, and on Behalf of the other Land Owners and Inhabitants of the Counties of Inverness, Ross, Cromarty, Sutherland, Caithness, and the Orkney Islands, and Boroughs therein, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Rivers called Bewly, Conon, and Helmsdale, run across the Country immediately

to the Northward of Inverness, from the Mountains* to the East Sea; that it is the singular Condition of those Three Rivers to be absolutely without a Bridge, from their Sources down to their respective Friths, from which uncommon Circumstance, the large and populous Northern District above mentioned is sometimes utterly inaccessible, and always reached through dangerous Fords and Ferries, with great Inconveniency, and not unfrequently with the Loss of Lives; and that the Funds and Abilities of the said District have been totally exhausted, by* making long Tracts of good Roads, and constructing numerous Bridges, some on large, and others on smaller Streams, without the Assistance, hitherto, of any public Aid, to effect those laborious and expensive Undertakings in the Counties to the Northward of the said Rivers; and that Two of the said Rivets, Bewly and Conon, run partly through, ind partly Contiguous, to Two of the most considerable of the late forfeited Estates, now restored to the Heirs of the former Proprietors, and, during the Time the said Estates were in the Hands of the Public, the Commissioners appointed for their Management entered, at different Times, upon various Proceedings,' for building Bridges on the said Rivers Conon and Bewly, and paying the Expences out of the Rents of the said Estates; but these Rents having been, from Time to Time, otherwise applied, neither were the said Bridges, nor any other public Work, carried on upon the said Northern,

Estates, nor in that Quarter' of the Highlands where they lie, although their Rents were regularly levied for the Public, and were intended by Parliament for general Improvements in those Parts, as well as in other Quarters of Scotland; and that the late Grants of the forfeited Estates are charged with. Payment into the Exchequer in Scotland, of certain Sums, subject to the future Disposition of Parliament, it bang understood to be the liberal Intention of Parliament to dispose of those Sums in useful and necessary public Improvements in Scotland, the Bridges above mentioned are conceived to be primary Objects of that Description, as nearly serving to complete the only Part that now remains unfinished of a Line of Communication from one End of the Island to the other, and the Expence of building the aforesaid Bridges is computed at about £. 12,000: And therefore praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for appropriating the Sum of £. 12,000, of the unexhausted Balance, which is subject to the Disposition of Parliament, directed by an Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, to be paid into the Court of Exchequer in Scotland, by the several Persons to whom the forfeited Estates in Scotland are granted, towards building Bridges over the Rivers Bewly, Conon, and Helmsdale, in North Britain.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Persons whose Names are FM thereunto subscribed, being Planters and Proprietors of Trade Lands in East Florida, on Behalf of themselves and others, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, by several Acts of Parliament, great Encouragement hath from Time to Time been given, and large Premiums allowed, for the Importation of Naval Stores, and Indigo, from the British Plantations in America, which were not continued after the Year 1782, by Reason, as the Petitioners apprehend, of the Rebellion' then subsisting in roost

- of

5 Geo. Ill- 8° Mariiu . Sai

t>/ His Majesty’s Provinces in America; and that iiince the Year 1782, and more especially since the Cession of East Florida to the Crown of Spain, the Petitioners have imported from the said Province, into 'Great Britain, divers Articles of Naval Stores and Indigo, upon which no Premiums have been allowed; and that East Florida, having ever persevered in its > Loyalty to the King, and Attachment to the Laws and Constitution of Great Britain, the Petitioners conceive they are entitled to the Indulgence of the same Premiums as were allowed to them, and to the Planters in the other Provinces of America, previous to the Interruption of the Commercial Intercourse between the Two Countries; and that the said Premiums, as the Petitioners understand, were calculated, and allowed, as an Equivalent to the Duties payable upon the Importation of the said Naval Stores, but that, by the several Additions of Five per Cent, upon the said Duties, the Premiums, had they been lately allowed, would not have been equal to the Whole of such Duties: And therefore praying, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as the House shall think fit

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

and the said Act contains a Clause, which enacts, that it shall not be lawful for any Brewer, or Seller of Beer or Ale, living or carrying on his or her Brewery without the said City of Glasgow, and Liberties thereof, or without the Villages of Gorbels and Port Glasgow, to import, or sell, any Beer or Ale, into, or in, the said City and Villages of Gorbels and Port Glasgow, or the Liberties or Privileges thereof, unless he or she do previously give Notice to the Magistrates of Glasgow, or to their Collector of the said Duty, at their Office at Glasgow, or Port Glasgaiv, respectively, and agree to be subjected to, and charged with, the Payment of the said Duty by the said Acts granted and made payable, for all the Beer and Ale which shall be brewed by such Brewer, or Seller of Ale and Beer, living or carrying on his or her Business without the said City and Villages, or the Liberties or Privileges thereof, and that every Brewer, or Seller of Ale or Beer, who shall import, or sell, any Ale or Beer, into, or in, the said City, or Villages, or Liberties or Privileges thereof, respectively, without having given such previous Notice, and agreed, as aforesaid, shall be charged with, and liable to, the Payment of the said Duty, to the Magistrates and Council of the said City, or their Collector or Collectors respectively, for all the Ale or Beer brewed by him or her during Twelve Calendar Months immediately preceding his or her committing such Offence; and that the Petitioners conceive the said Clause to be unjust and oppressive, as it subjects them to the Payment of the said Duty for all the Ale and Beer they brew, if thtly import or

A Petition of the Inhabitants of Pulborough, West Anin Navi* Chiltington, Stopham, Hardham, Fittleworth, Petworth, 8ation* and the adjacent Parishes, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for amending and improving the Navigation of the River Arm, from Houghton Bridge, in the Parish of Houghton, in the County of Sussex, to Pallenham Wharf, in the Parish of Wisborough Greeni in the said County, and for continuing and extending the Navigation of the said River A run from the said Wharf, called Pallenham Wharf to a certain Bridge, called Newbridge, situate in the Parishes of Pulborough and Wisborough Green, in the said County of Sussex; and Setting forth, That, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it will be very injurious and oppressive to the Petitioners and others, Owners and Occupiers of Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, for, by the said Bill, a Toll of Nine Pence for every Ton of Timber, Planks, Coals, Lime, Corn, and Grain, and Six Pence for every Ton of Firewood, Chalk, Soil, and Dung, carried on the present Navigation between Houghton Bridge and Pallenham, is imposed, and is to be collected at such Places as the Company of Proprietors shall appoint for that Purpose, although on the present Navigation no Toll is payable, and repeated Declarations have been made that none was intended to be imposed; and, the Petitioners believe, that great Injury will be done to the Lands and Grounds where the Locks, &c. are to be erected; and Representing to the House, That, as no possible Advantage can accrue to the Petitioners from the extending the Navigation from Pallenham Wharf to Newbridge, they ought not to contribute to the Expence thereof, which they must do, to a very considerable Amount, if the present Bill passes into a Law: And therefore praying, That they may be

heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill’s passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That Mr. William Egerton have Leave to Leave of go into the Country for Three Weeks, on his private Absence,

Richmond Mr. Ambler reported from the Committee, to whom Poor and the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Streets. principal Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of Richmond) in the County of Surrey, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the Relief and " Employment of the Poor, and for repairing the " Highways, paving, cleansing, lighting, and watch-" ing the Streets and other Places in the Town and " Parish of Richmond, in the County of Surrey, and " for removing and preventing Annoyances, Obstructions, and Encroachments therein, and for shutting " up a Road from the late Horse Ferry at Kew, to " West Sheen Lane, near Richmond Green, and for " amending and keeping in Repair the Road from " Kew Bridge to Richmond" was read: And Mr. William Stallard being examined, said, That the said Act has, in many Respects, been found inadequate to the salutary Purposes for which it was made — That since the passing of the said Act, the Poor of the said Parish have greatly increased, and by Reason of the Defects in the Law under which they are governed and supported, they are very ill provided for, and are maintained at a very large Expence, by Means whereof the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish are greatly burthened by heavy Rates: Then Mr. William Smith being examined, said, That he is a Surgeon — That he knows the House which now is, and for several Years last past has been occupied as a Workhouse, for the Reception and Employment of the Poor of the said Parish; that the same is in a very confined and bad Situation, and is in a very ruinous State and Condition, and much too small to admit the Number of Poor Persons of the said Parish, who are proper Objects of Relief, therein: And

Mr. Stallard, being again called in, confirmed the before-mentioned Evidence of Mr. Smith; and added, That the said Wrorkhouse is now held under a Lease which is near expiring: Then

Mr. Smith, being again called in, was examined, and said, That the Church Yard of the said Parish is the only Burial Ground or Cemetery within the said Parish, and is situate very near the Middle of the Town of Richmond — That the same is so very small, that from the Number of dead Bodies which have been buried therein, the Ground is raised more than Two Feet above the original Level, whereby it is become a real and great Nuisance to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and that the same will in a short Time, if not prevented, become very unwholesome and dangerous.

A Petition of the severaj Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Acting Commissioners under an Act. for repairing the Roads from Maidenhead Bridge to, Reading, and also under an Act for repairing the Highways between the Bear Inn, in Reading, and Punt field, in the County of Btrksy and other Roads, in ijie said Act mentioned, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for paving t,he Footways in the Town of Reading, in the County of Berks, for cleansing, lighting, and watchipg the Streets, Lanes, Passages, and Places in the said Town, and for removing Encroachments, Obstructions, and Annoyances therefrom, and preventing the like for the- future; apd Setting forth, That there is a Clause in the said Bill, impowering the Commissioners to erect a Turnpike Gate, or Bar, on every public Road leading to the said Town, within One Mile thereof and to take a Toll thereat from

all Passengers, in Manner therein stated, and also, to take an additional Toll at all the present Turnpike Gates within a certain Distance of Reading, at parti- cular Times, which, together, make a very considerable Part of the \ ear, so that a Person, travelling from London to Bath, would, on this Plan, be liable to pay an additional Toll, on each Side of the Town, towards repairing the Footways only, on which he would never step; and that the said Commissioners under the Turnpike Acts already have a Power of lighting that Part of the Town through which the Bath Road leads, and this Power has been by them exercised whenever they have thought proper, and also full Power to cleanse and repair the same; and that there is another public Road leading from London to Bath, through Basingstoke, which is at present used by many People, and possibly many more Travellers may be induced to prefer that Road, if such additional Tolls should be laid on, which would lessen the Securities of those Persons who have advanced Money for the Repair of the said Roads; and that no public Notice has been given of any Intention of erecting new Turnpike Gates, or of laying on the additional Tolls, which the Petitioners always conceive to be necessary on the Renewal or Alteration of any Turnpike Act; and therefore, as Trustees in Behalr of the Persons who have advanced Money on a Security of the present Tolls, and also in Behalf of all Travellers, praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that such Part of the said Bill, as relates to the said additional Tolls, may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names arc thereunto subscribed, being Acting Commissioners, under an Act, made for repairing and widening the Road from Shillingford, in the County of Odford’ through JValtingford and Pangborne to Reading, in the County of Berks, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That there is a Clause therein, impowering the Commissioners to take an additional Toll at all the present Turnpike Gates on the Roads leading to the said Town, and within a certain Distance, at particular Times, which, together, make a very considerable Part of the Year; and Alledging, That the Tolls at the present Turnpike Gate near Reading, are necessarily very high and oppressive to the Traveller, viz. Two Pence for each Horse, and Ten Pence for a Coach, or Chaise and Pair, which are as high as by the said Act can be imposed, and, if those Tolls are raised, Travelling on this Road will be very much discouraged, and the Security to those who have lent Money on it will be greatly endangered, and the Petitioners rendered unable to raise Money to discharge the present Loans, if required; and that no public Notice has ever been given of any Intention of laying on those additional Tolls, which the Petitioners always conceived to be necessary previous to the Alteration of any Turnpike Act, and, if such Notice had been given, most probably those Persons who have advanced Money on the Security of the said Tolls would themselves have petitioned the House; and therefore, as Trustees for such Mortgagees, and for such Persons as necessarily Travel the said Road, praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that such Part of the said Bill, as relates to the said additional Tolls, may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

A Petition of Sir James Campbell, of Aberuquhill, Baronet, Sir William Stirling, oi Ardoch, Baronet, John Francis Erskine, Esquire, of Marr, Robert Graham, Esquire, of Gartmore, James Erskine, Esquire, of Card-ross, George Drummond, Esquire, of Blairdrummond, John Ramsay, Esquire, of Ochterlyre, William Stirling, Esquire, of Keir, and others thereunto subscribing, Freeholders, Justices of Peace, and Commissioners of Supply, in the County of Perth, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That in the Bill respecting the Highways, Bridges, and Ferries in the County of Perth, the Petitioners presumed to think there were many Things exceptionable, and by no Means expedient or calculated to attain the Purposes proposed by the Bill, yet they agreed to forego their Opinion, in Deference to that of the Majority, except as to One Article, which appeared to them to be of such Importance, as to make it their Duty to state it to the House j the Eighth Clause concludes with a Proviso, " That in case any Person shall think him-<fi self aggrieved by the Lists so made up, it shad " be lawful for him to appeal to the next General " Meeting of the Justices of Peace and Commissioners of Supply, at Michaelmas, or to the Meeting " following, that shall happen within the Space of

" One Year after the making up of such Lists, but

" ings, shall take place and remain to be the Rule,

" and the Determination of such General Meeting shall be final to all Intents and Purposes, without x " any Appeal or Review by any other Court being 4< competent;" by the Twenty-fourth Clause, respecting the shutting up of old Roads, and making new ones, after pointing out the Steps to be taken in such Cases by the General Meeting, and Committee appointed by them, as more particularly mentioned in the Clause, it. is provided, u That- in case any of

Vol. 40.

the said Parties shall think theriiselves iaggrieved " by the Judgment of the kaid Committee thereon, " it shall be lawful for him to appeal to the next u General County Meeting, who shall immediately " hear and determine the same; and in case any of " the said Parties shall be dissatisfied with the Judgment of the said General Meeting thereon, it shall " be competent to them to apply to the Court of " Session for Redress, and, in case the said Court of " Session shall affirm the Judgment of the said General Meeting, they shall award the full Costs of " Suit;" and by the Thirty-ninth Clause, it is provided, " That in case any Person or Persons shall " consider themselves aggrieved by any Thing done " in pursuance of this Act, and for which no particular Remedy hath been already hereby directed of " appointed, it shall and may be lawful to the said " Person or Persons to appeal for Redress to the " then next General Meeting of the said County, " who are hereby authorized and required, provided " Five Justices of the Peace shall be present, to " take Cognizance thereof, and to hear and determine such Appeal, and to award such Costs of " Suit as they shall think proper, and their Judgment thereupon shall be final to all Intents and " Purposes, without any Advocation, Suspension, or " Review, by any other Court, being competent;" thus, except as to Questions respecting new or shutting up old Roads, it is meant that the Judgment of the General Meeting, provided Five Justices of the Peace be present, shall be final without Review; and that it is obvious, that in the Execution of this Act many Questions may arise, which may materially affect Property, and be extremely interesting both to Individuals and to the Public, it appears therefore to the Petitioners to be a Matter of the most serious Concern, to guard, as much as possible* against a partial Execution of the various Powers thereby conferred, and, for this Purpose, that the Proceedings of the General Meetings should, in all Cases, be subject to the Controul of the Court of Session; and that the Petitioners consider that a Gra?* dation of Judicatory is the best Expedient for preserving pure the Fountains of Justice; in other Questions of Civil Right it is open to every Individual, who may think himself injured by the Decree of an inferior Judge, to apply to the Supreme Court for Redress; this is a Constitutional Privilege belonging alike to all Orders of Men, a Privilege which the Petitioners would not wish to forego for themselves, and which, as charged with the Interests of those who may come after them, and of the County at large, they do not think they are entitled to surrender; and that at the Era of the Resolution it was thought necessary, by the Claim of Rights, to secure to the Subject the Right of appealing to the Parliament of Scotland, from the Judgments of the Court of Session, though that may, in general, be supposed to consist of Jbdges in every Respect the best qualified in the Kingdom; if it be supposed that even the Decrees of that Court may be charged with Error or Injustice, the Petitioners cannot see any Reason for concluding that, especially in a Country so extensive, and of which those in the Commission of the Peace must be so numerous, a Court consisting of any Five Justices of the Peace, should be less fallible; on the contrary, besides the Infirmities of Passion and Caprice, incident to them, in common with other Men, the Petitioners should apprehend, that, from being more exposed to the Influence of local Prejudice, of Connection with the Parties, and of personal Interest, it would be essentially necessary that their Judgments should be subject to the Controul of a superior Jurisdiction: In these Sentiments the Petitioners are confirmed by the Experience of other Counties, who have obtained Statutes upon the Plan of the present Bill, as far as the Petitioners have been able to learn or observe,

the''Exclusion of the Controul of the Court of Session has, in many Instances served only to secure complete Effect to Injustice and Oppression; and the Distinction made in the Bill, it is presumed, will not merit the Approbation of the House: The Cases in which the Review of the Court of Session is admitted, are those in which Persons of Property may be supposed to be chiefly concerned: The Cases in which the Review of that Court is excluded, are those which may be supposed more immediately to interest the lower Classes of People, though these are certainly entitled to every legal Remedy which the highest enjoy: And therefore, for these Reasons, the Petitioners hope, that the House will be of Opinion, that the Bill ought not to pass, except with a Proviso, that, in every Case, the Proceedings of the General Meetings of the County shall be subject to the Review of the Court of Session.

Mr. Alderman Watson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Alder, men, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; mid he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same w as read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from Blackfriars, in the City of London, to the opposite Side, in the County of Surrey, and to make Ways and Passages to and from the same, on each Side of the said River; and also an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for completing the said Bridge, and the Avenues thereto on the London Side of the said River, were read; by which last mentioned Act it appeared, that the said Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, were empowered to embank a certain Part of the North Side of the said River, within the Limits therein described, and for the Purpose of providing a Fund to defray the Expences of lighting, watching, cleansing, and repairing the said Bridge, when built, that they were also empowered to charge the Ground to be obtained by the said Embankment with certain Quit Rents to arise therefrom.

Mr. Robert Milne, Surveyor, being then examined, said, That the said Bridge and Embankment are completed, as directed and required by the said Acts - — That the Produce of the Fund arising by virtue of the said Acts, and thereby made applicable to the Support and Maintenance of the said Bridge, and of the lighting, watching, and cleansing thereof, amounts to no more than One hundred and Seventy-five Pounds per Annum; but that there are some other small Pieces of Ground, at present under Dispute, which, if let by the City of London, may form an Addition to the said Fund of about Ten Pounds per Annum: And he produced to your Committee an Estimate of the Expence of watching, lighting, cleansing, watering, and repairing the said Bridge, by which it appeared that the Annual Charge thereof will be Five hundred and Ninety-nine Pounds and upwards. — And being further examined, he said, that all the Particulars of the said Estimate, except the Watering, are expressly directed to be done by the said Acts of Parliament, and that the Calculations are formed upon a Plan of performing the said Works, in such a Manner as will be but barely sufficient for the Safety and Accommodation of the Public. — And being further examined, he said, it is apprehended that a Sunday Toll, on Carriages and Horses passing over the said Bridge, would be the most eligible Way of obtaining an Income sufficient to make up the Deficiency of the present Fund applicable to the above-mentioned very useful and necessary Purposes; and that the Passage to and from London, over the said Bridge, is the only Avenue to the Metropolis at which a Sunday Toll is not paid at this Time.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for laying a Toll upon all Horses and Carnages passing on a Sunday through any Turnpike to be erected at or near Blackfriars Bridge, towards increasing the Fund for watching, lighting, cleansing, watering, and repairing the said Bridge: And that Mr. Alderman Watson,

Mr. Alderman Newnham, and Sir Joseph Mawbey, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Richard Gterard, Esquire, being examined, said, ^That the several 'Works by the said Acts authorized and directed to be performed, have been executed, and have greatly tended to the Advancement of Trade* and the Security of Shipping — That the Trade of the said Town has of late Years greatly increased, and that the Ships and Vessels, using the said Port of Liverpool, are*: more numerous than they formerly were; and that the Three Wet Docks, and the Dry Pier, already built in the said Harbour, are not sufficient for the Ships and Vessels coming therein to lade and unlade; and that it is necessary to erect One or more additional Wet Dock or Docks, with proper Piers, and other Works, for the Accommodation of Shipping within the said Port.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enlarge the Term and Powers of several Acts relating to the Harbour of Liverpool, and for making Two additional Docks and Piers in or near the Port of Liverpool: And that Mr. Gascoyne, Junior, and the Lord Penrhyn, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir Adam Fergusson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Archibald Earl of Dundonald* was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and , is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Letters Patent, granted in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, under the Great Seals of England and Scotland respectively, securing to the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, the sole Privilege and Authority of making, using, exercising, and vending, within Great Britain, for the Term of Fourteen Years, his Invention of a Method of extracting or making Tar, Pitch, Essential Oils, Volatile Alkali, Mineral Acids, Salts, and Cinders, from Pit Coal, were produced to your Committee: And,

Dr. Bryan Higgins being examined, was asked, Whether he had attended to Lord Dundonald's Method of extracting Tar and Pitch, and what was his Opinion of the Benefit to be derived therefrom by the Public ? who said, That he had not seen the actual Process on the great Scale, but he was informed by a Model, and by considering the Principles of the Process, that it is a considerable Improvement, superior to any of the Methods by which Mineral Pitch or Tar has been heretofore extracted — That he conceives the Process to be simple and easy, and to promise the greatest Produce, with the smallest Expenditure of the Fuel.

And being asked, Whether he knew that Tar, Pitch, Essential Oils, Volatile Alkali, Mineral Acids, Salts, and Cinders, have been extracted from Pit Coal by Lord Dundonald's Method ? he said, All the Sea Coal that he has ever known yields Oil, which, by Rectification, may be divided into a fine Oil and Pitch, and at the same . Time yields Volatile Alkali, which is a valuable Article.

And being asked, Whether this Tar is superior to the Foreign Vegetable Tar? he said, From general Principles he infers that it is superior to Vegetable Tar in Duration, and the Preservation of Timber, because it is less poluble in Water, resists Menstrua generally with greater Force, penetrates the Wood more freely, and seems in drying to acquire a firmer Consistency. — Then,

Mr. John Hall, Master of the Swan Tender, was called, and asked. Whether he had made use of the Coal Tar, as prepared by Lord Dundonald? he answered, That in November 1782 the Sxvan Tenders Bottom was payed $ith it at Dundee, after an Hour's Boiling, to bring it to a proper Consistence, without the Addition of Pitch — That the Swan has been Two Voy-agesto Shetland; Twice to Plymouth; Twice to Mcmcl, in the Baltic; Once from London to Alloa; from whence she returned to London again, where she now is — That she was afloat during that whole Time, except Twice, to examine her Bottom, when the Stuff was found perfectly firm, and still continues so — That after Vo l. 40. J

the Stuff had been on the Bottom Twelve Months, it was covered with Barnacles, which were easily removed by Brooms, without affecting it — That on Tuesday last, the 8th March, he examined her Bottom, in the Presence of Captain Shanks of the Navy, and several other Gentlemen, and found, by taking a Chip off the Plank with the Stuff, to the Depth of nearly a Quarter of an Inch, that the Wood was perfectly fresh and dry, and there was no Appearance of any Worm having penetrated into it.

And being asked, Whether the Ship, since she was payed with this Stuff, had lain any Time in the Medway ? he said. She had lain there, at different Times, in all about Three Months.

And being asked, If he knew that Ships Bottoms are apt to suffer more by the Worm in the Medway than in any other Part of the Coast of Great Britain ? he said, The Minerva Tender, built in 1776, except Two Voyages in the Coal Trade,1 was chiefly employed at Sheerness, and in the Medway — That in Two Years she was so much worm-eaten, that she was with Difficulty kept afloat, and was obliged to be sheathed; since which the Sheathing is much eat, though properly payed for the Purpose with Turpentine, White Lead, and Rosin.

And being asked, Whether he thought the Minerva would have suffered so much if she had been upon any other Part of the Coast of Great Britain ? he said, From the Experience he has had, he thinks there is 110 Port in Great Britain where the Worm does so much Damage as in the Medway.

And being asked, Whether, upon the Whole, from his Experience, he thought that the Tar prepared by Lord Dundonald was preferable to the usual Mode of paying Ships Bottoms? he said, The Experiment tried on the Swans Bottom confirmed him in the Belief that it is preferable; not only on Account of its Duration, but, that a less Quantity of Coal Tar covers more Space, from the Smoothness of its Quality, than the usual Mixture, and makes Stuff without the Addition of Pitch.

And being asked, Whether, when the Bottom of the Swan was last examined, there was enough of Stuff remaining upon it to prevent the Wood from Injury ? he said, Except where it had been rubbed off by Lighters, Boats, and other Accidents, there now remains a sufficient Quantity to preserve the Bottom.

And being asked, Whether that would have been the Case if the Ship had been payed in November 1782, in the common Way, with Vegetable Tar and Pitch? he said, As the Barnacles have been Twice scraped off, he presumes the Stuff would have come off had she been payed in the common Mode; and that he knows no Instance of a Ship, payed in the common Mode, having lasted so long in good Order as the Swan has — That Ships bound on IVcst India Voyages generally have their Bottoms payed in the qommon Mode every Voyage, which seldom exceeds Nine Months; and that if the same Number of Voyages he had made in the Swan had been made by a Ship payed in the old Way, she must have been payed about Three Times.

And being asked, What was the Condition of his Ship’s Bottom when first payed writh Coal Tar? he said, For Eighteen Months previous to the paying she had not been upon the Ground; that the Weed, on her Bottom was Fourteen Feet long, with a Number of Muscles as close as possible to her Bottom — That he has not discovered One Weed or Muscle since the Stuff' wras first laid on, nor any Thing but Barnacles, which were rubbed off without affecting the Stuff, as before mentioned.

And being asked, Whether there was any considerable Difference of Expence between paying with Coal Tar, and the other Stuff usually made use of? he said, It wotfld require Two Barrels and a Half of 7 Y Vegetable

A Petition of the Callico Manufacturers and Printers of the County Palatine of Lancaster, and Counties adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are exceedingly alarmed at the Resolutions brought before the House relating to the Commercial Regulations betwixt Great Britain and Ireland, which, if carried into Effect, they have no Doubt will, in their Consequences, be greatly injurious to the Commerce and Manufactures of this Country; and that the principal Part of the Expence in the various Articles of the Cotton and Callico Manufacture, together with the Printing, consists in the Price of Labour, which is greatly enhanced by the many heavy Taxes with which this Country is burthened, and the People of Ireland being, in a great Measure, free from Taxes, the Price of Labour is consequently very low; and that, to cany on the same Extent of Business in this Country as in Ireland, a much greater Capital will be required, on Account of the Difference in the Price of Labour, and the very heavy Duties on the Bleaching and Printing Cotton Goods; from these Considerations the Petitioners have sufficient Reason to fear that this valuable Branch of Manufacture, which at present is computed to employ upwards of Five hundred thousand People, will be immediately very much injured, and the Consumption of this Country will in Time be wholly supplied by the Manufactures of Ireland; and that the Petitioners are apprehensive that no Duties laid on the Importation of Irish Manufactures will be a sufficient Security to the British Manufacturer, as it is well known that high Duties continually operate as an Inducement to smuggle: And therefore praying, That the House will take the same into Consideration, and prevent those Resolutions from passing into a Law; and that they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, in Support of the Allegations contained in this Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, Vo t. 40.

to whom it is referred. to consuler further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland', and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs and Excise do attend the said Committee, Tomorrow Morning.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go, with the Mace, to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker; and One hundred and Twenty-four Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked; die Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of alb the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Name of Sir Thomas Dundas, Baronet, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioners; and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Twenty-seven other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of William Young, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Sitting Members; and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Twenty-two other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That, in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Twenty-six other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Six, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Ten, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; and Ten, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete;

Lists of the said Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

Mr. Young reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir George Collier, Knight, late Commander in Chief of His Majesty’s Fleet in America, together with the Captains, whose Names are thereunder signed, in Behalf of themselves, and others, and also of the Officers and Men under their Command, on the late Expedition to Penobscot, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as folio weth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Gazette Extraordinary, published by Authority, dated the 24th of September 1779, was produced, and read, whereby it appeared, that the said Sir George Collier had, by a Letter to Philip Stephens, Esquire, dated from on Board the Reasonable^ in Penobscot Bay9 August 20th, 1779, given Information to the Lords of the

Admiralty, that in consequence of his having received certain Information that His Majesty’s Garrison at Penobscot was besieged by a considerable Rebel Armament of Troops and Ships from Boston, he had proceeded with the Squadron to the Relief of the Place, and had taken, blown up, and destroyed the whole Fleet, not a single Vessel of any Kind having escaped — That General Lowell, who commanded the Rebel Army, and Commodore Saltonstall the Fleet, had fixed on the said 20th of August to have made a general Assault on the Fort and Ships, which the Appearance of His Majesty’s Squadron had happily prevented — That such of their Army and Sailors as had escaped were then exploring their Way through thick Woods and desart Wastes, and that he had enclosed a List of the Rebel Fleet, as follows: .
