may be Appropriated without Delay, and paid into the Exchequer, we are of Opinion, that the Receiver General should, at the Foot of his Weekly Certificates to the Commissioners of the Customs, state the Sum of Duties then remaining in his Hands, and for what Reason they are not paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer: And, since it appears, from the Manner in which the Appropriation of the Payments into the Exchequer, by the Receiver General, is formed, that the Duties paid in neither are nor can be ranged with Accuracy under those Branches to which they in Fact belong, we think the Commissioners of the Customs warranted by constant Usage, and ought, to order the Controller General to apply such Duties, remaining in the Hands of the Receiver General, in the Manner which best suits his Arrangement of the Receipts of the Week.

The Subject that has occurred to us, as the most important in this Inquiry, is the Intricacy and Perplexity that involve the Collection and Accounts of this Part Of the Public Revenue. The Examination shews us, that the Number of Rules required in the Computation, and the Number of Branches under which the Accounts of these Duties are kept, are the principal Sources of this Evil. The obvious Remedy is, to reduce the Number of these Rules and Branches, as near as Circumstances will admit, to Unity, and to introduce a systematic Simplicity and Uniformity into the Manner of keeping the Accounts. This Regulation is become an Object of high and urgent Importance for the Attention of the Legislature. The Number of Accounts are increased in almost every Session of Parliament: Seven new Accounts were created by the Acts of the last. The Merchant, ignorant to what Duties he is liable, must rely upon the Officer. The Labour of the Officer is become great: The Number of Entries Inwards, in the Four Months ending with October last, was Fifteen thousand Three hundred and Forty-two: They have sometimes amounted to Four hundred in One Day. The Collectors at the Out Ports, by their frequent Applications to the Board, profess themselves ignorant. Errors in the Computations are daily; the Science difficult, possessed by few, and in Danger of being lost; and this in a Branch of the Revenue productive, improving, and essential to the Support and Credit of the Nation.

In a Revenue that embraces such a Variety, it is hardly possible to introduce, at once, Regulation coextensive with the Objects. It must be a Work of Time. A practicable System must be formed upon Principle, and carried by Steps and Degrees into Execution.

In almost every Instance of Goods liable to Duties, in order to obtain the Amount, it is necessary to have recourse to Two Rules of Computation at least; in many to Five. As a Proof of the Multiplicity and Intricacy of them, we have procured from Mr. Richard Frewin, the Examiner of the Duties Inwards, and inserted in the Appendix, Examples of the Rules by which the Computation must be made, both upon the same and different Articles.

The Three Rules adopted by the Act of Charles the Second, The Tonnage, The Poundage, and The Specific Duty, are simple. The Rate per Ton, or the Value by the Measure, Number, or Weight, being given, or a certain Sum imposed upon a defined -Article, the Amount of the Duty upon any given Quantity is easily Found. These Rules should, therefore, be retained or adopted, wherever the Subject Matter is of such a Nature as to be capable of the Application. The Rules by which the Computation is made, of the Duties to be paid upon each Article, may be reduced to One, by applying the Rule to be retained or adopted, in such a Manner, as to produce

the same, or nearly the same Sum, as is produced by the Rule to be rejected.

Where the Operation produces a Fraction, as it frequently must, the Duty should be increased to an Integral. The Public stand in need of every Advantage, and the Merchant will profit by the Regulation.

Wine requiring Two Rules, and unrated French ordinary painted Paper requiring Five, to ascertain the Duties, arc Two Examples, by which the Practicability of this Regulation may be tried.

Wine is distinguished into Four Kinds: French, Portugal, Spanish, and Rhenish. French is liable to Fifteen different Duties; the rest to Thirteen. They are all Duties of Tonnage, except the Two Imposts 1779 and 1782; and, therefore, requiring only Two Rules of Computation, the one grounded upon the Quantity, the other upon the Aggregate of the subsisting Duties. By substituting Two additional Duties, of Four Pounds Seven Shillings and Sixpence each, per Ton, upon French Wine, in the Place of the Imposts, each Impost will be converted into a Tonnage, and the Amount of the Duties will continue nearly the same. The like Alteration may, with equal Facility, be made in the other Three.

The French Paper pays Fourteen Duties. The First Eight are each a Poundage upon one Value: The next Two, a Poundage upon another Value: The Eleventh is a Duty upon the Measure: The Twelfth, upon the Quantity; and the Two last are the Imposts. f

Suppose the Poundage upon the First Value to be the Rule to be retained — Twenty-two and One Half per Cent. upon the Value will give the Ninth and Tenth Duties; Twelve and One Half will give the Eleventh; One Half per Cent. the Twelfth; and Six and Five Eighths something under the Imposts: Or, suppose them to be all changed into a specific Duty upon the Measure — One Shilling and Five Pence Three Farthings per Yard, will give Seven Pounds Seven Shillings and Eleven Pence, which is something more than the present Duty upon a Ream, as stated in the Example before us.

This Substitution may sometimes be attended with Difficulty. The Rules may be grounded upon Qualities or Circumstances so widely different, that One Rule, though it may in any given Case produce the same Sum, yet in other Cases it may fail to produce the Quantum of Duty intended by the other Rule: For Instance, in the Article of Skates, the Five First Duties are each a Poundage upon the Value, taken at One Shilling and Three Pence per Dozen. In the

Impost 1690 the Value is departed from, and the Duty is laid upon the Weight of Wrought Iron, Five Shillings per Hundred. ‘ This produces, upon the Fifty-six Dozen, weighing Two Hundred, and Two Quarters, Twelve Shillings and Sixpence. Seventeen Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Two Pence per Cent. upon the Rate will produce nearly the same Sum; but, should the same Number weigh Twice as much, the substituted Rule will produce but Half the Duty intended. This Difference may be corrected by taking the mean Weight per Dozen, and producing, by the favoured Rule, the Duty arising from that Weight.

It is probable there are few Instances, where the Amount of the Duties is so nicely calculated, that a small Variation will disturb the State of the Commerce carried on in any Article.

The Management of this Revenue will derive Relief from the Simplicity introduced by this Regulation; but far more important and extensive will be the Effect, if all Distinction of Branches in the Customs can be abolished, and One entire Sum only be the Duty to bp collected upon each defined Subject of

25 Geo. III. ai° Martii. 669

Duty, and One Head of Customs comprehend the Whole of this Revenue. There will then be no longer a Necessity for that Multiplicity of Computations and Entries; One Sum will frequently stand in the Place of Fifteen, always in the Place of many, upon the Warrants, Bills, and Instruments, and in all the Cash Books and Accounts above referred to There will be an End of Appropriations of Receipts and Payments, of Branches overpaid and underpaid, and of that perpetual Violation of the Truth of the Receipt, by placing Duties received in one Branch among Duties received under another, as delivered to the Receiver General, and by him into the Exchequer; a Violation rendered unavoidable under the present System, without incurring the Danger of a much greater Evil, Confusion in the Accounts, perpetually increasing: But, above all, this Regulation, as tending to a Diminution of the Charges of Collection, co-operates to that great Object always to be kept in View, the Reduction of the Public Expences.

That the Amount of the Duty to be paid upon every Article, under every given Circumstance of Importation or Exportation, may be ascertained, the Laws continuing as they now stand, is apparent from the Books of Rates, that have from Time to Time been composed by Officers employed in the Management of this Revenue; which Books, Alterations in the Duties have rendered of no Use. Such a Composition must precede, and be the Ground of this Regulation; but this is a Work of Time and Labour: The Subjects of Commerce, with their various Modifications and Circumstances, are numerous; the Sum of the Duty upon each Species must be ascertained before it can be imposed; and a temporary Suspension of Legislative Interposition, so far as to effect a Variation in the Duties, is necessary for the Completion of the Work.

The Measure of Duty to be assumed should be that best adapted to the Nature of the Subject Matter, and that is, in general, the Measure by which the Merchant purchases and sells. If he buys and sells by the Ton, the Number, or the Weight, the Rate should be upon the Ton, the Number, or the Weight; and the Sum of Duty should be an Integral, capable of Integral Divisions.

Since the Reduction of all the Branches of these Duties to one Head seems to us practicable, as well as highly expedient, as far as it concerns the Office of the Customs, it remains for us to inquire, whether the same Reduction can be effected in the Office of the Receipt of the Exchequer.

The Legislature direct the Distinction of the Accounts, but without expressing the Reasons: We must learn them from the Construction of the several Acts. In general, an Act that imposes a Duty, appropriates that Duty to some specific Service: Whilst that Appropriation continues, a distinct Account must be kept of the Produce of the Duty, in the Offices both of the Customs and Exchequer, in order that the Sum received on that Head of Duty may be issued for the Service to which that Duty is destined by the Legislature — and because, where the Service is limited, as it generally is, if the Duty exceeds it, it is necessary to know the Quantum of the Excess, as being Public Money, whether that Excess is appropriated or not: If the Duty is deficient, it is equally necessary to know the Quantum of the Deficiency, as it must be supplied from some other Fund. Unless then all Distinction of Appropriation of the Custom Duties can be put an End to in the Exchequer, the Distinction of Accounts must continue in the Office of the Customs.

The Appropriation of a Duty to a Service, is an

Vol. 40.

Act of the Legislature, , similar to other Acts, subject Thirteenth continually to the Legislative Will and Authority, Report directed to the Public Good. The Legislature are on Public bound to provide for every Public Service as it arises, Accouats-and as long as it exists; but in what Manner, and out of what Fund, that Provision shall be at first made, and how long it shall continue the same, is in the Wisdom of Parliament. The Legislature can by no Act so connect the Provision with the Service, be that% Service what it may, but that, whenever the Public Good requires it, the Provision may be varied, blended, diminished, transferred, or abolished, by the Power that created it, provided sufficient remains for the Service, or another equally ample and secure, in the Judgment of Parliament, be substituted in its Stead.

The Supreme Power is bound to watch over, and to modify and adapt its Provisions to the Exigencies of the Times, and the Vicissitudes that must arise in the Course of human Events. Limited only by the immutable Principles of Reason and Justice, it cannot be restrained or fettered by the Acts of antecedent Legislatures; nor can it, by its own Acts, divest itself of the Right of exercising, or communicate to others any Check upon the Exercise of, this or any other Power inherent in its Nature, and essential to the Execution of that Trust, which is the sole End and Purpose of its Institution, the Promotion of the Public Good.

But, not to rest upon general Reasoning only, we examined into the Appropriations themselves, and the Power that has been exercised by the Legislature over them; and for that Purpose we procured, from the Auditor of the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, an Account of the Number of Branches under which N*6p. the Accounts of the Customs are kept in that Office, and to what Charges or Services those Branches are severally applicable. The Branches are ranged, in this Account, in the Order in which we received them from the Custom House: The Titles of them, in Use both at the Custom House and the Exchequer, are inserted; and, that we might the more easily refer to them, we have added the Numbers.

It appears, in this Account, that the Number of Heads in the Exchequer is less by Three than the Number at the Custom House. The Heads, Number Forty, and Forty-two, are omitted in the Exchequer; for the Duties collected under those Heads in the Customs, are directed by the Receiver General, upon his Payment of them into the Exchequer, to be placed to such Branches as he particularly mentions.

The Heads, Number Forty-four and Forty-five, though separate in the Customs, are blended together in the Exchequer, as arising from the same Subject, and neither of them appropriated. The Duties under the First Head, intituled " Customs," are collected under Three separate Branches; but they are paid into the Exchequer in Moieties, under the Heads of The Half Subsidies 1712 and 1714*

As many of the Duties are carried over to various Funds, that it might appear at one View what Duties are carried to each Fund, we required from the same Office, an Account to what Funds the Duties of the n°-0. Customs are carried, when paid into the Exchequer, ' and what Branches of those Duties are kept under distinct and separate Heads. This Account shews us, that Six of them are carried to the General Fund; Thirteen, and a Moiety of the Duties under the Head of Customs, to the Aggregate Fund; Six, to the South Sea Fund; and Eleven, to the Sinking Fund: That Eight are unappropriated; and the remaining Twenty-four, with the other Moiety of the Customs, are kept under distinct and separate Heads, and appropriated to specific Services.

The Appropriation of these Funds does not appear in these Accounts; and, therefore, we applied to the 8 H same

Being thus furnished with the Knowledge of the Appropriation of every Custom Duty, in the Office of the Receipt of the Exchequer, whether by itself, or in common with other Duties; and being assisted by the Information of Mr. Hughson, Clerk of the Debentures in that Office; we are enabled to form some Judgment, whether any Objection arises to this Plan of Consolidation from the Circumstance of the Appropriation.

In the Account of the Funds to which the Duties are carried, there are Three Distinctions: The Unappropriated Duties — The Duties carried over to the Compound Funds — and, Those kept under separate and distinct Heads.

The Fii*st Class, not being appropriated at all, an Account of the Produce of them is laid before Parliament some Time in every Session, and that Produce is applied to the current Services of the Year. There does not appear to us eny Reason why this Produce, being applicable every Year to whatever Service Parliament . think fit to direct; it, should not b$ received into the Exchequer as One Sum, and these Eight Branches be united and blended together under One Head.

The Duties of the Second Class, being carried over to their respective Funds, are mixed with certain other Duties, collected together from almost every Source of Revenue. The Number and Variety that compose N* 76. each Fund, appear in an Account from the Exchequer, of the several Duties of which the General, Aggregate, South Scay and Sinking Funds are respectively composed. The Duties thus brought together form in each Fund One compound Cash; out of which the Services to which the Fund is made applicable are supplied as they arise. In this Issue all Distinction of separate Appropriation is done away; there is no Connection between any one of the Services and any one of the component Branches; the entire compound Fund is made Subject to each Service separately, and to all of them tal^en together.

It is true, that the Distinction in the Receipt shews how much each Branch contributes to the common Stock for any given Period. But that Knowledge seems to be mere Matter of Curiosity; no Use is made of it; it is the Ground of no Operation of Finance; the Quantum of the Produce has no Relation to the Quantum of any particular Service: The Fund receives the Whole; and, whether it be more or less productive, equally affects every Service; if the Fund produces -enough for every Service, it is immaterial what Share each Branch contributes to it.

It is frequently necessary, for the Regulation of the Commerce upon any particular Article, to know the Annual Amount of the Duty produced by it; but that Knowledge cannot be collected from the Sum produced by any of these Branches, because the Sum paid into the Exchequer upon any Branch, does not distinguish from what Articles the Duties arise which compose that Sum; it comprehends the Aggregate of the Duties collected upon every Article that has been imported or exported, within the Time of the Collection, liable to the Duty. This Knowledge is obtained from the Inspector General of Imports and Exports, who keeps an Account of every Species of Goods, whether imported or exported; and, the Quantity of the Goods, and the Rate of the Duty, being given, the Sum of the Duty produced by it in any given Time is easily computed.

Since the Distinction of the Branches thus earned over in the Receipt of the Exchequer seems to us to be of no Use, we are of Opinion, that all the Branches of the Custom Duties, carried over to these Four Funds, and amounting together to Thirty-seven* may

be added to the Eight unappropriated branches, and the Produce of them paid as One Sum, under One Head, into the Receipt of the Exchequer.

Of the Twenty-five remaining Branches, Twenty-two are appropriated to the Payment of Annuities; One, to the Coinage; and the other Two, to the Encouragement of the Growth, One 6f Cotton in the Leeward Islands, the other of Hemp and Flax in England and Scotland.

As to the Coinage Service, the Act of the Eighteenth of Charles the Second, Chapter the Fifth, imposed Two Duties, the one on Wine, the other on Spirits, and directed the Produce to be distinguished and kept apart in the Offices both of the Customs and Exchequer, and to be applied to no other Use but that of defraying the Expence of the Mint. One of these Duties, that on Spirits, is, by the Ninth of George the Second, Chapter the Twenty-third, Section the Seventeenth, carried and appropriated to the Uses of the Aggregate Fund.

At present, the whole Produce of the remaining Branch, the Duty on Wine, is applied to the Coinage; but, this Service generally exceeding the Produce of the Duty, the Deficiency is paid out of the Supplies of the Year.

Nothing has as yet been issued of the Duties collected for the Encouragement of the Growth of Cotton in the Leeward Islands; nor has there been any Demand from England for any Part of her Share in the Produce of the other Branch. Scotland has received Payments on Account of her Share, which is Seven Fifteenths of the Produce.

It cannot be material out of what Duties these Ser^ vices are supplied:' They may, whether limited or fluctuating, be made a Charge upon any sufficient Fund, or upon that of which these Three Branches may form a Part — The Twenty-two remaining Branches are appropriated, each to the Payment of some particular Annuity, granted between the Year 1706 and the present Time.

The Public Creditors are of Two Descriptions; Bodies Corporate, and Individual Proprietors of particular Government Securities. These latter are no otherwise connected than as Proprietors of Shares in the same Fund or Annuity. At the Creation of these Annuities, the Legislature has always appropriated some existing Branches of the Public Revenue, or created some new Branches, either in the Act that grants the Annuity, or in some subsequent Act, as a Fund out of which the Annuity is to be paid. The Act of the Fifth of William and Mary, Chapter the Twentieth, which incorporated the Bank of England, and the Act of the Ninth and Tenth of William the Third, Chapter the Forty-fourth, which gave Rise to the East Ifidia. Com-

n, each imposes a Variety of new Duties; and, out e Produce, appropriates a certain Sum to the Use of those Persons who should become Subscribers to a Loan proposed to be advanced to Government, upon the Terms mentioned in the Act The Act of the Ninth of Queen Anne, Chapter the Twenty-first, which erected the South Sea Company, creates a Fund, out of Duties then existing, to answer the Annuities granted by that Act, to those Proprietors of certain Public Debts, who should subscribe them into the Stock of the Company. In all the Acts which have occurred to us, for raising Money by granting Annuities to Individuals, until within these few Years, the Funds appropriated for the Payment of the Annuities have been inserted in the same Act: But of late Years, the Annuities have been granted by one Act, and the Funds created by some subsequent Act of the same Session. In this latter Case, the Subject does not lend his Money upon the Credit of any particular Security. Ignorant what it will be, he leaves the Choice of the Fund to the Legislature, and relies for the Payment 5 of

35 Geo. III. Martii. 6ji

of his Anrtuity upon such as they shall think pro-

per to adopt.

Where the Security is coupled with the Loan in the same Act, the Subject expressly accepts the Security as held out to him, and lends his Money upon the Credit of it: And yet the Legislature, representing all the Creditors of Government, as well as the rest of the Subjects, and consulting their Good as blended with the Common Good, do retain, and must, from the Nature of its Institution, for ever retain, a Power over that Security, to be exercised at whatever Times, and in whatever Manner, the Common Good requires. The only Right vested in the Creditor, and which the Legislature cannot, without Injustice, infringe, is, the Right to the full and regular Payment of ms Annuity, and the Re-payment of his Principal according to the Terms of his Loan; and this Right subsists in ftfll Force, independent of any Appropriation. Should both the Specific and Supplemental Funds, proposed and accepted as the Securities, fail, his Right to his Principal and to his Annuity does not fail: The whole Property of the Public, the Real and Personal Estate of every Subject, the Produce of his Labour, is liable and bound to the Payment of every Debt contracted for his Defence, Security, and Protection.

If the Creditor derives, from the Act that creates the Loan, any exclusive Right to the Fund destined to the Payment of his Annuity, it must be a Right to that Fund exactly in the State in which he accepts it as his Security; for there is no Reservation or Limitation annexed to his Acceptance. Such a Right in the Creditor would exclude the Right of the Legislature, unless he consents not only.; to change the Fund, but to make any Alteration in the Duty arising from any one Article of Commerce that contributes to that Fund. On the contrary, any Principle that empowers the Legislature to Vary One of those Duties, equally empowers them to change the Fund. The only Difference is, the Degree of Violation of the Right of the Creditor in the one Case, and the Extent to which the Legislative Power is exercised in the other. The continual Exercise of this Power over the appropriated Duties, without the Consent of the Public Companies, and of the Proprietors of the Government Securities, is a Proof of the Legislative Right, and establishes the Principles upon which we have suggested this Right to be grounded.

That we might the more easily trace the Alterations that have been made in the Duties appropriated for the Annual Payments of the Sums granted to the Public Companies, at their First Creation, to answer the Interest of the Debts contracted by them with Government, we procured from the Auditor of the Receipt of N#77. the Exchequer, an Account of the several Duties out of which the Annuities of the Bank, South Sea Company, and East India Company, on Account of their Stock, are severally paid. To enumerate the Variety of Changes that have from Time to Time been made in them is needless; a few Instances are sufficient for our Purpose.

The Act that incorporates 4he Bank of England, imposes a Tonnage Duty on Ships, and an Excise Duty on Beer and other Liquors, and charges this compound Fund with the Annual Payment of One hun-£. 100,000. dred thousand Pounds to the Use of the Company. In Three Yearn after, by the Seventh and Eighth of WilSam the Third, Chapter the Thirty-first, the Tonnage Duty is taken off, and another substituted in the Place.

The Act of the Seventh of Anne, Chapter the Se-vehthj appropriates the Two Thirds Subsidy, and certain Dufies on Coffee and other Articles, imposed by former Acts, to the Annuity payable upon the enlarged Capital of the Bank of England. — The Act of the

Great Raisins is an Article liable to the same Duties. The Act of the Fourteenth of His present Majesty, Chapter the Seventy-fourth, reduces the Rate payable upon the Importation of them, from One Pound Ten Shillings, to Ten Shillings only, per Hundred Weight, without substituting any other Duty in its Stead, and consequently diminishes the Security pledged for the Payment of all those Services to which the Three Subsidies above mentioned are made liable.

By an Act of the last Session, Chapter the Sixteenth, the additional Duty of One per Cent, and Part of the Aliens Duty, both of them Parts of the Branch of Customs, are discontinued, and no Duty imposed to supply the Place of them.

The Officer will, by these Means, be relieved from all Computation upon this Article; and his Entries will be rendered simple. One Sum may be paid into the Exchequer, under the same Head of Subsidy on Spirits, and the Whole carried, as the Produce of Five of the Branches is now, to the Aggregate Fund; and the Deficiencies that may arise from thence, in the Funds Of which these Six last Duties now form a Part, may be charged upon the Aggregate Fund, just in the same Manner as the Deficiencies in the Funds to which the Five first were applicable now stand charged by the same Act.

No Reason occurs to us, why the same Steps may not be taken with regard to Wine, Tea, Sugar, Tobacco, Linen, Salt, Coals, and any other extensive and productive Subjects of the Custom Duties. The proper Rule of Computation may be established; the Aggregate of the Duties obtained; the Sum paid into the Exchequer, under the Head of the Duties upon that particular Article, and carried to the Sinking Fund; and that Fund be made liable to such Deficiencies as may be occasioned by this Alteration. — The Office of the Customs will find immediate Benefit from such a Regulation; and the Plan will be continually approaching nearer to its Completion.

If the Principles on which we have endeavoured to establish this Consolidation of the Custom Duties be well founded, they lead to a still more important and extensive Regulation.

We cannot presume to pronounce, without a previous Examination, that they can be applied to such other Offices of the Revenue as are perplexed with a Multiplicity of distinct Accounts; but it is highly probable, that Distinction, in every Office, is, for the most Part, rendered necessary upon the same Ground of Appropriation; and if so, it may upon the same Principles be abolished. This will open the Way to a great Measure of Financial Regulation — to the Introduction of the most simple of all Modes of Account into the Depository of the Public Treasure — the Formation of One Fund, into which shall flow every Stream of the Public Revenue, and from whence shall issue the Supply for every Public Service.

The Public Creditor may safely rely upon this Fund for the Payment of his Annuity: The Excess of it will be the same as the Excess of the Sinking Fund would be, were that Fund to continue in its present State.

How far the Produce of the Sinking Fund has exceeded the Charges upon it, appears from the* Account N°79. of the Surplusses for these last Ten Years. The Sum therein stated as the Surplus of the last Year is incom-£.1,600,000. plete: It amounted to above One million Six hundred thousand Pounds more; which Sum has been issued to supply the Deficiencies of the Taxes for Five Quarters, occasioned in Part from the Interest of the Loans often taking Place long before the Taxes raised for the Payment of the Annuities commenced, and still longer before any Part of them were received — and in Part from the Unproductiveness of other Duties. The Usage has been, to replace these Deficiencies to the Sinking Fund from the Supplies of the Year.

Thus, One great Fund of Revenue, composed of the Annual Income of the State, will be the ample Security Vol. 40.

Martii. 73

to every Public Creditor for the Payment of his An- Thirteentk nuity; and the collateral Security to that Fund, the Report Property of the Nation. on PuWlc

This Plan is consistent with every Distinction of Ac- Accounts, count in the Exchequer, that may be necessary to preserve the Knowledge of the Produce of each of the several leading Branches of Revenue, and the Quantum and Circumstances of the Issue for any particular Service.

There is no Danger of confounding the Receipts, or of the Issues exceeding the Sums voted or appropriated to each Service.

We have confined this Inquiry to the Collection of the Duties in the Office of the Customs, the Payment of them into the Exchequer, and the Manner in which the Accounts of them are kept in both Offices.

What remains, and will be the next Object of our Examination, is the Diminution of the Produce of these Duties by the Charges of Management; which, though a Branch of the same Subject, is capable of a distinct and separate Consideration. The Objects it involves are numerous, and of Moment to the Public: The Investigation must, from the Nature of them, require much Time and Attention. Had we waited until that Investigation could have been completed, our Report, already sufficiently voluminous, must have been delayed to a distant Period: And, should the Materials we have thus collected be deemed a sufficient Ground for the Exertion of the Wisdom of Parliament, the Public might have been deprived of the early Benefit of Regulation essential to the Security and good Management of their Revenue, and to the Facility and Accuracy of their Accounts, in Two of their most important Offices.

APPENDIX.

N# 1.

The Examination of Charles Harris, Esquire,

Deputy Auditor of the Imprest; taken upon Oath, 30th June, 7th and 9th July, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That the Materials sent to the Auditor of the Imprest, by the Receiver General of the Customs, from whence his Account is made out, are — a Book of Account, containing Entries of all his Receipts and Payments, under every Head of Duty —

Books containing Entries of the Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills — the Quarterly Establishments — Lists of Salaries and Allowances — and, a List of the Tallies, with the Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills — Receipts of the Parties, or their Agents or Assigns — and Tallies.

The Charge upon the Receiver General consists of — the Balance remaining due on the preceding Account, either in Money, or unsatisfied Bonds and Imprest Orders — and, of the Money and Bonds received by him, during the Time of the Account. —

The Auditor charges the Receiver General with this Sum, in consequence of an Account, delivered by the Controller General to the Auditor, containing a Charge upon the Receiver General, of all the Sums received by him, in Money and Bonds, during the Time of the Account, upon the several Branches of the Customs. This Account is signed by the Controller General, and sworn to by him, before a Baron of the Exchequer; and upon the Authority of this 8 I Account

Thirteenth Report on Pnbiic Accounts.

21 ° Martii. A* 1785.

Account, the Auditor charges the Receiver General, after examining and seeing that the Totals, under each Head of Duty, agree with the Account of the Receiver General.

The Vouchers for the Discharge are — Tallies — the Quarterly Establishments — Debentures — Certificates — Portage Bills — Treasury Warrants — Orders of the Commissioners — and, the Receipts of the Parties.

The Sums paid by the Receiver General into the Exchequer, are vouched by the Tallies; the Number of Tallies for the Year of this Account is One thousand Five hundred and Twenty-four. The Receiver General produces a Receipt for every Payment. The Authority for every Payment is either entered in the Office, or produced by him.

The Authority for the Payments, upon the Quarterly Establishments in the Port of London, is the Warrant of the Treasury, annexed to the List; that for the Payment of the Patent Officers in the Port of London> and for some at the Out Ports, and in the Plantations, is the Patents themselves, entered in the Auditor’s Office.

W'here a Payment is made pursuant either to a Treasury Warrant, or the Order of the Commissioners of the Customs, the Warrant or Order must be produced. Payments for Incident Charges and Allowances must be certified by the Controller General, and allowed by the Commissioners of the Customs.

The Authority for allowing the Payment of the Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills, is the Signature of Four Commissioners of the Customs; they all contain the Signature of various other Officers, but whether they are such Officers as the Instruments Vequire, the Auditor of the Imprest can have no Cognizance. The Vouchers are all compared with the Entries of those Payments in their respective Books, and the Totals of the Payments under each Branch of Duty in those Books, are compared with the Entries of the like Totals in the Receiver General’s Book of Account.

It is no Part of the Business of the Auditor, to take Notice out of what Fund the Payment is made; nor can he form any Judgment at what Rate the Computation is made upon the Receipt of any Duty: There are certain Officers in the Customs appointed to that Service. After this Examination, the Account is reduced into the Official Form: The Articles in the Charge are similar to those in the Account of the Receiver General ;* the Articles in the Discharge are ranged in a Manner different from the Arrangement in his Account. The Accountant ranges his Payments under the Heads of Duty out of which they are made; the Auditor, according to the Usage of his Office, ranges them either under Heads of Service, or from the Authority under which they are paid, or the Instruments by which they are paid. The Balance being found to agree, the Receiver General swears to the Truth of his Account before a Baron of the Exchequer. The Attestation is wrote at the Foot of the Account of that Branch of the Duties called the Customs, for there the Balance of the whole Account appears; every other Duty being balanced in his Book of Account, and the Balance paid by him into the Exchequer. The Account is then passed through the several Offices of the Treasury and Exchequer.

N# 2.

The Examination of Charles Harris, Esquire, Deputy Auditor of the Imprest; taken upon Oath, August 2d, 3d, 10th, 13th, 17th, and 20 th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That the Materials received by the Auditor of the Imprest, from the Controller General of the Customs, from whence the Auditor forms his Account, are, First, The General Book of Account, which comprehends the Totals of the Annual Receipts and Payments of all the Collectors in London, and at the Out Ports, during the Period of the Account, with the Debts depending, and Overpayments, both of the Year preceding the Account, and of the Year under Examination; all arranged under their separate and respective Heads of Duties.

Secondly, The London Accounts, which are Books containing Weekly Accounts of the Receipts of the Duties in the Port of London by each Collector, with his Payments to the Receiver General.

Thirdly, The Quarterly Accounts of each Collector at the Out Ports, which contain his Receipts of Duties during the Quarter, but neither his Remittances to the Receiver General, nor his Payments over to other Collectors.

Fourthly, The Receipt Book, which comprehends Entries of the Totals of the Weekly Receipts of every Duty in the Port of London, and of the Quarterly Receipts by the Collectors at the Out Ports.

Fifthly, Accounts of Payments by the several Collectors, under particular Heads.

Sixthly, A Book, containing Entries of all the Payments for Salaries and Incidents, by all the Out Port Collectors.

Seventhly, Separate Debenture, Certificate, and Portage Bill Books, with the Vouchers for all the Payments.

The Charge upon the Controller General consists of, First, The Arrears depending upon the Receivers and Collectors, at the Foot of the preceding Account; each Article contains the Total Sum in Arrear, of Monfey and Bonds, under each Head of Duty, and is taken from the preceding Account.

Secondly, The Money received, and Bonds given, for the Duties during the Year of the Account.

Thirdly, The Over-payments, or Sums paid by them during the Year of the Account, more than they have received under the several Heads of Duties.

The Discharge contains, First, The Over-payments, or Sums appearing to be due to the Collectors upon the several Heads of Duties, at the Foot of the preceding Account, and are taken from that Account.

Secondly, The Money remitted to, and accounted for by, the Receiver General.

Thirdly, The Money paid for Salaries and Incidents at the Out Ports.

Fourthly, The Allowance of Four Pence in the Pound for collecting the Coinage Duty.

Fifthly, Payments upon Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills.

Sixthly, The Balance, consisting of Arrears in Money and Bonds, remaining due from the several Collectors.

The Charge upon the Controller General of the Sum received in Money and Bonds during the Year, is taken from the Receipt Book. The Articles in that Receipt Book are taken from the London and Quarterly Accounts; these Accounts are signed by certain Officers, generally by the Collector and Controller of the Duty; upon this Signature, and the Oath of the £ Accountant,

Accountant, the Auditor relies for the Truth of this Charge.

The Article of Over-payments is copied from the Controller General’s Book of Account; the Auditor relies upon his Oath for the Truth of it. Frequently Collectors receive Money and Bonds from other Collectors; of this the Auditor has no Cognizance, but from the Entries in the Controller General’s Account, in which the Money and Bonds received from, and paid to, other Collectors, are Two Heads; the Auditor, in forming the Official Account, charges and discharges the Collectors of these Sums, as he finds them entered in the General Account, upon the Authority of the Controller General; these Payments to other Collectors occasion a Variation in the Overpayments, and prevent die Auditor from checking the m.

In the Discharge, the Vouchers for the Salaries at each Out Port are, the Quarterly Establishments, signed by Four Commissioners. The Vouchers for the Incidents are, a List of the Payments, with the Bills annexed; this List includes the Salaries, and is sworn to by the Collector before his Controller. An Abstract both of the Salaries and Incidents is signed by the Controller General, and allowed by Two Commissioners; each Voucher must have a Receipt.

The Allowance for the Coinage Duty, being Four Pence in the Pound on the Sum collected, is computed upon the Sum charged to be received for that Duty in the Receipt Book.

The Vouchers for the Payments upon Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills, are, the Instruments themselves, properly authenticated.

The Auditor examines and forms the Account in the following Manner: —

In the Charge, he compares the Entries of the Ar* tides of the Receipt in the London and Out Port Accounts, with the correspondent Entries in the Receipt Book.

In the Discharge, the Vouchers for the Salaries and Incidents are compared with the Entries in the Lists, which are cast up and computed, and the Totals compared with the Entries of those Totals in the General Salary and Incident Book, and those Entries with the corresponding Entries in the General Book of Account. — The Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills, are compared with the Entries in their respective Books; the Totals in those Books are cast up, and compared with the Entries in the Controller General’s Account; this Account being found to be right, the Auditor reduces it into the Official Form.

In the Charge, the Entry of the Arrears in the Account depending consists of the Totals of the Arrears of each Duty; but the Entry of them at the Foot of the preceding Account contains also the Debts due from each Collector on each Head of Duty: These Arrears are either Debts due from the Collectors in Office, or from Collectors enumerated in the Even and Dormant Schedules, entered upon Accounts of former Years; or from the Collectors enumerated in the Open or Fluctuating Schedule, at the Foot of the preceding Account.

The Articles that compose the Sum received by the Collectors in Money and Bonds during the Year, are taken from the General Account: The Entries of the Over-payments are taken from the same Account. In the Discharge, the Entry of the Overpayments is taken from the last Article in the Charge of the preceding Account, with this Difference; — in that Account is entered the Over-payments of each Collector upon each Head of Duty, but in the Account depending, the Entry is the Total of the Overpayments upon each Head of Duty only. This Examinant saith, That he is Assistant to Tl’ll* liam Mellish, Esquire, the Receiver General of the Customs; he has been about Thirty-two Years in the Office of the Receiver General, and Two Years Assistant; he settled the Account of the Receiver General of the Customs for the Year 1781, and transmitted it to the Auditors of the Imprest. The Sum with which the Receiver General stands charged, consists of Cash — unsatisfied Bonds — and, Imprest Orders. The Bonds are to the King, payable to the Receiver General, and given for Duties on Tobacco. An Imprest Order, is the Order of the Commissioners to the Receiver General to advance a Sum on Account, with the Receipt of the Person to whom it is issued, annexed. Neither the Bonds nor Imprest Orders are sent to the Auditor, and therefore the Receiver General is charged with the Amount of them as Cash. — All the Money in the Hands of the Receiver General arises either from Payments made to him by the Collectors of the Customs, or from Bonds or Bills discharged; the Bonds in his Custody he receives from the Collector Inwards in the Port of London. — The Collectors in the Port of London are making Daily Payments, and every Saturday send to the Receiver General an Account of the whole Sum they have paid in during the Week, distributed under its proper Heads of Duty. — The Collectors at the Out Ports remit to him their Receipts in Bills or Notes, and generally with an Account under what Heads of Duties the Money is to be placed. — The Account sent to

The Sums paid into the Exchequer by the Receiver General are ranged under their respective Heads of Duties. — Debentures for Drawbacks and Bounties are sometimes paid by the Collectors pursuant to the Orders of the Commissioners, in which Case the Collectors pay those Debentures to the Receiver General as Cash. After the Year’s Account is completed, it is sent to the Office of the Controller General, and the Charge upon the Receiver General is checked by him, and each Article marked off.

Every Saturday the Total Sum of Cash received by the Receiver General during that Week is paid into the Bank, and placed to his Account: A Certificate of such Receipts as can be applied, and of the Payments during that Week, is laid before the Lords of the Treasury and the Commissioners of the Customs, upon the Tuesday following; and on the Wednesday the Balance is paid into the Exchequer.

Where a Sum advanced by the Receiver General upon an Imprest Order is expended, the Person wrho has received the Imprest produces to the Receiver General a Bill for the Services performed by him, the Amount of which is certified by the Controller General; he gives a Receipt for that Amount, and takes back the Imprest Order, and the Bill is the Voucher for the Re

on Account of the Customs; and where his Receipt exceeds his Expenditure, he remits the Balance to the Receiver General. — Every Collector in the Port of London delivers to the Controller General-a Weekly Account of his Receipts and Payments: The Rule of the Office is, to deliver every Tuesday the Accounts of the preceding Week. The Collectors at the Out Ports remit their Receipts to the Receiver General by Bills and Notes; the Controller at the Out Ports sends at the same Time, or soon after, an Abstract of the same Bills or Notes to the Controller General; by these Means he has full Knowledge of all the Sums paid into the Hands of the Receiver General. — Every Saturday the Receiver General sends to the Controller General an Abstract of the Money received by him, by Bills turned into Cash, to the preceding Tuesday inclusive; this Abstract is examined, and sent back to the Receiver General; — every Tuesday he delivers to the Board this Abstract, and a Certificate of all his Receipts to the Saturday preceding, inclusive, containing Money, Bonds, and Money arising from Bonds or Bills discharged, together with his Payments, all digested under the proper Heads of Duties; this Certificate is signed by him, and delivered with the Abstract to the Controller General: Thus, by the Accounts of the Collectors and Controllers, and by the Admission of the Receiver General, a complete Annual Charge, containing an Account of the Total Sum received by him from every Collector, under each Head of Duty, is formed against him, and sent by the Controller General to the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest. — The Con-

The Sums with which every Collector stands charged are, Debts in Money and Bonds, under each Head of Duty, depending at the End of the preceding Yean The Debt in Money is either the Balance remaining in his Hands, or remitted by him to the Receiver General by Bill not due; thq Bonds are those given for Duties by the Merchants, and remaining in his Custody at the End of the Year — the Money and Bonds received by him from the Merchants during the Year — the Interest he receives on those Bonds — and the Money and Bonds he receives from other Collectors. The Sums of which he discharges himself are, the Over-payments made by him on each Head of Duty in the Account of the preceding Year. — An Over-payment is, the Balance due to him upon that Head of Duty, that is, where he has paid, on Account of a Duty, more than he has received — Payments made by him for Salaries, Incidents, on Debentures, and Certificates — Remittances to the Receiver General — and Money and Bonds delivered to other Collectors.

The Money received, and the Bonds taken, by a Collector in the Port of London, appear from the Account made up and signed by him every Week. The Account of the Collector Inwards is countersigned by the Surveyor General, or Surveyor, and by the Controller and Examiner of the Port of London — ^That of the Collector Outwards is countersigned by all the same Officers, except the Examiner — The Account of the Collector of Coals is countersigned by his Controller and Examiner; and those of the Collectors of Wool and Leather, and of White Woollen Cloths, are countersigned by their respective Controllers, the Surveyor General, or Surveyor. The Controller General relies upon the Countersignature of the Accounts of these Collectors, that they contain all the Money and Bonds received by them. The Money and Bonds received by a Collector at the Out Ports appear by his Quarterly Account, signed by him, and sometimes by his Controller, and by a similar Quarterly Account sent up, and signed by the Controller at the same Port. The Collectors Account is examined, and an Abstract made of it, by the Examiner, who signs and sends it to the Surveyor of the Out Ports; he compares it with the Controllers Account, which is sent to him, and signs the Abstract; this Abstract, so signed, is the Authority for the Controller General to charge the Collector.

The Weekly Accounts of the Collectors in the Port of London, and the Quarterly Books of the Collectors of the Out Ports, are sent to the Auditors of the Imprest, as Vouchers for the Charge upon the Controller General.

The only Collector in the Port of London who makes Payments, is the Collector Inwards; he pays Debentures for Drawbacks and Bounties, and Certificates for Over-entries and Damages. Every Debenture and Certificate payable by him, or by the Receiver General, or by the Collectors at the Out Ports, requires the Signature of various Officers, and, if payable by the Receiver General, must be signed by Four Commissioners of the Customs — The Collectors pay it pursuant to the Directions of the several Acts of Parliament. The Authority for the Payments made by the Collectors at the Out Ports is the Establishments sent to them every Quarter, signed by Four Commissioners, or Orders for particular Payments, signed in the like Manner; these Establishments and Orders, with the Receipts of the Persons entitled, are the Vouchers for the Collectors; they are transmitted to the Board, examined by the proper Officers, and delivered to the Controller General, and aje his Vouchers to the Auditor.

The Examination of Mr. Joshua Powell i taken upon Oath, August 6th, nth, 17th, and 20th>

1784.

This Examinant saith, That in the Account of the Controller General, the Receiver General is charged with all the Bonds remaining in his Custody at the End of the preceding Year, and with the Bonds received by him during the Year of the Account, and with the Interest received on those Bonds; he is discharged by the Sum he receives from the Bonds paid off: The Sum of Bonds remaining in his Custody at the End of the preceding Year is taken from the last Account; the Sum of Bonds received by him during the Year is taken from the Account of the Collector Inwards, who is the only Collector that delivers Bond? to him. The Controller General knows what the Total of the Bonds amounts to upon each Duty, but he is ignorant of the particular Circumstances of each Bond; many of them appear to be of a long Date: The Sum due upon Bonds in the Hands of the Receiver General for the New Subsidy, which expired the First of August 1714, is Ten thousand Six hundred and Sixteen Pounds Nineteen- Shillings and Four Pence Halfpenny; the Total Sum due on Bonds for this Duty, in the Hands of all the Collectors, including the Receiver General, is Thirty-seven thousand Five hundred and Fifty-four Pounds Sixteen Shillings and One Penny Halfpenny. The Receiver General is placed among the Collectors in the Account of the Controller General, as accountable for the Bonds he receives, and the Interest paid on those Bonds, because, by receiving the Bonds, he stands in the Place of the Collector from whom he receives them; and the General Account comprehends an Account of all the Bonds due for the Customs in the Hands of every Accountant, and for every Branch.

The Money and Bonds received from other Collectors consist either of Money paid to a Collector by other Collectors, pursuant to Orders of the Board, or Money or Bonds received from his Predecessor, or his Representatives.

Every Collector is subject to be called upon for the Payment of Drawbacks upon certain Foreign Goods exported; in some Articles the Drawback is for the whole Duty, in some for a Part: He may be also called upon for Bounties upon certain Goods imported or exported. He may be called upon for these Payments when he has no Money in his Hands liable to those Payments, but. has Money sufficient upon other Branches of Duties: The Consequence of

his making such a Payment is, he becomes indebted to that Branch out of which he makes the Payment, and has Credit on that Branch out of which it ought to have been paid, if he had been in Cash upon that Branch^-rthis is called an Over-payment. Hence almost every Collector has an Account of Over-payments, and Debts depending, though he may have remitted the Balance of his Cash to the Receiver General; and upon his Death or Resignation his Accounts of the different Branches of the Duties will not be balanced, though. he may not be indebted to Government: Thus almost every Collector, from a remote Period, has an Account of Over-Payments and Debts depending still open in the Customs; and this Account has been constantly accumulating and increasing, in Proportion to the Increase of the Number of Branches of Duties: To prevent the swelling the General Account, by inserting this Account of each Collector dead or out of Office under each Head of Duty, they are inserted in Three Schedules; One of them, called an Even Schedule, comprehends a Set of Collectors, in which the Sum of the Over-payments of each is balanced by the Sum of their Debts depending; the last Even Schedule was formed in the Year 1776, and contains the Names of One hundred and Forty-four Collectors: The Second, called The Dormant Schedule, includes those Collectors whose Over-payments are not balanced by their Debts depending, which Debts are principally considered as desperate; this Schedule is also dated in 1776, and contains the Names of Two hundred and Forty-four Collectors: The Fluctuating Schedule contains the rest of the Collector^ who are dead, and their Accounts either not Even, or, if Even, not yet transferred to the Even Schedule, and those Collectors in Office, so far as they have had no Transactions under particular Heads of Duties during the Year of the Account; this Schedule is formed every Year.

A Debenture for a Drawback or a Bounty is made out, and generally paid at the Port from whence the Goods are exported: If it is a Debenture for a Drawback, and the Collector has no Money on that Head of Duty, he pays it out of ftuch Duties as are in his Hands, at his own Option.

In general, the Act that gives a Bounty upon the Exportation of any Goods, directs out of what Duty that Bounty shall be paid; sometimes it directs the Bounty to be paid out of any Money in the Hands of the Collector. There are Five Branches, called The Excepted Branches, Three on Coals, and Two on (Coinage, out of which po Bounties should properly be paid; the Duties on Coals are considered neither as Exports new Imports, but as Duties paid Coast-wjse, and therefore no Bounty is to be paid opt of them: The Coinage Duties, being originally laid for the special Purpose of the Mint, are likewise exr cepte<D but if the Collector has no other Money in his Hands than what has arisen from the excepted Branr ches, he would pay the Bounty out of them, in which Case the Controller would correct his Account, by making him indebted upon the excepted Branch, for the Sqm he has paid, and overpaid upon that Branch liable to the Bounty. Many of the Ports are called Negative Ports, the Duties there collected not being sufficient to defray the Expences; this renders it necessary for the Board to order Money to be remitted to them from other Collectors. The Usage is, to send to the Collector that wants Money, an Order or Draft upon the Collector Inwards of the Port of London, payable to the Collector at the Out Port: This Order is negotiable, and when paid by the Collector Inwards is his Voucher to the Controller General, who keeps it in his Possession, and does not send it to the Auditor: the Auditor has no Knowledge of this Transaction, nor is it necessary he should, 7

provided the Two Heads in the General Account of Money and Bonds received, and Money and Bond* delivered over, are Even.

The Controller General admits the Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills, upon the Authority and Signature of the Examiner; he admits the Payment of the established Salaries, upon the Authority of the Establishments themselves, signed by Four Commissioners; and of Lists of all the Payments, with the Receipts annexed, signed and sworn to by the Collector before, his Controller, who signs his Name to it; and for each incidental Payment above Forty Shillings, an Order must be produced, signed by Four Commissioners. After the Articles in the Quarterly Account have been examined by the Con* troller General, he signs to the Amount of the Iisf, and Two Commissioners sign the Allowance of it No other Account is passed of the Remittances, either of the Duties received in Scotland or in the Plantations, except that, in the Account of the jRe-eeiver General, he is charged by the Controller General with the Sums he receives for these Duties during die

The Collectors at the Out Ports, and in the Plantations, and the Receiver General in Scotland, send no Account to this Office of their Remit* tances to the Receiver General. — The Supervisor generally every Quarter compares the Entries of the Payments of the Receiver General, by virtue of Treasury Warrants, or Orders of the Commissioners, with the Vouchers, and signs his Name to each of them, as a Certificate to the Auditor that they have been examined by him. N* 11.

The Examination of William Suckling, Esquire; taken upon Oath, 12th and 22d of November, and 1st December, 1784.

This Examinant saith. That he is Deputy Collector of the Duties Inwards in the Port of London; he holds his Office by Deputation from Sir Banks Jenkinson, the Collector Inwards; he has been Deputy Collector about Twelve Years.

All the Duties Inwards are collected by Three Receivers, under and subject to the Controul of the Deputy Collector; One is the Receiver of the Grand Receipt, that is, of all the Duties Inwards, except the Duties arising from Imports from the Plantations, and from Wine, each of which has a separate Receiver, by reason of the Magnitude of the Revenue arising from them, and the Quantity of Business they occasion. The Duties are paid by the Merchant, either to the proper Receiver, or to the Receiver General, and usually after they have been computed by some known Officer belonging to the Customs; sometimes they are paid to the Receiver General by the Merchant or his Agent, without the Intervention of the Receiver.

If the Duty is paid to the Receiver, the Merchant produces to him the Warrant and the Six Bills, with the Duties computed on One Bill; this Computation must appear upon the Face of it to have been made by some known Officer, or marked by the Clerk of the Rates: The Receiver receives the Duties, enters them in Figures upon the Warrant, under their several Branches, signs his Name to the Total, retains the Bill, and delivers the Warrant and the other Five Bills to the Clerk of the Warrants; sometimes the Receiver requests the Merchant to pay the Duties to the Receiver General, and upon Production of his Receipt enters the Duties upon the Warrant. Where the Merchant pays the Duties to the Receiver General, before he applies to the proper Receiver, he relies upon the Accuracy of his own Computation as to the Payment in, but must procure the Computation, either of the proper Officer, or of the Clerk of the Rates, before he produces his Warrant, Bills, and Receipt, to the Receiver.

When the Business of the Day is closed, the Receiver is bound by his Instructions to pay into the Office of the Receiver General all the Cash he has received during the Day, reserving only enough to answer such Demands as he is informed are likely soon to be made upon him, on Account of the Revenue; these Daily Payments to the Receiver General are Payments on A\ccount.

On the last Day of every Week every Receiver appropriates the Total Sum paid on his Account to the Receiver General during the Week, under the proper Branches: This Appropriation is signed by the Receiver and the Cashier of the Receiver General.

The Receiver enters from his Bill, in his Cash Book, the Duties he has received on every Warrant, under their several Branches. As often as the Business will permit, the Controller, the Surveyor, the Surveyor General, and the proper Examiner, bring to the Office of each of the Three Receivers their several Cash Books, containing Entries of the Duties, similar to those in the Cash Books of the Receivers; each Article is read by One of them, whilst the others attend to their own Entries: After this Examination each Receiver and Check cast up to a Total the Daily Receipt of each Branch; from these Daily Totals a Weekly Total is formed every Week of each Branch, and One Total formed of the several Branches; and these several Totals are compared and examined in like Manner as the separate Articles of the' Daily Receipt.

Vol. 40.

In the Grand Receipt, where the Duties are so numerous, the Number of Daily Warrants so great, and the Computation so varied, Errors in the Computation must frequently arise; he believes seldom a Day passes but there is some Difference in the Computation of the different Checks; where the Difference appears, tha Article is marked to be re-computed.

The Payments made by the Receivers are — Sums to the Receiver General — certain Debentures paid by them, and taken as Cash by the Receiver General — and certain other Debentures paid by them, and delivered to the Controller General, as Vouchers in their Accounts with him- — and Imprest Orders by the Receiver of the Wine Duties.

After the Weekly Accounts are agreed, the Receiver draws up an Account, with a Duplicate of the Weekly Receipt, which comprehends the Weekly Totals under each Branch, and the Payments during the Week, which include the Weekly Totals paid to the Receiver General under each Branch, and the Debentures delivered up to the Controller General: This Account and Duplicate are signed by the Receiver, the Computer, the Examiner, and some One other of the Checks; the Account is sent to the Controller General, and the Duplicate to the Controller of the Receiver General’s Issues; the Signature of the Receiver goes to both Sides of the Account, the Signature of the rest to the Charge only.

The Deputy Collector has under him Six Officers, holding their Appointments by Deputation from the Patent Collector Inwards. — These Six Officers are, the Clerk of the Ship’s Entries, the Clerk of the Rates, the Three Receivers, and the Clerk of the Certificates; each of these has the same Powers with the Deputy Collector, and acts for the Patentee, in the same Manner as the Deputy Collector. — The Report of the Captain of a Vessel is always sworn to before, and signed by, One of these Deputies, and One of his Checks.

The Weekly Account of each of the Three Receivers, after it has been signed by the several Checks, is brought to the Deputy Collector; the Total Sums received and paid, are entered from this Account in his Cash Book, and he transmits the Account to the Controller General. — Every Quarter the Deputy Collector examines the Balance Books of the Receivers, in which Books the Receipts and Payments of every Branch during the Quarter are brought to a Balance, and the Difference between the Sum of the Receipts and the Sum of the Payments in each Branch, must agree with the Balance of his Cash Book.

The only Bonds taken by the Receiver of the Grand Receipt, are the East India Company’s Bonds. For every Ship the Company enter into Four Bonds; One for the rated Duties, payable in Twelve Months, by equal Half Yearly Payments; One for the unrated Duties; One for the 18 per Cent. on Muslins; and the Fourth for the 15 per Cent. on Callicoes: These Three payable within stated Times after the Sales of the specific Goods. After the Goods are landed, the Surveyor of the East India Company’s Warehouses sends to the Collector the Warrant, signed by Eight Officers, containing those Circumstances, relative tq the Goods landed, that are essential to the Computation of the Duties; the Bills for the Receiver and Checks are sent by the Company; the Warrant and Bills pass the Offices in the usual Manner: These Bonds are retained by the Collector, until the Duties are paid by the Company, unless delivered over by the Order of the Board to the Solicitor, to be put in Force.

The only Bonds taken by the Receiver of the Plantation Duties, are Tobacco Bonds. After the Duties for the Quantity of Tobacco specified in the Warrant have been computed, and entered upon the Warrant and Bills, the Bond is given for the Sum of the Duties, payable within Fifteen Months from the Ship’s

Report;

Thirteenth Report on Public Accounts.

684 - ai MarA. 11$5,

Thirteenth Report; if paid before, a Discount is allowed for prompt Payment:. This Receiver delivers the Bond to Accounts! the Receiver General. ' His Weekly Account contains separate Accounts of the Duties he has received in Cash, and the Bonded Duties, and in his Discharge the Duties he has paid, and the Bonds he has delivered to the Receiver General; these are the only Receipts and Payments in his Weekly Account; the Collector enters these Totals in his Cash Book. The Discharge in the Weekly Account of the Receiver of the Plantation Receipt contains his Payments to the Receiver General only. The Discharge of the Receiver of the Wine Duties contains also the Money he has paid upon Imprest Orders, and these are his only Payments.

After the Sales of the unrated Goods, for which the Bonds are given by the India Company, and deposited with the Collector Inwards, the Duties are computed and entered upon the Warrants and Bills, and paid to the Receiver of the Grand Receipt: Upon the Certificate of the Computer and Controller, that all the Goods contained in the Warrant have been sold, and the Duties brought to Account in the Kings Books, the Collector delivers up the Bond.

W. Suckling.

N# 12.

The Examination of Mr. James Deacon; taken upon Oath, November 24th, and 29th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Receiver of the Grand Receipt under the Collector Inwards; he has been in this Office from October 1771; he holds it by Deputation from the Patentee. He receives the Duties either from a known Officer in the Long Room, or from the Merchant, in consequence of a Bill being produced to, and left with him, on which the Duties appear to be computed either by the Clerk of the Rates, or some known Officer: The Duties upon the Bill are computed according to the Rule in Use at the Custom House, but he enters them in his Cash Book in the Net Sums, under the different Heads. Sometimes the Merchant himself pays his Duties into the Treasury, and produces to the Receiver the Receipt of the Receiver General. The Treasury closes at Two o'Clock; before that Time the Receiver pays into it, generally, all the Duties he has received during the Day, retaining only such a Sum as he is informed, or has Reason to believe, will be soon demanded of him on Account of Debentures. The Receiver, to accommodate the Merchants, continues at his Office until Three, or later; the Duties he receives after Two he retains until the next Day. All his Daily Payments to the Receiver General are Payments on Account of the Duties, and consist of Cash, and Debentures paid in as Cash; these Payments are examined and agreed every Day, by a Clerk in each Office; at the End of the Week the Total Sum paid’ in during the Week is appropriated by the Receiver in Concert with the Receiver General, who frequently wanting a Sum under some particular Branch, for the Regulation of his own Accounts, desires the Receiver to appropriate, out of the Duties he has paid in, the Sum he wants to that particular Branch; the remaining Sum he^ divides among the remaining Branches; in the succeeding Week the Branch so overpaid has a less Sum appropriated to it, in consequence of the former Over-payment: This Weekly Appropriation is signed by the Receiver, examined, and agreed by a Clerk in the Receiver Generals Office, and left with him.

The Receiver every Week pays in, as near as he can, the Balance of the Duties remaining in his Hands, and draws out an Abstract comprehending all his Receipts, and his Payments to the Receiver General, during the Week; the Receipts contain the Daily Totals under each Branch, and each Branch is cast up to a Total, and One Total formed from the Brandies.

The only Payments in this Abstract are those to the Receiver General, except at the End of the Quarter, when the Abstract of the last Week contains also those Debentures either for Drawbacks or Bounties, which have not been paid in as Cash to the Receiver General, and have been paid by the Receiver during the Quarter, appropriated under their several Branches: Some Debentures are paid indiscriminately, either by the Collector Inwards, or the Receiver General, at the Option of the Merchant; some must be paid by the Receiver, because the Receiver General has no Branch open for the Appropriation; some must be paid by the Receiver General, because the Controller General, who passes the Account of the Receiver, has no Branch open: The Receiver signs this Weekly Abstract, and a Duplicate; the Abstract is sent to the Controller General, and the Duplicate to the Controller of the Receiver General’s Receipts and Issues: In this Abstract the Payments to the Receiver General are not accurately appropriated, but every Quarter the Receiver appropriates all the Sums he has paid upon the Debentures, which he sends as his Vouchers to the Controller General, with that Weekly Abstract. The Bonds given by the India Company for the rated Goods are deposited with the Receiver; the Bonds are not for the Duties, but for a certain Sum to secure the Duties: After the Duties are computed the Receiver enters in separate Accounts in his Cash Book these Bonded Duties, under their respective Branches; these Entries are compared with the similar Entries of the Checks; they are entered in the Weekly Abstract, in like Manner as the Duties received, but under the Head of Bonds charged: Sometimes, before the Six Months allowed for the Payment of a Moiety of the Duties are expired, the India Company pay in to the Receiver, Debentures on Account; the Receiver pays them to the Receiver General as Cash, and in his Account with him appropriates the Amount of these Debentures; when the Company have paid in the complete Moiety of the Duties, the Receiver is discharged to the Amount of those Duties in the Bonded Account, and charged with the actual Duties he receives in his Cash Account. The Number of Branches of Duties in his Department are Fifty-three.

The Duties upon India Wrought Silks are received by the Receiver, under the Head of £. 5 per Cent, on prohibited Goods, which is a Part of Customs; but the Drawbacks are paid under the Head of India Wrought Silk, 1776. The Controller General has that Head, but the Receiver General has not.

The Controller General has no Account open with the Receiver on Account of the Drawback of the Coinage Duty, and therefore he delivers the Debenture he pays for that Drawback to the Receiver General. The Acts of Parliament relative to the Customs, and the Branches, are become so numerous and so intricate, that the Business is transacted with the utmost Difficulty to the Merchant, and to the great Hazard of the Officer,

Ja. Deacon.

T. Anguish,

Geo. Drummond\

Will* Roe.

N° 13.

The Examination of Mr. Henry Gyles; taken upon Oath, the 30th November 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he has been informed, and believes, that Mr. Lancelot Reed, late Receiver of the Plantation Duties, died on Saturday last: He saith, That he hath been appointed by the Deputy Collector to execute the Office of Receiver of the Plantation Duties in the Absence of the Receiver. These Duties are received from the Merchants in consequence of the Warrants and Bills, in like Manner as the Duties on the Grand Receipt, and are entered in the same Manner in the Cash Book, under their proper Branches. Every Day, before the Treasury closed, he paid to the Receiver General nearly the Amount of the Duties he had collected during the Day, except such Sums as he had paid on Debentures, and retaining such Sums as he expected would soon be demanded of him for the Payment of Debentures — these Daily Payments to the Receiver General were on Account: At the End of the Week he delivered to the Receiver General all the Debentures he had paid during the Week, with a List of them, and appropriated all the Money he had paid to the Receiver General during the Week, and the Money he had paid upon Debentures, under their proper Branches, and put the Initials of his Name to this Appropriation.

The Receiver General gave him a List of the Branches, with the Sums he wished should be paid in upon those Branches — he appropriated those Sums accordingly: The Sum received under any particular Branch very seldom (if ever) agreed with the Sum paid under that Branch. At the End of the Year the Branches are brought as near as can be to a Balance, but for these last Four Years they have not been balanced; such has been the Increase in the Number of the Branches, that the Clerks have not been able to keep up in their Computations, and Entries in their Cash Books. The Receiver of the Plantation Duties receives Tobacco Bonds; these Bonds are given for the Duties, after they have been computed upon the Warrants; the Receiver charges himself with these Duties under their several Branches in his Account of Bonds charged; every Month he delivers all the Bonds, with a List, to the Receiver General, and his Account of Bonds is discharged; the discharging the Bonds is a Transaction with the Receiver General: His only Payments are to the Receiver General, and Debentures.

Henry Gyles.

T. Anguish,

Richd Neave,

Sam1 Beach croft,

N° 14.

The Examination of Mr. William Mucklow; taken upon Oath, October 19th and 22d, 1/84.

This Examinant saith, That he is Receiver of the Duties on W ine and Vinegar, under a Deputation from Sir Banks Jenkinmi, Baronet, who is the Collector of the Duties Inwards.

After the Entry of the Ship, a Warrant and One Bill is usually brought to the Collector Inwards, by some Officer in the Long Room, employed by the Metqhant, containing1 the Name of the Ship and of the Master, ,the /Port of Lading, ;the Description of the Wme, md the Duties payable under their several

NQJU 40.

Branches cast up to a Total, and signed by the Butler; Thirteenth this Signature implies that he has received his Prisage; Report until which the Collector is forbid by Act of Parlia- on Public ment to receive the Duties. The Collector, relying Accounts' upon the Computation of the Officer, receives the Duties, signs the Warrant, and keeps the Bill; the Warrant is carried to the Examiner. The Collector, after the Tuesday s Examination, enters in the Cash Book, from the Bill retained by him, the Duties he receives, under the Heads of their several Branches. —

Every Tuesday, or soon after, the Entries of the Duties upon every Bill of the Week preceding are examined with the Entries upon the similar Bills of the Computer, the Examiner, the Controller, the Surveyor, and Surveyor General.

Every Saturday, or soon after, the Weekly Receipts under each Branch are cast up to Totals, and reduced to One Total; and the Payments which are made during the Week to the Receiver General (which are the only Payments made by the Collector of the Wine Duties, except Debentures, which are delivered as Cash to the Receiver General, and Imprest Orders, which are allowed as Payments by the Controller General) are also cast up to a Total, and the Entries of every Article under each Brandi, and the Totals, are compared with the like Entries of the Five Officers above mentioned.

An Account and Duplicate is made out of the Weekly Totals of each Branch, and compared with the similar Accounts of the Computer, the Examiner, the Controller, and either the Surveyor or Surveyor General: The Account is signed by the Computer, with the Initials of his Name, and by the Collector himself, and by the rest, with their Names, and transmitted to the Controller General; the Duplicate is signed by the Collector and Controller, and transmitted to the Controller of the Receiver General’s Issues and Payments.

The Office of Collector Inwards has, ever since he has been in the Office, which is upwards of Forty Years, been executed by Deputy: the Principal has never, to his Knowledge, executed any Part of the Business, except signing a Warrant upon his being sworn into the Office. '
