N° 15.

The Examination of Mr. William Sims; taken upon Oath, the 27th October, 8th, 10th, and 16th November, 20th and 24th December, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Clerk of the Rates, called also Computer of the Duties, under the Collector Inwards, in the Port of London; he has been Six Years in this Office, and holds it under an Appointment by Sir Banks Jenkinson, Patent Collector Inwards. The Business of the Collector Inwards is executed by his Deputies, and their Assistants; he executes ho Part of it himself. The Clerk of the Rates is an Assistant to the Collector; it is his Business to compute the Duties for the 1 Collector upon all Goods imported into the Port of London; to compute the Drawbacks 'upon all Foreign. Goods exported; to keep an Account of both; and to prevent, as far as he is able, Entries contrary to Law.

The usual Course of transacting the Business of this Office is in the following Manner: — The Merchant or his Agent produces the Warrant and Six Bills to the Clerk of the Rates. The Warrant, and Two of

8 M the

686 ai° Martii. A. 1785.

Thirteenth Report on Public Accounts.

the Bills, are sometimes with, and sometimes without, the Duties; Four of the Bills are always without them: But they all contain those Circumstances relative to the Ship and Goods, by which the Duties are to be computed. Where the Bills contain the Duties, the Clerk of the Rates puts his Initials upon One or both of the Bills, as his Testimony of the Accuracy of the Computation; if they do not vcontain the Duties, he computes them upon One of the Bills, and enters upon the Bill designed for the Receiver as many Sums as there are Branches, computed in the Manner made use of in the Custom House, and cast to a Total, but omitting the Titles of the Branches. The Warrant and Bills are carried to the Receiver of the Duties, who retains the Bill on which the Duties are entered, and delivers the Warrant, with the other Bills, to the Clerk of the Warrants. The Clerk of the Rates takes from that Office the Bill on which the Duties are cast, and from thence enters them in Net Sums in his Cash Book, under their several Branches. Where there are several Articles in One Bill subject to the same Branches of Duties, though the Computations are different, the Sums payable on each Branch are blended together into One Sum. The same Course is not always pursued, the Hurry and Multiplicity of Business preventing it — Every Day, after the- Receiver has finished his Business, the Warrants, completely signed, are brought by the Clerk of the Warrants to the Clerk of the Rates, and Two of the following Officers, the Controller, the Surveyor, the Surveyor General, and Examiner, attend with their Bills, generally by Weekly Turns: The Clerk of the Warrants reads each Article of the Goods in the Warrants, whilst the other Officers attend to the same Entries in their Bills. If the Bill differs from the Warrant in the Description of the Goods, the Clerk of the Rates detains the Warrant until the Mistake is rectified: The Warrant is always checked by the Bills, before it is delivered to the Land Waiter. Every Entry of the Duties, in every Branch, in the Cash Books of the Clerk of the Rates, Receiver, Controller, Surveyor, Surveyor General, and Examiner, is compared by those Officers, as soon after the Entry of the Goods is made as Business will permit; and every Week the Receiver sends to the Clerk of the Rates an Account of the Totals of the Duties, under each Branch, received by him during the Week; the Clerk of the Rates compares this Account with the correspondent Entries of the Totals in his Cash Book, and if they agree, he signs the Receivers Account with his Name, and returns it to the Receiver.

These Entries in the Books of the Controller, Surveyor, Surveyor General, and Examiner, are Checks upon the Computer, and Charges upon the Receiver.

The Number of Entries Inwards in One Day, in the Customs, is frequently very great; they have sometimes amounted to about Four hundred: For these last Four Months of July, August, September, and October, they have amounted to Fifteen thousand Three hundred and Forty-two, which-, upon an Average of the Working Days, is about One hundred and Seventy-four each Day.

All the Custom Duties may be considered under Three Denominations, Tonnage, Poundage, and specific Duties on specific Articles. — Goods for Home Consumption, if not imported Duty-free, are liable to Three Duties at least, some to many more. The Duties upon unrated French ordinary painted Paper contain Fourteen Branches: The first Eight are a Poundage upon the Value before the Duties are paid, the next Tw o are a Poundage upon the Value including the Duties, the Eleventh is a Poundage upon the Measure, the Twelfth is a Poundage upon the Quantity, and the Two Imposts upon the Aggregate of the Duties: To obtain the Amount of these Duties requires Five Rules of Computation.

In computing a Drawback, the Merchant, or his Agent, brings to the Clerk of the Rates a Debenture and Certificate; the Debenture contains, amongst other Things, an exact Description of all the Goods entered by the Merchant for Exportation, and entitled to a Drawback, with the Dates when they were severally imported, and the Date when entered for Exportation, and to what Place. — It contains likewise all the Goods above enumerated which have been actually exported, certified by the Searchers, sworn to by the Exporter, and authenticated by the proper Officers. The Certificate is the actual Entry of the Merchant for Exportation, sworn to by him, and authenticated by the proper Officers.

The Clerk of the Rates computes the Drawbacks, and enters upon the Back of the Debenture, in Figures, the Sums under their different Branches, without the Titles: These Two Instruments are then carried to the Controller, for him to check the Drawbacks, and from him to the Collector Outwards, who detains the Certificate, signs the Debenture, and delivers it back to the Merchant, who carries it to the Examiner — he re-computes the Drawbacks, and enters the Branches, and the Sums, both in Words and Figures, on the Back of the Debenture, casts them to a Total, and signs it with his Name; it is then brought again to the Clerk of the Rates, who enters in a Debenture Book the Goods actually exported, and the Drawbacks under the several Branches, signs the Debenture, and delivers it back to the Merchant.

A Debenture frequently contains various Goods, imported by different Merchants at different Times; and Regulations of the Drawbacks by the Legislature relative to the same Article, may have intervened between the Periods of the Imports of that Article included in the Debenture. The Difference in the Articles, and the Difference of the Times of the Importation of the same Article, and of the Places to which they are to be exported, occasion a Difference in the Computation of the Drawbacks, and much Trouble to the Office. — The only Bonds given for Duties Inwards are on Tobacco and Goods imported by the East India Company.

Where the Duties upon the Import of Tobacco have not been paid, but a Bond has been given for them to the Collector, and a Merchant exports it, he delivers his Debenture for the Drawback to the Receiver General, in Discharge of the Bond given by the Importer, for so much as is included in the Debenture; if the Duties have been paid, he receives them back from the Receiver General, or from the Receiver of the Duties, upon producing his Debenture.

Where India Goods are exported, a Bond having been given for the Payment of the Duties, and not discharged, the Exporter carries the Debenture to the India Company, who allow him the Drawback, and deliver the Debenture to the Collector Inwards, in Diminution of the Duties secured by their Bond; this different Application of the Debenture renders it necessary to divide it into different Parts, where the same Debenture includes other Goods besides India Goods or Tobacco.

All Goods are either rated or unrated, or charged with a specific Duty; the rated Goods are those enumerated in the Book of Rates, the unrated are those upon which a Value is set upon the Importation; this Value is ascertained in some Cases by the actual Sale, in others, by the Oath of the Importer; and, as a Check upon that Oath, the Examining Officers (that is, the Land Waiters and Land Surveyors) are at Liberty to take the Goods from the Importer at the Value sworn to, he being paid back the Duties, and being allowed £.10 per Cent, upon the Value sworn to; These Goods must be sold publicly, and if sold for more than the Value sworn to, and the Duties, the Overplus is divided between the Crown and the

Officers;

25 Geo. III. 2i° Ma 687

Officers; if sold for less, the Crown sustains the Loss.

Upon the Sale of unrated Goods by the India Company, the Purchaser buys them free of Duties, and the India Company pays the Duties, consequently the Value they are sold at includes the Duties; in order therefore to compute the Duties to be paid by the Company, the Price they are sold for is reduced to a Sum called The Reduced Value, which being added to the Amount of the Duties computed upon that Sum, and to an Allowance for Charges, form together the Sum they are sold for.

This Examinant further saith, That he also examines the Duties on Coals, as a Check upon the Collector. — Every Quarter the Coast Collector sends to the Examiner a Quarterly List of the Coal Ships; from the Coal Meter he receives from Time to Time a Duplicate of the Certificate; and every Quarter from the Collector his Quarter Book: By a Comparison of the several Instruments, he checks the Quantities of Coals brought into the Port of London, and the Computation of the Duties received by the Collector, during the Quarter; he sees also, that every Coal Ship is accounted for by the Meter, and every Bond by the Collector; after this Comparison and Computation, the Examiner signs the Quarter Book of the Collector, and delivers it to the Controller General.

the Office of Deputy Prisage Master to the Duke of Thirteenth Grafton, who is Grantee from the Crown of Two Duties, fnPpublic Prisage and Butlerage. — Prisage was anciently a Right Accounts, in the Crown, to take One Ton where Ten Tons were imported, and Two Tons where Twenty or upwards were imported, by Natives not exempted; but this Duty has been compounded for Time immemorial, by the Payment of Two Shillings per Ton for all Wines imported.

The Prisage Tons are exempted by the Legislature from 'three Branches of the Duties, the Old Subsidy, the Additional Duty, and Coinage, but the Merchant has, Time immemorial, paid to the Patentee those Duties upon the Prisage Tons; he also pays him the Two additional Duties of the Years 1779 and 1782, upon those Three Branches: They are computed at the Time of the Entry, and paid to the Deputy of the Patentee. Aliens were not subject to Prisage; but in lieu of it, they paid to the Crown Two Shillings per Ton on all the Wines they imported, which Duty is called Butlerage: The Gross Amount of these Two Duties collected in the Port of London, in the Year 1781, was One thousand Eight hundred and Sixteen Pounds and an Halfpenny.

N# 16.

The Examination of Mr. Hutchinson Hothersall Browne; taken upon Oath, October 20th, 26th, and 27th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Computer of the Duties on Wine, under the Collector Inwards; this Office is a Branch of the Office of Clerk of the Rates, whose Duty it is to see that all the Duties Inwards, and all Drawbacks, are rightly computed. The Computer of the Duties on Wine does not compute the Drawbacks on Wine.

The Merchant, or his Agent, produces to the Computer a Bill, containing all the Circumstances on which the Computation is grounded: He computes the Duties, enters each Duty separately upon the Bill, omitting the Titles of the Branches, and casts the Duties up to a Total. After an Examination of every Branch in the Bill, with the similar Bills of the Examiner, the Controller, the Surveyor, and Surveyor General, each Article is entered under its proper Branch in the Cash Book, and a Daily Total formed of each Branch — Every Week these Totals are examined by the same Officers, and a Weekly Total formed of each Branch, and One Total of the Whole. The Collector sends every Week to the Computer his Weekly Account; the Computer examines the Totals of the Weekly Receipts with his Cash Book, signs it with his Initials, and returns it to the Collector.

Wines are distinguished under Four Heads, French, Portugal, Spanish, and Rhenish.

There are at present Fifteen separate Duties paid upon the Importation of French Wines, and Thirteen upon all the rest; and consequently the Total Sum of Duties paid for every Ton of French Wine consists of Fifteen different Sums, and is entered under Fifteen different Heads; they are all Duties of Tonnage, except the Two Imposts of the Years 1779 an^ 1782.

This Examinant saith, That the Duties payable to the Prisage Master are omitted both upon the Warrant and all the Bills; they contain those Duties only which are payable to the Crown. N* 22.

The Examination of Mr. Richard Frewin; taken upon Oath, August 18th, 24th, and 30th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Examiner of the Duties Inwards in the Port of London; he has been in the Examiner’s Office Twenty-two Years, and Principal about One Year and a Half. The chief Business of this Office is to see that all the Duties collected Inwards in the Port of London, except on Wine, are properly computed, and properly charged in the King’s Books, and that the Drawbacks are properly computed.

Upon the Arrival of a Ship in the River, the First Step taken by the Customs, is to put on board that Ship at Gravesend some Tide Waiters, to secure the Cargo from being smuggled; after which the Captain makes a Report on Oath, before the Collector Inwards, and his Controller, or the Surveyor or JSurveyor General, of the Cargo of the Ship; this Report includes all the material Circumstances relative to the Ship and Carso required by various Acts

Vol. 40.

of Parliament, and remains with the Collector. Upon Thirteenth this Report being made, it is clear that the Crown Rftp®rL has a Right to the Duties; that Right may, and has, upon particular Circumstances, been considered as accruing to the Crown before the Report The next Step is the Entry made by the Merchant; he generally brings to some Officer in the Long Room his Bill of Lading, or Description of his Goods; from hence a Warrant is made out, and signed by the Merchant, or his Agent, containing those Circumstances which are the Foundation of the Duties; from hence the Officer computes the Duties, enters upon the Warrant the particular Sums payable on each Branch of Duty, with the Total, and either receives it of the Merchant, or the Merchant pays it himself to the Collector; the Officer then makes Six Bills, which are Extracts from this Warrant; he carries and delivers to the proper Collector the Warrant and the Six Bills, and pays him the Duty, unless paid by the Merchant; the Collector signs the Warrant, which Signature is an Official Acknowledgment that he has received those Duties; he also puts a Date and a Number upon the Warrant, and the same Number upon the Bills; the Collector retains One Bill, and delivers the Warrant, and the other Five, to the Clerk of the Warrants, whose Business it is to procure to the Warrant the Signature either of the Controller, Surveyor, or Surveyor General, and of the Examiner; after he has procured these Signatures, he delivers One of the Bills, with the Duties entered upon it, to the Computer; the other Four to the Controller, the Surveyor, the Surveyor General, and the Examiner.

Every Day the Clerk of the Warrants, and the Computer, with Two of the other Officers, compare the Warrant with their Bills, after which the Clerk of the Warrants delivers it to the proper Land Waiter (taking his Receipt) as his Authority for directing the Goods to be landed; after the Ship is cleared this Warrant is deposited by the Land Waiter with the Jerquer.

The Examiner having received One of the Rills, computes the Duties, and enters them in a Cash Book under their several Branches; these Entries are, as soon as is convenient, compared with the like Entries in the Books of the Controller, the Surveyor, and the Surveyor General, all of whom are Checks upon the Collector; the Receipt of each Day, under each Branch, is cast up to a Total, and every Week these Daily Totals are compared with the like Totals of the other Three Checks, and each Branch cast up to a Weekly Total, and compared in like Manner; an Abstract is drawn out, in a separate Leaf in the Cash Book, containing these Weekly Totals under each Branch; these Totals are cast up together, and form the Total Sum of Duties received within the Week.

The Collector produces a similar Abstract, which is compared with the Abstract formed by the Examiner, and signed by him.

Before Goods can be entered Outwards, the Master of the Ship must enter his Ship Outwards with the Collector Outwards; the Merchant is thqn at Liberty to enter Goods on board of such Ship. When a Merchant is about to ship Goods entitled to a Drawback, he generally brings down to some Clerk or Officer in the Long Room the Particulars of his Entry, as — the Name of the Ship and Master — for what Place bound — the Quantity of the Goods to be exported — the Date of the Importation — and the Name of the Importer. A Bill containing these Particulars is drawn out, and delivered to an Officer under the Collector Inwards, called the Clerk of the Certificates, who having previously entered in his Books the Particulars of every Entry Inwards, is therehy enabled to examine this Bill, which having done, he keeps the same, and enters it in a Book kept by hfm for 8 N that

Thirteenth Report on Public Accounts.

690 219 Martn. A. 1785.

that Purpose. If it appears by his Books that the Merchant named as the Importer did pay Duties according to the Dates and Quantity expressed in the BiH, he writes off in the Margin of his Book the Quantity entered Outwards; he then grants a Certificate, signed by himself, of the Duties having been paid, describing the particular Branches of which they, are composed; this Certificate, with a Bill similar to that delivered to the Clerk of the Certificates, is given to the Controller, who keeps the Bill, and marking the Certificate with his Initials, returns the same to the Merchant. The Exporter, his known Clerk or Broker, makes Oath on the Certificate, before One of the principal Officers of the Customs, that the Goods therein mentioned are to be exported to the Place for which they are destined, naming the same, either on Commission, or on Account of the Exporter, as the Case may be. Certain Persons are deputed by the Collector Outwards, for the Purpose of writing Cockets, and thence called Cocket Writers, and to One of those the Certificate, thus sworn to, and Three other Bills, are carried; he makes out a Cocket, which is the Authority for shipping the Goods, and which contains the Substance of the Certificate; this Cocket, with the Certificate, and the Three Bills, is then delivered to the Collector Outwards, who marks the Cocket with his Initials, and retains One of the Bills; the Cocket, Certificate, and the Two remaining Bills, are then carried successively to the Controller and Surveyor General, who respectively mark the Cocket with their Initials, and the Register of Certificates does the same, retaining One of the Bills: The remaining Bill is left with the Copying Clerk Outwards, who marks the Cocket with his Initials, the Cocket is also marked by the Deputy Usher of the Long Room, with whom the Certificate is deposited; it is then sealed by the Controller, signed by the Collector Outwards, and also by the Controller, Surveyor, or Surveyor General, and delivered to the Merchant

The Merchant having thus made his Entry Outwards, and obtained his Cocket for shipping, endorses on the Back of the Cocket the Marks, Numbers, and Contents of each Package, with the Total Quantity shipped. A Bill is also made out by the Merchant, and endorsed in the same Manner as the Cocket, which Cocket and Bill are delivered to the Searchers, who examine the Goods, and if they find them correspond with the Endorsement, the Goods are permitted to be shipped, under the Care of an Officer: The Bill remains with the Searcher; but when the Ship comes to be cleared the Cocket is delivered to the Captain, and goes with the Ship.

The Certificate left with the Deputy Usher is the Foundation of the Debenture, it is by him delivered to the Collector Outwards, who therefrom makes out the Debenture, and delivers it either to the Merchant or his Agent (who is generally some Clerk in the Long Room) by whom the Debenture is carried to the Searchers, who examine it with the endorsed Bill left with them at the Time of shipping, and certify on the Debenture* under their Hands, the Quantity shipped, on which only the Drawback is afterwards computed: It is then returned to the Merchants

Agent, and Oath is made by the Exporter himself, before One or more of the principal Officers of the Customs, that the Goods are really exported, according to the Circumstances of the Entry; Oath is also made on the Back of the Certificate, "by the Importer of the Goods, that the Duties on Importation were paid for the Goods, according to the Dates therein mentioned, and also to whom they were sold or delivered; and if there are any intermediate Purchasers between the Importer and Exporter, thrir Oaths are also required, in order to identify the Goods. The Certificate is then signed by the Controller, and

delivered to an Officer under the Collector Outward*, in order to see that all the proper Oaths are made to it; he marks the Debenture with his Initials, and it is then, with the Certificate, delivered to the Register of Certificates, who examines the same with the Bill formerly left with him and entered in his Books, in which he now notes the Quantity shipped; the Debenture is then signed by the Register, and delivered with the Certificate to the Clerk of the Certificates, who writes it off in the Margin of the Book in which he had before entered the Bill, and signs the Debenture to which the Certificate is annexed: The Drawback is then computed upon the Quantity shipped; the Computation is made by an Officer under the Collector Inwards, called the Clerk of the Rates, who puts the same in Figures on the Back of the Debenture; the Debenture is delivered to the Controller, who checks the Computation, and if he finds it correct, marks it with his Initials; the Debenture and Certificate are then delivered to the Collector Outwards, who keeps the Certificate, and signs the Debenture, which is brought to the Examiner, who computes the Drawback, and if it is found right, inserts it in Figures on the Rack of the Debenture, and also describes the Title of each Branch, with the Amount in Words at Length, makes a Total of all the Branches, and signs the Debenture: The Clerk of the Rates then enters the Particulars of the Debenture in a Book, and signs it; the Controller does the same, and the Debenture is taken to the Register of Certificates, who enters the Total Amount in a Column left for the same in his Books, and makes out on the Debenture an Order for Payment of the Amount of the Drawback, according to the Total, as certified to him by the computing Officer?, and presents the same to the Commissioners for their Signature, which, when it is signed by Four of the Commissioners, is delivered to the Exporter, or his Agent, who sign a Receipt for the same. This Order for Payment is directed to the Receiver General of the Customs, or the Collector Inwards; from either of whom the Merohant, having signed a Receipt on the Debenture, may receive the Amount of the Drawback, leaving the Debenture with the Person from whom he receives the Money, whose Voucher it becomes.

N° 23.

The Examination of Mr. Richard Frewin; taken upon Oath, 12th and 23d October, 22d and 23d December, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That the Oath made by the Captain of a Ship in his Report, is always made before the Collector, and some One of the other principal Officers; and the Report is retained by the Collector; the Warrant is made out from the Bill of Lading by the Merchant, or the Person belonging to the Long Room employed by him; the Entry of the Duties upon the Warrant contains the particular Sums payable on each Branch, but not the Titles of the Branches: The Two Bills, the one for the Collector, the other for the Computer, contain the same Duties, but described in Sums of Twenty Times the Amount of the Sums upon the Warrant, a Mode of Computation made use of in the Port of London only, in order to avoid the Errors that might arise in computing the fractional Parts of the several Branches; the other Four Bills are without the Duties. The Date added to the Warrant by the Collector 4 is

is the Pay he receives the Duty, and the Number is according to the Order in which the Warrant i$ produced to him. — After the Warrant is signed by One of the principal Officers, and the Examiner, it is complete, and when delivered to the Land Waiter the Entry is completed. The Examiner enters upon the Bill the Sums payable on each Branch, confuted as above-mentioned, but the Entries in the CJash Bopk are the real Net Sums.

The Rules for computing the Duties are grounded upon the Acts that impose the Duties; they are various and numerous: There are very few Species of Gqods subject to Duties., but w hat require more Rules of Computation than One to ascertain the Duties; there are some particular Articles, on which it is necessary to refer to Five different Principles of Computation to obtain thp Amount. The Duties ppou Cordial Waters imported in Glass Bottles from Franc? consist of a Poundage Duty arising from the Bute, a Tonnage Duty arising from the Quantity, a Duty grounded upon the Size of the Bottles, a Duty comr pounded of former Duties consolidated, and Two separate Five per Cents, on all the other existing Duties. The Number of subsisting Branches of the Customs is Sixty-eight. — The Duties paid upon a single Species of Goods are frequently ranged under fifteen different Heads; and where an Entry contains Variety of Articles, the Duties to he paid frequently consist of Twenty Branches.

The Computation is become so intricate and extensive, that there are very few Persons who understand it perfectly, nor is it easy to procure Assistance: It is so little understood at some of the Out Ports, that the Officers are frequently obliged to apply to the Board fqr Information, and the References to the Officers in London occasion much additional Trouble to them.

Thp Duties are so complicated, that it is hardly possible fqr a general Merchant to know what Duties he may be liable to pay; he mnst often rely entirely upon the Officers of the Customs, and, according to the present System, it is hardly possible to frame a Table of Duties and Drawbacks clearly adapted to every Circumstance of legal Importation, so as to convey to him that Knowledge, without much Difficulty. The Foreign Merchant may be frequently

deterred from importing Goods, from his Imiorance of the Duties, and of the Legality of the Importation.

The First Head in the List of Duties is Customs, which comprehends Three several Duties; First, the old Subsidy — Secondly, the Petty Customs — Thirdly, the Additional Duty (the One per Cent. Duty, formerly a Part of the Customs, being repealed in the last Sessions;) these Three Duties are entered separately upon the Warrant, and in separate Columns in the Cash Bopk, but being all appropriated to the same Purpose, they are blended together in the Weekly Abstract, under the Head of Customs. The Head likewise of Sjlk and Lead, N# 66, contains Two Divisions, Silk imported, and Lead exported. These separate Duties are collected by different Officers, and paid by them separately to the Receiver General: The rest of the Heads in the List are single, and without Divisions.

The Computation of the Drawbacks is greatly more difficult than that of the Duties, from the Variety of Articles comprehended in One Entry, sometimes Twenty-five in Number, and from the different Rules by which the Drawbacks of the Duties which have been paid on the same Article are to be computed; and from the Drawbacks being in some Cases the Whole of the Duties paid, in others Portions only of those Duties, and different Portions on different Articles. N° 24.

The Examination of Mr. John Goldham\ taken upon Oath, 29th October, and 1st November,

1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Examiner of the Wine Duties in the Port of London; he has been in this Office about Twenty-four Years; he holds his Office under a Warrant from the Treasury. This Office is in the Department of the Collector Inwards; the Business is to compute all the Duties on Wine Inwards, and the Drawbacks on Wines exported. The Merchant, or his Agent, produces to the Examiner the Warrant and a Bill; the Bill contains — the Names of the Merchant — the Vessel — the Master — the Port of Lading — and, the Quantity, and Kind of Wine. The Warrant contains the Duties as computed by the Collector, and signed by him; the Examiner signs the Warrant under the Name of the Collector, and delivers i£ to thjB Clerk of the Warrants; the Examiner afterwards casts the Duties, and enters them upon the Bill under their several Branches, and makes a Total. Generally about Three or Four Dqys after lie has received the Bill, he examines and compares the Entries of the Duties upon it, with the like Entries upon the Bills of the Collector, Controller, Computer, Surveyor, and Surveyor General, and then enters them in his Cash Book under their several Branches, and forms Daily and Weekly Totals of each Branch. The Collector sends to the Examiner fiis Weekly Account, which the Examiner compares with his Cash Book, and if they agree, he signs the Account, and returns it to the Collector.

When a Drawback is to be paid, the Debenture, with the Certificate annexed, is brought from the Controller to the Examiner, to cast the Duties that are to be paid back. On the Back of the Debenture ary entered the separate Duties, as computed by the Computer, and signed with the Initials of the Controller; the Examinant re-casts the Duties, casts them up to q Total, adds his Initials, and returns it to the Person who brings it; it is then brought back, without the Certificate, to the Examiner, signed by an Officer under the Collector Outwards, with whom the Certificates

After a Portage Bill is made out by the Wine Jer-quer, it is brought to the Examiner, to 9ee that the Sum to be paid to the Master of the Ship is properly computed; the Examiner casts it, and signs his Name to the Bill.

The Examiner is paid a Salary of Eighty Pounds a Year, and certain Fees; the Salary is subject to the Land Tax, and the Civil List Duty, and he pays his Clerk out of it, which reduces it to less than Forty-eight Pounds a Year. — The Fees are One Shilling and Six Pence for each Debenture, paid by the Merchant (Six Pence of which he allows his Clerk) and One Shilling for each Portage Bill, paid by the Master of the Ship. — These Fees amount to about Fourteen Pounds a Year, which makes the Profits of his Office about Sixty-two Pounds a Year.

N* 25.

The Examination of Mr. William Bates; taken upon Oath, December 14th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Deputy Collector Outwards, by Deputation from the Duke of Manchester \ he is next to the Senior Deputy, who is a Bench Officer; he has been in this Office above Thirty-two Years.

After the Cocket is made out, the Deputy Collector compares it with the Warrant, and puts his Initials to it; it is then carried, with the Bills, to the other Checks, and after it is sealed, the Collector signs it with his Name. The Duties are generally entered

upon the Warrant and Cocket, by some Clerk in the Office, before the Cocket is carried to the Checks; they are always entered upon both, before the Receiver receives the Duty. The same Day, or the next Morning, the Checks attend the Collectors Clerk with their Bills, and compare the Entries of the Goods and Duties upon their Bills, with the like Entries upon the Warrant. After Goods are shipped, entitled to Drawbacks, the Deputy Collector makes out Debentures from the Certificates brought to him from the Usher; the Drawbacks are computed by the Collector Inwards — if for Bounties, by the Collector Outwards. The general Rule for computing Bounties, is a given Rale for a given Quantity; the Bounty is entered by the Collector 011 the Back of the Debenture in Figures and in Words. — Different Debentures for Boun- ties are made out for different Species of Goods: Where an Act of Parliament has given different Bounties upon different Kinds of the same Species of Goods, those Bounties may be included in the same Debenture. The Debenture is made out from the Entry, but the Bounty is computed from the Quantity certified by the Searchers to have been actually shipped. Where an Act of Parliament directs the Merchant to give a Bond upon the Exportation of Goods entitled to a Bounty, that Bond is taken by the Collector at the Time of the Entry: The Merchant is bound to the King, in a Penalty, not to re-land the Goods in any Place where he would not be entitled to the Bounty; this Bond is given up upon producing a proper Certificate of the landing the Goods. The Boun-

ties are entered in a Book, in a Column opposite to the Entry of the Goods.

N° 26.

The Examination of Mr. James Dodson; taken upon Oath, October 13th and 15th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Receiver of the Customs Outwards in the Port of London} by Deputation from the Duke of Manchester, who is the Collector Outwards.

After a Ship is cleared of her Cargo Inwards, or when she goes out upon her first Voyage, the Master or Owner, or his Agent, enters her with the Collector Outwards, describing all those Circumstances relative to the Ship, directed by Acts of Parliament; this Entry is inserted by the Collector in a Book, for public Inspection. Where a Merchant intends to export ‘British Manufactures, he or his Agent brings to a Clerk in the Collectors Office a Warrant, describing the Goods he intends to put on board that Ship; this Warrant being reduced into the Form of Office, is signed by the Person who brings it, and remaius with the Collector; the Officer makes out, on Parchment, a Cocket, which is a Copy of the Warrant; to this Cocket the Collector puts the Initials of his Name; Four Copies are made of it, and it is carried with the Copies to the Controller, who adds his Iuitials to the Cocket, and keeps One of the Copies; it is then carried to the Surveyor, the Surveyor General, and Copying Clerk Outwards, each of whom adds his Initials, and keeps a Copy; the Cocket is then brought back to the Controller, who puts to it the Seal of Office, after which the Collector signs his Name to it, and either the Controller, the Surveyor, or the Surveyor General, adds his Name; it is then delivered to the Merchant, as his Warrant to the Searcher, to permit him to ship his Goods. — As soon as the Cocket is made out, the Collector computes the Duties, enters them upon the Cocket, under their proper Branches, and, upon receiving them, signs his Name under the Duties, as his Receipt. Three of the Copies, for the Controller, the Surveyor, and Surveyor General, are intended as Checks upon the Collector, as it is the Duty of each of these Officers to compute the Duties upon their Copies.

The Duties are entered in a Cash Book, under their respective Branches; the Daily Receipt and the Weekly Receipt of each Branch is cast up to a Total; and every Week these Totals are compared with the Three Checks, the Controller, the Surveyor, and the Surveyor General; after they have agreed, the Collector makes out an Account, and a Duplicate, containing the Totals of the Week’s Receipt, and the Payments to the Receiver General, being the only Payments made by the Collector Outwards; these Accounts are signed by the Collector, and either by the Controller, Surveyor, or Surveyor General; the Account is carried to and left with the Controller General, and the Duplicate with the Controller of the Receiver General’s Issues.

The Number of Branches of the Duties on Exports are Eleven. — Coals exported, otherwise than to Ireland and the British Plantations, pay Six Dudes — the Subsidy Outwards — the Duties of the Years 1714, 1757, and 1765, which are Duties of Poundage; and — the Imposts of the Years 1779 and 1782, which are £ 5

per

25 Geo. III. U'Marti

per Cent. each upon all the subsisting Duties prior, to 1779: The Duties upon Coals so exported are computed upon a Chaldron, according to the Measure at Newcastle; but the Duties upon Coals brought into the Port of London are computed upon a Chaldron, according to the Winchester Measure, that is, in the Proportion of Eleven to Twenty-one, and the Drawback is paid according to the Winchester Measure. These different Rules of Computation occasion much Trouble to the Office; it tenders it necessary to reduce to the Newcastle Measure the Coals, which are all received in the Port of London by the Winchester Measure, and accordingly the Quantities exported are entered according to both Measures upon the Cocket

*The Examination of Mr. James taken

upon Oath, 25th November, 1784

This Examinant saith. That the Daily Receipt of the Duties Outwards is not very considerable; and therefore he pays them only Once a Week, upon the last Working Day of the Week, into the Treasury; the Average Weekly Collection amounts to between Two and Three hundred Pounds. The Duties are never entered from the Bills in the Cash Book until the Day after the Receipt of the Duties: He pays to the Receiver General an entire Sum, as near the Amount of his Balance as may be, and appropriates this Sum generally to One Branch only, that on which the greatest Sum has been received during the Week. The Duties received are all appropriated, and placed under their proper Branch^; but jt ii not the Practice to appropriate the Payments jt& the Receiver General in the same specific Sums as in the Receipts; it would create much Trouble to the Office: Sometimes the Receiver General desires a certain Sum to be appropriated to a certain Head, which occasions Underpayments upon the rest of the Branches; by this Practice the Appropriation of the Payments never corresponds with the Appropriation of the Receipts; this W'eekly Appropriation is signed by the Receiver, marked by the Cashier of the Receiver General, and left in the Receiver General’s Office. The Weekly Account delivered by the Receiver to the Controller General contains the same Appropriation of the Sum paid in to the Receiver General as is contained in that delivered to the Receiver General. The Receiver of the Duties Outwards neither receives Bonds, nor pays Debentures. At the End of every Quarter the Weekly Totals of the several Branches of the Receipts and Payments are cast up to Totals, and the Receipt of the last Week is appropriated amongst the Branches of the Payments of that Week, in such Proportions as that the Receipts and Payments on the several Branches shall Balance as near as possible. The Debtor Side of this Account is compared with the like Accounts of the Controller, Surveyor, and Surveyor General.

James Dodson.

N* 32.

'The 'Examination of Mr. Thomas Sutton; taken upon Oath, August 25th and 31st, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is One of the Deputies for Foreign Business to the Collector Outwards, and has been so for about Four Years, and has been in the Office about Twenty-two Years.

When Goods on which by Law a Bounty is payable are intended to be shipped, the Exporter makes out a Warrant, and Four Bills, which express the Ship’s and Captain’s Names, the Port.of Destination, the Name of the Exporter, and the Quantity and Quality of the Goods, arranged under the different Heads to which they belong. The Warrant and Bills are brought to the Office of the Collector Outwards, where the Warrant remains, and is entered in a Book kept for that Purpose, and a Cocket for shipping the Goods is made out, and marked with the Initials of the Collector’s Deputy: This Cocket, with a Bill, is taken to the Controller’s Office, where it is examined 2 to

as Geo. III. ai Mar til.

to see if it agrees with the fill, and if k does, it is marked wkh his Initials, and the Bill is kept; it is then carried, with a like Bill, successively to the Surveyor, Surveyor General, and the Copying Clerk Outwards, who each keep a Bill, and having examined the Cocket, mark it in the same Manner. The Cacket, thus marked, is taken back to the Control* ler’s Office, and there sealed with his Seal of Office, and carried to the Collector’s Office, where the Exporter having entered into a Bond for the Exportation of the Goods mentioned in the Entry, the Collector’s Deputy, whose Initials had before been put to it, signs the Cocket, and then the Deputy Controller signs it, and it is complete.

The Merchant having obtained the Cocket, endorses upon it an Account of each Package, and the Contents thereof, actually intended to be shipped, and makes out another Bill, on which he also makes the like Endorsement; and when the Goods are upon the Quay for shipping, he delivers the Cocket to the Patent Searchers, and the Bill to the Controlling Searchers; from each of these Offices One Searcher goes to examine the Packages, and compare them with the Endorsements; if they find them agree, the Goods may be shipped, under the Care of the proper Officers. The Cocket is entered in the Searcher’s Office, in a Book kept for that Purpose, by the Patent Searchers Clerk, and where the Quantity shipped is less than the Quantity expressed in the Cocket, he enters in the Margin of the Book the Quantity shipped, taken from the Endorsement on the Cocket.

The Controlling Searchers, from the Endorsement on the Bill which is left in their Office, enter iu their Book of Shipping the Quantity shipped.

The Requisites of Law being complied with, Debentures for Bounties are made out in the Cqllector s Office Monthly, One Month under another. When the Time for making out the Debenture arrives, the Clerks in the Collector’s Office in that Department fill up the Debenture from the Bond, and deliver it to the First Clerk in the Department for Foreign Business, who compares it with the Bond, and also with the Entry formerly made by him of the Warrant, and writes it off in the Book in which that Entry was made, marking upon the Debenture the Number of the Entry. It is then signed by the Deputy-Collector, and entered in an Alphabetical Book Jkept for that Purpose, under the Letter of the Name of the Exporter, and is delivered to the Merchant, pr his Agent, who takes it to ,the Patent Searchers, where it is entered in another Alphabetical iBook, and the Searchers refer to -their Gravesend List, to see if the Ship has taken her final Clearance froip Gravesend* till when the Goods are not deemed to be exported, so as to be entitled to Bounty; they then compare the Debenture with their iBook, and certify, under the Hand of One of them, the Quantity shipped: The Debenture is wrote off in their Alphabetical Book, and delivered over to One of the /Controlling Search?* ers, who puts his Initials in -the Parent Searchers Book as a Receipt for the same, enters it in their own Alphabetical Book, compares it with their Book of Shipping, and signs to the Quantity shipped, unjler the Signature of the Patent Searcher.

The Merchant makes Oath at the Foot of the Debenture, before One of the principal Officers of the Customs, that the Goods certified by the Searchers to have been shipped are all of British Manufacture, and exported to Piurts beyond the Seas, on Commission, or on their own Account, as the Case may be, and not landed, or intended to be re-landed, in any Part of Great Britain, or the Islands of Faro or Ferro; After the Oath is made the Debenture is delivered to One of the Collectors Clerks, whose Department it is to

The Examination ‘of Robert Weston, Esquire; taken upon Oath, November 3d, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That in calculating the Deposit taken from the Factor upon the Entry, it is usual to take something more than the Amount the Duty is estimated at: The Sum payable upon a Chaldron by the Pool Measure being well known, it is easy to guess at nearly the Amount of the Duty upon the Quantity on the Cocket, though there expressed by the Newcastle Measure, which is considered nearly as Two to One.

After the Duties are computed upon the Certificate, the Collector settles the Amount of the Duties with the Factor; if the Deposit exceeds the Duties, the Overplus is returned to him, if it falls short, the Factor pays the Deficiency. After either the Deposit or the Duties are settled, the Usage in general is for the Factor to pay the Sum into the Hands of the Receiver General, and bring his Receipt to the Collector; these Daily Payments to the Receiver General are Payments not then appropriated, but on Account, and are settled at the Close of every Day with the Receiver General. — After the Receipt of the Week has been examined and agreed with the Controller, the Collector, retaining in his Hands a Sum to answer the Difference between the Deposits and the Duties, makes out an Account of his Receipts and Payments during the Week, and appropriates to its proper Branches the Amount of what he has paid during that Week into the Hands of the Receiver General; this Account, being examined by the Controller, is signed by the Collector, and transmitted by him to the Receiver General: Where a Bond is given for the Duties, and they are not paid within the Sixteen Days , upon the Receipt of the Duplicate from the Meter’s

Office, the Duties are Computed, and entered on the Back of the Bond, which is detained in the Office until the Factor produces the Certificate) and pays the Duties.

The Office of the Collector of the Coal Duties is in the Appointment of the Commissioners of the Customs; he is paid by a Salary, and has certain Fees; his Salary is Three hundred and Twenty Pounds a Year, which is reduced, by Taxes and Fees, to Two hundred and Sixty Pounds a Yean The Fees are certain Sams paid to him by the Factor, upon Bonds, Debentures, and Certificates, and amounted, in the Year 1781, to about One hundred and Forty-five Pounds Ten Shillings. He pays out of his Income Two Clerks, together One hundred and Twenty-four Pounds a Year.

N* 35.

The Examination of Mr. William Dobson; takeii upon Oath, November 2d, nth, and 16th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Clerk to Hugh Bishopp, Esquire, the Controller of the Coal Duty; he has been in the Office about Eight Years, and executes almost all the Business.

The Factor brings to the Controllers Office the Cocket* with an Entry Paper, which contains, amongst other Circumstances, the Quantity of Coals upon the Cocket, and the Sum deposited; if no Sum

appears upon the Entry Paper, it implies that a Bond is given to the Collector for the Duty; the Controller compares the Entry Paper with the Cocket, and inserts the Entry Paper in the Entry Book — the Cocket is taken to the Coast Office. Afterwards, the Factor brings from the Collector to the Controller, the Warrant, containing the Names of the Ship, the Master, and the Port of Lading, the Number of Chaldron, according to the Measure at that Port, the Date of the Entry, the Signature of the Collector, and the Deposit (if any). The Warrant is entered in the Deposit Book, and signed by the Controller; if it contains no Deposit, it is not entered, but only signed by the Controller; the Signature of the Collector implies that a Bond has been given to him for the Duties; the Factor then takes it to the Office of the Coal Meters.

After the Certificate on the Back of the Warrant has been filled up, and signed by the Sworn Coal

Meter, it is again brought to the Controller, with the Duties entered upon the Margin of the Certificate, as computed by the Collector, though not received by him; the Sums expressing these Duties are, One Sum for the Three Old Duties, with the Discount (if allowed) deducted from it, and One Sum for the Two Imposts, and the Total: The Controller computes the Duties, and either enters them on the other Margin of the Certificate, or ticks off the Sums as computed by the CollectorThe Controller enters the Total of the Duties in his Cash Book, and returns the Warrant to the Collector. Where the same Factor brings more Warrants than One, the whole Amount of those Warrants is entered in One Sum in the Cash Book; where the Warrants are brought by different Factors, the Sums entered are distinguished; by these Means the Controller charges the Collector with all the Duties he receives. — At the

Close

Close of the Day all these Entries are cast to a Total, and the Deposits taken are also cast to a Total, and brought in One Sum into the Cash Book, and charged against the Collector; he is discharged of the Deposits, as the Certificates are produced with the computed Duties upon them, and the Amount of the Deposits cleared is brought in One Sum to the Credit Side of the Cash Book. Where either a Deposit or a Duty has been paid into the Hands of the Receiver General, by the Direction of the Collector, at the Close of the Day the Collector produces the Receiver Generals Receipts to the Controller, who enters them in his Cash Book, in Discharge of the Collector; and these are the only Payments made by him. — The Collector keeps a Cash Book, and a Deposit Book; the Entries of the Total of each Day in these Two Books are every Day compared with the like Entries in the Books of the Controller; the Balance of the Collectors Receipts and Payments is the Cash remaining in his Hands at the End of the Day. The Controller keeps a Day Book, in which is entered, from the Certificates, the Number of Chaldron of Coals delivered; at the Close of the Week this Quantity is compared with the like Account kept by the Collector; both the Controller and Collector compute the Amount of the several Branches of the Duties upon that Quantity, and the Amount of every Branch is entered under its proper Head in the Week Book, and the Total of the Sums paid to the Receiver General during the Week is likewise ranged under the

proper Branches, which are Five in Number. The Weekly Account of the Collector, and a Duplicate of that Account, is examined by the Controller with his Week Book, and he signs his Name to both of them. The Collector's Week Book, and the Deposit Book, are both sent every Wednesday to the Board. Every Quarter the Weekly Receipts under each Branch are cast to Totals, and the Weekly Number of Chaldron are cast to a Total, both by the Collector and Controller, and the Duties computed upon that Number, to see that the Result agrees with the Totals of the Quarterly Receipts, and they compare together these Computations. The Collector sends every Quarter to the Controller his Quarter Book, containing every Circumstance relative to the Duties received during that Quarter; the Controller examines the Articles with the like Entries in his Entry Book — lie signs the Quarter Book, and sends it wdth his Day Book to the Examiner of Coal Duties. The Account of the Duties received by him, and paid to the Receiver General, is balanced every Quarter, and he retains in his Hands the Deposits not cleared, and the Day after the Quarter Day the Sum of Deposits not cleared is paid by him into the Hands of the Receiver General. It is the Usage in the Port of London, in order to encourage the speedy Payment of the Duties, to allow the Factor a Discount of 2f per Cent, upon the Amount of the Three Old Duties, provided he pays his Duties within Sixteen Working Days from the Date of his Entry, whether he makes a Deposit or gives his Bond. The late Increase of the Stamp Duties has induced the Factor to prefer Deposits to Bonds, to save the Stamp Duty: The Bonds are always payable within Three Months. Where a Bond is given, and Sixteen Days are elapsed and the Duties not paid, the Collector is charged with the Three Old Duties by the Controller, upon his receiving the Duplicate from the'Coal Meters Office, on which he calculates those Duties, but he is not charged with the Tw*o late Imposts, the Mode of keeping this Account not being yet altered and adapted to those Impositions. He is charged with the other Three, because he is supposed to have taken an effectual Security for the Payment of them. As the Deposits are paid into the Hands of the Receiver General, and all Payments to him by the Collector are at % Vol. 40.

The Two Duties of Three Shillings and Two Shil- ccouul*' lings a Chaldron, are called The Coast Duties, , and are paid at every Port; the Church Duty, which is Three Shillings, is paid in the Port of London only:

The -Coast Duties, and the Two Imposts, are drawn back upon Exportation. The Debenture for the Drawback is brought to the Controller with the Duties to be paid back computed, and entered by the Collector, and signed by him; the Controller examines them, signs his Name to the Debenture, and enters the Total Sum in his Debenture Book.

N- 36.

The Examination of Mr. Edward Millson; taken upon Oath, November 1st and 2d, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is One of the Two Clerks to the Fifteen Sea Coal Meters for the City of London, and has been so for Twenty-four Years; he and the other Clerk are appointed by them, and do all the Official Business, except that all the Warrants and Duplicates are signed by One Coal Meter; and they hold a Board once every Month, January excepted. — He understands, the Appointment of < the Sea Coal Meters is vested in the Corporation of the City of London; and the Office, when vacant, is sold for the Term of Twenty-one Years, by public Auction, in the Chamber of London, for the Benefit of the City: They have sold for upwards of Six thousand Pounds, and the last was sold for about Five thousand Three hundred Pounds; besides which, every Coal Meter pays an Annual Sum of One hundred Pounds to the Chamber of London: The Purchaser must be a Freeman of London; and in case of his Demise the Term is vested in his Representatives,

The Factor, or Agent for the Proprietor of the Coals, produces and leaves at the Office of the Coal Meters the Custom House Warrant of the Entry of the Coals, containing the Quantity, with the Fitter’s Bill from the Pit, containing both the Quantity and Description of the Coals, and the Port of Lading — the Quantity is generally the Number of Chaldron, by the Measure at the Port of Lading — the Chief of, the Coals come either from Sunderland or Newcastle, and there is no great Difference in their Measure — the Proportion of a Newcastle Chaldron to a London Chaldron varies in different Cargoes.

The Factor brings likewise a Coast Bill, signed by the Collector of the City Dues; this Coast Bill is. sent, w'ith the Fitters Bill, to the Lord Mayor; both are left in the Lord Mayors Office; the Lord Mayor sends to the Coal Meter’s Office a Permit for the unlading the Ship. — There are about Ninety Deputy Coal Meters, who are by Turns put on board the Ships, One to each Ship, to measure the Coals. He enters in his Book every Day’s Work, (that is, the Quantity delivered) by the London Chaldron — the Name of the Lighterman who has purchased them — and the Name of the Person employed by him to receive them. — After the Ship is cleared, he delivers a Copy of this Entry into the Office, together with another Account of the Names of the Purchasers, and the Quantity delivered to each; from these Two Papers, both signed by him, the Certificate is filled up on the Back of the Warrant, with the Number of London Chaldron delivered from that Ship, and is

The Factor pays at this Office One Shilling and Two Pence each London Chaldron, of which Ten Pence is the Orphans Duty, and is paid by the Receiver into the Chamber of London — Three Pence is paid to the Principal Coal Meters equally amongst them, and the remaining Penny to the Deputy who attends the Ship; upon this Payment the Factor receives back the -Tarrant, and takes it to the Custom House — The Coal Meters receive also a Halfpenny a Chaldron from the Custom House, subject to the Civil List Duty.

The Number of Chaldron of Coals brought into the Port of London in the Year 1781 w as Six hundred and Forty thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-eight; and the Net Profit of the Coal Meter was about Four hundred and Seventy-two Pounds Five Shillings and Three Pence.

N* 37-

The Examination of Mr. Humphry Bache; taken upon Oath, December 1st and 17th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he is Cashier to the Receiver General of the Customs; he has been in the Office of the Receiver General about Thirty-two Years, and Cashier about Two Years and a Half.

The Dufies arising from the Customs are paid either by the Collectors and Receivers, or by the Merchants, in the Port of London, and remitted by the Collectors at the Out Ports, into the Office of the Receiver General: Some of these are Daily, and others Weekly Payments; the Daily Payments are Payments on Account; the Weekly Payments, and the Remittances by the Collectors at the Out Ports, are appropriated., The Receivers pay Debentures, and deliver in those Debentures as Cash, or Duties received, to the Receiver General; the Receiver of the Grand Receipt pays other Debentures, which (by the Usage of his Office) he does not deliver to the Receiver General, but passes them with the Controller General. At the End of every Week every Receiver Inwards, and sometimes the Collector Outwards, has delivered to him, by the Receiver General, a Papei* informing him what Sums, of the Duties paid by him into the Treasury during that Week, are necessary to be appropriated under certain Branches; he delivers in to the Receiver General his Appropriation Paper, in which he complies with the Requisition of the Receiver General, and appropriates the Residue as he thinks proper.

The Collector of the Coal Duty appropriates his Receipt without the Intervention of the Receiver General; for the only Payments made by the 'Receiver General out of this Duty are the Drawbacks, and certain Salaries, and the Receipts under each Branch always exceed the Payments.

The Receiver General makes certain Payments out of certain Branches, pursuant either to Warrants of the Treasury, or Orders of the Commissioners; having paid into the Exchequer all the Duties he has received during the Week, he is continually making these Payments, without knowing whether he shall have

received at the End of the Week Money upon those Branches sufficient to answer those Payments: upon casting up his Payments under the several Branches, he regulates his Requisitions to the Receivers, and desires such an Appropriation, that no Branch of Duty id his Account may be overpaid. The last Day of every Week the Receiver General makes out Four Accounts or Certificates — One for the Treasury — One for the Commissioners — One for the Controller of the Receiver Generals Receipts and Payments — and One for the Exchequer; the Three First contain the Amount of the Duties received from the Collectors in the Port of London, and at the Out Ports, during the Week, appropriated under their proper Branches, and the Amount of the Payments. made by him under each Branch, and the Balances of each Branch paid into the Exchequer. The Account made out for the Exchequer contains the Surplusses of the Receipts above the Payments under each Branch, and are paid by him into the Exchequer; these Surplusses are the Receipts of the Duties as appropriated by the several Collectors, deducting the Payments made by the Receiver General; the Three First Certificates are signed by the Receiver General, and at the Beginning of the Week are sent to the Treasury, the Commissioners, and the -Controller of the Receiver General’s Receipts and Payments; on the Wednesday the Exchequer Account is carried thither, and the Total of the Duties is wrote in to the Offices of the Four Tellers, according to the Rule that govern those Offices; the Receiver General pays them by his Draft upon the Bank for the Amount. When the Tobacco Bonds are delivered to the Receiver General, by the Receiver of the Plantation Duties, which are the only Bonds delivered to him, he charges himself, in his Account of Bonds, with the Number of Bonds and the Amount of the Duties secured; Where the Tobacco is Warehoused, and the Merchant wants to take out a Part of it, and has not Time to procure a Computation of the Duties due on such Part, he deposits a Sum with the Receiver General as a Pledge for the Duties, and after they are computed this Deposit is appropriated, and goes in Part Discharge of his Bond; as the Duties on these Bonds are paid in to the Receiver General, lie charges himself with those Duties, and his Bonded Account is discharged.

The Receiver General makes no Alteration in the Appropriation of the Duties as transmitted to him by the Collectors at the Out Ports, or remitted to him by the Collectors in the Plantations.

H. Bache.

The Examination of Mr. John Dailey; taken upon Oath, January the 14th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That the Intention of sending the Weekly Abstracts of the Collectors to the Office of the Supervisor of the Receiver General’s Receipts and Payments, is to compare the Pajments made by the Collectors to the Receiver General with the Sums he charges himself with in his Weekly Certificate; the Supervisor has nothing to do either with the Receipts of the Collectors, or with their other Payments.

The Payments in these Abstracts to the Receiver General are appropriated under the same Branches as they are appropriated in the Weekly Certificate of the Receiver General.

The Supervisor is no Check upon the Sums received by the Receiver General from the Collectors at the Out Ports, the Plantations, and Scotland.

The Requisites of a Debenture, either for a Bounty or a Drawback, and the Manner of obtaining and paying it at an Out Port, are, in general, similar to the Practice io the Port of London.

The Examination of Mr. Joshua Powell; taken upon Oath, August 27th and 30th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That he has been a Collector at several of the Out Ports, and the Mode of collecting the Duties is in general the same throughout all of them: — ‘Upon the Arrival of a Ship in the Harbour, she is visited by the Tide Surveyor, who places Tide Waiters on board of her, for the Purpose of securing the Revenue, and preventing Smuggling: The next Step is, the Captains Report on Oath before the Collector, Controller, or Customer, a Copy of which is generally sent to the Tidfe Surveyor, that he may see that the whole Cargo is reported; after the Report the Merchant is at Liberty to enter his Goods, which he does by giving an Account of the Marks, Numbers, Packages, and Contents, from which the Collector makes out an Entry, which is* signed by the Merchant, and on which the Collector computes the Duties; this Computation is, or ought to be, examined by the Controller: The Entry is copied into separate Books by the Collector and Controller, with the Duties under their separate Heads, and where there fe a Customer it is, or ought to be, also entered by him: The Duties ire paid to i Vol. 40.

The Examination of Mr. Joshua Powell; taken upon Oath, October 19th, December 16th and 20th, 1784.

This Examinant saith, That in general the same Rules pursued in the Port of London, for collecting, computing, and keeping an Account of all the Custom Duties, are adhered to at the Out Ports, as far as Circumstances will permit. Every Out Port has It Customer, a Collector, and a Controller; it is the Duty of each to compute and keep an Account of all the Duties, except on Coals Coastwise, with which the Customer has no Business, because the Acts that? impose those Duties place them so peculiarly under, the Management of the Commissioners of the Customs, that the Collector receives them, and the Controller checks them, under the special Appointment of the Commissioners, and not by virtue of the Warrant of the Treasury; and therefore sometimes, at the Out Porta; the Customs and the Coal Duties are collected and controlled by different Persons: the Out Port Collector receives all the other Duties both Inwards and Outwards — The Customer, the Collector, and Controller, each send up a Quarter Book to the Office: In general, the Collector is Deputy Customer, and sends up a Quarter Book in each Capacity; the Collectors Quarter Book is lodged with the Examiner of the Out Port Collector’s Quarter Book; after Exa^ mination, he delivers it to the Surveyor of the Out Ports, with whom the other Two Quarter Books are lodged; he compares it with the Controller’s Quarter, Book, and delivers it back to the Examiner, who sends it to the Controller General — These; Officers are all Checks upon the Collector , at the Oat Ported as far as regards the Sum received: The Examiners are

700

the only Checks upon the Computation of the Duties. In the Port of London the Controller does not appear to be a Check upon the Payments made by the Collector, for he signs the Debtor Side of his Account only; but at an Out Port the Controller signs both Sides, and certifies the Balance.

The Collector at the Out Port sends every Quarter to the Board a particular Account of all die Bonds taken by him, and discharged during the Quarter; to the Controller General he sends Monthly and Annually an Account of the Amount only of the Bonds taken by him, and discharged on each Duty during the Month and Year; these Accounts are signed both by the Collector and Controller.

In the Port of London, the Collector and the Receiver General having settled the Appropriation of the Sums paid to the Receiver General, the Controller General receives from each of them the same Account of these Payments. The Receiver of the Grand Receipt is the only Receiver who makes Payments; he pays Debentures both for Drawbacks and Bounties; those which he sends to the Controller General as Vouchers in his Discharge are appropriated to their proper Duties; the Controller General makes no Alteration in the Appropriation either of these Receipts or Payments, but at many of the Out Ports the Appropriation of all their Payments is inaccurate; the Errors in the Payment of Debentures and Certificates are corrected by the Examiner; the Payment of Salaries and Incidents should be, pursuant to the Acts of Parliament, in Proportion to the Duties received under each Branch, but that is impracticable, from the Number of Branches, the Difference of the Sums received under those Branches, and the Variety of Payments, and therefore the Collector at the Out Port places them under such Heads as he thinks fit; the Controller General alters the Appropriation of these Payments, either to bring the Totals to round Sums, or to balance, as near as he can, the Receipts and the Payments upon the same Branch. The Collector at the Out Port sends every Month to the Board an Account of all his Receipts and Payments during the Month, which Account is sent by the Board to the Controller General; this Account seldom states to what Quarters the Payments relate, and therefore the Controller General cannot tell how to appropriate them; he sends up likewise an Annual Abstract of all his actual Receipts and Payments during the Year ending the 5th of January, and on it is endorsed the Amount of the Payments belonging to, or paid in each Quarter of the Year to the same Period; but this Annual Account, which includes Payments in the Lady Day Quarter which accrued in the Christmas Quarter, is not transmitted to the Controller General until after his Account of the same Year is made out, in which Account he has given the Collector Credit for Salaries and Incidents accrued during that Quarter, without knowing under what Heads the Collector will appropriate them in his next Annual Account of his Payments.

Besides the Three Collectors Inwards, Outwards, and Coals Coastwise, there are Two more Collectors in the Port of London — the Collector of Duties on Wool and Leather, and the Collector of the Duties on White Woollen Cloths — each has a separate Controller; the Duties received by these Two Collectors amount in the Year to very inconsiderable Sums: There are now no Custom Duties upon Wool — the Duties upon Leather and Woollen Cloths are Duties Outwards. The Account of the Gross Receipt of the Customs for the Year 1781, delivered to this Board, and dated the 4th of October last will not agree exactly with the Account of that Year passed in the Office of ftie Auditor; there are some Articles, both in the Receipts and Payments at the Out Ports, which were defective, and could not be rectified Time euough to

N* 42.

The Examination of Mr. Joshua Powell \ taken upon Oath, January the 19th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That the Books containing the Weekly Accounts of the Collectors in the Port of London, sent by the Controller General to the Auditor of the Imprest, contains the Weekly Certificates of the Collectors sent by them to the Controller General; the Certificates of each Collector and Receiver are bound up together; the Use made by the Controller General of these Certificates is, First, to charge the Collector with the Receipt, and in the next Place to discharge him of the Money paid by him to the Receiver General, and to charge the Receiver General therewith; and* to discharge the Collector of those Debentures, which he produces to the Controller General at the End of the Quarter, the Payment of which the Controller General is ignorant of until that Time; These Certificates are not considered as Cash Accounts, no Balance is drawn or earned over, nor does the Controller General examine the State of his Weekly Cash. If the Collector receives Bonds, the Controller General charges him with the Bonds, and discharges him of those Bonds by the Cash he admits to have received on those Bonds.

It is difficult to obtain the Annual Produce of the Duties upon any One Species of Goods, because the Duties arising from all the Good© are blended together under their several Branches The Inspector General of Imports and Exports keeps an Account of every Species imported and exported, and from knowing the Quantity of any Article, the Amount of the Duties may be computed: The Duties on Muslins and Callicoes, being by a lute Act formed into One Duty of £. 18 per Cent, a distinct Account is kept of the Produce, and the Receiver General appears in his Weekly Certificate to pay it as One Sum into the Exchequer; distinct Accounts are also kept of the Duties upon Linen, Yam, and Beaver Skins, but they appear upon the Receiver Generals Certificate to be-paid into the Exchequer, appropriated under their proper Branches.

The productive Articles of the Customs are, Wine, Tea, Tobacco, Linen, Silks, and Sugar.

The Examination of Mr. William Sims; taken upon Oath, January 27th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is One of the Foor Examiners of the Accounts of the Collectors at the Out Ports. The Out Ports are divided into Four Classes, and the Accounts of each Class are committed

to

2i° Ma.

Googh

35 Geo. III. 2t° Martii. 701

to One Examiner, and eadh Examiner has a different Class every Quarter, by regular Rotation; and therefore, in the Course of the Year, he examines One Quarterly Account of every Out Port.

Every Collector sends to the Board his Quarter Book, containing an Account of all his Receipts, and his Payments of Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills, during the Quarter,. appropriated under their proper Branches, with the Vouchers for those Payments: The Examiner takes the Quarter Book and Vouchers from the Secretary's Office; the Quarter Book contains the Circumstances of every Entry, and the Duties arising from that Entry; the Examiner computes every Article of Duty, and casts up the Totals; he computes the Sums paid on the Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills, from the Circumstances appearing upon the Face of those Instruments, and if he finds them right puts his Initials upon them. The Portage is an Allowance to the Master of a Vessel of a certain small Sum per Cent. upon the Amount of some of the Branches of the Duties arising from the Cargo, in Consideration of his making a just Report of his Cargo, and is paid to him upon his Requisition; in some Cases it is Six Shillings and Eight Pence, in others Ten Shillings per Cent. upon the Customs. The Examiner, at the Foot of the Quarter Book, forms an Abstract of the Receipt of the Quarter, comprehending the Amount of the Receipt upon each Branch, and signs his Name to this Abstract; he delivers the Quarter Book#to the Surveyor of the Out Ports, and the Vouchers to the Inspector of the Out Ports, with a Copy of his Abstract. Where there are Errors (and they are very frequent, especially in the Computations) the Examiner corrects them, surcharges the Collector with every Deficiency, and informs him of it The Surveyor returns to the Examiner the Quarter Book, with his Signature to it; the Examiner sends it to the Controller General.

W. Sims.

T. Anguish,

Geo. Drummond\

Willm Roe.

N*44.

The Examination of Mr. William Saxby; taken upon Oath, January 29th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Deputy Surveyor of the Out Ports, under Robert Thompson, Esquire, the Patentee. He receives from the Board the Quarter Books of the Out Port Customers and Controllers; these Books are designed as Checks upon the Collector’s Quarter Book; the Collector is, in every Out Port, except Five or Six, the Deputy Customer, and his Accounts as Deputy Customer are not always sent up regularly to the Board. The Surveyor depends upon the Account of the Controller; he receives the Collector’s Quarter Book from the Examiner, he compares together the Quarter Books of the Collector and Controller; if they agree he signs the Abstract of the Examiner; if they differ, he marks those Differences in the Margin of the Abstract of the Controller’s Quarter Book: He returns the Collector’s

Quarter Book to the Examiner; the Customer’s and Controller’s Quarter Books are deposited in this Office.

Wm Saxby.

The Examination of Mr. James Pawelt; taken Accounts, upon Oath, January 29th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Chief Clerk to William Eddington, Esquire, who is Patentee of the Office of Inspector of Out Port Collectors Accounts.

The Inspector receives, either from the Board or the Collectors themselves, a Quarterly Account from every Out Port Collector, containing all his Payments for Salaries and Incidents during the Quarter, sworn to by him before his Controller, and sigued by both of them, wdth the Establishment and the Vouchers for all the Payments. He examines and compares the Vouchers with the Entries of the Payments. The Authority for the Payments of the established Salaries is the Establishment, signed by Four Commissioners.

The Authority for the Payment of the incidental Salaries and Charges, are Orders signed by Four of the Commissioners. Every Out Port Collector sends up to the Board, generally every Quarter, a preparatory Account of Incidents, with the Bills; these Bills are referred to the Officers of the proper Departments, for their Examination and Report; upon their Report the Board issue their Orders to the Collector and Controller for Payment. The Inspector receives the Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills from the Examiner; he enters them in his Books, together with all the other Payments, and delivers the Account, with aH the Vouchers, to the Controller General
