N* 48.

Sir,

In Answer to your Favour of the First Instant, der siring me to answer the following Questions, relative to the Duty on Coals paid to his Grace the Duke of Richmond at this Port;

t( How much per Chaldron, and by what MeasureP — ^by whom? — at what Time? — and " upon what Account or Consideration paid ?

I acquaint you, That the Duty is 1/0. per Chalder, Newcastle Measure, (Eight of which Chalders are equal to Fifteen of Winchester Measure) and is paid by the Fitter, on Account of the Purchaser of the Coals, at the Time of clearing the Ships Coastwise, it not being due on Coals to Foreign Parts.

If by the Word "Consideration," is meant some Service or Thing done to the Trade on the Part of his Grace, I know not of any Consideration.

I am, Sir,

Your most obedient Servant,

JB. Conyers.

Custom House, Newcastle,

5 th February, 1785.

John Lane, Esq.

N# 49.

The Examination of William Stiles, Esquire; taken upon Oath, February 8th and 12th, J/8 5-

This Examinant saith, That he is Secretary to the Commissioners of the Customs; he was Deputy Controller of the Customs at the Port of Portsmouth for about Ten Years, and has been upwards of Thirty-eighth Years in the Service of the Customs.

When Goods are deemed liable to Seizure for any Cause of Forfeiture, any Officer or Officers of the Customs, empowered by Commission from the Board, seize and take them into Custody; it is their Duty to convey them to the Port nearest the Place of Seizure, and in the Port of London to deliver them to the Warehouse Keeper, and at an Out Port to the Collector and Controller, with a Note describing the Circumstances and Cause of the Seizure.

The Officer who has them in his Custody examines and delivers a particular Account of them to the Board; they refer this Account to their Solicitor, for his Report upon the Legality of the Seizure; upon that Report the Board direct him to pro* secute.

After Condemnation in the Court of Exchequer, a Writ of Delivery issues, directing the Goods to be sold, or otherwise disposed of, as the Law directs 2 If condemned before Two Justices, they make the like Order; the Warehouse Keeper, or the Collector and Controller, are directed by the Board to carry the Writ or Order into Execution; the Goods are sold publicly by Auction, the Price of them is paid to the Warehouse Keeper in London, and to the Collector at an Out Port The Accountant of Petty Receipts in London is the Check upon, and keeps the like Accounts with the Warehouse Keeper; the Controller at the Out Port is the Check upon the Collector.

The Accountant of Petty Receipts makes out an Account of the Sale, stating the Shares of each Officer, and the Share belonging to the Crown, after deducting the Expences of Condemnation; he lays this Account before the Board, they direct the Payments to be made to the several Officers; the Warehouse

Vol. 40. *

Keeper pays over the King’s Share to the Receiver of Thirteenth tines and Forfeitures for London. Report

At an Out Port the Collector and Controller are each to make out an Account of the Sale, distinguishing the Shares of the Officers, and the Share belonging to the Crown; they pay the Officers their Shares without any further Directions, and they remit the Share of the Crown to the Receiver of Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports.

The Weekly Accounts of the Collectors and Re--ceivers of the Duties in the Port of London, except the Receiver General's, are not of course laid before the Commissioners; they have no Knowledge of the State of those Recounts, nor do they ever, that he knows of, call fqif or examine the State of those Receipts and Payments; but the Board are very attentive to compel the Collectors and Receivers, as well as all Other Officers, to deliver in their Accounts to the proper Officers in due Time — they do hot examine the Accounts themselves.

W. Stiles.

T. Anguish,

Geo. Drummond\

N° 50.

The Examination of Mr.iVilliam Cooper; taken upon Oath, February 16th and lSth, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Solicitor for the Customs for the Northern Ports of England and Wales. There are Four Solicitors for the Customs, One for London and the Western Ports, One for the Northern Ports, and One for Bonds and Criminal Prosecutions — these Three are appointed by the Treasury; and One for Coast Bonds, who is appointed by the Board of Customs. The Two Solicitors for London, the Western and Northern Ports, receive Fines, and the Prosecutors Shares of Seizures and Forfeitures, where they are compromised, either by Delivery at the appraised Value, or upfcn a Composition by Li*-cence from the Court of Exchequer; or where the Seizure is delivered, upon Security to answer the Value in case of Condemnation. Where the whole Fine or Penalty is recovered, generally the Whole is paid of course by the Solicitor into the Exchequer; where it is compounded for, or recovered on a Bail Bond, the King’s Share only is paid by the Solicitor into the Exchequer, in the Case of the Bail Bond of course and in the Case of tlfe Composition, in consequence of a Warrant from the Treasury to the Commissioners of the Customs, directing what Share of it should be paid in as the King’s Share.

The Sum produced by a Compromise at the appraised Value, contains the Shares both of the Crow'n and Officers; the Share of the Crown is in general paid of course into the Exchequer; the Shares of the Officers, by Orders of the Board: Where the Sum produced is a Composition by Licence, the Solicitor receives the King’s Share only, and pays it into the Exchequer: Where the Sum produced is the appraised Value secured upon the Seizure being delivered, that Sum contains the Charges, the Shares of the Crown, and of the Officers: 'the Solicitor states the Law Charges in an Account delivered by him to the Board, and in general receives from them Directions to deduct the Charges, and to pay the Share of the Crown into the Exchequer, and the Shares of the Officers to them.

The Accounts of all the Solicitors are passed by an Officer, called The Auditor of the Solicitor’s Accounts; every Half Year the Solicitor passes an Account of his Law Charges, producing his Vouchers,

winch

704 216 Ma A. 1785.

Thirteenth Report on Public Accounts.

which are the Receipts: The Auditor allows the Payments of the Fees, upon the Authority of various Minutes of the Board; he ceftifies to the Board, r.t the Foot of the Account, that the Vouchers have oeen produced to him, and that the Fees are usual; the Board, having allowed this Account, direct the Payment

Every Year the Solicitor delivers to the Auditor an Account of all his other Receipts and Payments during the Year, with the Vouchers; the Checks upon the Receipts are the Orders of the Board, directing those Payments into the Hands of the Solicitor; the Vouchers for the Payments are the Tallies, and the Orders of the Board, with the Receipts annexed; the Auditor certifies to the Truth of this Account, and signs it; it is laid before the Board, and returned to the Solicitor, who keeps it with the Vouchers in his own Office. The Solicitors pass no other Accounts than these.

W. Cooper.

The Examination of Mr. Thomas Chauntrell;

taken upon Oath, February 11th and 12th,

1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is Warehouse Keeper in the Port of London, under the Collector Inwards, and also Deputy Receiver of the Fines and Forfeitures for London, styled in the Warrant Receiver tmd Accountant for the Money arising from the Sale of seized and condemned Goods, sold in London. The Offices of Warehouse Keeper and Receiver were united in the same Person, until about Two Years ago — they are now separated. Goods condemned or under-valued, or remaining in the King’s Warehouses above Six Months, the Duties not being paid or secured — Tobacco Ashes — refused Wines — and Goods sold for the sole Benefit of the Crown, are sold by the Warehouse Keeper by public Auction; the Money is paid by the Purchasers to the Deputy Receiver, within Fourteen Working Days after the Sale: A few Days after Payment the Surveyor of the Warehouse, the Receiver, the Warehouse Keeper, and their Controller, make up an Account of the Sale, containing the Circumstances of the Sale, and the Sum each Article is sold for — it is signed by all those Officers, and laid before the Board: Three Landing Surveyors attend the Sale, and make up a like Account, and lay it before the Board; these Two Accounts are delivered to the Accountant of Petty Receipts, who makes out the Shares of the Crown and Officers, and the Charges, and lays it before the Board. Pursuant to the Orders of the Board, the Receiver pays to the Officers their Shares; he retains in his Hands the Share of the Crown, to be disposed of as the Board shall direct.

The Accountant of Petty Receipts delivers to the Board from Time to Time a Memorial, stating the Balance in the Hands of the Receiver, and suggests what Part of that Balance.may be paid into the Exchequer; the Board direct it to be paid within Three Days, the Receiver pays it in accordingly, and takes a Tally, which he produces within Three Days to the Accountant of Petty Receipts, who is the only Auditor of the Receipts and Payments of the Receiver of The Fines and Forfeitures; the remaining Part of the Share of the Crown is paid away by the Receiver, for

Salaries, Incidents, and Imprests, pursuant to the Orders of the Board. The Balance in the Hands of the Receiver is frequently called for by the Board. The Net Proceeds arising from the Sale of the Goods undervalued, or remaining in the Warehouses, or Tobacco Ashes, or refused Wines, are all paid, gene* rally Half Yearly, into the Hands of the Collector Inwards; the Net Proceeds arising from the other Goods are carried to the Account of the King’s Share of the Produce of Seizures.

Tho1 Chauntrell.

The Examination of Mr. William ' JVtlliams; taken upon Oath, February 11th and V2tly

1785.

This Examinant saith. That he is Chief Clerk to the Receiver of Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports; he has been in this Office above Two Years. '

The Collectors at the Out Ports send to this Office an Account of their Remittances, which contains the Share of the Crown, and of those Officers who are paid in London; all these Remittances are ranged in this Office under the Head of Forfeitures. After the Bills are paid, a Cash Account is made out every Fortnight, and laid before the Board, including the Balance remaining in the Hands of the Receiver; the Shares of the Officers are paid pursuant to the Orders of the Board; the Board from Time to Time issue their Orders for the Payment of various Charges of Management. All the Payments which had been usually made by the Paymaster of Incidents, have fot these Two Years been made in this Office: The Receiver having in the last Year at Two particular Times/more in his Hand than he thought he should want, paid Two Sums into the Exchequer, amounting together to Two thousand Five hundred Pounds, without the particular Order of the Board, but in consequence of his Instructions, which direct him to pay every Fortnight into the Exchequer the Money remaining in his Hands on Account of the Crown; but since the Payment of the Incidents and Charges in this Office, the Receipt has been exhausted by those Payments, insomuch that he has been obliged to apply at different Times to the Board for Imprests, The Collector at the Out Ports sends Two similar Accounts of his Remittances, One to the Controller of the Receiver, the other to the Accountant of Petty Receipts. The Account of the Fortnight is examined and signed by the Controller, compared with the Books of the Accountant of Petty Receipts, and countersigned by him; this Officer passes the Account of the Receiver at least Once in every Year, and the Receiver passes no other Account.

The Bills and Cash are kept in an Iron Chest, to which there are Two Keys, One kept by the Receiver, the other by his Controller; it cannot be opened, unless both are present.

' IV. Williams.

The Examination of Mr. John Bastin; taken upon Oath, February 14th and 16th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is First Clerk to the Accountant of Petty Receipts; he has been in this Office about Twenty-three Years.

The Notes of Seizures in London are sent from the Warehouse Keeper, and entered in this Office the Tike Notes are sent from the Collectors and Controllers at the Out Ports to the Board, and entered in this Office. In London the Two Accounts of the Sale are sent to this Office, and the Three Divisions of the Produce formed from those Accounts, and the Account of that Division laid before the Board.

The Collector and Controller at an Out Port send from Time to Time to this Office an Account of his Remittances; and every Quarter he sends up a State of his Sales, comprehending both his Receipts and Payments, with the Vouchers for his Payments. The Orders of the Board Upon the Two Receivers in London ore entered in this Office,* previous to the Payment, and signed with the Initials of the Officer.

The Accountant of Petty Receipts passes the Accounts of both the Receivers, and of the Collectors, at the Out Ports, relative to the Produce of Seizures. The Account of the Receiver for London is passed after every Sale; he produces to this Office his Book, comprehending all his Receipts and Payments relative to that Sale, and the Balances remaining in his Hands on Account of former Sales, with the Vouchers, except the Tallies, which are produced within Three Days after the Payments are made into the Exchequer. The Receipt is checked by the Account of the Land Surveyors; the Payments are allowed upon com-

paring the Orders with the Entry of them in the Office Thirteenth Books, and seeing the Receipts annexed to those Orders. Hcport 7"he Accountant signs every Entry of Receipt and Public Payment in the Book with his Initials; the Book and c^ounti-Vouchers are deposited with the Accountant, and lie gives the Receiver a Receipt for them, which is his Acquittance.

The Receiver for the Out Ports makes out an Account every Fortnight of his Receipts and Payments during that Time, with the Balance of his last Account remaining in his Hands, and produces it, with the Vouchers, in this Office; the Accountant examines the Entries on the Receipt Side with the Entries of the Remittances in the Books of the Office, and the Payments with the Entries of the Orders, and with the Vouchers: He certifies at the Foot of the Account to the Truth of it, transmits the Account to the Board, and returns the Vouchers to the Receiver.

Every Quarter his Account, is finally passed, in the same Manner as that of the Receiver for London, and his Vouchers are deposited in this Office; but his Book of Account remains with him. In passing the Accounts of the Collectors at the Out Ports, the Accountant relies upon the Signature of the Controller appearing upon the Face of the Account, both as to the Receipts and Payments; and having compared the Vouchers, consisting of the Orders and Receipts, with the Entries in the Account, the Vouchers, with the Account, are kept in the Office. This is the final Audit of all these Accounts.

Jtf Bastin.

Na 63.

The Examination of Mr. Deacon; taken upon Oath, January the 19th, 1785.

The Examination of Mr. William Mucklow; taken upon Oath, January 2ist^ 1785.

This Examinant saith, That the Payments in the Weekly Abstracts contain only the Sums paid to the Receiver General, excepting the last Week of the Quarter. The Sum Total paid to the Receiver General is usually less than the Sum received. The Debentures paid during the Week, and to be delivered to the Receiver General as Cash, are generally not delivered until the Week after they are paid; and the Receiver is continually paying those Debentures, which he does not deliver to the Controller General until the End of the Quarter. There is no Check upon the Cash Account of the Receiver, nor does he give any other Account of the Debenture he pays, than those to the Receiver and Controller General.

The Balance Book contains the Weekly Totals of the Receipts and Payments under each Branch, as they are entered in the Weekly Abstracts, with the Balance on each Branch. The Receipts and Payments upon each Branch should be cast up every Quarter, and brought as near as may be to a Balance; but the Business has increased so much lately, from the Increase of the Number of Branches, that it has for some Time been impracticable to bring them to a Balance. This Balance Book is of no Use to any but the Collector, except that the Controller General examines it with his own Balance Book at the End of the Year.

Ja. Deacon.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Richd Neave,

Sam! Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will Roe.

N* 62.

This Examinant saith, That in the Accounts of the Wine Receipts and Payments, delivered every Week to the Controller General, the Receipt is of Money only, and is arranged under the same Branches as are entered upon the Warrants; the Payments are Sums to the Receiver General, including Cash, and Debentures paid to him as Cash, and Imprest Orders: The Payment of Debentures is Daily, of Imprest Orders uncertain; he does not pay to the Receiver General every Day all the Debentures he pays in that Day, it would be inconvenient to both Offices; he cannot pay in until the Monday or Tuesday the Debentures he pays on the Saturday, and therefore they cannot be brought to that Week’s Account, and for that Reason the Receipt of several Weeks appears to be greater than the Amount of the Payments in those Weeks; but at the End of the Quarter he balances his Cash Account as near as he can, by appropriating the Money remaining in his Hands amongst the Branches, so as to bring each Branch to a Balance, if the Hurry of Business will permit, and pays it into the Treasury; he credits himself every Week for the Imprest Orders paid during the Week, and once a Year he sends them to the Controller General, who allows them to him in his Annual Account.

The Imprest Orders are almost all paid out of One Branch — the Impost on Wines, and appropriated under that Branch; there is no other Check, that he knows of, upon the Cash Account, except the Two Accounts delivered to the Receiver and Controller General.

Wm Mucklow.

T. Anguish,

Richd Neave,

Geo. Drimmondy IViU" Roe.

The Examination of Mr. Henry Gyles; taken upon Oath, January 21st, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That he is npw appointed Receiver of the Plantation 'Duties. In the Weekly Accounts delivered to the Controller General, the Receipts, both in Money and Bonds, are appropriated under the same Branches as they are upon the Warrants; the Payments to the Receiver General are appropriated according to his Application, and include Cash and Debentures; the Bonds delivered to the Receiver General are appropriated under their true Branches. The Sum received during the Week generally exceeds the Sum that appears in the Account to be paid during the Week. The; Receiver General never takes in the Debentures paid either late on the Friday or on the Saturday, they cannot therefore be brought into the Account of the Week; and if the Receiver knows that Debentures will be brought to him for Payment, he retains Money for that Purpose: He makes up Officially no Weekly Cash Account,- npr is there any Check upon that Account.

Henry Gyles.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Geo. Drummond,

milm Roc.

N* 64.

The Examination of Mr. James Dodson; taken upon Oath, January 26th and 28th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That the Payt*ents into the Treasury, for about One Year, from the* End of May 1780, were not according to the usual Course of Payments; during that Year his Payments into the Treasury every Week, except in the Two or Three last Weeks in each Quarter, were much less than the Amount of the Receipts of each Week; he received Directions from his Principal, and did (pursuant to those Directions) pay the Remainder of those Weekly Receipts into a Bankers; from the 30th of May 1780 to the 9th of October, following, to his own Account, and from that Time to the 23d of June 1781, to the Account of his Principal: On the 5th of July 1780 he had drawn out of the Banker’s Hands, and paid into the Treasury, all the Sums he had paid in, except Two Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Nine Pence; this Balance increased so as to amount, upon the 9th of October, to One thousand One hundred and Sixty-five Pounds Ten Shillings, which he took from the Banker’s on the 10th, end paid into the Treasury that Day; he had, a few Days before, received Directions from his Principal, to place these Sums paid to the Banker, not to hi9 own Account, but to that of his Principal During the Time this Money continued placed to his own Account, he drew out no 4 , Part

25 Geo. III.

2i° Ma

711

Part of it for any private Use. In the last Two or Three Weeks of the Three succeeding Quarters* he received back from his Principal, Sums to reduce the Balance remaining on his Account at the Banker’s, and paid those Sums into the Treasury; the Balance left, upon the Account of his Principal, at the Banker’s, on the 5th January 1781, was Nine hundred and Fifteen Pounds and Eight Pence; on the 5th of April 1781 it was One thousand Two hundred and Ninety Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Four Pence; and on the 5th July 1781 it was Two thousand Five hundred and Forty-one Pounds Two Shillings and Four Pence. About Midsummer 1781, the Controller General objected to these short Payments; and being informed of the Reasons* he directed that the Balance should be paid into the Treasury: Upon Application to his Principal, he received from him at different Times, to the 28th of September following, One thousand Nine hundred and Fifty Pounds, and paid it into the Treasury; this left, upon the Account of his Principal, at the Bankers, Five hundred and Ninety-one Pounds Two Shillings and Four Pence, which, as he believes, still remains unpaid, for he as Receiver stands charged with it, and the Receiver General eannot receive it Officially but through his Hands. Ever since that Time, his Weekly Payments into the Treasury have nearly equalled his Weekly Receipts. The Receiver of the Export Duties makes out no other Cash Account than the Weekly Account delivered to the Controller General, and the Duplicate, nor is there any other Check upon his Cash Account He receives no Official Instructions, either from his Principal or the Board, relative to his Payments into the Treasury.

James Dodson.

N* 65.

The Examination of Robert Weston, Esquire; taken upon Oath, January 28th, 1785.

This Examinant saith, that the Difference in the Weekly Accounts, between the Receipts of the Duties, and the Payments to the Receiver General, arises, from the Difference between the Deposits taken, and the Deposits cleared, in each Week: The Deposits taken, are added to the Sum of the Weekly Receipt of Duties; the Deposits cleared, are deducted from that Amount, and the Balance is paid into the Hands of the Receiver General, arranged under the proper Branches; and therefore sometimes the Receipts exceed the Payments, and sometimes the Payments exceed the Receipts. The Appropriation of the Payments to the Receiver General in the Weekly Account, is the same as in the Appropriation Paper delivered in to the Receiver General.

Rob? Weston.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Rich? Neave,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

N* 66.

An Account of the Nature of the present System of computing the Duties of Customs: in which some of the Inconveniencies attending it are stated, and the different Principles from which those Duties originate are explained by Ex-

Thirteenth Report on Public Accounts

In endeavouring to explain the various -Causes of that Intricacy which now so generally pervades the whole System of computing the Custom Duties, it will not be necessary to enter into a State of those Duties prior to the Act of the 12th Cha? 2nd, Cap. 4, called The Act of Tonnage and Poundage; the Book of Rates established by that Act being still in force, it must be considered as the Foundation of the present Customs.

The Duties on Goods imported, at that Time, consisted of a Tonnage and a Poundage, Duty; the Principles of both were simple — Tonnage was a certain Duty on every Ton of Wine imported — Poundage, a Duty or Subsidy of 12 d. in the Pound, according to the Rate (which was supposed to be the Value) affixed to the Article in the Table of Rates; and on Goods not therein enumerated, it was payable on the Value, to be ascertained by the Oath of the Importer. So far the Duties might be well understood both by the Merchant and the Officer; but it should be observed, that even these Duties were somewhat perplexed by certain Allowances and Deductions for prompt Payment, by which Means the Net Duties have not at any Time appeared under the Authority of a Statute; a separate Operation by Figures was always necessary, and these Deductions generally occasioned the Amount of the Net Duty to be a nice Fraction: But these Discounts have been, within these few Years, abolished by the Authority of Parliament

A Deviation from the System of Tonnage and Poundage took place soon after the passing that Act, and was the primary Cause of the present Intricacy; for, had those Principles been strictly adhered to in the imposing new Duties, the computing Officers might easily have framed correct and explicit Tables of Duties and Drawbacks, whenever Alterations or Additions made new’ ones necessary: These Tables might have shewn w hat it is impossible to do at present, the Net Duties and Drawbacks on each Article, at One View and in One Sum. — The Impossibility of doing this under the present Laws, which impose the various Custom Duties, will be obvious, from the following Statement of the Nature of those Duties; which consist of

A Subsidy of Tonnage, 1 The Nature of which has A Subsidy of Poundage,/ been already explained.

An Impost or Duty originating in the Weight of the Article, which is an additional Duty, not springing from the Rate, is unconnected with foe Subsidy of Poundage, and requires a separate Operation*

See the Example annexed, N° 1.

An Impost Duty according to the Ton, by Gauge; which requires a separate Operation, where the rest of the Duties depend on the Rate or Value.

Example, N° 2.

An Impost or Duty on certain Articles, springing from their Value on Oath; this requires a separate Operation, the other Duties arising from the Rate.

Example, N° 3.

Vol. 40.

A Duty


Thirteenth Report on Public Accounts.

71a

A Duty arising from the Gross Price at which the Goods are publicly sold; this is a separate Operation, the other Duties springing from the Rate.

Example, N° 4.

A Duty arising from a specific Sum, charge4 to the Branch called The Old Subsidy, in lieu of the Duty springing from the Rate; this operates on some Articles, where the rest of the Duties still depend on the Rate.

Example, N* 5.

A Duty, not springing either from the Rate or Value, but arising from the Number of the Commodity.

Example, N° 6.

A Duty arising from the Measufe of the Article (being a Measure of Capacity) independent of the other Duties.

Example, N° 2.

A Duty arising from the Measure of the Article (being a Measure of Extent) unconnected with the other Duties originating in the Rate or Value on Oath.

Examples, N° 7 and 8.

A Duty arising from the Weight of the Commodity, where the rest of the Duties spring from the Value on Oath.

Examples, N° 9 and N° 18.

A specific Duty, charged in One Sum, independent of any Rate or Value whatever.

Example, N° 10.

A Duty on Unrated East India Goods, to be ascertained by the Price at the Company’s Sale, which Price is reduced to the Value of the Goods at Importation, by certain Deductions, in Proportion to the Duty and Charges.

Example, N° 11.

A Duty on Unrated East India Goods, to be ascertained by the Gross Price at the Company’s Sale, without any Deduction whatever.

Example, N# 12.

A Duty arising from the Value of the Goods, to be ascertained by Oath; without Abatement for any Duty whatever, and independent of the former Duties, whether springing from the Rate or Value.

Examples, N° 3 and N° 13.

A Duty which is a specific Sum, independent of the Rate or Value, and regulated by the Quality or Goodness of the Article.

Example, N° 14.

A Duty arising from a specific Sum charged on an Article, to be appropriated to Part of the former Duties only.

Example, N° 15.

A Duty arising from the Amount of Part of the Duties.

Example, N° iG.

A Duty arising from a specific Sum charged on an Article, but where a troublesome Operation, by Means of a feigned Rate, is necessary to appro-

A. 1785.

priate that Sum proportionately to the several Branches having Claims thereon.

Example, N° 17.

A Duty arising from the Total Amount of all former Duties, being the Two Five per Cent. Duties of the Years 1779 and 1782.

Exclusive of these several different Principles of Operation, the Difficulty of Computation is much increased by various other Causes, too numerous to mention, and too intricate to explain; such as the Difference of Duty occasioned by particular Circumstances of Importation, and local Distinctions. — Drugs, rated by the 12 Chas 2nd, Cap. 4, are subject to Treble Duty, unless imported in British Ships, and directly from the Place of their Growth; and Goods of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of the East Indies, France, or the French Plantations, are subject to much higher Duties than Goods of the same Kind, imported from other Places.

The Inconveniences arising from the present System are many, and material. — From its complicated Nature Errors must inevitably arise, which the utmost Diligence in the Officer cannot entirely prevent, and which the Merchant is frequently unable to discover.

The computing the several Duties on the Entries of each Day, w hen those Entries are not particularly numerous, w'ith the Posting them into the proper Books, so fully employ the‘/Officers in that' Department, that, from the Increase of Business at particular Times of the Year, it is not possible to prevent the public Accounts being retarded, and kept open much longer than they otherwise might be; nor can this be remedied by procuring further Assistance — A Science so complicated few are willing tp study; and of those who are ablef to instruct others, scarce any one can spare the Time from his constant daily Employment; and no Man, however extensive his Knowledge in other Respects, can be an Assistant any Ways useful in this Department, till he well understands the Nature of the several Duties. The Truth is, that the Number of Persons competent to this Business is gradually lessening, withbut the Appearance of others to supply their Places.

What has been said, relates principally to the Duties on Goods imported; of the Drawbacks (the Computation of which was always more intricate and perplexing than that of the Duties) it is sufficient to mention, that, from a Variety of Causes, the Difficulty of computing them is increased in a very great Degree — from the Increase of Difficulty, Errors and Delay must naturally arise — these are considerably augmented from the unavoidable Circumstance of blending in One Entry a Variety of Articles. — That the Examples annexed may be better understood, they relate to One Article only, and are each intended separately to explain a different Principle of Computation; but it will very often happen that several of these Principles operate in One Entry of Goods imported] and the Necessity of applying very many of them to ascertain the Drawback due on One Debenture for Goods exported, will also very frequently occur.

Thirteenth Report on Public Accounts.

Of the Nature of the Duties on unrated East India Goods it is not easy to convey, to Persons unacquainted with the general System of the Customs, a clear and precise Idea; it is attempted in the following Observations.

By the 2nd and 3d Ann, Cap. 9, it is directed,' That the Value according to which the Duties on unrated

East India Goods (which till that Time were ascertained by the Oath of the Importer) are to be paid in

future, shall be reckoned according to the Gross Price at which such Goods shall be sold, making certain Allowances therefrom; these Allowances were — so much as the Net Duties amounted to — Six per Cent, allowed the Company for Charges — and also so much as the Company shall allow the Buyers for prompt Payment —

the Remainder is what is called at the Custom House the reduced Value, and on which the Duties existing at

the Time of passing the Act (8th March 1703) have ever since been computed. The Reason that induced the Legislature to direct these Allowances was probably this — The Duties on unrated Goods were due on Importation, and were payable according to the Value, to be ascertained by the Oath of the Importer, and in which Valuation the Duties were not included — and, as unrated East India Goods are sold by the Company free of Customs to the Buyer, the Price will be increased in Proportion to the Amount of the Duty — therefore the altering the Mode of ascertaining the Value of those Goods, from the Oath at the Time of Importation to the Gross Price at the Sale, would have been a material Loss to the Company had not the Act which directed the Alteration provided ne Remedy — therefore the Deductions to be made are to be considered as reducing the Gross Price at the Sale as near as can be to the real Value of the Goods at the Time of Importation. The Operation is thus performed:

Certain Cowries sold at the East India Company’s Sale for -

From this Sum must be deducted the Allowance made to the Company for Charges; viz*. 6 per Cent....

And also as much as the Duties then payable amounted to.

TEA, sold for £. 100. Since the 15th September 1784.

The former Duties were, by the 24 Geo. 3rd, Cap. 38, repealed; and from the 15th September 1784 all Tea delivered by the East India Company became liable only to a Duty of £. 12. xo. per Cent, on the gross Price at their Sale; this Sum, being applicable to those Branches of which the former Duties were composed, the due Proportion to each can only be ascertained by the following Statement: — As £. 27. — xo, the former Total Duty on Tea sold for £100, is to £. 12. 10, the present Total Duty — so is £. 3. 12. 11, the former Old Subsidy, to the Portion now to be charged to that Branch. — The Subsidies 1747 and 1759 also require a separate Operation.

The Appropriation of the present Duty is as follows:

Although nothing can be more simple in its Nature, or more easily understood by the Importer or Exporter, than a Duty and Drawback of £.12. xo. per Cent, on the gross Price or Value of an Article, when that Value is ascertained by public Sale, yet to the Computing Officer, who is under the Necessity of preserving separately the precise Sum to be appropriated to each Branch, in the Proportions before stated, a new Source of Difficulty arises, and an Operation tedious and perplexing becomes unavoidably necessary.

N°73.

The Examination of John Hughson, Esquire; taken upon Oath, 28th February, 1st and 4th March, 1785.

This Examinant saith, That the Duties collected in the Customs under the Heads of Linen Yam, and Beaver Skins, are paid into the Exchequer under those Deads, but directed by the Receiver General to be placed in the Exchequer to some other Heads by him specified. The Two Duties upon Gum Senega, as being upon One Article, and both unappropriated, are consolidated in the Exchequer. — The Duties under the Title of Customs are paid into the Exchequer in Moieties, under the Heads of Half Subsidies 1712 and 1714.

Some Time in every, Session an Account is delivered to Parliament, containing the Sum produced by each of the unappropriated Branches; the Produce of these Branches is applied in the Appropriation Act to the Services of the Year.

The Services to which the Compound Funds are liable are paid as they arise, without any Priority.

The Sums payable to the South Sea Company upon their Original Fund are to be paid Weekly, if they require it. The whole Produce of the Coinage

Vox.. 40.

Duty on Wine is applied to the Coinage, and paid by a Warrant of the Treasury, to the Masters of the Mint in England and Scotland; it is generally deficient, and the Deficiency is paid out of the Supplies of the Year; it does not appear in the Exchequer what the Annual Allowance amounts to No Sum has yet been issued from the Exchequer for the Encouragement of the Growth of Cotton in the Leeward Islands. Sums have been paid, pursuant to Treasury Warrants* for the Encouragement of raising Hemp and Flax in Scotland; of the Produce is designed for Scotland\ and for England; nothing has been demanded from England.

The Surplusses, not only of the Compound Funds, but of the separate and distinct Funds, are, for the most Part, carried to the Sinking Fund, and that Fund is made liable to the Deficiencies, which are restored by the Supplies of the current or succeeding Year. The General, Aggregate, and South Sea Funds, always produce more than the Charges upon them.

A distinct Account is kept in the Receipt of the Exchequer of the Weekly Receipts of, and Issues out of, every Branch of Duty: All the Issues are directed by the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, pursuant to the Weekly Account of the Receipts, Issues, and Remains upon each Head of Duty, transmitted to 9 C them

Thirteenth Report on Public Account*.

Thirteenth lleport on Public Accounts.

74a 210 Martii. 1785.

them from the Exchequer; they direct the Sum, the Service, and out of what Branch, in which they are governed by the Account of the preceding Week; they direct no more to be issued from any Brandi than appears either to remain upon that Branch in the Account of the preceding Week, or to have been received on that Branch preceding the Day of the Issue, nor do they direct the Issue of Money Out of any Branch to any other Service than that to which that Branch is rendered applicable by the Legislature.

Where the whole Produce of any Branch is carried to a Compound Fund, the Service to which the Issue is directed must be the Service to which the Compound Fund is applicable. Where the Issue is directed out of a Branch applicable to specific Services, the Account of which is kept separate and apart, and the Surplus carried to a Compound Fund, the Title of the Service in the Treasury Directions shews whether the Issue is for the specific Service, which is always limited, or for a Service to which the Compound Fund is applicable.

The Reason why the Produce of the Sinking Fund for the Year 1784 is so small, is because the Deficiencies of the Anuuity Funds for that Year, and the preceding Quarter, have been paid out of that Fund, and not yet made good by Parliament; the Amount of these Deficiencies is One Million Six hundred and Six thousand Nine hundred and Fifty-four Pounds Fifteen Shillings and One Halfpenny.

John Ilughson.

T. Anguish,

Rich*1 Neate,

Uouse, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the "original Excellence of the Constitution of this Country, most ardently wish to have it maintained upoii the genuine Principles oh which it was founded; and that it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation; and that, ill the present State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, the Commons of this Realm are partially dnd inadequately represented, and consequently cannot have that Security for their Liberties which it is the Aim of the Constitution to give them: And therefore supplicating the House to take into their most serious Consideration the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy to this great Constitutional Evil as to t^he House may seem meet.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Cotton and others, of the County Palatine of Lancaster, ribt Trade, actually engaged in the Commerce of the said County, w as presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That, from their Knowledge of the Manufacture of the County, they are thoroughly sensible that an Act of the last Session of Parliament, for granting certain Duties on Cotton Stuffs, bleached or dyed, and on Licences for bleaching or dying the same, is, and will be, in its Consequences, in a very great Degree, destructive to the Trade of the County, and highly prejudicial to the general Weal of the Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the House will grant them such Relief in the Premises, as to their Discretion shall seem meet.

A Memorial and Petition of the Manufacturers of Ditto, White Cottons and Muslins, in the City of Glasgow, and the Neighbourhood, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Memorialists did not fail, during the last Session of Parliament, respectfully to state to His Majesty's Ministers, and to the Legislature, their serious Apprehensions of the dangerous Consequences likely to result from the Duty on Cottons and Muslins, then unhappily proposed as an Object of Revenue, and afterwards actually adopted as One of the Public Taxes: While the Memorialists were impelled, by a sacred Regard to the Laws of the Realm, respectfully to submit to the Burdens thus laid upon them, distressing and injurious as they are, the same Sentiments of Regard for their Country, and for the Preservation of a valuable Manufacture, urges them, on the present Occasion, to offer to Parliament their humble Representations on the Subject of the Tax in Question, which the Experience of a few Months has rendered more grievously distressing, than their utmost Apprehensions had formerly suggested to their Minds: Under Circumstances, therefore, of real, and not imaginary Distress, the Memorialists humbly represent to the House their serious Apprehensions, that all those Advantages which might reasonably be expected from a great and extended Branch of Trade, will be sacrificed to a System of Taxation, by no Means productive to Government, in so far as it is found impossible to apply the Rules of Excise to the various Circumstances attending the Progress of this Manufacture to Maturity, without such Inconvenience and Distress as will render it impossible to carry on the Trade; this Allegation has been sufficiently evinced and proved, by the various Representations of the Manufacturers of Manchester to His Majesty’s Ministers, exhibiting, in Detail, not only the specific Inconveniences which arise from the System thus unhappily introduced, but the Impossibility of executing the Requisites of the Law, without the most imminent Hazard of Forfeiture to the fair Trader, as well as the very great Risque of opening a Source of illicit Trade to such as were inclined to defraud His Majesty’s Revenue; the Hazards and Inconveniences attending the Introduction of a new Branch of Trade, are manifestly obvious, and the necessary and unavoidable Struggles to bring the same to Perfection, point out, in strong Colours, the Cruelty of disturbing Infant Manufactures in their Progress to Maturity; the Muslin Branch has already afforded Employment to many Thousands of the industrious Poor of both Sexes; its Progress, previous to the late unhappy Regulations, was rapid beyond all Example, and no Manufacture, established in this Part of the

united

25 Geo. III. li*Martii 749

united Kingdom, ever promised $6 fair to become & National Blessing, and to diffuse its Influence over a wide and extended Community, giving Employment and Bread to all Ages, and producing to the Country a liberal Return for the Labours of the industrious Poor: The Perseverance and Itigenuity thus manifested by the Muslin Manufacturers, in bringing to Per* section an Article of extensive Commerce, which, till now, was supposed to be capable of being produced in India alone, certainly merits the Attention of this House, to whom, as Guardians of the Manufactures of the Country, the Memorialists look up for that Favour and Protection which shall not only rescue them from the Fetters of Excise Laws, but also assist their Struggles in combating the strong Opposition which they experience from the extensive Importations of a similar Article pressed upon the Market by the East India Company, under Circumstances calculated to crush and to annihilate a Branch of Commerce already proved to be productive of the most extensive Advantages to the Nation; nor are the Discouragements, which ucheck and disturb this Infant Manufacture, confined alone to the Circumstances already mentioned; the Interference of the East India Company, in selling their Muslins by Auction, frequently at or under the original Cost, deprives the Memorialists of a fair and equal Market, and actually subjects them to the Loss of the whole Duty, which they have been unable to charge upon the Consumer, on account of the impolitic Competition, raised up by the Introduction of a Foreign Article: The Hardships attending the present Tax appear still in a stronger Point of View, when contrasted with the wise Policy of the Sister Kingdom, whose Legislature, ever attentive to the Improvement and Extension of Inland Branches of Trade, are, at this Moment, holding out the most liberal Encouragement for promoting a similar Manufacture; nor is it (unhappily for this Country) an ill-founded Assertion, that many ingenious Weavers, allured by the Advantages held out in Ireland, and dispirited by the ill-advised Restrictions and Burthens imposed in Britain, have actually removed to a Country, where the System of protecting and encouraging Manufactures, by Bounties, in Place of Imposts, must induce others to follow their Example, unless the present System shall be abandoned in Great Britain; nor ought the Memorialists to omit to mention, that the great Increase of the Muslin Branch in this Part of Great Britain has been occasioned by the Decline of the Manufacture of Lawns of all Kinds (for many Years a great Staple in Scotland) for which the Muslins are now used as a Substitute; and hence it appears, if the Country is deprived of the Cotton Manufacture, at a Period when the ancient Staple is also hurt, the Calamity will be doubly severe, and the Consequences to the lower Ranks, who assist in the auxiliary Branches of the Manufacture, will be distressing in the Extreme, as they cannot avail themselves of the Advantages held out to ingenious Artists, who, Individually, can suffer no material Loss, as their Emigration to Ireland, from the Vicinity of the Two Countries, is effected at so easy an Expence, as to render the Intercourse open to all who incline to listen to the liberal Encouragement held out by the Irish Manufacturer: In pursuing the Argument arising from the Contrast alius drawn, the Memorialists cannot, in Justice to their Country, conceal from this House the great additional Advantages which result to the Sister Kingdom from the Taxes of the last Session of Parliament, imposed on Cottons and Muslins; this Impost operates as a Bounty, in Addition to the liberal Aids of the Irish Legislature of near Ten pa' Cent. in Favour of the Manufactures of that Country at every Foreign Market; and, while the Memorialists applaud the Policy and Wisdom of the Sister Kingdom, in holding out such liberal Encouragement to those Sources of Vol. 40.

Wealth and Industry, upon which her true Interest depends, they look up with Confidence to- this House, for such an equal Adjustment of Commercial Privileges, as shall place the Manufactures in every Part of the Empire upon a fair and equal Footing; nor ought the Memorialists to conceal from the House the Sentiments they entertain of the Favour of Government, so liberally bestowed on the United Company of Merchants trading to the East Indies, in so far as the Public Aids thus afforded, have had a Tendency to check the growing Manufactures of the Country, by a System of Discrimination which exhibits the Monopoly of the Commerce of India, as highly favoured by Government, encouraged and protected by a Public Loan of One Million, free of Interest, while Taxes are levied on the Muslin Manufacture of Great Britain1, to fill the Treasury from whence this Aid is drawn, and drawn too for the Purpose of giving Aid to a Rival Manufacture, the Produce of a Foreign Country* thus raised and supported; not only from the Burthens imposed upon a similar Article produced in Great Britain, but also by a Reduction of Duties operating as an additional Distress upon the Industry of the Country: The Memorialists having, on many Occasions, experienced the nursing and protecting Hand of the Legislature, in the Operation of that Principle which removed every possible Obstruction to the Progress of useful Manufactures in Great Britain, and left the ingenious Artist free and unfettered, to pursue his Employment, cannot sufficiently lament the Fatality which has subjected even an Infant Branch to a Burthen which, from the Facts already stated, has proved not only ruinous to the Manufacturer, but unproductive to Government: And therefore praying*

That the House will take into their serious Considered tion the various Circumstances of Distress and Danger to which the Muslin and Cotton Trade ha9 been subjected by the Taxes of the last Session of Parliament, and that such Relief shall be granted, and such Arrangement made, for the Encouragement and Protection of this new and valuable Manufacture, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Land Owners, Merchants, Manufacturers, Dyers,

Bleachers, and others, interested in the Fustian Trade, in the Towns of Manchester, Salford,

Ashton, Bury, Chorley, Stockport, Macclesfield, and Chapel en le Frith, and in the Boroughs of Wigan and Newton, and of the respective Neighbourhoods of those Towns and Boroughs* in the Counties of Lancaster, Chester, and Derby, is referred.

A Petition of the Merchants, Tradesmen, and Commercial Manufacturers of the Town of Wolverhampton, was Intercourse presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, withlitUnd, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Commercial Arrangement between Great Britain and Ireland is very soon to come under the Consideration of Parliament, and that the Commerce of each Country should be regulated by Means of equalizing the Du ties in both; to obtain the End proposed, the Petitioners conceive either that each Country should admit the Produce, Wares, and Manufactures of the other Duty-free, or that the Duties payable in each should be so modified, that if Duties are laid on the Produce of either Kingdom in One, an equivalent Duty should be laid in that paying the Duty on the Ad* mission of the Produce of the other; and that, in order to place each Country upon an Equality in manufacturing, the Petitioners apprehend, that the Duties on Raw Materials for that Purpose, from 9 E Foreign

Sterling only is paid in the latter; and that the* ‘Petitioners are justly apprehensive, from this great Disparity of Duties, aided by lower Wages, and comparatively much lighter Taxes in Ireland, such Advantages will accrue in Favour of that Country, as nothing we-possess in Preference can compensate for, and that the certain and immediate Consequence must be Emigrations from this Kingdom, and, in the End, a Removal of the Iron Manufactory from it, on which the Existence of the said Town and Neighbourhood depends: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into their most serious Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the w hole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchant Venturers of the City of Bristol, under their Common. Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House of Commons in Ireland, that certain general Propositions, as a Foundation for new Regulations of the Commerce between Great Britain and Ireland\ have been voted by that House, from which, if agreed to by the Legislature of this Country, the Petitioners entertain great Apprehensions that most important evil Consequences will ensue to its Trade and .1

Manufactures, and eventually to the Landed Interest: That the Manufacturer in Great Britain, being obliged to advance to Government the heavy Duties and Excise imposed; upon bim; cannot support a Competition against the Irish Manufacturer, who bearing no Part of this Burthen, cau carry on an equal extensive Trade with a much smaller Capital; and that the just Retribution which our American Colonies make for the Expence of their Establishment, for the Support they receive by our exclusive Consumption of their Produce, and for the Protection afforded them by our Navy, will no longer exist, if Liberty be given to import West India Productions, either in their Raw or Manufactured State, from Ireland, greater Opportunity will be afforded for the illicit Introduction of them, and this Country will be deprived of the Advantage arising from the Supply of its own Markets, to which it is entitled both fronl Justice and Policy, and similar Mischief would accrue to the Revenue, and to the Carrying Trade of Great Britain, if the Import of Foreign Produce from Ireland be generally allowed; and that the Petitioiw ers entertain the most eprdial Wishes for the Increase and Extension of the Irish Commerce and Manufactures, in every Circumstance, not productive of essential Detriment to those of Great Britain, and submit to the House, whether, if the Spirit of those Resolutions should be adopted, it will be possible to prevent such Evil, unless the Legislature of Ireland will consent to impose Duties on Importation from Foreign States, equal to those now payable in Great Britain, the Manufacturers of Great Britain and Ireland be placed upon an equal Footing in respect40 the Burthens they bear, and the Staples of both Kingdoms be rendered liable to equal Duties on Import each into the other: And therefore praying. That when the particular Detail of the proposed Regulations shall be before the House, they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, respecting the 9ame; or that the House will afford the Petitioners such other effectual Relief in the Premises as it shall judge meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse betw een Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners be heard by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Sugar Refiners of the City Commerce! of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, thatwilh K certain general Propositions, as a Foundation for new Regulations of the Commerce between Great Britain and Ireland, are now under Consideration of the House, and the Petitioners are apprehensive of very important and injurious Consequences to their Manufacture, if the same should pass into a Law in their present Form; and Alledging, that the Petitioners have been at the Expence of upwards of £. 150,000 in Buildings and Utensils to carry on their Trade, and, should the Legislature of Ireland' under the Privilege of importing Raw and Refined Sugars through that Country to this, lay a heavy Duty on Loaf and Lump Sugar, and a small Duty on Bastard and Ground Sugars, and Molasses, they will effectually prevent our exporting the former to that Kingdom, and also to Foreign Markets, and enable them to send the--latter into Great Britain, at a less Price than it can be manufactured here under the Burthen of the high Duties, the high Price of Labour, and heavy Taxes, which would inevitahly tend to the Ruin of that valuable Branch of Trade in this Kingdom: And therefore

praying,

ingdon A Petition of the Chancellor, Masters, and Scho-

vigation. lars, of the University of Oxford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That certain Persons, chosen by the University and City of Oxford, were authorised by virtue of an Act, made in the Twenty-first Year of King James the First, to make the River Thames navigable from Burcot, in the County of Oxford, to the University and City of Oxford, and, in pursuance of the said Act, the said River was made Navigable for Boats, Barges, and Lighters, from Burcot aforesaid unto the said University and City, and divers considerable Sums of Money were at that Time, and have at several subsequent Periods, and particularly within’ these Ten Years last, been expended thereon, whereby the said Navigation is rendered safe, easy, and expeditious; and that the remaining Part of the said River, from Oxford to Leachlade, has been for many Years past, and still continues to be Navigable, and, as appears by Surveys accurately taken, may be so effectually improved and amended, as that the whole Navigation may become complete and certain, at a moderate Expence; and, the Petitioners apprehend, that Powers have been, already granted by Parliament for effecting the same; and that the Petitioners have been informed, that a Petition hath been presented to the House, for making a Navigable Canal from Leachlade, in the County of Gloucester, to Abingdon, in the County of Berks, and that a Survey hath been taken, describing the Line of the said intended Canal, which, if pursued, will, they apprehend, be a Diversion of the ancient Navigation by the River Thames, or Isis, and totally exclude the University and City of Oxford from the Benefits thence arising, to the great Inconvenience and Detriment thereof; and the Petitioners conceive, that by such Diversion of the Navigation, the Channel of the said River will be neglected and choaked up, whereby the Lands bordering thereon will become marshy, and prejudicial to the Health of the Inhabitants of the said University and City, and the Country adjacent: And therefore praying the House to take the Matter into their serious Consideration, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to join and communicate with the Line of the Thames and Secern Canal, in the Parish of Kemp ford, in the County of Gloucester, be brought in.

jrcourse County of the Town of Nottingham, was presented to

b Ireland, the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners engaged in the Hosiery and Stocking Manufactures, which create and constitute a very beneficial and important Branch of the Trade and Commerce of this Kingdom, are greatly alarmed and distressed at the Propositions lately laid before the House, for establishing, by Parliamentary Authority, a Commercial Intercourse between this Kingdom and Ireland; Vol. 40.

and that the Petitioners, till very lately, were totally unacquainted with the Object and Views of such Propositions, and therefore unable to form any Judgment how far they, or any other Commercial. Body of this Kingdom, might be affected thereby, or should have made an earlier Application to the House, to be relieved from those impending Evils which so formidably threaten the Stability, Prosperity, and Interest of the Manufactures of this Kingdom, and particularly that wherein the Petitioners are engaged; and that the Petitioners, impressed with the highest Sentiments of Veneration and Respect for the House, as the ancient and only Constitutional Guardians and Protectors of the Commercial Rights and Interests of this Kingdom, have presumed to offer their Apprehensions of die fatal Consequences and Effects which must necessarily result from-Measures attendant on the Estar blishment of such a Commercial Arrangement, humbly but confidently relying on an Intervention of the House, for preventing those Evils which, at present, too apparently and justly alarm the Petitioners, in common with the other Manufacturers of this Kingdom: And therer fore beseeching the House, That the said Propositions may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Pailiffs, Burgesses, and principal Severn Inhabitants, of the Borough of Tewkesbury, in the Navigation. County of Gloucester, and of the Proprietors and Occupiers of Lands lying contiguous to the Rivers Severn and Avon, within the Borough and Parish of Tewkesbury, and of the Bargemasters and Fishermen residing within the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Application is made for Leave to bring in a Bill for impoweripe certain Persons to improve the Navigation of the River Severn, from or near Stourport, in the County of Worcester, to or near the City of Gloucester; and Alledging, That the Petitioners, to their great Loss, have often experienced the fatal Effects of Floods, and are very apprehensive, that, if any Obstructions should be caused in the Severn (remarkable for its Rapidity) and within the Reach of Tide, their Lands upon the Banks of both the said Rivers would be rendered more liable to Floods, and consequently become much less valuable; and, they are w ell informed, that by removing the Shoals, or Banks of Sand, in the Severn, the River will be made much shallower above, and those Shoals, or Banks, so removed, will act as Obstructions below, and will certainly render its Navigation dangerous; and that the Petitioners apprehend the making Horse Towing-Paths on the Banks of The Severn, will essentially injure the Landed Property adjoining, by turning it into Common, and they conceive less Damage in the Track of Men than Horses, and by the best Information they can learn, from Barge Owners and Persons intelligent in Trade, Horse Towing-Paths will neither render the Navigation more expeditious and convenient, nor less expensive, than haling by Men, and it is their firm Belief, such Alterations will operate rather as an Advance, than a Reduction of the Price of Freight, and that the Navigation will be much injured thereby, and that those Men, who are employed in haling and navigating of Barges up and down the River, will be deprived of their Labour, and become a Burthen to Society, not being capable, by Habit, to pursue any other Occupation, and the least Number in that Employment, upon the said River, cannot be estimated at less than Two

thousand.

Severn Na- A Petition of the Bailiff, Aldermen, and Capital vigation. Burgesses, of the Borough of Bezvdleij, in the County of Worcester, in Common Hall assembled, under their Corporation Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Application is made for Leave to bring in a Bill for impowering certain Persons to improve the Navigation of the River Severn, from or near Stour port, in the County of Worcester, to or near the City of Gloucester; and Alledging, That the Borough of Btwdley aforesaid is an ancient Borough, and a Town of considerable Trade, and hath, for a great Number of Years last past, had large Quantities of Goods from the Port of Bristol, and other Places, earned up and down the River Severn, which, from Time immemorial, hath been a free River, and, if a Bill should pass into a Law, according to the Prayer of the said Petition, the Trade and Property of the said Town will be greatly prejudiced thereby; and that it appears to the Petitioners to be a partial Plan, and, if a Tonnage, or Duty shall be laid on the Vessels which carry Goods on the said River, and the Revenues arising from the said Duties shall only be appropriated towards improving, or attempting to improve, the Navigation of the said River towards Gloucester, the same will materially affect the Petitioners and the other Inhabitants of the said Borough, and be a Burthen on them, from which they can receive no Benefit: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may have such further and other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred.

Commercial A Petition of the Weavers and Inhabitants residing InUrcourse in the Town of Paisley, and its Vicinity, was presented with Ireland. to House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, consisting of many Thousands of His Majesty’s loyal and dutiful Subjects, have seen, with the greatest Concern, the Resolutions entered into by the House of Commons of Ireland, relating to a Commercial Intercourse betwixt that Country and Gi'eat Britain, and which are at present under the Consideration of the Parliament of Great Britain; and that the Petitioners are strongly of Opinion, that, were these Resolutions carried into a Law, the Consequences would be the most destructive and ruinous to the Trade and Manufacture of this Country, for the Irish, from the various Advantages of their Situation and Vol. 40.

Circumstances, will be able to undersell the Manufacturers of this Country in every Species of Manufacture, by which Means that Trade, which has hitherto supported the Petitioners, will be totally annihilated, and themselves and Families reduced to the greatest Distress: In these Circumstances, the Petitioners humbly pray, That the House will not pass the Resolutions above-mentioned into a Law, but will allow the Petitioners to be heard against them, by Counsel, at the Bar.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the operative Weavers in the City of Commercial Glasgow, Ruthcrglen, and Neighbourhood, consisting Intercourse of Thirteen thousand Two hundred and Forty-three with Irelandr Persons, assembled the 28th Day of March, Seventeen hundred and Eighty-five Years, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners,

His Majesty’s loyal and dutiful Subjects, have seen, with the deepest Concern, certain Resolutions relative to a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, which have passed in the House of Commons of Ireland> and which are presently under the Consideration of the Parliament of Britain; and that the Petitioners consider these Resolutions as destructive and ruinous to the Trade and Manufactures of this Part of the Country, and, if these Resolutions are passed into a Law, the Irish, from the many Advantages of Situation and Circumstances, will be able to undersell the Manufacturers in this Place in their own Market, as well as in every other; their Trade, by which the Petitioners have hitherto been supported, will be utterly ruined, and the Petitioners reduced to Beggary: In these Circumstances, the Petitioners humbly pray, That the House will be pleased not to pass the Resolutions above-mentioned into a Law, and will allow the Petitioners to be heard against them, by Counsel, at the Bar: This Petition is, after being fully considered, appointed to be signed by their Prseses, and other Managers specially authorized and elected for this Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Manufacturers and Traders of the Town and Neighbourhood of Derby, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive the Plan for a Regulation of the Commercial Intercourse between this Kingdom and Ireland\ now under the Consideration of Parliament, involves in it Consequences of the highest Importance to the Welfare and Prosperity of the Manufactures of the said Town and Neighbourhood: That, on every Principle of Reason and Justice, Ireland is entitled to, and ought to enjoy, every Benefit which may result from the Adjustment of a System of fair and equitable Commercial Regulations between the Two Kingdoms, founded on the Principle of an equal Participation of Burthens and Advantages; but the Resolutions adopted by the Parliament of Ireland appear to the Petitioners not to hold forth such a Participation of Burthens and Advantages, for the People of Ireland (where Taxes are comparatively low, and Labour cheap) being admitted to a full Participation of all the Commercial Advantages enjoyed by Great Britain (where Taxes are very high, and consequently Labour dear) will be enabled to bring their Produce and Manufactures to Market considerably lower than the People of this Country, whence the Emigration of our Manufacturers and Artificers will ensue, and the most fatal Consequences to the Commercial and Landed Interests of this Country may be reasonably apprehended: And therefore praying, That the said Resolutions may not pass into a Law, but that full Time may be allowed for Information on a Subject which merits the most complete and ample Investigation, and wherein the Interests of every Individual of the Community are so deeply concerned; and that a System may be formed, in which the Burthens and Advantages shall be reciprocally equal and proportional.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Cotton and Callico Manufacturers and Printers in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and Counties adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are concerned in a very extensive Manufacture of Cotton Goods for printing, and in the printing of Cottons and Callicoes, and this Branch of the Cotton Trade raises a very considerable Revenue to Government, and finds Employment for more of the industrious Poor than all the other Branches of the Cotton Trade; and that the Petitioners have been very much injured in their. Trade by a heavy Tax imposed the last Session of Parliament bn the Bleaching and Dying of Cotton Goods; that owing to the increased Capital required, and the Impossibility of advancing the Goods, their Trade has been very much on the Decline since that Period; that the Duties on this Manufacture, when printed, are so considerable, that they are very much evaded, by which thfc fair Trader sustains great Injury, as well as His Majesty's Revenue; that, owing to the great Importation of East India Callicoes, and the reduced Prices at which they are sold, the Petitioners are not only deprived of their Foreign Trade, but also of a Part of the Consumption of this Kingdom i And therefore praying, That the House will take these Premises into their Consideration, and re- peal the said Act, and that they may be he&rd by themselves, or Counsel.

A Petition of some of the principal Manufacturers Cotton of Manchester, was presented to the House, and read; Trade. Setting forth, That they see, with the most poignant Regret, the Calamities falling on the Manufacturers of this Kingdom, and in particular on those of Lancashire, and cannot help expressing their great Astonishment, that, whilst the Minister is proposing the most salutary Provisions for the Protection and Extension of the Irish Commerce and Manufactures, he is introducing Hosts of Excise Officers amongst those of this Kingdom, whose Operations are not only intolerably vexatious and ruinous, but also subversive of their Liberty, both as Citizens and Manufacturers; they conceive it their Duty at this critical Moment, to apprize the House of the Dangers arising from these ruinous Systems; the Petitioners are fully convinced, after a fair Trial, that the Cotton Manufactures of this Kingdom cannot long exist under oppressive and restrictive Excise Laws; and, if the Act, imposing a Duty on that Manufacture, is not repealed, they are extremely sorry to be under the Necessity of informing the House, that they shall be reduced to the sad Alternative of leaving this devoted Country, with their Families, Properties, and Dependants, and, for that Purpose, have already begun to stop their Manufactures:

And therefore the Petitioners, considering this House the Guardians of the Manufactures and Prosperity of this Kingdom, humbly beg they will take into their most serious Consideration the dreadful Consequences these Laws are likely to produce, and that such Measures may be adopted as to avert these impending Evils.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Land Owners, Merchants, Manufacturers, Dyers, Bleachers, and others interested in the Fustian Trade in the Towns of Manchestei', Salford, Bolton, Leigh, Waning-ton, Rochdale, Oldham, Ashton, Bury, Chor/ey, Stockport, Macclesfield, and Chapel cn le Frith, and in the Boroughs of IVigan and Newton, and of the respective Neighbourhoods of those Towns and Boroughs, in the Counties of Lancaster, Chesta%, and Derby, is referred.

Cotton A Petition of the Cotton Manufacturers in the

Trade. Neighbourhood of Manchester, commonly called

Country-Makers, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners beg Leave to represent the great Difficulties and Distress they are involved in since the Act imposing an Excise Duty on Bleached and Dyed Fustians became a Law: The Petitioners being Manufacturers of Fustians in the Neighbourhood of Manchester, and dispose of the same in an unfinished State to the principal Manufacturers of that Place, have, under full Confidence of that obnoxious Act being repealed, and also from the laudable Desire of employing the Poor, continued to Manufacture their usual Quantity of Goods, which ha9 likewise been the Means of preserving the Peace of that populous County; but they are extremely sorry to be under the Necessity of informing the House that they are now no longer capable of employing their Workmen, their Capitals being totally swallowed up in an immense Stock of manufactured Goods, which they cannot dispose of at any Price, owing to a general Stagnation in consequence of this arbitrary and ruinous Excise Law, their Credit is nearly exhausted, and they find themselves reduced to such an Extremity, that they fear universal Bankruptcy is like to take Piace amongst them, their poor industrious Mechanics are daily emigrating, for want of Employ, to other more hospitable Countries, who gladly embrace them; but what is still more to be dreaded, is the Hand of lawless Riots, which must soon take Place, if not timely prevented by the House: And therefore the Petitioners presume to make use of this Constitutional Mode of laying their Calamities before the House, not doubting that they wfill grant them speedy Relief, by repealing the impolitic Act passed last Sessions of Parliament, imposing au Excise Duty on Dyed and Bleached Fustians.
