Commercial A Petition of the Committee of Merchants, and the Intercourse principal Manufacturers of the Town and Neighbour-wuh Ireland. hood of Sheffield, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that there are now under Consideration certain Resolutions of the House of Lords, and the Commons of Ireland, which the Petitioners understand are intended to form the Foundation of a lasting Treaty of Commerce between Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners entertain alarming Apprehensions, that, if those Resolutions are adopted by the British Legislature, they would essentially affect the Iron Trade and Manufactures of Great Britain in general, and those of the Town and Neighbourhood of Sheffield in particular, and, as the preseut Duty on Bar Iron imported into this Kingdom cannot be reduced without great Injury to its Forges (which it is the Interest and Policy of this Country to encourage) the Duty on this Article when imported into Ireland should be equal to the Duties now paid on Importation into this Kingdom, otherwise the Iron Manufacturers of Ireland would have such decisive Advantage as might, in a short Space of Time, most materially injure, if not wholly destroy, the Iron Trade of the said Town and Neighbourhood in Foreign Markets, as the Petitioners % apprehend that at least Three Fourths of the Bar Iron Vql. 40;

employed in this Manufacture are imported from Abroad on a Duty of £. 2. 16s. per Ton, at the same Time that the Duty on the Importation of the same Material into Ireland does not now exceed Ten Shillings (Irish) per Ton: And therefore praying, That the House will grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Ironmasters, Nail-Manufacturers, Commercial and others concerned in the Manufacturing of Iron, hrtereoun* met at The Swan Inn, in Westbromwich, in the County wlt re m ' of Stafford, whose Names are thereunder written, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been informed, that certain Resolutions of the House of Commons of Ireland, relating to the Adjustment of a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and that Kingdom, have been presented to this House, as they understood, for Investigation, and that such Alterations might be made therein as should appear essential for the Protection of the Manufactures of this Kingdom, and to prevent a numerous Migration of Artists; and therefore, some Weeks since, a General Meeting, convened to take this important Business into Consideration, conveyed to a few Noblemen and Members of Parliament such Representations as, they apprehended, were material to the Iron Trade which had been long established in this Neighbourhood, but, the Petitioners being now assured that no Alterations whatever are intended to be made in those Resolutions, which, if carried into a Law, would be extremely injurious to the Iron Manufactures of this Kingdom, presume humbly to represent that the Petitioners alone employ many Thousand Persons in the Iron Trade; that the Duty upon Bar Iron imported into this Kingdom is £. 2. i6j. 1 d. per Ton, and in Ireland no more than 9s. 2d. English Money; and that, by the United States of America having become independent of this Country, the Irish accidentally possess the Liberty of exporting Iron Wares to those States free of Duty, and, now an Intercourse with them is opened, the Advantage to Manufacturers of Iron in Ireland is so great, that there can be no Doubt some of the substantid Manufacturers in this Vicinity will establish Works in that Country, and therefore, unless some effectual Means are adopted for the Protection of the Iron Trade in this Kingdom, many Workmen will be removed to Ireland: And therefore praying, That the Commercial Intercourse between Britain and Ireland may not be finally settled without equal Duties being imposed upon Bar Iron imported into both Kingdoms.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Intercourse Town of Lancaster, and others nearly interested therewith Ireland. in> whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Propositions now depending in Parliament, for regulating and establishing a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, have excited in the Petitioners well-grounded Fears and Apprehensions that the British Sail-Cloth Manufacture must be eventually ruined, should the said Regulations be carried into Effect: That the British Legislature hath heretofore considered the Manufacture of British Sail-Cloth an Object of so much Importance (not simply as a Manufacture only affording a comfortable Means of Support to great Numbers of His Majesty's Subjects, but more particularly as a Naval Store, which it has always been thought the Nation ought to be in full Possession of) as to encourage and protect the same by Bounties given upon the Exportation of British-made Sail-Cloth, and to impose Duties upon the Importation of Sail-Cloth from all other Countries; and that, if the Bounty heretofore paid upon the Exportation of British-made Sail-Cloth to Ireland be discontinued, and Irish Sail-Cloth be admitted into Great Britain Duty-free, Cheapness of Living, Exemption from Taxes, and consequent low Price of Labour in Ireland, will give that Nation a decided Advantage over, and enable the Irish to undersell the British Sail-Cloth

Manufacturer, both at Home and in all Foreign Markets, and in a short Time the British Navy must become dependent upon Ireland for a Supply of Canvas:

And therefore praying, That the Bounty given upon the Exportation of British-made Sail-Cloth to Ireland may be continued, and that Irish Sail-Cloth may not be admitted into Great Britain Duty-free; or that such other Means may be adopted, for the Preservation and Protection of the British Sail-Cloth Manufacture, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Fustians, Cotton commertiai Velvets, and other Cotton Goods, and of Linen Cloths Intercourse and Sheeting, in the Borough of Wigan, in the County with Ireland; Palatine of Lancaster, and other Towns adjacent, was presented to the House, dnd read; Setting forth* That the Petitioners are exceedingly alarmed at the Resolutions brought before the House relating to the Commercial Regulations between Great Britain and Ireland, which, If Carried into Effect, they have no Doubt, will be greatly injurious.to the Commerce and Manufactures of this Country i That the principal Parr of the Expence, in the various Articles in the Cotton and Linen Manufactures, consists in the Price of Labour, which is greatly enhanced by the many heavy Taxes with which this Country is burthehed, and the People of Ireland, being in a great Measure free from Taxes, the Price of Labour is consequently very low, and* that to carry on the satne Extent of Business in this Country as in Ireland, a much greater Capital will be required, on Account of the Difference in Price of Labour, and the heavy Duties bn the Bleaching and Dying of Cotton Goods: From these Considerations the Petitioners have Reason to fear, that those valuable Branches of Manufacture, which at this Time employ, and in a great Measure support, the greatest Part of the poorest People, will be very materially hurt, if not totally obstructed, and the Consumption of Cotton and Linen Goods in this Country, in Time, wholly supplied by the Manufactures of Ireland; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that no Duties, laid on the Importation of Irish Manufactures, will be a sufficient Security to the British Manufacturer from the above Effects, as it is too well known that high Duties continually operate as an Inducement* to smuggle: And therefore praying,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for erecting several public Buildings in the City of Edinburgh, and to impower the Trustees therein mentioned to purchase Lands for that Purpose, and also, for widening Vql. 40.

and enlarging the Streets of the said City, and certain Avenues leading the reunto: And also,

An Act passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for extending the Royalty of th6 City of Edinburgh over certain adjoining Lands, and for giving Powers to the Magistrates of Edinburgh for the Benefit of the said City, and to enable His Majesty to gi ant Letters Patent for establishing a Theatre in the City of Edinburgh, or Suburbs thereof* were read: And

Mr. Walter Ross being examined, said, That in consequence of the said Acts, public Buildings have been erected, and a Communication formed bjf a Bridge to the Northward; but the Avenues to the City from the South being still harrow, steep, and inconvenient, it is expedient to open a Communication by a Bridge over the Cow Gate, and by Streets from the said Bridge to the Squares, Streets, and Rows, on the South Side of the Oity- — that it is also necessary to form a Communication betwixt the Launmercate and the Streets on the West Parts of the new-extended Royalty, and to enlarge the public Markets, and make convenient Roads and Passages to them — that several Buildings in the University of Edinburgh are in a ruinous Condition, and the Apartments, from the Increase of Students, are incommodious, so that it is necessary wholly, or in Party to rebuild the same — that the present Mode of levying certain Taxes on the Citizens of Edinburghthe Liberties and Suburbs thereof, is attended with much Expence and Trouble* and that it is necessary to have the same established for supporting the Police of the City on a more equal Principle, and less expensive Collection — that it is also necessary to raise a sufficient Sum of Money by Way of Tax on the Inhabitants, to defray the Expence of lighting the said City and Suburbs — that a further Supply of Water is, by Reason of the Increase of the Number of Inhabitants, become necessary; and that it is also necessary to extend the Royalty over certain Grounds lately purchased by the City, and over Grounds belonging to such Persons as by their Title Deeds are bound to pay the ordinary Taxes payable by the Citizens; and that in order to carry these Measures into Execution, it will be necessary to purchase certain Lands and Houses, to equalize the Land Tax payable by the City and the Liberties thereof, to extend a Proportion of the said Tax over the Districts to the South of the City, and to obtain such Powers and Authorities as may be requisite for effecting the above-mentioned useful and necessary Purposes.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for opening an easy and commodious Communication from the High Street of* Edinburgh to the Country Southward, and also from the Lawn Market to the new-extended Royalty on the North, and for enabling Trustees to purchase Lands, Houses, and Areas for that Purpose, for widening and enlarging the Streets of the said City, and certain Avenues leading to the same, for rebuilding or improving the University, for enlarging the public Markets and Communications thereto, for regulating certain Taxes, for lighting the said City, for providing an additional Supply of Water, and for extending the Royalty of the said City: And that Sir Adam Fergusson, Mr. Henty Dundas, and the Lord Advocate of Scotland, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Commercial A Petition of the Sail Cloth Manufacturers of the

Intercourte Town of Kirkham, in the County of Lancaster, and

with Ireland, others materially interested therein, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, impressed with a just Sense of the great Importance of the Sail Cloth Manufacture, not only for the Protection of this Country, but the Maintenance of many Thousands of poor Families, are exceedingly startled at the Propositions now depending in the House, relative to the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, which, if passed into a Law, they have no Doubt will be big with the most destructive Consequences to the Sail Cloth Manufacture, and naturally to the Safety of this Kingdom; that the establishing the Manufacture of Sail Cloth within this Kingdom has ever been justly esteemed an Object of the greatest Importance for its own Protection and Defence, and there is no Naval Store more necessary for a Maritime Power, nor any Manufacture more deserving Encouragement from a Commercial Country; that Siis Kingdom might not be dependant upon any Foreign State for this essential Article in Time of War, as was formerly the Case, the Wisdom of the Legislature heretofore thought proper to impose very high Duties upon the Importation of Foreign Sail Cloth, and to grant Bounties upon the Exportation of British Sail Cloth, by Means whereof the Trade is extended to so great a Degree, as to be able to supply the Navy of this Kingdom with Expedition and Certainty in Time of War; and that, if the Bounty upon the Exportation of British Sail Cloth to Ireland is not continued, and the Admission of Irish Sail Cloth be permitted, exclusive of Taxes, into this Kingdom, the Price of Labour in Ireland, which is so much cheaper than in England, and their comparative Exemption from Taxes, will enable the Irish to manufacture Sail Cloth upon better Terms than the English, and consequently deprive this Kingdom not only of Foreign Markets, but Domestic Consumption; that, besides a total Subversion to this Country of the Sail Cloth Manufacture, important Consequences in Time of War may arise by establishing it in Ireland, from whence it must be brought for the Use of the British

Navy, and be subject to the Depredations of the Enemy; and that, amongst the various Branches of Manufacture now in a distressed Situation, there are none in so low a State, Qr requiring more Aid, than that of the Sail Cloth: And therefore the Petitioners hope,

That the Bounties granted Upon Exportation of British Sail Cloth to Ireland Uiay be continued as they now are, and that an Admission of the Irish Sail Cloth be not permitted into Great Britain free from Duty, or that such other Means may be put in Execution for the Preservation and Defence of the British Sail Cloth Manufacture, as to the House shall seem most necessary and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred ta consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the distressed Fustian Cutters in the Cotton Town and Neighbourhood of Manchester, was pre- Trade, sented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have been involved in the greatest Distress ever since the Act imposing a Duty on Bleached and Dyed Fustians took Place, and the principal Manufacturers have taken infinite Pains to obtain a Repeal of the said destructive Law, but hitherto without Effect; that the Petitioners have waited for that desirable Event with . an unexampled Patience, and although their Employers have, much to their own Detriment, kept the Petitioners from actually starving, yet they are nearly in that Situation; and that the Hardships of the Petitioners have been represented at different Times by Gentlemen sent for that Purpose, yet none are so able to describe Miseries, as those who feel them, and, as many considerable Manufacturers are now turning off their Workmen, the Petitioners Miseries will be thereby doubled, and, as Encouragement has been often held out to the Petitioners, inviting them to emigrate to Countries not subject to the British Crown, they apprehend their present Miseries, and future dreadful Prospects, will, if the Prayer of their Petition cannot be granted, at length force them from their Country: And therefore praying, That the House will grant a speedy Repeal of the said destructive Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy,

Commercial A Petition of the Manufacturers and Traders of the Intercourse Town of Paisley, was presented to the House, and read; with Ireland. Setting forth, That the Petitioners, impressed with the sincerest Wishes for the Prosperity of Ireland\ would cheerfully concur in any Measure which may serve to promote so desireable an End; at the same Time they cannot help being justly alarmed at some of the Resolutions for a Commercial Arrangement which has lately passed the Irish Parliament, and which are now waiting for the Approbation of this House, as they are persuaded these will, if passed into a Law, operate directly against that Principle which is declared to be the Basis of those Commercial Regulations; and that it appears to the Petitioners, by the Fourth and Seventh Resolutions of the Irish Parliament, that Linens, the great Staple of that Kingdom, will be for ever admitted into Britain free from Duty, whilst the greatest Part of the Manufactures of this Country, particularly those in which, the Petitioners are deeply interested, must for ever remain loaded with a heavy Duty on being imported into Ireland; that the Petitioners are fully convinced of the fatal Tendency.of these Resolutions, which they justly foresee, will be highly detrimental, and, in the End, will entirely revent the Exportation of many of our most valuable lanufactures; They therefore hope the House will

«Tuse their Assent to a System which will prove so estructive to this Kingdom, and consequently oc-sasion many Thousand useful Men to abandon their native Country; and that it appears to the Petitioners, a Commercial Arrangement on equitable Principles, which will admit a free Interchange of all Manufactures between Great Britain and Ireland, highly to be wished for, and would be mutually advantageous to both Countries; the Petitioners therefore hope, that the House will giant their Request, in rejecting the Irish Resolutions in their present Form, and, by allowing a free Interchange between both Countries, or permit them to be heard by Counsel at the Bar of the House, when they may have it in their Power more fully to state the fatal Effects of those Resolu-. tions*

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, was referred; That the* Committee had examined, and found that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, it not being intended to extend the Navigation beyond the Limits already authorized, nor to raise any further Sum of Money for that Purpose; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Two Acts, passed in the Sixth and Tenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a navigable Cut or Canal from the River Secern, between Bewdley and Tit ton Brook, in the County of Worcester, to cross the River Trent, at or near Heywood Mill, in the County of Stafford, and to communicate with a Canal intended to be made between the said River Trent and the River Mersey, were read. And,

Mr. James Penny being examined, said, That the said Company of Proprietors have proceeded in the Execution of the said Acts, and have at Length accomplished their Undertaking, in the Prosecution of which they have expended the Sum of £.170,000, which they were authorized to raise under the aforesaid Acts of Parliament

Then an Act, passed in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to enable certain Persons therein mentioned to make a navigable Canal from the Coal Mines lying near Stourbridge, in the County of Worcester, to join and communicate with the Navigation so made by the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, was also read; whereby it appeared, that there was a Clause inserted therein to enable the said Company, with the Aid of Commissioners, to regulate the Tonnage upon their own Navigation in Manner therein mentioned.

Mr. James Penny being further examined, said, That the said Company of Proprietors have not, by any of the said Acts, a Power to lower or regulate the Tonnage upon their said Navigation, without the Consent of the Majority of the Commissioners therein named — That unless the said Proprietors have it in their Power to regulate the Tonnage amongst themselves, the general Trade and Produce of the Country cannot be brought upon the Canal with Benefit to the Proprietors, and Advantage to the Public. — Then

Mr. Henry Penn being examined, said, That be is Owner of the Coal Mines upon the Line of the Bir-ming/idfn Canal — That he sold 1,083 Boat Loads of Coal, which were conveyed upon the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal within a Year, when the Tolls were lowered, but that since the Toflhage has been advanced, he has only sold 654 Boat Loads within the same Period — That the Bilston Mines are in a very declining State — -That if the Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal had a Power of reducing their Tonnage, the Bilston Collieries would be very much relieved — That the Bilston Coals are esteemed of a superior Quality to any that go to the Severn Market — That if the Tonnage upon the Staff* fordshire and Worcestershire Canal was lowered, he apprehends double the Quantity of Bilston Coals would be sent down the Canal.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill 16 enable the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, to lower and regulate the Tonnage upon the said Canal: And that Mr. Loveden Lcroeden and Sir Edward Littleton do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Commercial A Petition of the Manufacturers of Earthen Ware Intercourse in Staffordshire was presented to the House, and read; with Ireland, getting forth, That the Petitioners are greatly interested in the Commercial Regulations now negociating between Great Britain and Ireland, and are at the same Time fully sensible of the Importance of a fair and equal System being ^justed and finally settled between the Two Kingdoms; that they cannot help being apprehensive, however, that the proposed Resolutions of the Parliament of Ireland, if passed into a Law in their present Form, will be highly injurious to the Interests of the said Manufactory, inasmuch as they tend to lay the Foundations of a future and unequal Competition in our own as well as Foreign Markets, and such as may ultimately prove destructive of this valuable and extensive Branch of National Commefce: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves and their Counsel, against the proposed Resolutions of the Parliament of Ireland passing into a Law, and, that such Alterations may be made therein as to the House shall seem meet, in order that, whilst every reasonable and even liberal Encouragement and Assistance is afforded to the Trade and Manufactures of the Sister Kingdom, a due and prudential Regard may be had to the Commercial Interests of our own.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole Hopse, to whom it is referred tp consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse he.tween Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Considers- Wi tion the Petition of George Johnstone, Esquire, El© complaining of an undue Election and Return for the District of Burghs of Wigton, Whithorn, New Galloway, and StranroBwer, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with foe Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members, on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Three Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses; and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Thirty Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Peter Johnstone, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioner; and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Six other Members, then present w'ere drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of John Courtenay, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Sitting Member; and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Thirteen other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Commercial A Petition of the Merchants concerned in the Corn Intercourse and Malt Trade in the Burgh and Port of Great Yar-with Ireland, mouth, on Behalf of themselves and the Com Merchants in the several Ports within the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That much the greatest Part of the Exportation of Com and Malt from England to Ireland has been from the said Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, and principally from the said Port of Great Yarmouth, from which Port only, during the last Seven Years, 17L500 Quarters of Malt and Barley (being on an Average 24,500 Quarters Yearly) of the Growth and Produce of the said Two Counties, have been exported to Ireland, and the last Year 19,931 Quarters of Wheat and Wheat Flour, also the Growth and Produce of the said Counties, have been exported to Ire~

I land from the said Port of Yarmouth, and of course a

very great Number of Ships and Seamen were employed in transporting the same; and that the Petitioners had no Opportunity of applying to the Committee of Council, not having had any Notice of the said Committee sitting for the Purpose of Inquiry mentioned in their Report, until the Petitioners saw the said Report in Print, and, the Petitioners conceive that so much of the said Report as relates to Corn, does not contain sufficient Information relative to a Subject of such great Importance as the Corn Trade between England and Ireland, and therefore, if the House should proceed on the Ground only of the Information contained in the said Report, the Petitioners are seriously apprehensive that the very great Corn Trade carried on frotr^ the said Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, through the said Port of Yarmouth, will be greatly injured, if not totally lost: And therefore praying the House to postpone the final Adjustment of the Commercial Regulations with Ireland, so far as relates to the Exportation and Importation of Corn to and from Ireland, for such reasonable Time as may afford the Petitioners an Opportunity of offering further 1 Information; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by

themselves or Counsel, at the Bar of the House, in Support of this Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty's most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Nail Ironmongers in the Town Commercial of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, and others Intercourse concerned in the Manufacturing of Iron Wares in and Wlt re a<* near that Place, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that the House of Commons in Ireland have presented to this House certain Resolutions relative to the settling a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and that Kingdom; and that the Petitioners always understood, that the Resolutions of the Irish Parliament were each of them to undergo a minute Investigation, and that such Alterations would then be made therein, as to the House should appear necessary for the Prosperity, if not for the very Existence, of some of the Manufactures of this Kingdom, but the Petitioners, now finding that no Alteration whatsoever is to be made to the Resolutions of the Irish House of Commons, are greatly alarmed; and that the Petitioners employ many Thousand Persons in the making of Nails only, the greatest Part of which are shipped to the United States of America, and the Duty upon Bar Iron imported into this Kingdom is £. 2, 16$. id. per Ton, whereas the Duty paid in Ireland is only £.0. 9s. 2d. per Ton, English Money, and, besides this, the Duties, agreed to be laid by the Irish Parliament, in the Year 1778, on all Iron Wares exported by them to America, being now done away by the Independence of those States, these Considerations in

‘Favour

Commercial Intercourse with Ireland.

784 70 Afrilis. A* 1785.

Favour of Ireland, united, evidently give the Manufacturers of Iron in that Country a decided Advantage over us in the American Market, and must, in the End, prove ruinous to the Town and Neighbourhood of Dudley: And therefore praying, That the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland may not be finally adjusted, until an equal Duty be first laid on Bar Iron imported into both Kingdoms, which, the Petitioners hope, the House will see to be equitable and necessary on the present Occasion.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Glass Manufacturers in the Neighbourhood of Stourbridge and Dudley, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, that a System of Commercial Regulations is going to take place between this Kingdom and Ireland^ and that certain Resplutions relative thereto have been presented to this House, from 'the House of Commons in Ireland; and that the Alarms of the Petitioners are very greatly excited, by finding that the said Resolutions are not to undergo any Alteration by the House, and the Petitioners conceive the Glass Manufactories to be of Consequence to the Revenue and Trade of this Kingdom, and therefore merit the Consideration of the IJouse; and that the Glass Manufactories of this Kingdom must be entirely destroyed, if the Importation of Glass from Ireland is allowed Duty-free, and that Branch of Trade will be inevitably transferred to that Kingdom: That the Irish Manufacturer hath a considerable Advantage by not working under an Excise Duty, for, by not being subject to pay a Duty, he is enabled to purify his Waste Glass and Materials, which the English Manufacturer cannot do without being liable to pay the full Duty; and the Irish Manufacturer has likewise an Advantage in all Goods exported, on Account of paying no Excise Duty, as the Drawback allowed to the English Manufacturer is very inadequate to the Duty paid; and that the Glass Manufacturers in the Neighbourhood of Stourbridge and Dudley have at present an Advantage over the Irish in the Price of Coal and Clay, but, on Account of the heavy Land Carriage on the raw Materials and manufactured Goods, the Irish Manufacturers, from their advantageous Situation for the Export Trade, have an Advantage more than equal to the Difference of the Price of those Articles, and those Advantages, with many others, will give the Irish Manufacturers so great a Superiority over the Glass Manufacturers of the said Neighbourhood, as will totally destroy the Whole of the Business, unless timely prevented: And therefore praying, That the Commercial System of Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland may not. be concluded, without putting the Trade of the Two Nations upon an equal Footing, which, the Petitioners conceive, can only be done by imposing a Duty on the Irish Manufacturers equal to that paid by the English, and the same Drawback allowed them on Goods exported, as is allowed in England.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland\

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and ConmerJ Tradesmen of the Borough of Kidderminster, in thelDterc°n County of Worcester, was presented to the House, wilhIr^ and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, deeply impressed with the Importance of the Commercial Arrangements with Ireland, and strongly apprehensive that the Propositions for this Purpose submitted to the Consideration of Parliament, will, by no Means, produce that Equality between tire Two Kingdoms which is their proper and professed Object, but will prove highly detrimental to the Manufactures, Commerce, Landed Interest, and Public Revenue of Great Britain, pray that the same may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners would not object, but cordially agree, to any System that would establish and secure an equal Participation of Privileges and Burthens in both Islands, but it appears to the Petitioners, that, unless Ireland will agree to pay equal Duties with Great Britain on all its Imports, and an equal Excise on every Article of Manufacture and internal Consumption, and that the Net Produce of these Duties, and of this Excise, be applied to the general Support of the Empire, both in Peace and War, and that the same Regulations be adopted respecting the Exports from both Kingdoms, as well from one to the other, as from each to Foreign Parts, no Scheme of Equalization can be settled between the Two Kingdoms, and, even in this Case, Ireland will enjoy manifest Advantages over Great Britain in the Cheapness of its Labour and Provisions, and in its Freedom from Poor Levies and other Taxes, which will still continue to bear heavily on this Country, with a partial and an unequal Pressure; and that the Petitioners have Reason to believe, that some Manufactories are already carried on in Ireland in as great Perfection as in Great Britain, and to greater Advantage, and, if the above Propositions become a Law, other Manufactories may be removed from this Kingdom into Ireland, and the Produce sent here on such low Terms as immediately or eventually to injure similar Manufactures in this Country, and perhaps totally annihilate them, and the Revenue arising therefrom; that in particular, One of the principal Branches of Manufacture in Kidderminster, the Article of Silky Stuffs, would be immediately injured, and perhaps entirely lost, for, even at present, attended with all the Expence and Risque of smuggling, these Stuffs are brought from Ireland, and sold in that Market, from Twenty to Twenty-five per Cent. under our Manufactures, and whether other Articles may not immediately or eventually share the same Fate, the Petitioners leave for other Manufacturers particularly to state: And therefore praying, JThat the Propositions above referred to may not pass into a Law, that due Time may be allowed for the full Investigation of this extensive and weighty Subject, and, finally, that such Regulations may be adopted as may actually establish a real or near Equality in the Advantages and Contributions of both Kingdoms.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturer^ and Cotta Tradesmen in the Borough of Kidderminster^ in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners behold, with Concern, every Method of raising a Revenue by Taxes on Manufactures, and are more especially alarmed at the Introduction of the Officers of Excise into Manufacturers Warehouses and Work Shops, in as much as

a5 Geo. III. 7* AprjSg

that Freedom and Privacy, which Manufacturers should enjoy in the Exercise of their Business, - is thereby destroyed, their Operations cramped and impeded, and their Burthens and Expences greatly increased by additional Buildings and Servants, as well as by the Payment of the Duties imposed upon them; and that the Petitioners have observed, that the Manufacturers of Cotton have presented a Petition to Parliament for the Repeal of an Act, passed in the last Session, for granting certain Duties on Cotton Stuffs, bleached or dyed, and on Licences for bleaching and dying the same: And therefore praying, That the Prayer of the said Petition may be granted.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Abingdon A Petition of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, Manu-

Navigation. facturers, and other Inhabitants of the Borough of Ciraicester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed a Bill is depending in the House, for making a Navigable Canal from the Thames and Severn Canal, in the County of Gloucester, to join and communicate

with the River Thames, at or near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, which Measure, if carried into Execution, will lie of great National Utility, by opening an easy Communication between the interior Parts of the Kingdom, and the Port of London, and also of great Advantage to many of the Sea Ports of this Kingdom, and to several Manufactories in various Parts thereof, as well as of particular local Advantages to the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of William Robertson> in Name and Behalf of himself, and of the other Partners of the Iron Manufactory at Glasgow, in the County of Lanerk, under the Name and Firm of William Robertson and Company, of Thomas Edington, for himself, and in Behalf of the other Partners of the Iron Manufactory at Cramond, in the County of Edinburgh, under the Firm of Caddells and Edington, and of Peter Murdoch, for himself, and in Behalf of the other Partners of the Iron Manufactory at Dalnottar, in the County of Dumbarton, under the Firm of Murdoch, Gillies, and Company, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the above Companies have expended large Sums of Money in erecting Slitt and Forge Mills, and other Machinery for Manufacturing of Iron at the Places above-mentioned, and employ a great Number of Hands in carrying on their several Works; and that the Iron manufactured by the above Companies is Foreign Iron, which pays a Duty to His Majesty, at Importation, of £.2. 16s. 1 d.^ per Ton, whereas the Duty payable in Ireland\ upon

Vol. 40.

the Importation of this Article into that Kingdom, is no mbre than 95. 7d.\\ and that the greatest Part of the Articles manufactured by the Petitioners from Foreign Iron are exported to other Nations, and none of the Duty paid at Importation is drawn back upon the Exportation of the manufactured Articles; and, the Petitioners, being informed that certain Resolutions of the Parliament of Ireland, relative to the Trade of that Kingdom, are now under the Consideration of the House, and observing, that these Resolutions make no Provision for imposing the like Duties upon the Importation of Foreign Iron into Ireland which are now payable in Britain, beg Leave to suggest, that, unless the Duty at Importation is equalized in both Countries, the Manufacturers in Ireland will be enabled to undersell the Petitioners and the other Manufacturers of this Article in Britain, at every Foreign Market, by at least Twenty per Cent, on the original Cost of the raw Materials, not to mention another essential Advantage which the one Country has over the other, in Point of Cheapness of Labour; and, that there is no other Method whatever of equalizing the Duties upon the Article of Iron between the Two Kingdoms, other than that of imposing the same Duty upon this Article in both Kingdoms at

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upop the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Plate Glass Ordered\ That Sir William Dolben do make the Re-

Manufacture. port frotn the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Governor and Company of British Cast Plate Glass Manufacturers, was referred.

Sir William Dolben accordingly reported from the said Committee; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and -afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Wherq the same was read \ and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act to incorporate " certain Persons therein named, and their Successors, €( with proper Powers, for the Purpose of establishing " Orq or more Glass Manufactories within the Kingdom a of Great Britain, and for the effectually supporting " and conducting the same upon an improved Plan, in . a peculiar Manner, for the casting of large Plate u Glass," wras read: And,

Mr. Alexander Black being examined, said, That be is Secretary to the said Company — 'That, under the Sanction, Authority, and Encouragement of the said Act of Parliament, the Company have, with unremitting. Attention, endeavoured to forward the above-mentioned Work, not merely with a View to their own Emolument and Advantage, but as an Object of Public and National Concern — That the Result has been a complete Performance of every Thing (hat was held up as a Plea to warrant the Privileges granted by Parliament to the said Company, who have brought the Manufactory to such a Degree of Perfection, as to become an Object of Envy and Jealousy to the French Nation, in that Branch of Manufacture, which in France has been upheld for more than a Century, by peculiar Indulgences of Monopoly, and total Exemptions from Duty.

And he produced to your Committee a Copy of an Order of the French King’s Council of State, dated the 13th of October 1781, as published by . Authority; from which it appeared, that the Prch prietors of the Royal Glass Manufactory in France, haying represented to the King the Injury they should su^ain, if the new Duty on Glass, imposed by an Edict of the Month of August preceding, were to be rigorously levied on their Manufacture, the King in Council made the said Order, whereby the said Company of Proprietors weFe allowed to compound for the said Duties, at the Rate of 150,000 Livres per Annum, payable Quarterly; and that, as a further Encouragement, the whole Amount of the new Duty, as imposed by the said Edict, on such Glass as they should furnish for the Use of the Royal Palaces, or send Abroad, should be deducted from the said Composition: And it further appeared, from the said Order, that with a Yiew to enabling the said Proprietors to recover the Amount of the Duty which, under the said Composition, they should actually pay, tho Tarifte of their Prices of Glass was increased Ten per Cent.

And being further examined, he said, That the

Company of British Cast Plate Manufacturers have expended, in the Progress of their Works, upwards of One hundred thousand Pounds, without receiving any Dividend whatever, owing to a Variety of Circumstances, to which an Infant Manufactory, upon an entire new Plan, must necessarily be liable; in Confirmation of which, he produced to your Committee an Account, which is hereunto annexed, N° 1.

Mr. George Mackay being then examined, said, That, among divers Hardships and Difficulties the said Company had experienced, they had found the Duties payable to Government very oppressive, owing to the Mode in which they are collected, and the Manner in which Glass is made, by Casting, differing from all other B?'itish Manufactories, wherein the Glass is made by Blowing, and on which the Duties must fall lighter, though the Quantum of the Duty charged by Law on the Materials is exactly the same — That this appears to be owing to a Waste of Metal through the w hole Process of the Casting Work, exceeding in Quantity more than double the Waste of the Blowing Work; in Explanation and Confirmation of which, he produced to your Committee the Accounts hereunto annexed, N° 2 and 3. — And he added, That the Allowance of Waste, which is One Fourth Part of the whole Quantity of clean Metal in the Pot, is equal to both, and therefore it compensates for the Loss by Waste in a Manner much more advantageous to the Blowing, than it does to the Casting Glass Manufactory.

Mr. Black being again examined, said, That the Company have paid Duties upon an extra Waste of Metal, not known in the Blowing Glass Manufactory, to the Amount of more than /. 7,000.

Mr. Mackay being again examined, confirmed the preceding Evidence, respecting the Duties upon extra Waste; and added, that all the Drawback or Allowance the Company have been able to procure, has only reduced the said Over-charge to £. 6,801.2.10 f. as appears by the Account hereunto annexed, N° 2.

And being further examined, he said, That the actual Waste, as appears by the Accounts produced, is 59 and f per Cent, on the gross gauged Metal, instead of 25 per Cent, which is the Allowance from Government for the Waste — That this Excess has arisen from the peculiar Process in making Cast Plate Glass, unknown in England\ when the Acts were passed which laid the Duties — That the Operations peculiar to the Casting Work, which occasion such Waste, are chiefly the more frequent Breakage of Pots in the Furnace, and Loss of Metal therein, from its very great Heat, and particular Construction to admit the Cuvetts; the lading of the Metal out of the peat Pots in the Furnace into smaller ones, called Cuvetts; the scumming of the Cuvetts; the Metal adhering to the Bottom and Sides of the Cuvetts; the Metal forced over the End of the Table by the Roller; and the Heads or Lumps formed ori the Plates, by pushing them into the annealing Furnace, and squaring the Platea into proper Shapes; all which Waste, in the Casting Plate Glass, except the Breakage of Pots, as aforesaid, arises after the Officer has gauged the Metal, on which Gauge the Duty is paid; and that the Manufactory is further liable to a Variety of Accidents, which often destroy the Plates — That, on Account of the above Difficulties and Hardships, respecting the Duties, the Manufactory was stopped on the 18th of May 1784, has ceased working ever since, and cannot be carried on again without some Relief from Parliament. — And being asked, Whether he recollected any Application being made to the Excise Board, a few Years ago, for Relief, with respect to Payment of the G4ass Duty, on Account of Waste in manufacturing? he said, Such Application had been 6 made

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of One million Five hundred thousand Pounds be raised, by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament; and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged, with Interest thereupon, on or before the 5th Day of April 1786, to be exchanged and received in Payment, in such ‘Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply graqted to His Majesty, the further Sum of One Million be raised, by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament; and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged, with Interest thereupon, on or before the .5th Day of April 1786, to be exchanged and received in Payment, in such Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Gilbert, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Butler, the Marquis of Graham, Mr. Edward James Eliot, Mr. Aubrey, Mr. Attorney General, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Steele, and Air. Rose, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Yeomanry, and other Land Owners residing in and near the Market Town of Rochdale, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, having taken due Time maturely and dispassionately to consider the real Principles and natural Tendency of those Propositions now before the House, respecting the Commercial Regulations intended to be irrevocably established by them betwixt Great Britain and Ireland, are of Opinion, that, so far from being fair, open, candid, and equitable, that they are specious and delusive, by holding out to View Favours, that the Alovers of them canpot grant, and by flattering insinuations endeavouring to elicit and obtain from this Kingdom Favours which cannot be granted by her without materially injuring some of the most valuable Rights and Privileges of those several important and lucrative Alanufoctures, now so firmly established amongst us, and thereby greatly diminishing the Value of Landed Property; and that, by the late and present very flourishing State of those Manufactures, especially the Woollen and Cotton, Alultitudes of Strangers have been induced to settle amongst us, and, by such an Influx of People, the Prices of Provisions ^md Labour too have been advanced in a Proportion hardly known, or even to be credited, in most other Parts of this Kingdom, and that from the same Causes, the Poor Rates have been considerably ad-

Vol. 40.

vanced; but these burthens, heavy as they are, have hitherto been chearfully submitted to, under the Advantages resulting to the Landed Interest, by an increased and increasing Trade, but, should a neighbouring State enter into a spirited Competition with our Manufacturers in those Branches of Commerce, which there is the greatest Reason now to believe and expect, a State too in which both Provisions and Labour are comparatively so low, and in which Government Taxes are hardly known and felt, when this Kingdom is groaning and tottering under the heavy Burthen of them, the Consequence of such a Competition is so obvious as to require no Illustration; and the Petitioners, therefore, hope and trust, that they shall not be obliged to surrender any more of their just Rights and very valuable Immunities to the People of that Kingdom, without receiving some adequate Advantages in Return, and, such adequate Return, they conceive, cannot be expected from the Spirit or Tendency of the present Propositions, which hold out indeed the flattering artful Language of Equalization and the Shadow of Reciprocity, but without any rational Prospect of ever rendering to this Nation the Substance of either: Those memorable Words of Air.

Orde, " that Britain had removed all the Barriers which she had raised to protect her Trade; that her Monopolies are at an End, and that she is no longer secure of being the Emporium of Commerce," delivered in the Irish House of Commons, and delivered from such Authority too, have made a very deep and alarming Impression upon the Almds of the Petitioners, and given them some Reason to fear, that far more is meant by those Propositions than is expressed, and that we are about to sacrifice some very essential Advantages, in order to gratify the Ambition and aspiring Views of some of our restless Neighbours:

To this House, as to their Constitutional Sanctuary, the Petitioners, therefore, beg Leave to resort for Protection, confiding in the known Wisdom and Attention of its Members, that, if they see the Propositions in the same suspicious and dangerous Light as they appear to the Petitioners, they will not allow the same to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Mr. Gilbert took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, That they had heard Counsel and examined a Witness, in Support of the Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers and others resident in the Town and Neighbourhood of Manchester; and that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morn-7

ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January fast, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

MR. Frederick Montagu, from the Select Com- Elgin and mittee, who were appointed to try and determine the Merits of the Petition of Alexander Penrose Camming, of Altyre, Esquire; and also, the Petition of the Freeholders of the Shire of Elgin and Forres, thereunto subscribing; severally complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Shire, in- formed the House, that the said Select Committee have determined,

Mr. IPilmot reported from the Committee, to whom Coventry the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty Poll Booth, of the City of Coventry, and of the several Persons &c*-whose Names are thereutfto subscribed, Electors of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for better regulating Elections of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the City of Coventry, was read; wherein it is enacted, That the Returning Officer should at all future Elections cause the Booth for holding the Election to be erected in the widest and most convenient Part of the open Market Place, called Cross Cheaping, not contiguous to any other Building. Then,

Mr. Edward Inge being examined, said, That the Sheriffs caused a very expensive Booth to be erected at the last Election, about a Moiety of the Expence whereof was repaid them by the successful Candidates, but the other Moiety hath not hitherto been reimbursed, although the Payment thereof has been frequently demanded; therefore it is expedient that there should bp a Law, declaring at whose Expence the Election Booth should be erected for the future. — And the Witness apprehended, that it would tend to prevent Riots if the Sheriffs were authorized to take the Poll by Tallies, agreeable to the Plan adopted at the last General Election, which they cannot do at present without Agreement of the Parties.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the Manner of taking the Poll at Elections of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the City of Coventry,9 and for reimbursing the Returning Officers the Expence of erecting Booths for that Purpose: And that Mr.

Wilmot and Sir Sampson Gideon do prepare, and bring in, the same.

and that a Bill is now depending in the House for carrying into Execution the Purposes of the said recited Act, in which Bill is contained a Clause for ratifying and confirming certain Articles of Agreement, bearing Date the 29th Day of October 1783, between the Trent and Mersey Navigation Company, and the Coventry Navigation Company, by which a certain Agreement, entered into at a Meeting held at Coleshill, in the County of Warwick, upon the 20th Day of June 1782, by certain Delegates from the respective Companies of Proprietors of the Oxford, Coventry, and Grand Trunk Canal Navigations, and from certain Proprietors of, and Subscribers to, a then new-proposed Navigation, from the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury, to Birmingham, and from thence to join the Coventry Canal, in the Neighbourhood of Fazeley, was made binding and conclusive on the said Coventry and Trunk Companies respectively; by which Agreement it was understood, and agreed by such Delegates, on the Parts of their respective Companies, that the Tonnage to be taken for all Coals navigated from Birmingham throughout the intended Canal, to Fazeley, and upon all or any Part or Parts of the Coventry and Oxford Canals, should not exceed One Penny per Ton per Mile; and that, as the said Bill now stands, the Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal Navigation will, under such Agreement, be authorized to take One Third less Tonnage for Staffordshire Coals navigated from Birmingham to Fazeley, and upon all or any Part of the said Coventry Canal, than is by the said Act specified to be taken for Coals.navigated from the Warwickshire Collieries upon the same Canal, which the Petitioners conceive will be very injurious to the said City and its Neighbourhood, in as much as such partial Tonnage will operate to shut up the Warwickshire Collieries, and exclude those Coals from Market, and the Petitioners must, in such Case, depend solely on the Wednesbury Collieries, which are Fifty Miles from Coventry, for a Supply of Coals, which they cannot possibly obtain from thence in sufficient Quantities in hard Frosts; and that the Inhabitants of the City of Coventry, and its Neighbourhood, will be deprived of the Benefit resulting from many Thousand Pounds a Year now circulating in Specie amongst them, in Consequence of working the Warwickshire Collieries, to the great Advantage and Encouragement of the Manufactures of the said City, unless the House shall give Leave for a Clause to be inserted in the said Bill, that all Coals navigated upon the said Coventry Canal, or any Part thereof, shall pass at one and the same Rate of Tonnage: And therefore praying, That such Clause may be inserted in the said Bill, for equalizing the Tonnage of all Coals, so that the Tonnage, as well for Coals passing on the said Coventry and Oxford Canals from the Warwickshire Collieries, as for Coals passing on the said Canals from the Wednesbury, or any other Collieries, may be equal, and not exceed One Penny per Ton per Mile, as proposed by the said recited Agreement, made at Coleshill, with respect to the Wednesbury Collieries, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall appear just. and reasonable.

and that a Bill is now depending in the House, to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, and the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from Birmingham to Fazeley, to make a Navigable Canal from the said Trent and Mersey Navigation on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County, in which Bill is contained a Clause for ratifying and confirming certain Articles of Agreement, bearing Date the 29th Day of October 1783, between the Trent and Mersey Canal Navigation Company of the First Part, the Coventry Canal Navigation Company of the Second Part, and the Oxford Canal Navigation Company of the Third Part, by which a certain Agreement, entered into at a Meeting held at Coleshill, in the County of Warwick, upon the 20th Day of June 1782, by certain Delegates from the respective Companies of Proprietors of the Oxford, Coventry, and, the Trent and Mersey (therein called The Grand Trunk) Canal Navigations, and from certain Proprietors of, and Subscribers to, a then new'-proposed Navigation from the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury to Birmingham, and from thence to join the Coventry Canal in the Neighbourhood of Fazeley, was made binding and conclusive on the said Oxford, Coventry, and Grand Trunk Companies respectively, by which Agreement it was understood, and agreed by such Delegates, on the Part of their respective Companies, that the Tonnage to be taken , for all Coal navigated from Birmingham, throughout the intended Canal, to Fazeley, and upon all or any Part or Parts of the Coventry and Oxford Canals, should not exceed One Penny per Ton per Mile; and that, as the said Bill now stands, the Proprietors of the said Coventry and Oxford Canal Navigations will, under such Agreement, be authorized to take One Third less Tonnage for Staffordshire Coal navigated from Birmingham to Fazeley, and upon all or any Part of the said Coventry and Oxford Canals, than is by the said Acts specified to be taken for Coal navigated from the Warwickshire Collieries upon the same Canals, which, the Petitioners conceive, will be very injurious to the Towns and Neighbourhood of Nuneaton, Bedworth, and Polesworth, inasmuch as such partial Tonnage, in Favour of Staffordshire Coal, will operate to shut up the Warwickshire Collieries, and the Petitioners must, in such Case, although living on or near the Banks, and in the Midst of Collieries, depend on the Wednesbury Coal Mines, which are at a great Distance, for a Supply of Coal, and the Colliers now employed in working the Mines within the said Parishes will be destitute of Employment, and many Tradesmen will be deprived of a Subsistence! unless the House

shall give Leave for a Clause to be inserted in the said Bill, that all Coals navigated upon the said Coventry and Oxford Canals, or any Part thereof, shall pass at one and the same Rate of Tonnage: And therefore praying, That such Clause may be inserted in the said Bill for equalizing the Tonnage of all Coal, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall appear just and reasonable.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, Manufacturers, and others, of the Town and Neighbourhood of Ashton Underline, in the County of Lan-cast€7\ interested in the Welfare and Prosperity of this Kingdom, and of the Manufactories of the said Town and Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners having duly considered the Irish Propositions, now before this House, they cannot help being truly chagrined to see the Preference given thereby to Irish Commerce and Manufactures. The First Proposition is extreme*-Iy specious, and holds forth apparent Equality and Reciprocity; but they conceive, that Ireland, not having contributed a proper Quota towards the general Exigencies of the Empire, she cannot, in Justice, expect a Participation of all its Advantages; And representing to the House, That, in the Petitioners Opinion, Ireland has already experienced the greatest Cordiality and Beneficence from the British Parliament, and of which she has been scf sensible that Addresses expressive of her Gratitude have abounded from all Parts of that Kingdom: The Petitioners do not complain of what has been done; but to confirm these Propositions would, they conceive, not only put the Commerce and Manufactures of Ireland on a better Footing than those of this Kingdom, but also be a certain Means of encouraging Emigrations; for what Manufacturer will stay here to be harassed with almost unbounded Taxes, and, what is still worse, their Liberty and Property fettered and embarrassed by vexatious Excise Laws, when they can go to Ireland, with their Workmen, and manufacture Goods without those Restraints, and send them afterwards to the British Market ? And therefore praying, That the House will adopt such Measures as to prevent these Propositions becoming a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as-relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Operative Weavers in the Villages of Govan and Particle, and their Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen, with the deepest Concern, certain Resolutions relative to a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, transmitted from the House of Commons of Ireland, and presently under the Consideration of the Parliament of Britain 1 and that the Petitioners consider these Resolutions as destructive and ruinous to the Trade and Manufacture of this Country, and, if these Resolutions are passed into a Law, the Irish, from the many Advantages of Situation and Circumstances, will be able to undersell the Manufacturers in this Place in their own Market, as well as in every other, their Trade, by which the Petitioners have hitherto been supported, will be utterly ruined, and the Petitioners reduced to Penury and Want: And therefore praying, That the House will not pass the Resolutions above-mentioned into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much Vol. AO.

of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Inters course between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Commercial others, of the Town and Neighbourhood of Bolton, ^^ire^and in the County of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners see, with Regret, the alarming Tendency of the Irish Propositions :< When first they were introduced into the House, they conceived them only as the Outlines of a Plan subject to such Alterations as the House should think proper, but, to their great Astonishment, they now learn the Whole must stand or fall together; and that the Petitioners having thoroughly considered their dangerous Consequences to the Landed, Commercial, and Manufacturing Interests of this Kingdom, conceive they should be wanting in their ✓ Duty as good Citizens to the present Age (as well as to Posterity) if they suffered the same to pass unnoticed: Ireland already possesses great Commercial Advantages; she has lately (with great Reason) acknowledged the abundant Liberality of this Kingdom; but these Propositions, the Petitioners presume, if passed into a Law, must ultimately operate to the Destruction of the Manufactures of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the House will prevent the same becoming a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the^ 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

and, the Petitioners apprehend, that the vesting of the said Part of the Coventry Canal in the Proprietors of the said Trent and Mersey Navigation will materially affect and injure the Petitioners, and other Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal Company; A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manufacturers, Traders, and others, Inhabitants of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are duly sensible that it is of the utmost Importance that this Kingdom and Ireland should be united upon such Principles of Reciprocity and mutual Advantage as will equally conduce to the Welfare of both Countries; and that in settling a Matter of so great Moment, it should now be effected in such an equitable and permanent Manner, as to put an effectual Stop to any future Claims on the Part of Ireland on the one Hand, and that Great Britain on the other should not make any Concessions that she may be under the Necessity of retracting hereafter, and thereby endanger that Harmony and good Understanding so essential to the Interests of both; and that the Petitioners are fully convinced, both from the Evidence adduced at the Bar of the

House, and their own Knowledge, that the Propositions which have passed through the Irish Parliament, if admitted here in their present Extent, will not have these desired good Effects, but, on the contrary, will give superior Advantages to the Merchants and Manufacturers of Ireland, the certain Consequences of which will be a Decline in our Trade, in the Value of Lands, in Population, and in every Circumstance which constitutes the Prosperity of a Nation: And therefore praying, That the final Settlement of the proposed Commercial Regulations may be on such Principles as shall not give a decided Superiority to either Country in any Branch of Commerce.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland,

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Traders, c«i and others, of the City of Glasgow, was presented to Interame the House, and read; Setting forth, That the earnest Wish of the Petitioners is to see every Part of the British Empire firmly united by a fair and equitable System of Commerce and Interchange of Manufactures; but, from the most attentive Consideration of the late Resolutions of the Parliament of Ireland, they are fully convinced, that, if these Resolutions are passed into a Law, they will be so far from being conducive to the great and desirable End of establishing a firm and lasting Union, on Principles of mutual Advantage, that they will prove highly injurious to many of the Manufactures of this Country, and be a perpetual Source of Jealousy and Dissension between the Two Nations; and that it appeal’s to the Petitioners, that no System can be equal and permanent which does not comprehend an equal Share of Burthens as well as Advantages; and as, by these Resolutions, the principal Articles of Ireland are allowed to be imported into this Country Duty-free, while the Manufactures of this Country are to be for ever loaded with Duties on Importation to Ireland, and that the Duties on the Importation of many Foreign Articles are not proposed to be equalized, these and other Circumstances must give to the Kingdom of Ireland superior Advantages to what are enjoyed by the Manufacturers of this Kingdom, without subjecting them to the Burthens with which they are loaded, and therefore threaten a fatal Blow to the Trade and Manufactures, and consequently to the Landed Interests, of this Country: And therefore praying, That these Resolutions, in their present Form, may not

25 Geo. III. 11° Ap827

pass into a Law, but that the further Consideration of therri may be delayed until next Session of Parliament, in order that the House may be fully acquainted with the destructive Consequences that are likely to attend them, and may, from an accurate Investigation of the Trade and Manufactures of both ' Countries, form a System calculated to promote the general Good of both Nations, and to prove the Foundation of a lasting and unalterable Union and Friendship between the Two Countries.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates, to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.
