Commercial A Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Town Intercourse Council, of the Burgh of Dunbar, was presented to with Ireland. House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are well satisfied, that a Commercial Intercourse with Ireland, on a broad and permanent Foundation, is wise, and will be most beneficial to both Countries, but that a general Alarm prevails over the Country, with regard to the Terms held out to the Irish Parliament, and very many Manufacturers apprehend the most fatal Consequences to their Trade; and that the Country at large, although they wish well to the Principles of a Connection with Ireland, are dissatisfied with the little Time that has been given them for considering a Matter of such high Importance to both Kingdoms: And therefore praying the House to delay the Consideration of these Matters, that those most materially interested therein may have full Time to consider the Principles of the Connection, with its Consequences to both Countries.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Abingdon A Petition of the Commissioners appointed by an Navigation. Act of Parliament, passed in the Year 1777, for amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Road leading from the Turnpike Road, in the Parish of Asthall, in the County of Oxford, to the Turnpike Road at or near Buckland, in the County of Berks, and also of the Creditors who have advanced Money for completing that Road, according to the Powers by such Act given, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That before the passing of the said Act the said Road was, in many Parts, narrow, and out of Repair, subject to frequent Inundations, and consequently often impassable; and that the Petitioners, the said Commissioners, have borrowed several considerable Sums of Money, which have been expended in amending and altering, where necessary, and proper Arches erecting in the Course of the same, so as to make the said Roads safe and passable, but the Tolls taken at the different Gates authorized by the said Act to be erected, do not amount to a sufficient Sum to enable the Commissioners to keep the said Road in Repair, and to pay the Interest of the Money borrowed; and that the Petitioners are informed a Bill is depending in Parliament, for effecting a Navigable Cut or Canal from the Line of the Thames and Severn Canal, at or near Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester, to Abingdon# in the County of Berks,

which must not Only prove an Object of the utmost National Utility, but also will afford most essential Benefit to the Petitioners, as it appears, from the Plan of such intended Canal, that it will cross or intersect, at or near the Parish of Buckland, the said Turnpike Road, in which the Petitioners are, for themselves and circumjacent Country, peculiarly interested; and that the Town of Bampton, with other Towns, Villages, 8$c. in the Vicinage thereof, will draw large Supplies of Fuel, Merchandize, and Necessaries of Life, from such Canal, along the Road so constructed by the Petitioners, and through the Toll* Gates erected thereon, whereby the Tolls must be considerably augmented, and the Commissioners not only enabled to preserve the said Road in good Condition, but also to pay the Money borrowed, with all Interest due thereon, to the great Relief of such of the Petitioners who are Creditors, and much to the public Advantage: And therefore praying, That the Bill for making the Canal from Kempsford to Abingdon, as aforesaid, may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near the Town ,of Abingdon^ in the County of Berks, to join and communicate with the Line of the Thames and Severn Canal, in the Parish of Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester, be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Commissioners authorized and Abingdon appointed by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, %ana under the Great Seal of Great Britain, unto them directed, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, made in the One-and-twentieth Year of the Reign of the late King James the First, intituled, "An Act for " making the River Thames navigable for Boats,

" Barges, and Lighters, from the Village of Burcott,

" in the County of Oxford, unto the University and " City of Oxford,"- was presented to the House, and read; . Setting forth, That in pursuance of the said Act the River Thames was made Navigable, from Burcott aforesaid, unto the University and City of Oxford, and divers considerable Sums of Money were at that Time expended thereon by the University and City of Oxford, and the Inhabitants thereof, amounting in the Whole to about £.2,000; and that at several subsequent Periods, and particularly within the last Ten Years, the said Commissioners have laid out the Sum of £. 800, over and above the Annual Income arising from the Tolls and Duties on the said Navigation, in re-building the several Wharfs, Locks, and Pounds of the said River, within their Jurisdiction, so that the Whole of it is now in perfect Repair, by which the said Commissioners have contracted a Debt of £.721. is. 6d. which still remains due; and that a Petition hath been presented to the House, for making a Navigable Canal from Leachlade, in the County of Gloucester, to the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Bei'ks, and, the Petitioners conceive the making such Navigable Canal will not only destroy the Navigation of the said River Thames and Isis, from Leachlade to Oxford, and from Oxford to Abingdon, by which the Conveyance of Goods by Water Carriage to the University and City of Oxford will be totally annihilated, to the great Detriment thereof, but likewise will very materially injure the Estates of the several Land Owners lying near the said River, by rendering the valuable Meadow Lands a perfect Swamp, to the great Detriment thereof, and to the Health of the Inhabitants of the adjacent Country; and representing to the House, that the Wharfage, Tolls, and Duties on the Navigation within the Petitioners Jurisdiction* which have hitherto amounted to not les9 than ,£.13& per Annum, will be so reduced, as to be totally inadequate to the Discharge of the Debt already incurred,

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to join and communicate with the Line of the Thames and Secern Canal, in the Parish of jKempsford, in the County of Gloucester, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Representa- A Petition of the Freemen, Freeholders, and others, tion in Inhabitants of the Town of King's Lynn, was presented Parliament. to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are truly sensible of the great Excellence of the Constitution of this Country, and zealously attached to those Principles on which it was originally founded, and that for* Security in the Possession of their just Rights, it is indispensably necessary, that the whole Body of the People should be represented: That, at present, a very inconsiderable Part of the Nation have a Voice in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament, and the Representation is thereby rendered partial and inadequate: And therefore entreating the House to take into their most serious Consideration the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Commercial A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and intercourse others, in Aberdeen, thereto subscribing, was presented with Ireland. to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners were equally astonished and alarmed at the Ten Propositions, made by the Honourable Mr. Orde, in the House of Commons in Ireland,\ and now under Consideration of this House, for establishing a Commercial Intercourse betwixt Great Britain and that Kingdom, the Petitioners being unacquainted with any Reasons, of State or Necessity, which should induce Great Britain to make such a complete Surrender of her Commerce and Manufactures to the Sister Kingdom, as muss be consequent of these Propositions passing into a Law; and that a proportionate Participation of Burthens, as well as Advantages, is the only Foundation upon which a fair and equitable System or Treaty of Commerce can be established with Ireland; and, the Irish Resolutions, now before the House, holding forth no certain nor satisfactory Participation of Burthens, cannot be a proper Foundation for such a Treaty: And therefore praying, That the House will not adopt any Treaty of Commerce with Ireland, but on the Basis of its bearing a proportionate Share of the Burthens at present affecting, or which may hereafter affect, the People of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the jjConsideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse v between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Free Brothers of the Borough of Vol. 40.

Morpeth, in the County of Northumb&'layid, was pre- Representa-sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That tion in the Petitioners are Free Brothers of the Borough of Pad*1"6111-Morpeth, which Right they have acquired either by Patrimony, or by serving as Apprentices for the Term of Seven Years to the Trades to which they respectively belong; that the Right of voting for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Morpeth, is confined to a very small Number, who are, by the Custom of the Borough, called Freemen, and the Petitioners are entitled to every Privilege in the Borough with the Freemen, but that of giving a Vote at Elections for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the Petitioners, and the rest of the Free Brothers, are above double the Number to those Freemen who have the Right of voting for Members to serve in Parliament, and the Petitioners have been at very great Expence and Trouble, from Time to Time, in endeavouring to obtain the Privilege of giving their Voice at Elections, but hitherto without Effect; and, that the Petitioners, sensible of the original Excellence of the Constitution of this Country, most ardently wish to have it maintained upon the genuine Principles on which it was founded, and that it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation; and that, in the present State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, the Commons of this Realm are partially and inadequately represented, and consequently cannot have that Security for their Liberties, which is the Aim and Intention of the Constitution to give them:

And therefore supplicating the House to take their particular Case into Consideration; and also the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy to them, and to this great Constitutional Evil, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That’ so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to discontinue, for " a limited Time, the Payment of the Duties upon 16 Low Wines and Spirits for Home Consumption,

" and for granting and securing the due Payment of " other Duties in lieu thereof; and for the better " Regulation of the making and vending British Spirits, as well for Home Consumption as for Exportation; and for destroying all Home-made and " Foreign Spirits after the Condemnation thereof; " and for vesting in His Majesty the Duties of Excise within the Lands of Fcrentosh, in the County of " Inverness; and for discontinuing, for a limited Time, " certain Imposts and Duties upon Rum and Spirits " imported from the West Indies" as limits the Size of the Stills to be used in the Distillation of Corn Spirits, within the Parishes or Districts of certain Counties in the Highlands of that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Commissioners of Excise in Scotland be authorized to grant Annual Licences for erecting and working Stills, of certain Contents, for the Distillation of Corn Spirits, in the Counties of Orkney, Caithness, SutherlandRoss, Inverness, Argyle, Bute, Aberdeen, Forfar, Kincardine, Banff, Nairn, and Elgin, and certain Parts of the Counties of Stirling, Perth, and Dumbarton.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Twenty Shillings Sterling be charged upon every Gallon of the Contents of such Stills, to be paid by the Owners thereof.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the^aid Resolutions: And that General Murray, the Lord Advocate of Scotland, and the Marquis of Graham, do prepare, and bring in, die same.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to Mr. Mar-sham, Sir Joseph Mawbey, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker s Chamber.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Manufac- Trentj^ turers, and others, of the City of Coventry, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners find, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented, for Leave to bring in a Bill to make Navigable the Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, with some short Cuts -connecting the rewith, from Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, to Atherstone, in the County of JVarwick, with several short Cuts branching therefrom; and the Petitioners also find, that a Bill is depending in the House, for enabling the several Companies of Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, and from Birmingham to Fazeley, to make a Navigable Canal from The Trent and Mersey Navigation, on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County; and submitting to the House, that, if such Application for making Navigable the said Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, with the said several Cuts therefrom, should meet with the Sanction of Parliament, it will render the Completion of the intended Coventry Canal from Atherstone to Fazeley unnecessary, and every Communication intended thereby, and also by the said i intended Bill for making a Navigable Canal from Fradley Heath to Fazeley, will be effected, and at a much less Expence, with the Advantage of larger Boats, with greater Accommodation for the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize, as well with respect to an easier Tonnage and Freight, as to greater Safety and Dispatch, and unattended with the Loss of a large Quantity of rich and valuable Land, and without the Inconvenience of the Separation of Property, which must necessarily arise from the making a new Canal: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and that when such Bill, for making Navigable the Rivers Trent,

Tame, and Anker, shall be presented, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition, the same may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition’ of several Noblemen, and the humble Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, Traders, and Inhabitants of the Town of Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, and the Neighbourhood thereof, and also of the Bailiffs, Commonalty, and Inhabitants of the Borough of Tamworth, in the Counties of Stafford and JVarwick, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being Returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Seventy-five Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then draSvri by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Twenty-seven Members, thea present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And' the Name of the Honourable George Keith Elphimtone, being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Select Committee, that he had been afflicted with a severe Illness, from Which he was but very lately recovered, and that he could not possibly attend the said Committee, without great and manifest Detriment to the present uncertain State of his Health; and the Substance of what was so alledged by him being taken down by the Clerk* in Manner before mentioned, and the said Member having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon, Mr. Speaker putting the Question to the House, That the said Member (in respect of what he has now so alledged and verified)! be excused from serving On the said Select Committee; which being agreed to by the House, he was excused accordingly; ’ '

And the Names of Twenty-two 'other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to f

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioner be then heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County; and submitting to the House, that if such Application for making Navigable the said Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, with the said several Cuts therefrom, should meet with the Sanction of Parliament, it will render the Completion of the intended Coventry Canal, from Atherstone to Fazeley, unnecessary, and every Communication intended thereby (if completed) and also by the said intended Bill for making a Navigable Candl from Fradley Heath to Fazeley, will be effected, and at a much less Expence, with the Advantage of larger Boats, with greater Accommodation for the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize, as well with respect to an easier Tonnage and Freight, as to greater Safety and Dispatch,* and unattended with the Loss of a large Quantity of rich and valuable Land, and without the Inconvenience of the Separation of Property, which must necessarily arise from the making a new. A Petitioa of the Glass Manufacturers of London; Commercial Bristol, Navcastle, and Glasgow, was presented to the Intercourse House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners wlt reJ*n ' conceive that a Commercial Arrangement with Ireland is of very great Importance to this Kingdom, and to the Bj'itish Empire at large, but they have great Reason to believe that the Resolutions of the Irish Parliament, now under the Consideration of this House, will not put the Two Kingdoms upon Terms of Equality, but will, if passed into a Law, eventually prove highly detrimental to the Manufactures and Commerce of Great Britain, and particularly to the Manufacture in which the Petitioners are engaged; and that the Petitioners wish not, nor do they mean, to object to or oppose, any System which can or may be adopted for the Purpose of putting both Kingdoms upon Terms of Equality in respect to their Manufactures and Commerce, but, on the contrary, would chearfully and warmly support such System, but the Petitioners apprehend, that, unless Ireland will consent to pay equal Duties with Great Britain on all her Imports, and an equal Excise on her Manufactures,* and internal Consumption, for the Support of the Empire at large, and that the same Regulations and Laws be adopted and made respecting the Exports from both Kingdoms, as . well from one to the other, as from each to Foreign Parts, no Terms of Equaliza-' tion can be settled between the Two Kingdoms; and that if Terms of Equalization were to be settled between the Two Kingdoms as before mentioned, the Petitioners verily believe Ireland would still have and enjoy manifest arid great Advantages over Great Britain, inasmuch as His Majesty’s Subjects in this Kingdom are burthened with many very heavy and grievous Taxes, which the Petitioners apprehend and believe they are in a great Measure exempt from in-Ireland; and, moreover, the Manufacturers of Ireland\ from their local Situation, will have a great Advantage over the Manufacturers of this Kingdom, in sending their Manufactures to Foreign Markets, and are or may be, as the Petitioners believe, supplied with Coal, the Produce of that Country, the Petitioners having been credibly informed, that that Species of Fuel has been Jbund in various Parts of'

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Estates in the Hundreds of Tunstead and Happing, in the County of Norfolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is soliciting in Parliament for incorporating the aforesaid Hundreds, for the better Maintenance of the Poor within the same; and, the Petitioners having taken this Matter into Consideration, and being sensible that the Increase of their Poor’s Rates, for some few Years past, hath not been owing so much to any Neglect or Misapplication in the Disbursements, as from other Causes, which, in the general State of Things, have been unavoidable, they now look forward with Hope chearfully to provide for the necessary Support of their Poor, at a less Expence than if incorporated, and are perfectly satisfied in their present Situation, and fully persuaded it will not be for the Interest of the said Hundreds at large so to be incorporated, nor have a general Tendency to the better Maintenance of the Poor within the same, an Institution the Petitioners by no Means approve, nor can, with any Vol. 40.

Degree of Satisfaction, assent to: And therefore praying, That the Rill may not be allowed to pass, contrary to the Petitioners most earnest Wishes, and, they conceive, against their Rights and Privileges, in an equal Claim of being heard.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee to whom the Bill for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor within the Hundreds of Tunstead and Happing, in the County of Norfolk, is committed.

and that the Petitioners were elected by a Majority of legal Voters, but that Joseph Gouldsrnith, Esquire, who acted as Bailiff and Returning Officer at the said Election, in taking the Poll was guilty of the grossest Partiality and Injustice towards the Petitioners, by arbitrarily rejecting the legal Votes of several Persons who offered to vote for the Petitioners, and by admitting other Persons to vote for the said Sir Peter Parka* and Sir John Henderson who had no legal Right to, vote, and in many other Respects the said Joseph Gouldsrnith was guilty of unwarrantable Practices, as well previous to as during the said Election; and that several Persons, who voted for the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson, had previously asked, received, and taken Money, and other Reward, and had agreed, or contracted, for Money, Gift, and Reward, to give their Votes in the said Election, and had been guilty of other illegal and corrupt Practices, by Means whereof their Votes so given are, and ought to be declared to be, void; and that the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson, by themselves, or some Person or Persons employed by them, or One of them, did, by Gift or Reward, and by Promise, Agreement, or Security for Gift or Reward, corrupt and procure several Persons to give their Votes in the said Election, and, by the said and other undue Means the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson were returned to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port of Seaford, in Prejudice of the Petitioners (who were duly elected, and ought to have been returned) in Prejudice of the legal Electors of the said Town and Port, and in open Defiance of the Law and Freedom of Elections: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein as shall, upon Examination, appear to be just.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker; and One hundred and Forty Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides w ere called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked; the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses; and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Name of John Pollexfen Bastard, Esquire, being drawn, he wTas nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioners; and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Forty-nine Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That, in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Fifty-one other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Eight, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Ten, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; Sixteen, on . Account of their then serving on Select Committees; and Seventeen, on Account of their having already in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete;

The Counsel for the Sitting Members named John Strutt, Esquire, to serve on the said Select Committee.

And Lists of the said Forty-nine Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

Mr. Phelips, from the Select Committee appointed to try and determine the Merits of the Petitions of John Sinclair, Esquire, severally complaining of an undue Election and Return far the District of Boroughs of Kirkwall, Wick, Dornoch, Tain, and Dingwall, informed the House, That Major General Charles Ross, having been summoned to attend the said Committee, had returned an Answer by Letter, stating, that he was under Arrest, and did not think himself at Liberty to comply with the Order of the said Committee, without Permission from His Majesty.

Then Two Letters from Major General Charles Ross to the Chairman of the said Select Committee, dated this Day, together with a Letter from William Fawcett, Esquire, Adjutant General of His Majesty’s Forces, to the said Major General Ross, dated the 28th Day of February last, were delivered in at the Table, and read; and are as followeth; viz.

Sir,

Having just received your Order of Yesterday’s Date, for me to attend the Committee sitting on the Merits of the Kirkwall Election, I must inform you, Sir, that being under Arrest, and having only Li^ berty, through His Majesty’s most Gracious Indulgence, to go out for the Preservation of my Health, or upon my own private Affairs; therefore, I have a Doubt of the Propriety of my attending the Committee, which otherways I would obey with the greatest Readiness; and I have the Honor to be, with much Respect,

Sir,

Duke-Street, Your most humble

Westminster, and most obedient Servant,

A Petition of the Land Owners of the Manor of Richmai Richmond, otherwise West Sheene, in the County of P«. Surrey, and the Inhabitants of the Parishes of Rick mond and Kew, situate within the said Manor, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives His Consent, as far as His Majesty’s Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think lit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to repeal Part of an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty, for the Relief and Employment of the Poor of the Parish of Richmond, in the County of Surrey, and other Purposes in the said Act mentioned, ond for making npw Provisions for the Relief and Employment of the Poor, for the Repairs of the Highways, the paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets, and other Places, in the Town and Parish of Richmond aforesaid, and for the Removal and Prevention of Annoyances, Obstructions, and Incroachments therein; and Setting forth, that the Petitioners have Reason to believe, that Their Majesties intend, and are willing, to give up and relinquish all Right and Title to the Commons, or Soil of the Commons, called Pest House Common, arid The Hill Common, comprized within the said Manor, in order that such Parts of the said Commons, as may appear necessary, should be appropriated for building a proper Workhouse thereon, for the Use of the said Parish of Richmond, and that They likewise intend to assist the said Parish in

completing

Googh

25 Geo. III. 140 Afrilis. 847

Completing the same; and that the Petitioners are the principal Persons having a Right of Common within the said Manor, and are extremely desirous that the Commons aforesaid, or Parts thereof, should be inclosed, and appropriated for the Purpose before mentioned, the said Commons having been productive of little or no Benefit to any Persons for a long Time past, as well from their Vicinity to the City of London, as from their limited Extent, and the uncultivated State in which they have been suffered to remain; and Alleging, that the Footway leading from the North Eud of the Town of Richmond to the Hamlet of Kcw, along the Side of the Gardens, now in the Occupation, and, for the most Part, the Property of His Majesty, known by the Name of Love Lane, is seldom frequented, and does not afford a nearer and better Communication with any other Town, for the Purposes of Trade, or mutual Convenience, than may be had either by the public Highway, called Kew Lane, or by the Footway and Towing Path on the Side of the River Thames, both of which were raised by His present Majesty, and are still maintained at His Expenqe, and have been so raised and made

food within these few Years past; and that the said ’ootway, for these Reasons, and in this Manner, neglected, and, being extremely dangerous, from its great Length and Privacy, affords a safe Retreat for idle and disorderly Persons, and is become a real Nuisance to the Inhabitants residing near it, and particularly inconvenient to His Majesty, whose Gardens it intersects and divides for upwards of a Mile, and, the Inclosure of the said Bye-way will not be attended with Inconvenience to any Persons whatsoever; and that the Petitioners have Reason to believe that His Majesty will cause the said Footway to be shut up and discontinued at His own Expence, and will also make good, and keep in Repair, a new Communication from the said Footway to the public High Road, So as to answer every good Purpose which the said Footway is capable of producing: And therefore praying, That full and proper Powers may be given by and enacted in the said Bill, as will enable Their Majesties to grant, for themselves and their Successors, and that the said Parishes of Richmond and Kew may be impowered to inclose and cultivate, so much of the said Two Commons of the said Manor before described, as may be granted to them respectively by Their Majesties, and to appropriate Part of the Ground, Garden, and Fields, on which the said Work-house is to be built, and the Poor supported; and that His Majesty may he enabled to shut up the Footway leading from Richmond to Kew, as before described, at such Points as shall appear proper, at each End, with a Provision to require the Possessors of the Lands, on both Sides the said Footway so to be shut up, to make good, and keep in Repair, a new Communication or Footway, at the Point on the Richmond Side, at which the former one was discontinued, to the public Highway, called Kew Lane, with such further Relief and Assistance in the Premises, as shall appear to the House fit and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Ambler, the Lord Mahon, &c.: And they are to meet T.o-morrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the Merchants and principal Manufacturers of Broad Cloth, in the County of Gloucester, in Behalf of themselves and many Thousand others employed by them in the several Branches of the said Manufacture, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a large and very extensive Capital is employed by the Petitioners, in the Manufacture of Broad Cloths, and the Support of the Inhabitants of that most populous Country depends, in a great Measure, on the Prosperity of this particular Branch of the Woollen Manufacture; and that the Petitioners have attended, with the utmost Anxiety, to the Propositions admitted by the Irish Parliament, and now lying before the House to be passed into a Law, as a final Regulation of Commerce between the Sister Kingdoms: Relying on the good Disposition of His Majesty’s Ministers, the Petitioners have hitherto rested in confident Assurance that such Modifications would have been admitted as aj-e es? sential to the Trading Interests of the Petitioners, and the Petitioners beg Leave to assure the House, that they have too high a Sense of the natural Rights of Men, to wish to lay any Restraints on their Irish Brethren, unworthy People living under a Government free as that which they themselves enjoy; and, the Petitioners, therefore, most readily admit, " That " it is highly important to the general Interests of " the Bj'itish Empire, that the Trade between Great Britain and Ireland be encouraged and extended as " much as possible, and, for that Purpose, that the " Intercourse and Commerce be finally settled' and " regulated on permanent and equitable Principle^, " for the mutual Benefit of both Cowries, but loaded as this Country is, with an enormous Debt, and heavy Taxes, they are apprehensive that the Advantages of cheap Provisions, low Wages, and, comparatively, no Taxes, will enable the Irish Manufacturer to undersell the English at almost every Market, and even our own: They conceive it to be the mutual Interests of both Kingdoms, that the proposed System of Commercial Intercourse should be founded on such Principles of Justice and real Equar lity, as may finally remove all Jealousy and Misunderstanding; and with the utmost Concern, therefore,

Means this Country will be overstocked with Irish Goods smuggled, and which the Petitioners conceive will prove destructive to their Trade; and Representing to the House, that, in Consequence of the very heavy Duty on Silk, the Petitioners Trade has* been in a very declining Situation for several Years, which, with the additional Duty on that Commodity last Session, has so lessened their Home Consumption, that, for Want of Employment, the Consequence is, Poverty and Distress are deluging like a Torrent the whole Trade, and, if the Irish Resolutions should pass into a Law, their Trade is irretrievably lost and ruined, and Emigration and Depopulation must be the dreadful Consequence, the only Alternative left to fly from the Iron Jaws of extreme Misery and Want; and that the Petitioners beg Leave to state to the House, that the Nature of their Business is such as obliges them to bear a greater Share of the Burthen of the State than many other Manufacturers, for, although their Wages are much lower than many other Mechanics, yet they are obliged to occupy Houses of greater Rent and Taxes, particularly in the Articles of Window and Candle Tax, which since the additional Duty laid on those Articles, together with the increasing Parochial Dues, particularly Poors Rates, occasioned by the great Decay of the Silk Trade, that Poverty and Distress pervade the Streets, whereby Numbers are daily obliged to have Recourse to the Relief of a Workhouse, or are obliged to leave their Native Country, and thereby depriving the Community of many useful Subjects, and furnishing Foreign Nations with Arts and Mysteries, which, in the End, may prove exceeding prejudicial to the Trade, Commerce, and Revenue of this Country: And therefore the Petitioners beg Leave to lay their Distresses before this august Assembly, the only Saviours that can revive their drooping Trade, humbly imploring, in Behalf of themselves, and Thousands yet unborn, That the intended Propositions respecting Ireland may not pass into a Law, to the Ruin of their Trade, and that a few of the Petitioners may be permitted td prove the Allegations of this Petition at the Bar of the House, and that they will adopt such Measures as they shall think most conducive for promoting and encouraging the British Manufacture in all its Branches, whereby Thousands of His Majesty’s loyal and dutiful Subjects (Numbers of whom have chearfully fought the Battles of their Country, and are ready to step forth, if Occasion shall require, to face the Enemies of their Native Land) will be relieved from the greatest Misery and Distress.

the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been greatly and justly alarmed at the Resolutions lately passed in the Parliament of Ireland, respecting the proposed Commercial Treaty between that Country and Great Britain, now transmitted to the British Parliament for their Discussion and Approbation; Resolutions which at once appear to them to be partial, and no ways calculated to produce the Equality and Reciprocity which is held forth as the Basis for such a Treaty; and that the Petitioners are convinced, were these Resolutions to be adopted, and pass into a Law, most of the Manufactures of this Country must be greatly injured, if not entirely annihilated, and our Manufacturers and Traders be put to the disagreeable Necessity of transporting themselves to distant Climes, there to procure that Livelihood for their Families which cannot then be had at Home, to the certain Hurt of this Country, and of His Majesty’s Revenues; and that, before Ireland can be entitled to the many and important Advantages to be derived by them from these Resolutions passing into a Law, they must, in Reason and Equity, bear their Proportion of the Burthens and Taxes imposed upon the Manufacturers, Traders, and others, of Great Britaini, then will that Equality and Reciprocity take Place, which ought to be the Basis: And therefore most earnestly soliciting the House, That these Resolutions be not passed into a Law', at least that they shall be so altered and amended, that the Manufacturing Interests of this Country will not be in any Degree hurt or prejudiced thereby; and that Care will be had for securing the same.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Wing Wall of the River Stour Aqueduct, near Stour-ton, in the County of Stafford, for the Space of Eight Miles towards the Junction of the said Canal with the Birmingham Canal, and which w as to continue for the Term of Two Years, and no longer; and that such Reduction of Tonnage was made in Favour of the Bilston, Cosclcy, and Tipton Collieries, from an Apprehension that such Collieries, without such Allowance in their Favour, would not be able to send down Coals, as theretofore, to the Severn Market, and that the Collieries on the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals would engross that Part of the Coal Trade, but such Reduction was then expressly made for a limited Time only, in order that proper Relief might be given to such of the Parties who found themselves aggrieved at the Expiration of such Term; and that such Reduction of Tonnage, so made in Favour of Coals sent from the Bilston, Coseley, and Tipton Collieries, with the additional Tonnage imposed by the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Company, on all Coals coming down the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, operated so far in Prejudice of the Collieries lying on the said last mentioned Canals, as, in Effect, to exclude them from a Competition with the Bilston, Coseley, and Tip-ton Coals, in the Severn Market; and that, at a subsequent Meeting of the said Commissioners, holden on the 19th Day of March 1782, pursuant to public Advertisement, an Order, or Proposal, having been laid before them, by the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Car.al Company, to continue the said Reduction of Tonnage upon Coals navigated on the said Canal, within the Distance specified in their former Order, the Commissioners assembled at such Meeting, after having duly weighed and considered the same, did, by a Resolution, or Declaration in Writing, signify their Dissent thereto, and reject the same accordingly, which said Resolution, or Declaration, was signed by Fifty-four Commissioners, being a very large Majority of the Commissioners present at such Meeting; and that, in Consequence of such last mentioned Resolution of the said Commissioners, the Tonnage upon Coals navigated on the said Staffoi'dshire and Worcestershire Canal hath ever since remained upon the Footing the same was originally placed by the Legislature, and the different Collieries, which send Coals down the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, have been enabled to bring their Coals to Market without Prejudice to each other, and the Public and the Petitioners have been benefited thereby; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented to the House from the said Company of Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable them, without the Interposition of Commissioners, to lowTer and regulate the Tonnage upon their Navigation, or upon any Part or Parts thereof, in such Manner as they should, from Time to Time, see necessary; and, if such Bill should pass into a Law, it would be in the Power of the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal to lower the Tonnage partially upon Coals sent down their Ganal, from the Bilston, Coseley, and Tipton Collieries, so as totally to exclude Coals being sent from the Collieries on the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, and the Controul of the Commissioners interposed by the Legislature, under the express Agreement of the Parties, to prevent any such Partiality or Injustice, would be taken away, by Means whereof the great Object of the Petitioners, in making the said Stourbridge Navigation, in order to bring Coals into the Severn Market, would be defeated, and the Petitioners will be obliged to sit down, after having sunk upwards of £.50,000 in such Undertaking, with the Prospect of very little, if any, Return therefrom, whilst the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal are receiving very large and regular

Dividends from their said Undertaking, and the Owners and Proprietors of Mines lying on the said Stourbridge and Dudley Canals will be greatly injured, and the Public lose the Benefit of being supplied with Coals therefrom: And therefore praying the

House to take thq Premises into Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worccstei'shire Canal Navigation to lower and regulate the Tonnage upon the said Canal, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Gibraltar A Petition of Stephen Fuller, Rose Fuller, and John

Prize Money. Bowman, Esquires, Agents for the Gibraltar Head Money and Prize Money, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for authorizing the Prize Agents, appointed by the Officers of the Garrison of Gibraltar, to pay to the Agents of the Corps composing the said Garrison all such Sums, as shall remain or come to their Hands, of the Bounty allowed for the Destruction of certain Spanish Ships of War; and Setting forth, That an Act was made in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for authorizing the Treasurer of the Navy to pay to the Agent, or Agents, to be appointed by the Officers of the Garrison and Naval Department at Gibraltar, the Bounty Money therein mentioned, and, the Petitioners have been legally appointed Attornies and Agents for receiving such Bounty Money, and have received Bills on the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy for the same, agreeable to the Directions of the said Act, and they have also received Money for the Value of the Ship Saint Miguel find Stores, and also for a certain Quantity of Stores delivered into His Majesty’s Storehouses at Gibraltar, for all which Monies, and for such other Monies as they may hereafter receive on Account of the said Garrison and Naval Department, the Petitioners are ready to account to the Parties entitled thereto, upon the shortest Notice; and that, in paying the Money so by them received as aforesaid to the Officers and Men entitled thereto, the Petitioners have pursued the usual Practice and Course of Payment which has been established many Years in paying Navy Prize Money, and have regularly paid all such Persons as have been able to ascertain their Claims; and that the Petitioners have never heard of any reasonable Complaints of their Conduct in the transacting of this Business, and therefore are greatly surprized and concerned to find it is alledged in the said Bill, that great Inconveniencies and Difficulties have arisen in the Mode of Payment of the said Bounty Money by the Petitioners, on account of their limiting their Attendance to the First Friday in every Month, and that such Inconveniencies and Difficulties might be obviated, if the said Bounty Money and Prize Money were to be paid by the Regimental or other Agents, to the different Corps belonging to the said Garrison, who are or may be in constant Attendance; and that the Petitioners beg Leave to assure the House, that, so far from limiting their Attendance to the First Friday in every Month, as is alledged in the said Bill, they have given almost a regular Daily Attendance at their Offices for paying the said Bounty Money; and that, as the Petitioners are not conscious of having acted in any Manner contrary to the Trust reposed in them by the Persons by whom they have been legally appointed Attornies and Agents as aforesaid, they hope they shall not be divested

of that Trust until it shall have been proved to the House, that they have abused it, as the same would convey to the Public a Reflection upon their Conduct and Characters, And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration; and that they may be heard by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the said Bill, and in Justification of their Conduct and Characters, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That die said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if the^ think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Bill be printed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second TinJe upon this Day Sevennight.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Dudley Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act made in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Petitioners were authorized to make a Navigable Canal, within and from certain Lands of Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire, situate at Nether ton, in the Parish of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, to a Place called Black Dclph, upon Pensnet Chace, there to join and communicate with the Stourbridge Canal Navigation; and that the Petitioners, in pursuance of the said Act, have made and completed the said Canal, and the same hath been rendered navigable for more than Five Years last past, and the Petitioners have expended, in the said Undertaking, £. 9,000, and upwards, as well as the whole Income and Profits arising therefrom, amounting to the further Sum of £ 1,800, and upwards, and have not received any Dividends, or Return, for the Monies so laid out by them; and that the great Object

Vol. 40.

of the Petitioners, ill making the said Canal, was to convey Coals from the Collieries lying on and near to the Course thereof into the Severn Market, for the better Supply of the several Counties of Worcester, Gloucester, Hereford, and Warwick; and that, by a Clause in the Act for making the said Stourbridge Canal Navigation, the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal were authorized to impose a Tonnage upon all Coals brought down the said Stourbridge Navigation, and which should be navigated upon the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, not exceeding Two Pence a Ton per Mile, instead of One Penny Halfpenny a Ton per Mile, which they were before authorized to take on all Coals and Merchandize navigated on their said Canal, and the said last mentioned Company were also authorized to lessen and reduce the Tolls, Rates, and Duties, upon any Part of their said Canal, and for any Distance they should think fit, provided such Reduction w as made with the Consent of the major Part of the Commissioners, appointed by virtue of an Act* passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His said Majesty, for making the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation* assembled for that Purpose, of which Assembly Twenty-one Days Notice, at least, is required to be given in One of the Birmingham Newspapers, and that there be Twenty-one Commissioners, at least, present at such Meeting; and that such additional Tonnage on Coals, brought ,down the Stourbridge Canal into the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, was imposed on Account of the Collieries lying on the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals being nearer the Severn Market than the Bilston, Coseley, and Tipton Collieries, and navigating a less Distance on the Stuff fordshire and Worcestershire Canal, but under an express Agreement that the Power of lessening and reducing such Tonnage, as well as the Tonnage on ail other Coals navigated upon the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, should be placed by the Legislature under the Controul of Commissioners, whose Qualification is £.100 a Year Real Estate, in order to prevent any Partiality or Injustice being exercised, by the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Company, in Favoifr of any particular Collieries from which Coals might be sent on their said Canal, in Prejudice to other Collieries navigating on the same Canal; and that* as soon as the said Stourbridge and Dudley Canals became navigable, the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, on their own Authority, and without calling in the said Commissioners, in direct Violation of the said Clause, took upon themselves to reduce the Tonnage upon all Coals navigated on their said Canal, except what came down the Stourbridge Canal, at the same Time that they imposed and collected the full Duty of Two Pence a Ton per Mile on all Coals navigated from the said Stourbridge and Dudley Canals into the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal; and that afterwards, at a Meeting held the 21st Day of March 1780, a Reduction was made, with the Consent of the said Commissioners, of One Penny a Ton per Mile, on all. Coals navigated on the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, from the Distance of Sixty Yards from the East Wing Wall of the River Stour Aqueduct, near Stourton, in the County of Stafford, for the Space, of Eight Miles towards the Junction of the said Canal with the Birmingham Canal, and which was to continue for the Term of Two Years, and no longer; and that such Reduction of Tonnage was made in Favour of the Bilston, Coseley, and Tipton Collieries, from an Apprehension that such Collieries, without such Allowance in their Favour, would not be able to send down Coals, as theretofore, to the Severn Market, and that the Collieries on the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals would engross that Part of the Coal

Staffordshire, &c. Canal.

S6o 18° Aprilis. A, 1785.

Staffordshire, Trade, but such Reduction was then expressly made for &c. Canal* a limited Time only, in order that proper Relief might be given to such of the Parties who found themselves aggrieved at the Expiration of such Term; and that such Reduction of Tonnage so made in Favour of Coals sent from the said Bilston, Cosclcy, and Tip* ton Collieries, with the additional Tonnage imposed by the said Staff ordshire and Worcestershire Canal Company on all Coals coming down the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, operated so far, in Prejudice of the Collieries lying on the said Dudley Canal, as, in Effect, to exclude them from a Competition with the Bilston, Cose ley, and Tipton Coals, in the Severn Market; and that, at a subsequent Meeting of the said Commissioners, holden on the 19th Day of March 1782, pursuant to public Advertisement, an Order or Proposal having been laid before them, by the said Staffordshire and Worcester shire Canal Company, to continue* the said Reduction of Tonnage upon Coals navigated on their said Canal within the Distance specified in their former Order, the Commissioners assembled at such Meeting, after having duly weighed and considered the same, did, by a Resolution, or Declaration, in Writing, signify their Dissent thereto, and reject the same accordingly, which said Resolution, or Declaration, was signed by Fifty-four Commissioners, being a very large Majority of the Commissioners present at such Meeting; and that, in Consequence of such last mentioned Resolution of the said Commissioners, the Tonnage upon Coals navigated on the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal hath ever since remained upon the Footing the same was originally placed by the Legislature, and the different Collieries, which send Coals down the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, have been enabled to bring their Coals to Market without Prejudice to each other, and the Public and the Petitioners have been benefited thereby; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented to the House from the said Company of Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable them, without the Interposition of Commissioners, to lower and regulate, the Tonnage upon their Navigation, or upon any Part or Parts thereof, in such Manner as they should, from Time to Time, see necessary, and, if such Bill should pass into a Law, it would be in the Power of the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal to lower the Tonnage partially upon Coals sent down their Canal from the Bilston, Coseley, and Tipton Collieries, so as totally to exclude Coals being sent from the Collieries on the Dudley Canal, and the Controul of the Commissioners interposed by the Legislature, to prevent any such Partiality or Injustice, would be taken away, by Means whereof, the great Object of the Petitioners in making the said Dudley Canal, in order to bring Coals into the Severn Market, would be defeated, and the Petitioners will be obliged to sit down, after having sunk upwards of £. 10,800 in such Undertaking, with the Prospect of very little, if any, Return therefrom, whilst the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal are receiving very large and regular Dividends from their said Undertaking, and the Owners and Proprietors of Mines lying on the said Dudley Canal will be greatly injured, and the Public lose the Benefit of being supplied with Coals therefrom: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Parishes of Kingsrvinford and Dudley, in the Counties of Stafford and Worcester, respectively, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, the said John Lord Viscount Dudley and Ward, is the Owner of very large and extensive Coal Mines, and the other Petitioners are also Owners and Proprietors of very considerable Coal Mines, situate within the said respective Parishes, and upon which Collieries have been planted, at the Expence of many Thousand Pounds, on and near to the Line of the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, and very large Quantities of Coals have, since the making of the said Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, been raised at such Collieries, and sent down the said last mentioned Canals into the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, for the Supply of the Severn Market, and the adjacent Country; and that, previous to the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal being opened, the Forges and Iron Works on the River Stour, the Salt Works at Droitwich, and a very considerable Part of the County of Worcester, were supplied with Coals from the Collieries situate within the said Parishes, and, by Means of a Communication between the said* Stafford* shire and Worcestershire Canal, and the Birmingham Canal, the Collieries lying on the said last mentioned Canal, which before never had any Intercourse wife, or. and that, as soon as the said Stourbridge Canal became navigable, the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and JVoixestershire Canal, on their own Authority, and without calling in the said Commissioners, in direct Violation of the said Clause, took upon themselves to reduce the Tonnage on all Coals navigated upon the said Canal, except what cape down the said Stourbridge Canal, at the same Time that they imposed and collected the full Duty of Two Pence a Ton per Mile on all Coals navigated from the said Stourbridge Canal into the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal; and that afterwards, at a Meeting, held the 21st Day of March 1780, a Reduction was made, with the Consent of the said Commissioners, of One Penny a Ton per Mile on all Coals navigated on the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, from the Distance of Sixty Yards from the East Wing Wall of the River Stour Aqueduct, near Stourton, in the County of Stafford, for the Space of Eight Miles towards the Junction of the said Canal with the Birmingham Canal, and which was to continue for Two Years, and no longer; and that such Reduction of Tonnage was made in Favour of the Collieries lying on the said Birmingham Canal, from an Apprehension that such Collieries, without such Allowance in their Favour, would not be able to send down Coals as theretofore to the Severn Market, and that the Collieries on the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals would engross that Part of the Coal Trade, but such Reduction was then expressly made for a limited Time only, in order that proper Relief might be given to such of the Parties who found themselves aggrieved at the Expiration of such Term; and that such Reduction of Tonnage, with the additional Tonnage imposed by the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Company on all Coals coming down the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, operated so far in Prejudice of the Collieries lying on the said last mentioned Canals, as, in Effect, to exclude them from a Competition in the Severn Market with the Collieries on the said Birmingham Canal; and that, at a subsequent Meeting of the said Commissioners, holden on the 19th Day of March 1782, pursuant to public Advertisement, an Order or Proposal having been laid before them by the said Staffordshire and JWorcestershire Canal Company, to continue the said Reduction of Tonnage upon Coals navigated on their said Canal, within the Distance specified in their former Order, the Commissioners assembled at such Meeting, after having duly weighed and considered the same, did, by a Resolution or Declaration in Writing, signify their Dissent thereto, and reject the same accordingly, which said Resolution or Declaration was signed by Fifty-four Commissioners, being a very large Majority of the Commissioners present at such Meeting; and that, in Consequence of such last mentioned Resolution of the said Commissioners, the Tonnage upon Coals navigated on the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal l*ath ever since remained upon the Footing the same Voi~ 40.

was originally placed by the Legislature, and the dif- Staffordshire ferent Collieries which send Coals down the said Staff- &c* Canal. fordshire and Worcestershire Canal have been enabled to bring the ir* Coals to Market without Prejudice to each other, and the Public and the Petitioners have been benefited thereby; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented to the House by the said Company of Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable them, without the Interposition of Commissioners, to lower and regulate the Tonnage upon their Navigation, or upon any Part or Parts thereof, in such Manner as they should, from Time to Time, see necessary, and, if such Bill should pass into a Law, it would be in the Power of the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, by their own mere Act, and without the Interposition and Consent of the Commissioners, to lower the Tonnage partially on Coals sent down their said Canal from the Collieries lying on the said Birmingham Canal, so as totally to exclude and prevent Coals being sent from the Collieries lying on and near to the said Stourbridge and Dudley Canals,' which would entirely defeat the great Object in making the said Canals, and the Public would be deprived of the Benefit of being supplied with Coals from the said last mentioned Collieries, and the Petitioners would be obliged to sit down and discontinue the working of their Mines, after having expended many Thousand Pounds in planting the same, without any Prospect of an adequate Return, and the said Comf-pany of Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestet'shire Canal might, as soon as they had shut up the Collieries on the said Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, independent of the Commissioners, raise thet Tonnage on the Coals sent from the Collieries on the said Birmingham Canal again to its full Denomination; and that the Petitioners submit to the House, that if the additional Tonnage of One Halfpenny a Ton per Mile, imposed on all Coals coming down the Stourbridge Canal, and navigated on the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, was taken off, and the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Company were to reduce and equalize their Tonnage on all Coals navigated on their Canal, between the Point of Junction of the Stourbridge Canal with the said Staffffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, and Stourport, where the said last mentioned Canal falls into the River Severn, all Coals, sent down the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal into the Severn Market, would partake of the Advantage of such Reduction, and the Public would be greatly benefited thereby: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to ' lie upon the Table, until the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation to lower and regulate thp Tonnage upon the said Canal, be read a Second Time: And the Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favpur of the said Bill, against the said Petitions.

Commercial A Petition of the Master Printers in Edinburgh, ntercourse whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented nth Ireland. to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that certain general Propositions, as a Foundation for new Regulations of the Commerce between Great Britain and Ireland, have been voted by the House of Commons in Ireland, and are now under the Consideration of the British Parliament, and, the Petitioners are apprehensive, if the same should pass into a Law in their present Form, the most injurious Consequences would ensue to their Trade and Manufacture; that one of the principal Branches of their Business consists in reprinting Books after the Time limited to Copy Right by the Statute of Queen Anne is expired; these are all printed on British Paper, which pays a Duty of no less than about 23 pei' Cent, and this Duty, when the Paper is exported to Ireland, is drawn back, by which Means the Printers in Ireland are furnished with this Article 23 per Cent, below what is paid for the same by the Printers of this Country, and consequently, as the Price of Labour and Provisions is lower in Ireland than here, they can supply the Market with printed Books proportionably cheaper than the Printers of this Country; that formerly this was of little Consequence to the Printers here, as Books originally published in Great Britain were prohibited from coming to this Country from Ireland after being re-printed there, under severe Penalties; if, however, the Resolutions of the Irish Parliament are adopted, in their present Form, the Case will be materially altered, the Printers in Ireland, being then under no Restraint, will: not only be enabled to undersell the Printers of this

Country in a Foreign Market, but even at Home, to the

freat Detriment of their Trade and Business, as well as tuin of a numerous Body of Journeymen and their Families: And therefore praying the House to take the , Premises into their most serious Consideration, and to

- grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall

seem meet.

Wool- Ordered, That Sir George Howard do make the Re-

combing. port from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Manufacturers of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the several Counties of Northampton, Huntingdon, Cambridge, and the Isle of Ely, Bedford, Leicester, and Rutland; and also, the Petition of the Manufacturers of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the County of Lincoln, were severally referred.

Sir George Howard accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. Robat Godby being examined, said, That the Yams spun in the Counties of Northampton, Huntingdon, Isle of Ely, Bedford, Leicester, and Rutland, have greatly decreased in their Value, owing to the fraudulent Reeling thereof, and that in consequence of the Preference given to Yams of other Counties, where Regulations have taken place under Acts of Parliament, passed for that Purpose, their Trade is in a declining State for Want of proper Regulations. — And the Witness added, that he has had a large Quantity of Yarns returned to him for being short Reeled.

Then, to prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Samuel Coddington being examined, said, That the Yarns spun in the County of Lincoln have greatly decreased in their Value, owing to the Want of proper Regulations to prevent the fraudulent Reeling thereof, by which Persons dealing therein chuse to purchase their Yarn in Places where they are under Regulations established by Act of Parliament. — And being further examined, he said, that he has been obliged to submit to Drawbacks after he has sold his Yarns, by Reason of the short Reeling thereof, and that Persons dealing therein have been much aggrieved by false Reeling. — And he added, that he apprehends, that if the Reeling the Yarns was put under proper Regulations, it would be of great Advantage to Trade, and to the Public.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for more effectually preventing Frauds and Abuses committed by Persons employed in the Manufactures of Combing Wool, Worsted Yam, and Goods made from Worsted, in the Counties of Bedford, Huntingdon, Northampton, Leicester, Rutland, and Lincoln, and in the Isle of Ely: And that Sir George Howard, Sir John Thorold, and Mr. Lancelot Brown, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Ironmasters, and others concerned in the making of Iron in Great Britain, and of the Manufacturers of Iron in the several Counties of Salop, Worcester, Stafford, and Warwick, met together at their Quarterly Meeting at Stourbridge, the 8th of April 1785, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Plan for a more familiar Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland is now under Consideration, and that certain Resolutions on this Subject have already passed the Houses of Lords and Commons in that Kingdom; and that the Petitioners have the most alarming Apprehensions, that these Resolutions of the Irish Parliament would, if adopted here, be attended with very ruinous Consequences to the making and manufacturing of Iron in this Kingdom; and, that in settling a Commercial Treaty with Ireland, the Petitioners apprehend, the principal Regulations ought to be an entire Abolition of Duties on Articles the Growth, Product, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom, when imported into the other, or, if Duties were thought necessary, that they should be laid ad Valorem on all Articles the Growth, Product, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom, when imported into the other, and that the Duties on all Articles used in Manufactures, when imported from Foreign States, into either Kingdom, should be precisely the same; and that, at the same Time the Petitioners make these Representations, they hope the House will excuse the Liberty they take of giving their Opinion, that an Union between Great Britain and Ireland, on a liberal Plan, would be attended with far more beneficial Consequences than any Commercial Arrangement, for, they apprehend, nothing short of this will remove Jealousies respecting Trade and Manufactures, and cement the Two Nations together in indissoluble Friendship, and, in the present State of the Business, the Petitioners see so many Difficulties, that they think it indispensably necessary, that more Time should be allowed for mature Consideration: And therefore

praying, That the House will not come to any final Resolution respecting the more familiar Intercourse between this Kingdom and Ireland, till next Session of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said . Petition be referred. to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Then a Petition of the Honourable General James Murray, late Captain General and Governor in Chief of the Island of Minorca, and Vice Admiral of the same, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioner, during his exercising the said Offices in the Island of Minorca, judged it expedient, for the Good of His Majesty’s Service, to suspend James Sutherland, Esquire, Judge of the Vice Admiralty Court there, until His Majesty’s Pleasure should be known, and, having signified to the King’s Ministers his having so done, they were pleased to continue the said Suspension for a considerable Length of Time, and to refuse to suffer the said James Sutherland, Esquire, to return to the said Island, to exercise the said Office, without his consenting to make a public Submission to the Petitioner, and the Petitioner agreeing to receive the same; notwithstanding which, the said James Sutherland brought an Action for Damages against the Pe* titioner, for having so suspended him, and obtained a Verdict against the Petitioner, for £ 5,000, which the Petitioner has paid, together with the Costs, and other Charges, amounting to £5,536. 5 & 3 d.; and that His Majesty having been graciously pleased to take the Petitioner’s Case into Consideration, and accept his Prayer for Relief, the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury did, on the 15th of December 1783, make a Minute, directing that the Amount of tho Judgment, and the Petitioner’s legal Costs, in Consequence of the said Verdict, should be ascertained, and that they would then issue Money for the Discharge thereof; and, that the Petitioner not having hitherto received the said Sum, and finding that he cannot have such Relief without the Aid and Assistance of the House, therefore prays the House to grant him such Relief, and that the said Sum of £ 5,000, and the Costs, paid by him to the said James Sutherland\ and the Petitioner’s own Costs in the said Action, together with his other subsequent Expences incident thereto, may be repaid to him.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Dempster, Mr. Sheridan,

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

Mr. Harrison reported from the Committee, to whom Beverley, ac. the Petition of Sir Henry Etherington, Baronet, Joseph Drains Robinson Pease, Esquire, and of the several Persons *

whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Pro* prietors of Lands in Woodmansey, Thearn, Beverley,

Beverley 'Parks, Figham, Skidby Carr, and Skidby Ings, all in the Parishes of Saint John in Beverley, and Skidby, in the East Riding of the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Bills of Drainage, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Joseph Dickenson being examined, said. That within the said several Townships and Places mentioned in the Petition, there are divers large Tracts of Ground, which are subject to be Overflowed during a considerable Part of the Year — That they are capable of being drained, and would thereby be greatly improved — That he is an Engineer, had surveyed the Whole of the Lands, and that an Outfall may be easily made into the River Hull, contiguous to which they lie.

And being further examined, he produced to your Committee an Estimate of the Expence of the proposed Drainage, by which it appeared, that the first Cost of the main Drain will be about £. 2,500, andt together with other requisite Expenditures, will be discharged by a Payment of about Two Pounds per Acre, the Lands to be drained amounting to 1,500 Acres — That the Expence of keeping open the Drainage, and other Charges of the Commissioners, will amount to about 100 per Annum — That some of the Land is now worth but little or nothing, and that the Improvement is estimated to he from Five to Fifteen Shillings per Acre, when drained.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for draining, preserving, and improving certain Low Grounds and Carrs, in the several Parishes of Saint John in Beverley, and of Skidby, in the East Riding of the County of York: And that Mr. Harrison, Sir John Thorold, Mr. Long, and Mr. Buncombe, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Henry Bagshaw Harrison being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the Act, and have borrowed a considerable Sura of Money, which has been laid out according to the Directions of the said Act — That the Sum of^£. 1,876 now remains due, which Money cannot be repaid, nor the Roads kept in proper Repair, unless the Term granted by the said Act is further continued, and the Powers thereof altered and enlarged.
