A, PETITION of the Commissioners appointed . by, and for putting in Execution, an Act of Parliament made for improving and completing the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and Isis, from the City of London to the Town of Cricldade, in the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to join and communicate with the Line of the Thames and Severn Canal, in the Parish of Kemp ford, in the County of Gloucester; and Setting forth, That the said Canal will be a Diversion not only of the ancient and natural Course of Navigation from Leach-lade to Abingdon, by the River Isis, but of the Trade and Business carried on between those Places by Means of the said Navigation, and will, in its Consequences, deprive the Whole of the River Navigation of a considerable Stream of Water, and be otherwise injurious to the same; and that an Act passed in the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, to improve and complete the Navigation of the said Rivers from London to Cricldade, in the County of Wilts, and the said River Thames has been considerably improved and amended from London to Mapledurham, in the County of Oxford; and, that when the Amendments and Improvements are carried throughout the remaining Course of the said Rivers Thames and Isis, agreeably to the Intention of that Act, the said Navigation from Leachlade to Abingdon will, in the Opinion of able and experienced Surveyors, be rendered safe, cheap, and easy, by the Expenditure of a Sum of Money considerably less than the Expence of making and completing such Navigable Canal: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by jthemselves or 3 Counsel,

Sir George Howard presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for more effectually preventing Frauds and Abases committed by Persons employed in the Manufactures of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the Counties of Bedford, Huntingdon, Northampton, Leicester, Rutland, and Lincoln, and the Isle of Ely: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Lord George Cavendish presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for dividing and inclosing the Commons, Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, Commonable Lands, and Waste Grounds, within the Liberty of Holbrooke, in the Parish of Duffield, in the County of Derby: And the same was received; and lead the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Lord George Cavendish presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " widening and repairing the Road leading from Ashborne, in the County of Derby, over Belpar Bridge, " to the present Turnpike Road from Sheffield and " Chesterfield to Dei'by, at or near a Place called Openwood Gate, and from Belpar Bridge to Ripley, in the County of Derby:' And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

An ingrossed Bill for continuing the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acts, of the Second and Ninth Years of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Roads from The White Post, on Haseldens Wood, in the Parish of Cranbrooke, to Appledore Heath, and from Milkhouse Street, in the same Parish, to Castlederis Oak, in the Parish of Bid-denden, and from the Turnpike Road, in the Parish of Tenterden, through Rolvenden, to the Turnpike Road, in the Parish of Newenden, in the County of Kent, was read the Third Time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, declaring, that no Person shall pay more than One Toll in a Day.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for continuing the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acts, of the Second and Ninth Years of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Roads from The White Post, on Haselderis Wood, in the Parish of Cranbrooke, to Appledore Heath, and from Milkhouse Street, in the same Parish, to Castledens Oak, in the Parish of Biddenden, and from the Turnpike Road, in the Parish of Tenterden, through Rolvenden, to the Turnpike Road, in the Parish of Newenden, in the County of Kent.

Ordered, That Mr. Marsham do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Ordered, That Mr. Holdsworth have Leave to go into the Country for Three Weeks, on his private Affairs.

Ordered, That Mr. Penruddocke have Leave to go into the Country for a Fortnight, on his private Aflairs. '

A Petition of the several Merchants, Factors, and Corn and others, concerned in the Importation and Exportation, Grain-and in the manufacturing, of Corn and Grain, within the Town and Port of Southampton, and the Creeks thereto belonging, whose Names are thereunder subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, An Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for further regulating and ascertaining the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain within several Ports " and Places therein mentioned," and for extending the Powers and Provisions thereof to all Places within that Part of Great Britain called England; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe with Concern, that, by certain Clauses in such Bill, the Powers delegated to Grand Juries, at the Quarter Sessions of their respective Counties, by divers Acts of Parliament, to enquire and present, on their Oaths, the Prices of English Corn and Grain, in order to regulate the Importation of Foreign Grain, are to be totally annihilated, and that, instead thereof, a new System is intended to be substituted, by vesting in a, single Individual, in the City of London, a Power to inspect the Weekly Returns of the Co nfactors at Mark Lane (by many of whom he is to be elected and maintained) and to compute and form, from thence, the Average Prices, which being laid before the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Justices of the Peace, at their Quarter Sessions, and afterwards published in the Gazette, are to be deemed (without the least Respect to the Difference and Fluctuation of the Average Prices in any other Part of the Nation) the general Average Prices of this Kingdom, and the Importation and Exportation of Com

2$ Geo. III. 2a0

and Grain, as well at London as at every Out Port, are to be accordingly governed thereby; and that, the Petitioners apprehend, if such Clauses should pass into a Law, the most grievous Injuries and Distress would result therefrom to many Thousands of His Majesty’s Subjects, and it would open a Door to Monopoly, Partiality, and Inconvenience: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the Clauses above-mentioned from passing into a Law; or permit the Petitioners to be heard, by their Counsel, if the Nature of their Case shall require the same.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Menai Bridge in Road towards Ireland.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders, and Owners and Masters of Ships, of the Port of Saint Ives> was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appears, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Bridge or Embankment over an Arm of the Sea, between the Counties of Carnarvon and Anglesey, called The Sir eights of Menai, at a Place near Port ha-et/m-y or Bangor Perry, called Ynysgeint: And Alledging, That the free Navigation of The Streights of Menai is an Object of public Importance, the said Streights being navigable throughout for Ships of large Burthen, frequented by some Thousand Sail in the Year, and in particular by many Vessels, which on certain Winds, have a secure and speedy Passage there, when they could not otherwise proceed to their Destinations; and that the making a Bridge or Embankment as aforesaid will very materially injure, if not totally ruin, the Navigation of the said Streights, and thereby be detrimental to the Trade and Commerce, Maritime Strength, and Revenue of this Nation, and to the Interests of the Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying, That the Bill for making a Bridge or Embankment as aforesaid may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Noblemeu, and the humble Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and others, of the County of Anglesey, and of other Parts of Great Britain, and also of the Kingdom of Ireland, is referred.

District in particular, if a Branch of Road was made from or near the Filth Mile Stone, on the present Turnpike Road leading from Swansea to Rosilly, over Fairwoods Common, to the Opening of the Rond leading to Kilvrough, by the Smith’s Shop, through Part of the Parishes of Bishopston, Penardand I Is ton; and that, as far as the Petitioners are concerned in the said Tolls, they think it would tend to improve them, and accommodate a large Part of the Country: And therefore praying, That the said Branch of Road may be inserted in the Bill for regulating the Turnpike Roads through the County of Glamorgan.

Stafford\ to Atherstone, in the County of Warwick, with several short Cuts branching therefrom; and the Petitioners also find, that a Bill is depending in the House, for enabling the several Companies of Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, and from Birmingham to Fazeley, to make a Navigable Canal from The Trent and Mersey Navigation, on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County; and submitting to the House, that, if such Application for making navigable the said Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, with the said several Cuts therefrom, should meet with the Sanction of Parliament, it will render the Completion of the intended Coventry Canal from Atherstone to Fazeley unnecessary, and every Communication intended thereby, and also, by the said intended Bill for making a Navigable Canal from Fradley Heath to Fazeley aforesaid, will be effected, and at a much less Expence, with the Advantage of larger Boats, with greater Accommodation for the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize, as well with respect to an easier Tonnage and Freight, as to greater Safety and Dispatch, and unattended with the Loss of a large Quantity of rich and valuable Land, and without the Inconvenience of the Separation of Property, which must necessarily arise from the making a new Canal: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and that when such Bill for making navigable the Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, shall be presented, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition, the same may pass into a Law.

Setting forth, That the Property of the Petitioners, comprized in the above-mentioned Acts, is various and different, some consisting of Buildings, some of Land, and others of both Buildings and Land; and, the Petitioners severally suffered great Damage in their respective Properties by the Restrictions contained in the first-mentioned Act, to various and different Amounts, according to the Circumstances of their respective Cases; and that by a Clause in the said Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for reimbursing the Proprietors of the above-mentioned Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, the Damages suffered by them in consequence of the Restrictions contained in the said Act of the Twenty-second Year of His present Majesty (which last Act is repealed by the said Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty) the awarding such Damages is referred to the sole Consideration of the Commissioners for putting the last mentioned Act into Execution, or any Five or more of them, widiout the Medium or Inquest of a Jury; and that the Petitioners severally attended the said Commissioners at their Meeting, held under the said Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty, according to the Directions of the said Act, and proved their respective Cases, and the Damages severally sustained by them in consequence of the Restrictions contained in the said Act of the Twenty-second Year of His present Majesty, but the said Commissioners awarded them no Damages; and that the Clause in the above-mentioned Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, referring the Damages suffered by the Proprietors to the sole Consideration of the Commissioners, without the Interference of a Jury, provides that the Award of the said Commissioners shall not he final, unless the 7 1 sams

Com and A Petition of the Merchants concerned in the Cram. Corn Trade, of the Town and Port of Great Yarmouth, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for further regulating " and ascertaining the Importation and Exportation " of Corn and Grain within several Ports and Places " therein mentioned," and for extending the Powers and Provisions thereof to all Places within that Part of Great Britain called England; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are convinced, the said Bill has been framed evidently with a View to create a Monopoly of the Com Trade in Favour of the Cornfactors of London, to the Prejudice of the Landed Interest of the Kingdom in general, especially of the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, to the great Injury of the Corn Trade in the Out Ports of different Counties, and particularly to that of the Town and Port of Great Yarmouth: And therefore praying, That the same may not be passed into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the several dangerous and partial Regulations contained in the said Bill.

Ditto* A Petition of the several Merchants, and others,

concerned in the Importation and Exportation, and in the Manufacturing, of Corn and Grain, within the County of Southampton, and the Creeks thereto belonging, whose Names are thereunder subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice' of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe with Concern, that, by Voi. 40.

certain Clauses in such Bill, the Powers delegated to Grand Juries, at the Quarter Sessions of their respective Counties, by divers Acts of Parliament, to enquire and present, on their Oaths, the Prices of English Cora and Grain, in order to regulate the Importation of Foreign Grain, are to be totally annihilated, and that, instead thereof, a new System is, intended to be substituted, by vesting in a single Individual, in the City of London, a Power to inspect the Weekly Returns of the Corn Factors at Mark Lane (by many of whom he is to be elected and maintained) and to compute, and form, from thence, the Average Prices, which being laid before the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Justices of the Peace, at their Quarter Sessions, and afterwards published in the Gazette, are to be deemed (without the least Respect to the Difference and Fluctuation of the Average Prices in any other Part of the Nation) the general Average Prices of this Kingdom, and the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain, a3 well at London as at every Out Port, are to be accordingly governed thereby; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if such Clauses should pass into a Law, the most grievous Injuries and Distress would result therefrom to many Thousands of His Majesty’s Subjects, and it would open a Door to Monopoly, Partiality, and Inconvenience: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the said Bill from passing into a Law; or permit the Petitioners to be heard, by their Counsel, if the Nature of their Case shall require the same.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Manufacturers ^and Inhabitants commercial of the City of Coventry, and the adjacent Manufac- intercourse, turing Parishes, was presented to the House, and with Ireland, read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are greatly alarmed at the Resolutions brought before the House, respecting the Commercial Regulations now depending betwixt Great Britain and Ireland, which, if carried into Effect, vrill be very injurious to the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, and more particularly to the Manufacture of Ribbands carried on in the City and Neighbourhood of Coventry, and that the Duty on Raw and Thrown Silks, imported into Great Britain, is much higher than in Ireland, and, the Petitioners having been informed, that it is not intended to equalize the Duty, by subjecting the Irish to the same Duty on the Importation of Silk as is paid in Great Britain, but by laying a Duty on Irish manufactured Goods when imported into this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners have no Doubt that this Mode of equalizing the Duties will be very injurious to the Silk Manufactures of Great Britain, as it will give great Encouragement to Smuggling; the equalizing Duty, added to the Protecting and Excise Duties, amounting to a very large Proportion of the Value, and Silk Goods, especially the Article of Ribbands, being more peculiarly exposed to Smuggling, on account of their small Bulk, in Proportion to their Value; and that the Duties on the Materials

Mr. Wyndham Grenville reported from the Committee who were appointed to search the Journals of this House, touching the Usage of the House in Cases of Reports of Committees of Privileges or Elections, respecting the Conduct of Returning Officers, and to report the same to the House; That the Committee had examined the Matters referred to them, and bad searched Precedents for that Purpose; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee appointed to search the Journals of this House, touching the Usage of the House in Cases of Reports of Committees of Privileges or Elections, respecting the Conduct of Returning Officers,

Having, in Obedience to the Commands of the House, carefully examined the Journals with respect to the Matter referred to them, beg Leave to report* That they have found a great Variety of Cases relating thereto; but, as they conceive that these differ from each other in several very essential Points, they have thought it their Duty to state to the House the Substance of each, referring to the Journals themselves for the whole Proceedings at large, which could not have been here inserted without swelling this Report to an unreasonable Size. They have also thought it right to class them under such general Heads as might, in their Opinion, tend to give a clearer View , of the Subject; observing, however, with respect to this Arrangement, that in many of the earlier Cases it is Matter of much Difficulty and Doubt, because the whole Pro^ ceedings were not at that Time entered on the Journals, but only such Notes and Abstracts of them as were made by the Clerk.

And, a a the Order of this Arrangement depends on the different Forms in which Reports have been made to the House from the Committees of Privileges and Elections, they think it right, in the First Instance, to state, that the earliest Entry which they find on the Journals, of the Appointment of any suck General Committee, occurs In the Proceedings of the 2 2d of March 1603; though there is Reason to believe that the Practice began somewhat earlier. The Committee then appointed, was a Select Committee for Matters of Privileges and Elections, consisting only of particular Members named by the House. And Ibis Mode of Appointment was continued till 1673, when an Order was made (October 30th) That all who came should have Voices; which Order has since that Time always been adopted.

Your Committee now proceed to state the different Cases upon your Journals, under the following general Heads:

I". Cases where the House has proceeded against Returning Officers, on Reports from Committees, containing Resolutions respecting only the Merits of the Return or Right of Election, unaccompanied by any other Matter.

II\ Cases where the House has proceeded against Returning Officers, on Reports from Committees, containing Resolutions eliminating the Returning Officer, but unaccompanied by any State of the Case, or of the Evidence produced before them.

IIP. Cases where the House has proceeded against Returning Officers, on Reports from Committees, containing Resolutions respecting only the 10 R Retort*

Wycombe, May 5th, 1660. Report received respecting the Double Return, with the Resolutions of the Committee thereon. — The Mayor ordered to attend to amend the Return. — May 9th, The Mayor amends’ the Return, and the House resolve, 44 That the Mayor be committed to the Serjeant at Arms, 44 until further Order, for his Abuse in making a false Return."

East Loo, May 5th, 1660. Report received, That the Mayor had made a Double Return, and that none of the Persons so returned ought to sit till the Merits were determined. — House resolve, 44 That the Mayor be summoned to appear at the Bar of the House, to answer his Misdemeanor in making an insufficient Return of Members; and that he bear the Charge of the Summons." — May 26th, A Petition from the Mayor read, and the House resolved, " That the Mayor be discharged from his further Attendance, 44 he paying the Charge of the Summons."

Having thus reported the Substance of the different Cases in which the House have proceeded against Returning Officers on the Ground of Reports from Committees of Privileges or Elections, your Committee proceed to state Instances which they have found on the Journals, of a contrary Nature. Of these, your Committee have found only Four, which are as follow:

Grimsby, May .5th, 1675. Committee report the State of the Case, and Two Resolutions; 1st, That Sir Christopher Wj'ay is duly elected; 2d, That the Sheriff of Lincolnshire be sent for in Custody for making

an undue Return.---- On Question, the House agreed

to the First, and disagreed to the Second, of these Resolutions.

Southwark, February 7th, 1711. Report received, containing Three Resolutions; 1st, That the Bailiff could not, under the Circumstances there stated, proceed to a Scrutiny; 2d, That Edmund Halsey not duly elected; 3d, That Sir George Matthews duly elected; — and, stating the whole Case and Evidence

produced to the Committee.---- The House agree to

the Three Resolutions, and then resolve, " That the " Bailiff was guilty of arbitrary and illegal Proceedings, in Breach of the Privilege of the House, " and tending to the Subversion of the Freedom of " Election." — Ordered, " That the said Bailiff be, " for his said Offence, taken into Custody of the Serjeant at Arms."

Arundel, Februwy 22d, 1693. Committee report the Evidence and Three Resolutions; 1st, Respecting the Right of Election; 2d, Lord Waulen not duly elected; 3d, Mr. Cook duly elected. — House agree — Motion being made to send for the Mayor in Custody, it passed in the Negative.

Bedford, April 16th, 1728. Committee report the Case and Evidence with Four Resolutions, respecting 10 S the

§94 2 5° —

the Merits of the Election; to which the House agreed. It was then moved, That the Mayor, by not returning Mr. Metcalfe, was guilty of a manifest Violation of the Laws, and Breach of Privilege — The< House divided, and it passed in the Negative.

Your Committee think it proper to add, That there are a great variety of Cases on the Journals, where the House have not proceeded against Returning Officers, when Committees have reported against the Return, and even when they have accompanied their Report with Evidence which appears to affect the Returning Officer; but your Committee conceived it to be as useless, as it would have been difficult, for them to have enumerated every such Case, as an Attempt of that Nature would have required an In-' vestigation of the Whole of the Evidence reported on > each Case.

Your Committee have found, That on the nth of January 1694, a Select Committee was appointed by the House, "to inspect Precedents;" what Censures have " been inflicted upon Officers making false Rer " turns, and to report the same." And that on the 6th of Febrtmy following the y made a Report, containing only the Case of York above reported. They were then directed to examine further; and in the next Session a similar Committee was appointed, but it does not appear that any further Report was made.

Your Committee having now stated to the House, the Whole of what they have been able to discover on the Subject referred to them, have only to request the Indulgence of the House for any Omissions which may have been made in the Course of so extensive a Research into a Subject, dispersed over every Part of the voluminous Records of the House.

Ordered', Jhat suCha Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr, Speaker, and One hundred and Twenty-two Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses; and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Six Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Right honourable William Wyndham, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioners; and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Thirty-two other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of John Parry, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Sitting Members; and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Eleven other Members, then present, w>ere drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That, in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Seventeen other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Three, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Three, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; and Eleven, on Account of their having already, in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete;

Lists of the said Names tfere delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

A Petition of the several Proprietors of the Oxford Canal Navigation, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from rITie Trent to The Mersey, and the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from Birmingham to Fazeley, to make a Navigable Canal from the said Trent and Mersey Navigation, on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford\ to Fazeley, in the said County, and to amend an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making a Navigable Canal from The Trent to The Mersey; and Setting forth, That the said Bill hath been applied for, by the Company of Proprietors of The Trent and Mersey Navigation, in Conformity to Articles of Agreement entered into between that Company, the Company of Proprietors of the Oxford Navigation, and the Company of Proprietors of the Coventry Navigation, and it appears to the Petitioners indispensably necessary, for the Completion of the Plan intended, by the said Articles of Agreement, to be carried into Execution, that all the contracting Parties should be bound, by the Authority of Parliament, to fulfil the Engagements they have, by the said Articles, pledged themselves to perform: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass, and that the Powers and Provisions thereof may be sufficiently extensive to bind all the Parties who have agreed to the carrying into Execution the very useful Plan thereby meant to be completed, to perform their respective Undertakings, and that, if necessary, they may be authorized and impowered so to do.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition.

A Petition of Owners of Shipping employed in His Majesty’s Service, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, during the late War, supplied His Majesty's Navy and Victualling Boards with Ships, for Transports and Victuallers upon Freight, for which they received Navy and Victualling Bills, the Amount whereof was usually paid them in Cash, by the Treasurer of the Navy, within Two Years of the Date of their Bills, from which Circumstance the Petitioners were able to form an Idea of their Value, and to govern themselves thereby in making future Contracts, and the Petitioners (from this regular Mode of Payment) had it in their Power to raise Sums of Money on the Credit of their Navy Bills, by paying a moderate Discount to Brokers, and other Persons, w ho make it their Business to purchase such Bills; and that the Petitioners have been at a great Expence in fitting their Ships for long

and dangerous Voyages; at et Time when Naval Stores were excessive high, and are now also obliged to advance large Sums of Money, from Time to Time, in defraying Seamen's Wages and paying Tradesmen’s Bills, which, together with the Lass of Employ for their Ships since the Peace, has reduced their Value near Fifty per Cent. and is now become a Matter truly alarming to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners find themselves very much distressed in not. being able to raise Money on the Credit of their Navy Bills, without paying the enormous Discount of Ten oi\ Twelve per Cent. more than they bad Reason to imagine at the Time they contracted with His Majesty's Boards, which Contracts were accepted by the Petitioners at low Rates of Freight, on a Supposition, and under a firm Belief, that their Navy Bills would be regularly paid as usual, which not being the Case, the Petitioners feel themselves greatly injured by having to pay the above heavy Discount, owing entirely to the Uncertainty of the Time when such last mentioned Bills will be paid off, some of Which have already run near Three Years, and, as the Petitioners cannot receive either the Principal or Interest, they have often been obliged to sell some of their Bills, subject to such Discount, in order to raise Money for their Necessities, and (the Purchasers, well knowing their Distresses, take an Advantage of the Times, and become Gainers by the Purchase of those Navy Bills at the same Time) that the Petitioners become Losers by their Contracts, in Consequence thereof; and that the Petitioners have ever been ready to risque their Property for His Majesty's Service, and (finding the Profit of their Trade, by unforeseen Events, falling into the Hands of others, who have had neither Trouble or Risque) are reduced to tl» Necessity of applying to the House for Redress: And therefore praying, That the House will take their great Losses into Consideration, and order those Navy and Victualling Bills to be paid off, or grant the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several of the Inhabitants and Land Richmond Owners of the Town of Brentford\ in the Parish of Poor* Great Ealing, and Parts adjacent thereto, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to repeal Part of an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty, for the Relief and Employment of the Poor of the Parish of Richmond\ in the County of Surrey, and for other Purposes in the said Act mentioned, and for making new Provisions for the Relief and Employment of the Poor, for the Repairs of the Highways, the paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets, and other Places, in the Town and Parish of Richmond aforesaid, and for the Removal and Prevention of Annoyances, Obstructions, and Incroachments therein; and Setting forth, That* by the said Bill, it is proposed to shut up a Lane* called Love Lane, leading from the North End of the Town of Richmond to the Hamlet of Kew, which, the Petitioners conceive, will be a manifest Prejudice to tbs Town of Brentford, and Parish of Great Ealing, and Parts adjacent, by diverting the Trade from the Market of the said Town of Brentjord; and that the Footway, through the said, Lane, to the said Town of Brentford, is almost solely used by Persons concerned in Trade and Traffick having Occasion to resort to the Town of Brentford, the Inhabitants whereof are chiefly dependent on their respective Trades for Support, and w here the Produce of the Parish of Ealing, and Parts adjacent, are usually brought to Market; and that the Petitioners, so far from considering the said Footway dangerous, do generally use the same, both in the Day Time and in the Evening, as being, in their Opinion, and from Experience, safer than any other, no Robbery, or other Molestation, having happened there for many Years past, and the Convenience of crossing the Water desirable, from the Ease and Convenience thereof, particularly to Persons carrying Burthens; and that the Petitioners would chearfully relinquish their Right of Way in a Case where Pleasure only would result to them from the Use thereof, but, on the present Occasion, the Trade of the Town of Brentford, and the Sale of the Produce of the Parish of Ealing, and Parts adjacent, is likely to be very materially injured, by the Intercourse being cut oft; which the present Footway encourages with the Town of Richmond, and Parts adjacent thereto: And therefore praying, That the House will take the same into their serious Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be heard by themselves or their Counsel, against that Part of the said Bill; and that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee; That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

The House resumed the Consideration of the Amendments made by the Lords to the Bill, intituled, An Act for appointing Commissioners to enquire into the Fees, Gratuities, Perquisites, and Emoluments, which are, or have been lately, received in the several Public Offices therein mentioned, to examine into any Abuses which may exist in the same, and to report such Observations as shall occur to them for the better conducting and managing, the Business transacted in the said Offices.

Ordered, That Mr. Rose do carry the Bill to the Lords, and acquaint them, that this House hath agreed to the Amendments made by their Lordships to the said Bill, with several Amendments to One of them; to which Amendments this House doth desire the Concurrence of their Lordships.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the Jurisdiction of the Court of Admiralty, which, before the Treaty of Union between the Two Kingdoms, was stiled, " The High Court of Admiralty " of Scotland" and for discharging and abolishing the Payment of Fees and Perquisites to the Judge of the said Court; and for the Punishment of Persons destroying Ships: And that the Lord Advocate of Scotland and the Marquis of Graham do prepare, and bring in, the same.

And the said Motion was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into Elections — a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for County the better securing the Rights of Voters at County Voters-Elections.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Robert Smith took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Robert Smith reported’ from the Committee,

That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Robert Smith accordingly reported from the Said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place: and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerks Table: Where the Report was read.

And it appearing, that, from the many Alterations made in the said Bill, it would be more convenient for the House, that the said Bill should be withdrawn, and another Bill presented instead thereof;

Ordered, That Leave be given to withdraw the said Bill, and present another Bill instead thereof.

Ordered, That the Lord Mahon, Mr. Robert Smith,

Mr. Buncombe, and Mr. Wilberforce, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven- Elections — night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, Bribery and upon the Bill to explain, amend, and reduce into One Expence. Act of Parliament, all the Laws now in being for preventing Bribery and Expence in Election of Members to serve in Parliament.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Abingdon A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and Free-

Navigation. holders of the Town and Neighbourhood of Stroud, in the County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is depending, for enabling certain Persons to make a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to join and communicate with the Thames and Severn Canal, at some Place at or near Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester, which Canal, if executed, will not only prove a great National Benefit, but also be of particular Advantage to the Petitioners: A*nd therefore praying the House to permit the same to pass into a Law.

Ditto. A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are

thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, and believe, that, by a Paper annexed to a Petition to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to communicate with the Thames and Severn Canal, in the Parish of Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester, it is stated, that the Petitioners were neuter to the Plan of making such Canal; and Representing to the House, that they, or any of them, are not, not ever were, neuter to the said Plan, but have always been much averse to the same, and always declared their Disapprobation thereof in the fullest Terms, because they apprehended that such Canal would be a very great Injury to their Estates, which will be cut through, and intersected, in making the same, and, that the said Canal will be of no material Advantage to the Country in general: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as may seem meet; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by Counsel, upon the Matters here stated.

l)itto. A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are

thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed, by the Votes, that Leave hath been given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to join

and communicate with the Line of the Thames and Sevan Canal, in the Parish of Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester; and Alledging, that the Petitioners are Owners and Proprietors of several Mills upon the said River, between Abingdon and Leachlade, and, if the said Canal is permitted to be made, the same must wholly, or in a great Measure, be supplied with Water from the said River, which will deprive the Petitioners of the Benefit of the said Water for working their Mills, which, in dry Seasons, will be a very great Loss and Inconvenience to the Petitioners, as it will many Times render them incapable of carrying on their Businesses, and at others greatly retard and hinder the same: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as shall appear just and reasonable;

and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, in Opposition to the said Bill.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Abingdon thereunder subscribed, was also presented to the House, Navigation, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed by the Votes, that Leave hath been given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to join and communicate with the Line of the Thames and Severn Canal, in the Parish of Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester, which Canal will be a Diversion of the ancient and natural Course of Navigation From Leachlade to Abingdon, by the said River Thames and Isis, and of the Trade and Business carried on . between those Places; and Alledging, that the Petitioners are Owners and Proprietors of several Locks,

Weirs, and Pounds, upon the said River, bfctweeii Leachlade and Abingdon, to which all Boats and Barges passing through the same pay certain Rates and Duties, and, if' the said Canal is permitted to take Place, all the Boats and Barges, navigating between Leachlade and Abingdon, will pass down the said Canal, and not along the said River Navigation, whereby the Petitioners will lose all the Rates and Duties payable at their said Locks, Weirs, and Pounds:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Considerations, and grant them such Compensation for the said Rates and Duties payable at their said Locks, Weirs, and Pounds, and such other Relief as shall appear just and reasonable; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, upon the Matters here stated.

A Petition of Charles Long, Esquire, was also pre- Ditto, sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is informed, and believes, that, by a Paper annexed to a Petition to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to communicate with the Thames and Severn Canal, in the Parish of Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester, it is stated, that the Petitioner has assented to making such Canal; and Representing to the House, that his Assent to the said Bill was obtained by false Suggestions and Information given to him by the Promoters of the Bill, for that they represented to him in London, that Sir Robert Throckmorton, the Reverend Mr. Loder, and his Neighbours in general, bad consented to the Canal Scheme, whereas, when the Petitioner came into the Country, he found the Scheme opposed by the said Sir Robert Throckmorton and Mr. Loder, and reprobated by the Country in general, and the Petitioner is convinced of the Inutility of the same, and of the great Injury which will be done to his Estate by making it: Ahd therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to absolve him from his Consent obtained by the Means aforesaid, and grant him such further Relief as may seem meet; and that the Petitioner may be heard, by Counsel, upon the Matters here stated.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Ditto, thereunto subscribed, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, and believe, that, by a Paper annexed to a Petition to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Canal from the River Thames, or Isis, near Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to communicate with the Thames and Severn Canal, in the Parish of Kempsford, in the County of Gloucester., it is stated, that the Petitioners have assented to making such Canal; and Representing to the House, that the Petitioners, or any of them, never did, directly or indirectly, give their Consent to the making such Canal, but always have, in the fullest Manner, declared their Disapprobation thereof, because they believed, and still believe, the making such Canal to be

Road, whom the Petition of several Trustees for putting in Execution an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for amending the Road from Aylesbury, in the County of Buckingham, through Thame and Little Milton, to the Turnpike Road between Bensington and ShiOingjord, in the County of Oxford, and of several other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the'25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with* and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them* to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read. And,

Mr. Giles Prickett, Clerk and Treasurer to the Trustees, being examined, said, That a great Progress hath been made in repairing the Roads comprized in the said Act, in the doing of which, a considerable Sum of Money, borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls, hath been expended, and still remains charged thereon, and that the Money so borrowed cannot be paid off, and the Roads be completely amended and kept in Repair, unless the Term and Powers of the Act "be enlarged.

And being further examined, he said, That it would be of great public Advantage if Provision was made for amending the Road from the present Turnpike Road opposite Rook's Lane, through the liberties of New Thame, Old Thame, and Thame Parky the Liberty or Hamlet of Attwgton, and Liberty of Postcomb, to the Turnpike Road between Tetsworth\ and Postoomb, in the said County of Oxford.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twelve thousand and Eighty-seven Pounds Seven Shillings and Eight Pence Halfpenny, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the same, to make good the Deficiency on the 5th Day of July 1784, of the Fund established for paying Annuities granted by an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1758.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, ^hat a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Fifty-nine thousand Six hundred and Twenty Pounds One Shilling and Nine Pence Farthing, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the same, to make good the Deficiency on the 5th Day of July 1784, of the Fund established for paying Annuities granted by an Act, made in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1778.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Fifty-eight thousand Five hundred and Fifty-one Pounds Four Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the same, to make good the Deficiency on the 5th Day of July 1784, of the Fund established for paying Annuities granted by an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1780.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, the said Act of the Fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign was read. And,

A Member present informed the Committee, That a considerable Progress hath been made in amending the several Roads therein described; in the doing of which a large Debt had been contracted, which cannot be discharged, nor can the Roads be completely amended, and kept in Repair, unless the Term and Powers of the Act be enlarged. And that the several Pieces of Road alluded to in the said first-mentioned Petition are narrow, ruinous, and incommodious; and that it will be of public Utility to include the same within the Powers of the said Act.

To prove the Allegations of the Four last mentioned Petitions, Mr.. Thomas Thomas being examined, said, That the several Pieces of Road described in those Petitions are narrow and incommodious, and incapable of being properly amended, and kept in Repair, by the ordinary Course of Law; and that it will be a Convenience to the Public, and to the Neighbourhood, to extend the Powers of the said Act to these Roads also.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for amending, widening, and u keeping in Repair, several Roads leading from the " Town of Cardiff,\ and several other Towns and " Places, in the County of Glamorgan" and for altering, repairing, and widening certain other Roads within the said County: And that Sir Herbert Mack-worth and Mr. Edwin do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Commercial Dealers, in the City of Brechin, North Britain, was Intercourse presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, WIthIreland. That the Petitioners are very sensible of the many Ad-, vantages that might arise to Great Britain and Ireland from a permanent System of Intercourse and Commerce betwixt them, established on just and reciprocal Principles* but, so far as the Petitioners are able to form a Judgment of the System adopted by the Resolutions of the Irish House of Commons, they are fraught with Danger to the Manufactures, as well as the Landed Interest of this Kingdom, and in particular alarming with respect to the Linen Manufactures, which are the Staple Article in that Part of the Country; and the Petitioners apprehend, that in all Equity, if Ireland is to have an equal Share of all the Commercial Benefits of the Empire, she should take a proportional Share of all the Burthens: And therefore praying, That the House will not, in this ‘

Session, determine on this Subject, but will1 allow more Time for digesting and settling a Matter of so very great Importance to this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and L'eland.

Mr. Phelips reported from the Committee, to whom York the Petition of the Governor and Company of Under- Building takers for raising Thames Water in York Buildings, was referred; That the Committee had examined the " Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the Mouse; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act, passed in the Second and Third Years of King William and Queen Mary, was read; whereby it appeared, that the said Governor and Company were in*? corporated and enabled to purchase, enjoy, and alien Lands and Hereditaments, Goods and Chattels, and to do and execute all other Things by their Name of Incorporation that to them shall appertain, and to use a Common Seal; and the said Act appointed a Governor and Six of the said Company to be called Assistants, to have the Direction of all the Affairs of the said Company.

And it appeared that the said Company, in pursuance of the Power vested in them by the said Act, did, in the Year 1719, order a Subscription to be opened for raising a Stock of £1,200,000, to be laid out in the Purchase of Estates in Great Britain, to be a Fund for granting Annuities for Lives, and for assuring Lives for the Benefit of all the Subscribers to the said Joint Stock.

It further appeared, that the Sum of £308,093.14.7. was by the said Company invested in the Purchase of certain Estates in Scotland, of the Annual Value of £ 12,000, more or less, and in Northumberland, of the Annual Value of £ 2,684, more or less, which Estates were sold under the Authority and Directions of an Act of the Fourth of George the First, for Sale of the Forfeited Estates in Great Britain and Ireland: And, in pursuance of PoNVers vested in the Company by Two other Acts of the Sixth and Seventh Years of the said King’s Reign, in order to raise Money the better to enable them to make good their said Purchases, they granted Annuities for Lives, to the Amount of £ 12,000 per Annum, by Bonds to the Annuitants, and charged the said Company’s Lands in Scotland with the Payment of the said Annuities.

It further appeared, that, subsequent to this Transaction, the Affairs of the said Company were, by Mismanagement and Misconduct in the then Directors, greatly deranged and embarrassed, and their Estates and Property were loaded with divers Incumbrances,

A Petition of Stephen Fuller, Rose Fuller, and John Gibraltar Bowman, Esquires, in Behalf of themselves, and of James Prize Money. Simpson and James Deze, Esquires, who are resident at Gibraltar, was presented to the House, and read;

Reciting an Act, made in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for authorizing the Treasurer of the Navy to pay to the Garrison and Naval Department at Gibraltar, the like Bounty for destroying certain Spanish Ships of War, as is allowed to the Officers and Men on Board any of His Majesty’s

Gibraltar Prize Money.

920 2° Man, A. 1785.

Majesty’s Ships of War, taking or destroying Ships of War belonging to the Enemy; and Setting forth, That, by a rower of Attorney, bearing Date the 27th of October 1782, duly executed by Sir George Augustus Eliott, Governor of the Garrison of Gibraltar, by Sir Robert Boyd, the Lieutenant Governor, by the Generals, Officers, Non-commissioned Officers,. Soldiers, and others of the said Garrison, or the major Part of them, the Petitioners (together with Mr. Stephen Robinson, since deceased) and the said Messrs. Simpson and Deze, of Gibraltar, were duly appointed their Attornies and Agents, to solicit, transact, and take Care of all their Concerns and Interests in the Spanish Battering Ships, and Spanish Ship of War Saint Miguel, and in all Head Money, Bounty Money, or other Monies arising therefrom, with the fullest Powers for receiving the same, and thereby allow ing to the Petitioners (and the said Stephen Robinson, since deceased) and the said Messrs. Simpson and Deze, the usual and customary Commission thereon; and, the Petitioners likewise received a like Power of Attorney, bearing Date the 30th of September 1782, from Sir George Augustus Eliott, Sir Roger Curtis, and the Majority of the Naval Officers, Seamen* and Marines of the said Garrison and Naval Department, whereby they were, in like Manner, impowered to act for them; and that, under the Authority of the said Act of the Twenty-third of His present Majesty, and pursuant to the before-mentioned Powers of Attorney, Bills were issued by the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Navy, for the before-mentioned Bounty Money, and delivered by the Treasurer of the Navy to the Petitioners, as Agents for the said Officers, Soldiers, Seamen, and Marines of the said Garrison; and that, upon the 21st of July 1784, His Majesty was pleased, by Warrant under His Sign Manual, to appoint the Distribution of £30,000, being nearly the Amount of the Bounty Money, to and between the Military and Naval Departments, in the Proportions therein mentioned, and the Petitioners immediately requested Sir Robert Boyd, the Lieutenant Governor of the said Garrison, then and now resident here, to appoint a Broker, to cooperate with the Broker named by the Petitioners in selling the said Navy Bills to the best Advantage, for the Purpose of making the most speedy Distribution of the Bounty Money, pursuant to His Majesty’s said Warrant, and Sir Robert Boyd did accordingly appoint a Broker, agreeable to the Petitioners said Request; and that thtf said Navy Bills were accordingly sold by the said Brokers with as much Expedition as a beneficial Sale thereof would permit, and, in order that every possible Delay might be avoided in making the Distribution, the Petitioners did, in the mean Time, and before all the Navy Bills were sold, publish Notice in the London Gazette* agreeably to the Directions of certain Acts of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of His present Majesty, appointing the 7U1, 8th* gth, 10th, and 11th of December 1784, for the Payment of the several Military and Naval Departments, in the Order particularly mentioned in the said Advertisement, and thereby giving Notice that the Shares not then demanded would be recalled at the Place appointed on the First Friday in every Month, for Three Years to come, which Term of Three Years is the Term appointed by the before-mentioned Acts of the Nineteenth and Twentieth of His present Majesty, at the Expiration of which the then non-claimed Shares are to be accounted for and paid over by the Prize Agents to the Treasurer of Greenwich Hospital, for the Use and Benefit of the said Hospital; and that, although the Recall Days Were so fixed for the First Friday in every Month, agreeably to the constant Usage and Custom in the Payment of Prize Money, the Petitioners, being anxious to give every possible Dispatch and Facility to the Distribution and Payment of the said Bounty Money, have caused constant Daily

Attendance to be given at their respective Counting Houses in London, from the said First Day of Payment to the present Time, for the Purpose of paying all the Officers and Men, as well of the Military as of the Naval Department; and, in consequence of such unremitted Attendance, the Petitioners can prove, to the Satisfaction of the House, that the Payments which have been made on the Recall Days, on the First Friday in the Months of January, February, March, and April, amounted only to £2,634, or thereabouts, and that the Payments, made in the Intervals of the said Recall Days, amounted to £ 8,980, and upwards; and, the Petitioners have, in no one Instance, had any Complaint made by any of the Officers, Soldiers, Seamen, or Marines, or by any Person, on their, or any of their Behalf, that any Inconvenience or Difficulty has arisen in the Mode of Payment which the Petitioners have so adopted; and that, -notwithstanding such the Attention, Assiduity, and Facility which have been uniformly given by the Petitioners, to the Distribution of the said Bounty Money, agreeably to His Majesty’s said Warrant, a Bill has been brought into the House, upon the Petition of the said Sir Robert Boyd only, for authorizing the Prize Agents, appointed by the Officers of the Garrison of Gibraltar, to pay to the Agents of the Corps composing the said Garrison, all such Sums as shall remain or come to their Hands, of the Bounty allowed for the Destruction of certain Spanish Ships of War, the Preamble whereof contains a Recital of Inconveniencies and Difficulties which do not, nor have at any Time, existed, and the said Bill contains Clauses and Provisions which are founded upon the Misrepresentations so contained in the Preamble to the said Bill, and are not only unnecessary and useless, but injurious to, and destructive of, the Rights with which the Petitioners are duly and legally invested, under the Powers of Attorney, given them by the Governor and the several Officers, Soldiers, Seamen, and Marines of the said Garrison, and which have been recognized by, and received the Sanction of, the before-mentioned Act of the Twenty-third of His present Majesty, and which Powers, being neither revoked, or sought to be revoked, by the Persons who executed the same, the Claims in the said Bill are equally injurious to the Rights of those Individuals who have so intrusted the Receipt of their Shares in the said Bounty Money, and also their Concerns and Interests therein, to the Petitioners, and the said Messrs. Simpson and Deze, and which Powers will necessarily be annihilated without the Consent of the Parties executing the same, if the said Bill, as now framed, shall pass into a Law; and that the said Bill also contains a Clause, disposing of the Sum of £423. 1 i s. 4 d. Surplus of the said Bounty Money, although Directions have been given, by His Majesty’s said Warrant, concerning the Application of the same, or some Part thereof, and likewise a Clause respecting the unclaimed Shares of the said Bounty Money, totally Vepu^nant to the Directions of the several Acts of Parliament now in force concerning the Application of the unclaimed Shares of Prize and Bounty Money: And therefore praying, That they may be at liberty to attend, by Counsel, before the Committee of the House on the said Bill.

Commercial A Petition of the Manufacturers and Woolstaplers Intercourse of the County of Southampton, was presented to the with Ireland. j.jousej ancj reac|. Setting forth* That the Petitioners are sensible of the Advantages which would arise, as well to England as to Ireland, from the Settlement of a permanent and mutual Treaty df Commerce, and are therefore far from wishing to impede Government in making such a Treaty, but, apprehending the Resolutions of foe Irish' Parliament by no Means calculated to produce so desireable an Event, the Petitioners judge it expedient to communicate their Sen-'timents before a final Regulation takes Place, having too high an Opinion of the House to suppose they will promote the Establishment of those Resolutions /Unless they can be regulated in such a Manner as Vol.40.

will place the Interests of both Countries on a fair and equitable Footing; The Petitioners are of Opinion, that the 3d, 4th, 7th, and 9th Resolutions of the Irish House of Commons are very incompetent to produce the much-desired Plan of Equalization, but, on the contrary, are likely to undermine British Manufactures, and that the Mode proposed of equalising Duties, by laying them on, or taking them of, specific Articles, will not be productive of reciprocal Advantages; The Petitioners conceive it may not be improper to state, that there is a very lar^o Quantity of Irish Yarn imported Annually into this Country, the Introduction of which they apprehend of great Service, as it furnishes Employ for a Number of their Poor, but, if the Resolutions pass info a Law in their present Form, they imagine that Ireland Svjh work up her own Materials, and, from the Ipequar lity of Taxation, fyc, will not only supplant them in Foreign Markets, hut also in the Home Trade, the fatal Result of which appears too obvious: The Price . of Labour and Provisions being so much lower in Ireland than in England, the Petitioners think it necessary, in order to produce Equality, that the Situation of the Two Countries should be strictly compared, ip order that such Regulations may be made as will promote the general Welfare of both, and the Petitioners, 'having impartially investigated the Irish Propositions, are unanimous in their Opinion, that, if they pass into a Law, it will be exceedingly injurious to all foe Manufacturers of Low Woollens apd Worsted Stuffs, and think it necessary to remark, foat Irish Wool is particularly well adapted for making such Goods, and, as there is a large Consumption of them in this Country (owing to foe Number of Poor employed in its many extensive Manufactures, who are chiefly Cloathed therewith) they suppose the Sister Kingdom will seek a Market here for those Articles, and will inevitably supplant them in the Home Trade, unless such a Duty be imposed on the Importation of Irish Stuffs and Coarse Woollens, as will put jt out of the Power of Ireland to meet them on unequal Terms in their own Markets; and that foe chief Articles the Petitioners manufacture am Worsted Stuffs,

Coarse Woollens, and Yarn, for Sale, which being wrought with Wool the Produce of our own Land, and considered as the Staple Commodity of this Kingdom, they think it would be very impolitic to give Ireland the Preference in these Branches, especially as her Exports already so much exceed those of this Country, and she enjoys such manifest Privileges in the Linen Trade; and that the Petitioners, being well satisfied that the Duties proposed to be laid on the Importation of Irish Stuffs and Coarse Wollens are not sufficient to protect the Home Trade, with Grief and Concern observe, that a Ratification of the Irish Resolutions will not only prove injurious to most Branches of the English Manufacture, but will also be detrimental to the Landed Interest, and ultimately tend to exalt Ireland at the Expence of Britain, and destroy those Springs of Emulation and Improvement which arise in a Commercial Country, and are essential to the Manufacturing Interests of this Kingdom: And the Petitioners therefore hope the House will remove the Subjects of their Apprehensions, by such Alterations and Modifications as to, foe House shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of, the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manu- Stafford,? facturers, and principal Inhabitants of the Borough of &c: Navi-; Tewkesbury, in the County of Gloucester, was presented satioD' to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Leave hath been given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation to lower the Tonnage upon what Parts or Lengths of their Canal they shall please, without the Interference of the Commissioners whom Parliament appointed for the Protection of the public Interest; and that the Petitioners are well satisfied with the Integrity of the present Commissioners, and think a Power of such Importance to the Public better lodged in the Hands of Men of Fortune and Honour than in those of interested Individuals, and, the Petitioners firmly believe, if such Bill passes into a Law, a partial Lowering of Tonnage will immediately take Place, having little Expectation of Justice being done where Competitions subsist; that they have sensibly felt the Advantages of the Collieries near the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals, and are very apprehensive, if the Attempt succeeds, they will be deprived of those useful Sources, and the Stourbridge and Dudley Canals rendered of no Service to the Petitioners and the Public at large: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon ths Table, until the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation to lower and regulate the Tonnage upon the said Canal, be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manu- Dodley facturers, and principal Inhabitants of the Borough Canal, of Tewkesbury, in the County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed, by the Votes, that Leave hath been given to bring in a Bill for extending the present Dudley Canal into the Birmingham Canal, at or near Tipton, by which a shorter Communication will be opened between the Birmingham Market and Bristol; and that the Petitioners are well assured, that, if such Bill passes into a Law, it will be attended with great National Importance, by bringing the Produce of many valuable and extensive Mines of Limestone, Coal, and Ironstone, into the Severn Markets, by lowering and regulating the Price of those necessary Articles, and by causing a Reduction in the Freight of all Merchandize navigated upon The Severn; all which the Petitioners conceive to be of great Consequence to themselves, and to the Public in general: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may be permitted to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill, for extending the present Dudley Canal from the Termination thereof, in certain Lands of Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire, within the Parish of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, to join and communicate with the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, at or near Tipton Green, in the County of Stafford\ be brought in.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending, for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for further regulating and " ascertaining the Importation and Exportation of

Corn and Grain within several Ports and Places " therein mentioned," and for extending the Powers and Provisions thereof to all Places within that Part of Great Britain called England, whereby the general Average Prices of Corn and Grain, in the several Parts of this Kingdom, are to be ascertained, by the Returns of the Com Factors in the City of London, according to the Prices in that City; and Alledging, That large Quantities of Corn and Grain are exported from, and imported into, the Port of Bristol\ to the Vol. 40.

Mail. 93 f

great Behefit of that Place, and of the neighbouring Counties, and such Exportation and Importation have been regulated by the Prices of Corn, as found by the Grand Jury at the Quarter Sessions, by due Enquiry upon Oath, which Regulations, the Petitioners ap* prebend, are better calculated to answer the Purposes intended by the Legislature, than those proposed by the said Bill: And therefore praying, That such Clauses of the said Bill as relate to, or affect, the Manner of ascertaining the Prices of Corn and Grain out of the City and Port of London, may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Clauses, if the Nature of their Case should require the same.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Common- torn and fclty of the Society of Merchants Venturers of the City Grain-of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive, that the Provisions of the said Bill, if it was to pass into a Law, would tend to deprive the Port of Bristol from obtaining a Foreign Supply, even in Times of the greatest Need, and establish a Monopoly of the Corn Trade in the Port of London; and that considerable Districts, in the several Counties which are situate near, or have Communication with, the Port of Bristol, do not grow Corn sufficient for their own Consumption, but depend chiefly on the Bristol Market for a Supply, and, any Attempt to regulate the Importation of Corn and Grain, into the Port of Bristol, by the Price of Com at the Corn Exchange within the City of London, would be injurious in the Extreme to the Inhabitants of Bristol, and its Dependencies:

And therefore praying to be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to * lie upon the Table, until the said Bill he read a Second Time; and the last mentioned Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Shoes, and of Tanned and Wrought Leather, in the Town of Staf- ford, and Neighbourhood, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth; That the Propositions, now depending in Parliament, for regulating and establishing a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, have excited, in the Petitioners Minds, well-grounded Fears and Apprehensions, that the Manufacturers of Shoes, and of Tanned and Wrought" Leather, must be eventually ruined, should the Resolutions be carried into Effect: That the British Legislature hath heretofore considered the Tanned and Wrought Leather Manufactures of so great Importance, that the Importation of them from other Countries hath been either totally prohibited, or permitted only under such Duties as were a virtual Prohibition, and that, if these Prohibitions are removed with regard to the Irish Manufactures of Leather, the Petitioners, labouring under many heavy Burthens of Taxes, from which our Sister Kingdom is free, have not the smallest Hope left of being able to maintain themselves and Families in this Country, in Opposition to so formidable a Rival: And therefore praying to be heard, by themselves and Counsel, against those Propositions passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners be heard by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, in Support of their Petition, if they think fit.

Sir William Augustus Cunynghame reported from the Glasgow Committee, to whom the Petition of Peter Murdoch, Two Pcdm Robert Cowan, James Gordon, James Hopkirk, and James Scots‘ Warrochy all Partners in a Brewing Business in the Village of Anders town, near Glasgow, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared, by an Act, passed in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for continuing and rendering more effectual an Act, passed in the Ninth Year " of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for " continuing the Duty of Two Pennies Scots, or OneSixth of a Penny Sterling, on every Pint of Ale " or Beer that shall be vended or sold within the City " of Glasgow, and for extending the same over the Villages of Gorbals and Port Glasgow, and Privileges " thereof, for the Benefit of the said City and VII-" lages," (after reciting an Act passed in the Parliament of Scotland in the Year 1693, an Act passed in the Third Year of the Reign of her Majesty Queen Anne, an Act passed in the First Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the First, an Act passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the Second) the aforesaid Duty was granted and continued for a new Term of Thirty-eight Years.

That the said Act of the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty King George the Second, contains the following Clause: " And whereas of late " Years sundry Persons have erected Breweries in the " Neighbourhood of the said City of Glasgow, and the u said Villages of Gorbals and Port Glasgow, and have " imported large Quantities of Ale and Beer into the " said City and Villages, for the Consumption of the " Inhabitants thereof, and have refused to make Payment of the said Duties by the foresaid Acts

Then John Mortland, Esquire, being examined, said, That the said Clause is unjust and oppressive, as it subjects the Petitioners to the Payment of the said Duty for all the Ale and Beer they brew, if they import or sell the smallest Quantity within the aforesaid City or Villages, whereas it is apprehended they ought*only to pay the said Duty for all such Ale or Beer as they shall sell within the City of Glasgow, or the Villages of Gorbals and Port Glasgow, or the Liberties or Privileges thereof.
