Town of Poofe, in the County of Dorset, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for further regulating and ascertain-u ing the Importation and Exportation of Corn and " Grain within several Ports and Places therein mentioned," and for extending the Powers and Provisions thereof to all Places within that Part of Great Britain called England; and Setting forth, That the said Bill will, if suffered to pass into a Law, invest the City of London with a full Power of Controul over the Out Ports of this Kingdom, as far as respects the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the Laws now in force for ascertaining the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain, are founded in sound Policy, and, having for their Object the general Benefit of the Public, have stood the Test of many Years Experience with National Advantage, and, therefore the Petitioners fear, that the proposed Alteration in the Mode of ascertaining the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain, will be of the greatest Injury to many Thousands of His Majesty’s Subjects, and give the greatest Encouragement to Monopoly and Oppression; and that it frequently happens, as the Petitioners are informed, that the very large Importation of Corn to the Port of London in One Quarter of a Year, reduces the Prices of Middling British Corn and Grain so far below the Standard for Importation, that, at the next Quarter Sessions, the Port is shut against the Importation of Foreign Corn and Grain, whilst, at many Out Ports in the Kingdom, the Average Prices fully justify the Necessity of allowing a free Importation;

and that the Regulation proposed by the said Bill, as far as respects the Exportation of Corn and Grain, will prove, in many Parts of this Kingdom, highly prejudicial to Commerce, and a great Discouragement to Cultivation and Agriculture, as the Average Prices of Com at the London Market may frequently, from a Variety of Circumstances, exceed the limited Exportation Prices, at a Time when the Prices in the Out Ports are considerably below the Standard prescribed by Law, and, the Petitioners are apprehensive, that the said Bill will be greatly injurious to the Landed Property of this Kingdom, and be attended with the utmost ill Consequences to the Community at large: And therefore praying, That the House

will take the Premises into Consideration, and permit the Petitioners to be heard, by Counsel, at the Bar of the House, in Support' of their Allegations, and against the said Bill passing into a Law, if the Nature of their Case shall require the same.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of Stephen Fuller, Esquire, Agent for Jamaica, was presented to the House, and read;

Vo l, 40.

Setting form, That the Petitioner has been commanded, by the Assembly of Jamaica, to represent to the House the Grievances which that Island labours under:- — 1st, By a Deprivation of that Intercourse with the Continent of North America which used to furnish the said Island with Supplies of such Species as are absolutely necessary for the Sustenance of the Inhabitants, the Existence and Support of their Settlements, and the Cultivation and Package of their various Products, an Intercourse which afforded a Certainty of those Supplies in a regular unfailing Succession, answerable to their wants, and which, at the same Time that it assisted the Staple Products of the Island with Materials essential to their Progress, Mahufac- ture, and Export, added the farther Encouragement of receiving Payment chiefly in Rum, of which important Article little more than One-Fifth, of the An-. nual Crop can be reasonable expected to find a Vent and Consumption in this Kingdom: — 2dlv, By the heavy Duty oti Sugar (amounting in some Cases to nearly Three-fourths of the original Value) aggra- vated, and rendered more burthensome to the Planter, by the Mode of Collecting: — And 3dly, By the Duties on Rum, in respect to which, although they have been indulged with some Alleviation, yet those Duties still remain so high as to preclude it from an extensive Consumption: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them a limited Intercourse with the Continent of America, in American Vessels of a limited Size, and navigated by a limited Number of Hands; and that the House wilL grant such Relief as to them shall seem^ meet in regard to the Duties on Sugar and Rum, and the Mode of Collection; and that he may be heard by his Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. j

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, Jamaica Copies of the Naval Officers Quarterly Accounts of Trade. British and Foreign Vessels entered and cleared out in the Island of Jamaica, from the 29th of September 1783 to the 29th of September 1784.

" Cotton not painted, printed, stained, or dyed in " Foreign Parts," on all Linens, Stuffs made of Cotton and Linen mixed, and Stuffs wholly made of Cotton Wool, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu thereof, an additional Duty of Two Pence per Square Yard, over and above tiite Duties now payable thereon, be laid upon all Linen and Stuffs, and upon all Stuffs wholly made of Cotton manufactured in Great Britain, to be printed painted, stained, or dyed in Great Britain (except such as shall be dyed throughout of One Colour only, and except such whereof the greatest Part so Value shall be Woollen) of the Value of more than Sixteen

Pence per Yard, iand under Two Shillings and Six Pence per Yard, according to the Value of the same in London, or the nearest Market Town, by the Running Yard, and at the Time the same shall be first presented to the Excise Officer to be measured and taken Account of.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu thereof, an additional Duty of Four Pence per Square Yard, over and above the Duties now payable thereon, be laid upon all Linen and Stuffs, and upon all Stuffs wholly made of Cotton, manufactured in Great Britain, to be printed, painted, stained, or dyed in Great Britain (except such as shall be dyed throughout of One Colour only, and except such whereof the greatest Part in Value shall be Woollen), of the Value of Two Shillings and Six Pence pet' Yard, and upwards, according to the Value of the same in London, or the nearest Market Town, by the Running Yard, and at the Time the same shall be first presented to the Excise Officer to be measured and taken Account of.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu thereof, an additional Duty of Eight Pence per Square Yard, over and above the Duties now payable thereon, be laid upon all Foreign Callicoes, to be printed, stained, painted, or dyed in Great Britain, except such as shall be dyed throughout of One Colour only.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duties shall also be subject and liable to the additional Duties of Five Pounds per Centum, Five Pounds per Centum, and of Five Pounds pei' Centum, laid by Three Acts, of the Nineteenth, Twenty-first, and Twenty-second Years of His Majesty’s Reign, for granting additional Duties upon the Produce of the several Duties under the Management of the respective Commissioners of Excise in Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Seven thousand Seven hundred Thirty-seven Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Ope Penny Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of several Battalions of Foot for different Periods in the Year 1784.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Ninety-seven thousand Seven hundred and Three Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account of the Reduced Officers of His Majesty s Land Forces and Marines, for the Year *7*5-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred Thirty-five Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Allowances to the several Officers and Private Gentlemen of the Two Troops of Horse Guards reduced, and to the superannuated Gentlemen of the Four Troops of Horse Guards, for the Year 1785.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty-seven thousand and Eight hundred Pounds One Shilling and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account of the Commissioned Officers of His Majesty’s British American Forces, for the Year 1785.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Seven hundred Thirty-six Pounds Eleven Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to make good a Deficiency on the Sum granted upon Account of the Commissioned Officers of His Majesty’s British American Forces, for the Year *783.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Four thousand Three hundred and Eight Pounds Eleven Shillings and Three Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to make good a Deficiency on the Sum granted upon Account of the Commissioned Officers of His Majesty’s British American Forces, for the Year 1784.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Five hundred and Thirty-five Pounds and Six Pence, he granted to His Majesty, upon Account of several Officers late in the Service of the States General, for the Year 1785.

And that, in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, an Act w^s made for repairing the Road from Ashborne aforesaid to join the said Road from Sheffield to Derby, and a certain other Road therein mentioned, and that a Rill is depending in the House, for enlarging the Term, and continuing the Powers, of the said Act; and that, soon after the passing of the said Act, the Trustees for the Care of the said Road caused a Turnpike to be erected within the Distance of Twenty-eight Yards from a Road leading out of the said Turnpike Road to the said Mill, through which Turnpike all Persons Travelling between the said Mill and the Town of Ashborne, with Horses and Carriages, are obliged to pass, but, soon after the said Gate was erected, the said Trustees agreed to compound with the Occupier of the said Mill for the Sum of Five Shillings pel' Annum in lieu of all Tolls payable for, or in respect of, his Horses and Carriages passing and re-passing through the said Turnpike, which Composition was continued, from Year to Year, so long as the Trustees continued to receive the Tolls; and that, for several Years past, the said Tolls have been let upon Lease, since which Time the Composition has been very considerably increased, and the present Lessee now refuses to make any Composition with the Occupier of the said Mill, and insists upon receiving the full Tolls dt the said Turnpike, which will be a very great Hardship upon the Occupier of the said Mill, and, at the Expiration of the Term of his Lease, will very materially affect the Petitioner’s Estate: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that a Clause may be inserted in the said Bill for fixing a reasonable Composition in lieu of Tolls for all Horses and Carriages passing and re-passing to and from the said Mill.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Dudley Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, was Canal, presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That by Two Acts, passed in the Sixth and Tenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Bersons were incorporated by the Name and StHe of " The Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire <c and Worcestershire Canal Navigation," and were authorized to make and maintain a Navigable Cana! from the River Severn, between Bewdly and Tilton Brook, in the County of Worcester, to cross the Rivet Trent, at or near Haywood Mill, in the County of Stafford, and to communicate with a Canal then intended to be made between the Said River Trent and the River Mersey, and to raise and contribute amongst themselves the Sum of £. no,(too, for the Purpose of carrying the sard Acts into Execution; and that the said Company of Proprietors, their Successors and As Signs, in pursuance of the said Acts, have made and completed the said Navigation, in doing which, and in making necessary Alterations and Improvements therein, to accommodate public Business, the said Company have expended the Money allowed to be raised under their Acts of Parliament, together with a Considerable Part of the Income of the said Navigation, amounting together to a very large Sum of Money, and the Navigation, with its Works and Appendages, isr now complete, and of the greatest public Utility, and is become interesting to the said Company; ancf (hat, in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, atl Act Was obtained to enable certain Per- -Sons thereby incorporated, by the Name of f‘Th4 u Company of Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal

" Navigation," to make and complete a collateral Branch of Navigation from Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, through many large Collieries, in the Counties of Worcester and Stafford, to join and communicate with the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, at Autherky, in the County of Stafford\ in order to bring Coal from those Mines upon the said General Canal Navigation, as well as Merchandize, from and towards the Town of Binning-liam; and that, by another Act, passed in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, certain Persons were incorporated by the Name of " The " Company of Proprietors of she Stourbridge Navigation," and were thereby impowered to make and complete another collateral Branch of Navigation from and out of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, at a Place called Stewponey, to the Town of Stourbridge, and some Coal Mines in the County of Worcester; and, in the same Sessions, another Act was obtained to extend the said last mentioned Canal to some Coal Mines upon the Estates of the Right honourable John Lord Viscount Dudley and Ward, and others, lying in the County of Worcester, which lust-mentioned Canal is called u The Dudley Canal Navigation;" and, in both the said last mentioned Acts, there is a Clause to prohibit each of the said Companies of Proprietors, their Successors or Assigns, or the said Lord Viscount Dudley and Ward, his Heirs and Assigns, or any other Person or Persons, to extend either of the said last mentioned Navigations, or any collateral Branch thereto belonging, to any Place or Places whatsoever, lying or being within the Distance of One Mile and an Half of the Birmingham Canal Navigation, or the collateral Cuts thereto belonging, or within the Distance of One Mile and an Half of any Part of them, or either of them, either by a Canal, Cut, Sluice, Tunnell, or otherwise howsoever, and also, from making or extending, at any Time, any Cut, Sluice, Trench, or Tunnell, from the said Birmingham Canal, or collateral Cuts, to either of the said Canals and Cuts, or to any Part of them, or either of them, or within the Distance of One Mile and an Half of either of the said Canals and Cuts, or any Part of them, without the Consent of the Company of Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal, or their Successors or Assigns, under their Common Seal for that Purpose first had and obtained; and, in the Stourbridge Canal Act, there is also a Clause, founded upon an Agreement between the said Company and the Petitioners, for protecting the Interest of the Mine Owners upon the Line of the Birmingham Canal, as well as the Interest of the Petitioners, in the Admission of the Stourbridge Canal into the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill hath been presented, by the Company of Proprietors of the Dudley Canal Navigation, for Power to extend their Canal, so as to make a Communication by a Canal Navigation between the Birmingham and Dudley Canals, and to make Reservoirs of Water to supply the same.; and that the Petitioners apprehend that the Consent of the Birmingham Canal Company, under their Common Seal, for making such proposed Extension and Communication, hath not been obtained, which Consent, the Petitioners conceive to be absolutely necessary, before any Act or Powers can be granted to carry the Design into Execution; and that if such a Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners conceive it will be injurious to a great Part of the Iron Manufactory, be a Means to form a Monopoly of the Coal Trade, and be very injurious many Coal Mines, upon the Birmingham Canal, as well as to the Interest of the Petitioners generally, as such Extension is formed to operate against the Petitioners original Navigation for Twelve Miles and an Haiti if not for the full Distance from Authcrley to Stour-

port, whereby the Petitioners Interest will be greatly intruded upon, and materially injured, and the Public will receive no further Benefit than by the present Line of Navigation: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and that they may be heard, by themselves*or Counsel, against the Whole of the said Bill, or against any Part thereof, and that their Interest in the Staffordshire and Worcester shire Canal Navigation may be secured to them, or the said Bill not pass into a Law.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Ptpys and Mr. Thomson:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, as relates to the Distillation of Corn Spirits in small Stills, in certain Counties or Districts of the Highlands in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland; and for authorizing the Commissioners of Excise in Scotland to grant Licences to Persons, living in the said Counties or Districts, to distill Spirits from Barley, Bear, or Big, the Growth of the said Counties, and for imposing a Duty on such Licences; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords. have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for amending and widening the Roads leading from New Street and Pig Street, in Penryn, in the County of Cornwall, to Redruth, in the same County; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Common Fields and Waste Lands within the Manors of Kinnerley and Melverley, in the County of Salop) without any Amendment: And also,

Vo i, 40,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing certain Commons and Waste Lands within the Townships of Pickering and Newton, in the North Riding of the County of York; with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, Ati Act td effectuate a Partition of the Estates of Job Hanmer, Esquire, the Reverend Erasmus Wanen, Clerk, and Sir Thomas Charles Bunbury, Baronet, in the Counties of Suffolk and Essex; to which the Lords deSirfe the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Mr. Dempster reported from the Committee, td whom the Petition of George Ross, of Cromarty, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the Said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; arid he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; Alexander Gray, Esquire, being (examined, informed your Committee, That Cromarty Bay has at all Times been a most safe Road-stead to Ships of all Nations, overtaken with Storms, in any Part of the German Ocean, and the Erection of a Pier and Harbour has been judged beneficial to Navigation in general, and to the Commerce of Scotland in particular.

And it appeared by certain Documents adduced to your Committee, and by the Testimony of the above Witness, that the Petitioner, George Ross, Esquire, is Proprietor of the Barony of Cromarty, arid of the Port and Harbour; and that hehas given up to the Public the Ground and Coast necessary to be occupied by the said Harbour and Pier.

It also appeared, that the Sum of £.5,000 has been granted by His Majesty, out of the Produce of the Forfeited Estates in Scotland, towards erecting the said Harbour and Pier.

Then a Member present informed your Committee, That the Main Pier is erected, and Two other Piers or Jetties are begun to be erected, in order to complete the said Harbour.

And Mr. Gray further informed your Committee; That he has examined the Accounts, and it appears that upwards of £.5,000 has already been expended, arid has not proved sufficient for erecting and completing the said Piets and Harbour. — And the Witness added, That it will require £. Soo more than what has been already expended, to complete the Work, whifch the Petitioner, has undertaken to advance; but the said Hdrbour and Piers cannot be maintained and preserved without such Tolls are levied as may be adequate to that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better preserving and maintaining the Piers and Harbour of Cromarty, in North Britain: And that Mr. Dempster and the Lord Advocate of Scotland d4 prepare, and bring in, the same.

Resolved, That this House will, at the Rising of the House this Day, adjourn till Monday Morning next

A Petition of the Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Creditors of the Governor and Company of Undertakers for raising the Thames Water in 7

York Buildings, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for altering and' amending an Act, passed in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for expediting the Sale of the Estates in Scotland belonging to the York Buildings Company, for c< the Relief of their Creditors," in order to have the unsatisfied Purchase Money of the said Estates paid into the Bank of England, to be distributed1 among the several Creditors, under the Direction of the Court of Chancery, and the Surplus to remain for the Benefit of the Stockholders; And setting* forth, That, the said Governor and Company having become Insolvent, the Petitioners were under the Necessity of taking the proper and legal Steps,* according to the Forms of the Law of Scotland, for establishing their respective Debts, which are now* become chargeable on the said Company’s Estates in that Country, and, the same having been sold, the Price only remains to be divided amongst the Peti- tioners, and the other Creditors of the said Company, for which Purpose the Laws now in force are sufficient, without the further Aid and Authority of Parliament; and that, the Petitioners apprehend, the' above Bill is introduced merely for the Purpose of Delay, and to retard the Payment of their just Debts:

And therefore praying to be heard, by themselves' or Counsel, against the same being passed into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that: the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they7 think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert took the Chair of the Committee.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

The Lord Beauchamp reported from the Committee, appointed to enquire what Proceedings have been had in the Execution of an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the effectual Transportation of " Felons and other Offenders; and to authorize the ix Removal of Prisoners in certain Cases; ants for " other Purposes therein mentioned," and to report their Opinion to the House, what further Measures may be necessary to carry the Purposes of the said Act into Effect; and who were impowered to report their Proceedings, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had made a Progress in the Matter they were appointed to enquire into; and had directed him to make a Repbrt thereof to thd House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed*; viz.

Your Committee beg to inform the House, That id the Course of thfe Enquiry which they have instituted, such important Intelligence has been laid before them, of the Consequences to be apprehended from transporting Criminals to that Part of Africa, which lies within the Tropic^, that they have thought it their Doty immediately to submit it to the Wisdom of the House.

Mr. Recorder of London being examined, informed the Committee, That as soon as the Act of last Session passed, the Judges at The Old Bailey adopted a new Form of Sentence for Transportation, pursuant to the Direction of the said Act, leaving it to the King in Council to declare the Place to which the Convicts so sentenced should be seftt; but in some few Instances they specifically sentenfced them to be sent to Africa — That Government having given Orders for the Removal Of 100 Convicts from Newgate, for the Purpose of being sent to Africa, he had prepared a List, from the best Information he could obtain, as well from the Evidence given on their respective Trials, as from their Demeanor during their Confinement in Newgate, of such Convicts as seemed most proper to be sent to that Part of the World; which List amounted to between 90 and 106, including Women — That afterwards the necessary Orders of Council and of Court were made, to authorize the Removal of these Offenders; but it being jhdged inconvehient, at that Time, to remove the Women, and One or Two of the Men having died, the Number actually removed amounted only to 78 — That at the last Old Bailey Sessions 5 Persons were sentenced to be transported to Africa, the fest of the Transports receiving the general Sentence; and that he has now a List of the remaining Prisoners lieforc him, in order to select as many as will complete

thu Number ofi 00 — That all’the Convicts so selected, especially the Women, are of the most desperate and dangerous Disposition, deserving, for the Sake of public Example, great Severity of Punishment — That he does not knows of any Persons, who, having been capitally convicted, after receiving the King’s Pardon on Condition of being transported to America* have since been ordered for Transportation to Africa'; but that many, who were originally sentenced to America, are now' destined to Africa.

Thomas Buttei'sworth Bailey, Esquire, an acting Magistrate for the County of Lancaster, being examined* acquainted the Committee, That the Magistrates at the Quartet Sessions have experienced great Difficulties in inflicting the ’Punishment of Transportation for Seven Years, the Sentence being for Transportation generally, to some Parts beyond the Seas, as the Mag-’ nitude of the Punishment is rendered very uncertain, from the Difference of the Climate and Country to which they may be sent, and from the Uncertainty of the Offenders being able to return after the Expiration of the Teriti — That under this Embarrassment they have sentenced Persons to Imprisonment in England for different Terms, whom otherwise they would have sentenced tb Transportation — That in consequence of this a very great Accumulation of Prisoners has taken place in the County Gaol, and other Prisons, where there fe not Accommodation for them. — He further said, That these Prisoners are maintained1 out of the County ifcates, at a great Expence, and that being closely ironed they cannot work — That some of them have been confined Three Years, or Three Years and a Half, since they were sentenced to Transportation — That there is no stated County Allowance — That they are maintained under discretionary Orders from the Magistrates when they visit the Prisons — And that, if the Law remains as it is, the Evil will be greatly increased. — Being asked, What Steps the Magistrates of the County of Lancaster have taken to carry the Act of last Sessions into Effect ? he informed the Committee, That they appointed Two of their own Body to contract for the Transportation of Offenders; and that he, as Chairman of the Quarter Sessions m January last, sent to His Majesty’s Secretary of State for the Home Department an Account of the Number of Prisoners under Sentence of Transportation, and requested to know His Majesty’s Pleasure concerning them, that they might be sent to the respective Places of their Destination without Delay — to which nb Answer has yet been received — That the Justices did not think themselves authorized to make any Arrangement for the temporary Confinement of these Prisoners, Without His Majesty’s Order by Sign Manual — and that they have not applied for such Order, being in constant Expectation of an Order for their Removal — That the Two Magistrates appointed under the Act to contract for the Transportation of Offenders, have not been able to execute it, from not knowing to what Place they were to be conveyed. — That the Law appears to him defective, inasmuch as it gives no Power to compel Masters of Ships to take them — and that no Captains of Vessels are willing to undertake that Service, there being no Persons in that Country, as in London, who have ever made a Trade of conveying Transports beyond Sea.

Richard Akerman, Esquire, produced to the Committee a List of the Prisoners in Newgate, another Session having taken Place since the last Return — and he acquainted the Committee, That in a few Days the Number of Prisoners in his Custody will amount to 600, owing tb the Influx from the other Gaols, for the Purpose of Trial at the ensuing Sessions — That the present Number is double of what it usually was Five* or Six Years ago — and that, from the full State of the Gaol, it has happened that Convicts under Sentence of Death could not be kept in separate Cells, as was usually the Practice — and that the same inconvenience 2 ‘ may

the Transportation of Convicts to any Part of America ? he informed the Committee, That Mr. Moore, a Merchant in London, took on board 150, whose original Sentence had been America at large, a Part of whom made their Escape, and the Remainder were admitted into the American States — That the same Experiment was tried a Second Time, but that it did not succeed, Captain Moore s Vessel being refused Admittance into their Ports; upon which they were carried down to Honduras, where they got into Quarrels with the Log Wood Cutters — And the Witness added, That this Measure was not authorized by Government. Mr. Nepean being asked, Whether there is any Plan for sending Convicts to Cape Breton, or any of the British Settlements in America ? he said, That there have been strong Representations made against it from Nova Scotia — That he believes there are very few Settlers in Cape Bretony and that he has heard of no Plan for sending them to Canada.

Mr. John Barnes acquainted the Committee, That he is an African Merchant — That he originally proposed the Idea of sending Convicts to Lemane, in the River Gambia, and that in different Conversations with Lord Sydney the Plan has been formed — That when he first thought of the Measure, the African Committee was much pressed to receive a Number of Convicts, which they refused, as highly dangerous, and in that Refusal Mr. Barnes concurred — lie further said, That he has been Twice on the Gambia, the last Time in 1757, when he returned from being a Prisoner at Goree — That in the Year 1753 he w'ent very high up the River, within Seven Leagues of Cuttejar — That he has Twice passed the Island of Lemane, but never landed on it — That it appeared to him a very fine Island, 10 or 12 Miles in Length — That the Land is high, and, as he understands, never flooded — That Part of it is clear and cultivated — That there are Rice Grounds and Guinea Corn — He passed on the North Side — the Channel there is about One Mile and a Half over — South Side much narrower, and shallower Water, but not fordable — He understands it belongs in Part to the King of Lemane on the North Shore of the River, and Part to a King on the South Side of the River — That the Natives are the best-disposed People in the World, strict and fair in their Dealings — That they have great Abundance of Provisions, animal and vegetable — That the Climate is generally esteemed better than lower down the River, or even at Yannimaroo, where the Crew of his Vessel proved sickly on their Return, though during the Voyage they had no Siek; but he added, that he had no Experience of the Climate but during the dry Season — That his People had no Worms in their Legs, and that he never found the Well nor River Water unwholesome — He further said, That James Fort has been generally esteemed unhealthy, but that might be owing to the bad Construction of the Fort, and the Method they have of living the re — That all great Rivers within the Tropics are full of Crocodiles and Hippopotami, and wild Beasts on both Banks, and that they are covered with Mangrove Trees as far as the Salt Water reaches — That there arc many Islands in the Gambia, but Lemane appears the most healthy, and the highest — That there is Wood upon it — That between Yannimaroo and the Island the River is all in One Channel, about Two Miles in Breadth, and that an armed Vessel could not prevent Boats passing in the Night. — He further said, That Lemane would maintain 3 or 4,000 People, and that 2 or 300 armed Europeans could not liberate themselves from it, on Account of the different Rivers running into the Gambia, and because the Blacks would not suffer them to be in their Country; though he added, that if they had Craft and Arms they might seize a Vessel, and escape by Water, or they might buy Canoes of the Natives. —

He further said> That he supposes Europeans could not bear the Cultivation of Lands so well within the Tropics as in temperate Climates; but that they could cultivate Corn and Rice on the Island for their own Subsistence, without Prejudice to their Health, if properly instructed — That Grain is about Four Months in coming to Maturity — That if the Island was ceded by Stipulation, the Natives would certainly be ready to assist the Settlers — That Europeans will gradually become inured to the Climate; and that Convicts, deprived of all the Means of Debauchery, would stand a good Chance of living. — He further said, That the Mortality mentioned by another Witness, at Galam, was owing to the Detachments being sent up too late in the Season, when the Country had been long flooded. — Being further examined, he said. That he never had any Experience of Field Work being performed by an European on the Coast of Africa, though he had seen Artificers among the French Garrison that came down from Galam; and that he had known a French Gentleman who had lived there 30 Years — That he has also seen E?iglish Masons and Carpenters (but no Labourers) do Out Door Work at Senegal, even after the rainy Season began. — Being asked, Whether the Natives would admit a Colony of Convicts into their Country ? . he said, He believed so, if they were paid a stipulated Rent — That all our Settlements in Africa have been so acquired; but that he never heard of any Attempt to make a Treaty with, them for an Establishment of Convicts — That Great Britain at present possesses no other Lands in the Gambia but the Island of Saint James, which is about Half a Quarter of a Mile in Length; and that since the Peace not above Three or four Vessels have, traded there in a Year. — He also said, That if the Natives received an Injury from One of the Convicts, they would revenge it only on the Individual, unless Satisfaction was denied them by the Settlement at large.

Mr. John Nevan, a Captain in the African Trade, acquainted the Committee, That he was last Year up the River Gambia — That his Vessel w as stationed opposite Yannimaroo, which is considered as the healthiest Spot on the River, for Six Months, between February and August — That when he anchored there, his Crew' (Men and Boys) consisted of Twenty-one, of which he lost Six by the Country Fever — That he owed his own Preservation to Bitters and Bark — and that not a Man escaped the Contagion, though the Crew constantly slept on board — and that had they been suffered to sleep on Shore, the Mortality would in his Opinion have been greater — That he saw Five European Traders, Three of whom had Houses at Yannimaroo — They had a very wretched Appearance, being quite pale and emaciated, and hardly able to crawl; and that they told him they regularly fell sick in August, though they had a constant Supply of Medicines — -The Witness further said, That be had gone up in his Long Boat as far as Fattitenda, and had landed at several Places on the Island of Lemane, having gone up one Channel and come down the other — That the Island seemed to be rather higher than the Banks of the River, which are covered with Mangrove Trees — and that the Country is marshy, and without Hills — That the Northern Channel is about Half a Mile broad, and the Water is at least Eight Feet deep in the Month of May — That the Southern Channel is about a Quarter of a Mile wide, but he cannot ascertain the Depth of Water, as no Vessel ever attempts to go through it, but the Country Boats — That he supposes the Island cannot be a Mile in Breadth, and that no Part of it appeared to be cultivated — That he saw only a few Blacks on the Island, and believes they came over from the main Land — That when he left the Country the Princes on both Banks opposite Lemane were at War — and he understands that they belong to different Sovereigns.

25 Geo. III. 9"

Being further asked, HoW many of his Crew might* probably have survived, if the Ship had remained a whole Year at Yannimaroo? he answered — Not One, as the Rains were sometimes so incessant for 48 Hours together, that the Crew were not able to stir out of their Cabins, and that when he came away, only himself and Two Men w’ere capable of doing Duty on board. — He also added, That from the Shallowness of the Water, a Sloop of War of Fourteen Guns could not be stationed at Yannimaroo, and that without a Guard Ship it would be impossible to confine the Convicts within the Island. — Being asked, What would be the Consequence of putting 200 Male and Female Convicts on Shore at Lemane unarmed, with Six Months Provision, with Articles of Trade, and without any Government, but such as they might establish amongst themselves? he. answered, That if they had Goods, and no Arms, the Natives would murder them, and seize their Goods — but that if they were armed, there probably would be a Conflict with the Blacks, who being more numerous must ultimately prevail — and that he had known different Instances of Vessels being attacked by them for the Sake of Plunder. — Being further asked his Opinion of the probable Consequence on the Trade in the River Gambia, of the projected Colony of Convicts in Lemane? he said, That the Consequence would be very prejudicial, as the Traders would not venture up the River — and that he would rather trust the Blacks than them. — He further said, That the Natives would not, in his Opinion, trade with them; and that, on account of the Climate, the Convicts could not subsist themselves by Labour — That the Island must be first cleared, and then it is uncertain of what Quality the Soil may be.

Mr. Thomas Nesbitt informed the Committee, That he was Supercargo of a Ship in 1780 — That he went into the River Gambia for the Purpose of trading in Wax and Ivory — That not meeting with either, he only stayed Four or Five Days; and was prevented going higher up, by the Information he received, that Captain Heatly, who had been up the Gambia, and continued there a Twelvemonth, lost all his Crew — That he has frequently been in Company with French Traders, who had been up the River, and who informed him, that they generally lost most of their Crews, although they took the utmost Care of them, and fed them differently from the English — That he has always understood that the River runs a great Length through a very flat Country. — Being further examined, Whether he thought it probable that the Natives would permit an Establishment of Convicts among them? he said, It appeared to him very doubtful; but that at all Events no European Trader would venture up the River; and that the Natives would revenge the Loss of their Trade, by extirpating the Convicts from the Island. — He further said, That supposing the Convicts to exist after their Provisions were expended, which he does not think probable, they could not, if confined to any One Spot, subsist by their Labour; if they were at Liberty to remove from One Part of the Continent to the other, they would have a better Chance — That a Settlement on the Coast, where there is Access for Assistance from Europe, is much safer than an Inland Situation, the Sea Breezes being found to mitigate the bad Effects of the Climate — and that it made a most material Difference as to Health, whether the new Settlers were under Military Discipline, or consisted of disorderly Persons, who were left to regulate and take Care of themselves. — Being asked, Whether an armed Vessel, stationed in the River near Lemane, for the Purpose of confining Convicts, would have the desired Effect? he said. Certainly not: and that giving Rewards to the Natives, for apprehending all the Runaways, would be Vol, 4(X

Man. p57

attended with great and useless Expence, as the Natives could not be depended on; and would sometimes steal them from the Island, either to obtain the Reward, or to employ them in their own Armies — and that the Country being divided among a great Number of Princes, it is impossible to guard against these Inconveniences by Treaty.

Mr. Henry Smeathmany who resided near Four Years on the Coast of Africa, and chiefly at Sierra Leonat informed the Committee, That he had made many Observations on the Character of the Natives, and that they are exceedingly vindictive, of which he knew many Instances, but one in particular: — The Commander of a Danish Vessel ordered the Head of a Chief of the Country to be held down to a Grind Stone, and the Hair and Skin ground off together — Near Three Years after, this Chief and his People cut oft’ a French Ship, and murdered most of the Crew, by way of retaliating on White Men, which led him to think that the Natives would take their Revenge on the first Europeans which fell in their Way, for any Injury which our Convicts might do them. — He further said, That if 200 Convicts were left on an Island in the River Gambia, without any Medical Assistance than what they might give to each other, not One in 100 would survive the first Six Months, as Persons long confined in Prisons are peculiarly unfit to struggle with an African Climate — That they would be incapable also of Labour, from being long kept in Irons on Board of Ship; and that the Salt Provisions brought from Europe would soon become rancid and unfit for Use; in which Case they must depend on the Mercy of the Natives, who might or might not be disposed to assist them.

Mr. John Boon was also examined; who informed the Committee, That he has been Surgeon to the Army in Africa, and has resided Three Years at Senegal — And being examined as to the Nature of the Climate, he said, That from about the Middle of July to the Beginning of November, Putrid Fevers usually prevail; and that Fluxes are very, general from December to the End of March; and that the former Disorder is the most fatal to Europeans, Two Thirds of the King’s Forces having perished every Year — That the Natives are not so liable to the Contagion; and to avoid it, they usually remove into the inward Parts, at some Distance from the Coast — And. he added, that in Persons affected by this Disorder, the Blood is so inclined to Putrefaction, that Gentlemen frequently died in the Space of Three or Four Hours — That the higher up the River, the more fatal the Disease — And Mr. Boon mentioned, as an Instance, the Detachment sent up every Year to Galam, consisting of a Captain, Lieutenant, Ensign, Surgeon, and a Company of Foot, from 50 to 100 Men, during the Three Years he was there, of which not One ever returned. — He further said, That he always heard of the same Sickness attending the People on the Gambia, as at Senegal; and that he thinks the Climate must be nearly the same on both Rivers — That a Field Labourer on either could not live a Month, unless he bad an able Surgeon with him, well acquainted with the Diseases of the Coun-. try; because the Soldiers who suffered in the Manner above-mentioned at Senegal, had the Advantages of being under Military Discipline, were furnishea with Provisions, with Wine and Medical Assistance, and* were exempt from Labour; yet, for Eleven Months out of the Twelve, mcfst of them were unable to do Duty. — Being examined as to his Opinion, what would be the Effect of any Convention formed with the Natives to receive a Colony of Felons, and other desperate Persons we might chuse to send out ? he answered, That no Reliance could be placed on the Faith of the Natives — That they would rob any Settlers ..... Sir George Young being also examined, acquainted the Committee; That he had been Four Times at Gambia and Senegal — That the Rains commence, on the Coast of Africa, in May, and increase till July or August\ which produce a malignant Fever, which proves very fatal to Europeans — That he supposes a Ship of War, which was to continue on any Part of the Coast, within the Tropics, during the rainy Season, would - bury 9-ioths of her Crew — And that if she was stationed the whole Year up the River, at Yannimaroo, not an Individual of the Crew would survive — That he had always considered Gambia as the most unhealthy Part of the Coast; but that at Fattitenda, 900 Miles up the Country, where the Hills commence (the whole Country being flat and unhealthy, as far as that Pass) the Climate is somewhat better, owing to the Commencement of the Freshes; and that the Sea flows 6 or 700 Miles up the River — That there are many Ponds, left by the Rains, on each Side of the River, until the hilly Country begins, which stagnating from the Heat of the Weather, produce Vermin of all Sorts, and consequently Putrid Fevers.

Sir George Young confirmed the Testimony of other Witnesses with regard to the Impossibility of restraining a Colony of Convicts, without Order or Government, within the'Limits assigned to them; and also expressed his Apprehension that none of the Traders, who now navigate the River in their Long Boats, after such an Establishment took'place would venture up it, for fear of being plundered, — He also said, tliaLt another Mischief would arise from a Colony of Convicts, that the Natives being unable to distinguish them from other Europeans engaged in the same Commerce, would consider every White Man as an English Thief, and behave to him accordingly — That if the Convicts were armed they would probably kill and rob the Natives, or if unarmed, the Natives would rob and kill them — and that a Colony so constituted would not subsist by Labour, but by. Enter-prize and Piracy. — Being asked his Opinion of the Natives; He observed, That they were very peaceable, if well treated, but very revengeful, if insulted ~He also believes that no Prince of the Country will cede any Part of his Territpry for a Colony of Convicts, if he knows them to be such. — Being further examined as to the Practicability of Europeans subsisting themselves by Field Labour within the Tropics; he said, That it had never been attempted, as Death would be the Consequence of their continuing an Hour exposed to the Sun — And as a Proof of the UnheaFthiness of the Climate, which is universally the Ca$e below the Freshes; he said, That he landed at Albreda, opposite to Swansea Fort, where there was only One French Woman, all the Men, except her Husband, being dead, and he was gone up the Country to trade; and while Sir George Young was there, $He heard that he also was dead, and every White Man that went with him, which was a very common Case, for she had had Five Husbands in Three Tears. — The Witness also acquainted the Committees, That to convey 300 Male and Female Convicts to the River (Zambia, with proper Attention to their Health, would require not less than Four Vessels, of *bput 150 or 200 Tons, with 30 Seamen to each Vessel, which must be Well secured, and the Convicts ironed every Night; and that a Man of War would be necessary to convoy them to the Place of their Destination.

" ML Call, a Member present, informed the Committee, That having been at Senegal and Gambia, in the Year 175°> he had an Opportunity of seeingmany Traders, both English and French^ as also the Frenoh

Garrison at Goree, and the Remains of the Garrison at James Forty which was reduced by Sickness, from 25 or 30 Men to 5 or 8; and the Officers being all dead, a common Soldier had succeeded to the Command — That the Europeans almost generally laboured under Fluxes or Fevers — That he did not see above Two Persons, in the Character of Gentlemen or Officers, who appeared to be in Health — That the Captain of the Vessel in which he was embarked permitted no Person to sleep in the Fort, or the Village on the opposite Side of the River, which was reported to be much more unhealthy than either of the Fi'ench Settlements at Goree or Senegal — That he has heard the Country a great Way up the River Gambia is much more healthy than near the Sea Coast; but from the Information of the French Governor at Goree, it appeared, That Mons. St. David, who Two or Three Years before had sent 300 Men up the River Senega^ w'ith Tools for working in the Gold Mines, had returned with only Three of their Party living, the Tools being also reduced to the Size of a large Wire, and totally corroded with the Rust, from the Influence of the Climate — That the Banks of the River Gambia being higher, and less flooded, the Country from that Circumstance may be less unwholesome. — Being examined, as to the Etfect of Military Discipline in Tropical Climates, he said, He was clearly of Opinion, that Military Discipline not only contributes to tbs Health of those who are subject to it, but lhajt any give® Number of Men, properly attended to by their Officers, and not employed in Duties of Fatigue, will be infinitely more healthy than the same Number of People not subject to any Controul on their Conduct. — Being further asked his Opinion, in what State of Health Person* are likely to arrive and continue, who are taken out of a Prison Ship, and conveyed in Ivpns 400 Mile* into the Continent of Africa, up the River Gambia? Mr. Call saidt That it was his Opinion they would ajv rive there in a very debilitated State, as unable aft perhaps unwilling to undertake any laborious Work j and that they would soon fall a Sacrifice to the Oik mate or the Natives, or else make some Attempt to liberate themselves; which, if they were in Force, it would not be difficult for them to effect, by the Sei of a Vessel lying in the River. — Being examined* as to the probable Effect of sending a Set of despe* rate and disorderly People into -the Country, without any one to contFoul or command them, and without Arms to defend themselves, Mr. CaH confirmed tha Testimony of other Witnesses, by giving it as lm Opinion, that they would make Depredations on the Property and Families of the Natives, which of course would instigate them to Acts of Revenge, and pro* bably would lead to the Extermination of the Cou* victs; and that if they were armed, their Attempt* upon the Property of the Natives would only be at* tended with greater Force, and the Result must be* one or other of the Events which he before pointed out — Mr. Call being desired to explain his former Answer, that the Convicts might probably seize foe, Country Boats, or master some European Vessel, for the Purpose of making their Escape; and being fur--ther asked. Whether such a Vessel as Mr. Nepean mentions in his Evidence, or an armed Sloop, might not only prevent such Escape; but also protect the Convicts themselves from the Violence of the Natives, as well as the Natives from their Depredations? he said. That undoubtedly a Vessel of Force, by which ha means one properly armed, and manned with One hundred Men or upwards, would keep both Europeans and Natives under some Subjection, as far as such a Vessel could extend her Influence; but as the Vessel would be stationed in the River near Yannimaroo, it could not have that Effect Fifty or Sixty Miles higher up; and it is very probable the Crew would be sq reduced in foe sickly Season, that unless !! Mr. Sturt, a Member present, informed the Committee, That he went to Africa ill 1782, with Three Sloops of War, and the Mackard Transport in Company, with 350 Convicts on board, wdiich were carried to Cape Coast Castle — That they were enlisted as Soldiers, and w*ere under military Discipline, with proper Officers to watch over their Conduct — That daring the Voyage they behaved very well, for Fear of the Men of War; but the Witness concludes, that had the Fleet been separated, they would have run away with the Ship — That about 20 or 30 of them died on their Voyage; and that, after their landing, they were so riotous, that their Officers were afraid of their Lives — And as a Proof of the bad Policy of sending our Convicts to Afnca} he said, that many of them deserted to the Dutch, and manned Two or Three Forts, which the British Fleet afterwards attacked — That the Witness afterwards heard, that Part ’ of these Convicts had taken a Portuguese Vessel — That the Remainder either died, or escaped into the Country, except a fewr, who remained with Captain M'Kenzie, their Commander.

Commodore Thompson informed the Committee, That he now commands His Majesty’s Ships on the Coast of Africa, and was there last Year from April to June — That he has only been in the Mouth of the Gambia, but has heard different Accounts of the Health of the interior Parts of the Country — That some Travellers report them, at the Distance of 5 or Coo Miles from the Coast, to be more healthy; but Commodore Thompson added, he had always remarked the contrary in the Countries where he has been, in -similar Parallels of Latitude — That most People, both French and English, who have traded upon the River, have described the Country as unhealthy — That the Europeans who liad resided there some Time appeared to him sickly and debilitated; and that he should imagine not 2 in 100 would exist there, if compelled to support themselves by Field Labour. — Being asked his Opinion of the Natives, Commodore Thompson answered, That they were generally Thieves, and w'ould plunder whenever they had an Opportunity — That on the Shore a Man might pass in Safety; but if he enters the Woods, he runs the utmost Risk of being murdered — And that, from Reports, and the History of the Country, he believes the Inhabitants of the Inland Country to be worse than those on the Sea Coast — That the probable Behaviour of a Colony of Criminals under no Government or Subordination, instead of altering the Disposition of the Natives, and reconciling them to an English Settlement in the Heart of their Country, would incense them to the highest Degree, and render them still more barbarous — That working in the Sun produces a Fever, which is certain Death; and that, consequently, no European could subsist by Field Labour in that Part of Africa which lies within the Tropics. — Being asked his Opinion of what would be the Condition of a King’s Ship stationed the Year round above Yannimaroo? he answered. That he imagines very few would survive to return. — Being further asked, If the Natives were to receive an Injury from any of the Convicts, what would be the Consequence to Other Europeans? he said, They would immediately demand a Punishment adequate to the Injury, an Vo l. 40.

Hint’the Offender might be given up to them; if that TraDSPofN Demand was not, or could not be complied with, they would revenge themselves on the first Europeans ' they could find; of which Commodore Thompson mentioned an Instance in regard to 6ome Marines of the Ship which he commanded, who strayed into the Woods between Goree and Gambia, and were robbed by the Negroes: On the Complaint of Commodore T/wmpson to the Negroe Captain of the Village, he took the Offenfcters, and brought them to him, and, after compelling the Restitution of the Articles stolen, he took out his Knife, and cut Three Marks on the Cheeks of the Offenders, and dismissed them. Some Marines afterwards robbed the Negroes; the Captain of the Village came to him to have the Effects restored; he asked for the People to be punished, which they were, and he was satisfied: But Commodore Thompson added, that if Satisfaction had not been mutually given, Hostilities would instantly have ensued.

— Being asked, Would they not soon be apprized of the Situation of this Colony of Convicts, arid consequently consider them as a distinct Set of People, so as not to retaliate upon innocent Traders for any Injury that the Convicts might do them? he said.

That undoubtedly they would consider the Convict as the Criminals of our Country; but if they could not secure the Convicts who hhd offended them, that they would iixliscriminately fall on any Europeans they might meet, to satisfy their Revenge. — Being asked, What Strength Great Britain has in the Gambia to keep 2 or 300 armed Convicts in Order? he answered, None. — And being further asked, What Mode could be adopted to keep them under Subjection in Lemane? lie said, That he could suggest none* as he thiuks it impracticable. — That they would escape with the Canoes, or perhaps swim out of the Island; at least, that no Vessel of War stationed at Yanmmaivo could prevent their Escape, as the upper Part of the River is full of small Islands — That he lms always heard Lemane mentioned as an Island very productive of Rice, and consequently swampy and unhealthy. — Being further examined, Whether the Natives would cede a Tract of Land for a valuable Consideration, on which a Cdony of Convicts under no Coercion or Government might establish themselves? lie said, That according to his Knowledge of the Disposition of the Negroes, for a present Gratification they would sell any Thing, and cut off the Settlers afterwards. — Being asked, Whether he knew the Fate of the 350 Convicts sent to Cape Coast as Soldiers? he acquainted the Committee, That all he heard of them was, that about 20 of them went to>

Sea on a Piratical Intent, and wfere never heara of afterwards; there were Three at Cape Coast, One a Serjeant at Dick's Cove, 'Two at Annamaboey One at Tantumquerry, and One at Accra — That this was a(

Year and a Quarter after they got there — Commodore Thompson further said, That sending Convicts into the Service of the African Cotapariy has been the Occasion of perpetual Commotion among the Natives, and has endangered in different Instances the Safety of the British Forts — and Commodore Thompson earnestly stated to the Committee, That from the present Circumstances of our African Trade, and the Rivalship of other Nations, it is peculiarly necessary to cultivate the good Opinion of the Natives of the Country; and instead of sending Persons of the worst Characters to Africa, to be very careful in the Choice of Persons to be employed in that Service, as from the small Number of Europeans, to whom a Fort, or other important Trust is committed, the personal Character of every Individual is more essential than in any other Situation which can be thought of, which he explained by the following Fact: When Mr. Wall was Governor of Goreef he, contrary to the Laws of that Country, seized several Chiefs, and sold them

Mr. Spencer Stanhope reported from the Committee, to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting Two Thirty-sixth Shares of the Navigation of the River Douglas, alias Asland\ in the County of Lancaster, Part of the settled Estates of Edward Holt, Esquire, in Trustees, to be sold, and for laying out the Money arising by such Sale in the Purchase of Lands and Hereditaments, to be settled in lieu thereof, to the same Uses, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to he true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Bill to the House, without any Amendment; and he delivered the Bill in at the Clerk’s Table.

And the said Bill was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass.

Ordered, That Mr. Spencer Stanhope do carry the Bill to the Lords; and acquaint them, that this House hath agreed to the same, without any Amendment.

Menai A Petition of the Merchants and Traders, Own-

toidoe. ers an(j Masters of Vessels, of the Port of Swansea, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appears, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented lor Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Bridge or Embankment over an Arm of the Sea between the Counties of Carnarvon and Anglesey, called The Streights of Menai, at a Place near Porthaethwy, or Bangor Ferry, and Alledging, That the free Navigation of The Streights of Menai is an Object of public Importance, the said Streights being navigable throughout for Vessels of very large Burthen, and frequented by some Thousand Sail in the Year, when they could not otherwise proceed to their Destination; and the making a Bridge or Embankment will very materially injure (by the additional Force of the Current) if not totally ruin the Navigation of the said Streights, and thereby be detrimental to the Trade and Commerce, Maritime Strength, and Revenue, of this Nation, and to the Interests of the Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying, That the Bill for making a Bridge or Embankment as aforesaid, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and others, of the County of Anglesey, and of other Parts of Great Britain, and also of the Kingdom of Ireland, is referred.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Proprietors of the Coventry Canal Navigation, in Behalf of themselves and several other Proprietors of the said Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is depending in the House for enabling the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, and the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from Birmingham to Fazeley, to make a Navigable Canal from the said Trent and Mersey Navigation on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County, in which Bill is contained a Clause for ratifying and confirming certain Articles of Agreement entered into between the said Trent and Mersey Canal Navigation Company, the said Coventry Canal Navigation Company, and the Company of Proprietors of the Oxford Canal Navigation, upon the 29th of October 1783, and declaring the 6ame to be binding and conclusive upon the said several Companies respectively, and in which Articles, a prior Agreement, entered into at a Meeting held at Coleshill, in the County of IVanvick, upon the 20th of June 1782, by Delegates from the respective Companies of Proprietors of the said Offord, Coventry, and Trent and Mersey (therein called The Grand Trunk) Canal Navigations, and from certain Projectors of, and Subscribers to, a then new-proposed Navigation from the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury, to Birmingham, and from thence to join the Coventry Canal in the Neighbourhood of Fazeley, and which the Petitioners observe to be fully recited and set out in the said Bill, was made binding and conclusive on the said Oxford, Coventry, and Grand Trunk Companies respectively; and the Petitioners further observe by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented for Leave to bring in a Bill to make Navigable the Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, with short Cuts connecting the rewith from Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, to Atherstone, in the County of Warwick, with several short Cuts branching therefrom; and that the Petitioners acknowledge the several Agreements as stated, but beg Leave to submit to the House, that the original Agreement, entered into by the Delegates on the Part of the Proprietors of the Coventry Company, and afterwards confirmed by that Company by the Articles above stated, was so entered into and 'confirmed for the Purpose, as is recited in the said original Agreement, of effecting a general Communication between the Oxford, Coventry, and Grand Trunk Canals, the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wed-nesbury, and the Town of Birmingham, and, upon this Public Ground, the said Agreements were acceded to on the Part of the Coventry Company; and that the said Coventry Company, in executing their Canal to its present Termination at the Town of Atherstone, which is about Sixteen Miles and Three Quarters, did, about Thirteen Years ago, expend the Whole of the Monies raised for the Purpose of completing the said Canal to its originally intended Junction with The Grand Trunk at Fradley Heath, the same amounting to £. 50,000, a Sum considerably exceeding the Estimate of the late Mr. Brindley of the Expence of completing the Whole to such Junction; and that, from the Time of the Expenditure of the Whole of the said £ 50,000, the Dividends made to the Proprietors of the Profits of the said Coventry Canal, have not, upon an Average, amounted to £. 2 per Centum per Annum, and the Smallness of the Dividends have not arisen from any extra Expence, Accidents, or Losses, but from Want of a sufficient Trade upon the said Canal, to make it a productive Revenue, and, exclusive of the said £.50,000, the said Company have, from their low Dividends, sustained a Loss of upwards of £. 20,000, computing £.5 per Centum Interest for their Capital; and that, at the Time of making the said Agreements, sanguine Expectations were entertained, that the Money necessary for carrying the same into Execution would have been raised, as the effecting a Communication with The Grand Trunk, and other Canals, was an Object which the Generality of the Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal were assiduous to attain, though some others, by disapproving of the Agreements, appeared not to be Friends to the Measure; and that, before the Scheme of the said lliver Navigation was known to the Coventry Company, various Expedients were devised, but which proved ineffectual, for the Purpose of raising Money to effect the above Communication, which Communication was then thought practicable in no other Way but by an Extension of the Coventry Canal in its present Parliamentary Line, and to which Line, it is the Intent of the Bill now depending, to confine it; and that the Proprietor’s of the said Coventry Canal have never lost Sight of the great National Object of completing, and rendering effectual, for all the Purposes of Commercial Intercourse, the Inland Navigation of the Kingdom, by a Communication of Canals, and, had they not been deceived by Mr. Brindley's Estimate of* the Expence, on which they relied, the Whole of their Undertaking had been long since completed, and it is now become very doubtful whether the Coventry Company can, in their present Situation, raise Money sufficient to complete their Undertaking; and that tb$ Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal did, at a General Meeting held the 29th Day of March last, under their Common Seal, declare their Resolution of not proceeding in an Application to Parliament for Powers to enable them to complete and execute the said Coventry Canal in the Manner proposed by the said Articles, because they were of Opinion, that the proposed Scheme for making Navigable the said Rivers, would be more advantageous to the Public, and because, as the Petitioners were informed and believed, the whole Money necessary for. completing the said River Navigation, was then already subscribed; and that the Object and Design of such Agreements was a Public Accommodation, and as the same is attainable in another, and, as the Petitioners are firmly persuaded, a better Mode for the Public, the Petitioners hops that they shall not uqw be obliged to fulfil the said

Agreements;

as Geo. III. 9° Mail

' Agreements; and that the Petitioners, and the other Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal, have had Surveys and Levels laid before them for making Navigable the said Rivers, as stated in the said Petition, and, the Petitioners conceive, that such River Scheme will, on an accurate Investigation, be found to answer every Public Idea, and all the avowed Public Objects of an Extension in the present Line of the Coventry Canal to Fazcley, and the Grounds of their Opinion in this Respect have arisen from a careful Examination of such Surveys and Levels, and the Information of able and experienced Engineers on the Subject, together with the Knowledge of several of the Petitioners of different Parts of the Country in the Course of the said -projected River Navigation, and the Cuts to be connected with it; and that the said River Navigation and Cuts will be executed with much less Expence, and will be used with the Advantage of Boats larger and better accommodated for the Conveyance of Merchandize, and will be attended with an easier Tonnage and Freight, and a less Waste of Land, than the Extension of the Coventry Canal, in its present Line to Fazeley, and also with the Advantage of conveying Goods in such larger Boats without unloading the whole Length from Gainsborough to Coventry: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into their Consideration, and not make the Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal liable to be called upon, in a^compulsory Way, to complete, or carry forwards, their said Canal, by any Enacting Clause in the said Bill: and that, when a Bill for making Navigable the said Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, shall be presented, pursuant t9 the Prayer of the Petition for that Purpose, that the same may pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, and that such Relief may be given to the Petitioners, and the said other Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal Navigation, in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet

A Petition of the Agents for the American Loyalists, America* in Behalf of themselves, and their Constituents, being Loyalists, offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners are Subjects of the British Empire, and, in common with their Fellow 9 ' Citizens,

j

35 Geo. III. 9° Mali. 971

Citizens, entitled to its Protection find Justice, and that by the immutable Principle* of natural Equity, and the fundamental La\Vs of all Civil Societies, the Expences, Burthens, and Sacrifices, necessary to the Common Benefit and Safety, ought to be equitably borne by all the Citizens, in a just Proportion; and that the Duties of Allegiance and Protection which form and support the Union of Society are reciprocal between the Subject and Sovereign, and mutual Considerations for each other, and therefore the Subject, who fulfils his Duty of Allegiance in Times of Public Danger, id certainly entitled to Public Protection and Indemnity; and that it* the Years 1764 and 1767, When a violent and riotous Opposition arose in Arrie-rica to the Sovereign Authority of Parliament, both Houses, by their Resolutions, declared, " That such kt Persons who had manifested a Desire to comply *£ with, or to assist in* carrying into Execution any 4t Acts of the Legislature, relating to the Colonies u in North America, ought to have full and ample *c Compensation for any Injury or Damage sustained *c on that Account," and that such Persons were entitled to, and should assuredly have, the Protection of the House of Commons of Great Britain; and that in 1775, when a dangerous Rebellion against the Sovereign Rights of the British Legislature had broke out in America, His Majesty conceived that the Aid of His Subjects would be necessary to reduce it, and therefore, by His Proclamation, He called on all for their Assistance; and, that none might neglect or violate their Duty through Ignorance thereof. He further declared; " that all His faithful Subjects were bound 16 by Law to be aiding and assisting in suppressing " the Rebellion, and that there could be no Doubt €t of the Protection which the Law would afford to " their Loyalty and Zealand that the Petitioners, in dutiful Obedience to the Call of their Sovereign, tod the Two Houses of Parliament, and, relying on the Justice and Protection thus held up before them* have* alone, stept forth from the great Body of British Subjects, who were equally called on, and equally interested in, the Public Safety, and, in Consequence of their loyal and zealous Exertions, have been deprived of their Fortunes by the Insurgents, and have besides encountered a Variety of the most imminent Dangers, and suffered extreme Distress, from which their Fellow Subjects have been entirely exempt, and for which this House can make them no adequate Compensation; and, that moreover the Estates and Fortunes of the Petitioners, which the British Government, by the essential Laws of its Union, was bound to regain, and restore to them, have been devoted and (ceded by that Government to the American States, as the Purchase and Price of Peace for the whole Empire; thus circumstanced, the Petitioners conceive, that they have, under the fundamental Laws of the British Constitution, the Resolutions of both Houses of Parliament, the Royal Faith pledged to them itt His Majesty’s Proclamation, and under all the Precedents of Parliamentary Justice, 011 similar, and much less meritorious Occasions, not only an equitable, blit ft lawful Right, to a just Compensation for their Estates and Property, so devoted to the National Peace and Safety* and nothing less than an equal Distribution of their Losses thus incurred among their Fellow Subjects, who are in the Enjoyment of the Benefits and Security so purchased at their Efcpence* tan be consistent with Law and Justice; and that in the Year 1783, sensible of the Justice due to the Pie* titioners, Parliament passed an Act, appointing Com-hiissioners to enquire into their Losses thus sustained* for the Purpose of making them due Compensation* and, the Commissioners, having investigated a large Number of their Claims, have made Tw*o several Reports thereof to the Lords of His Majesty’s Tre*" Vol. 40.

sury, which, the Petitioners have Reason to b&ievfe, American contain their Decision on what has been lost by the Loyalists, respective Claimants, who anxiously expected that the said Reports would have been laid before the House, in order that Compensation might be made to those comprehended in them; and that it is impossible to describe the poignant Distress under which many of the American Loyalists now labour, and which must daily encrease, should the Justice of Parliament be delayed until all the Claims are liquidated and reported, but the Petitioners would be greatly deficient in their Duty to their Constituents, if they should omit to represent to the Consideration of the House, that Ten Years have elapsed, since many of them havte been deprived of their Fortunes, and, with their helpless Families, reduced, from independent Affluence, to Poverty and Want, some of them are now languishing in British Gaols, others indebted to their Creditors, who have lent them Money barely to support their Existence, and who, unless speedily relieved, must sink more than the Value of their Claims when received, and be in a worse Conch tion than if they never made them; others have already sunk under the Pressure and Severity of their Misfortunes; and others must, in all Probability, soon meet the same melancholy Fate, should the Justice due to them be longer postponed, notwithstanding the temporary Support which the Petitioners thankfully acknowledge has been given from His Majesty’s Civil List, and re-imbursed by Parliament: but that, on the contrary, should Provision be now made for Payment of those whose Claims have been settled and reported, it will not only relieve them from their Distress, but give a Credit to the others, whose Claims remain to be considered, and enable all of them to provide for their wretched Families, and to become again useful Members of Society: And therefore praying, That the House will take their Case under Consideration, and make such Provision for the Payment of the Sums adjudged to be due to the respective Claimants* as the House shall think reasonable; or, if this cannot be done; in the present Session, That (he House would, by a Vote, now declare, that the Claims re* ported, and to be reported by the Commissioners, shall be considered as a Part of die Unfunded Debts Of the Nation; and, that if any Doubt should remain respecting their Right to the Sums reported to be due, that they may be beard by Counsel at the Bar of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Joseph Wilkes, of Overseal, in the County of Leicester, Gentleman, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is One of the Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, made by virtue of an Act passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for making a Navigable Cut or Canal from the River Trent, at or near Wilden Ferry, in the County of Derby, to the River Mersey, at or near Runcorn; and that a Bill is now depending before the House, for enabling the Company of Proprietors of the said Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey (commonly called The Grand Trunk Company) and the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from Birmingham to Fazelty, to make a Navigable Canal from the said Trent
