Trent and Mersey Navigation, on Fradiey Heath, in the County of Stafford, to in the said County,

by which Bill it is proposed, that the said Trent and Mersey Company, and Birmingham and Fazeley Company, shall make and compleat a Line of Canal or Cut, from Fradiey Heath to Fazeley, which belongs to, and ought to be performed by the Coventry Canal Company, in pursuance of the Powers vested in the said Coventry Canal Company, by an Act made in the Eighth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign; and, by the said Bill, the Property of the said Grand Trunk Company is intended to be made a collateral Security for the Expence to be incurred in making their Part of the said Cut from Fradiey Heath to Fazeley, and thereby the Property of the Petitioner, and the other Proprietors of the said Grand Trunk Company, is exposal to Loss, and -may be much injured; and that in the said Bill is contained a Clause for enabling the said Coventry Canal Company to purchase and redeem the Property of so much of the said Cut from Fradiey Heath to Fazeley, as is intended by the said Bill to be vested in the said Grand Trunk Company, if the said Coventry Canal Company should choose so to do, within a certain Time therein specified; and, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Property of the Petitioner, and the other Proprietors of the said Grand Trunk Company, will be subjected to an inevitable Loss and Expence, for, if the Undertaking of the said Cut from Fradiey Heath to should appear, and have the Prospect of producing an ample Revenue, the Coventry Company will have a Power to repossess themselves of the said Cut; but, should the Undertaking be attended with greater Expence than the Tolls arising therefrom will be likely to satisfy and compensate, then the Loss will fall upon the Petitioner, and the other Proprietors of the Grand Trunk Company: And the Petitioner, therefore, in Behalf of himself and the other Proprietors of the Grand Trunk Company, begs Leave to address himself to the Justice and Equity of the House, That neither the Property of the Petitioner, nor of the said Grand Trunk Company, may be invaded or diminished by the said Bill; and that he may be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, that it may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Cheesemongers of the Cities of Trent, Tame, London and Westminster, and of the Borough of South- &c. Canal. work, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners find, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented for Leave to bring in a Bill to make navigable the Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, with some short Cuts connecting the rewith, from Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, to Atherstone, in the County of Warwick, with several short Cuts branching therefrom; and that the Petitioners are considerable Dealers, and very materially concerned in the Carriage of Cheese, the Produce as well of the Counties through which the said Rivers so intended to be made Navigable run, as of the adjoining Counties; that Cheese is a valuable and perishable Article, and the Petitioners, and the Trade in general, have suffered very great Loss and Inconvenience from the Construction and Narrowness of Canal Boats, and, if the said Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, are made Navigable, the Petitioners apprehend that a considerable Advantage will arise in the Carriage of the Commodity in which they are concerned, as well as of other Goods and Merchandize, from the Construction and larger Size of the Boats that will be navigated upon the said Rivers, which will tend to the Decrease of the Rates of Tonnage and Freight, and be attended with greater'Safety and Dispatch: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that, when such Bill for making navigable the said Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, shall be presented, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition, the same may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee to whom the Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, Traders, and Inhabitants of the Town of Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, and the Neighbourhood thereof, and also, of the Bailiffs, Commonalty, and Inhabitants of the Borough of Tam-worth, in the Counties of Stafford and Warwick, and ethers whose Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the further Sum of One Million be raised by Loans, or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament, and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged,

with Interest thereupon, oh or before the 5th Day of April 1786, to be exchanged and received in Payment in such Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons interested in, or entitled unto, any Bills payable in Course of the Navy or Victualling Offices, or for Transports, which were dated on or before* the 30th Day of June 1783, who shall, on or before the 5th Day of June 1785, carry the same (after having had the Interest due thereupon computed up to the 5th Day of July 1785, and marked upon the said Bills at the Navy or Victualling Offices respectively) to the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, shall have in Exchange for the same, from such Treasurer, or his Paymaster, or Cashier, a Certificate to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, for the Amount of the Principal and Interest computed thereupon, and the Persons who shall be possessed of such Certificates, upon Delivery thereof to the said Governor and Company of the Bank of England, shall be entitled, in respect of the same, to One hundred and Eleven Pounds Eight Shillings Capital Stock for every One hundred Pounds contained in such Certificates, and so in Pro-ortion for any greater or lesser Sum, such Capital tock to be attended with Annuities after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, to commence from the 5th Day of July 1785, payable Half Yearly, in lieu of all other Interest, the said Annuities to be irredeemable until Twenty-five Millions of the Public Debt, bearing Interest at the Rate of either Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, or Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, shall have been redeemed or paid off; and that all Persons interested in, or entitled unto, such Navy, Victualling, and Transport Bills, made out between the said 30th Day of June 1783 and the 1st Day of January 1785, who shall, on or before the 5th Day of June 1785, carry the same (after having had the Interest due upon such of the said Bills as now bear an Interest, computed and marked upon the said Bills, to the 5th Day of July 1785, at the Navy and Victualling Offices, respectively) to die Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, shall have, in Exchange for the same, from such Treasurer, or his Paymaster, or Cashier, a Certificate to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, for the Amount of the Principal and Interest computed thereupon, after deducting therefrom a Sum at the Rate of Five Shillings pet Centum upon the Amount of such Principal and Interest for every Month, between the 1st Day of July 1783 and the Day on which such Bill was made out, and the Persons who shall be possessed of such Certificates, upon Delivery thereof to the said Governor and Company of the Bank of England, shall be entitled, in respect of the same, to One hundred and Eleven Pounds Eight Shillings Capital Stock for every One hundred Pounds contained in such Certificates, and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Sum, such Capital Stock to be attended with Annuities after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, to commence from the 5th Day of July 1785, payable Half Yearly, in lieu of all Interest, the said Annuities to be irredeemable until Twenty-five Millions of the Public Debt, bearing Interest at the Rate of either Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, or Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, shall have been redeemed or paid off, the Whole of the said Annuities to be charged upon a Fund to be established in this Session of Parliament, and for which the Fund commonly called The Sinking Fund, shall be a Collateral Security.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons interested in, or entitled unto, any Debentures payable out of His Majesty’s Office of Ordnance, which were dated bn or before the 31st Day of December 1783, who shall, on or beforb the 5th Day of June 1785, carry the same to the Treasurer of

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties riow charged upon Male Servants, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid or payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards raSsing the Supply granted to His Majesty* there be charged upon and paid to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, by every Person who shall retain or employ any Male Servant, or Servants, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, the several Yearly Sums following, that is to say, for One Male Servant, and not more than Two Male Servants, the Sum of One Pound Five Shillings each; for Three, and not more than Four Male Servants, the Sum of One Pound Ten Shillings each; for Five, and not more than Seven Male Servants, the Sum of One Pound Fifteen Shillings each; for Eight, and not more than Ten Male Servants, the Sum of Two Pounds each; and for Eleven Male Servants, and upwards, the Sum of Three Pounds for each, except those Servants who shall be retained or employed solely for the Purposes of Husbandry or Manufactures, or of any Trade or Calling by which the Master or Mistress of such Servants earn a Livelihood or Profit.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a proportionable Part of the said Duties be applied to the Uses to which the former Duties were applicable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to |iis Majesty, there be charged and paid to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, by every Person who shall retain or employ any Female Servant, or Female Servants, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, the several Yearly Sums following, that is to say, for One Female Servant, the Sum of Two Shillings and Six Pence; for Two Female Servants the Sum of Five Shillings each; and for Three or more Female Servants, the Sum of Ten Shillings each; except those Servants who shall be retained or employed solely for the Purposes of Manufactures, or of any Trade or Calling by which the Master or Mistress of such Female Servants earn a Livelihood or Profit.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every House, or other Building, now, or hereafter to be erected, any Part of which shall, for the Time being, be used as a Shop publicly kept open for the Purpose of carrying on any Trade, or in which shall be gold any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, by Retail, or upon every Building, or Place, used as a Shop only for the Purposes before mentioned, there Vojl. 40.

shall be charged a Yearly Duty, according to these- Waysan^ veral and respective Rates following, thereon, over Means, and above all other Duties now payable, that is to say, for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Five Pounds, and not exceeding Ten Pounds, the Annual Sum of One Shilling in the Pound of such Rent; for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Ten Pounds, and not exceeding Fifteen Pounds, the Annual Sum of One Shilling and Three Pence in the Pound of such Rent; for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Fifteen Pounds, and not exceeding Twenty Pounds, the Annual Sum of One Shilling and Six Pence in the Pound of such Rent; for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Twenty Pounds, and not exceeding Twenty-five Pounds, the Annual Sum of One Shilling and Nine Pence in the Pound of such Rent; for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Twenty-five Pounds, and upwards, the Annual Sum of Tw'O Shillings in the Pound of such Rent.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duties now charged upon, and payable by, Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid or payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Rates and Duties granted by an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for repealing an Act,

" made in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting " to His Majesty certain Duties on Licences to be " taken out by all Persons letting Horses to Hire for " travelling, in the Manner therein mentioned, and " certain Duties on all Horses let to Hire for the " Purposes of travelling Post, and by Time, and " upon certain Carriages therein mentioned/* and for " granting other Duties in lieu thereof;’* and also, by an Act, made in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for granting to His Majesty an additional Duty " upon Stage Coaches, and other Carriages therein " mentioned," shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid and payable, except only such Monies as shall have been received, or shall be payable, by the several Postmasters, Innkeepers, and other Persons, for and on Account of the said Rates and Duties, and which shall be unaccounted for and unpaid by them to the several Collectors appointed, by virtue of the said Act, to receive the same, and the several Bonds given in pursuance of the said Act.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Postmaster, Innkeeper, or other Person, in the Kingdom of Great Britain, who shall let to Hire any Horse for the Purpose of travelling Post by the Mile, or from Stage to Stage, or being a Person usually letting Horses to Hire, shall let to Hire, for a Day, or any less Period of Time, any Horse for drawing any Coach, Chaise, or any other Carriage, used in travelling Post, or otherwise, by whatsoever Name such Carriages now are, or hereafter may be, called or known, for or in respect whereof any Rates or Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise now are made payable by any Statute or Statutes heretofore made, and now in Force, shall yield and pay Annually unto His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, the Sum of Five Shillings for a Licence for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for and in respect of every Horse hired by the Mile or Stage, to be used in travelling Post, in the Kingdom of Great Britain, there be charged a Duty of One Penny Halfpenny for every Mile such Horse shall be hired to travel Post, such Duty to be paid

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for and in respect of every Horse hired for a Day, or less Period of Time, for drawing on a Post, or other public lload, any Coach, Chaise, or any other Carriage used in travelling Post, or otherwise, by whatsoever Name such Carriages now are, or hereafter may be, called or known, for or in respect whereof any Rates or Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise now are made payable by any Statute or Statutes heretofore made, and now in Force, there shall be charged, if the Distance shall be then ascertained, the Sum of One Penny Halfpenny per Mile, and, if the Distance shall not be then ascertained, there shall be charged the Sum of One Shilling and Niue Pence, for and in respect of each Horse so hired, such Duty to be paid by the Person or Persons, by whom such Horse shall be so hired or used.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person who shall keep any Coach, Berlin, Landau, Chariot, Calash, or other Carriage, with Four Wheels, or any Calash, Chaise, Chair, or other Carriage, with Two Wheels, by what Name soever the same now is, or hereafter shall be, called or known, to be employed as public Stage Coaches, or Carriages, for the Purpose of conveying Passengers for Hire to and from different Places in tha Kingdom of Great Britain, shall yield and pay Annually unto His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, the Sum of Five Shillings for a Licence for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Coach, Berlin, Landau, Chariot, Calash, or other Carriage, with Four Wheels, and every Calash, Chaise, Chair, or other Carriage, with Two Wheels, by what Name soever the same now is, or hereafter shall be, called or known, to be employed as public Stage Coaches, or Carriages, for the Purpose of conveying Passengers for Hire to and from different Places, in the Kingdom of Great Britain, there shall be charged a Duty of One Penny for every Mile such Carriage shall travel, to be paid by the Owner or Owners thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a proportional Part of the said Duties be applied to the same Uses - as the former Duties were applicable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be raised, levied, collected, and paid to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, by all Persons uttering or vending, in Great Britain, any Gloves, or Mittens, made of Silk) Leather, or any other Material, by Retail, a Stamp Duty of One Shilling, for a Licence to be Annually taken out for that Purpose.

Rcsolvedy That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be charged upon every Pair of Gloves or Mittens, above the Value of Four Pence, and not exceeding the Value of Ten Pence, a Stamp Duty of One Penny; and of the Value of Ten Pence, and under the Value of One Shilling and Four Pence, a Stamp Duty of Two Pence; and above the Value of One Shilling and Four Pence, a Stamp Duty of Three Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, all Persons using or exercising the Trade or Business of a Pawnbroker, within the Cities of London and Westminster, the Parishes of Saint Mary le Bone, and Saint Pancras, in the County of Middlesex, or within the Distance of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, or within the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, shall take out an Annual Licence, and be charged with a Stamp Duty of Ten Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, all Persons using or exercising the Trade or Business of a Pawnbroker in any other Part of the Kingdom of Great Britain, shall take out an Annual Licence, and be charged with a Stamp Duty of Five Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Allowances for Waste on White and Refined Salt, and Rock Salt, carried Coastwise, be reduced.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be ‘issued and applied the Sum of Sixty-six thousand One hundred and Sixty-one Pounds Three Shillings and Five Pence Halfpenny, now remaining in the Exchequer, being the Overplus of the Grants for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four.

Com and A Petition of the Magistrates, Merchants, and chief

Grain. Inhabitants of the Town and Port of Whitehaven, in the County of Cumberland, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for further regulating and u ascertaining the Importation and Exportation of " Corn and Grain, within several Ports and Places <c therein mentioned," and for extending the Powers and Provisions thereof to all Places within that Part of Great Britain called England; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive, the said Bill contains sundry Clauses, which, if passed into a Law, would be productive of much Injury and Distress to great Numbers of His Majesty’s Subjects; and that the Principle of the said Bill, which proposes to divest the Grand Jurors, at Quarter Sessions, of the Power delegated by former Acts, which authorized them to ascertain and certify the Average Prices of Grain within their respective Counties, and transferring such Authority to an Individual in London, is d dangerous Innovation, and that the Average Prices of Grain in the London Market can never be a Criterion for the whole Kingdom, the Experience of any particular Month in the Year will sufficiently prove; and that the Petitioners, in common with some Millions of His Majesty’s Subjects residing at a great Distance from the Metropolis, apprehend a Variety of evil Consequences from the proposed entire Change in the System which has long been attended with such happy Effects in permitting, as the Necessities of the Times required, either the Importation or Exportation of Grain at the Ports of the respective Counties; and, the Petitioners conceive, this Privilege would be frequently infringed, if not totally abrogated, by the said Bill, as the Average Prices of Com in the London Market may frequently, from a Variety of Circumstances, exceed the limited Importation Prices at the very Time when the Average Prices at the Out Ports ‘may be at, or under, the limited Prices for Exportation, and so vice versa; and that, when the ^Averages Prices at the London Market prohibit the Importation of Foreign Grain, the Average Prices in the Northern Part of the Kingdom may be, as they have frequently been at former Periods, in the Proportion of Sixty to Forty-eight, and, in such Circumstances, the Petitioners, and great Numbers of

His Majesty’s Subjects, can have no Alternative but by having recourse to London for a Supply, which, when loaded with the additional Expences of Freight, Insurance, Commission, 8$c. will occasion an Advance of at least Sixteen per Cent. above what the Inhabitants of London will be charged, and , an unsur-mountable Disadvantage will arise from such Circumstances', as the Grain cannot be brought through so tedious a Passage without receiving evident Damage, as a Proof of which, the Petitioners wish to advert to the constant Practice of Underwriters, who uniformly refuse to insure Grain otherwise than free of all partial Damage: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the said*

Bill from passing into a Law.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, and other Corn and Inhabitants of the City of Exeter, whose Names are Grain, thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House,' and read; likewise Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That, the Petitioners apprehend, the Object of such Bill is, that the Prices of Cora and Grain, throughout the Kingdom, should be regulated from the General Average Prices thereof at Mark Lane, within the City of London, to be ascertained in such Manner as in the said Bill is mentioned, and, that from thence, the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain, as well at London as at every Out Port, should be governed, without any Reference to the Difference and Fluctuation of the Prices in different Markets; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the Law, as it now stands, with respect to the Importation and Exportion of Corn and Grain, has been attended with great Advantage, and that, at present, the Prices are fairly and impartially ascertained in the Country by Persons most competent to the Subject, but, on the contrary, the Petitioners apprehend, that the Plan, for regulating the Prices of Corn and Grain, proposed by the said Bill, is liable to very great and serious Objections, and, if passed into a Law, will subject the Petitioners, and all Persons resident in Parts of the Kingdom at any considerable Distance from the Metropolis, to great Inconvenience, Injury, and Oppression: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into their Consideration, and that the said Bill, in its present Form, may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be permitted to be heard, by their Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as materially affect their Interests.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Commercial A Petition of the Tanners of London, was presented Intercourse to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the with Ireland. Petitioners, during the Time that the Propositions for settling the Commercial Treaty with Ireland, now before the House, have been pending, have been anxious to procure every Degree of Information on that complicated Subject, and, lest they should proceed on Misinformation, have deferred petitioning till this late Period, convinced, however, that if the proposed Regulations are passed into a Law, the Manufacture of Tanned Leather, already in a declining State, will be left in a Situation which will enable Ireland to rival her in this Staple Commodity of the Kingdom, and render the various Disadvantages under which this Country now labours perpetual; and that the Petitioners are constrained, by a Sense of that Duty they owe to themselves, as well as to Posterity, and also from an ardent Wish for the Prosperity of the Manufactures of this Kingdom, to represent to the House the alarming Situation in which they conceive this important Branch of Manufacture . will be placed, and, confiding in the Wisdom of the House, express their Hopes, that such Measures may not be adopted in the Settlement of the Commercial Treaty with Ireland, as shall prove destructive to the Manufacture of Tanned Leather in this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the Propositions passing into a Law;

Ditto. A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council

of Montrose, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are fully sensible of the many Advantages which would arise to Great Britain as well as to Ireland, if a permanent Treaty of Commerce between them could be established on Principles really reciprocal, but, as far as they are able to judge of the System contained in the Resolutions passed in the Parliament of Ireland, they cannot but regard them as big with Danger to the Trade, Manufactures, and "Landed Interest of this Kingdom; they consider them as particularly alarming with respect to the Linen Manufacture, the Staple Article of this Part of the Country, which is already in a declining State, the fine Fabricks being almost entirely engrossed by the Irish, and the coarser depending altogether on the Bounty granted in this Kingdom for Exportation; and that the Petitioners think that, on the Principles of natural Justice, Ireland cannot claim an equal Share of all the Commercial Benefit, without taking upon herself a proportional Part of all the Burthens of Great Britain: For these, therefore, and other important Reasons, which have been urged in the numerous Petitions already presented to the House, the Petitioners pray, That the House will not determine any Thing during the present Session of Parliament on a Subject when a Decision once given cannot easily be retracted, but will allow Time and Leisure to digest proper Measures for settling a Treaty which, 'in its Consequences, may so materially affect Ages yet unborn.

A Petition of the Merchants, Factors, and others concerned in the Importation and Exportation, and in the Manufacturing, of Corn and Grain, within the Port of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the lleign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, u An Act for further regulating and ascertaining the (€ Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain " within several Ports and Places therein mentioned," and for extending the Powers and Provisions thereof to all Places within that Part of Great Britain called England; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe with Concern, that, by certain Clauses in such Bill, the Powers which have, for a great Number of Years, been vested in the Grand Juries at the Quarter Sessions in the several Counties, by divers Acts of Parliament, to enquire and present, on their Oaths, the Prices of English Corn and Grain, in order to regulate the Importation of Foreign Grain, are to be totally annihilated, and, the Petitioners conceive, the Provisions already established for regulating the Importation and Exportation of Grain, which have stood the Test of so many Years Experience, are founded in great Wisdom and sound Policy, having for their Basis the Encouragement of Agriculture, the Promotion of Trade and Navigation, and the general Benefit of the Public, therefore the Petitioners are justly alarmed lest any Alteration thereof may be attended with very pernicious Effects; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the intended Bill has for. its Object a dangerous Monopoly (however specious the Pretence) and, if suffered to pass into a Law, would be highly injurious to the Kingdom in general, and to the County of Devon in particular, as it would be in the Power of a few opulent Vol. 40.

and interested Individuals so to manage the Average Prices of Corn in Mark Lane, as to prevent the Export and Import thereof at any of the Out Ports of the Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their most serious Consideration, and that the Regulations for the Import and Export of Corn and Grain may remain as they now stand, without any Alteration whatsoever.

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, Burgesses, Merchants, and Inhabitants, of the Borough and Parish of Barnstaple, in the County of Devon, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That, the Petitioners conceive, the Provisions already established, as to the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain, are founded in Wisdom and true Policy, and are extended to the general Benefit of the Public, therefore the Petitioners fear any Innovation - or Alteration thereof, as intended by the present Bill, may have a very dangerous Effect, especially as it carries a strong Appearance of a Monopoly and Partiality to the London Market; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the providing against Calamities that may happen for Want of, as w^ell as supplying, the Necessaries of Life, by the quickest Dispatch, and most reasonable Manner, has been ever the Object of Legislative Attention, and therefore conceive, that, should the present Bill pass into a Law, these salutary Measures will be defeated, as too much Time will be taken up in notifying the Prices of Grain to the remote Parts of the Kingdom, by which Means, in Times of Scarcity, many Thousands of His Majesty’s Subjects may be reduced to the greatest Distress: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the said Bill from passing into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table* until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Commercial others, of the Town and Neighbourhood of Man-Chester, was presented to the House, and read; Set- w ting forth, That the Petitioners are very sensible of the many Advantages which would arise, as well to England as to Ireland, from the Establishment of an equitable and permanent Treaty of Commerce with their Sister Kingdom, and are therefore far from wishing to impede Government from making such a Treaty; but, before the Resolutions of the Irish Parliament pass through the House, the Petitioners beg Leave to call its Attention to the following Facts and Considerations: The Petitioners beg Leave to inform the House, that, prior to the Excise Laws being introduced into the Cotton Manufactures of England and Scotland\ a very formidable and successful Experiment was made in Ireland to establish that most valuable Manufacture, and since the Introduction of the said Excise Laws, which operate as a considerable Bounty on the Irish Manufacture, the Petitioners have every Reason to apprehend that the British Market itself will soon be supplied from Ireland, should these Resolutions pass into a Law: That, besides the Excise Laws under which the Cotton Manufacture now groans, the Petitioners beg Leave to draw the Attention of the House to other Circumstances, highly advantageous to Ireland, the Cheapness of Provisions, the Difference in the Price of Labour, the almost total Exemption from internal Taxation, comparatively with England: That the raw Material, in some Branches of the Manufacture of Manchester, is the Product of Ireland; that this Material can be carried through the first Stages of the Manufacture much cheaper in Ireland than in England; that when in this Stage, namely, Linen Yarn, it is essentially necessary to the carrying on several Branches of the Petitioners Business; that they have purchased Annually, upon an Average of Four of the last Years, Linen Yarn to the Amount of £-176,531. 8 s. 9 d. and of Worsted Yarn to the Amount of £.36,079. 6$. 3^. making together the Sum of £.212,610. 155.; that these raw Materials the Petitioners pay, upon some of them, above £. 10 per Cent.; and, upon an Average of the whole Linen Yam, hot less than £ 7 £ per Cent, more than the Irish Manufacturer, in Duties imposed by Ireland, and in Freight, Insurance, Commissions, and sundry other Charges; and that, if this Yam was to be spun in England, it would come much dearer to them, from the greater Expence of Living, and the heavy internal Taxation under which the Petitioners labour; and that the Petitioners hope, when the House considers the many Advantages Ireland will enjoy over England, that, in order to create and establish a fair and equitable Treaty between the Manufacturing Interests of both Nations they will think that no Treaty ought to be made but what is established upon such Principles of Equity that will preclude each Country from any just Cause of Complaint; but the Petitioners observe, with equal Sorrow and Surprize, that, when the Terms of the present Resolutions are compared with the local Situations, and other Circumstances of the Manufacturers of the Two Kingdoms, the Advantages appear to be

d

25 Geo. in.

12' Mail.

987

11 on one Side, all in Favour of Ireland; and the Petitioners beg Leave to state the Disadvantages they labour under now, and have for some Time suffered in their Foreign Markets, through the partial, not to say impolitic, Laws in Favour of Irish Linens, to the Exclusion of other Linens from our Market, and the Depression of our own: In Russia there is now existing an Impost of £.30 per Cent. ad Valorem, upon some of our English Manufactures, and in Germany a prohibitory Edict is now hovering over our Heads, suspended for a short Time, but which, in all Probability, the Determination of the British Legislature on the Irish Resolutions will decide; but, instead of leaving an Opening for a Commercial Regulation with those States who are so able, and have hitherto shewn themselves willing, upon the Principles of Reciprocity, to increase, in a very considerable Degree, the Consumption of British Manufactures, the Legislature of this Country should preclude themselves from the Power of hearkening to fair and advantageous Offers, and should lightly and precipitately bind themselves from ever doing so, it may merit the most serious Consideration of die House, what Measures the Petitioners, as Subjects and Manufacturers of this Nation, are to expect from Powers so circumstanced; but the Petitioners do not confine their Views to the Danger arising, immediately and directly, from these Resolutions, as affecting the Manufacturers of Man-Chester only, but feel themselves equally entitled, as Subjects of this Country, to protest against all the Propositions, taken aggregately, as , a new and destructive System of Commercial Policy, particularly the 2d, 3d, and 5th Resolutions, which, by universally undermining the Commercial Interests of Great Britain, must consequently affect every Trade and Manufacture»within it, the Prosperity of which depend evidently upon the general Wealth, Commerce, and Prosperity of the whole Nation; the Interest of all the different Branches of Trade and Manufacture in a Country must ever be nearly the same; if a Nation is impoverished and depopulated by a general Decline of its Commerce, every particular Trade and Manufacture, which can only flourish from the Population and Riches of the whole Country, must languish and decline; if the Revenue be affected, as it must be by the Consequence of the 2d, 3d, and 5th Resolutions upon general Commerce and Manufactures, new Burthens must fall upon the Subject, and upon all the Necessaries of Life in this Country, and these new Imposts must operate as direct Burthens upon every Manufacture, the Cheapness of which depends on the Cheapness of Labour, and of the Materials of which they are composed; and that the Petitioners have too high a Sense of the Liberality and Generosity of the Irish Nation to suppose them capable of even wishing to rise to Greatness upon the Ruins of the British Nation: And therefore praying, That the House will reject the whole System before them, as unjust, unwise, unreasonable, and impolitic, not having either Equity, Equality, or Reciprocity, for its Basis.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Tanners, and other Dealers iri Commercial Tanned Leather, in London, was presented to the Intercourse House, and read; Setting forth, That a Petition has *lth Ireland* been already presented to the House by the Tanners of London, setting forth, in general Terms, the great Injury likely to be produced to the Manufacture of Leather, by the proposed Commercial Treaty with Ireland, in which Petition they did implore the Aid and Protection of the House, and to be allowed to lay the Particulars of their. Case before them, by Evidence, and to be heard by their Counsel upon it; and that the said Petition has, as the Petitioners are informed, been referred to the Committee on the Irish Propositions, but the House not having been pleased to permit any Counsel, or Witnesses, to be heard in Support thereof, nor to receive, in that Mode; the very important Information which was intended to be laid before the House, the Petitioners hope they shall not be deemed w anting in Respect to the House, if, upon a Subject in which they are Individually so deeply interested, and which on account of the Magnitude and Extent of the Manufacture, the Number of Persons employed in it, and the large Revenue Annually yielded from it to the Public, justly ought to be, and ever has been deemed, a great Object of National Concern, they presume to solicit the Attention of the House to some of the Facts which might have been substantiated by Evidence, if, to the Wisdom of the House, it had appeared proper to hear it, and upon which the Apprehensions ’ and Alarm of the Petitioners are principally founded;

The Petitioners conceive, that, in taking a comparative View of the State of this Manufacture in England and Ireland\ many natural ‘Advantages will be found to be possessed by the latter, exclusive of the general ones of Situation, which must, unless counterbalanced. by Regulations favourable to the English Manufacturer, unavoidably tend to depress the Manufacture of England, already very materially affected, if not to transfer the Whole of it to Ireland; and the Petitioners therefore beg Leave to observe, that Ireland, being a Grazing Country, abounds with Raw Materials for the Manufacture of Leather,‘ very considerable Quantities of which have been Annually exported to this Country, the Petitioners are not pre* pared to say, with Precision, what Quantities, but they believe, in some Years, not less than from 60 to 70,000 Raw Hides, and from 26" to 24,000 Dozen

the Quality of the Goods is also unavoidably injured by salting or drying, the Only Methods of curing them for Exportation; add to which, the important Consideration of the Difference in the Price of Labour, not being less than £.30 per Cent, in a Manufacture carried on, principally by Labourers, in whom very little Skill is required: The Petitioners are aware, that it has been uYged, the Advantages Ireland has in her Raw Material is counterbalanced by the high Price which she pays for her Bark imported from this Country, and therefore beg Leave to state to the House what they know of this Pact, which is, that the Irish Agent can buy Bark &s cheap as the English Tanner, after which, no Dufy being imposed on that Article, it may, from the Vicinity of our Coasts to Ireland, be exported at a Freight of about 17$. per Ton, which is less than the Same Article costs by Land Carriage, to many of the British Manufacturers, and thus the Irish Tanner may have this important Article nearly as cheap as the Manufacturer of this Metropolis, and even cheaper than the British Tanner in some Parts of this Island; and that the Petitioners beg Leave to call the Attention of the House to the rapid Effects produced by these Advantages, since the Allowance given to their Operation by the Act of Parliament, passed in the Year 1780, since which Time, it appears, that the Imports of Raw Material into this Country have gradually declined, and the Exports of Manufactured Leather in Ireland have rapidly increased, its, by Reference to the Custom House Books of Ireland, they apprehend, will irtcontrovertibly appear, ted therefore the Petitioners think they may fairly Assume; that, no new Markets having been opened, those Customers have been served from Ireland, which were, before that Period, supplied from the English Market, and which, indeed, the declining State of the Manufacture of Tanned Leather, in this Country, fully evinces, it having gradually been falling in Price, owing to the diminished Demand for Exportation both of wrought and unWrought Leather, and which declining State of the Manufacture must soon have compelled the Petitioners to apply to Parliament for Relief; and that the Petitioners beg Leave ftlrther to State to the House, that, in the Article of Cut Leather (considerable Quantities of which are exported from this Country, and which being allowed no Drawback, go Abroad, with the full Duty of £. 15 per Cent. Whefeas Ireland having no internal Duty on ner Leather, and h Very trifling one on her Exports) the Irish Manufacturer will, if the present Propositions pass into a Law, be for ever enabled to undersell the Manufacturer of this Country by £. 15 pet Cent, a Consequence this, the Petitioners conceive to be truly alarming; and also the Petitioners beg Leave further to represent, that the Manufacture of Leather, in this Country, which has ever been considered as one of its staple Commodities, cannot, in the Conception of the Petitioners, be fully secured by any countervailing Duties, not only from the probable Inadequacy of them in any Mode of Regula-tidh, to the Duty paid by the English Manufacturer On the Whole Hide or Skin, but also because the Du-ife* Which AfA intended to countervail, amounting, as

A. 1785.

the Petitioners are informed, to about £. 25 per Cent* will hold out a strong Temptation for Smuggling;, which will be greatly facilitated by the close Package of Shoes, and Cut Leather; and that the Petitioners also conceive themselves bound1, under the present Circumstances, to represent to the House, the Injury that the Revenue must suffer by the Decline of the Manufacture of Leather, a Consideration, they apprehend, that enters deeply into this Question, anrf is, in the highest Degree, worthy the Attention of the British Legislature: That, labouring under these general Disadvantages in their Competition with the Irish Manufacturer, the Petitioners still hoped for Protection and Relief, from the Check which the Possession of Bark enabled England at any Time to impose on the Irish Trade, if such a Check was found necessary; the Petitioners also relied on deriving some Assistance from the Prohibition imposed on the Export of Raw Hides from England, by the Statute of the 13th and 14th of Charles the Second,

Chap. II. Sec. 7, under the Penalty of £.500, th*

Pain of perpetual Disability to trade or deal in Leather for the future, and the Danger of committing what the Legislature in that Act has declared to be a Common Nuisance; the Petitioners had also placed considerable Dependance on the Prohibitory Duties now imposed on any Leather, wrought or unwrought; imported from Ireland into this Country, whereby the English Market is preserved entire to the English Manufacturer; and the Petitioners therefore, with the deepest Concern and Alarm, find themselves no\V threatened with the Ruin of all these Hopes, and the utter Preclusion for ever of every possible Assistance and Support from them, should the Propositions now under Consideration be passed into a Law, whereby the Power of clicking the Article of Bark is for ever given up, the free Admission of the Irish tanned Leather and manufactured Goods are let into the English Market freed from the Prohibitory Duty, and an Option is left to Ireland, by the Seventh Proposition, of effectually excluding the English Manufacturer from the Purchase of Raw Hides in Ireland, by imposing the same Prohibition on the Export of them, that now exists in England on the Export of the same Article, a Danger, which the Petitioners conceive, they will not be deemed unwarranted in their Apprehensions of, from the recent Duty imposed on the Export of this Article by Ireland, and the additional Motives that will stimulate them to it, after they are furnished with the Means of manufacturing the Commodity at Home, for the free Supply of every Market, Domestic, English, and Foreign; and that the Natural Advantages enjoyed by Ireland in respect to this Manufacture, will in this Manner be left to have their full and uncontrolled Effect in Favour of the Irish Manufacture, and, at the same Time, the English Legislature will be for ever precluded from the Power of affording any Relief to the English Manufacturer, or of putting him on an equal Footing with the Manufactured in Ireland: All which Premises, the Petitioners implore the House to take into their Consideration, and to afford to the Trade and Manufacture of the Petitioners such Protection and Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending in the House for enabling the Company of Proprietors of the Trent and Mersey Canal Navigation, and the Petitioners, to make a Navigable Canal, from the said Trent and Mei'sey Navigation, on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County, and to amend an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making a Navigable Canal from The Trent to The Mersey, which Bill recites certain Articles entered into between the Company of Proprietors of the said Trent and Mersey, Oxford, and Coventry Canal Companies, for the Ratification of a certain Agreement of Delegates from the said respective Companies, as also of a Set of Subscribers to a new Canal from the Coal Works to Birmingham, and from thence to Fazeley, held at Coleshill, upon the 20th Day of June 1782; and Alledging, That, by the Acts of Parliament passed for making the said Coventry and Oxford Canals, the Proprietors therein respectively incorporated, their Successors and Assigns, are entitled to' take Three Halfpence per Ton per Mile for all Coals navigated along such respective Canals, and, that Part of the original Line of the said Coventry Canal which lies between Atherstone and Fradley Heath, at the Time of the Meeting of the said Delegates at Coleshill, was, and still remains, unexecuted; and that the Petitioners understand, that the Meeting of Delegates at Coleshill was held with a View that the unexecuted Part of the said Coventry Canal from Atherstone to Fazeley, and the unexecuted Part of the said Oxford Canal from Banbury to Oxford, might be compleated, and that the then projected Canal from the Staffordshire Coal Mines to Birmingham, and from thence to Fazeley, was to be undertaken and executed, in order to supply the upper Parts of Warwickshire and Oxfordshire with Coal from such Staffordshire Mines, that Part of the Country having the retofore rested upon a Supply from the Warwickshire Coal Mines in the Neighbourhood of Bedworth and Griff; and that such Staffordshire Coal Mines lying more remote from the Warwickshire and Oxfordshire Markets than the before-mentioned Warwickshire Coal Mines by Forty-six Miles, it became absolutely necessary, from the Amount of Tonnage and Freightage upon the Staffordshire Coals in passing such Forty-six Miles, that they should afterwards pass along the Coventry and Oxford Canals at One Penny per Ton per Mile only, instead of Three. Halfpence, which was to be continued to be paid for the Navigation of the Warwickshire Coals, in order that the Staffordshire Coals might have a Chance of selling with the Warwickshire Coals at the above Markets; and that the Petitioners, fully relying that the Staffordshire Coals were to pass along the said Coventry and Oxford Canals at One Penny per Ton per Mile, and that the Warwickshire Coals were to continue to pay Three Halfpence per Ton, without future Reduction, for the Reasons above stated, agreed to extend their then Birmingham Canal from Birmingham to Fazeley, and to be

substituted in the Place and4 Stead of such new Subscribers, and, by an Act of the Twenty-third of His present Majesty, are so substituted; and that the Petitioners, from the most indubitable Conviction that the Rates of Tonnage above mentioned were to* remain unalterable, have expended upwards of £. 20,000 in Part Execution of the Powers of the said Act of the Twenty-third of His said Majesty, and, if they should be obliged to extend their Canal from Birmingham to Fazeley, and to join the Proprietors of the said Trent and Mersey Canal in executing the unfinished Part of the said Coventry Canal lying between Fazeley and Fradley Heath, with the other Works authorized by the said Act of the Twenty-third of His present Majesty, they must expend upwards of £. 80,000 more; and that, in the Committee to whom the Consideration of the Bill now pending was referred, a Clause hath been received, whereby all Coals, whether the Produce of Mines in Wanvickshire or Staffordshire, are authorized to pass upon all, or any Part, of the said Coventry and Oxford Canals, at one and the same Rate of Tonnage per Ton per Mile, and such Clause, though called a Clause of Equalization, is in Fact the very Reverse, and, if permitted to stand part of the Bill, will not only take away the very Foundation upon which alone the Petitioners would ever have consented to execute a Canal from Birmingham to Fazeley, or to have joined with the Proprietors of the Trent and Mersey Canal in finishing that Part of the Coventry Canal lying between Fazeley and Fradley Heath, but amounts so far to a Prohibition upon the Exportation oiStaffoi'dshire Coals into Warwickshire and Oxfordshire, as not to afford a Sum adequate to the Repairs only of the intended Canal, without calculating any Thing by Way of Profit or Interest upon the enormous Expenditure of £.100,000; and that the Petitioners have . hitherto preserved good Faith writh the several contracting Parties, and are yet desirous to proceed in the Execution of the Powers granted by the said Act of the Twenty-third of His present Majesty, in case the true Spirit and Intention of the Meeting of Dele-. gates at Coleshill is strictly adhered to: And therefore praying, That the Clause received by the Committee for such pretended Equalization may be expunged from the said Bill, or that the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the same.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee to whom the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, and the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from Birmingham to Fazeley, to make a Navigable Canal from the said Trent and Mersey Navigation, on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County, and to amend an Act passed in the Sixth Year of the Reten of His present Majesty, for making a Navigable Canal from The Trent to The Mersey, is committed.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Tradesmen of the Borough of Kidderminster, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have great Satisfaction in observing that the House has thought proper to alter and amend the Propositions originally laid before it, for settling a Commercial Treaty with Ireland; and, the Petitioners conceive, that, as great Good has arisen from the Enquiries which the House has already made on this extensive and important Subject, so, further and considerable Advantages will be most probably derived from the further Investigation of it; and that the Petitioners would not do any Thing, wantonly and unnecessarily, to delay any Measure of Government, but as the new Resolutions can neither be very speedily communicated to distant Parts of the Nation, nor be at once sufficiently understood in any Part, therefore the Petitioners pray, That the House would forbear coming to a speedy Decision, and be pleased to receive such further Information as may be offered on this Business.

A Petition of the Nail Ironmongers in the Town of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, and others concerned in the manufacturing of Iron in and near that Place, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are happy to observe, by the Votes of the House, that the Eleven Resolutions of the Irish Parliament, for settling a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and that Country, are to undergo some material Alterations; and that, as these Resolutions comprehend a vast Extent and Variety of Matter, and which, it is apprehended, will, in its Consequences, powerfully operate on the Iron Trade of this Country in a Manner that the wisest and best-informed Persons cannot hastily judge of, or foresee, especially as the Alterations intended to be made are not at present clearly understood by the Petitioners, the Petitioners therefore pray, That the House will give sufficient Time for obtaining a more perfect Knowledge of the Alterations intended to be made in the above Resolutions, and also for the deliberate Consideration of them, before they pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Glass Manufacturers in the Neighbourhood of Stourbridge and Dudley, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are much alarmed at finding the Irish Resolutions are likely to pass into a Law without such Regulations being made as will prevent the Trade of this Kingdom being injured: And therefore praying. That such Resolutions may not pass into a Law until sufficient Time be allowed to lay before the House the great Injury their Manufactory will sustain, and to consider of such Modes as will put the Trade of both Kingdoms upon an equal Footing, and such as, the Petitioners hope, will meet the Approbation of the House.

And the said Petitions wrere severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Com-V«l. 40.

mittee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Treat anjl thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and the Mersey other Proprietors of the Coventry Canal Company, CanaL was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from The Trent to The Mersey, and the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from Birmingham to Fazeley, to make a Navigable Canal from the said Trent and Mersey Navigation, on Bradley Heath,in the County of Stafford, to Fazeley, in the said County, and to amend an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making a Navigable Canal from The Trent to The Mersey; and Setting forth, That it is stated in the said Bill, that the Proprietors of the Coventry Canal Com- pany did, by Articles of Agreement, under their Common Seal, and bearing Date on the 29th Day of October 1783, consent that so much of the Line of Navigation extending from Fradley Heath to Fazeley aforesaid, as w as vested in the Coventry Canal Company, should be given up to the Canal Company from The Trent to The Mersey, commonly called The Grand Trunk Company, and to the Company of Proprietors of the Birmingham and Fazeley Canal; and Representing to the House, That the Petitioners conceive, that, however the Common Seal, when duly and legally affixed, may be deemed conclusive upon all the Proprietors of the said Company, as to Transactions within the Powers given to the Company by the said Act whereby they were incorporated, yet it can never, in Law, nor, as the Petitioners hope, in the Judgment of the House, be considered of such Validity as to bind the Proprietors in Matters totally foreign to, and out of the Powers and Intentions of, the said Act, and to oblige them to give up an Interest and an Estate solemnly vested in them by the said Act; and, they conceive that, as the Surrender intended to be enforced by the said Articles will affect every Individual in the said Company, the Consent of every Individual to this Alienation of their fundamental Rights and Property ought to have been obtained and proved before Parliament, in order to induce the Legislature to pass such a Law, and thereby alter and take away the private Estate of such Individuals, secured by the Faith of Parliament; and that several Proprietors of the said Company never did consent to this Surrender of their Property, and the Common Seal w’as put to the said Articles at so distant a Period as the 29th of October 1783; and that, although such Articles as before stated were entered into, yet the said Company of Proprietors of the said Coventry Canal Navigation, after due Deliberation, are now desirous that the same should not be carried into Execution, and, they did, at a Meeting held on the 29th of March last, pursuant to a special Notice, duly given for that Purpose, under their Common Seal, declare their Resolution of not proceeding in an Application to Parliament, for Powers to enable them to complete and execute the said Coventry Canal in the Manner proposed by the said Articles: Under these Circumstances the Petitioners hope that the Legislature will not compel a Body of Proprietors to give up their Estate and Interest in any Part of their Property, contrary to their Inclination; and, for these, and other Reasons, the Petitioners trust in the Equity and Justice of the House, that the said Bill will not pass into a Law, and that they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, that the same may not pass into a Law.

Intercourse monalty of the Society of Merchant Venturers, of the

with Ireland. of under their Common Seal, was pre-

sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that the leading Proposition for regulating the Commercial Intercourse between Great Jiritain and Ireland has been agreed to, but that many Alterations have been introduced by the Committee of the House, of the Purport of which the Petitioners are not fully informed: And the Petitioners conceiving their Interest, as a Commercial and Manufacturing City, very materially concerned in so important a Business as the Adjustment for ever of the reciprocal Trade of the Two Kingdoms, therefore praying, That proper Time may be given them, to weigh well and consider the Nature and probable Effects of the Alterations, and whether they tend to give such Relief to the Petitioners as they, in their former Petitions, presented to the House, respecting the Irish Resolutions, humbly prayed for.

A Petition of the Commercial Committee, and other Merchants and Manufacturers, of the Town of Birmingham was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that certain general Propositions, relative to a Commercial Treaty with Ireland\ have been agreed to in a Committee of the whole House, and that others are proposed to be brought forward; and they also observe, that His Majesty’s Ministers have . held out sundry new Propositions, or new Modifications of the former Propositions, the Nature of which the Petitioners are not yet fully informed of, but have Reason to fear that they contain many Articles which may essentially affect the Trade and Manufactures by which the Petitioners, and many Thousands of others, are maintained; and that (lie Petitioners did, in a former Stage of this Business, represent to the House the bad Effects which, they had Reason to fear, would arise to the Trade and Manufactures of Great Britain in general, and to those of the Town and Neighbourhood of Birmingham in particular, if the Resolutions of the Parliament of Ireland on this Subject were adopted in Great Britain, and they still adhere to the Sentiments contained in the said Petition, and beg Leave to refer the I louse to the same; and that the Petitioners conceive, that, notwithstanding the tedious Investigation which this Subject has undergone before the House, all the Dangers to which the Trade and Manufactures of this Nation will be exposed by such a Treaty are not yet fully laid open, and, it is with great Concern they observe, that no adequate Means are proposed to be adopted, to guard them against those Dangers which have been pointed out, and that Concessions are proposed to be made to Ireland, in regard to her principal Article of Export, which, if granted, would for ever preclude Great Britain from using the Means by which she cpuld most easily remedy any inconveniencies that

arise from the Privileges which have been already granted to Ireland; and that the Petitioners are afraid, that, if these Resolutions should be passed into a Law, contrary to the general Sentiments and Interests of the Trading and Manufacturing Part of this Nation, it may produce Effects fatal both to our Commerce and internal Peace: And therefore praying the House to defer their final Determination ou this most important Subject until the next Session of Parliament, or until the Propositions themselves, and the proposed Modifications of them, may be better understood, and the Dangers to w’hich our Manufactures and Commerce are exposed, may be more effectually guarded against.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Earthen Ware of the County of Stafford, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners understand, that various Alterations are to take place in the Irish Resolutions, in which they, with other Manufacturers, may be greatly interested: And there- fore praying for Time to consider the said ne*r Resolutions, and how their Trade may be thereby affected.

A Petition of the Mayor, Capital Burgesses, Merchants, and Cornfactors, of the Borough Town and Manor, and Port of Bideford, in the County of Devon, and Creeks belonging to the Port aforesaid, whose Names are thereunder subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for further regulating " and ascertaining the Importation and Exportation " of Corn and Grain within several Ports and Places " therein mentioned," and for extending the Powers and Provisions thereof to all Places within that Part of Great Britain called England; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, with Concern, that, by certain Clauses in such Bill, the Powers delegated to Grand Juries at the Quarter Sessions of their respective Counties, by divers Acts of Parliament, to enquire and present on their Oaths the Prices of English Corn and Grain, in order to regulate the Importation of Foreign Grain, are to be totally annihilated, and, instead thereof, a new System is intended to be subj stituted, by vesting in a single Individual in the City of London, a Power to inspect the Weekly Returns of the Cornfactors at Mark Lane (by many of whom he is to be elected and maintained) and to compute, and form, from thence, the Average Prices, which, being laid before the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Justices of the Peace, at their Quarter Sessions, and afterwards published in the Gazette, are to be deemed (without the least Respect to the Difference and Fluctuation of the Average Prices in any other Part of the Nation) the general Average Prices of this Kingdom, and the Importation and Exportation of Corn and Grain, as well at London as at every Out Port, are to be accordingly governed thereby; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if such Clauses should pass into a Law, the most grievous Injuries and Distress would result therefrom to many Thousands of His Majesty's Subjects, and it w'ould open a Door to Monopoly, Partiality, and Inconvenience: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the Clauses above mentioned from passing into a Law; or permit the Petitioners to be heard, by their Counsel, in Support of their Allegations, if the Nature of their Case shall require the same.

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Coun«> cil assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is ordered to be brought in for charging a Yearly Duty upon every House, or other Building, used as a Shop, wherein Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, shall be sold by Retail; and that the Petitioners have always been, and still are ready and willing to bear their Part of the necessary burthens of the State, upon a fair and equal Taxation, but that the Tax intended to be raised by the said Bill will, in the Judgment of the Petitioners, be partial, unjust, and highly oppressive upon Trade; and that the present accumulated Load of Taxes, under which the Inhabitants and Traders of the City of London more particularly labour, are become extremely burthensome; that London and Middlesex pay Eighty Parts out of Five Hundred and Thirteen of the whole Land Tax Annually raised in this Kingdom, and, although the Tax now proposed is denominated a Shop Tax, yet it is to all Intents and Purposes an Extension of the House Tax upon Shopkeepers only; that the Retail Dealers in the Metropolis are, from their local Situation, subjected to the Payment of large Rents, and, as the Tax now proposed to be laid upon them will greatly add to their present Burthens, the same must eventually tend to the Decrease of their Trade, and a consequent Diminution of the Revenue, and the Petitioners conceive, that it is a false and groundless Idea, to suppose that Taxes on the Conduct of Trade, or of Traders personally, fall eventually on the Con-/ sumer, it being a notorious Fact, that the Prices of all Commodities are regulated by the natural Force of the Supply at Market, combined with the State of the Demand: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their serious Consideration, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Hawkers and A Petition of the Manufacturers and Printers of Pedlars. Silk, Linen, and Cotton Handkerchiefs, Callicoes, 8$c. of the Town of Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is intended to be brought into the House, for the Repeal of the several Acts of Parliament for licensing Hawkers and Pedlars; and Representing to the House, That many very great Advantages have resulted from the said Body of Men to the Manufacturers of the Town and Neighbourhood of Manchester, as well as to many of the Manufacturers in other Parts of this Kingdom, and the Quantity of Goods purchased by that Class of Dealers is much more considerable than may have been apprehended, and, from the Mode of their Sale, which is generally from House to House in Country Villages and Districts, remote from Towns where Shopkeepers reside, great Quantities of British Manufactures are sold, which otherwise would not be disposed of; and that the Petitioners will be obliged, in case the intended Bill should pass into a Law, to discontinue the manufacturing and printing great Quantities of Goods which they sell to the said Class of People, and thereby His Majesty’s Revenue will be considerably diminished, and great Numbers of industrious -Families be thrown out of Employ; and that great Numbers of Hawkers and Pedlars in Lancashire, Staffordshire, Derbyshire, Yorkshire, and Cheshire, who have been brought up to the said Business from their Infancy, and have, by CEconomy, Industry, and Perseverance, been enabled to support themselves and Families with Credit, and to discharge, by regular and early Payments, the Debts owing to the Petitioners, will (in case the said Bill be passed into a Law) be also thrown out of Employ, and the Petitioners thereby become considerable Sufferers, and themselves and their Families, to the Amount of many Thousands, having no other Business, become Burthens to their respective Parishes: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the said Bill from passing into a Law.

A Petition of the Merchants* Manufacturers, and Inhabitants of the City of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill being brought into Parliament by the Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, for them to lower the Tonnage of Freight without the Controul of Commissioners appointed by a former Act, the Petitioners express their entire Confidence in the Wisdom of Parliament, that they will enforce such Regulations as may prevent partial Advantages, to the Injury of others, and to the Detriment of the City of Gloucester, and the Public in general.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, to low er and regulate the Tonnage upon the said Canal, be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Inhabitants of the City of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending for extending the present Dudley Canal into the Birmingham Canal, by which a much shorter, cheaper, and quicker Communication will be opened between Binningharn and the City of Gloucester, and many valuable Mineral Productions, now buried, will be brought to Market, which the Petitioners conceive to be of great Advantage to themselves and the Public; And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for extending the present Dudley Canal from the Termination thereof, in certain Lands of Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire, -within the Parish of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, to join and communicate with the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazqley Canal Navigations, at or near Tipton Green, in the County of Stafford, be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and Manu- Commercial facturers of the City of Bristol, was presented to the In.t®rcouJr8e House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners wlt rtan having observed, by the Votes, that the Propositions for regulating the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland had been agreed to, but had first undergone many Alterations in the Committee of the House, the Petitioners, who conceive their Interest, as a Commercial and Manufacturing City, very materially concerned in so important a Business as the Adjustment for ever of the reciprocal Trade of the Two Kingdoms, therefore pray, That proper Time may be given them to weigh well and consider the Nature and probable Effects of the Amendments, and whether they tend to give such Relief to the Petitioners, as they, in their former Petitions presented to the House respecting the Irish Resolutions, prayed for.

A Petition of the Tanners, Curriers, Shoemakers, Dittos and the rest of the Manufacturers of Leather in the Town and Neighbourhood of Wrexham, in the County of Denbigh, was also presented to the House, and read; Praying, That the House would postpone, for a Time, passing into a Law the Propositions, as they now stand, in Favour of Ireland, till they are more maturely considered and investigated: The Petitioners would have thought of petitioning the House before now, had they known from what Cause their Trade, and the Revenue of course, has been so very materially injured; It seems, that in 1780 a Bill was brought into the House, and passed into a Law, granting to Ireland a free Export of all her Manufac- tory to any Foreign Market, since which Time no Trade in the Kingdom has suffered such a Decline, the Reasons of which, the Petitioners beg Leave to observe to the House, are many, and obvious; the'

Irish Manufacturer of Leather, not being shackled by the Restrictions of Excise Laws, can emplby a Currier to shave and pare down, out of the Wooze, all the rough and gross Matter of the Leather in the Process of manufacturing it, w'hich will enable him to do it sooner with One Half of the Labour, and with One Third of the Bark, that the English Manufacturer can; in Ireland, One Man may follow the Business of a Tanner, a Currier, and a Shoemaker, which, in England, by the British Laws, he is prolii-bited from by severe Penalties, which certainly gives a manifest Advantage to the Irish Trader in supplying Foreign Markets; the Imports of Raw Hides ana Skins into the Ports of Liverpool and Chester, since the Period above-mentioned, have decreased more than One Half, and the Exports of Tanned Leather from those Ports (which formerly was very considerable) is now, and has been for several Years past,* entirely at a Stand: From the above' and many other Reasons which the Petitioners could adduce, it is evident, that the Irish Manufacturer of Leather, having Liberty to export Boots, Shoes, and Saddles, and all other Manufactory of Leather to this Country,

1004 *3° M J. 1-785,

will be enabled to sell them upon such Terms that will entirely ruin the Trade of the English Manufacturer: The Petitioners further beg Leave to observe to the House, that under the distressing Circumstances of their Trade being taken from them, in addition to the heavy Burthen of Taxes which Government have thought proper to impose upon diem, they have very heavy Parish Rates to pay for the Maintenance of a numerous Poor, and for the Repairs of Church and High Roads, which nothing but Trade can support: They therefore hope that the House will take their Case into serious Consideration, and grant them that Protection which Policy dictates, and Justice requires, or a general Bankruptcy will be the Consequence.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s moot Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland\
