Canal. thereunto subscribed, Proprietors of the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appears by the Votes, that a Bill hath been presented by the Company of Proprietors of the Dudley Canal Navigation, for Leave to extend the said Dudley Canal, so as to join and communicate with the said Bh'mingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations; and Representing to the House, That the Canals already made, and at a very considerable Expence, extend to the same Points, and to the same . Markets, as the Canal so prayed for would, if made, extend to, and every public Advantage is - derived from them which could be derived from the said proposed Junction; and the Petitioners apprehend that such Junction might be a Means of advancing the Price of Coals at the Mines upon the Line of the old Bir~ mingham Canal, which, of course, would be very prejudicial to the Manufactories of Hardware, and to the Public in general, and that the Petitioners have not given their Consent to the said proposed Junction, but, on the contrary, object thereto: And therefore x praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for extending the present Dudley Canal from the Termination thereof, in certain Lands of Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire, within the Parish of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, to join and communicate with the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, at or near Tipton Green, in the County of Stafford\ be read a Second Time.

Staffordshire A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Set. Canal. ’ thereunto subscribed, Barge Masters, Boat Owners* and Dealers in Coal upon the River Severn, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a Bill is depending in the House to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, to lower and regulate the Tonnage upon the said Canal j and Representing to the House, that, whilst the Tonnage on Coal raised at the Bilston Mines was lowered, the Petitioners had an extensive Trade, and full Employment for their Vessels, in supplying the different Markets upon the Severn with the Produce of those Mines, as well as of the Coal Mines lying on the Line of the Dudky and Stourbridge Canals, by. which they obtained a comfortable Support for themselves and Families, but, since that lonnage was again advanced, the Trade of the Bilston Coal has declined, and thrown the Stour-

bridge and Dudley Coal Trade into the Hands of the Stourbridge Coal Committee Company, who are bo-come the principal Dealers in, and Carriers of, that Coal to the different Markets upon the River Severn, and they have sold the Coal cheaper at those Markets than the Petitioners can possibly afford to do, by which Means the Petitioners have lost all Benefit of the Stourbridge and Dudley Coal Trade, and, the Trade of the Bilston Coal being greatly reduced and injured by Means of the high Tonnage, many of the Petitioners have been obliged to give up the Coal Trade, and are reduced to the Necessity of hiring their Vessels to, or becoming the Carriers for, the Stourbridge Committee Company, or else to let their Vessels lie idle, which is very prejudicial to the Interests of the Petitioners and the Public, and tending to create a Monopoly in the Hands of the Stourbridge Coal Committee Company; and that the Petitioners apprehend, in case the said Bill should pass into a Law, the same will be a Means of restoring the lost Trade to the Petitioners, and of bringing the different Mines to Market upon nearer Terms of Equality, and thereby prevent a Monopoly: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Stafford thereunto subscribed, Owners and Occupiers of Coal&c CallL Mines in the Neighbourhood of Bilston and Conseley, in the County of Stafford\ was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented by, and on the Behalf of, the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire arid Worcestershire Canal Navigation, for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable the said Company to lower and regulate the Tonnage upon their said Canal, without the Interposition of Commissioners, so as nevertheless that the same shall not exceed the Rates of Tonnage at present allowed by certain Acts of Parliament in the said Petition recited; and that the Petitioners arc the Owners and Occupiers of certain large and extensive Coal Mines in the Neighbourhood of Bilston and Coascky, upon the Line of the Canal extending from Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, to Authcrhy, in the County of Stafford, where the same joins and communicates with the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, and the Petitioners conceive, that if Powers were given to the said Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, to lower and regulate the Tonnage upon the said Canal, the same would tend greatly to the Interest of the Public, and of the Petitioners, by enabling the Petitioners to send their Coals to the Severn Market at a lower Rate than at present, and the same would be of further public Utility: And therefore praying, That the House will give Leave to the said Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, to bring in a Bill according to the Prayer of their said Petition, and that the said Bill may pass into a Law.

1 Ireland, Petition of the Master Silk Weavers in Manchester, in the County of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners having already laid before the House the Grievances which they believe they shall be subjected to from the former Propositions respecting the Irish Com* mercial Regulations, if they should pass into a Law, now apprehend, that the Alterations and Additions made to them are of very great Moment to the Petitioners, as well as to the Kingdom in general, and therefore request, That they may not suddenly be carried into Effect, but sufficient Time be allowed for the mature Consideration of them by the Petitioners.

A Petition of the Company of Bottle and Flint Glass Makers at Warrington, in the County of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Manufacture of Glass in Great Britain employs a great Number of Hands, and produces a very considerable Yearly Revenue, and is consequently of much National Concern, both as an Article of Commerce, and as a fit Subject of Taxa-. tion; but that the Regulations and Restraints prescribed by the Excise Laws for ascertaining and charging the Duties imposed, and for rendering them productive, are, in their Operation, peculiarly hard and injurious, as they restrain the Petitioners, and the Glass Makers in general, from bringing their Metal to the utmost Degree of Purity, oblige them to work up a considerable Part thereof (paid for as pure) into Articles of inferior Price, and do not allow an adequate Drawback on Exportation; and that these internal Duties imposed on the Glass Manufactures of this Kingdom, with the Restraints necessarily concomitant to guard against Fraud, cannot be countervailed by any Duty to be laid on the Importation of Glass from Ireland, or any other Place not subject to the like Impositions and Restraints, and, that while this Kingdom, loaded with an enormous Debt, is compelled to resort to an internal Duty on her own Manufactures towards the raising of her necessary Supplies, Ireland, labouring under no such Burthens or Restraints, will be enabled not only to undersell us at Foreign Markets, but to ruin our Revenue and Trade at Home, by smuggling in upon us her Manufactures and Produce, which the Vicinity of her Situation will render completely easy; and that, so burthened, and under the absolute Necessity of imposing internal Taxes, the Petitioners conceive, that no Regulations of Intercourse and Commerce can be settled between this Kingdom and Ireland on equitable Principles, unless the Produce and Manufactures of Ireland be subjected to the like internal Duties and operative Restraints with those imposed on the Produce and Manufactures of Great Britain: And therefore praying, That, in settling the Trade and Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, effectual Care may be taken of the Prosperity of Great Britain, and the general Interest of the British Empire.

A Petition of the Glass Manufacturers of London, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, understanding that several Additions and Alterations have been made in the Irish Resolutions now before the House, by which the particular Manufacture the Petitioners are engaged in may be injured, they therefore pray the House not to pass the said Resolutions into a Law, till the Petitioners can have Time to inform themselves how far they may be affected thereby.

A Petition of the Sail Cloth Makers in the City of London, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners being fully convinced of the great Importance of the Sail Cloth Manufacture to this Kingdom, as a Naval Store, and the Vol. 40.

Necessity there is of its being encouraged here, so that the Navy may have an ample Supply of this Article in Time of War, as it hath hitherto had, without being under the Necessity of depending on any other Country, from whence it cannot be brought, in Time of War at least, without Danger of Capture from our Enemies, and, as this Manufacture cannot be supported in Time of Peace without the Aid of Bounties to encourage the Exportation to Ireland and Foreign Parts, which the Wisdom of Parliament hath hitherto seen necessary, and have adopted for a long Series of Years, to the great Improvement of the Manufacture, but, should the Resolutions in Favour of Ireland, now before the House, respecting the Bounty on Exportation of British Canvas to Ireland, pass into a Law, the Petitioners are under the most painful Apprehensions, from the Certainty of the Irish engrossing the Export Trade, that the Manufacture itself will be lost to this Country, and many thousands of His Majesty’s Subjects rendered destitute of Subsistence: And* therefore praying, That, as the House hath seen the Necessity of making some Alterations in those Resolutions in Favour of other Branches of Trade and Manufacture in this Country, they will make such farther Alterations as will effectually prevent this essential Manufacture from being removed to Ireland, or any other Place.

A Petition of the Paper Makers and Stationers of the City of London, and its Neighbourhood, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners understand that, contrary to general Expectation, a Variety of Alterations have been proposed in the Treaty with Ireland, in which, although Provisions seem to be made for protecting some particular Branches of Commerce, no Protection is to be granted to the Petitioners, as far as the Petitioners understand the aforesaid Propositions as now altered, these Propositions containing new, important, and complicated Matter, which will require much Time and deliberate Consideration clearly to understand; and as the Petitioners are of Opinion, that it is not consistent with sound Policy and true Wisdom to determine a Matter of such Magnitude with Haste and Precipitation, they therefore request the House will allow sufficient Time to reflect how far the Manufacturing Interest of this Kingdom, and that of the Petitioners in particular, may be affected by the passing the aforesaid Propositions into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom.it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Haw kers and Pedlars within the Hawkers and Cities of London and Westminster, and the Neighbour- Pedlars-hood thereof, was presented to the House, and read;-Setting forth, That the Petitioners have heard, with the utmost Astonishment and Affliction, that a Measure has been introduced into the House for their utter Extermination, uncensured, unsummoned, unheard, untried, and uncondemned, and therefore claim it as their Birthright and Inheritance, as free Citizens, that they be confronted with their Accusers, that their Charge be delivered to them, and that they may have an Opportunity of being heard, by themselves and

Counsel, before any Measure so harsh and unprecedented shall be adopted by the House, as to permit a Law to be brought in for their Suppression; and they believe it to be their Utility to the general Interests of the State that makes them obnoxious to some Part of the Community, who have an immediate private Interest in their Suppression: That the Petitioners are informed, there is a Standing Committee of this House, called the Committee of Commerce, and therefore crave it as their Right, before any Bill shall be brought into the House for depriving them of Bread, to have their Characters and Conduct, as likewise the Nature and Extent of their Commercial Dealings, enquired into by that Committee, and the Petitioners have no Doubt but that every Enquiry respecting them will terminate in a Report evincing their Innocence and Utility, and protecting them against the Effects of the many malicious Calumnies and groundless Charges to which they have been continually exposed from those who have an immediate private Interest in their Suppression; and that the Petitioners compose Part of a Body consisting of Tourteen hundred Persons, at least, In England alone, many of whom have Wives, Children, aged Parents, and indigent Relations, who depend for Subsistence on the Fruits of the Petitioners Industry: And therefore praying to be heard, by themselves and Counsel, against any Measure that may tend to their Injury or Suppression.

Setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in the last Session of the late Parliament, for establishing certain Regulations concerning the Portage and Conveyance of Letters and Packets by the Post between Great Britain and Ireland\ the Petitioners are deprived of that Part of the Privilege of franking printed Vottfs, Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, which extended to Ireland\ and which Privilege had been enjoyed by the Clerks in the Offices of His Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State' from the original Establishment of the Post Office, and was expressly Confirmed to them by the Act of the Fourth Year of His present Majesty; and, the said Privilege has been a Source of considerable Advantage to many of the Petitioners, and might naturally be expected to prove so ta all of them in a Course of Succession, and in Proportion to the Extent of their Connections; and that, notwithstanding the Grant from Parliament out of the Revenue of the Post Office in Favour of the Petitioners, which commenced in the Year 1769, upon the Abolition of their Privilege of franking Letters, they still find that their Appointments in the Offices are much inferior to those of the Clerks in the other great Offices of State, which renders them the less able to bear so considerable a Diminution of their Incomes, many of the Petitioners deriving the chief Support of their Families from their Official Situation, whilst it is well known that the constant Duty of the Offices, precludes them from pursuing any other Employment, and that the Confidence reposed in them is of the most important Nature; and that the Petitioners are the more encouraged to submit their Losses on this Occasion to the Consideration of the House, as it is an acknowledged Principle of Parliament, to provide a Recompence for such Individuals as suffer by any Regulations made for the Public Benefit, it being evident that a very considerable Increase of Revenue will arise, both in Great Britain and Ireland, from the Post Tax laid on Newspapers by the Acts passed in both Kingdoms for that Purpose: And therefore

praying, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and grant them such Compensation, for their Losses above-mentioned, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referfed to the' Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon tfo’s Day Sevennight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Then

Thomas Fansfiaxv, Esquire, being examined, said, That in the Year 1752 he was appointed by the City of London Collector of the said Toll or Duty; that he executed the said Office himself for Twelve Years, and since that Time the Office has been executed by Mr. William Read, as his Deputy — That the Duties he collected were upon Com, Coals, and for Ground-age, which was paid for every Coal and Com Vessel anchoring in the Port of London, which Duties he received for the Use of the Mayor and Commonalty and Citizens of the City of London, and paid the same, from Time to Time, into the Chamber of the said City. Then

Mr. William Read being called, informed your Committee, That he has acted as Deputy to Mr. Fanshaw for near Twenty-five Years, and has collected the said Toll or Duty of One Farthing per Quarter upon Com Inward, and accounted for the same to the City of London — That the said Duty has usually been collected from the Masters of Ships bringing Corn, immediately upon their Entry at the Custom House; and that such Duty was afterwards returned to such of the Proprietors of Corn as were Freemen of London, or to their Factors on their Behalfs, upon their producing Notes for that Purpose — That the Tenor of the Notes, claiming a Return of the Duty, were in various Forms (to wit) " my Property " — " are on "my Account" — "are mine" — " belonging to me" — "the Property of me" — " on my Account" — " received so much Corn," with their Names simply subscribed; and that several of the Factors, who sometimes made use of the Expression, " the Corn is my " Property," at other Times merely signed their Initials; and that the Witness always returned the Money, under the Idea that the Com was their own Property, and did not conceive it was claimed otherwise; if he had, he should not have returned such Duty — The Tenor of the Notes being so various,

it was the Custom of the Office to return the Duty upon all such Notes, till some little Time before the Dispute which arose about the Year 1772, when it was suspected that Demands were made by the tree-men Factors for the Return of the Said Duty upon Corn that was not their own Property.

The Witness then produced to your Committee an Account of the Yearly Receipts of the said Duty, from the Year 1754 to 1775, inclusive, together with the Amount of the Duty returned, and the Net Produce paid into the Chamber of London; which Account is hereunto annexed, N* 1.

And the Witness further said, That he has attended the Trials at Law upon Questions respecting the Payment of the said Duty, where it has been proved, that the Duty so paid back to the Corn Factors has not been accounted for or allowed to their Employers. — And he added, that if such Claim were to be established, it would totally annihilate the Duty, the Witness not knowing of any Corn Factor who is not a Freeman of the City of London.

Mr. Fanshaxv being again called, confirmed Mr. Read's Evidence, as to the Manner of the Receipt and Return of the Com Duty during the Time he acted personally as Collector. — He also agreed, that the Claim now set up would annihilate the Duty. And

Philip Wyatt Crcrwthei’, Esquire, Solicitor to the City of London, being examined, said, That the first Ground upon which the Return of the said Duty wras claimed, was that of an Exemption, but which Ground was afterwards relinquished; and they now rest their Claim upon a Right to receive the Duty to their own Use, as Freemen Factors of the City of London, although the Corn so consigned confessedly belonged to, and was the Property of, Non-Freemen.

And the Witness added, That in Consequence of several Decisions in the Courts of Law, respecting the City’s Right to the said Duty, no Redress can (as he is advised and believes) be had by any Mode of legal Proceeding.

Mr. Joseph Bushnany Assistant Comptroller of the Chamber of the City of London, being examined, said. That the City of London have, from Time to Time, expended large Sums of Money in the Conservancy of the River Thames, and the Maintenance of the Port of London, with the public Stairs and Landings adjoining to the River. Then

Mr William Montagu, principal Clerk in the Chamberlain’s Office, produced to your Committee an Account of the Money expended by the City of London, in keeping in Repair the Avenues to the River Thames, and the public Stairs and Docks thereof, and on Account of the Conservatorship of the said River, from Christmas 1764 to Christmas 1784; which is hereunto annexed, N* 2.

A Petition of the Justices of Peace, Commissioners lf of Supply, and other Heretors of the County of Fife,

met at Cupar, on the 17th Day of May 1785, was also 5- presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

r That the Petitioners are fully sensible of the Justice

I V 0 l. 40.

by the Chancellor of His Majesty’s Exchequer, are still, in the Petitioners Opinion, notwithstanding such Alterations, of such a Tendency as must, in a short Time, totally ruin their Businesses in this Country, and consequently involve the Petitioners, and their Dependents, in the greatest Distress: The Petitioners, therefore, confiding in the Wisdom of the House in the forming of a Commercial Treaty between Great Britain and Ireland, which will lie for ever irrevocable, earnestly intreat the House to deliberate upon, and defer coming to any Decision on, a Question of so much National Importance, till sufficient Time hath been had for the due Consideration of the whole System now before the House.

A Petition of the Tanners, Curriers, Cordwain-ers, Sadlers, and others, of the . Town and Neighbourhood of Manchester, interested in; the Leather Trade, was likewise presented to the House, and read, Setting forth, That the Petitioners are justly alarmed at the Irish Propositions now before the House, and which, though considerably altered from the original Propositions moved by Mr. Orde in the Irish House of Commons, and afterwards in this House by the Chancellor of His Majesty’s Exchet quer, are still, in the Petitioners Opinion, notwithstanding suefi Alterations, of such a Tendency, as must, in a short Time, totally ruin the Manufacture of Leather in this Country, and consequently involve the Petitioners, and their Dependents, in the greatest Distress: The Petitioners therefore, confiding in the Wisdom of the House in the forming of a Commercial Treaty between Great Britain and Ireland, which will be for ever irrevocable, earnestly intreat the House to deliberate upon, and defer coming to any Decision on, a Question of so much National Importance, till sufficient Time hath been had for the due Consideration of the whole System now before the House.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 25th Day of January last, as relates to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for extending the present Dudley Canal from the Termination thereof in certain Lands of Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire, within the Parish of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, to join and communicate with the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, at or near Tipton Green, in the County of Stafford; And setting forth, That the Canals already made, and at a very considerable Expence, by the Petitioners and others, have already opened a Communication with large Tracts of Coal and Mines, which appear, by the said Bill, to be the Objects of the said intended Extension, and the Petitioners apprehend, that such Extension would not afford a cheaper Conveyance for Goods and Merchandize between the Town of Birmingham, and the Port of Bristol, and the intermediate Places, as stated in the said Bill, nor will the same be of great Public Utility, but such Extension will materially injure the Property of the Petitioners, as, they apprehend, it will render nearly useless Twelve Miles and an Half of their Navigation, without any Compensation being provided by the said Bill, or offered them for the same, whilst they observe, that a Compensation is to be given to the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Company for the Loss of Tonnage which they would otherwise sustain by Reason of such intended Canal taking Place, and, that Powers are intended to be given to the Stourbridge Canal Company to lower and reduce the Rates of Tonnage on their Navigation, but no such Power is offered to the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and that the Interest of the Petitioners may be properly secured, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, in Support of their Petition, and against the said Bill.

Maiu A. 1785.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Hawkers and A Petition of the licensed Hawkers and Pedlars trad-Pedlars. ingfrom Halifax and its Neighbourhood, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been regularly bred up to, and exercised their Trade and Calling of Hawkers, §c. by the Authority of several Acts of Parliament,

which having imposed the Duties payable by the Petitioners for their Licences, held out to them the Hope of their enjoying a permanent Protection and Security, to which they conceive themselves equally entitled with any other Class or Description of the Subjects of this Kingdom, and cannot forbear to hope the same Protection will be continued to the Petitioners, otherwise it must unavoidably be attended with their utter Ruin, and without any Crime proved, or even surmised, unless by some interested Individuals; and Representing to the House, That, so far from the Trade of the Petitioners being detrimental to the Manufacturers or Traders, the Petitioners conceive that it is directly the contrary, for that it is of great Advantage to the Internal Commerce of this Kingdom, as, by the Petitioners, Goods are introduced into remote Parts in great Abundance, to the Encouragement of the Manufacturers, and great Increase of the Revenue; and that the Petitioners, from thd Nature of their Trade, being obliged to have great Stocks of Goods on their Hands, which they generally sell upon Credit to labouring Manufacturers and Mechanics, the Petitioners compute they have no less owing them of outstanding Debts in the Country than £.40,000, and they now stand indebted in large Sums to the different Merchants and Manufacturers of London, Glasgow, Manchester, Leicester, Nottingham, Carlisle,

6*. &;c. fyc. which, if the Petitioners be prohibited from following their lawful Calling, will reduce them to Beggary, and be a Means of making their Creditors Bankrupts, as the Petitioners will be totally unable to collect their outstanding Debts, if the Laws are repealed that protect them; and that the Petitioners have ahvays chearfully submitted to and paid, and are still w filing to pay, whatever Parliament hath or may think proper to impose upon them, as their reasonable and proportionable Share of the necessary Supplies to be raised for the Exigencies of Government, and, the Petitioners, independent of these Considerations, conceive that to deprive them, or any other Body or Class of Men, without any Fault of their own, of the Power of exercising their honest and lawful Callings, and thereby condemn them, indiscriminately, to Poverty and Distress, and that without any possible Advantage to the Public, the Petitioners submit would be an Act of unprecedented Cruelty and Oppression: And therefore praying, That the House will suffer them to retain the Enjoyment of the Common Privileges of the other Subjects of this Realm, and not pass any Act for the Repeal of those Laws by which they are at present protected therein.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Jeremiah Osborne, Junior, being examined, said,

That the Parish Church of Christ Church, otherwise The Holy Trinity, is very much out of Repair, and being situate at the Corner of Two of the principal Streets of the said City, the one Street being between 17 and 18 Feet wide, \ and the other between 18 and 19 Feet wide, and by reason of some Houses and Tenements adjoining near to the said Church, the Passage is rendered narrow, inconvenient, and dangerous — That the taking down the said Church, and the Said Houses and Tenements, and the rebuilding of the said Church nearly on the present Scite thereof, so as to widen the Streets adjoining; would be of great Advantage both to the Parishioners and the Public, by enlarging a Passage in the Center of the said City.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for re-building the Parish Church of Christ Church, otherwise The Holy Trinity, within the City of Bristol* and for widening the Streets adjacent thereto: And that Mr. Brickdale and Mr. Cruger do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Commercial A Petition of the Importers of Irish Linen Yarn, in Intercourse the Town of Manchester, was presented to the House, with rc and anj rea(j. setting forth, That the Petitioners are very apprehensive, that the Propositions for a Commercial Treaty with Ireland, even in their altered: State, will greatly affect and prejudice themselves and others, and the said Propositions being of such infinite Magnitude and Importance, and in their Nature irrevocable, the Petitioners dread the Consequences of their being finally concluded upon before Time is given for a more deliberate and hill Investigation of their Nature, Tendency, and probable Effects: And therefore praying the House not to precipitate the Business to a Conclusion at this advanced Period of the Session, as they hope and trust that, if further Time is granted, some more fair and equitable System- may be formed, by which Ireland may gain every reasonable Advantage, without so materially affecting the Interests of Great Britain.

Mali. A. 1785.

A Petition of the Small Ware Manufacturers of the Commercial Town of Manchester, in the County of Lancaster, was Intercourse also presented to the House, and read: Setting forth, With re and* That the Petitioners* having heard of the Resolutions moved in the Irish House of Commons, and afterwards introduced into this House, humbly express their great Regret at so dangerous and destructive a System, and, as the Petitioners have been very recently informed of several Alterations made in such Resolutions, they therefore entreat the House not to come to any decided Vote upon such Alterations until Time hath been allowed to consider their Tendency and Operation, as such Alterations are to establish a par-manent, unalterable, and irrevocable Treaty between England and Ireland.

A Petition of the Check Manufacturers of the Town of Manchester, in the County of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That the Petitioners, justly alarmed with the injurious Tendency of the Resolutions moved in the Irish House of Commons on the 7th of February last, and afterwards introduced into this House, now humbly express their great Regret at so dangerous and destructive a System, and, as several Alterations have been made in the proposed System, the Petitioners entreat the House not to come to any determinate Vote upon them, until Time hath been allowed to consider the Tendency of such Alterations, which are to be the Basis of an eternal and irrevocable Treaty between England and Ireland.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, was likewise presented to the House, and read: Setting forth, That the Petitioners beg Leave to approach the House with the warmest Sentiments of Veneration and Respect, for the late salutary Interposition of its Wisdom and Authority in altering and amending the dangerous Principles of the Irish Propositions, which so imminently threatened the Welfare and Prosperity of the Manufactories of the said Town; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that such Alterations and Amendments have been brought forward and effected by the Alarm which the said Propositions had so justly given to the Manufacturers in general of this Kingdom, whose Petitions to the House contributed to that deliberate Inquiry and Investigation which could alone prevent the dangerous Effects which,’ the Petitioners presume, would inevitably have succeeded a precipitate Adoption of those Propositions; and that the Petitioners, so far as they are capable of judging, conceive that very great and alarming Evils are to be dreaded to the Manufactories of the Town of Nottingham, and of the Kingdom in general, if such Propositions, even in their present altered and improved State, should pass into a Law, and that nothing but the Wisdom and Virtue of the House, repeatedly employed in exploring the Principles and probable Effects of such Propositions, can afford the Petitioners a Confidence or Hope against the Adoption and Consequences of so dangerous a System: And therefore beseeching the House, That the said Propositions may not, in any State or Form whatsoever, during the present Session of Parliament, be carried into a Law, nor receive the Sanction of the House, but that further Time may be granted for investigating a Subject of such infinite Importance to the Commercial Interests of this Country.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Manufacturers and Wholesale Haw Traders in Kendal, in the County of Westmoreland, was Pedl presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners have, for many Years past, been acquainted and had Dealings with the licensed Hawkers and Pedlars trading from Kendal aforesaid, whom 5 they

5 Geo. III.

3 b° Mai

they have experienced to be a most frugal, industrious* and useful Class of People, and not only greatly instrumental in promoting the Trade and Business of the Petitioners and the Manufacturing Trade of this Kingdom in general, but also of the greatest Utility and Convenience to that Part of the Country in which they travel, particularly to such Parts as are remote from any Market Town, and where a great Majority of the Inhabitants are not in Circumstances to take frequent Joumies to purchase Goods, and the Expences and necessary Loss of Time of which Journies would make so heavy an Addition to the real Cost of those Goods as greatly to discourage the Consumption of, and thereby tend to the Decrease of the Demand for, the Manufactures of the Nation, and of the Revenues thereof; and that many of the Petitioners have, on the Faith of several Acts of Parliament, which, in the Petitioners Apprehension, secured to the said Hawkers and Pedlars a permanent Protection in their Business, and from long Experience of their Integrity and Uprightness in their Dealings, from Time to Time sold very large Quantities of Goods to them on Credit, and which being again sold on Credit, not only their Trade with their Customers, but also their Dealings and Trade with the Petitioners, have been long ago thereby reduced and brought into a regular Channel, and of course the Debts due from them to the Petitioners constantly amount to large Sums of Money, which are again due to them the said Hawkers and Pedlars, in small Debts, from a very great Number of People, unknown to, and at a great Distance from the Petitioners, and, from this Circumstance, it would be impossible for such Debts to be collected by any Persons but those in the same Trade, and who could sell Goods at the same Time they made such Collection; and that, in case the Trade of the Hawkers and Pedlars should be prohibited, a great Part of the Debts due from them to the Petitioners must be unavoidably lost, and the Petitioners Trade, and also the Demand for, and Consumption of, the Manufactures of this Kingdom, reduced, to the great Loss of all, and the utter Ruin of some, of the Petitioners, and the manifest Disadvantage and Decrease of the Public Revenue; and Representing to the House, That the Conduct of the said licensed Hawkers and Pedlars has been such as to entitle them to Encouragement and Protection, and the Petitioners cannot refrain from expressing their Astonishment and Concern at any Attempt to withdraw that Protection, and to introduce any Law which must condemn a most useful Class of Men indiscriminately, and without Cause, and not only without Advantage to, but to the manifest Disadvantage of, the Public, to a State of Vagrancy, Beggary, or compelled Idleness and Inaction, and be attended with so heavy a Loss to such of the Petitioners as have the greatest Part of their Fortunes intrusted in their Hands: And therefore praying, That the House will not pass any Act for the Repeal of those Laws which protect the Trade of the Hawkers and Pedlars, but suffer j them to continue the Exercise of such their Trade, and

( to enjoy the common Privileges of every Description of the Subjects of this Realm.

Ordered, That the said. Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ways and Means.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties granted by an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, on Certificates issued with respect to killing of Game, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid or payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person in Great Britain, who shall use any Dog, Gun, Net, or other Engine, for the Destruction of Game (not acting as a Gamekeeper under or by virtue of a Deputation or Appointment duly registered) shall previously deliver in a Paper, or Account in Writing, containing the Name and Place of Abode of such Person, to the Clerk of the Peace, or his Deputy, or to the Sheriff or Stewart Clerk of the County, Riding, Shire, Stewartry, or Place where such Person shall reside, and annually take out a Certificate thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Certificate issued to any such Person shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Two Pounds Two Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Deputation or Appointment of a Game-keeper, granted to any Person by any Lord or Lady of a Manor in England\ or the Dominion of Wales, shall be registered with the Clerk of the Peace of the County, Riding, or Place, and every such Deputation, or Appointment, by any Proprietor of Land in Scotland, shall be registered with the Sheriff, or Stew-art Clerk of the County, Stewartry, or Place, in w:hich the said Manor, or Lands, respectively lie, and the Gamekeeper so appointed shall annually take out a Certificate thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Certificate issued to any Person under any Deputation or Appointment of Gamekeeper, shall be ingrossed; written, or printed, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Ten Shillings and Six Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person, exercising the Trade of a Coach-maker, be obliged to take out a License, and pay annually for the same the Sum of Twenty Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Twenty Shillings be laid upon every Four-Wheeled Carriage, upon which a Duty of Excise is now charged, to be paid by the Maker thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Ten Shillings be laid upon every Two-W.heeled Carriage, upon which a Duty of Excise is now charged, to be paid by the Maker thereof.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

American A Petition of the Society of Owners and Masters of inaShips belonging to the Port of London, associated for ra c* the Protection of Shipping at the said Port, and now consisting of upwards of One hundred and Seventy Members, was presented to the House, and read; Setting torth, That the Petitioners have observed, with great Concern, that Attempts are making, by a Petition to the House from the West India Planters, to shew that there is a Necessity for opening a Commercial Intercourse between the United States of America and His Majesty’s Colonies and Plantations in The West Indies, by allowing the Inhabitants of those States to import Lumber, and other Articles of their Produce, into The British West India Islands in their own Ships; that such Necessity has arisen from a Want of British Ships sufficient for the Purpose of carrying on such Trade, and that such Want of Ships has been owing to that Loss which unavoidably attends the performing of such circuitous Voyages as those from hence to The West Indies by the Way of North America; and, the Petitioners, in Opposition to the Authors of such ill-founded and erroneous Suggestions, beg Leave to inform the House, That the British Ships employed in the West India Trade are more than sufficient for the carrying of all such Supplies as The British West India Islands may want from America as well as from Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners are Proprietors of Two hundred Sail of Ships, whose Burthens amount to upwards of 60,000 Tons (being only a Part of those employed in the West India Trade) and that, as many of them will be obliged to go from England to The West Indies in Ballast, through the Want of Freight Outwards, their Owners will be glad to let such Outward-bound Ships to those Planters and Merchants as shall be willing to engage to load them with Lumber or Provisions from any Port in The American States to The West India Islands, at the Freight now given to American Ships, or for such Freight as was given from their several Ports before the late War; and Representing to the House, That many of the Petitioners Ships, through the Want of Outward Freight, scarcely earn the Expellees they incur during their respective Voyages, and that, should the Ships of the United States be permitted to enjoy a tree Intercourse with The British West India Islands, a considerable Part of the carrying Trade of those Islands will soon be lost, and the Remainder much reduced in its Value, if not rendered absolutely ruinous to the Petitioners, and the Whole, or nearly the Whole, of that valuable Trade will thereby fall into the Hands of The American States, the Manufactures of all the European Nations, as well as those of Ammca, will be carried to The British West India Market, and the Naval Power of Britain

Vol. 40.

Matt. 1033

reduced in Proportion to the Loss sustained in her Commerce; that the Protection of her remaining Navigation will be rendered difficult and precarious, her distant Dominions exposed to Devastation and Conquest, and even her own much-envied Independence imminently hazarded: And therefore praying, That the House will take the above Facts into their most serious Consideration, and endeavour, by a due Exertion of their Wisdom and Power, to prevent those Evils which have a manifest Tendency so materially to affect the Interest of the Petitioners, narrow the Navigation of Britain, and involve her in Difficulty and Ruin.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Tanners, and others concerned in Commercial the Manufacture of Tanned Leather, within the West Intercourse Riding of the County of York, was presented to the with Ireland-House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, by the Votes, that certain Propositions for settling a Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland are pending before the House; and that the Petitioners, from a deliberate Consideration of the Effects the said Propositions, if passed into a Law, will have upon the Tanned Leather Manufacture of this Kingdom, are deeply sensible that not only the Petitioners will be most materially injured by the inevitable Depression the said Manufacture must undergo in this Kingdom, and that a very great Number of Persons brought up to, and now employed in, that extensive Manufacture will be deprived of their usual Means of providing for themselves and Families, but that the very considerable Revenue arising therefrom to this Kingdom will be very sensibly diminished: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Propositions, so far as the same concerns the Petitioners, and that such Relief may be granted to them as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House* and read; Setting: forth* That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending in the House, to repeal the several Acts for licensing Hawkers and Pedlars; and Alledging, That.numerous and important Advantages have resulted from the said diligent and useful Body of Men to the Trade and Manufactures of these Kingdoms, particularly in the various Branches of Silk, Cotton, Linen, and Worsted, and in almost every Article of Female Attire, whether for Use or Ornament; and, the Laws now in Force seem to have held out Promises of Permanence and Stability to that Branch of Traffic, the Taxes imposed thereon being, by the Acts of the Fifth and Sixth of Queen Anne, to continue from the 23d of June 1710, for 96 Years, and for One whole Year thence next immediately ensuing after the Expiration of the said Term of 96 Years; and that this Sanction of the Legislature of Britain has induced Numbers of industrious Traders to employ large Capitals in that Line of Business, and to give Credit, to a considerable Amount, in scattered Villages, remote Districts, and Houses far distant from Towns and Shopkeepers, which Debts can only be recovered by a Continuance of their stated Visits, and, if lost, would involve Thousands of worthy Families in Distress and Ruin: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Wholesale Dealers within the City of London, was presented to the House, and read 5 Setting forth, That the Petitioners are grieved *0 fend tihat a Proposal has beet) made to suppress HawJcere and^ Pedlars, and, in their Opinion, if such an Act takes Place, it:will not only be the total Ruin of upwards of One thousand Four hundred industrious Tradesmen, who are of great Utility to Commerce in general, and the Manufactories of this Kingdom in particular, but also of many of the Petitioners, and others, who trade with diem, and give them Credit to a considerable Amount; and that the Petitioners, having been many Years resident Traders of the City of London, from their Experience are convinced, that, by the Means made Use of by Hawkers and Pedlars, travelling from House to House, to Villages and Farm Houses remote from Market Towns, a greater Quantity of Goods are sold than could otherwise be disposed of, and the Inhabitants are thereby supplied with Necessaries which otherwise could not be procured without Loss of Time and additional Expence, and, the Petitioners, having had many and extensive Dealings with Hawkers and Pedlars, are enabled, from Experience, to assure the House, that that Description of People are, in general, honest, industrious, and punctual, that many of them have Wives and Families depending upon their Industry for Support, and, the Petitioners are fully convinced, that nothing more is requisite to secure those Persons the Protection of the House, but a full Enquiry into their Characters, and the Nature of the Trade which they carry on: And therefore praying, That so oppressive an Act may not be suffered to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of all the Taxes, Customs, Rates, and Duties, of every Kind, paid or collected in the Counties of Argyle, Inverness, Ross, Sutherland, Caithness, and Orkney and Shetland, as also the Net Amount of the said Taxes, Customs, Rates, and Duties, distinguishing each Tax, each Parish or District, and Port, so far as the same can be made up from Materials actually in Possession of the several Boards or Offices for the Receipt of the Public Revenue at Edinburgh, from the Year 1774, up to the latest Period the said Accounts can be made up.

Ordered, That there be laid before this Horse, an Account of the Gross and Net Amount of the above Taxes, Customs, Rates, and Duties, for the Year 1765, and for the Year 1782.

PETITION of the Merchants, Manufac- Hawkers an turers, and Wholesale Dealers, in the Town of Eed!*1-8* IVigart, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and its Neighbourhood, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, And read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending in the House to repeal the several Acts for licensing Hawkers and Pedlars; and Alledging,

That numerous and important Advantages have resulted, from the said diligent and useful Body of Men, to the Trade and Manufactures of these Kingdoms, particularly in the various Branches of Silk,

Cotton, Linen, and Worsted, and in almost every Article of Female Attire, whether for Use or Ornament; and, the Laws now in Force seem to have held out Promises of Permanence and Stability to that Branch of Traffic, the Taxes imposed thereon being, by the Acts of the Fifth and Sixth of Queen Anne, to continue, from the Twenty-third of June 1710, for Ninoty-six Years; and for One whole Year then next immediately ensuing after the Expiration of the said Term of Ninety-six Years; and that the Sanction of the Legislature of Britain has induced Numbers of industrious Traders to employ large Capitals in that Line of Business, and to give Credit to a considerable Amount, in scattered Villages, remote Districts, and Houses far distant from Towns and Shopkeepers, which Debts can only be recovered by a Continuance of their stated Visits, and, if lost, would involve Thousands of worthy Families in Distress and Ruin:

And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Journeymen Silk Weavers of Hawkera Manchester, and its Environs, was presented to the M* House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are justly alarmed at the Proposition lately made in the House for abolishing the granting of Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars, as the same, if carried into Effect, will prove very destructive to that Branch of Business, which not only produces a considerable Revenue to Government, but gives Employment to the Petitioners, and a comfortable Support to themselves and their numerous Families, who must be otherwise thrown out of Employment, and be thereby reduced to the utmost Distress: And therefore praying the House to take this Petition into Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Lrneh, Chtoh, Silk, m Thread Hawked Manufacturers of the Town of Paisley, and Neigh- Pefe bourhoot), was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is depending in the House for abolishing the Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars; and Representing to the House, That, under the Sanction of repeated Acts of Parliament, the Hawkers and Pedlars have carried on their Trade, in which they have employed considerable Sums of Money, and by their Industry and Perseverance have contributed greatly to the Extension of many of the Manufactures both of England and Scotland, by introducing them into Parts of the Country where they could not otherwise have been Sold, and, the Petitioners are convinced, that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it will very materially injure the Manufactures of Scotland in general, and the Town and Neighbourhood of Paisley in particular, and will not only lessen His Majesty’s Revenue, but will deprive many industrious People of Employment and Subsistence, and will also be highly injurious to that Class of Men, who have their whole Property engaged in the said Business: And therefore praying the House, to take this Matter into their serious Consideration, and to give such Relief as to them may seem fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Tablq.

A Petition of the Hawkers and Pedlars in the Parish of Allstonfield, in the County of Stafford, was pre- M*-seated to the House*, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners hear, with the utmost Concern, that a Bill is intended to be brought into Parliament for the Repeal of the several Acts for granting Licences p to Hawkers and Pedlars; and that, the Petitioners a having been brought up from their Infancy in that Business, and relying on the Faith of Parliament that the same would be permanent and lasting, at least Z till

Pays and leans.

'blic

" counts.

5 Geo. III.

to53

kill the Expiration of the A^t of the Fifth of Queen jinne^ have fully employed themselves therein, and therefore totally unacquainted with any bther Business by which they can procure a Livelihood for themselves and Families, and especially as their Habitations are in a remote and barren Part of the Country, the Lands whereof are not capable of such Cultivation as (were the Estates their own) would produce a sufficient Maintenance; and that the Petitioners, having conducted themselves with Industry, Reputation, and Propriety, have gained Credit with a great Is umber of Manufacturers in many principal Towns in the Kingdom, with whom they have contracted Considerable Debts, and, from the Nature and Extent of the Petitioners Trade through most of the small Villages in the Kingdom, they have likewise been under the Necessity of giving great Credit, many of which Debts, in case their Trade is discontinued, they will be unable to recover, and therefore not able to pay the Manufacturers, the natural Consequence of which must bring on the Ruin of the Petitioners, and their. Families to the Parish; and that the Petitioners have always paid with Chearfulness the Duties Annually charged on their respective Licences, and, had the Legislature thought it expedient to have made any Addition thereto* they would have exerted their utmost Endeavours to have complied with every additional reasonable Requisition, and therefore cannot avoid thinking it particularly hard, that, out of the great Number of different Trades in this Kingdom, they only should be selected for Destruction, and, the Petitioners conceive, that it is contrary to the Spirit of Justice, and the Rights of Humanity, to abolish an Avocation which has hitherto been countenanced by successive Acts of the Legislature, by a Law whose Principle is pregnant with as many dreadful Consequences to the Rights of Property as that which makes an ex post facto Law so greatly inimical to the Liberty of the Subject: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law; and that they may be heard, at the Bar of the House, by themselves and their Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Staffordshire, A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are &c. Canal. thereunto subscribed, Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, and others, Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, have, at a very considerable Expence and Risque, made and corn-pleated a Canal Navigation from the River Severn, between Bewdley and Titton Brook, in the County of Worcester, across the River Trent, at or near Haywood Mill, in the County of Stafford, to join a Canal (now called The Grand Trunk Canal) made between the said River Trent and the River Mersey, and that the great Inducement to the said Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation to undertake the making of their said Canal, was the Advantage expected to arise from Coals and Merchandize to be navigated on the said Canal in general, and particularly from A ut her ley, near Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford (where the said Canal joins and communicates with the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations) to the River Secern, which is a Distance of Twenty-five Miles, and great Quantities of Coals, from Coal Mines which lie upon the Line of the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, and all the Goods and Merchandize conveyed,by Water between the Town of Birmingham and the Port of Bristol, and the intermediate Places, have been, and are, brought along the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, to Autherley, and from thence, along the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, to the River Severn, at Stourport, by which Means the Proprietors of the said last mentioned Navigation derive a very considerable Annual Income and Advantage; and that the Dudley Canal Navigation, by Means of its Junction with the Stourbridge Canal Navigation, opens a Communication with the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, at or near Stour ton, in the said County of Stafford, which, by the Course of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, is about Twelve . Miles and an Half distant from the said River Se-

vern; and that a Bill is now depending in the House, and before a Committee, for extending the present Dudley Canal from the Termination thereof, in certain Lands of Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire, within the Parish of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, to - Voi,. 40.

join and communicate with the Birmingham and Bir~ minghxm and Fazeley Canal Navigations, at or near Tipton Green, in the County of Stafford; and, the Petitioners observe, by the said Bill, that its Object is to open a Communication with large Tracts of Coal, Limestone, and Ironstone, lying upon the Line of such Extension, and to afford a shorter and cheaper Conveyance of Goods and Merchandize between the Town of Birmingham and the Port of Bristol, and the intermediate Places; and that the Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation have not the Power in themselves to reduce the Rates of Tonnage taken upon their said Canal, wherefore such intended Extension of die Dudley Canal will be very injurious to the Proprietors of the said Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, by drawing the Carriage of Coals lying upon the Line of the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, and also of Goods and Merchandize, out of and into the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, by the Way of such Extension, instead of passing on by the Way of Autherley, by which Means the said Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation will be deprived of the Advantage which they would otherwise receive from the Carriage of such Coals, Goods, and Merchandize, between Autherley and Stotirton, if such intended Extension did not take Place; and that, the Petitioners conceive, if the Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation were empowered of themselves to reduce and regulate the Tonnage upon their said Canal, it would be a Means of enabling them to preserve some Part of the said Carriage upon their Canal, at the same Time that the Public would be benefited by the Reduction of such Tonnage: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the said Company of Proprietors of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation may have Leave to introduce into the said Bill proper Clauses to impower them to reduce and regulate the Tonnage upon their said Canal, and that their Interest may be secured to them; and that they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; And that they do exexamine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House;

' And it is referred to Sir Edward Littleton, Mr. Gilbert, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Bill to repeal the Duties on Male Servants, and for Supply Bill; granting new Duties on Male and Female Servants, Servant*, was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Ways and Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re- Mean*, ferred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be charged upon, and paid to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, within the Kingdom 12 N of

1058 9° Junii. A, 1785,

Ways and of Great Britain, by every Male Person never having Means. been married, who shall retain or employ any Female Servant or Servants, the' several additional Yearly Sums following, that is to say, every such Person who shall retain or employ One Female Servant, and not more, the additional Sum of Two Shillings and Six Pence; for Two Female Servants, and not more, the additional Sum of Five Shillings each; and for Three or more Female Servants, the additional Sum of Ten Shillings each.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be charged upon, and paid to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, by every Male Person never having been married, who shall retain dr employ any Male Servant or Servants, the additional Yearly Sum of Twenty-five Shillings for every Male Servant who shall not be retained solely for the Purposes of Husbandry, or Manufactures, or of any Trade or Calling by which the Masters of such Servants earn a Livelihood or Profit.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for and upon every Warrant, Mandate, or Authority, granted to any Solicitor, Attorney, Notary, Proctor, Agent, or Procurator, in Great Britain, to institute, commence, or to defend any Suit, or Prosecution, in any of His Majesty's Courts at Westminster, or in any Ecclesiastical Court, or in any of the Courts of Admiralty, or Cinque Ports, or in any of His Majesty's Courts in Scotland, the Great Sessions in Wales, or in any Courts in the Counties Palatine, or in any other Court holding Pleas, where the Debt or Damage shall amount to more than Forty Shillings, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Solicitor, Attorney, Notary, Proctor, Agent, or Procurator, admitted or inrolled in any Ecclesiastical Court, or in any Courts of Law or Equity in Great Britain, when such Courts shall hold Pleas of more than Forty Shillings, shall, previous to his commencing or defending any Suit or Prosecution, take out Annually a Certificate of such his Admission or Inrollment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for and upon every such Certificate, so taken out by any Solicitor, Attorney, Notary, Proctor, Agent, or Procurator, who shall reside in any of the Inns of Court, or in the Cities of London or Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, the Parishes of Saint Pancras and Saint Mary le Bone, or within the Bills of Mortality, or within the City of Edinburgh, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Five Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for and upon every such Certificate, so taken out by any Solicitor, Attorney, Notary, Proctor, Agent, or Procurator, who shall reside in any other Part of Great Britain, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Three Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Allowances now made for Waste or Leakage to Brewers selling Beer, or Ale, in less Quantities than a Cask containing Four Gallons and a Haiti be discontinued.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in upon the Five last of the said Resolutions: And that Mr.

A Petition of the Wholesale Dealers and Manufacturers in the Town and Neighbourhood of Bolton in the Moors, in the County of Lancaster, w^as presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending in the House, to repeal the several Acts for licensing Hawkers and Pedlars; and Representing to the House, That many Advantages have resulted from the said diligent and useful Body of Men to the Wholesale Dealers and Manufacturers of the Town and Neighbourhood of Bolton, as well as to the Trade and Manufactures of other Parts of this Kingdom; and, the Laws now in Force seem to have held out Promises of Permanence and Stability to that Branch of Traffick, the Taxes imposed thereon being, by the Acts of the Fifth and Sixth of Queen Anne, to continue from the 23d of June 1710, for Ninety-six Years, and for One whole Year then next immediately ensuing after the Expiration of the said Term of Ninety-six Years; and that the Sanction of the Legislature of Britain has induced Numbers of industrious Traders to employ large Capitals in that Line of Business, and to give Credit, to a considerable Amount, in scattered Villages, remote Districts, and Houses far distant from Towns and Shopkeepers, which Debts can only be recovered by a Continuance of their stated Visits, and, if lost, would involve Thousands of worthy Families in Distress and Ruin: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the said Bill from passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That this House will resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the State of the Hawkers and Pedlars, and of the Nature and Condition of their Trade;

It passed in the Negative,

Commercial A Petition of the Proprietors and Occupiers of otercourse Buildings and Lands, and the Manufacturers and nth Ireland. Tradesmen, of the Town and Environs of Bromsgrove, f in the County of Worcester, was presented to the

c House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are alarmed at the Propositions now under Consideration of the House, intended to form a Treaty between Great Britain and Ireland, which, if carried into a Law, the Petitioners are apprehensive, will prove a continual Source of Uneasiness and Complaint to this Kingdom, as well as a lasting Injury to the Landed Interest, Trade, and Public Revenue, and, they conceive it unreasonable that Ireland should demand an equal Participation of the General Privileges and Protection of the British Empire, without a pro-; portionate Contribution towards its General Expences

and Support; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that many Manufacturers in their Neighbourhood will T: receive very great Injury from these Propositions, if

carried into a Law, unless guarded by a better Secu-; rity than is therein contained, and, that no Agreement between the Two Kingdoms can be equitable,

Vol. 40.

which doth not establish such Duties and Regulations, in both Kingdoms, as to put every Article of Commerce and Manufacture upon Terms of Equality; and that the different Manufactories in the Petitioners Neighbourhood, of Wool, Hats, Hemp,

Flax, Leathei4, Paper, drid Iron (especially the latter) employ many Thousand Persons, and the Petitioners have already experienced a rapid Increase of the Poors Rates, equal at least to One Fourth of the improved Rents (a Burthen unknown to Ireland) and, they apprehend, the intended new Regulations between the Two Kingdoms will induce the useful Manufacturers to emigrate) and leave a Part of their Families bur-thehsome to the Petitioners, by which Means the Poors Rates must vet inevitably increase: That the Linen Manufactories of the Neighbourhood of Bromsgrove are already very greatly injured by the free Admission of Irish Linens into this Kingdom, and will (if such' new Regulations take Effect) threaten a partial, if not a total, Destruction; and, that the Consideration which it is proposed for Ireland to give for this intended Participation is in itself inadequate, and no sufficient Security seems to be given for the Payment of such Consideration, which, the Petitioners apprehend, nothing short of a Real, Substantial, and Solid Union of the Two Kingdoms can effectually accomplish, and, they conceive, that Arrangements so important and extensive require the utmost Deliberation: And therefore praying, That the House will continue to extend its Enquiries on so interesting a Subject, so as to obtain the fullest Information on every Article of Manufacture, Commerce, and Revenue, involved in this weighty Business.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
