Richard Townsend, sworn.

I was Returning Officer at the last Election for Crieklade — This is the Poll. [Delivers it in.]

Withdrew.

Robert Smith, sworn.

As to the Conduct of the Returning Officer.

I attended as Agent for Heneage and Nicholas, at the last Election at Crieklade, from the Beginning to the End; my Employment was to take an' Account of the Votes as they came, with the Objections made to them by Counsel, and the Opinion of the Returning Officer — I took Minutes of what passed at the Poll — This is the Book in which I took the Minutes, and it has ever since been in my Custody — it only contains respecting the Borough Votes. — Previous to the Poll, Two or Three Days, I was in the Streets with Mr. Heneage and Lqccden, and it was proposed by them, that it w.ould be a very extensive Poll, and it might be as well to have Two or Three Places for the polling* — I looked upon that to be an Application on Behalf of the Petitioners — The Returning Officer was present* and it was made to the Returning Officer. — He said, it had not been usual at any other Election, and he could not think it necessary. — It was argued, that the Right of Election was so extended, it would save Confusion — The Hundreds are very extensive, and he knew it — I don’t know any particular Stress was laid on that. — On the First Day of the Poll I understood it was agreed upon by every Body that the Poll should close at Four o’Clock in the Evening — it was agreed so by the Counsel before the Business began — On the 8th of April — The Returning Officer declared he would not poll a Man in the Borough till all the Hundreds were polled — On the First Day many Hundreds came in with Gentlemen — I' believe near 100, on the Behalf of the Petitioners, were obliged to go away unpolled, much dissatisfied to find they could not poll — I think the First Proposal was, that they should sit till about Two o’Clock, then adjourn for an Hour to Dinner, and then come again, and go on till Eight o’Clock at Night — That he refused, and said he should close at Four; the Reason given for the Request was, that the Freeholders might not be obliged to come again on another Day — The Poll began on the First Day about Twelve or One o’Clock. — On the Saturday I attended the Poll till the Close of it — it was proposed, That^he Poll should continue till about Four o’Clock, and that they should adjourn it then, and if necessary come again; and the Reason given for it was this, there were several Farmers on both Sides, I suppose; I knew several on our Side had Occasion to go to

Marlborough Market, and said on Friday Night they could return from Market on Saturday Evening, and come and poll — This Proposal was acceded to by the Returning Officer, and every one on his Behalf — what I recollect was, the Returning Officer declared he should only adjourn for an Hour, and that he should come again* provided any of the Freeholders came to poll; and if none came, he should only go as Matter of Form, and adjourn till the Monday Morning — this 1 believe was acceded to by all Parties present — I was present, I speak with Certainty — in my Presence it was acceded to — not One objected to it, as I heard* — After Dinner the Returning Officer and

Mr. Myers came into our Room just as we had dined — Myers said, 44 Are any of your Freeholders come in?" — the Returning Officer by. — Myers attended, I believe, as the Assistant and Adviser of Mr. Townsend — he sat at his Right Hand, and very often declared what he thought right; and said, he (the Returning Officer) should abide by his Opinioii. — We said to Myers, Not that we know of — Then they said, they should only go down to adjourn the Court^-don’t remember any Thing said by the Returning Officer about going to the Poll — I did not go down, thinking the y only went down to adjourn the Poll; but in about Five or oix Minutes afterwards a Message was brought to our Lodgings, that the Candles were lighted in the Hall, that the Returning Officer was there, and began to poll the Borough Votes — I then went down, as did every Body; when I got down, I found Mr, Mills there; there was a Place set apart for the Voters to go up and poll — few but Gentlemen from any where but there; when I came I found that particular* Spot full of People, Voters in the Borough — I don’t believe there was a Freeholder — They were beginning to poll the Borough, there were Two polled that Night — there was an Objection made to polling the Borough by Mr. Mills, as Counsel for the Petitioners, in general charging the Returning Officer with Breach of Promise — Mr. Mills objected to it, because be had promised he would poll only Freeholders that Night. — No Freeholders came in, and therefore it was intended he should adjourn the Court till Monday Morning — The Objection was not attended to tUL near an Hour; he said he should go on, he was not to wait there to do nothing. — Mr. Mills insisted the Returning Officer was guilty of a Breach of Promise, and that he ou^ht not to have done it. — Mr. Mills demanded to adjourn, which he would not do — the Freeholders were not at that Time exhausted-after that Ninety were polled — on Monday Morning — — I don’t mean any were then in the Town. — Mr. Townsend said it was only a Farce, we might as well go on, for we had no more Freeholders to poll, we were quite exhausted — it was near Two Hours before the Poll was closed — it was all Altercation — The Borough Voters who polled were the Two Fawkes. — On the Friday Morning, previous to the Beginning of the Poll, I applied to Mr. Kinnier, a Voter — he had before declared himself a Friend to the Petitioners, and I applied to him to poll; he said he had no Objection; and I told him it would be an Inducement to the Returning Officer to take the Votes promiscuously. — He went and offered to poll on the Friday Morning — Townsend asked him what he came there for? He said, to vote for Heneage and Nicholas. He said, You don’t mean to poll as a Burgess? for if you do, I shan’t take you now; I am not come to the Town yet; but, says he, 44 if you like it, you may poll as a Freeholder/’ and went away. — The Returning Officer said, what he had often said before, he never would poll a Burgess, while there was a Man in the Hundreds to poll — he said so an Hundred Times — There was no Agreement made about it between the Candidates. — On the Motiday Morning I went early to the Poll — at the Beginning — Ninety

Freeholders

5 Geo. lit 13® JttmL io6t

Freeholders polled tbit £>ay — I believe the First who offered were Borough People: — He began the Borough People on the Monday Morning. — Mr. Mills insisted he had a Right to examine all the Voters who came to poll in the Borough as to their Right of voting — this was when they were beginning to poll — I don’t believe One had polled: He said he had a

Right to examine into every Vote. — There is no Oath taken at Cricklade — with respect to the Leaseholder a particular Claim was made; it was insisted on, that when the Leaseholders came up to poll, they should not only be examined with respect to their Lease, by whom granted, and for what Number of Years, but that they should produce it; this was insisted on by Counsel on Behalf of the Petitioners. — *No Copyholders of the Borough offered to claim all the Election. — A Resblution of the Committee, of 1775 was read to the Returning Officer. — I do not believe there was a Man polled in the Borough who was not objected to on the same Ground as the First — several Voters applied to the Returning Officer for Advice, when Mr. Mills questioned them. — When he insisted on the Production of the Lease, the Returning Officer said, No, the Inhabitants were not obliged to produce any Lease, when called for by Counsel, or any other Person — I took down his Words — Several referred to the Returning Officer, when they were asked where they lived, and the Nature of their Leases, — many of them — the Officer gave the same Answer — said they were not obliged to answer any Question whatever. — That was the general Answer be gave to all; and said, " I know he is a good Vote, and will admit him." — The Officer did not acquaint the Petitioners Counsel on what Grounds he knew the Voter had a good Vote. — I remember William Dash coming to poll — he was objected to as being on the Poors Rates — the Objection was made by the Counsel, and by a Mr. Bird, a Freeholder of the Borough — he said he knew the Returning Officer had paid him himself — that was the First Pauper objected to — the Returning Officer admitted the Vote — don’t know he made any Answer to the Objection — the Rates had been inspected by Agents on Behalf of the Petitioners, and they had taken Extracts from those Rates, of People having received Alms — I inspected them myself — the Extracts were offered to be produced as Evidence to shew the Voters received Alms — it was hinted to me, and other Agents, that there were several Pau-

!)ers — that the Agents for the Sitting Members had nspected the Books, and taken Extracts from them;

I came in when One of the Two Borough Votes was polling, on the Saturday — they were the only Two that polled that Evening, 1 believe — I came in when they were polling the last Man — we were all taken by Surprize.

British Mr. Alderman Hammet reported from the Corn-

Assurance mittee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons

iet*’ whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and others, Members of a Society called or known by the Description of The British Assurance Society, and now held at the Queens Arms Tavern, Newgate Street, in the City of London, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared from the Testimony of Mr. Christopher . Howard Bullock, and Mr. Joseph Potter, that about

the Year 1773 the Petitioners, and several others (Mechanics, Tradesmen, Artificers, and Labouring Persons) established a Fund for the Relief of themselves and Families in Cases of Sickness, and other Misfortunes, and held Meetings, and chose certain Persons to collect and apply, under stipulated Rules, the Subscriptions from Time to Time made — That about the Year 1779 the Society very much increased, from which, and on Account of some Variance happening amongst the Members, it became necessary to regulate their former Rules and Orders, and accordingly a Deed (by Way of Policy) with certain Covenants therein specified, was prepared, and the Petitioners were stiled therein The British Assurance Society, an Exemplification of which Deed w>as, for the Purpose of every Member having Access thereto, as Evidence, inrolled in the Court of King’s Bench in Trinity Term 1779 — That since the making of the said Deed, several other Persons have become Members of the said Society, and the same are daily encreasing; yet, notwithstanding the Covenants in the said , Deed, the Petitioners, for Want of being regularly incorporated, find, that they cannot carry into Execution several of the salutary Regulations proposed by their original Institution, and thereby many Persons, who would willingly become Members of the Society, are prevented from so doing through Doubts of the said Society’s Property being sufficiently secured by the present Mode of Establishment — That, for Want of Incorporation, the Society can neither sue, or be sued, but are reduced to the Necessity of proceeding in the Names of certain Members appointed for that Purpose, which not only occasions great Expence, but is constantly attended with Delays and Difficulties.

It also appeared, from the Testimony of the before-mentioned Witnesses, that as the said Society’s Stock is daily encreasing, it has been considered that if the same was placed out on Government Security, or Freehold Lands, in the Name of the Society, not only every Member w ould be better secured in his just Claims, but the Stock would be thereby much im-Vol. 40.

Junii. 1069

proved — That by the Rules and Regulations of the said Society, not only the several Parishes in and round this Metropolis, but also some of the most distant Parishes in the Kingdom, will be greatly disencumbered of their Poor, from several Members of the Society and their Families being, by the Benefits of the said Institution, prevented becoming burthensome to their respective Parishes.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a. Bill for incorporating the Members of a Society called The British Assurance Society: And that Mr. Alderman Hammet and Mr. Beaufoy do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Offices and Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to E^ploy-indemnify such Persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments, and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications ' within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes; and to indemnify Members and Officers in ^Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or having been stamped, have been lost or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; and to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the Execution of Indentures of Clerk3 to Attornies and Solicitors, was committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for rendering valid the Proceedings of Trustees for the Care of Turnpike Roads, at Meetings where Persons have acted without being duly appointed, and for indemnifying such Persons.

A Petition of the Merchants, ManufacUiFers, and

Junii. . 1785.

Wholesale Dealers, of Whitehaven, in the County of Hawkers and Cumberland, was presented to the House, and read; Pedlars. Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending in the House, to repeal the several Statutes made for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars; and Representing to the House, That many great and important Advantages are derived from the said useful and industrious Class of Tradesmen, the Quantity of Goods bought and disposed of by them being considerably more extensive than hath been generally conceived, and the Mode of their Sale, which is wholly confined to small Villages and Places remote from general Markets, tends very greatly to diffuse the Manufactures of the Kingdom in general, and is a Source of great Convenience to those Inhabitants who live at a Distance from the principal Towns, great Quantities of Goods, of almost every Description, being thereby vended in detail, which the remote Inhabitant could not find Leisure to seek, and, when Necessity might compel him to go from Home, the Expence of his Journey would frequently be as great as the Object of his Purchase; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it will tend greatly to lessen the Consumption of many principal Articles of Manufacture, will consequently curtail the manufacturing thereof, and throw many Manufacturers out of Employment, and must also, in many Cases, prove prejudicial to His Majesty’s Revenue, without taking into Consideration that Loss which will be occasioned by the Want of the Duty on Licences, and, the numerous Body of Men who are now employed in that Branch of Commerce, and who have been bred up therein from their Infancy, who have exerted their Industry, and placed their whole Dependence in Life, under the Sanction and Protection of the Legislature of this Kingdom, will thereby be thrown out of Employment, and they and their Families be reduced to Indigence and Poverty: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and prevent the said intended Bill from passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Iron Masters, Nail Manufacturers, and others, concerned in the Iron Trade, at West Bromwich, in the County of Stafford, and Neighbourhood thereof, whose Names are thereunder written, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That very large Sums of Money are employed in making Bar Iron in Britain, which could not be done to Profit, if there ‘was not some Duty laid upon the Importation of Foreign Iron, and which is now £.2. 16$. id. per Ton, and in Ireland only () 6*. 2 d. English Money; and, many Thousands of Manufacturers have, for a great Number of Yeafs, been employed upon Iron Wares exported from Britain to America, to which Country nearly the Whole of our Export Trade in that Article has been confined; and that, in the Year 1778, Liberty was given to export Iron Wares from Ireland to America, provided a Duty of £.3. 3s. lid. per Ton was imposed thereon, as an Equivalent for the Difference of the Duties then paid in Britain and in Ireland upon the Importation of Bar Iron, and, since that Time, a farther Duty of 7 s. 7 d. per Ton has been laid upon Bar Iron in Britain, so that the true equalizing Duty should ndw be £.3. ibs. 3d. per Ton; and that, when the Resolutions of the House of Commons in Ireland, relative to a Commercial Intercourse between the Two Kingdoms, came under the Consideration of the Iron Masters, Nail Manufacturers, and others, at a public Meeting held upon the 21st Day of February last, at West Bromwich, it was not understood by the Petitioners, that the Irish were at Liberty to export Iron Wares to the United States of America free of the equalizing Duty of £.3. 3$. 11 d. as settled in 1778; but, at a Second Meeting of Iron Masters and Nail Manufacturers, at the same Place, on the 18th Day of March last, a Petition to this House was signed* representing, that they employed many Thousand Persons in making of Nails and other Iron Wares^ and that, by the United States of America having become independent of this Country, the Irish had accidentally acquired the Liberty of exporting Iron Wares to those States free of Duty, by which the Advantage to Manufacturers in Ireland was so great that there could be no Doubt some of the substantial Manufacturers in this Vicinity would establish Works it that Country, unless some effectual Means were adopted to prevent the Removal of Workmen, and therefore they prayed, that the Commercial Intercourse with Ireland might not be finally settled without equal Duties being imposed upon the Importation of Bar Iron into both Kingdoms; and that the Petitioners being, since that Time, informed, that it is not probable that either the equalizing Duty, as Settled in the Year 1778, will be continued, or Iron Wares exported from Ireland to the United States of America, or that the Duty to be paid in Ireland, on the Importation of Bar Iron, will be made equal to that in Britain, they consider it their indispensable Duty to their Neighbourhood, and to their Country, again humbly to make these Representations of the Situation of the Nail and IronWare Trade, now that the great Advantage of removing Workmen to Ireland is publicly and generally known, and to declare that they have no Doubt there is a Necessity for taking immediate Measures to prevent the planting a considerable Part of the Nail and Iron Ware Trade in that Country, where so many Advantages would attend the carrying it on, besides the important one here stated; and, they very much fear, if Establishments should be begun in Ireland, by any of the Petitioners, or by many others who are equally qualified, there would be no Probability of the Trade ever returning to this Country: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to adopt such effectual Methods for the Protection of the Iron Trade in Britain, as to the House shall seem meet, and that

ahd that the Proprietor of the said Manufactory is willing to desist from carrying on his Trade there, provided an Indemnification be given him for the Loss and Injury he may sustain by removing it; and, the Petitioners would raise, among themselves, a Sum of Money to provide such an Indemnity, but, by Reason of the grievous Losses they have recently sustained by the said Fire, they are totally unable so to do: And therefore praying, That* in Consideration of these Circumstances, they may have Leave to present a Petition praying for Relief, notwithstanding the last Day for receiving Petitions is passed.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, and others, have sustained a very great Loss and Damage in their Pro- perty by a Fire, which happened on the 7th Day of May last, in or near a Manufactory of Turpentine, Pitch, and Tar, in the Occupation of Mr. Edward JVebster, situate in Hai'sey Dawn aforesaid, and, the Petitioners conceive the carrying on of such Businesses subjects the Houses and Buildings in the Vicinity of the Manufactory to constant and very imminent Danger of Accidents by Fires, notwithstanding the Regulations provided by Law respecting the Situation of Turpentine Manufactories; and Representing to the House, That, on the Spot where the Houses, Warehouses, and other Buildings, lately belonging to the Petitioners, stood, such Trades are particularly hazardous and alarming, the Streets being narrow, and the Warehouses therein, and on the Bank of the River, being always full of Goods and Merchandize, to a very great Value, and that the Proprietor of the said Manufactory of Turpentine, Pitch, and Tar, situate in Horsey Down, at the Request of the Petitioners and the Neighbourhood, is willing to desist from carrying on his Trade there, provided an Indemnification be given him for the Loss and Injury he may sustain by removing his Manufactory to another Place; and that the Removal of so dangerous a Trade would not only be a great Satisfaction and Security to the Petitioners, but of great Benefit to the Neighbourhood for a great Extent, and to the Shipping which resort to the Warehouses on the Side of the River where the said Manufactory now stands, and, the Petitioners would chearfully raise among themselves a Sum of Money to provide such an Indemnity to the Proprietor thereof as aforesaid, but, by Reason of the grievous Losses they have recently sustained by the said Fire, they are totally unable so to do: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that an adequate Indemnification may be provided, for the above Purpose, by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as the Circumstances of their Situation may be found to merit and require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof* and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Mr. Henry Thornton reported from the Committee, to'Turpentine whom the Petition of the several Persons whose Names Manufac-are thereunto subscribed, Owners of Houses and Estates tones* in Potters Fields, within the Parish of Saint John, Horsey Dozen, and Borough of Southwark, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Richard Davis being examined, said, That in consequence of a Fire which happened upon the 7th of May last, in or near a Manufactory of Turpentine,

Pitch, and Tar, belonging to Mr. Edward Webster, situate in Horsey Dozen, very considerable Loss and Damage have been sustained by the Petitioners and others, to the Amount of between and £.500,000 —

That the Witness’s Loss was very considerable — That it is computed that 1,000 Ton of Hemp, near 10,000 Barrels of Pitch, Tar, and Turpentine, a great Quantity of Oil and Logwood, besides other Articles, were totally destroyed; together with near 700 Ton of Tea belonging to the East India Company.

That the carrying on of such Businesses subjects the Houses and Buildings in the Vicinity of the Manufactory to constant and very imminent Danger of Accidents by Fire, notwithstanding the Regulations provided by Law, respecting the Situation of Turpentine Manufactories — That on the Spot where the Houses, Warehouses, and other Buildings lately destroyed stood, such Trades are particularly hazardous and alarming, the Streets being narrow, and the Warehouses therein and on the Bank ot* the River being always full of Goods and Merchandize to a very great Value.

And the Witness further said, That the Removal of so dangerous a Trade would not only be a Satisfaction and Security to the Petitioners, but of great Benefit to the Neighbourhood for a considerable Ex^ tent, and to the Shipping which resort to the Warehouses on the Side of the River where the said Manufactory now stands; and that the Petitioners would chearfully raise among themselves a Sum of Money, for the Purpose of indemnifying the Proprietor of the said Manufactory, for the Loss and Injury he may sustain in removing the same to anodier Place (which, at the Request of the Petitioners and the Neighbourhood, he has consented to do) but, by Reason of the 12 T grievous

m

Graumanns

frievous Losses they have recently sustained by the said ire, they are totally unable so to do. Then,

Mr. Webster being examined, informed your Committee, That he has been in Possession of the said Ma-nufactory near 20 Years — That he holds the Whole of his Premisses by Lease, of which 27 Years are unexpired — That when he first went there, the Manufactory stood clear of Buildings; but since that Time, several Buildings have been erected round it — That in case a fair and adequate Indemnification is granted to him, he is willing to remove the said Manufactory to another Situation, in order to accommodate the Neighbourhood — That he has had an Estimate made of the Expence he should sustain by building a new Manufactory in another Place. — And he produced to your Committee the said Estimate, which amounts to £. 6,200.

And being asked, What would be the Expence of re-building his Warehouses upon the present Scite ? He said, he supposed about £. 1,500 would reinstate what he has lost; and that his Turpentine Manufactory is the least damaged.

Then an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for making " more effectual an Act, made in the Sixth Year of " her Majesty’s Reign, for the better preventing of cc Mischiefs that may happen by Fire," was read; whereby it was enacted, That it should not be lawful for any Person or Persons to distil or boil any Turpentine, nor draw any Oil of Turpentine and Rosin by distilling of common Turpentine, nor boil the said Oil and Turpentine together, above the Quantity of Ten Gallons at One Time, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Borough of Southwark, and Liberties thereof, in any Worldiouse contiguous to any other Building, but should stand distant from any other Building, at least 50 Foot, except such Houses as were then built in Southwark, and used for the said Trade, and except the Still and Furnace built by Daniel Toombes, at his House at Holborn Bridge, for the Distillation of Oil of Turpentine, under the Penalty of One hundred Pounds.

Then Two Acts, made in the Twelfth and Fourteenth Years of His present Majesty, for regulating Buildings and Party Walls within the Cities of London and Westminster, were also read; by which it appeared, that the said Act of Queen Anne was repealed, and the Restrictions and Penalties therein contained were re-enacted, without any Exception in Favour of Manufactories then existing.

Then Mr. Webster being again called, informed your Committee, That at the Time of passing the said Acts of the Twelfth and Fourteenth Years of His present Majesty, he was not aware of the Restrictions contained in them; and that he did not even know, till after the late Fire, that such an Act existed.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the Borough of Penryn, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, the Petitioners are sensible, the Exigencies of the State are such as to require new Taxes, but that the Tax imposed on Retail Shops is in many Instances very burthensome; and, that the only Alleviation the Petitioners can point out to themselves in the present Case, is a repeal of the several Acts for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars, and the Petitioners rely on the Wisdom of Parliament for a Repeal of those Acts, and that a Prohibitory Act may be passed, to prevent those itinerant Traders from carrying on their Traffic, so very prejudicial to the fair resident Tradesman, who is so heavily burthened with Parochial

and other Taxes; and that the Hawkers and Pedlars are greatly prejudicial to the Revenue of this Kingdom, by the illicit Trade they carry on, and are a Nuisance to the Community at large, by their frequent Impositions, and the Petitioners hope that the Idea which was held forth, when the Shop Tax was first proposed, of abolishing all itinerant Traders, will not be abandoned.

A Petition of the several' Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Retail Shopkeepers residing in or near the Borough of Truro, in the County of Cornwall: And also,

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the Town of Penzance, in the County of Cornwall;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, though already heavily burthened with Parochial Rates and numerous Taxes, are truly sensible that the Exigencies of the State require other Taxes to be imposed, and that they must contribute their Part, but, at the same Time, they represent to the House, that the levying a Tax upon Shops will operate as a most partial and oppressive Tax upon Shopkeepers, unless the several Acts for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars be repealed, or such considerable Duties imposed on their Licences, or otherwise, as will prevent them from underselling, and thereby injuring, the Shopkeepers, who already pay Duties on almost all the Articles they deal in; and that the House Tax, Window Tax, Commutation Tax, Insurance Tax, and the Taxes on Bills of Exchange and Re* ceipts, heavily affect them, but the greatest Evil which the Petitioners experience, and which they submit to the Consideration of the House, -is the long Credit the Retail Shopkeepers are compelled to allow to their Customers, whilst the Haw kers and Pedlars, who pay few Taxes, carry off the Ready Money, which often should have been applied to pay Book Debts too long outstanding for the Interest of the Retail Shopkeepers, and to the Injury of their Families: And therefore praying ing the House, to take their Case into Consideration, and to give them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet A Petition of the Shopkeepers resident within the Borough of Lancaster, in the County of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the late Tax upon Shops, added to the several Parliamentary and Parochial Taxes before imposed upon them, will become a very excessive Burthen upon their Trade, unless the several Acts of Parliament granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars be repealed, as the Petitioners had every Reason to expect; and that the Hawkers and Pedlars have many Opportunities of dealing in Contraband Goods, and should they be permitted to carry on their Traffic, which at present is free from all Taxes whatsoever, their Licences only excepted, it would tend to increase the Number of such itinerant Traders, and lessen the Number of Shopkeepers, to the great Detriment of the Revenues of this Kingdom; and that, if the Hawkers and Pedlars were suppressed, they would not necessarily be reduced to Indigence, because they have an equal Right to keep Shops, and follow a fair and open Trade, with their Fellow Subjects: And therefore

praying, That the several Acts of Parliament for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars may be repealed, and a prohibitory Act passed, to prevent such itinerant Traders, if, in the Wisdom of Parliament, it should be thought proper.

Commercial A Petition of the Landholders and Commissioners

Supply of the County of Aberdeen, was presented w! re an. House, and read; Setting forth, That, on the Introduction into this House of the Propositions for a Commercial Intercourse with Ireland, in their original Form, the Commissioners of Supply of the said County, under the deepest Sense of the destructive and dangerous Tendency of these Propositions, did, in the firmest though most respectful Terms, signify to the Public their Sense of that important Measure, in a Resolution unanimously adopted at a Meeting called for that special Purpose, on the 12th of March last; and that the Commissioners of Supply, being afterwards advised that the only Constitutional Mode of submitting their Grievances, on this Occasion, to the Consideration of Parliament, was by presenting a Petition to this House, did accordingly, at their Annual General Meeting, on the 30th of April last, resolve on and prepare a Petition to the House, praying that these Propositions might not pass into a Law, which was signed by the Praeses, in Name, and by Appointment of the Meeting, but the ‘Petition was refused to be received, on Account of its not being signed by each individual Commissioner; the Petitioners, however, are happy to see that the general and decided Voice of the Commercial and Manufacturing Interest of Great Britain, confirmed by the Evidence which has been given‘ at the Bar of the House, in Support of the numerous Petitions which were presented from other Counties and Corporations, have induced the House to make such Amendments and Alterations upon the Propositions originally presented as appear to have a Tendency to correct, in some Degree, the ruinous Consequences with which they must have been attended, both to the Commercial and Landed Interest of these Kingdoms; at the same Time, the Propositions, as now amended, embrace Objects of so vast Magnitude, so nice Disquisition, and so essential Importance to the Prosperity of the whole Realm, that the Petitioners have not hitherto been able, in the short Time that has elapsed since the amended Propositions were made, to form a proper Judgment how far they ought to be adopted, and, as the Commercial Treaty to be framed on these Reso« Jutions will be for ever binding on both Kingdoms, so that no Alteration can be made thereon, the Petitioners are hopeful that full Time will be given to the Subjects of both Kingdoms to deliberate on and investigate this important Subject, and therefore that the final Adjustment of this Treaty will be postponed to the next Session of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Petition do He upon the Table.

Paisley Two A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names Pennies are theronnto subscribed. Inhabitants of or near to the

Town of Paisley, and affected by the Bill herein after complained of, for and in Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, that a Bill is depending in the House, for a Renewal of the Act which imposes a Duty of Two Pennies in the Pint of Ale and Beer within the Town of Paisley, and for authorizing the Magistrates and Town Council thereof to levy the said Impost, or Duty, of Two Pennies Scots, or One Sixth Part of a Penny Sterling, over and above the Duty of Excise paid or payable to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer that shall be either brewed, brought into, tapped, or sold within the said Town of Paisley, and Liberties thereof, and a certain other District surrounding the same; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the establishing such a Duty of Two Pennies Scots on every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer in Manner mentioned in the said Bill, is not only highly unjust, partial, and oppressive to them, and many other. Individuals, but also, extremely prejudicial to the Public Revenue; and, the Petitioners are of Opinion that these Impost Duties granted to several Towns, for limited Times, in this Part of the united Kingdom, are incompatible with its true Interests, and act in direct Opposition to a Reform in the National Revenues so necessary for the Prevention of Frauds, and Imposition of New or Additional Taxes upon the People of this Realm, and, it i3 an incontrovertible Fact, that the Duties of Excise upon Beer have decreased in the Proportion of One Half in almost every Town in Scotland\ where those Impost Duties have been established, and, by the Records of the City of Edinburgh, it is ascertained that the Quantities of Bejer, brewed in that City in the Year 1776, was only equal to Two Seventh Parts of the Quantities brewed, and for which Duties were paid in the Year 1724, although in the intermediate Space the Inhabitants of that City have very much increased in Number, which the Petitioners ascribe solely to the Existence of those Impost Duties in that City; and that the Petitioners likewise conceive, that the said Bill is not only unwise and impolitic in its Principle, but also partial, unjust, and oppressive in its Provisions and Operation, as, among others, it subjects all such of the Petitioners as are concerned in the Brewing Business to pay this Impost Tax for all they brew, whereas, in Equity and Justice, the Petitioners contend that, if they are to be subjected to this Tax, they ought only to be subjected to the Duty for what is sold and consumed within the Town; and upon these Grounds, and sundry others, which the Petitioners are ready to offer at the Bar of the House, they hope and trust the House will see sufficient Reason for rejecting this Bill altogether, or at least so to modify and explain it, as to make it less partial, burthensome, and intolerable, than it must be if passed in its present Form ': And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the above Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief therein, and in the several Matters and Tilings above complained of, as to the House may seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to continue, and render more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for laying a Duty of Two Pennies Scots, or One-Sixth Part of a Penny Sterling, on every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer which shall be brewed for Sale, brought into, tapped, or sold, within the Town of Paisley, and Liberties thereof, in the County of Renfrew, for improving the Navigation of the River Cart; and for other Purposes, is re-committed; and that the Petitioners’ be heard,

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the County of the Borough of Carmarthen, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have long laboured under great Inconveniences and frequent Losses from the unfair Practices of Hawkers and Pedlars, who generally sell some Articles at or under Prime Cost to delude the Unwary, while, on other Articles, they take exorbitant Profits; and that the Petitioners are subject to high Rents, to Parochial Offices, always troublesome, though necessary, and Parish Rates and Taxes unfelt by the Pedlar and Hawker, and the Petitioners frequently sustain considerable Losses from the Uncertainty of the Returns of Hawkers (who always carry off ready Cash, while the Shopkeeper is obliged to give long Credit) and, when the Petitioners have laid in an Assortment of Goods, which they have a Certainty of disposing of in a reasonable Time, and thereby flatter themselves with the Hope of making regular Returns, the Hawker comes in the Instant, and, by a pompous Advertisement, blasts their Hopes, and too often their Credit also; and, the Petitioners conceive the Revenue will not be much, if any Thing, injured by the Suppression of the Licences of Hawkers and Pedlars, nor even themselves injured, since they will continue to have the like Chance with the fair Trader whenever they shall be disposed to bear the like Burthens; and that the Petitioners, although already labouring under a Load of Taxes, chearfully submitted to the Tax on Retail Shops under, they trust, a well-grounded Hope that the Licences of Hawkers and Pedlars would be totally done away, and the Grievances aforestated removed; and that the Petitioners are alarmed at the Petitions presented to the House for the Continuance of the Licences of Hawkers and Pedlars, who, if suffered to continue travelling from Place to Place under the Protection of Law, will greatly injure the fair Trader, and render the Petitioners incapable of paying their Rents, the numerous Taxes, and supporting their Families: And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and afford them such Relief, as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers in Kendal, in the Hawkers County of Westmoreland, was presented to the House, and Pedlars, and read; Setting forth, That the Tax imposed on Shops, added to the great Weight of Parochial Taxes, will fall very heavy upon their Trade, against which the Petitioners were flattered that the several Acts for granting Licences to Hawkers were to be repealed, to enable them to pay such Tax; and, the Petitioners are satisfied ho public Inconvenience can arise from suppressing such Licences, as the remote Places might and would be supplied with Goods by the Retail Shops now established in all Parts of the Country, and where many more would be opened, if Goods were not introduced by the Hawkers; and that the Petitioners do now, and always have, sold the Goods manufactured in Great Britain upon more reasonable Terms than the Hawkers and Pedlars ever have or can do; and, if the Hawkers and Pedlars were suppressed, they would not necessarily be reduced to Indigence, Misery, and Inaction, as they have an equal Right, with their Fellovv-Subjects, of opening Shops, and following a fair and open Trade, and they would thereby become more useful Members of Society; and that, if the Hawkers and Pedlars were prohibited, a great many more Shops, would be opened, the Inland Trade guarded against Smuggling, and the Revenues of the Kingdom greatly enlarged and secured: And therefore praying, That the several Acts of Parliament for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars may be repealed, and a prohibitory Act passed, to prevent itinerant Traders from carrying on their Traffic, so prejudicial to the fair resident Tradesman.

A Petition of the Manufacturers, Wholesale Traders, and Inhabitants of Kendalin the County of Westmoreland\ was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, with Concern, seen by the Votes, an Opposition made to the intended Bill for suppressing Hawkers and Pedlars, as they conceive the Trade of Hawking has been, and is, a Means of conveying and selling prohibited Goods, to the great Injury of the Revenue, and the fair Trader; and that by the Means of itinerant Dealers, stolen Goods are frequently disposed of, and, if Hawking was suppressed, the same Quantity of Goods, the Produce of the Manufactories of this Country, would still be sold that ever has been, and such Suppression would not eventually injure the Trade and Manufacture of this Kingdom, but would greatly increase the Revenue, and shut a great Avenue against Smuggling: And therefore praying, That an Act may be passed for repealing the several Acts of Parliament for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars.

A Petition of the several Tradesmen, Shopkeepers within the Town of Dover, in the County of Kent, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners having long experienced the Injuries derived from licensing Hawkers and Pedlars, and finding that the Tax on Shops hath passed the Royal Assent, and that the Chancellor of the Exchequer hath since moved the House that certain additional Duties may be laid on Hawkers and Pedlars, and that another Set of Persons, not exactly of that Description, but who, instead of travelling with Parcels and Bundles, usually take Rooms, and hold temporary Auctions in various Towns, Cities, and Corporations, are equally Objects of Taxation, the Propriety of which the Petitioners are well

A Petition of Edward Webster, Esquire, Proprietor of the Manufactory of Turpentine, Pitch, and Tar, in Potters Fields, within the Parish of Saint John, Ho?'-scy Down, in the Borough of Southwark, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner observes, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented to the House, stating, that a Fire having lately happened in or near his said Manufactory, it is expedient to remove the same for the Purpose of securing the Houses, and other Buildings, in the Vicinity thereof from similar Accidents in future; and that the Petitioner is willing to remove his said Manufactory, provided an adequate Compensation be given him for so doing: And therefore praying, That, in case it should be deemed requisite, for the Security of the Neighbourhood, and the Benefit of the Public, that his Manufactory at the Place above-mentioned should be discontinued, a reasonable Satisfaction may be made to him for removing the same, and that he may be permitted to state to the House the Loss and Damage he must sustain by such Removal.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Supply, Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re-, ferred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Fifty thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to be applied as a Payment for present Relief, and upon Account, to such Persons who have suffered in their Rights and Properties, as have given satisfactory Proofs of their Losses to the Commissioners appointed by an Act, made in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, " An tc Act for appointing Commissioners to enquire into " the Looses and Services of all such Persons who " have suffered in their Rights, Properties, and Professions, during the late unhappy Dissections in " America, in Consequence of their Loyalty to His Majesty, and Attachment to the British Government," to be distributed and paid under the Direction of the said Commissioners, in a Proportion not exceeding Forty Pounds per Centum, to such of the said Persons as bore Arms, or rendered Services in America, and in a Proportion not exceeding Thirty Pounds per Centum to such others of the said Persons as were resident in America during the War.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to be paid to Mr. Henry Phillips, on his making a proper Discovery, for the Use of the Public, of the Composition of his Powder for the Destruction of Insects.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the further Consideration of the First of the said Resolutions be adjourned till Friday Morning next;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the said Resolutions were severally read a Second Time; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

AP E T I TIO N of the Retail Shopkeepers residing within the Town of Falmouth, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill having lately passed both Houses of Parliament, and received the Royal Assent, for imposing and levying a Tax on all Retail Shops within the Kingdom of Great Britain, whereby the Petitioners will be greatly affected and oppressed (the said Tax operating partially on the Petitioners, as they conceive) unless the several Acts of Parliament, now in being, in Favour of the Hawkers and Pedlars within this Kingdom, be repealed, such Itinerants being inimical to the resident Traders, who are obliged to pay large Rents for their Shops, and are already most heavily burthened with Parochial and other Taxes: And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and repeal the said Act for imposing and levying the aforesaid Shop Tax, or otherwise grant them Relief, by repealing and abolishing the several Acts of Parliament made, as aforesaid, in Favour of the Hawkers and Pedlars, who are so injurious to the fair Trader.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House, an Account of the Money granted in the Year 1783, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the Twenty-third of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for extending and improving the Trade to " Africa" and that they have invested the Money granted in 1784 for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast; and that the said Forts and Settlements were delivered to the Petitioners in a very ruinous Condition by the Royal African Company, and the Sums Annually granted by Parliament for their Support and Maintenance being nearly expended in the Civil and Military Establishments, and in the necessary Contingent Charges, there remained little or nothing for the Purpose of Repairs; and that the Petitioners, by Advices from Africa, find that a very considerable Expence has been incurred by the Hostilities on that Coast between the Subjects of this Country and of the States General of the United Provinces, for which no Provision has been made, but, not having received a compleat Account of the said Expenditure, they cannot at present ascertain the exact Amount thereof, or the Debt now due to the several Officers and Servants of the Petitioners, for Want of the general Books to the End of the Year 1784: And that the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for extending and improving the British Trade to Africa, therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum as may be necessary for the effectual Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements in Africa, for the Payment of the Debt abovementioned, and likewise such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the 'Table.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now read.

Mr. Henry Thornton reported from the Committee, Turpentine to whom the Petition of Edward Webster, Esquire, Manufactory. Proprietor of the Manufactory of Turpentine, Pitch, and Tar, in Potters Fields, within the Parish of Saint John, Horsey Dozen, in the Borough of Southwark, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards deli* yered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as folloVveth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Webster informed your Committee, That he is willing to remove his Manufactory to another Place, provided a reasonable Compensation is made to him for the Expence he must sustain in so doing. Then,

Jacob Lerouw, Esquire, a Surveyor, being examined, said, That he had made an Estimate of the Expence of building such a Manufactory as is now standing upon Mr. Webster s Premisses — And he produced the said Estimate, by which it appeared, that if the Building contains the Turpentine, Pitch, and Tar Manufactory together, the Expence will be £.3,600, besides a further Sum of £. 780, for Utensils, and for a Cone over the Building, and also for paving Gangways, and other Parts, similar to the present, making together the Sum of £.4,380.

It also appeared by the said Estimate, that if the Building was to contain the Pitch and Tar Manufactory only, the Expence w'ould amount to £, 2,470 in the Whole.

And the Witness being asked, What would be the Expence of removing the Turpentine Manufactory alone ? he said, It will make a Difference of near £. 400, if it should be built separate from the other Works; in w;hich Case the Estimate would amount to £.2,300 on Account of the additional Walling, and an 1

additional House.

And being asked, What Deductions were to be made from the Sums in his Estimate? he said, One Fifth Part of the Whole, by Way of Abatement for 12 Z Repairs,

G

Supply Bill Suit.

1098 33* Junii. A. 1785.

Repairs, and the Length of Time the Building Part will last beyond Mr. Webster's I^ease, of which Twenty-seven Years are unexpired. Then,

Mr. Samuel Robinson, a Surveyor, being examined, said, That be had made an Estimate of the Expence of building a Pitch and Tar Manufactory, and also a Manufactory for Turpentine; — That the Pitch and Tar Manufactory will cost £ 1,975. — And if the Turpentine Works are also removed and re-built, in Addition to those for Pitch and Tar, the Expence will be £ 1,275 more, making together the Sum of £3>25°i but that if the Turpentine Manufactory was to be removed alone, the Expence would amount to £ 2,500.

And the Witness further said, That he made those Estimates upon a Calculation that the Buildings would last 27 Years, and therefore no Deductions were to be made therefrom; but that he thinks the new Buildings will be in a better Condition at the End of 27 Years than the old Buildings, if repaired, would be.

And being asked, What would be the Expence of repairing the present Buildings? he said, About £1,200; — £800 of which Mr. Webster will receive from the Insurance Office.

And Mr. Webster informed your Committee, That if his Two Manufactories were to be separated, it would cost him £. 50 a Year for additional Clerks. Then

Mr. John Crutchfield, a Turpentine Distiller and Colourman, was asked, What would be the Difference of Expence of carrying on Mr. Webster's Business if his Manufactory was removed to the Water Side at some distant Place ? he answered, That if the Ware-houses were not to be removed, or if the Manufactory should be distant from the River, there would be an additional Charge for Carriage, &c. of Six Pence a Barrel, which, on 5,000 Barrels, would amount to £125 a Year, which he judges of from the Situation of his own Warehouse in Caswell Street. And,

Mr. Francis Henry Shepherd, a Pitch and Turpentine Distiller in Sun Tavern Fields, being called, was asked, What would be the Difference of Expence upon 5,000 Barrels of Tar and Turpentine per Annum, in carrying on a Manufacture at a Distance from the River ? he said, That it cost him about £100 a Year for Wharfage; and if he were to pay for Cartage, and did not keep his own Horses, it would amount to £ 75 more — And he added, That his Manufactory cost him £.3,000 building, including Two Dwelling Houses, and, with the Expence of Utensils, it amounted to £.5,000. Then

Mr. Richard Davis, Owner of certain Hemp Warehouses adjoining to Mr. Webster's Premisses, being examined, said, That the Removal of the said Manufactory will not only be of great Advantage to the Neighbourhood, but would also tend to the Security of Government Stores, of which he has always had from 10 to £.50,000 Worth deposited in his Warehouses at a Time, during the last 5 or 6 Years. And,

Mr. James Brownley, a Storekeeper to the Victualling Office, being called, confirmed Mr. Davis's Evidence; and added, That those Warehouses are more convenient, both from their Situation and Extent, for the Purpose of depositing Government Stores, than any other Place adjoining the River.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie. upon the Table.

40 Pedlars. of t[ie Qty of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners presented a Petition to the House, praying that the Hawkers and Pedlars might not be abolished, as they constitute the best Part of the Petitioners Customers,-and as the Petitioners conceive them to be highly useful in the Sale of the Manufactures of this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is brought in to restrain the said Hawkers and Pedlars from vending their Merchandize in Corporate and Market Towns, and imposing divers other Restrictions upon them in the Exercise of their Trade, which, the Petitioners apprehend, will prove highly detrimental to the Business of the Petitioners, and injurious to the State: And therefore praying to be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as impose upon the said Hawkers and Pedlars the said Restrictions.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for granting to His Majesty additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, be read a Second Time.

Sir William Lemon, according to Order, reported frbm the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the Encouragement of the Pilchard Fishery, by allowing a farther Bounty upon Pilchards taken, cured, and exported, was committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were . Mr. Beaufoy reported from the Committee appointed to enquire into the State of the British Fisheries, and into the most effectual Means for their Improvement and Extension, and to report the same, from Time to Time, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had made a further Progress in the Matters to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Buss* or other Fishing Vessel, properly fitted out and furnished, as by Law required for Vessels entered for the Bounty, should be allowed to clear out of any Port of Great Britain, at any Time between the 1st Day of June and the ist Day of October, and to proceed immediately to her Fishing Station, and to cast her Nets, without being obliged to rendezvous at any other Port or Place.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Masters of Busses, and other Vessels employed in the Herring Fishery, should be at Liberty to purchase Fresh Herrings of the Boat Fishers (being British Subjects) and to ship the Herrings which they shall take, or which they shall purchase as aforesaid, on board any attendant British Vessel, with Permission to land the same, under proper Regulations, in any of the Ports of Great Britain, upon Oath being made, by the Master of the smaller Vessel so landing them as aforesaid, or by the Owner of the Fish, that the Fish were, to the best of his Knowledge and Belief, caught by British Subjects; provided, that if the attendant Vessel, which shall sail with such Fish, shall land them at any other Port than that from which the principal Vessel cleared out, a proper Certificate of the Number of Barrels of salted Fish so landed shall be obtained from the principal Officer of the Customs at such Port, before the Bond for the Duties on the Salt taken on board the principal Vessel shall be Vol. 40.

discharged; and provided also, that tio BusS of Vessel* returning to Port within the Space of Twelve Weeks after her Clearance Outwards, unless with a full Cargo* the Whole of which shall have been taken, and cured* or salted, by such Buss, or Vessel, should be entitled to a Bounty. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That, for reviving and encouraging the Cod Fishery in the North Seas, and in Icelandy the Owner of any Vessel employed therein should be at Liberty to use* in the said Fishery, British-made Salt Duty-free, and to Warehouse, under the Key of the Officer* any surplus Sait remaining in such Vessel upon her Return to the Place of her Outfit, under the like Rules and Regulations as are provided for surplus Salt brought back in Vessels employed in the Herring Fishery.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That all Busses, and other Fishing Vessels, should in future be permitted to be entered for the Bounty* without any Limitation of their Burthen or Tonnage* except that no Vessel of less than Twenty Tons should be entitled to any Bounty, and except that no Buss, or other Vessel, should be entitled to the Bounty for more than Eighty Tons, although of a larger Burthen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Busses and Vessels, employed in the Herring Fisheries, should be at Liberty, during the Time of their Continuance at Sea, to catch and cure God, *

Ling, and Hake, as well as Herrings, and should be subject to the same Regulations, and have the same Privilege of curing the said other Species of Fish with Salt Duty-free, as in the Case of Herrings; but that no Bounty should be allowed on the Exportation of the said other Species of Fish, and therefore, that such other Fish should be marked by cutting their Tails in the Manner prescribed for marking Fish cured for Home Consumption.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee.

That the Duties payable upon Fish caught and cured by British Subjects (such Fish being entered and landed as by Law required for Fish cured for Home Consumption) should cease, and be discontinued.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

The said Report is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

N. B. A printed Copy is with the Original.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers residing in the seve- Hawkers atd ral Cities, Towns* and Villages, in the County of Pedlars. Kent) was presented to the House, and read; Setting' forth, That the Petitioners, already contributing considerably more than their Proportion to the Exigencies of the State in the numberless Taxes and Duties on Trade, humbly presume to represent to the House; that the Tax lately imposed on Retail Shops is a partial Tax, peculiarly grievous and burthensome to them, being, as they conceive, an additional Tax on their Houses, over and above that which the Petitioners are charged with by an Act of the Nineteenth of His present Majesty, in common with other Housekeepers, the said Tax being, though nominally charged upon their Shops, yet actually charged and assessed according to the full Annual Value or Rent of their several Houses; that the Petitioners sustain very great Injury in their Trade from Hawkers and Pedlars, who, Travelling with Goods for Sale from Town to Town, and from one Village to another, are paid for their Merchandize in ready Money, and are liable to no Losses, yet, not having any settled Place of Abode, avoid the Payment of all Taxes, and contribute nothing to the numerous Parochial Assessments, whilst the Petitioners are subject to every Charge, by Reason of their Residence, are obliged to give long Credit in their Dealings, and are frequently subject to great Losses; and that the Petitioners are particularly injured by the Trading of Hawkers and Pedlars in the said County, by Reason of its Situation and Adjacency to the Coast of France, an Opportunity being thereby afforded such Traders of vending contraband and smuggled Goods, and likewise of imposing on the inexperienced Part of the Public damaged English Goods, which they pretend to be contraband, or smuggled, and cheap Bargains to the Purchasers: That the Petitioners had Reason to expect, from the Declaration of His Majesty’s Minister when the said Tax on Shops was first proposed, that the Act of Parliament for licensing Hawkers and Pedlars w ould have been repealed, which would, in some Measure, have lessened the Burthen of the said Tax on the Petitioners, and they have therefore hitherto forborne to represent their Uneasiness on Account of such Tax; and the Petitioners beg Leave further to represent to the House, That, labouring under the before-mentioned Disadvantages, and burthened with Taxes and Contributions to so great an Amount, their Trade must very shortly be annihilated, unless some Means be adopted for their Relief: And therefore praying,

That the House will take the Subject of this Petition into Consideration, and repeal the said Act for licensing Hawkers and Pedlars, and also to pass a prohibitory Act to restrain such Description of Persons from vending Goods.

A Petition of Edward Webster, Esquire, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is possessed of, and, Tor near Twenty Years past, has uninterruptedly carried on, a very extensive Manufactory of Pitch, Tar, and Turpentine, in Potters Fields, within the Parish of Saint John, Horsey Down, and Borough of Southwark; that the said Manufactory is of a very ancient Date, and, on that Account, was One of those expressly exempted from such of the Penalties created by an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for making more effectual an Act, made in the Sixth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, for the better preventing of Mischiefs that may happen by Fire, as related to distilling Turpentine within the Limits therein specified; and that Two Acts were passed in the Twelfth and Fourteenth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, called The Builders Acts, whereby the said Act of the Seventh of Queen Anne was repealed, but the Provision and Restriction respecting Turpentine Manufactories are repeated and re-enacted, the same as in the Act of Queen Anne, though the Exemption in Favour of the Petitioner’s said Manufactory was, by some Error, as he presumes, unintentionally omitted; and that, on the 7th Day of May last, by an unknown Accident, a dreadful Fire broke out on or near the Petitioner’s said Premisses in Potters Fields, whereby nearly all his Warehouses were consumed, though the Manufactory itself (the Fire not having been occasioned by any Process therein) suffered but little Injury: That the Conflagration having communicated to the Neighbouring Houses and Warehouses, and done very considerable Damage, the Inhabitants presented a Petition to the House, praying, That, in case the Petitioner should be willing to remove his said Manufactory, an adequate Compensation might be given him for the Expence he would incur and Damage he might sustain by so doing, and the Petitioner, being well inclined to comply with the Wishes of h\i Neighbours in that Respect, presented a Petition to the House on the 21st Day of this Instant June, stating his being willing to remove his said Manufactory on receiving sufficient Amends, and praying that he might be at Liberty to prove what Expence and Damage he should incur and suffer thereby, which, in the Opinion of skilful and experienced Surveyors, and Persons acquainted with the Nature of his Business, will amount to full £.5,000, as appears by the Report from the Committee, to whom his said Petition was referred; and that the said Acts of the Twelfth and Fourteenth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign passed without the Petitioner’s having any Suspicion that they contained Clauses whereby he was to lose an Exemption he and his Predecessors had enjoyed for so long a Course of Yearfs, and it was not till since the above-mentioned dreadful Fire, that either he, or any of his Neighbours, discovered that, by the said Omission in the said Acts, he has, in Aggravation of his Misfortune, no Right to continue his Manufactory in its present Situation, which is, in all Respects, the most commodious and advantageous of any within the Bills of Mortality: And therefore praying either that the Exemption in Favour of his said Manufactory, which the Petitioner has lost, not by any Neglect or Miscon--duct on his Part, may be renewed, and that he may be indemnified against all Penalties he may have incurred under the said Act of the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty, or that, in case it should be deemed expedient for the Safety of the Neighbourhood, and the Benefit of the Public, that his said Manufactory should be removed, he may have an adequate Compensation allowed him for removing the same. 1

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Thornton, the Lord Mahon, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Hawkers and A Petition of the Shopkeepers resident in the Town Pedlars. Corporate of Scarbrough, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sitting on high Rents, are heavily burthened with Parliamentary Aids, exclusive of great Parochial and other Assessments, at a Time when the Trade of the Town is in a considerable Degree fallen to Decay, owing to the constant Resort of Hawkers, Pedlars, Petty Chapmen, and other itinerant Traders, many of whom contribute very little, and the far greater Part not any Thing, towards the Exigencies of the State, but, on the contrary, are in the Extreme detrimental to the Revenue, as they are known to carry on an illicit Traffick, over the Inland Country, from the Ports on the German Ocean; and that the Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, often travel in Company, under the Sanction of One Licence, which, in Opposition to an express Act of Parliament, they lend to each other, to avoid the Penalties of the Law, and the inferior Class, in the Course of their Itinerancy, too frequently commit Burglaries, and other great Depredations: That the permitting Manufacturers, their Children, Apprentices, Servants, and Agents to carry Abroad, and sell by Retail the Goods of their own Manufacturing, isdn no Way beneficial to the reputable Manufacturer, nor does any Way increase the Consumption, but has become very destructive to the Traffic of great Towns, by the collusive Arts of the inferior Manufacturers apd itinerant Traders, who expose and vend innumerable Goods, of different Manufacturers, under the Pretence of being their Servant or Agent, and actually go Abroad armed with Indentures of Apprenticeship, Letters of Attorney, and other Credentials calculated to evade Justice; and that Numbers of profligate Tradesmen, in Contemplation of Bankruptcy, become itinerant for the sole Purpose of Vo l. 40.

Corporate, and Market Towns, as are not the Seats of Manufactory, and cause the Destruction of the resident and established Tradesmen now bearing the Mass of Taxes, and must consequently greatly decrease the National Revenue: And therefore, as some Compensation for the Burthen of Taxes sustained by the Petitioners, praying a Repeal of the Acts of Parliament now in Force for granting Licences to Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, that all Hawkers, Pedlars,

Petty Chapmen, Manufacturers, and other itinerant Traders, may be restrained from vending by Retail their Wares within the Liberties and Jurisdiction of Cities,

Towns Corporate, and Market Towns, and that such other Relief in the Premises may be granted to the Petitioners, and the resident Tradesmen of Great Britain, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Landholders of the Shire ofof Hectors. Haddington;

Were severally presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the original Excellency of those Laws which ought to regulate the Qualifications for electing the Representatives in Parliament of the several Counties in Scotland, have, with deep Concern, observed the most alarming Devices put in Practice to evade the Laws and Constitution of their Country, by Means of separating Superiority from the Property of Land, and making fictitious Alienations of naked Superiority, for the Purpose of creating nominal and unsubstantial Qualifications; and that, by the Creation of such fictitious Qualifications, Persons possessed of no real or substantial Interest in Land, must always influence Elections, and even are or may become the Majority of Voters at the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for all the Shires in Scotland, the fatal Consequences of which Abuse are too obvious to need Illustration:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises under Consideration, and to apply such Remedy, as to the House may seem fit

A Petition of the Freeholders of the Shire of Ber* wick, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the Wis- dom and Excellency of the Plan on which the Laws respecting Freehold Qualifications in the Counties of Scotland were enacted, have, with deep Concern, observed various Devices put in Practice to pervert these Laws, and corrupt the System of Parliamentary Representation; and that they have, with peculiar Regret, observed the Principal of those Laws departed from, and their wise Intentions defeated, by the creating of Qualifications to vote on fictitious Grants of Wadsett and Conveyances of bare Superiority in Life Rent only, and not in Perpetuity, and, through such Contrivances, Persons possessed of no substantial Interest in Land ate raised to the same Consequence in 13 C Elections

A Petition of the Heritors, or Landed Proprietors, of the Shire of Inverness, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen, with extreme Concern, the most alarming Abuses put in Practice of late Years in the Election of Commissioners of Shires to serve in Parliament for that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, by Means of separating Superiority from the Property of Lands, for the Purpose of creating nominal and unsubstantial Qualifications for Electors of Members of Parliament, and, by the Creation of such nominal Qualifications, Persons' possessed of no Property are, or may become, the Majority of Voters at the Elections of Members of Parliament in all the Shires in Scotland; and that, in particular, the Voters now upon the Roll of Freeholders in the Shire of Inverness amount to Ninety-two Persons, of whom only Sixteen are qualified Electors by virtue of their Property within the Shire, and the Petitioners apprehend, the Landed Proprietors of the Shire are the only Persons Constitutionally entitled to elect the Representative of the Shire in Parliament; and that the Petitioners are deeply interested in National Prosperity, and submit, with the Patience of good Subjects, to the Imposition of every necessary Tax for the Support of Government, they are conscious of bearing in their Breasts the strongest Attachment to the British Constitution in all its Branches, they feel themselves animated with the Love of their Country, and they are disposed, upon every proper Occasion, to assert the Honour of the British Nation; if Abuses are suffered to be put in Practice, and Measures are countenanced which do most effectually deprive the Petitioners of their Constitutional Rights and Privileges, they cannot but entertain the most disagreeable Apprehensions in regard to the Existence of that happy Constitution, which is so admirably calculated to secure to the Subjects of this Kingdom the Blessings of a free and well regulated Government: And therefore praying the House to take under Consideration the Abuses complained of, that the Representation of that Part of Great Britain called Scotland may be put upon a legal and Constitutional Footing.

A Petition of the Landholders of the Shire of Linlithgow, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the original Excellency of those Laws which ought to regulate the Qualifications for electing the Representatives in Parliament of the several Counties in Scotland, have, with deep Concern, observed the most alarming Devices put in Practice to evade the Laws and Constitution of their Country, by Means of separating Superiority from the Property of Land, and making fictitious Alienations of naked Superiority, for the Purpose of creating nominal and unsubstantial Qualifications; and that, by the Creation of such fictitious Qualifications, Persons possessed of no real or substantial Property in Land must always influence Elections, and even are, or may become, the Majority of Voters at the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for all the Shires in Scotland; and that the fatal Consequences of this Abuse are obvious, for the Voters upon the Roll of the Shire of Linlithgow amount to Fifty-seven, of whom Twenty-one only are qualified Electors in virtue of their Property within the County: And therefore praying the House to take
