The House being informed that the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door; they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor and Aldermen of the City of London, in Court of Aldermen assembled.

And then they withdrew'.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, are greatly, and, as they conceive, most justly alarmed, at a Bill depending in Parliament, for the further Prevention of Crimes, and for the more speedy Detection and* Punishment of Offenders against the Peace, in the Cities of London and Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, and certain Parts adjacent to them; and, they think it a Duty incumbent upon them, as Magistrates who are materially concerned in the Administration of Justice in so considerable a Part of the District proposed to be the Object of that Bill, to take the First Moment that offers for expressing flieir Apprehensions of the mischievous and dangerous Effects of a Law, which, under Colour of correcting Abuses, overturns the Forms established by the Wisdom of out* Ancestors for regular Administration of Justice, and goes to the entire Subversion of the Chartered Rights of the greatest City in the World, and the Destruction of the Constitutional Liberties of above a Million of His Majesty’s Subjects; and that the Petitioners forbear to state any of the numerous and weighty Objections which occur' to them to the particular Clauses and Provisions of the Bill, because the Principle of the Bill, establishing, in Defiance of Chartered Rights, a System of Police altogether new and arbitrary in the Extreme, creating, without Necessity, new Officers, invested with extraordinary and dangerous Powers, enforced by heavy Penalties, and expressly exempted from those Checks, and that Responsibility, which the Wisdom of the Law has hitherto thought necessary to accompany every extraordinary Power, appears to them so mischievous, that no Amendment or Modification can or ought to reconcile the Nation to such a Measure: And therefore most earnestly praying the House, no longer to entertain, or give Countenance thereto, but by an immediate Rejection of the Bill, to quiet the Minds of His Majesty’s Subjects, and relieve them from the Dread of being reduced under the Scourge of such a System.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

George Shepley being examined, said, That Mr. Webster had carried on the Business of making Turpentine at the Manufactory in Potter's Fields near Twenty Years —

That by the late Fire, which appeared to begin at or near Mr. Webster's Premisses, a small Part of the Manufactory was burnt, and nearly the Whole of the Warehouses destroyed.

An Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for the better " Regulation of Buildings and Party Walls, within " the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and other the Parishes, Precincts,

" and for the more effectually preventing Mischiefs 4t by Fire, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and other the Pa-4i rishes, Precincts, and Places, within the Weekly u Bills of Mortality, the Parishes of Saint Mary-leBon, Paddington, Saint Pancras, and Saint Luke at tc Chelsea, in the County of Middlesex; and for indemnifying, under certain Conditions, Builders and <c other Persons, against the Penalties to which they are " or may be liable, for erecting Buildings within the u Limits aforesaid contrary to Law/’ were then read; whereby it appeared, that the said Act of the Seventh of Queen Anne was repealed; and that the Provisions therein contained, respecting Turpentine Manufactories, were repeated and re-enacted; but that the Exception in Favour of the Turpentine Manufactories in Southwark was omitted,

Mr. Timothy Newland being then examined, said. That he had known the Turpentine Manufactory in Potters Fields, now Mr. Websters, upwards of 62 Years — That it was formerly the Property of Mr, Symonds — That when he first knew it there were Two Men employed therein, who told him they had worked there a great Number of Years, and that at that Time the Building appeared to be very old, and was supported by Buttresses — That ever since he knew the Borough of Southwark there had been no other Turpentine Manufactory but that in Potter's Fields, which is in the most convenient and advantageous Situation of any he knew.

Sir Robert Taylor being then examined, said, That he had, as an Architect, given what Assistance and Information he could to to the Gentlemen of the Law, by whom the said Act of the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty was drawn — That the Act of the Twelfth being found very inaccurate in many of its Clauses, it was absolutely necessary to pass the Act of the Fourteenth, by which the former one was repealed, and that at that Time there were a great Number of Actions brought, in Consequence of the various Inaccuracies it contained — That the Clause respecting Turpentine Manufactories was copied from the Act of the Twelfth, without any Reference being had to thh Act of Queen Anne, then no longer in Force — That Mr. Webster's Manufactory was never attended to, nor thought of, in penning that Act; and that the Clause respecting Turpentine was inserted merely for the Sake of including all former Provisions relating to Fires in Oue Act; and that the Act of Vol. 40.

'unit. in}

the Twelfth of His present Majesty was framed under the Advice and Inspection of Mr. John Phillips, a Builder, since deceased.

Mr. John FAnson] being then examined, said, That he was Agent and Solicitor for Mr. Webster — That he was enmployed by him as such when he purchased the said Turpentine Manufactory — That neither he nor Mr. Webster, to his Knowledge, ever knew that the Exception in Favour of the said Manufactory in Potter's Fields had been lost, by Means of the said Acts of His present Majesty’s Reign, till since the late Fire; for if Mr. Webster had known it, the Witness believes he should have been consulted thereon — That Mr, Webster's Neighbours having objected to his carrying on his Works, he had applied to the Witness, to know whether he had a Right so to do; on which he looked into all the said Acts, and then for the first Time discovered that Mr. Webster had, by the said Acts of the Twelfth and Fourteenth of His present Majesty, lost the Exception, under which the Manufactory in Potter's Fields had been carried on from the Year 1708, and long before, to the present Time, as the Witness has been informed. Then

Mr. Luke Ideson, Vestry Clerk of Saint James'i Parish, said, That he was employed as Solicitor to the Builders to draw the Act of 12th George III. and that he remembers some Conversation about Continuing the Exemption of the Turpentine Manufactories, and that he remembers hearing some of the Builders say, that the Manufactory of Tombes, at TIolborn, was to their Knowledge removed, but they did not know whether there was any Manufactory of Turpentine continued in Southwark; if any Application was made by any Turpentine Manufacturers in Southwark, they said they would continue the Exemption, but if hot, he was ordered to leave it out — That he did not send to esquire, nor did he give any Kind of Notice to any Proprietor in Southwarkalthough Notice was given to the Fire Offices,

Carpenters, and other Descriptions of People interested in the Bill, whose Approbation was obtained; and that the said Exemption was never inserted in the Bill.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers in Warrington, in the County of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Tax lately imposed upon Retail Shops is likely to prove a very great Burthen upon the Petitioners, of which they were not unaware, but, lulled into a Belief that their Hardships would be in some Measure alleviated by the Abolition of Hawkers and Pedlars Licences, they desisted from troubling the House with their Complaints: With Grief and Disappointment, however, they learn, that only an additional Duty (so small as no wise to promise a Reduction of the Number) is proposed to be laid on such Licences, and therefore they think it their Duty to their Country and to themselves, to represent, that the Number of Hawkers and Pedlars travelling in and about the County of Lancaster, and the Neighbourhood of Warrington in particular, many of them not Housekeepers, and consequently not labouring under an equal Pressure of Taxes, is very injurious to the Petitioners: That many other Circumstances concur to enable the Hawker and Pedlar to undersell the fair Trader, such as the Travelling without a Licence, or (as is too generally practised) under the Sanction of another's, the Trading

in smuggled and (not unfrequently) in stolen Goods, which their Licence affords them continual Opportunities of doing with little Fear of Detection: These, and the Frauds and Impositions often practised upon the ignorant, render them not injurious to Shopkeepers only, but a Nuisance to the Country; and, the Petitioners conceive, that, were the Office of an Informer held in less Abhorrence than it at present generally is, it will be impossible, by any Regulations or Restrictions whatever to guard against the Frauds and Evasions which may and will be exercised by Hawkers and Pedlars, or to put the Shopkeeper upon an equal Footing with them, by any other Means than that of an absolute Prohibition: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Hardships of their Case into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as they shall be found to merit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers of the Town and Hawkers and Borough of Ipswich, in the County of Suffolk, was Pedlars, presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the Burthen of the Shop Tax lately levied upon them, feel themselves exceedingly aggrieved, and, agreeable to a respectable Meeting of the Trade of the said Town of Ipswich, and Places adjacent, the 21st of this Instant June, the Petitioners beg Leave to present the following Resolutions: " That it is unanimously the Opinion of " this Meeting, that a Repeal of the Acts of Parliament " now in Force, for granting Licences to Hawkers " and Pedlars, will be a Measure of great Benefit to " the Community at large, as well as to the resident " Traders in particular, their Licences being a Cover " to the vending of smuggled and stolen Goods, and c< many other illicit Practices;" and " That such a <c Repeal will be <some Compensation to the fair and " reputable Tradesmen of this Kingdom, for the heavy " Burthen they will sustain by the Tax imposed on " Retail Shops: " And therefore praying the House to take into Consideration the above Resolutions, and that the several Acts for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars may be repealed, that the Retail Trade may be on a more fair and equitable Footing.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Thomas Macknight, James Parker, and William ATCormick, in Behalf of themselves, and the Heirs of their deceased Partner William Aitchison, Owners of the Ship Belville an4 Brigantine Betsey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, having suffered a considerable Loss t)f Property by the Capture of the Ship Belville and Brigantine Betsey, under the Prohibitory Act, intended to have presented a Petition to the House for that Redress which they were informed it was competent to Parliament alone to give, but were prevented by the Sickness of one of their Number, and by other unavoidable Circumstances, from presenting it within the Time limited for that Purpose: And therefore

praying the House, that, in' Consideration of the Circumstances above-mentioned, Leave may be given to present their said Petition.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition as desired by the said Thomas Alacknight, James Parker, and William ATCormick.

Then a Petition of Thomas Alacknight, James Parker, and William ATCormick, in Behalf of themselves and the Heirs of their deceased Partner William Aitchison, Owners of the Ship Belville and Brigantine Betsey, being offered to be presented to the House,

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners were particularly called upon by the Governors of North Carolina and Virginia, at the Beginning of the late unhappy Dis-sentions in America, to assist in supporting His Majesty’s Government in that Country, and distinguished themselves by their Loyalty and Attachment to the British Constitution, in consequence whereof, their Property in America hath been confiscated, but the above-named Vessels, having escaped the Hands of the Congress, were captured by His Majesty’s Ships of War in the Beginning of the Year 1776, and condemned in British Courts of Admiralty as the Property of Inhabitants of Colonies declared by the Vol. 40.

Prohibitory Act of Parliament to be in a State of Rebellion, which Law was made on the 24th Day.of December 1775, and took Effect in America from the 1st Day of January 1776; and that the Petitioners Ship Belville was loaded in Pasquotank River North Carolina, in the latter End of the Year 1775, was regularly, cleared out from His Majesty’s Custom House of Port Roanoke for Cadiz in Spain, and sailed on this Voyage 150 Miles to Ocracoke Bar, where she was taken in the Month of December by a Vessel belonging to the Committee of Safety, the Commander of which, afraid of being captured by a British Ship of War which hove in Sight, threw the Belville'$ Cargo overboard, and carried her across The Shallows to Newbern in North Carolina, where she was detained till William McCormick gave Bond and Security to pay to the Convention the Value of this Ship and her Cargo, provided the Petitioners other Property, which by this Time had been seized by Order of the Committee of Safety, should be finally confiscated; and that William M'Cormick, being permitted to re-load the Ship on those Terms, she proceeded on her Voyage to Cadiz, but was captured on the Coast of Spain by One of His Majesty’s Ships of War, and, being carried to Gibraltar, was libelled in the Court of Admiralty, on the Prohibitory Act, as the Property of Inhabitants of a Colony in Rebellion, and, notwithstanding it was proved in the Course of the Trial, that the Owners, far from countenancing the Rebellion, were faithfully and firmly attached to the British Government, yet the Prohibitory Act, containing no Exception in Favour of Vessels belonging to good Subjects, the Judge found himself obliged to condemn the Belville and her Cargo as a Prize to the Captors; and that the Petitioners Brigantine called The Betsey was also captured by a British Ship of War in the Beginning of the Year 1776, while she was carrying Provisions from North Carolina to the Earl of Dunmore, Governor of Virginia, for the Use of His Majesty’s Troops then at Norfolk; notwithstanding this Voyage was undertaken for His Majesty’s Service, at the Request of the Governor of Virginia, and at the Risk of William ATCormiclcs Life, had the Destination of these Provisions been discovered before he got out of North Carolina, yet this Vessel and her Cargo were also condemned under the Prohibitory Act of Parliament; and that the Petitioners having been plundered by the Americans for their Loyalty on the one Hand, and thus punished as Partizans of Rebellion on the other, they are stripped of their All, and, from a State of Affluence, reduced to the Necessity of depending for Subsistence on an Allowance-from Government, which has been hitherto granted to them in common with other American Sufferers; with them the Petitioners patiently wait, and hope for Compensation for their Losses in America arising from the Law's of Congress; but the Loss of these Ships and their Cargoes flowing directly from the Operation of an Act of the British Legislature (surely not meant to injure good Subjects) the Petitioners are informed, can only be made good to them by the Bounty of Parliament, the Petitioners Solicitations for Payment having only obtained from His Majesty’s Ministers repeated Acknowledgments of the Justice of their Claim; and that, in the Month of June 1783, on the Second Reading of the Bill appointing Commissioners for enquiring into the Losses and Services of the American Loyalists, the Case of these Vessels was particularly stated in the House of Commons as a Case that deserved Relief, and though it did not come within the Letter or Spirit of the Bill then reading, the Sense of the House appeared to be, that the Petitioners should lay their Case respecting the Loss of these Vessels before the Commissioners, to the End that, on their Report of the Facts, the

House

A. 1785.

in 6

30° Junii.

House might determine tvhat was lit to be done for their Relief; and that the Petitioners have accordingly laid this Case before the Commissioners, in a Memorial separate and distinct from their Claims as American Sufferers, and, the Commissioners having examined the Facts above stated, the Petitioners trust they are ready to report thereon, when required so to do, and believing that Parliament alone can redress the Injury they have sustained by the Operation of the Prohibitory Act, and knowing that it hath ever been the Practice of the British Legislature to indemnify innocent Sufferers under Laws made for the Public Service, the Petitioners are encouraged to have Recourse for Relief to that Power from whose Act this Misfortune hath befallen them; and that the Petitioners do now submit this Case respecting the Loss of these Vessels to the Consideration of the House, trusting that the Evidence they have laid before the Commissioners of American Claims respecting their Loyalty, Services, and Sufferings, in Support of Government, will induce those Gentlemen to give such an Account of their public Conduct as must convince the House that the Petitioners have acted the Part of loyal and faithful British Subjects, at the Expence of every Thing dear and valuable to them: And therefore praying, That the House will take this Case into their serious Consideration, and do thereon what to them shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Thomas Rich, Mr. Dempster, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

Parish Rates, and other Taxes, unfelt by the Hawkers and Pedlars; and, that there is another Set of Persons, not exactly of that Description, but who, instead of Travelling with Parcels and Bundles, usually take Rooms, and hold temporary Auctions in various Towns, Cities, and Corporations, who always carry off Ready Cash, while the Shopkeeper is obliged to give long Credit, and, besides these, there are a certain Species of Tradesmen who pretend to be Manufacturers of Goods, which they sell in Corporate Towns, but who are not so in general, and, being encouraged under that Pretence, are equally injurious to Shopkeepers within Towns, Cities, and Corporations; and that the Petitioners, although already labouring under a Load of Taxes, chearfully submitted to the Tax on Retail Shops, under, they trust, a well-grounded Hope that the Licences of Hawkers and Pedlars would be totally done away, and the Grievances be* fore stated removed: And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and to relieve them from the great Oppression under which they la-bour, both in respect to Hawkers and Pedlars, Temporary Auctions, and also Manufacturers of Goods brought into Corporate Towns, and there sold by Retail, and that the several Acts of Parliament for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars may be repealed.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers, Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Halifax, in the County of Yoi'k, w as also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are materially affected by the Bill lately passed, imposing a Duty upon Retail Shops, and are far from being averse to bearing such equal and just Proportions as the Exigencies of the State may require, but, conceiving the Partiality of the present Tax to operate most immediately upon the Petitioners, they presume they have a Claim upon the House to palliate the Measure, and to render the Petitioners the Relief they now seek, as an Equivalent for the Payment of the said Tax; and that the Petitioners would have sought earlier Redress, and instructed their Representatives to have opposed the Progress of the said Bill through the House, had not they been induced to believe, upon the Introduction of the said Tax, that an Equivalent would have been granted them, by abolishing the Licences granted to Hawkers and Pedlars, so much to the Injury of the fair Trader: But, apprehensive that such Equivalent is likely to be withheld from them, they therefore pray, That House would take the same into their serious Consideration, and afford them the promised Relief, by an entire Abolition of the granting of Licences to the Hawkers and Pedlars of this Kingdom, which will, in this Case, better enable the Petitioners to pay the said Duty.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie tipon the Table.

Prayers.

A PETITION of the Shopkeepers and other ib cktisui Inhabitants of the City of Exeter, was present* ed to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Sale of Goods and Merchandizes by Hawkers and Pedlars is highly injurious to the Public and the Revenue, tending to promote the vending of stolen and smuggled Goods, and other illicit Practices, and much more liable to Fraud and Deceit than the Dealings of resident Traders, who are well known, and whose Characters are at Stake for carrying on their Trades upon fair and reasonable Terms; and that the Encouragement usually given to Hawkers and Pedlars upon their coming to any City or Town is to the greatest Degree detrimental to the fair resident Trader; inasmuch as there are many Instances, even in the City of Exeter, of those Persons receiving, during a Week or Fortnight’s Residence therein only, many Thousand Pounds in ready Money, when the resident Traders, who have been under the Necessity of giving Credit, remain at the same Time unpaid, and their Stock in Trade, which they must be supplied with, is left on their Hands a considerable Time without the usual Demand for it: That the entire Suppression of those Traders, or at least a Prohibition of them from coming into any City, Town Corporate, or Market Town, would be some Compensation to the resident Traders of this Kingdom for the grievous Burthen laid upon them by the late Tax on Retail Shops, which will operate as a partial and oppressive Impost falling heavily on a particular Description of Men, who already contribute more than their Proportion to the Exigencies of the State; and, the Petitioners conceive, that, if the Hawkers and Pedlars are permitted to sell their Goods in Cities, Towns Corporate, and Market Towns, on Market Days, it would, in a great Measure, counteract the good Intention of the proposed Regulation: And therefore praying, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and grant them Relief, either by suppressing Hawkers and Pedlars, or prohibiting them from vending their Goods within Cities, Towns Corporate, and Market Towns, or within the Space of Two Miles thereof, at any Time whatsoever, or to give the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. John James Hamilton, according to Order, re- Brittt ported from the Committee of the whole House, Fhbtria to whom it was referred to consider of the Report which, upon the 27th Day of June last, was made from the Committee appointed to enquire into the State of the British Fisheries, and into the most effectual Means for their Improvement and Extension, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Buss, or other Fishing Vessel, properly fitted out, and furnished as by Law required for Vessels entered for the Bounty, shall be allowed to clear out of any Port of Great Britain, at any Time between the First Day of June and the First Day of October, and to proceed immediately to her Fishing

Station,

Duties on Tobacco.

5 Geo. Ill* 5° Julii. 1125

Station, and to cast her Nets, without being obliged to rendezvous at any other Port or Place.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Masters of Busses, and other Vessels, employed in the Herring Fishery, shall be at Liberty to purchase Fresh Herrings of the Boat Fishers (being British Subjects) and to ship the Herrings which they shall take, or which they shall purchase as aforesaid, on board any attendant British Vessel, with Permission to land the same, under proper Regulations, in any of the Ports of Great Britain, upon Oath being made, by the Master of the smaller Vessel so landing them as aforesaid, or by the Owner of the Fish, that the Fish were, to the best of his Knowledge and Belief, caught by British Subjects; provided that, if the attendant Vessel, which shall sail with such Fish, shall land them at any other Port than that from which the principal Vessel cleared out, a proper Certificate of the Number of Barrels of Salted Fish so landed shall be obtained from the principal Officer of the Customs at such Port before the Bond for the Duties on the Salt taken on Board the principal Vessel shall be discharged; and provided also, that no Buss, or Vessel, returning to Port within the Space of Three Months after her Clearance Outwards, unless with a full Cargo, the Whole of which shall have been taken, and cured, or salted by such Buss, or Vessel, shall be entitled to a Bounty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for reviving and encouraging the Cod Fishery in The North Seas and in Iceland, the Owner of any Vessel employed therein shall be at Liberty to use, in the said Fishery, British-vndide Salt Duty-free, and to Warehouse, under the Key of the Officer, any surplus Salt remaining in such Vessel upon her Return to the Place of her Outfit, under the like Rules and Regulations as are provided for Surplus Salt brought back in Vessels employed in the Herring Fishery.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Busses, and other Fishing Vessels, shall in future be permitted to be entered for the Bounty without any Limitation of their Burthen or Tonnage, except that no Vessel of less than Twenty Tons shall be entitled to any Bounty, and except that no Buss, or other Vessel, shall be entitled to the Bounty for more than Eighty Tons, although of a larger Burthen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Busses and Vessels, employed in the Herring Fisheries, shall be at Liberty, during the Time of their Continuance at Sea, to catch and cure Cod, Ling, and Hake, as well as Herrings, and shall be subject to the same Regulations, and have the same Privilege of curing the said other Species of Fish with Salt Duty-free, as in the Case of Herrings, but that no Bounty shall be allowed on the Exportation of the said other Species of Fish, and therefore, that such other Fish shall be marked by cutting their Tails in the Manner prescribed for marking Fish cured for Home Consumption.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Beaufoy, Mr. John James Hamilton, the Marquis of Graham, and Mr. Dempster, do prepare, and bring in the same.

A Petition of the Importers, Dealers, and Manufacturers of Tobacco, in the City of Glasgow, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, at a Time when the House overflows with Petitions from every Corner of the Kingdom, the Petitioners, however averse they may be to increase the Number, find themselves called upon by that Duty which they owe to themselves and to the Public, to lay before the House the alarming Situation of the Vol. 40.

Tobacco Trade in their Part of the Kingdom, the smuggling of that Article, in great Quantities, being carried on with the utmost Ease and Security, in open Defiance of the Laws, and to the great Injury of His Majesty's Revenue; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that internal Regulations only, for the Purpose of checking this illicit Trade, however salutary they may appear, will be found ineffectual Palliatives, unless the Duties, at the same Time, are considerably reduced: And therefore requesting the House, That the Axe may be at once applied to the Root of this pernicious Traffic, by ordering such a Reduction of the present high Duties on that Article as, in the Wisdom of Parliament, may seem necessary for removing the Temptation,'by which the Attempts of the Smuggler will be rendered abortive, the fair Trader protected, and His Majesty’s Revenue increased.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Lord Beauchamp reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Thomas Macnight, James Parkery and William M'Cormick, in Behalf of themselves and the Heirs of their deceased Partner William Aitchison, Owners of the Ship Belville and Brigantine Betsey, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Macnight being examined, said, That the Ship Belville was loaded, and passed Pashquotank River, in North Carolim9 in the latter End of the Year 1775, and the Restraining Act was then in Force, but did not apply to that Colony — That they took out a regular Clearance at His Majesty’s Custom House at Port Roanoke: That she was laden with Pipe Staves and Bees Wax — That on their Passage they were taken, in the Month of December, by a Rebel Vessel, which carried her into Newberriy where she was detained till Mr. M'Cormicl: gave Bond and Security to pay the Value of the Ship and Cargo — That Mr. M'Cormick being permitted to re-load on those Terms, proceeded on his Voyage to Cadiz, and was captured on the Coast of Spain, by the Enterprize, commanded by Sir Thomas Rich, and carried to Gibraltar, where she was libelled in the Admiralty Court, under the Prohibitory Act, as the Property of Inhabitants of a Colony in Rebellion, and condemned as a Prize to the Captors, notwithstanding the Owners were proved to have been faithful Subjects, as the Act contained no Exception whatsoever in their Favour.

Mr. William McCormick informed your Committee, That when he was examined upon Oath before the Commissioners for settling the Claims of American Loyalists, he stated, to the best of his Belief, that the Vessel in Question, including Outfits, Repairs, Provisions, and Advance of Wages to Seamen, amounted to about £. 2,000 Sterling — That upon quitting America, he was obliged to leave his Books and Papers, and has never been able to recover them — Then,

Mr. Thomas Bell, Merchant and Ship and Insurance Broker, acquainted your Committee, That he has had great Experience in the Trade from North Carolina to Europe, and believes, that a Ship of the Size and Description of the Belville, and so equipped, was worth about £. 1,800 at the Port of London.

And it appeared to your Committee, by a Certificate of Mr. James Duff, His Majesty’s present Consul

at Cadiz, being the original Port of Destination, that the Cargo actually sold at £.1,600 Sterling, after it had been re-shipped at Gibraltar, where it had been condemned. And,

Mr. Mackmght said, That the Interest of the above Sums, at the Rate of £. 5 per Cent. calculating from the Time the Ship was taken, amounts to £. 1,530, which Sum, being added to the Value of the Ship and Cargo, makes the Whole amount to £. 4,930.

Mr. McCormick being further examined, said, That the Brigantine Betsey was also captured by a British Ship of War, in the Beginning of the Year 1776 —

That she was taken upon her Voyage with Provisions to the Army under Lord Dunmore, and under the Authority of His Lordship’s Pass, but was captured by Captain Eastwood, and carried to St Kitt's, where she was condemned as belonging to Subjects in Rebellion — That she was intended to proceed, after delivering the Provisions at Norfolk, with Hogshead Staves to the West Indies: And he further said, That he had made an Affidavit before the Commissioners above mentioned,

That the News of the Declaratory Act having passed had not reached him in North America — That he bad also made an Affidavit, that the original Cost of the said Ship amounted to £.1,000 Sterling, including the Outfits, at the Time she sailed. And,

Mr. Bell stated, That a Ship of the Size and Description of the Betsey, would be worth £.7. 10 s. per Ton. And,

Mr. McCormick further said, That he had declared on Oath, before the Commissioners, that the said Ship was 180 Tons Burthen; and that the Value of her Cargo w'as £.500 Sterling — And added, That, valuing the Ship at £. 1,000, and the Cargo at £. 500, as abovementioned, the Interest for Nine Years amounts to £.675 Sterling. Then,

A Member present informed your Committee, That he personally knew the Petitioners, Mr. Parker and Mr. Macnight; and said, they both distinguished themselves for their Zeal and Loyalty to His Majesty’s Government, and both took an active Part in the Field in Support thereof.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A PETITION of the Shopkeepers in the Towi* Hawkers of Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford, and Pedlars, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners, patiently bearing the numerous Taxes in common with their Fellow Subjects, now labour under a new and particular Impost, which, under the present Circumstances, whilst it materially' affects the opulent, will severely distress the middling, and reduce to Ruin the inferior, Class of Tradesmen; and that, during the Progress of this Tax in the House, His Majesty’s Minister held forth some Alleviation of that rigorous Burthen, by declaring his Intention to annihilate the Hawkers and Pedlars, a

1

6° Julii.

A. 1785.

' Body of Men not more pernicious to the fair Trader, than destructive to His Majesty’s Revenues, and, under such Expectations, the Petitioners remained silent; but finding themselves deceived, they submit the Protection of their Trade to the Wisdom and Justice of the House: And, as the most effectual Mode of enabling them to pay this great additional Tax, and of securing their present Property, therefore praying, That the Acts of Parliament for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars may be repealed.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers and others, Inhabitants of the Town of Leeds, in the Borough of Leeds, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are sensible that the Exigencies of the State are such as to require new Taxes, but that the Tax imposed on Retail Shops is, in many Instances, very burthensome, and the only Alleviation the Petitioners can point out to themselves, in the present Case, is a Repeal of the several Acts for granting Licences to Hawkers and Pedlars; the Petitioners, therefore, rely on the Wisdom of Parliament for a Repeal of those Acts, and that a Prohibitory Act may be passed to prevent those itinerant Traders from carrying on their Traffic, so very prejudicial to the fair Resident Tradesman, who is so heavily burthened with Parochial and other Taxes, and the Petitioners are sensible that the Hawkers and Pedlars are very prejudicial to the Revenue of this Kingdom, by the illicit Trade they carry on, and are a Nuisance to the Community at large by their frequent Impositions, and therefore hope that the Idea which was held forth when the Shop Tax was first proposed, of abolishing all itinerant Traders, will not be abandoned.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Tablq.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the County- Hawker*

Town of Cardigan, and its Vicinity, was presented and Pedlars, to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the 13 K Petitioners,

1138

12° J

A* 1785.

Petitioners, although bending under die Weight of accumulated Taxes, forebore to increase the Number of Petitions presented to the House in Opposition to the Shop Tax Bill, under the Idea arising from an express Declaration, that, in Compensation to the settled TVader, every Species of Hawkers and Pedlars would be suppressed; but the Petitioners are greatly concerned to find their well-founded Expectations likely to be frustrated by a Bill now depending in the House, for permitting those itinerant Traders under additional Duties, and therefore beg Leave to represent, that, while such Permission, under whatever Restriction, exists, the Hawker and Pedlar will necessarily continue to derive considerable and many unfair Advantages over the settled Trader, from his unfixed Mode of Traffic, and that, while the Petitioners are obliged, by their Situation, to pay numerous and heavy Parish Rates, and other local Taxes, to discharge troublesome Parochial Offices, to vend their Goods, at a very moderate Profit, on long Credit, and to sustain frequent and weighty Losses from fraudulent Customers, the itinerant Dealer is generally subject to none of those Inconveniences, few of that Description having any fixed Place of Residence, they aVe^ consequently free from Parochial Rates and Offices, their Advertisements draw in the Customers of the resident Trader, who purchase of them, for ready Money, Goods which might be bought in fixed Shops on Credit, and equal Terms, not to mention the Facility with which Hawkers dispose of contraband Goods, encouraged by the almost Impossibility of detecting them, from the short Continuance of their Abode in any one Place; and that the Petitioners are far from wishing to deprive any Description of honest Men of the Means of subsisting, but they are of Opinion, that, were Hawkers and Pedlars Licences totally abolished, the present travelling Traders would be induced to establish Shops, and share with other Shopkeepers their Advantages and Inconveniences: And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An King’s Act to authorize the Lord Steward of the Household, Bounty to the Lord Chamberlain, the Master of the Horse, the the IndiSeDt‘ Master of the Robes, and the Lords of the Treasury, respectively, to pay Bounties granted by His Majesty to Persons in low and indigent Circumstances; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act Turpentine to amend so much of an Act, passed in the Four- M"ufac* teenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for tonei* the further and better Regulation of Buildings and Party Walls, and for the more effectually preventing Mischiefs by Fire within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and other the Places therein mentioned, as relates to Manufactories of Turpentine; for extending the Provisions of the said Act so amended to Manufactories of Pitch, Tar, and Turpentine, throughout that Part of Great Britain called England, and for indemnifying the Proprietor of a Turpentine Manufactory in Potters Fields, in die Borough of Southwark, against the Penalties he may be liable to under the said Act, and for excepting, for a limited Time, his said Manufactory from the Provisions therein contained; without any Amendment:

And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Supply Bill; Act for reducing the Allowances for Waste on SaltSalu and Rock Salt, for regulating the Exportation of Salt to Jersey, Guernsey, Alderney, and Sark, for repealing the Laws allowing the Use of Foul Salt for Manure only, for allowing a Drawback on the Exportation of Glauber or Epsom Salts, for restraining Fish Curers from being Dealers in Salt; for regulating the Exportation of Herrings from The Isle of Man; for better securing the Duties on Salt, and for indemnifying Persons who have been guilty of Offences against the Laws relating to the Duties on Salt: without any Amendment.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Elections — thereunto subscribed, Electors of the City and Liberty p°l,s and of Westminster, on Behalf of themselves and other ScrutlQitt* Electors of the said City and Liberty, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to limit the Duration of Polls and Scrutinies, and for making other Regulations touching the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for Places within England and Wales, and for Berwick upon Tweed, and also, for removing Difficulties which may arise for Want of Returns being made of Members to serve in Parliament; and Setting forth. That the Petitioners are advised that the said Bill hath a direct Tendency to establish the Legality of the High Bailiff’s Conduct in continuing a Scrutiny upon the late Election of Members for the City of Westmbister for many Months after the Return of the Writ, and consequently to

deprive

Elections-Polla and Scrutinies.

GEb. III.

i 4° J

1143

deprive the Electors of the said City, or their Representatives, of that further Redress which they conceive the Law, as it now stands, would indisputably afford them; and that even admitting the Law at present to be defective, which the Petitioners utterly deny, the Petitioners have Reason to apprehend that no competent Provision is made to guard against similar Evils arising in the Execution of Writs upon a General Election in future; and, that the said Bill doth also contain Clauses which will inevitably increase, in a very dangerous Degree, the Powers of Returning Officers at popular Elections, and enable them, should they be so inclined, to exercise, with Impunity, a corrupt Partiality in making their Returns of Members to serve in Parliament: And therefore praying, That a Business of so much Moment, and so peculiarly interesting to the Petitioners, may not, at this late Period of the Sessions, be decided upon; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel* against the said Bill being passed into a Law.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read the Third Time; and that the Petitioners be at Liberty to be then heard, by their Counsel, in Support of their said Petition, against the said Bill;

Then several Amendments were made by the House to the Bill.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned till Monday Morning next.

Conference A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Anguish and Mr. with Lords.. Montagu:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords do desire a present Conference with this House, in the Painted Chamber, upon the Subject Matter of the Conference on the 31st Day of Max) last.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Resolved, That this House doth agree to a Conference with the Lords, as is desired by their Lordships.

And the Messengers were again called in; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them therewith.

And then the Messengers again withdrew.

Ordered, That the Managers who managed the last Conference do manage this Conference.

And the Names of the Managers were called over; and they went to the Conference.

And being returned;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported, That the Managers had met the Lords at the Conference, which was managed, on the Part of the Lords, by the Lord Steward of His Majesty’s Houshold; and that the Conference was to acquaint this House, that the Lords, having taken into their Consideration the Resolutions communicated to the Lords by this House at a Conference on the 31st Day of May last, relative to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, have concurred with the said Resolutions, with several Amendments; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer also reported, That the Lords at the Conference delivered to the

Royal Assent A MESSAGE by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher to Bills. of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission aforementioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Osborne, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty a certain Sum of Money out of the Sinking Fund, and for applying certain Monies therein mentioned for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-five; and for further appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament; and for providing a Compensation to the Clerks in the Offices of the Principal Secretaries of State, for the Advantages such Clerks enjoyed before the Commencement of an Act, made in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for establishing certain Regulations concerning the Portage and Conveyance of Letters and Packets by the Post between Great Britain and Ireland.

An Act for granting to His Majesty a certain Sum of Money, to be raised by a Lottery.

An Act to explain and amend an Act, made in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Rates and Duties upon Bricks and u Tiles made in Great Britain, and for laying additional Duties on Bricks and Tiles imported into " the same."

An Act to repeal the Duties upon Flasks in which Florence Wine and Oil is imported; to permit the Importation of Wines in small Casks for private Use; to revive, continue, and amend so much of an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty, as allows the Exportation of certain Quantities of Wheat, and other Articles, to His Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in America; for disallowing the Drawback on the Exportation of Snuff; for continuing the Permission to land Rum or Spirits, of the British Sugar Plantations, before Payment of the Duties of Excise; for reviving and continuing the Premiums upon the Importation of Pitch, Tar, and Turpentine from East Florida into Great Britain; for allowing a Bounty upon the Exportation of Silk Gauzes, and a Drawback upon the Exportation of Raw Silk.

An Act for repealing the Duties on Linens to be printed, painted, stained, or dyed in Great Britain, imposed by an Act, made in the last Session of Par-3

liament, and for granting other Duties in lieu thereof, and on Cotton Stuffs, Muslins, Fustians, Velvets, and Velverets,x wove in Great Britain, to be printed, stained, painted, or dyed, and upon the Importation of Linens, Cotton Stuffs, Muslins, Fustians, Velvets, and Velverets, printed, stained, painted, or dyed in Foreign Parts.

An Act for altering and amending an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act " for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on all " Gold and Silver Plate imported; and also certain " Duties on all Gold and Silver Wrought Plate made " in Great Britain."

An Act for further postponing the Payment of the Sum of Two Millions advanced by the Governor and Company of the Bank of England towards the Supply for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-one.

An Act to exempt Carriages carrying the Mail from paying Tolls at any Turnpike Gate in Great Britain.

An Act for reducing the Allowances for Waste on Salt and Rock Salt; for regulating the Exportation of Salt to Jersey, Guernsey, Alderney, and Sark; for repealing the Laws allowing the Use of Foul Salt fof Manure onfy; for allowing a Drawback on the Exportation of Glauber or Epsom Salts; for ,restraining Fish Curers from being Dealers in Salt; for regulating the Exportation of Herrings from The Isle of Man; for better securing the Duties on Salt; and l*or indemnifying Persons who have been guilty of Offences against the Laws relating to the Duties on Salt

An Act to amend so much %of an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the further and better Regulation of Buildings and Party Walls, and for the more effectually preventing Mischiefs by Fire within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and other the Places therein mentioned, as relates U) Manufactories of Turpentine; for extending the Provisions of the said Act so amended to Manufactories« of Pitch, Tar, and Turpentine, throughout that Part of Great Britain called England; and for indemnifying the Proprietor of a Turpentine Manufactory in Potters Fields, in the Borough of Southwark, against the Penalties he may be liable to under the said Act; and for excepting, for a limited Time, his said Manufactory from the Provisions herein contained.

An Act for the Encouragement of the Pilchard Fishery, by allowing a farther Bounty upon Pilchards, taken, cured, and exported.

An Act to authorize the Lord Steward of the Houshold, the Lord Chamberlain, the Master of the Horse, the Master of the Robes, and the Lords of the Treasury, respectively, to pay Bounties granted by His Majesty to Persons in low and indigent Circumstances.

An Act for the further Encouragement of the British Fisheries.

An Act to prohibit the Exportation to Foreign Parts of Tools and Utensils made use of in the Iron and Steel Manufactures of this Kingdom, and to prevent the seducing of Artificers or Workmen employed in those Manufactures, to go into Parts beyond the Seas.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Pepys and Mr. Thomson:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing the Duty imposed on Tea, by an Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, and for granting other Duties in lieu thereof; for repealing $0 much of several Acts as relates to the Removal of Tea; for directing the Officers of Excise to examine and certify the Exportation of Exciseable Commodities; and for better securing the Duties on Candles; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing an Act, made in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty a Stamp Duty u on Licences to be taken out by certain Persons uttering or vending Medicines, and certain Stamp " Duties on all Medicines sold under such Licences, u or under the Authority of His Majesty’s Letters a Patent," and for granting other Duties in lieu thereof; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to extend the Provisions of an Act, made in the Twenty-third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, foi granting to His Majesty a Stamp Duty on the Registry of Burials, Marriages, Births, and Christenings, to the Registry of Burials, Births, and Christenings of Protestant Dissenters from the Church of England \ without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for extending the Time limited by an Act of this Session, for delivering in Navy, Victualling, and Transport Bills; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The House was moved, That the several Resolutions relative to the Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland\ as agreed to by both Houses of Parliament, in this Session, might be read.

And the same were read accordingly; and are as followeth; viz.

Vol. 40.

Resolved, I. That it is highly important to the ge- Commercial neral Interests of the British Empire, that the Inter- Intercourse course and Commerce between Great Britain and Ire- With Ireland-land should be finally regulated on permanent arid equitable Principles, for the mutual Benefit of both Countries.

Resolved', II. That it is consistent with the essential Interests of the Manufactures, Revenue, Commerce, and Navigation of Great Britain, that a full Participation of Commercial Advantages should be permanently secured to Ireland, whenever a Provision equally permanent and secure shall be made by the Parliament of that Kingdom towards defraying, in Proportion to its growing Prosperity, the nesessary Expences, in Time of Peace, of protecting the Trade and general Interests of the Empire.

Resolved, III. That, towards carrying into full Effect so desireable a Settlement, it is fit and proper that all Articles, not the Growth or Manufacture of Great Britain or Ireland, except those of the Growth,

Produce, or Manufacture of any of the Countries beyond The Cape of Good Hope, to The Streights of Magellan, should be imported into each Kingdom from the other reciprocally, under the same Regulations, and at the same Duties (if subject to Duties) to which they would be liable when imported directly from the Country or Place from whence the same may have been imported into Great Britain or Ireland respectively, as the Case may be; and that all Duties originally paid on Importation into either Country respectively, except on Arrack and Foreign Brandy, and on Rum, and all Sorts of strong Waters not imported from the British Colonies in The West Indies, shall be fully drawn back, within a Time to be fixed, on Exportation to the other, but, nevertheless, that the Duties shall continue to be protected and guarded, as at present, by withholding the Drawback until a Certificate from the proper Officers of the Revenue in the Kingdom to which the Export may be made shall be returned and compared with the Entry Outwards.

Resolved, IV. That it is highly important to the general Interests of the British Empire, that the Law’s for regulating Trade and Navigation should be the same in Great Britain and Ireland; and therefore that it is essential, towards carrying into Effect the present Settlement, that all Laws which have been made, or shall be made, in Great Britain, for securing exclusive Privileges to the Ships and Mariners of Great Britain, Ireland, and the British Colonies and Plantations, and for regulating and restraining the Trade of the British Colonies and Plantations (such Laws imposing the same Restraints, and conferring the same Benefits, on the Subjects of both Kingdoms) should he in Force in Ireland, by Laws to be passed in the Parliament of that Kingdom, for the same Time, and in the same Manner, as in Great Britain.

Resolved, V. That it is further essential to this Settlement, that all Goods and Commodities of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of British or Foreign Colonies in America, or The West Indies, and the British or Foreign Settlements on the Coast of Africa, imported into Ireland, should, on Importation, be subject to the same Duties and Regulations as the like Goods are, or from Time to Time shall be subject to, upon Importation into Great Britain', or, if prohibited to be imported into Great Britain, shall be. prohibited in like Manner from being imported into Ireland.

Resolved, VI. That, in order to prevent illicit Practices injurious to the Revenue and Commerce of both Kingdoms, it is expedient, that all Goods, whether of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of Great Britain or Ireland, or of any Foreign Country, which shall hereafter be imported into Great Britain

Resolved\ VII. That, for the like Purpose, it is also expedient, that when any Goods, the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of the British West India Islands, or any other of the British Colonies or Plantations, shall be shipped ffcm Ireland for Great Britain, they shall be accompanied with such original Certificates of the Revenue Officers of the said Colonies, as shall be required by Law on Importation into Great Britain; and that, when the whole Quantity included in One Certificate shall not be shipped at any One Time, the original Certificate, properly indorsed as to Quantity, should be sent with the First Parcel; and to identify the Remainder, if shipped within a Time to be limited, new Certificates should be granted by the principal Officers of the Ports in Ireland, extracted from a Register of the original Documents, specifying the Quantities before shipped from thence, by what Vessels, and to what Ports.

Resolved\ VIII. That it is essential, for carrying into Effect the present Settlement, that all Goods exported from Ireland to the British Colonies in The West Indies, or in America, or the British Settlements on the Coast of Africa, or to the Countries beyond The Cape of Good Hope to The Streights of Magellan, should from ^3 Time to Time be made liable to such Duties and Drawbacks, and put under such Regulations, as may be necessary, in order that the same may not be exported with less Incumbrance of Duties or Impositions than the like Goods shall be burthened with when exported from Great Britain.

- Resolved, IX. That it is essential to the general

Commercial Interests of the Empire, that, so long as the Parliament of this Kingdom shall thipk it advise-able that the Commercq to the Countries beyond The Cape of Good Hope to The Streights of Magellan, shall be carried on solely by an exclusive Company, having Liberty to import into the Port of London only, no Goods of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of the said Countries should be allowed to be imported into Ireland but through Great Britain; except Dye Stuffs, Drugs, Cotton or other Wool, and Spiceries, which may be Imported into Ireland from Foreign European Countries, so long as the same are importable from Foreign European Countries into Great Britain: And that it shall be lawful to export such Goods of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of any of the Countries beyond The Cape of Good Hope to The Streights of Magellan, from Great Britain to Ireland, with the same Duties retained thereon as are now retained on their being exported to that Kingdom, but that an Account shall be kept of the Duties retained and not drawn back on the said Goods exported to Ireland, and that the Amount thereof shall be remitted, by the Receiver General of His Majesty’s Customs in Great Britain, to the proper Officer of the Revenue in Ireland, to be placed to the Account of His Majesty’s Revenue there, subject to the Disposal of the Parliament of that Kingdom; and that the Ships going from Great Britain to any of the said Countries beyond The Cape of Good Hope to The Streights of Magellan, should not be restrained from touching at any of the Ports in Ireland, and taking on board there any of the Goods of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of that Kingdom; and that no Ships be allowed to clear out from Ireland for any of the said Countries, but such Ships as shall be freighted by the said Company, and which shall have sailed from the Port of London: And that, whenever the Commerce to the said Countries shall cease to be so

carried on solely by such an exclusive Company, the Goods, the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of the said Countries beyond The Cape of Good Hope to The Streights of Magellan, should be importable into Ireland from the British or Foreign Settlements in The East Indies, subject to the same Duties and Regulations as the like Goods from Time to Time shall be subject to on Importation into Great Britain; and if prohibited to be imported into Great Britain, should in like Manner be prohibited from being imported into Ireland.

Resolved\ X, That no Prohibition should exist, iu either Country, against the Importation, Use, or Sale of any Article, the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of the other, except such as either Kingdom may judge expedient, from Time to Time, upon Corn, Meal, Malt, Flour, and Biscuits; and except such qualified Prohibitions, at present contained in any Act of the British or Irish Parliaments, as do not absolutely prevent the Importation of Goods or Manufactures, or Materials of Manufactures, but only regulate the Weight, the Size, the Packages, or other particular Circumstances, or prescribe the Built or Country, and Dimensions of the Ships importing the same; and also except on Ammunition, Arms, Gunpowder, and other Utensils of War, importable only by virtue of His Majesty’s Licence; and that the Duty on the Importation of every such Article (if subject to Duty in either Country) should be precisely the same in the one Country as in the other, except where an Addition may be necessary in either Country, in consequence of an Internal Duty, on any such Article of its own Consumption, or an Internal Bounty in the Country where -such Article is grown, produced, or manufactured; and except such Duties as either Kingdom may judge expedient, from Time to Time, upon Corn, Meal, Malt, Flour, and Biscuits.

Resolved, XI. That, in all Cases in which the Duties on Articles of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of either Country are different, on the Importation into the other, it is expedient that they should be reduced, in the Kingdom in which they are the highest, to an Amount not exceeding the Duties which were payable in the other on the 17th Day of Map 1782, so that in every Case in which any Article was charged w>ith a Duty, on Importation into Ireland, of Ten and a Half per Centum, or upwards, on the 17th Day of May 1782, the Amount of the Duties so reduced shall not be less than the said Duty of Ten and a Half per Centum, unless in Cases where any Articles are importable Duty-free into either Kingdom from the other, which Articles shall hereafter be imported Duty-free into each from the other respectively; and that all such Articles should be exportable, from the Kingdom into which they shall be imported, as free from Duties as the similar Commodities or Home Manufacture of the same Kingdom.: Provided always, That >vhen any such Articles shall be liable, in either Country, to any Duty on being exported to any Foreign Country, the same Articles, when re-exported from either of the said Kingdoms into which they shall have been so imported as aforesaid, shall pay the like Duties as if they had been originally exported from the Kingdom of their Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, to such Foreign Country.

115B 250 Julii. A. 1785.

His Majesty’s Speech at the Opening of the present Session, and the Resolutions of the Two Houses of Parliament in Ireland, which were laid before us. by His Majesty’s Commands, on the 22d Day of Febru~ ary last. '

That, after a long and careful Investigation of the various Questions necessarily arising out of this comprehensive Subject, we have come to the several Resolutions which we now humbly present’ to His Majesty, and which, we trust, will form the Basis of an advantageous and permanent Commercial Settlement between His Majesty’s Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland:

That we have proceeded on the Foundation of the Resolutions of the Parliament of Ireland; but, in "considering so extensive an Arrangement, we have found it necessary to introduce some Modifications and Exceptions, and we have added such Regulations and Conditions as appeared to bs indispensably necessary for establishing the proposed Agreement on just and equitable Principles, and for securing to both Countries those Commercial Advantages to an equal Enjoyment of which they are in future to be entitled:

That His Majesty’s Subjects in Ireland, being secured in a full and lasting Participation of the Trade with the British Colonies, must, we are persuaded, acknowledge the Justice of their continuing to enjoy it on the same Terms with His Majesty’s Subjects in Great Britain:

And it is, we conceive, equally manifest, that, as the Ships and Manuel's of Ireland are to continue, in all Time to come, to enjoy the same Privileges with those of Great Britain, the same Provision should be. adopted in Ireland as may be found necessary in this Country, for securing those Advantages exclusively to the Subjects of the Empire: This Object is essentially connected with the Maritime Strength of His Majesty’s Dominions, and consequently with the Safety and Prosperity both of Great Britain and Ireland:

We therefore deem it indispensable that these Points Should be secured, as Conditions necessary to the Existence and Duration of the Agreement between the Two Countries: They can only be carried into Effect by Laws.to be passed in the Parliament of Ireland, which is alone competent to bind His Majesty’s Subjects in that Kingdom, and whose Legislative Rights we shall ever hold as sacred as our own:

It remains for the Parliament of Ireland to judge, according to their Wisdom and Discretion, of these Conditions, as well as of every other Part of the Settlement proposed to be established by mutual Consent:

Our Purpose in these Resolutions is, to promote alike the Commercial Interests of His Majesty’s Subjects in both Countries, and we are persuaded, that the common Prosperity of the Two Kingdoms will be thereby greatly advanced; the Subjects of each will in future apply themselves to those Branches of Commerce which they can exercise with most Advantage, and the Wealth, so diffused through every Part, will operate as a general Benefit to the Whole:

We have thus far performed our Part in this important Business, and we trust, that, in the Whole of its Progress, reciprocal Interests and mutual Affection will insure that Spirit of Union so essentially necessary to the great End which the Two Countries have equally in View:

In this Persuasion we look forward with Confidence, to the final Completion of a Measure which, while it tends to perpetuate Harmony and Friendship between the Two Kingdoms, must, by augmenting their Resources, uniting their Efforts, and consolidating their Strength, afford His Majesty the surest Means

of establishing, on a lasting Foundation, the Safety, Prosperity, and Glory of the Empire.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty upon the said Resolution.

And a Committee was appointed, of Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir George Hmvard, Mr. Henry Dtindas, Mr. Attorney General, Mr. Jenkinson, Mr. Secretary at War, the Lord Mulgrave, Mr. Solicitor General, the Master of the Rolls, Mr. Rose, Mr. William Wyndham Grenville, the Lord Mahon, the Marquis of Graham, Mr. Steele, Mr. Gilbert, or any Five of them: And they are to withdraw immediately into the Speaker’s Chamber.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported from the Committee appointed to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place*; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign, Addrs*

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, thereon, the.....Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, have taken into our most serious Consideration the important Subject of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, recommended in Your Majesty’s Speech at the Opening of the present Session, and the Resolutions of the Two Houses of the Parliament in Ireland, which were laid before us, by Your Majesty's Command, on the 22dof February last.

After a long and careful Investigation of the various Questions necessarily arising out of this comprehensive Subject, we have come to the several Resolutions, which we now humbly present to Your Majesty, and which, we trust, will form the Basis of an advantageous and permanent Commercial Settlement between Your Majesty’s Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland.

We have proceeded on the Foundation of the Resolutions of the Parliament of Ireland; but, in considering so extensive an Arrangement, we have found it necessary to introduce some Modifications and Exceptions, and we have added such Regulations and Conditions as appeared to us indispensably necessary for establishing the proposed Agreement on just and equitable Principles, and for securing to both Countries those Commercial Advantages to an equal Enjoyment of which they are in future to be entitled.

Your Majesty’s Subjects in Ireland, being secured ii> q. full and lasting Participation of the Trade with the British Colonies, must, we are persuaded, acknowledge the Justice of, their continuing to enjoy it on the same Terms with Your Majesty’s Subjects in Great Britain.

And it is, we conceive, equally manifest, that, as the Ships and Mariners of Ireland are to continue in all Time to come to enjoy the same Privileges with those of Great Britain, the same Provisions should be adopted in Ireland as may be found necessary in this Country, for securing those Advantages exclusively to the Subjects of the Empire. This Object is essentially connected with the Maritime Strength of Your Majesty’s Dominions, and consequently with the Safety and Prosperity both of Great Britain and Ireland.

We therefore deem it indispensable, that these Points should be secured as Conditions necessary to the Existence and Duration of the Agreement between the Two Countries they can only be carried into Effect by Laws to be passed in the Parliament of Ireland; which is alone competent to bind Your Majesty’s

It remains for the Parliament of Ireland to judge, according to their Wisdom and Discretion, of these Conditions, as well as of every other Part of the Settlement proposed to be established by mutual Consent.

Our Purpose in these Resolutions is to promote alike the Commercial Interests of Your Majesty’s Subjects in both Countries; and we are persuaded that the common Prosperity of the Two Kingdoms will be thereby greatly advanced, the Subjects of each will in future apply themselves to those Branches of Commerce, which they can exercise with most Advantage, and the Wealth so diffused through every Part will operate as a general Benefit to the Whole.

We have thus far performed our Part in this important Business; and we trust, that in the Whole of its Progress, reciprocal Interests and mutual Affection will insure that Spirit of Union, so essentially necessary to the great End which the Two Countries have equally in View.

But your Committee beg to submit, it was their de- cording to the following Order; — First, those Parts cided Opinion, that the Idea of composing an entire of Africa which already belong to the Crown of Great Colony of Male and Female Convicts, without any Britain, or which may probably be acquired for the Pur-other Government or Controul but what they may pose in Question.^Seamdly, the Provinces as well as from Necessity be led to establish for themselves, can Islands which are subject to His Majesty in America. answer no good or rational Purpose — That such an — A$d, lastly, such other Parts of the Globe as have
